name: Gassy Waters: Advances in Understanding and Measuring Gas Fluxes Across the Aquatic Continuum
description: Aquatic ecosystems, including ponds, lakes, streams, rivers, coastal zones, and human-made environments (e.g., hydroelectric reservoirs), play a vital role in the cycling and exchange of greenhouse gases (GHGs) such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous oxide (N2O). These gassy waters act as both sources and sinks of GHGs, as well as other gases like volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and trace pollutants. Gas fluxes are shaped by a complex interplay of biogeochemical, hydrological and ecological processes which are spatially variable and temporally dynamic.
lead_organizer: Konstantinos-Marios Vaziourakis, Uppsala University
co_organizers: Marco dos Santos, Energy Planning Program/COPPE/UFRJ
Ulisse Cardini, Genoa Marine Center - Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn
Jorge Machado Damazio, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
Todd Kana, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science
Abigail Lewis, Smithsonian Environmental Research Center

presentations.title: IT'S A GAS: REVIEWING THE CURRENT STATE OF OUR KNOWLEDGE AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS OF BIOGENIC GAS FLUXES ACROSS THE LAND-OCEAN CONTINUUM
presentations.abstract: When we measure gas fluxes we are–in the broadest sense–capturing the breath of ecosystems. As such, gas fluxes give insights into critical ecosystem processes, and they can help us understand how these processes change through space and time. Gas fluxes can also provide an integrative signal of physical, chemical, and biological conditions. Yet measuring gas fluxes in aquatic environments is extremely challenging. Beyond logistical considerations, which are numerous – there is work to be done to better understand where, when, and how frequently to sample. Recent research for example has demonstrated that traditional sampling schemes might capture some types of gases well, while missing the dynamics of others. Additionally, as climate change alters ecosystem phenology, our windows of sampling need to be adjusted to include dormant season measurements and pulsed events like winter thaws. There is also a need for enhanced sampling capabilities including increasing our capability for high resolution measurements across aquatic ecosystems as well as lowering the barriers to technology access. Additional efforts are needed to develop better proxies for gas fluxes so we can improve global scaling efforts. In this talk we will provide an overview of our current understanding of aquatic gas fluxes across the land-ocean continuum. We will share recent exciting advancements, discuss ideas for improving gas flux collection and scaling, and highlight emerging ideas that can guide future research. We aim to synthesize the state of the field and motivate others to join efforts to enhance measurements of aquatic gas fluxes.

presentations.title: Greenhouse gas dynamics of Canadian Prairie Pothole wetlands: A regional synthesis of aquatic emissions
presentations.abstract: Canadian Prairie Pothole Region (PPR) wetlands across the northern Great Plains are glacially formed ecosystems that store carbon yet emit substantial greenhouse gases (GHGs), primarily CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O. Despite extensive agricultural drainage, the remaining wetlands persist as biogeochemical hotspots whose net climate impact reflects a balance between carbon sequestration and GHG production. Progress in quantifying these impacts has been limited by the absence of representative, seasonal and region-wide data on aquatic GHG emissions. To help address this gap, we compiled more than 2,500 measurements from wetlands across all three Canadian Prairie Provinces during the ice-free season, and evaluated four major emission pathways: diffusive fluxes of CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O, and CH₄ ebullition. Our talk will present a preliminary estimate of emissions from roughly 1 million open-water wetlands in the Canadian PPR. These steps provide essential foundations for developing a comprehensive regional emissions budget for PPR wetlands, improving inventories, and guiding conservation actions that sustain biodiversity while reducing wetland GHG emissions under a changing climate.

presentations.title: GREENHOUSE GAS DYNAMICS IN STREAMS IMPOUNDED BY LOW-HEAD DAMS IN WISCONSIN, USA
presentations.abstract: Low-head dams are widespread and alter hydrology and biogeochemistry in streams, influencing greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics. By slowing flow, trapping nutrients, and flooding the riparian zone, these small impoundments can create ideal conditions for GHG production. Despite comprising over 99% of all dams globally, the effects of low-head dams on carbon and nitrogen cycling in small fluvial systems remain understudied. Thus, we measured dissolved CO2, CH4, and N2O in paired free-flowing stream reaches and downstream impoundments created by low-head dams at 9 sites throughout Wisconsin, USA, during summer 2025, and deployed high-frequency sensors that captured CO2 and CH4 fluxes every minute for 2 days. Spearman rank correlations suggest that changes in hydraulic residence time were indirectly influencing GHG concentrations by altering nutrient retention, and GHG concentrations were frequently higher within the impoundments relative to upstream reaches. On average, impoundments saw an increase of 14.6 μM CO2, 0.16 μM CH4, and 4.1 nM N2O. Our results suggest that small impoundments, by lengthening hydraulic residence times, can increase nutrient retention and transformation and consequently amplify dissolved GHG concentrations, highlighting the importance of accounting for these systems in large-scale carbon and nitrogen budgets.

presentations.title: GREENHOUSE GAS FLUXES ALONG THE AQUATIC CONTINUUM: COMPARING GROUNDWATER SPRINGS AND STREAMS ACROSS LAND USES IN A TROPICAL HIGHLAND SYSTEM, EAST AFRICA
presentations.abstract: In sub-Saharan Africa, groundwater-fed springs are vital for human welfare, facing unsustainable management through overextraction and pollution. While ecological, social benefits, and threats to groundwater systems have been documented, their contribution to atmospheric greenhouse gas (GHG) budgets remains largely overlooked. To assess their role in GHG emissions, we measured CO2, CH4, and N2O across highland tropical groundwater-fed springs and streams to examine how hydrological sources and land use (Forested, Agricultural, and Mixed Forest-Agricultural) influence emissions in Taita Hills, Kenya. GHGs were measured using the headspace equilibrium technique. In situ measurements (pH, EC, DO, stream velocity, discharge) and laboratory analyses (NO3--N, NH4+-N, DOC, TDN) were conducted. On average, springs differed significantly from streams with higher N2O (0.63 ± 0.03 SE µg N L-1) and CO2 (3616 ± 151 SE µg N L-1) concentrations, while the streams had higher CH4 (11.29 ± 0.5 SE µg N L-1). Structural equation models revealed that environmental drivers showed greater variance in springs compared to streams for N2O (65% vs. 33%) and CH4 (62% vs. 30%), whereas CO2 was more predictable in streams (53%). In springs, N2O production was strongly coupled with redox potential and DO, with agricultural land use acting as a major NO3 source and directly increasing N2O, suggesting nutrient enrichment. CH4 was controlled by redox and oxygen, but more sensitive to land use in springs. In both systems, the dynamics of CO₂ were influenced by oxygen consumption. However, while CO2 levels rose with agricultural land use in streams, they declined in springs. This likely indicates the presence of deeper groundwater that is rich in NO₃⁻ and low in CO2, or changes in carbonate chemistry. These results show groundwater and surface water environments emit higher GHGs with intensified land use, demonstrating the importance of including ground and surface water interfaces in aquatic GHG evaluations.

presentations.title: LEVERAGING NEW HIGH-FREQUENCY MEASUREMENTS OF pCO₂, pCH₄, AND pN₂O IN A LARGE RIVER TO EXPLORE TEMPORAL VARIABILITY AND BIOGEOCHEMICAL CONTROLS
presentations.abstract: Rivers can be substantial and highly variable sources of CO2, CH4, and N2O to the atmosphere. Understanding the biogeochemical controls on these gases in rivers has been largely limited by measurement techniques. Most observations of dissolved gases in rivers come from discrete grab sampling, which limits the temporal resolution of observations and can preclude capturing the dominant sources of variability and biogeochemical controls on these gases (e.g., in situ metabolism, wind, light, and hydrologic events). Here, an autonomous headspace equilibrator is described that allows for long-term observations of pCO2, pCH4, and pN2O at per second intervals. In addition, five months of high-frequency, concurrent pCO2, pCH4, and pN2O measurements from the Connecticut River that were collected using this system are presented. All three gases were found to be highly variable: pCO2 ranged from 40 µatm to 3300 µatm; pCH4 ranged from 100 µatm to 590 µatm; and pN2O ranged from 0.35 µatm to 1.61 µatm. The three gases exhibited distinct temporal patterns, attributable to different biogeochemical controls. For instance, pCO2 was predominately controlled by aerobic metabolism and exhibited pronounced diurnal fluctuations inversely related to dissolved oxygen. In contrast, pCH4 and pN2O were controlled by temperature and river discharge, although there was a brief week-long period when pN2O experienced an unexpected and strong diurnal signal. This multi-month, high-frequency time series of pCO2, pCH4, and pN2O allows for the quantification of within-reach temporal variability and novel insights into the complex biogeochemical processes that govern greenhouse gas emissions from large rivers.

name: Temporal Trajectories in Aquatic C Cycling on a Changing Planet
description: The importance of aquatic ecosystems on the global C cycle is well established but constraining the stocks and fluxes of C into and through these systems is a moving target. Additionally, though there is a close relationship between terrestrial and aquatic systems, full integration of C balances across the land-aquatic continuum are rarely carried out, making it difficult to consider the overall landscape balance.
lead_organizer: Adam Heathcote, St. Croix Watershed Research Station
co_organizers: Jean-Francois Lapierre, Université de Montréal - GRIL

presentations.title: GLOBAL CHANGE AND THE TEMPORAL SCALING OF CARBON DYNAMICS IN LAKES: CONSTRAINTS AND POSSIBILITIES
presentations.abstract: In the ca. 20 years since Jon Cole and colleagues submitted their initial synthesis of the carbon cycle in lakes (Ecosystems vol. 10; 2007), aquatic organic carbon (OC) dynamics has become a major focus of limnological research reflecting their key role in the earth's carbon cycle. Contemporary monitoring programmes have reached decadal timescales at multiple sites and there has been considerable progress on constraining gas fluxes as well as OC sequestration rates, driven in part by methodological progress. In this same period, global change processes affecting lakes have intensified. Both the transfer of carbon from land to water (both as DOC and POC) as well as autochthonous production in lakes are strongly affected by multiple drivers (disrupted nutrient cycling, altered hydrological pathways and intensified thermal budgets) which makes identifying drivers of change difficult. In this context, longer temporal perspectives (both contemporary monitoring and sediment archives) are vital to help with defining background rates and natural variability. In this review, I assess progress and constraints in three main areas of carbon dynamics in lakes: defining past and present carbon sequestration rates; determining long-term DOC interactions between land and water and finally, carbon mineralization rates in space and time. I illustrate these issues and how they are affected by multiple global change drivers with examples from different lake types in both natural and culturally-impacted landscapes. Where possible I will suggest possible solutions to the key problems.

presentations.title: Climate-driven global divergence in sedimentary carbon mineralization rates between shallow and deep lake areas
presentations.abstract: Lake warming, a major consequence of global climate change, strongly influences ecosystem functioning and carbon cycling. While warming effects on lake organic carbon (OC) dynamics have been examined locally, their spatial heterogeneity within lakes and temporal dynamics over pluri-decadal scales remains poorly quantified. Using long-term monitoring data from 822 lakes worldwide (1921–2022) and 401 French lakes (1959–2019), we assess the extent to which climate-driven shifts in temperature and oxygen concentrations have influenced OC mineralization rates in the sedimentary compartment in shallow and deep areas. Littoral zones consistently exhibit higher mineralization rates (319 mg C m⁻² d⁻¹) than deep areas (112 mg C m⁻² d⁻¹), and this spatial decoupling has intensified over the past three decades as littoral temperatures have risen more rapidly (+35 mg C m⁻² d⁻¹), with models projecting an even greater divergence under continued warming. Deep-water deoxygenation intensifies this pattern, particularly in hypoxic lakes receiving predominantly allochthonous carbon inputs. By incorporating lake-specific sediment surface areas, we refine global estimates of OC mineralization across 637 lakes worldwide, revealing a projected increase in summer decoupling of +0.7 t C yr⁻¹ by 2100. Overall, warming and deoxygenation intensify benthic littoral-pelagic decoupling of OC mineralization across all lake sizes, yet incorporating carbon stocks and organic matter inputs remains essential for accurate global carbon budget estimates.

presentations.title: Cross-regional patterns in carbon sedimentation and storage in boreal and temperate lakes
presentations.abstract: We present a multi-region study aimed at identifying and assessing the main local and climatic drivers explaining carbon (C) storage in lake sediments across diverse landscapes of Quebec and Central Sweden. Fifty-eight lakes from four regions were mapped with a triple-beam echo-sounding system to derive an accurate basin-wide three-dimensional representation of Holocene sediment distribution and organic C content and a subset of 31 lakes were cored and dated using 210Pb to estimate more recent organic C burial rates. Long term (Holocene) C accumulation rate varied between 0.4 and 8.0 g C m-2 yr-1 and revealed a latitudinal gradient with boreal lakes storing the most organic C in their sediments. Recent organic C burial rates ranged from 1.2 to 29.4 g C m-2 yr-1, with the highest rates seen in the southernmost temperate region of Quebec. We developed an empirical model that combined metrics of lake shape and size with catchment productivity, and it explained 61% of the variation in long-term C accumulation rates. The most important factor, catchment net primary productivity, explained 28% of the variance and indicated the importance of organic C fixed and transported from terrestrial vegetation in the watershed. Lake shape and size were also important indicating that large and flat lakes tend to accumulate less carbon per unit area than small and deep lake basins. In three of the regions, we also compared more recent and long-term accumulation rates and found that recent rates are consistently elevated across all regions with the biggest changes seen in the more developed regions of southern Quebec and boreal Sweden. These results provide precise estimates of whole-lake Holocene organic C storage in boreal and temperate lakes and highlight the temporally dynamic nature of lakes as C sinks with increasing magnitude and variability of organic C burial evident across all regions.

presentations.title: Combining field observations and laboratory experiments to identify rates and drivers of organic carbon cycling driven by sediment transport in the Arctic
presentations.abstract: Rivers are both important vectors of lateral export of terrestrial carbon to the oceans and key reactors releasing about twice as much carbon to the atmosphere annually. Understanding the fate of organic carbon mobilized from floodplain deposits is therefore essential for predicting carbon cycle feedbacks and future climate. Recent advances in fluvial geomorphology and hydrodynamics have improved our understanding of suspended sediment transport mechanics, creating a new physical framework for investigating biogeochemical processes. Field observations from rivers globally show distinct differences between the rates of organic carbon oxidation in floodplains and in active transport. Across the Yukon River catchment in interior Alaska, USA, our data show distinct microbial communities between these two conditions, suggesting a major influence of transport processes, though mechanisms linking transport and decomposition are poorly understood. We conducted mesocosm flume experiments designed to reproduce realistic flow conditions. Using sediments from the Yukon River floodplains, we compare the effects of static and flowing conditions on carbon outgassing and lateral transport. Carbon dioxide flux measurements were combined with metagenomic sequencing to assess microbial community responses to transport conditions and compared to parallel geochemical and microbial analyses of field samples of floodplain and suspended sediments. We show how physical transport conditions influence organic carbon decomposition rates and microbial community structure in Arctic river sediments.

presentations.title: CATCHMENT-SCALE CARBON BUDGETS ACROSS A RANGE OF HYDROCLIMATIC CONDITIONS IN THE ARCTIC
presentations.abstract: Arctic climate has been changing at an unprecedented rate and the consequences for carbon cycling and coupling between terrestrial and aquatic systems are still unfolding. While air temperatures have been increasing across the Arctic, precipitation changes have been less coherent. Shifts in hydroclimate will shape hydrological connectivity and linkages between aquatic systems and the surrounding landscape, ultimately affecting the fate of carbon and its sources across Arctic catchments. Here, we compiled a novel dataset characterizing carbon burial, emissions, and export from 29 catchments in Scandinavia and Greenland that span a large gradient of hydro-climatic conditions. We analyze temporal shifts in carbon burial, its quality and sources (isotopic signatures and FTIR), and contextualize the magnitude of the carbon sink in inland waters with regards to contemporary annual carbon emissions to the atmosphere and downstream export across hydro-climatic gradient.

name: Physical Limnology: Dynamics, Drivers, and Change in Inland Waters
description: This session explores the physical processes that govern the behaviour of lakes and inland seas, emphasizing the role that physics of mixing, transport and stratification have in driving biological and chemical processes in aquatic systems. We invite contributions that investigate the physical dynamics of lakes across spatial and temporal scales, from ponds and small lakes through to large systems such as the Great Lakes.
lead_organizer: Mathew Wells, University of Toronto
co_organizers: Sally MacIntyre, University of California, Santa Barbara

presentations.title: Impact of sediment heating on ice-covered lakes
presentations.abstract: In early winter, after the formation of the ice cover, the under-ice hydrodynamics of lakes are often governed by the release of summer-accumulated heat from the sediment. This serves as the main driver for circulation and mixing during the lightless Winter I period. The circulation patterns can differ from year to year, depending on the amount of heat stored in the sediment, the lake aspect ratio (area of shallow pelagial sediment compared with the entire surface of the lake bottom), Coriolis forces, and the stratification of the water column during the preceding autumn. These processes enhance the vertical heat flux, but remain poorly understood, and thus are not parameterized in commonly applied lake models. This process-based study investigates the impact of sediment heating on under-ice lake hydrodynamics, to ultimately understand how the circulation patterns control mixing and biogeochemistry (e.g., deep-water oxygen transport). Idealized, three-dimensional numerical simulations are performed to explore a wide parameter space of physical variables that can influence the stratification, basin-scale circulation and dissolved oxygen concentrations under the ice. Specifically, we focus on the effect of the sediment heat flux, bottom slope, initial stratification and Coriolis force. Our results will contribute to the understanding of under-ice lake processes, their parameterization in lake-scale models, and their impact under changing lake ice patterns.

presentations.title: Interaction between turbulent mixing and the bottom boundary layer in a deep lake: Potential role of long-linear internal waves
presentations.abstract: The development of the bottom boundary layer (BBL) in deep lakes is a critical process contributing to hypoxia, which severely deteriorates benthic habitats, particularly in profundal zones. Despite its ecological significance, research on lacustrine BBL dynamics remains insufficient. Understanding its mechanisms (formation, maintenance, decay) is urgently required to predict future water quality changes under global warming. Therefore, this study aims to elucidate the BBL's spatio-temporal dynamics in a large lake, such as Lake Biwa. This investigation uses high-resolution vertical profiles of water temperature and dissolved oxygen (DO) from intensive field observations at Lake Biwa's almost maximum depth station during 2019. BBL thickness was operationally defined and estimated based on observed vertical DO gradients. To quantify turbulence for vertical mixing, Thorpe displacement and Thorpe length scales were calculated for the entire water column. These parameters were then used to estimate the viscous dissipation rate, a key metric for turbulence intensity. Furthermore, analysis of the density difference ratio indicated that available turbulent kinetic energy likely influences BBL thickness. Additionally, preliminary correlations with meteorological data suggest that long-linear internal wave dynamics, potentially internal Poincaré waves, play a significant and complex role in governing BBL structure and dynamics.

presentations.title: Seasonal Thermal Control of Exchange Dynamics and Circulation Regimes in the Interconnected Lake Michigan-Huron System
presentations.abstract: The Lake Michigan-Huron system functions as a single hydrodynamic unit yet each lake exhibits distinct thermal and circulation regimes shaped by basin morphology and seasonal stratification. Using 3D hydrodynamic modeling validated against temperature profilers, acoustic doubler current profiler, and water level data (2018-2021), we demonstrated that Lake Michigan sustains stronger summer stratification (epilimnetic temperatures: 22.8 ± 2.0 °C versus 15.7 ± 3.2 °C in Huron) and higher stability (Brunt-Väisälä frequency N2 up to 3.54 × 10-3 s-2), while Lake Huron occasionally experiences inverse winter stratification (February-March). Exchange through the Straits of Mackinac shows a persistent eastward net transport, driven by Helmholtz resonance (dominant period: 2.83 days). Moreover, spectral energy in winter currents in the Straits is nearly 10 times that of summer, coinciding with a shift from baroclinic two-layer summer exchange to barotropic winter flow. Newly deployed surface drifters in northern and southern Lake Huron (August-October 2025) provide direct Lagrangian observations of surface current transport in this large interconnected system. These findings underscore how seasonal thermal structure governs inter-lake coupling, circulation patterns, and hydraulic residence times, key processes controlling contaminant transport, ecological connectivity, and climate resilience in large, interconnected lakes.

presentations.title: Novel year-round observations reveal spatial variability and seasonal timing of thermal mixing in a large dimitic lake
presentations.abstract: In dimictic lakes, the timing and spatial progression of seasonal mixing events regulate lake's ecosystems. However, most previous studies rely on single-site thermal profiles, limiting the ability to resolve lake-wide variability in stratification and overturn dynamics. Here, we present a three-year, spatially resolved temperature dataset for Lake Simcoe, a large and deep, dimictic lake in Ontario, Canada, consisting of benthic temperatures from 44 Innovasea receivers (2021/2022, 2022/2023, and 2024/2025) and vertical profiles from five thermistor chains (2024/2025). We find that the timing and duration of fall overturn are strongly related to local water depth, i.e., shallow sites begin overturning up to ~10 days earlier than the deep basin. Likewise, in spring, shallow regions warm more rapidly, ~20 days for temperatures to firstly rise from 4 °C in the shallowest sites to 4 °C across the entire lake to stop the spring overturn. Although Lake Simcoe is typically ice-covered from January to April and exhibits inverse winter stratification, with near-zero temperatures in shallow areas and ~2 °C water in the deep basin, ongoing climate warming is shifting these patterns. Later ice-on dates and earlier ice-off dates are associated with progressively lower water temperatures at the times of freeze-up and breakup, indicating a transition from a seasonally weakly stratified winter regime toward one that is increasingly mixed. These findings highlight the importance of spatially distributed observations for understanding the formation of thermal habitat and provide essential insights for the management of cold-water fisheries in large inland lakes.

presentations.title: The Long and Winding Road to Meromixis
presentations.abstract: The exclusion of salt when ice forms on a brackish lake can result in a freshwater cap with sufficient salinity stratification to supress spring and fall turnover, resulting in meromixis. The conditions required for the establishment of meromixis, along with the processes involved, are not well understood. Here we examine the evolution of meromixis in the Zone 2 pit-lake at Colomac, Northwest Territories, Canada. This pit-lake was intentionally destratified using aeration to enhance biological remediation of contaminants. This effectively created an inadvertent geophysical-scale laboratory experiment providing us with an opportunity to study the details of the transition from holomixis to meromixis. We studied in detail each of the steps from complete mixing during aeration to the establishment of meromixis. During this period there were approximately twenty identifiable phases contributing to the transition to meromixis. Most importantly, in the first winter after destratification, salt excluded from the ice mixed to the bottom. This, along with the fresh water cap from the ice melt, established a salinity stratification. Mixing of the fresh water cap in the following fall, established a weak chemocline. In the second winter, salt excluded from the ice remained within the mixolimnion. In the subsequent 15 years, the pit-lake has been meromictic. Understanding these processes is important to characterizing the likelihood that meromixis will be established in these low salinity systems, and to planning managing water quality in natural and constructed water bodies.

presentations.title: INTER-LAKE HETEROGENEITY OF THERMAL DYNAMICS ACROSS DIFFERENT CLIMATIC REGIONS ON THE TIBETAN PLATEAU
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
presentations.abstract: Thermal dynamics (seasonal stratification and mixing) plays an important role in the spatial/vertical distribution of heat, nutrients, dissolved oxygen and aquatic organism habitats within the lake water body. Numerous lakes on the Tibetan Plateau (TP) have undergone significant changes under global warming in the past few decades, attracting considerable attentions from both the scientific community and governmental administrations. However, in-situ water temperature observations remain scarce for most TP lakes, leaving some essential scientific questions unresolved. To clarify the thermal circulation type and explore the underlying impact of climate change on the thermodynamics of lakes on the climatically sensitive TP, we established a water temperature monitoring network in 2019. This network spans six representative lakes in distinct climate zones (monsoon, monsoon-westerlies transition, and westerlies zone) from eastern to western TP. In this study, we report preliminary results based on high-frequency water temperature profile dataset, which has successively captured the seasonal and spatial heterogeneity in thermal structures. All lakes exhibited significant thermal stratification, with the stratification period ranging from late March to early November. Noteworthy, the climate determined salinity gradients play a more noticeable force on lake thermal dynamics. As salinity increased from monsoon- to westerlies-dominated regions, the annual bottom water temperature presented a decrease trend, and reached the minimum value of -5 ℃ in Longmu Co, a hypersaline lake located in the westmost area of the TP. In addition, relatively high salinity also caused early under-ice thermal stratification (not inverse stratification), even lasted to autumn mixing. To explore the inter-annual responses of lake thermodynamics to climate change of lakes on the TP, in the follow-up, the salinity alternations should be thought highly. View Additional Details

name: Sustaining Safe Drinking Water and Healthy Aquatic Ecosystems in the Asia-Pacific (2nd AP-GLEON)
description: Securing safe drinking water without sacrificing ecosystem health is an urgent, shared challenge across the Asia-Pacific. The Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Global Lake Ecological Observatory Network (AP-GLEON) tackles this challenge by pairing high-frequency, in-situ sensor networks with satellite and drone imagery and by leveraging the value that comes from an open, collaborative community of researchers, managers and technologists.
lead_organizer: Christopher Keneally, The University of Adelaide
co_organizers: Arianto B. Santoso, National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN)
Man Xiao, State Key Laboratory of Lake Science and Environment, Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

presentations.title: Climate-driven shifts in salinity and water level shape phytoplankton communities in a shallow coastal lagoon
presentations.abstract: Coastal lagoons support high biodiversity and provide many ecosystem services but are under threat from climate change. Understanding how phytoplankton community structure responds to climate-induced changes in environmental conditions is critical for assessing the impact of climate change on ecosystem function. This study investigated patterns in phytoplankton abundance and diversity across a wide range of environmental conditions, from extreme dry (drought) to extreme wet (flood), by analysing a 16-year dataset (2007–2023) in the Coorong, South Australia, a coastal lagoon of international importance. Multiple statistical analysis techniques, including correlations, analysis of principal coordinates, biota and environmental matching, distance-based linear modelling and generalised additive modelling were employed to identify the key drivers of phytoplankton community dynamics. Salinity and water level were highlighted as principal drivers of change in the abundance and diversity of the phytoplankton community, with distance from the ocean inlet and water temperature also significant, but to a lesser degree. Phytoplankton communities were characterised by salinity-derived habitats, from freshwater to extreme hypersaline, facilitating predictions of the phytoplankton community under future climate change. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the environmental drivers of phytoplankton community structure in coastal lagoons and supports the development of predictive tools for coastal lagoon management to adapt to the inevitable impacts of climate change.

presentations.title: Nutrient‑reduction targets for cyanobacterial bloom control in Lake Taihu, China
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: According to the year-round total phosphorus (TP) monitoring data from 17 national water quality monitoring sites in Lake Taihu, the Class III level (China's surface water quality standards) of TP, defined as a TP concentration lower than 0.05 mg/L, has been attained since 2007. In order to elucidate the concurrent environmental and ecological variation with the decrease of TP, the long-term variation of the monitoring data was analyzed using the ecological monitoring data of the Taihu Laboratory for Lake Ecosystem Research (TLLER) from 2005 to 2024. The findings of this analysis indicated that the low external loads of TP and total nitrogen (TN), coupled with the low intensity of the Microcystis bloom from 2022 to 2023, established a significant foundation for the low TP observed in 2024. The inertia of the low bloom intensity in 2023 resulted in an extremely low bloom intensity in the first half of 2024, which further caused a relatively low annual average of TP in 2024. Conversely, the increase in bloom intensity in the second half of 2024 was due to the increase in external loading of TP and TN, as well as the extremely high autumn precipitation and air temperature. The findings of this study indicate that a reduction in external TP and TN loading had significantly suppress the bloom intensity in Lake Taihu. However, it is important to note that climatic conditions, such as temperature, rainfall, and wind wave, continue to exert a substantial influence on bloom intensity.

presentations.title: Remote sensing inversion of algal blooms and analysis of bloom outbreak mechanisms in the terminal reach of Ganjiang River
presentations.abstract: Remote sensing inversion of riverine algal blooms is often affected by boundary effects from riparian wetlands, and the accuracy of traditional methods is limited in narrow and elongated water bodies. The terminal reach of the Ganjiang River, as a typical sensitive water area, still lacks a clear understanding of its bloom outbreak mechanisms. Based on Sentinel-2 and Landsat series satellite data, this study proposes an improved method integrating inward-masking technology with the Floating Algae Index (FAI) and Otsu thresholding, which effectively suppresses nearshore interference and enables accurate extraction of blooms in elongated rivers. Using this method, we reconstructed the bloom outbreak processes of the Ganjiang River from 2019-2024. The results reveal that algal blooms exhibit pronounced seasonality, primarily occurring in late summer and early autumn (August -September), dominated by small-scale outbreaks. Blooms were significantly aggregated in the nearshore slow-flowing zones along the windward banks of the southern and middle branches of the river, with intensity gradually decreasing from the littoral zone toward the thalweg. Driver factor analysis using a Random Forest regression model indicates that daily maximum temperature is extremely significantly correlated with bloom area, with a contribution of 47.1%, far exceeding that of nutrients (29.9%), wind speed (9.3%), discharge (7.3%), and precipitation (6.4%). Accordingly, combined with the analysis of bloom dynamics and environmental conditions under typical heatwave events(≥35℃for three consecutive days), this study suggests that under meso-eutrophic background conditions, low discharge and water retention in summer–autumn provide the basis for bloom accumulation, while extreme heatwave events as the dominant drivers.

presentations.title: Contrasting effects of nitrogen depletion and fixation on filament length of Raphidiopsis raciborskii
presentations.abstract: Raphidiopsis raciborskii is a globally distributed harmful species that frequently forms blooms in freshwater, and high morphological plasticity has been observed. Filament length essentially affects population ecological role as the association to grazing susceptibility in aquatic ecosystems. We hypothesized that nitrogen depletion directly promotes filament shortening, as results heterocyst formation may actually prevent filament shortening for nitrogen fixation and supplement. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a monoculture experiment using non nitrogen-fixing and nitrogen-fixing strains, along with a confirmatory field investigation in 100 reservoirs. Our results revealed the filament shortening of both strains as the response to stress of nitrogen depletion, while nitrogen supplementation via heterocyst-based nitrogen fixation mitigated further filament shortening, resulting in significantly difference in filaments composition between the two strains population, of more short filaments (< 50 μm) in non-nitrogen-fixing population (N8) than nitrogen-fixing population (N1). The investigation confirmed that filaments of R. raciborskii varied in 7 μm to 800 μm, and heterocysts was scarcity in field waters. The levels of dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) significantly explained population's filaments composition among 60 samples, of which only one reservoir was of DIN < 0.1 mg/L. In the nitrogen depleted reservoir, shorter filaments (< 50 μm) was of 70% population biomass. Consequently, we suggest that the ecological role and impact of R. raciborskii blooms in nitrogen-depleted reservoirs require re-evaluation.

presentations.title: Effects of environmental extremes on bloom-forming cyanobacteria: Mesocosm studies across different continents
presentations.abstract: We used in-lake and ex-lake mesocosms to simulate how projected environmental changes may affect harmful cyanobacterial blooms. Experiments were conducted at the in-lake IGB LakeLab facility (Lake Stechlin, Germany) and the ex-lake Smart EcoLake facility (Lake Taihu, China) using replicated control and treatment manipulations. We examined responses of Planktothrix rubescens in LakeLab and Microcystis and Dolichospermum species in Smart EcoLake. LakeLab treatments applied artificial mixing to disrupt the thermal stratification supporting a deep chlorophyll maximum (DCM) of P. rubescens. The DCM reformed rapidly but showed altered dynamics, likely linked to elevated surface nutrients and increased competition in the mixed layer following mixing. Smart EcoLake treatments involved heating (+4, +8 °C) and cooling (−4, −8 °C) relative to controls. Phytoplankton diversity declined within days in heated treatments, with Dolichospermum biovolume increasing relative to Microcystis. These mesocosms provide insights into how bloom-forming cyanobacteria may respond to a warmer, more variable climate. Traits such as nitrogen fixation, buoyancy, and toxicity will confer selective advantages for different cyanobacteria species and strains, with indications that P. rubescens and Dolichospermum blooms may become more common in the future.

presentations.title: Danish⁠–Australian Networks for Low-Cost Global Methane (CH4) and CO2 Monitoring in Aquatic Ecosystems of the Asia⁠–Pacific Region
presentations.abstract: Reservoirs and lakes release large quantities of greenhouse gas (GHG), perhaps even more than expected due to ebullitive (bubble) events. This is especially true in areas with limited measurements, such as the Global South. A Danish-Australian network will expand the area of open-source, low-cost methane and CO2 sensors across Oceania, to help feed data into lake carbon models and test mitigation scenarios. In doing so, the project aims at aligning with the Global Lake Ecological Observatory Network (GLEON) Asia-Pacific Working Group's drive for high-frequency lake data. We hope to reach out to everyone interested in emissions of GHG, in particular, people located in the Asia-Pacific region. This project aims to create a collaboration hub between Denmark and the Asia-Pacific region, with bases at the University of Southern Denmark, DK, and the Adelaide University, AU, to stimulate cooperation in methane and CO2 monitoring in aquatic ecosystems. The project will host a variety of activities, including workshops, seminars, conferences, and summer/winter schools to allow for knowledge sharing and to equip all participants with the know-how of how to build their own low-cost methane and CO2 sensors. This presentation will report on our initial progress following project kick-off in early 2026.

name: The Next Frontier in Aquatic Sciences: Linking Remote Sensing, Data Science, Modeling, and Open Science to Better Understand Aquatic Ecosystems
description: In times of an increasingly uncertain climate and growing demand for water resources, there is a need for assessing how aquatic systems worldwide are responding to co-occurring human and climatic disturbances. Over the past half century, remote sensing technology, high performance and cloud computing infrastructure, machine learning techniques, open data practices, and widened training in computer programming have created extraordinary opportunities to expand aquatic science research across spatial and temporal scales.
lead_organizer: Robert Ladwig, Aarhus University
co_organizers: Rachel Pilla, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
Laura Soares, Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research

presentations.title: Clarifying the trophic state concept to advance freshwater science, management, and interdisciplinary collaboration across spatial and temporal scales
presentations.abstract: For over a century ecologists have used the concept of trophic state to characterize biological productivity. Since measuring productivity can be challenging, multiple trophic state classification schemes, each relying on a suite of proxies for productivity, have emerged to meet use-specific needs. Most commonly, chlorophyll, phosphorus, and Secchi depth are used to discriminate trophic state based on autotrophic production alone, while phosphorus, dissolved organic carbon, and true color are used to discriminate trophic state based on both autotrophic and heterotrophic production. Both classification schemes aim to characterize an ecosystem's function broadly, but the relative emphasis on heterotrophic and autotrophic processes masks critical nuances. Moreover, differing classification schemes can create inconsistent understanding and can lead to narrowed interpretation of ecosystem integrity. These inconsistencies in classification schemes may be compounded when interdisciplinary projects employ varied trophic state classification schemes. Even with these shortcomings, we argue that trophic state is useful for distilling complex aquatic ecosystem function into a set of generalizable expectations, which can be used to contextualize, compare, and project ecosystems across scales. We explore the consequences of using contrasting trophic state classification schemes with data from the US EPA National Lakes Assessment, highlighting how an improved understanding of the trophic state concept advances freshwater research, management efforts, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

presentations.title: LAKE SURFACE AREA VARIABILITY OVER FINE SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL SCALES
presentations.abstract: Changes in lake surface area have extensive impacts on water accessibility and greenhouse gas emissions, as well as habitat and nutrient availability. However, little research has been done to quantify global surface area dynamics over time scales except the decadal. This study explored lake area's seasonal variability and periodicity for 700,000 lakes from 2001-2023. The periodicity, calculated using wavelet analysis, was dominated by lakes with a 12 month signal, showing that they peak consistently once per year. These lakes also had lower seasonality. A high periodicity did not always come with a low seasonality; Indian lakes often had a 12 month periodicity and a higher seasonal variability. A significant number of lakes had a reduced periodicity or no periodicity at all. For example, lakes in central Australia and central Asia had a lower periodicity as well as a higher seasonal variability. This highlights the irregularity of these lakes' annual cycles, and the importance of regular monitoring. This study investigated the cause of this spatial heterogeneity by examining precipitation periodicity, which aligned with the surface area periodicity in some regions but not in others, including western Europe. A 6 month periodicity in surface extent and precipitation was found in equatorial Africa, highlighting the potential influence of the intertropical convergence zone. Other variables such as landcover and lake depth were also explored. These trends in spatial and temporal variability are important to incorporate into lake management to best conserve these ecosystems.

presentations.title: Quantifying Long-Term Post-Wildfire Hydrologic Recovery: A Continental-Scale Remote Sensing Analysis
presentations.abstract: Remote sensing has transformed our understanding of watershed hydrology by providing broad spatial and temporal coverage of landscape change. The increased intensity of wildfires and their watershed impacts can be studied at a large scale, allowing us to ask: How does wildfire affect long-term Evapotranspiration (ET) rates? Post-wildfire reductions in ET are well documented: vegetation loss decreases ET, increases streamflow, and enhances the transport of fire-derived pollutants. However, few studies have examined how wildfires shape long-term ET recovery, and none have addressed delayed canopy mortality (DCM), the multi-year demise of trees following an initial fire. Does DCM significantly prolong ET recovery in burned landscapes? By synthesizing multiple remote sensing products, we quantify the relationships among burn severity, forest change, and watershed-scale hydrologic fluxes across 180 fires in the US from 1999 to 2024. We compare ET fluxes across a continuum of DCM intensity and unburned reference catchments to test whether DCM prolongs the time required for ET to recover to pre-fire levels. We also use USGS stream gages to link downstream streamflow response with wildfire behavior. We find that high-DCM burns prolong ET suppression relative to low-DCM burns, sustaining high streamflow for longer and potentially amplifying downstream ecological impacts.

presentations.title: DELINEATING PERMANENTLY INUNDATED AREAS OF RESERVOIR ARMS TO QUANTIFY THE SPATIAL HETEROGENEITY OF WATER COLOR
presentations.abstract: Reservoirs are spatially heterogeneous with the main pool often differing substantially from the reservoir arms. Remote sensing has advanced our understanding of surface water dynamics, but large-scale applications often prioritize analysis near the reservoir center or deepest point. Field data from the arms also remain scarce compared to near the dam. Selecting representative locations within reservoir arms is complicated by diverse morphometries, variable sizes, and fluctuating water availability. To address this gap, we developed a standardized and scalable method that uses open-source data to identify points within reservoir arms, applied it to more than 100 morphometrically distinct systems, and compared satellite-derived water color (dominant wavelength) at those locations with values obtained at the center. We used the permanent water occurrence from the JRC Global Surface Water product to ensure each reservoir-arm point corresponded to a water pixel, identified the tributary inlet by intersecting the minimum-water polygon with the HydroRIVERS river network, and successfully delineated arm locations using a reproducible geospatial framework. Using 10 years of monthly observations across a subset of seven reservoirs, we found that the dominant wavelength was, on average, 6.7 nm longer in reservoir arms compared to main-body sites (95% CI: 5.7-7.6 nm; p<0.0001). The next step is to programmatically apply this approach to all major Texas reservoirs.

presentations.title: Global inland water quality climate data records from the ESA Lakes Climate Change Initiative: progress on global datasets and applications to climatological studies
presentations.abstract: Lakes act as sentinels of climate change, responding both directly to atmospheric forcing and indirectly to changes within their catchments. The increasing availability of openly accessible satellite products has greatly expanded opportunities for inland water research. Within this context, the Lakes_cci project (ESA Climate Change Initiative) provides a multi-decadal, multi-sensor, globally representative climate data record of water-leaving reflectance (Rw) and optical–biogeochemical water-quality products for over 2,000 lakes worldwide, alongside other essential lake variables describing physical properties. We introduce an upgraded processing chain based on an improved atmospheric correction algorithm (Polymer v4.17) and a comprehensive recalibration of algorithms for the retrieval of chlorophyll-a (Chla), total suspended matter (TSM), coloured dissolved organic matter (aCDOM(440)) and the diffuse attenuation coefficient of downwelling irradiance (Kd). For all three sensors, Chla, TSM, aCDOM(440) and Kd retrievals yielded correlation coefficients exceeding 0.8, 0.75, 0.7 and 0.9, respectively. The combination of improved atmospheric correction and rigorously assessed, OWT-based water-quality retrievals underpins the v3.0 release of the Lakes_cci climate research data package, anticipated for open access in early 2026.

presentations.title: Assessing natural resilience: comparative analysis of storm-driven morphological changes in reflective and dissipative coastal profiles in a data-scarce region.
presentations.abstract: Sandy coasts, particularly in data-scarce regions like Mozambique, are increasingly vulnerable to cyclone-induced flooding and erosion, while their natural resilience is being progressively reduced by climate change. This study assesses the protective capacity of dunes by using Cyclone Eloise as a case study and also a set of synthetic storms with varying significant wave heights Hs under nine different MWL and five return period (TR) scenarios. The XBeach model in 1D surfbeat mode is used to simulate the hydrodynamic and morphological response of two distinct beach profiles (reflective and dissipative) to better assess beach-dune resilience under 80 different scenarios. These scenarios combined two profile settings with varying dune heights, return periods, and MWL. The results revealed a nonlinear relationship between hydrodynamic drivers and morphodynamic responses, leading to a dune resilience threshold that corresponds to a critical dune height of approximately 3 m. The primary factor in dune resilience was found to be its height, as dunes below this threshold are likely to fail under most MWL-increase conditions. However, higher water levels dramatically increase the morphological response, transforming a medium-sized dune from moderately eroded to near-total erosion. Although dissipative profiles demonstrate greater natural resilience, as expected, this advantage attenuates under extreme cyclone conditions. These findings provide critical thresholds for conditions where the dune is no longer able to protect the backshore against flooding, underscoring the need to dissuade infrastructure development in a changing climate.

name: Advances in Nutrient Accounting Approaches for Management of Inland and Coastal Waters: Concepts, Methods and Applications
description: Methodological development of nutrient budget approaches to estimate anthropogenic nutrient sources to watersheds and their delivery to receiving waters has been an active area of research in recent decades. Upscaling and downscaling to address regional and local management questions are also of vital importance.
lead_organizer: Dennis P Swaney, Cornell University

presentations.title: Rethinking Nutrient Budgets as a Framework for Food, Water, and Climate Sustainability
presentations.abstract: Nutrient budgets track nitrogen and phosphorus fluxes across landscapes and are central to informing action on sustainable agriculture, clean water, and climate mitigation. As their use expands across scientific, regulatory, and policy domains, including efforts to meet Sustainable Development Goals, expectations for accuracy, transparency, and comparability have grown. Yet current approaches remain fragmented, with varying assumptions, data sources, and definitions yielding conflicting results. Here we identify 25 key challenges that limit the coherence and utility of nutrient budgets. These include data gaps, inconsistent coefficients and assumptions, and inadequate treatment of uncertainty, alongside emerging complexities from dietary shifts, and climate extremes. We organize these challenges around core issues related to input quantification, transport and transformation, and aligning scale with decision making needs. We also highlight tensions between granularity and generalizability and identify important opportunities for innovation. By rethinking nutrient budgets as integrated sustainability tools, and mapping pathways toward consistency, we advance here a shared framework for environmental accounting across science, policy and practice.

presentations.title: STREAM RESTORATION SHOULD BE PRIORITISED BASED ON DISPROPORTIONATE CONTRIBUTION TO RIVERINE NITROGEN EXPORTS
presentations.abstract: The amount of nitrogen (N) exported from rivers and streams remains high in many parts of the world, resulting in adverse impacts downstream and, ultimately, in coastal environments. Understanding where N exports are most intense, and the factors driving them, is therefore key to provide mitigation strategies to improve aquatic ecosystem health. Here we present a detailed analysis of riverine N exports from multiple (65) nested and independent subwatersheds of 8 major tributaries of the St. Lawrence River in Quebec, Canada. Based on drainage area, a proxy for discharge, we found that around half of watersheds exported more N than expected relative to one another. However, there was a large variability in absolute amount where one tributary alone accounted for a third of all exports. We then quantified land use in terms of kilograms of N imported on land as a consequence of human activities with the Net Anthropogenic Nitrogen Input approach. This enabled us to distinguish among four main sources of N: atmospheric, urban, crop-intensive or livestock-intensive agriculture. Combining landscape and limnoscape degradation indices allow us to explain why certain river sections were exporting disproportionate amounts of N downstream, and provide the knowledge of which regions (in-field vs in-stream) should be prioritised for restoration purposes.

presentations.title: THE PREDICTIVE CAPACITY OF A BALANCED NUTRIENT BUDGET FOR INVESTIGATING WATERSHED DISTURBANCE
presentations.abstract: Nutrient budgets can inform lake research and management in the absence of long-term water quality data. However, most existing budgets omit permanent burial or estimate it empirically using nutrient concentrations at spring overturn. Doing so limits the predictive capacity of nutrient budgets due to incompleteness or by restricting predictions to annual time steps. We developed phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N) budgets for Lake McDonald, Montana, USA for water years 2008 through 2023 by quantifying source contributions from its catchment and the atmosphere and losses via permanent burial (using paleolimnological techniques) and via the outflow. On average, 2,391 kg of P and 5,851 kg of N were buried annually, compared to 1,179 kg of P and 113,507 kg of N exported via the outflow. We evaluated the predictive ability of these budgets by comparing nutrient budget-based predictions of lake water nutrient concentrations to measured values resulting in a root mean squared error of 1.79 μg-P L−1 and 79.9 μg-N L−1. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of nutrient budgets as diagnostic tools by simulating wildfire-enhanced nutrient loading to assess plausible causes of a nutrient enrichment event detected in Lake McDonald in 2018.

presentations.title: IMPROVING THE SCIENTIFIC FOUNDATION FOR NUTRIENT OFFSETTING IN AUSTRALIA
presentations.abstract: Nutrient offsetting can serve as a nature-based solution where point source polluters may choose to pay for non-point source, catchment restoration, which is offset against their nutrient discharge. We reviewed a range of nutrient offsetting projects across Australia and found that investment was constrained by the high uncertainty in the science around nutrient offsetting. This means that investing in grey infrastructure provides more certainty than investing in nature-based solutions. Therefore, despite its potential, nutrient offsetting lacks scientific robustness for expansion geographically, as well as constraining market investment. There is a lack of knowledge of the equivalency of nutrient sources from both point- and non-point sources which may be used for offsetting projects, in terms of the impact on aquatic ecosystem health. Therefore, we used two ecosystem measures to compare a range of nutrient sources, i.e. algal response bioassays and oxygen demand bioassays. We focussed on nitrogen, and found that total dissolved nitrogen (a mixture of dissolved organic and inorganic nitrogen) was a much better measure for comparisons than total nitrogen, despite it being widely for nutrient offsetting. Organic carbon availability in different sources was also an important measure of ecosystem responses.

presentations.title: A BAYESIAN DYNAMIC SPARROW NUTRIENT ACCOUNTING FRAMEWORK TO QUANTIFY WETLAND CONTROLS ON INTERANNUAL PHOSPHORUS BUDGETS TO LAKE ERIE
presentations.abstract: Effective nutrient management in the Lake Erie basin requires closing watershed phosphorus (P) budgets across wet and dry years and quantifying how landscape features, such as wetlands, attenuate anthropogenic loads. We develop a dynamic configuration of the SPAtially Referenced Regression On Watershed attributes (SPARROW) model, implemented in a Bayesian framework, to construct annual total P (TP) material balances for Canadian tributaries to Lake Erie from 2003 to 2020. Annually updated hydrologic, land-use, and watershed-attribute datasets allow source contributions and delivery processes to vary interannually, extending conventional single-year SPARROW applications into a time-resolved nutrient-accounting framework. We explicitly represent wetland-mediated retention by combining SPARROW with annual Sub-Pixel Water Fraction mapping to estimate wetland extent and hydrologic connectivity, separating connected from isolated wetlands as distinct compartments in the TP budget. This separation provides empirical, basin-scale evidence of the potential of connected and unconnected wetlands to act as nutrient-attenuating best management practices (BMPs). We summarize annual TP budgets and their uncertainties using Sankey diagrams, offering managers an intuitive, probabilistic view of sources, retention pathways, and deliveries to Lake Erie to support regional P-reduction planning.

presentations.title: ASSESSING THE ROLE OF HYDROLOGICAL VARIABILITY AND WETLAND CONNECTIVITY IN PHOSPHORUS LOAD DYNAMICS IN LAKE ERIE- A HIERARCHICAL SPARROW MODELLING APPROACH
presentations.abstract: Managing eutrophication in lake ecosystems requires understanding how hydrological variability and landscape features shape nutrient dynamics. Variable hydrologic conditions can drive fluctuations in phosphorus loading, complicating mitigation efforts. This study applied a hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the SPARROW (SPAtially Referenced Regression On Watershed attributes) model to the Canadian side of the Lake Erie drainage basin to evaluate how total phosphorus (TP) export, delivery, and retention vary across contrasting flow regimes and wetland connectivity. Long-term discharge records from 68 gauging stations (2000–2020) were used to classify years as wet, normal, and dry, enabling calibration data to be grouped by hydrological regime classes. To capture the role of wetland connectivity on phosphorus attenuation, our model distinguished between connected wetlands intersecting or adjacent to stream networks and isolated wetlands, using data derived from Sub-Pixel Water Fraction (SWF). Model results indicate that hydrologic conditions strongly shape TP export coefficients, with wet years amplifying nonpoint source contributions from croplands and urban land uses relative to dry years. Wetland retention responses also varied by hydrological class. Isolated wetlands showed higher TP retention during wet years, whereas connected wetlands showed higher retention during dry years.

name: Aquatic Sciences on Ice: Physical and Abiotic Processes
description: Ice-covered periods define the physical environment of aquatic systems across much of the globe, from seasonally frozen lakes and rivers to perennially ice-covered polar waters. This session focuses on ice itself: its formation, structure, and evolution, alongside the physical and abiotic processes that operate during the ice-covered season.
lead_organizer: Ryan Hutchins, Toronto Metropolitan University

presentations.title: ION EXCLUSION DURING DIRECTIONAL FREEZING IN ICE RINKS AND LAKES AND IMPLICATIONS FOR LAKE UNDER-ICE STRATIFICATION AND ICE QUALITY
presentations.abstract: Freezing redistributes dissolved ions between ice and water, but quantitative data on how this process varies across freshwater systems remain limited. Understanding ion exclusion in natural ice formation is critical because solute buildup beneath ice can influence density gradients, oxygen depletion, and nutrient cycling during winter. We quantified ion inclusion rates during directional freezing in both engineered and natural settings to identify how source-water chemistry governs solute retention. Controlled ice rink experiments with waters of 5, 80, and 220 mg L⁻¹ total dissolved solids showed high inclusion (40–95 percent), whereas natural lake ice incorporated only 2–47 percent of dissolved ions. Among lakes, inclusion rates were higher in soft water but absolute ion concentrations in the ice were similar between soft and hard water systems, suggesting a threshold effect in top-down freezing. Once a critical ionic strength is exceeded, most solutes are efficiently excluded, enhancing salinity-driven stratification and altering under-ice chemistry.

presentations.title: NON-DESTRUCTIVE IN-SITU QUANTIFICATION OF SPORTS ARENA ICE CLARITY USING IMAGE PROCESSING
presentations.abstract: The quantification of ice clarity in winter sports has been an ongoing challenge. With the lack of a standard, existing methods are either destructive or require extensive experimental setup, making it difficult to apply in the setting of ice sports restricted by both accessibility and cost. The clarity of ice depends on factors such as water quality, inclusions of air bubbles, thickness, and usage. We developed a method to quantify ice clarity by capturing images of arena ice and analyzing the images using edge detection image processing algorithms. The variance of the image indicates the presence of detected clear edges, which in turn can be used to evaluate the clarity of ice. This method is flexible and low-cost, making it accessible to the general public without the need to purchase any specialized equipment or destroy the ice sheet.

presentations.title: THE EFFECTS OF CHANGING WINTERS AND LAKE ICE LOSS ON UNDERWATER LIGHT AND THERMAL STRATIFICATION
presentations.abstract: Shifts in climate are changing lake thermal stratification and light attenuation, which are key physical drivers of lake ecosystem structure and function. In northern temperate dimictic lakes, the summer stratified season is becoming both stronger and longer. At the same time, winters are warming, leading to reduced lake ice cover and thickness. Warmer winter conditions not only shorten the duration of ice cover but also affect ice transparency and snow that accumulates on the lake surface. Here, we examine how changing lake ice cover is affecting mixing dynamics and mean light throughout all seasons using mean daily mixed layer irradiance (E24) as a proxy, with a focus on winter. We use a gradient of lakes with various winter conditions including long ice cover, intermittent ice, and no ice. E24 is higher in lakes with clear ice cover than during summer stratification, indicating that warming winters could potentially increase phytoplankton growth.

presentations.title: SNOW, HYDROLOGY, AND LIGHT: CONTROLS ON UNDER-ICE OXYGEN IN SEASONALLY ICE-COVERED LAKES
presentations.abstract: Winters are changing rapidly with warming temperatures, declining ice duration and dwindling winter snowpack. Ice covers more than half of the world's lakes each winter, and conditions under ice can impact ecosystem function in subsequent ice-free seasons. In this study we use 16 lake-years of high frequency temperature and oxygen observations from three lakes of varying morphometry in the southern Rocky Mountains to investigate the drivers of both inter- and intra-annual patterns of bottom-water oxygen concentration under ice. We provide evidence that snow accumulation on the lake surface is associated with decreased light availability and declines in oxygen concentrations, particularly early during the first half of winter. Additionally, in some lake-years we see evidence for hydrologically-mediated or convective mixing that re-oxygenates the bottom waters in mid-winter or the month(s) leading up to ice-clearance.

presentations.title: HOW LAND COVER SHAPES LAKE ICE PHENOLOGY
presentations.abstract: Lakes are experiencing shorter ice durations in response to a warming climate. Although the meteorological factors influencing ice phenology (timing of ice-on and ice-off) are well understood, the impact of surrounding land cover on lakes is rarely examined. In this study, we investigated how land cover types- such as forest, cropland, and developed land- affect the timing of ice-on and ice-off. Analyzing 47,000 ice phenology records and surrounding land cover types from 2982 lakes across five eastern U.S. states (Minnesota, Wisconsin, New York, Maine, Michigan), we found increasingly variable ice-on and ice-off dates, thus higher unpredictability in ice phenology patterns as land cover shifted from forested to agricultural, to moderately urbanized, and finally to highly urbanized areas. We also noted that while ice cover duration decreases across all regions, forested regions experience higher rates of decline in ice duration.

presentations.title: POND ICE MANIPULATION ALTERS WINTER GREENHOUSE GAS DYNAMICS
presentations.abstract: Nearly half of all lakes and ponds experience winter ice coverage annually. However, climate change is shortening winters and diminishing their severity, resulting in altered ice dynamics that has shifted some dimictic lakes to become warm, monomictic without sustained ice. This loss of winter ice cover is likely to dramatically shift the ecology of lakes both in the winter and potentially in the next growing season. In this study, we used experimental ponds to manipulate ice cover to assess impacts to biological, chemical, and physical processes. We compared four control ponds with nearly four months of ice cover to four ponds where we reduced ice cover and kept them isothermal. The ponds with reduced ice cover averaged four degrees colder and had greater light availability than control ponds. Control ponds had significantly higher accumulation of GHGs, lower oxygen concentrations, and greater primary productivity during ice cover.

name: Seasonal Confluences: Ecology Under Ice and Its Year-Round Effects
description: Rapid changes in ice cover on water bodies worldwide create an urgent need for research focused on ecological and biogeochemical dynamics under ice, as well as their influence on cross-seasonal processes in freshwater ecosystems. Yet winter remains an understudied season in aquatic ecology.
lead_organizer: Rebecca North, University of Missouri-Columbia
co_organizers: Catherine Girard, Université du Québec à Chicoutimi
Marie-Pier Hebert, Université du Québec à Chicoutimi and Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL MEMORY– WHAT IS IT AND HOW CAN IT ADVANCE LIMNOLOGY?
presentations.abstract: Ecological memory (EM), a concept implicit in ecology, describes how past states of communities and ecosystems can shape present and future dynamics. While EM has been applied across subfields of ecology, there has recently been a resurgence in the use of this term in limnology from its original introduction in 1992. Here, we propose that EM offers a framework for linking the timing, duration, and strength of antecedent conditions to present-day ecological or biogeochemical dynamics in inland waters. In this talk, we draw on recent examples in limnology where EM is already evident, such as the expansion of under-ice hypoxic zones in lakes due to intensifying summer anoxia and long lags between P-remediation and water quality improvements. We additionally highlight statistical techniques for quantifying EM, including approaches borrowed from other disciplines. Because winter conditions often encode the physical, chemical, and biological conditions that shape processes during the more often sampled 'open-water seasons', the rapidly developing field of winter limnology is uniquely positioned to advance EM research.

presentations.title: ANALYZING SEASONS AND SEASONALITY IN LAKES AMID GLOBAL CHANGE
presentations.abstract: Within-year seasonality plays a fundamental role in shaping lake ecosystem function worldwide. However, definitions of seasons vary widely, and phenomena traditionally associated with specific seasons are shifting in time as a result of climate change. There is a growing need to critically evaluate how seasons and seasonality are represented in lake ecosystem research. Here, we reviewed existing literature and analyzed high-frequency data from 12 lakes (78 ºS to 60 ºN) to conceptualize seasonality in lake ecosystems. We found that a wide range of criteria are commonly used to delineate seasons in lakes, including fixed dates (e.g., months, solstice/equinox), environmental thresholds (e.g., air temperature and precipitation cutoffs), and lake-specific indicators (e.g., beginning and end of ice cover, spring algal bloom). Using different criteria to define the same season often resulted in significantly different interpretations of ecosystem states within that season.

presentations.title: Predicting Phenological Mismatch in Lakes
presentations.abstract: In temperate regions, spring lake conditions are rapidly changing due to increased climate and weather variability. It is now common to observe 20–40-day shifts in ice-off date from one year to the next. This creates unpredictable spawning and growing seasons for biological communities and decouples photoperiod and temperature conditions which have driven the evolution and life histories of aquatic organisms for centuries. We use high frequency and spatially diverse sampling to investigate how physical conditions and biological residents in lakes interact in early, late and average ice off years. For example, walleye spawn immediately following ice-off each summer regardless of calendar date. In contrast, the boom-and-bust transition from Daphnia to Holopedium happens the same calendar week each summer regardless of ice off.

presentations.title: Interannual seasonal variability impacts microbial ecological dynamics in Lake Champlain
presentations.abstract: Lake Champlain experiences increasingly ice-free winter conditions. Evidence from temperate lakes suggests that under-ice microbial dynamics play important roles in lake biogeochemistry, and that winter processes set the stage for subsequent spring and summer phytoplankton and cyanobacterial blooms. Littoral surface water samples were collected for -omics analysis at three Lake Champlain bays that span trophic status, Missisquoi, St Albans, and Malletts, from December 2022 to spring 2025. NMDS analysis reveals significant dissimilarity between seasons, and between some of our sites. Shannon diversity is lower in both bloom-prone bays in winter or spring as compared to summer. Cyanobacterial analyses of bloom-prone Missisquoi Bay and St Albans Bay displayed distinct microbial dynamics compared to the non-bloom reference site, Malletts Bay. Key taxa, including Roseomonas, Sediminibacterium, and Arenimonas, emerged as potential contributors to bloom initiation or persistence.

presentations.title: Seasonal Shifts in Primary Production Across Trophic Gradients
presentations.abstract: Rapid climate change is reshaping lake ecosystems in many ways, including through changes in trophic status, water temperature, and ice cover duration. This study examines primary production within the nutrient-color paradigm, focusing on ten Minnesota and Wisconsin lakes of different trophic status across the full annual cycle. Using a 13C-based approach, we measured planktonic productivity in both open water conditions (summer) and under ice and snow (winter). 13C enriched bottles were incubated in situ at varying depths for 24 hours. In winter, we conducted snow removal experiments to assess the effect of snow cover on production. We observed large differences in production between lakes and seasons, related to trophic status and light availability. While under-ice production rates were generally lower than open water rates, some lakes supported high production rates when sufficient light reached the water column.

presentations.title: SEASONAL PHENOTYPIC PLASTICITY IN ALPINE COPEPODS: INSIGHTS FROM DIFFERENTIAL GENE EXPRESSION ANALYSES
presentations.abstract: Alpine lakes are harsh environments characterized by pronounced seasonal variation, including fluctuations in UV radiation in clear lakes and mineral turbidity in glacier-fed lakes. Copepods, microscopic crustaceans inhabiting these ecosystems, have developed diverse strategies to endure such dynamic and stressful conditions. In this study, we investigated the physiological responses of the copepod species Cyclops abyssorum tatricus from two contrasting alpine lakes -one glacially turbid and the other clear- over a seasonal cycle. Using comparative transcriptomics, we identified key molecular adaptations to environmental stressors. For example, the expression of small heat shock proteins (Hsp20), markers of stress response, differed significantly between the two lakes. In the clear lake, Hsp20 gene expression was consistently downregulated, with the lowest levels observed at the end of the ice-free season (November). In contrast, Hsp20 was upregulated throughout the study period in the turbid lake.

name: Novel Concepts and Methods in Food Web Research
description: Food web research is becoming increasingly interdisciplinary driven by the need to tackle crucial questions at a time when ecosystems are being impacted at unprecedented scales. With the emergence of big data and novel tools some of these complex questions can be better addressed.
lead_organizer: Katalin Patonai, Université de Montréal
co_organizers: Ferenc Jordán, Institute of Biological Research
Simone Libralato, National Institute of Oceanography and Applied Geophysics - OGS

presentations.title: HOW ROBUST ARE FRESHWATER FOODWEBS TO MAJOR ECOSYSTEM PERTURBATIONS?
presentations.abstract: Understanding how ecological systems respond to disturbance remains a central challenge in ecology. Here, we examine the robustness of freshwater food webs to a major perturbation: the transformation of rivers into reservoirs. Using data from 17 reservoirs in Québec, sampled over 20 years before and after impoundment, we analysed the response of predator–prey fish communities across a broad biomass gradient. We applied the Predator–Prey Power Law (PPL) framework to this type of perturbation for the first time, and we showed that this scaling relationship remains remarkably stable, indicating persistent interaction mechanisms at the ecosystem scale. However, by using different scalings, linking production fluxes, biomass, and productivity between prey and predators, we revealed that the intensity of energy use and storage by predators has changed significantly, without altering the trophic control forces (i.e. top-down and bottom-up). This transition is partly explained by marked demographic and physiological shifts in predators, leading to higher mean biomasses after impoundment along the PPL, and producing a more 'bottom-heavy' mean biomass pyramid.

presentations.title: QUANTIFYING IMPACTS OF BIOLOGICAL INVASIONS IN FRESHWATER COMMUNITIES IN ITALY
presentations.abstract: Biological invasions threaten the biodiversity and functioning of aquatic ecosystems. While there are more and more documented cases of species invasions, the impacts on food web community structure are very complex and difficult to quantify. Here, we investigated how aquatic communities have changed over the past 30 years in an invasional hotspot in Italy, the lower Po River Basin. Analyses of fish and macroinvertebrate communities in early and late invasion stages showed food web simplification characterized by reduced species richness, fewer trophic interactions, and less clustered networks. Environmental data indicated a shift towards turbid, hypoxic conditions consistent with bioturbation and vegetation loss caused by the invasive grass carp. Native predators such as Esox cisalpinus were replaced by tolerant non native species such as Silurus glanis, indicating trophic reorganization. Late-stage communities were dominated by asymmetrical bottom-up trophic interactions. These findings align with the invasional meltdown hypothesis.

presentations.title: Food webs with high zooplankton turnover are less stable: a 24-year mechanistic analysis
presentations.abstract: Biodiversity is declining at an unprecedented pace, and freshwater ecosystems are among the most affected. Understanding how freshwater ecosystems respond to biodiversity loss is critical for predicting ecosystem function in a changing world. We used the high-resolution inference method FLUXNET to develop mechanistic food web models of the plankton community in Müggelsee over 24 years (1994-2017). The models predict daily concentrations and carbon fluxes between 40 phytoplankton and 40 zooplankton species for each year. We analyzed plankton community vulnerability by eliminating individual species and quantifying the resulting change in concentration of other species. There is a strong correlation between vulnerability and zooplankton turnover and vulnerability and interaction strength distribution. Further analysis showed that the invasive quagga mussel substantially alters carbon flux pathways through the plankton network.

presentations.title: ASSESSING THE POTENTIAL FOR HYPOXIA-INDUCED SHIFTS IN TROPHIC DYNAMICS FOR MYSIDS IN THE CHESAPEAKE BAY REGION
presentations.abstract: Environmental change from anthropogenic stressors on a global basis is degrading biological communities and impacting trophic structures.
