Animals that are well-adapted to naturally fluctuating conditions, such as hypoxia, can serve as models for understanding organismal responses to anthropogenic forcing in coastal ecosystems. For example, bottom-water hypoxia may lead to habitat compression, making some typical habitats inaccessible. Mysids, which are small omnivorous crustaceans, engage in vertical and horizontal migrations on sub-daily to seasonal timescales. In this Chesapeake Bay-based study, we tested the hypotheses that: 1) localized hypoxia decouples mysids from benthic trophic pathways, 2) a shift to pelagic pathways reduces mysid trophic position, and 3) these hypoxia-induced changes associate with shifts in basal resources fueling mysid growth. Mysids were sampled and analyzed for the stable isotope composition of bulk tissues (δ15N and δ13C) and compound-specific amino acid δ15N and δ13C values (CSIA-AA).

presentations.title: TOP PREDATORS AS SENTINELS: UNRAVELING TROPHIC SHIFTS IN A DARKENING FJORD USING dDNA AND STABLE ISOTOPES OVER THE LAST 20 YEARS
presentations.abstract: The Greater Oslofjord, like many other coastal systems, is undergoing rapid ecological shifts driven by climate change, coastal freshening and darkening. To understand how these bottom-up stressors restructure food webs, we utilized a multi-trophic approach, analyzing three sympatric predators (approx. 500 individuals): Harbour seal (Phoca vitulina), Great Cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo), and Atlantic Cod (Gadus morhua). We combined dietary DNA (dDNA) metabarcoding with stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) to trace temporal and spatial changes in food web utilization over the last 20 years. We observed distinct dietary variations linking predator foraging behavior to environmental gradients. This included observable changes over the last 20 years, such as an increase in invasive species in their diet and a shift in the composition of zoo- and phytoplankton.

presentations.title: REVISED ESTIMATE OF PRIMARY PRODUCTION REQUIRED FOR FISHERIES IS THREE TIMES HIGHER THAN PREVIOUSLY THOUGHT, REVEALING WIDESPREAD ECOSYSTEM-LEVEL OVERFISHING
presentations.abstract: Primary production required (PPR) to support fisheries links food-web energetics to sustainability, yet the last global assessment, over 30 years old, relied on simplified trophic assumptions. We reassess PPR using a data-driven, species- and ecosystem-specific method (PPR2.0) that exploits the full structure of marine food webs. First, we show that standard calculations using mean trophic level and a single global transfer efficiency systematically underestimate PPR because they use averages for convex functions (Jensen's inequality) and ignore between-ecosystems and within-species variability. We instead estimate species-specific PPR from detailed diet matrices, accounting for cycles and detrital pathways. Incorporating updated catch, bycatch and mariculture data, we find that global PPR is roughly three times higher than previous estimates, requiring ≈25% of marine NPP rather than 8%. Under legacy methods only about 15% of LMEs breached this sustainability threshold, while PPR2.0 reveals that in fact more than half do so, indicating widespread ecosystem-level overfishing.

name: Drying Waters: The Science and Management of 'Temporary' Aquatic Ecosystems
lead_organizer: Rachel Stubbington, Nottingham Trent University
co_organizers: Ryan Burrows, University of Melbourne and Melbourne Water
Lena Fehlinger, GEA, Universitat de Vic UVic-UCC
Lenka Kuglerová, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
description: Temporary aquatic ecosystems—which sometimes dry out—are widespread and diverse in Earth's critical zone, and their extent is increasing in both space and time due to climate change and other human pressures.

presentations.title: LEAF LITTER DECOMPOSITION IN AN EPHEMERAL RIVER NETWORK OF THE BRAZILIAN SEMIARID REGION
presentations.abstract: Most rivers from hot tropical semiarid regions of Brazil are naturally ephemeral, with flow periods occurring for a few weeks or months on an annual basis. While biogeochemical processes have been intensively studied in non-perennial rivers and streams worldwide, the leaf litter decomposition (LLD) of terrestrial plant material in ephemeral river networks have been rarely explored. The lack of water for long periods during the dry season may alter decomposition patterns. In ephemeral rivers, LLD could be mostly driven by abiotic processes such as photodegradation and/or be highly influenced by short pulses of microbiological activity following rainfall events. We quantified the LLD rates of four native species in two different habitats: dry sediments (DS) and isolated pools (IP). Preliminary results indicate that LLD from DS did not vary spatially, but temporally, with the lowest decomposition occurring during the mid-dry season. Conversely, LLD varied both spatially and temporally in IP. Findings show decomposition processes are strongly suppressed during prolonged dry phases, but rainfall events can temporarily stimulate decomposition in this hot tropical semiarid environment.

presentations.title: Seasonal and Hydrological Drivers of Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Mediterranean Temporary Waters
presentations.abstract: Inland waters play a key role in the global carbon cycle by emitting CO₂ and CH₄. We measured CO₂ and CH₄ fluxes across three seasons under both wet and dry conditions in 20 Mediterranean ponds using closed static chambers. Ponds acted as net sources of both gases, with significantly higher fluxes in the wet than in the dry phase. In the wet phase, dissolved oxygen was the main driver for both gases, together with temperature for CO₂ and CH₄, and—for CH₄—open-water percentage and chlorophyll-a. In the dry phase, sediment properties dominated, with water content and temperature interaction driving CO₂ fluxes, and DOM properties such as SUVA and FI shaping CH₄ fluxes. Hydroperiod length did not explain differences. CO₂ was the major contributor to GWP (~70% dry, ~90% wet).

presentations.title: Intermittent Waters, Shifting Carbon: DOM Signatures Across the Largest Floodplain of the St. Lawrence River
presentations.abstract: River floodplains are increasingly subject to hydrological intermittency, altering both habitat structure and biogeochemistry of drying waters. In the major floodplain of the St. Lawrence River (Québec), shifts in land use may modify DOM composition. We investigated DOM concentration, composition and biodegradability along a gradient from row-crop fields to grasslands and natural forests. Water from 12 tributaries was also sampled. Fluorescence and absorbance properties (PARAFAC), DOC concentrations and degradation experiments were measured. DOM from agricultural areas contained higher proportions of protein-like and labile material; DOM from natural habitats was richer in humic, aromatic and more recalcitrant compounds. Tributary DOM also differed from field-derived DOM.

presentations.title: CHANGES IN FREQUENCY AND INTENSITY OF HYDRIC FLUCTUATIONS AFFECT STRUCTURE, FUNCTION AND RESILIENCE OF BENTHIC MICROBIAL COMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: Phototrophic biofilms are exposed to multiple stressors, including more frequent and intense drying events. River biofilms were exposed to different drying-rewetting cycles in a mesocosm study for 41 days. Biofilms were exposed to 4 drying regimes differing in amplitude (24h or 72h cumulative drying over 96h) and frequency. Drying amplitude and frequency strongly shaped biofilm structure and functioning. For 24h cumulative drying, fragmentation of the drought period reduced biofilm biomass inhibition compared to continuous drought. Impacts persisted after re-submergence, revealing persistent legacy effects.

presentations.title: Characterising the effects of drying on the taxonomic diversity of microbial biofilms in seasonally intermittent chalk streams
presentations.abstract: Chalk streams are groundwater-fed systems in southern England with seasonally drying headwaters (winterbournes). We characterised seasonal changes in biofilm diversity using amplicon sequencing. Higher prokaryote and eukaryote diversity in perennial reaches with diversity peaking in autumn; winterbourne diversity lowest during autumn flow cessation. Proteobacteria dominated during flowing phases; Actinobacteria became dominant during drying. Algae dominated eukaryote community most of year, but Fungi began to dominate during drying transitions, comprising >50% after flow cessation and >80% after 2-month dry period.

name: Invasive Bivalves in Freshwater and Marine Systems
lead_organizer: Bastiaan Ibelings, University of Geneva
description: Molluscs are the second largest group of animals, and in freshwaters molluscs include some of the most threatened and most invasive species. Particularly Dreissena rostriformis bugensis and D. polymorpha (quagga and zebra mussels) have established themselves as important drivers of change in freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: Blooms like it hot, but mussels do not: Influence of invasive quagga mussels on cyanobacteria during heatwaves
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract: We combined laboratory experiments, long-term field monitoring, and ecosystem modeling to investigate whether temperature constrains mussel control of cyanobacteria. Lab filtration rates of quagga mussels on cyanobacteria/green algae across 24-33°C decreased within 27.6-30.2°C breakpoint window. Among cyanobacteria, Dolichospermum was palatable; Aphanizomenon, Anabaenopsis, Microcystis non-palatable. 10 years of lake data confirmed this thermal window. PCLake+ ecosystem modelling under RCP scenarios shows mussel-mediated HAB suppression persists under RCP 4.5 and 2.6, but under RCP 8.5 summer cyanobacteria return.

presentations.title: HOW SWITZERLAND TRIES TO KEEP SOME OF THEIR PRE-ALPINE LAKES FREE OF QUAGGA MUSSELS AFTER RECENT INVASIONS AND MASS ABUNDACES IN SOME LAKES
presentations.abstract: Quagga mussels were discovered in Switzerland in 2014 and have colonised more than 10 lakes. Eleven Swiss cantons have decided to stop spread by issuing an obligation to clean boats before changing water bodies. This system, comprising certified cleaning stations, web campaign and online certificates, was set up within a year. We discuss current spread, potential consequences, and the recently implemented compulsory boat cleaning regulations.

presentations.title: EARLY INVASION DYNAMICS OF CORBICULA FLUMINEA AND ITS CO-OCCURRENCE WITH NATIVE FRESHWATER MUSSELS IN A NEWLY INVADED NEW ZEALAND RIVER SYSTEM
presentations.abstract: In May 2023 Corbicula fluminea was detected for the first time in New Zealand, in the Waikato River catchment. Surveys at 25 wadeable sites confirmed spread across multiple hydro-lakes and riverine stretches. Annual monitoring 2023-2025 revealed nearly 50-fold density increase (27 to 1,360 clams m-2). Depth-stratified surveys at 9 sites in Lakes Karāpiro and Maraetai (2024-2025) quantified C. fluminea and kākahi co-occurrence. C. fluminea densities increased in mid-to-deep zones (9-12 m); kākahi peak at 4-6 m, indicating depth partitioning.

presentations.title: JUST HANGING IN THERE AFTER 50 YEARS: THE INVASIVE BIVALVE CORBICULA FLUMINEA IN A NORTH CAROLINA USA LAKE
presentations.abstract: Lake Waccamaw is a shallow blackwater lake in North Carolina where Corbicula was first seen ~50 yrs ago. A quantitative survey by Porter and Horn (1981) found highest densities in shallow sand along the northern shoreline. Marked individuals showed very low growth rates and low O:N ratios indicating energetic limitations. Periodic die-offs occurred but Corbicula persists at very low densities. What can we learn from constrained populations?

presentations.title: TROPHIC IMPACTS OF QUAGGA MUSSEL DISPLACEMENT OF ZEBRA MUSSELS IN LAKE SIMCOE, ONTARIO
presentations.abstract: In 2010, zebra mussels were displaced by quagga mussels (D. rostriformis bugensis) in Lake Simcoe. May-Aug 2025, samples of DIC, macrophytes, algae, benthic invertebrates, zooplankton, and fish were collected from nearshore and offshore zones for stable isotope analysis. Hypothesized rerouting of energy pathways toward benthic deepwater zones. Such a shift could increase food availability for benthic feeders like whitefish.

presentations.title: BOOM OR BUST? FOUR DECADES OF DREISSENID INVASION IN THE LAURENTIAN GREAT LAKES
presentations.abstract: Using four decades of data from US EPA Great Lakes Biology Monitoring Program, we synthesized long-term trends in dreissenid density and biomass across the four lower Great Lakes. Invasion dynamics, population size, growth, and mussel longevity are governed by lake morphometry. Productive nearshore zones show boom-and-bust cycles. Offshore deep populations stabilizing in density but accumulating biomass — long-term phosphorus sink. Lake Erie western/central declining due to recurring hypoxia.

name: Bridging the Fresh/Salty Divide
lead_organizer: Jemma Fadum, Carnegie Institution for Science
co_organizers: Laura Falkenberg, University of South Australia
description: While the fields of limnology and oceanography are closely related, individuals working in inland and marine ecosystems rarely find themselves in conversation. To provide a platform for knowledge exchange across the Fresh/Salty divide, we invite submissions on coastal/ocean ecosystems with translatable findings to freshwater, inland water research with implications for oceanography, and/or studies spanning a salinity gradient.

presentations.title: Double Diffusion in an Ice-covered Freshwater Lake
presentations.abstract: Double diffusion occurs in quiescent regions of oceans and saline lakes. Results here are the first showing salt fingers and the diffusive mode of double diffusion occur under the ice in freshwater lakes with low specific conductance. Calculations indicated 90 to 100% of lake-wide solute increase for several months following ice-on was from cryoconcentration. Rρ and Ɍ ratios indicated salt fingers below ice. Increases in SC above sediments after ice-on imply localized density increases conducive for intrusive flows. Diverse solutes including oxygen and DOC released by cryoconcentration.

presentations.title: Comparison of Aquatic and Marine Manganese Oxidation Along an Oxygen Gradient
presentations.abstract: Mn oxide formation is critical across marine and aquatic environments. We compare Mn oxide formation in Steel Lake, Minnesota (freshwater) and the Baltic Sea. Both well stratified with high Mn (>10 µM). MnOx peaks at base of oxycline. Oxidation in Steel Lake primarily microbially mediated except at MnOx peak; in Baltic Sea, nearly uniform abiotic Mn oxide formation occurs throughout oxycline. Despite similar water column signatures, vastly different biotic/abiotic contributions.

presentations.title: Coastal Biogeochemical and Microbial Responses to Exports from a Small Rain-dominated River Plume in the Northeast Pacific Coastal Temperate Rainforest
presentations.abstract: Hyacinthe Creek/Bay (Quadra Island, BC) river-ocean estuary system. Samples at 0, 15, 50 cm depth across 7 sites in freshwater plume (0-27.9 PSU). Surface samples revealed distinct biogeochemical/microbial signatures distinct from underlying waters, vertical plume extent <15 cm. Nutrient/carbon increased with distance from river inflow. Microbial communities exhibited horizontal and vertical structure, supporting river-to-sea microbial continuum.

presentations.title: Intra-specific genomic variation across distant oceans reveals signatures of seasonal and ENSO-driven selection in microbes
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Marine Sciences (ICM), CSIC, Barcelona, Spain
presentations.abstract: Coastal microbiomes from Blanes Bay (Mediterranean) and Newport Beach (Pacific). 15 and 10 years of monthly metagenomic sampling. 1,535 MAGs in Blanes; 1,068 MAGs + 187 SAGs in Newport. 615 shared species-level genomes; 16 shared at strain level. Focusing on shared Prochlorococcus lineage (>96% ANI), detected recurrent mutations and seasonal pN/pS patterns. Detected potential ENSO imprint in Newport: higher pN/pS aligned with El Niño events.

presentations.title: Physical forcing shapes microbial community structure in the Lower Laurentian Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Five lakewide sampling campaigns in Lake Ontario (May, Sept 2023) and Lake Erie (May, Aug, Sept 2024). 16S rRNA gene sequencing, flow cytometry, and EPA water quality data. Great Lakes microbial communities consistently include core assemblage of cosmopolitan taxa, reflecting strong homogenizing selection and efficient lakewide dispersal. Physical disturbances (tributary inputs, upwellings, cyanobacterial blooms) promote localized proliferation of rare taxa.

name: High Arctic Limnology in Rapidly Changing Landscapes
lead_organizer: Frédéric Bouchard, Université de Sherbrooke
co_organizers: Isabelle Laurion, Institut national de la recherche scientifique
description: As climate change accelerates across the circumpolar North, High Arctic limnoscapes are emerging as key sentinel environments. Permafrost plays a central role in shaping local to regional limnological processes.

presentations.title: 50-YEAR AND 20-YEAR RECORDS OF LAKE BIOGEOCHEMICAL CHANGE FROM PERMAFROST DEGRADATION
presentations.abstract: 50-year record (Toolik Lake) and 20-year record (Wolverine lakes chain) show doubling of conductivity and major ions related to increased weathering as summer thaw deepens. Toolik increases roughly linear; Wolverine major ion increases linear for ~15 years but reversed in recent years. Lakes impacted by shoreline thermokarst failures: major ion chemistry and light extinction increased rapidly but recovered within one to several years.

presentations.title: HIGH-RESOLUTION GREENHOUSE GAS FLUX DATA FROM ARCTIC EPHEMERAL PONDS
presentations.abstract: Bihourly CO2 and CH4 emissions data 2023, 6 weeks, opaque automated flux chambers, three ephemeral ponds in Arctic polygonal landscape on Bylot Island, Nunavut (73°N). Initial spike during snowmelt, stabilization for ~1 week, then increase as ponds warmed and dried. CO2 peaked at maximum solar radiation; CH4 peaks variable, lagged by up to 12 hours.

presentations.title: BIOCHEMICAL HOMEOSTASIS IN DAPHNIA ACROSS A GRADIENT OF ARCTIC LAKE CONDITIONS
presentations.abstract: Daphnia responses across 14 shallow lakes/ponds in Iqaluktuuttiaq region (Nunavut), spanning gradients in DOC (8.4-29.2 mg/L), P (6.7-32.3 µg/L), and permafrost disturbance. Despite variable conditions, Daphnia show only minor shifts in stable isotope and FA profiles. Strong correlations between adult and ephippial isotopes suggest stability extends to future generations.

presentations.title: Energetics and Seasonal Evolution of a Meltwater Pond on the Milne Ice Shelf, Nunavut
presentations.abstract: Limnological experiment at meltwater pond (1.5m deep, 0.02 km2) on Milne Ice Shelf May-July 2025. Heat budget analyzed using bathymetry, temperature, meteorological measurements. Pressure sensors estimated ice ablation rate. Residual net heat flux aligns with observed melting rate ~3 cm day-1.

presentations.title: EARLIER ICE-OFF, LONGER GROWING SEASONS
presentations.abstract: Multi-year datasets from two high-latitude lakes assessing how earlier ice-off events influence phytoplankton structure, productivity and oxygen. Prolonged open-water periods favor fast-growing taxa, alter seasonal succession, potentially shift trophic interactions. Oxygen saturation high and stable compared to longer ice-cover years.

presentations.title: INVESTIGATING ENVIRONMENTAL DRIVERS OF MICROBIAL COMMUNITY COMPOSITION IN GLACIALLY-FED LAKES IN THE ARCTIC
presentations.abstract: Microbial community composition in 6 glacially-fed Arctic lakes. Sampled summer 2025 in Kangerlussuaq (W Greenland) and Jostedalsbreen (Norway), differing in nutrient and DOM features. DNA, nutrients, turbidity, DOC, DOM. Metagenomics and 16S rRNA.

name: Advances in Lipid Biomarker Approaches
lead_organizer: Benjamin Gwinneth, Université de Montréal
description: Lake sediments preserve an extraordinary archive of environmental change. Among the most rapidly advancing tools for accessing these archives are lipid biomarkers.

presentations.title: SEDIMENT BIOMARKERS TRACK A SEABIRD COLONY RESPONSE TO PAST CHANGES IN CLIMATE
presentations.abstract: Dated sediment core from Cape Vera Devon Island tracking inputs from large northern fulmar colony via d15N, sterols, stanols, and biogenic elements. Compared with GDGTs that track recent temperature records to show how northern fulmar populations responded to past climate.

presentations.title: LONG CHAIN N-ALKANES IN LAKE SEDIMENT TRACK DIFFERENCES IN ADJACENT LAND VEGETATION
presentations.abstract: 19 lakes across 4 Saskatchewan ecoregions. Significant correlations between n-alkane ratios C31/(C27+C31) and herbaceous-to-tree ratio. Distinguishing Prairie Grassland from forested. C/N and δ13C not effective. Lignin-derived phenols influenced by other factors.

presentations.title: Compound-Specific Isotope Analyses of n-Alkane Biomarkers Reveals Source-Dependent and Persistent Priming Effects in Incubated Sediments
presentations.affiliation: Concordia University and Geotop Research Center
presentations.abstract: Spiking coastal sediments with marine OC (Nannochloropsis) and terrestrial OC (corn leaves). Result: 10.3% and 30.4% stimulation of sedimentary OC decomposition lasting 32 days. Synergistic enhancement with 1:1 mixtures. Sources can turn long-term sinks into sources.

presentations.title: REFINING THE USE OF GDGTS AS PALEOCLIMATE PROXIES IN EASTERN AND WESTERN CANADA
presentations.abstract: Two lake sediment transects in Canada (Western parallel to Rockies; Eastern southern to northern Quebec) for temperature calibrations. MBT5'Me index inversely correlated with latitude.

presentations.title: NORTH PACIFIC CLIMATE VARIABILITY INFERRED FROM A 600-YEAR SEDIMENTARY LIPID BIOMARKER RECORD IN CULTUS LAKE, BC
presentations.abstract: Lake-specific brGDGT calibration for Cultus Lake. brGDGT Ib showed strongest thermal sensitivity. ~600-year record (since ~1400 CE) shows multi-centennial temperature variability consistent with tree-rings and Mt. Logan ice core. Tracks δ15N (Pacific salmon) until late 19th century when anthropogenic N loading caused decoupling.

presentations.title: GDGTs AS PROXIES TO TRACK URANIUM MILL ACID ROCK DRAINAGE IN WHISKEY LAKE, ON
presentations.abstract: Sediment cores from Whiskey Lake exposed to acidic loading from uranium mines (~1955-1996). GDGT cyclization correlates with decreasing pH. Results show utility of GDGTs in tracking acid rock drainage in lake sediments.

name: Effective Strategies for Controlling Algal Blooms
lead_organizer: Alan Wilson, Auburn University
co_organizers: H. Dail Laughinghouse, University of Florida
description: Algal blooms in freshwater and marine systems are often dominated by toxigenic cyanobacteria or dinoflagellates. This session shares experiences evaluating diverse techniques for controlling algal blooms.

presentations.title: SYSTEM ANALYSIS GUIDED TACKLING OF EUTROPHICATION AND CYANOBACTERIAL BLOOMS
presentations.abstract: Restoration of eutrophic water bodies should begin with system analysis. Case studies from Netherlands. Tailored package of measures needed; single-measure focus should be abandoned. Adequate monitoring crucial. Widespread (diffuse) nutrient loading requires ongoing maintenance or repeated interventions.

presentations.title: Lake Geneva, a success story of eutrophication control through phosphorus reduction, but...
presentations.abstract: Lake Geneva environmental change over 60 years. Long-term P target set in 1960s now reached. Yet hypoxia in deeper parts back due to climate change — 309m deep lake hasn't fully mixed since 2012. Other major issue: invasive quagga mussel and lake benthification. Pelagic foodweb weakening.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF NITROGEN DIVERSION ON LAKE PRODUCTION, CYANOBACTERIAL BLOOMS, AND PHYTOPLANKTON TOXICITY: A 30-YEAR WHOLE-CATCHMENT EXPERIMENT
presentations.abstract: Catchment-scale experiment (52,000 km2) where urban N pollution reduced >90%, leading to ~50% decline in total N flux to lakes after 22 years. No change in total P. Comparison of 4 reference and 3 impacted lakes: no substantial change in chlorophyll/Secchi after 8 years; surface blooms intensified due to warming, anoxia. Up to 85% of water column N derived from sediments.

presentations.title: Climate Change Intensify the Variability of Cyanobacterial Blooms in Large Shallow and Eutrophic Lake Taihu, China
presentations.abstract: Lake Taihu eutrophication and cyanobacterial blooms since 1980s. Most severe bloom in 2017 (1582 km2). Decline 2021. Bucket model: warm winter 2016-2017 triggered early bloom, increased pH and reduced DO activated sediment P release establishing positive feedback. Loop broken by sharp PAR decrease in spring 2021.

presentations.title: Mitigation of harmful algal blooms using cultivable seaweeds
presentations.abstract: Studies demonstrating HAB-mitigating effects of seaweeds. Ulva spp. on M. polykrikoides and D. acuminata; Ulva and S. latissima on A. catenella and Pseudo-nitzschia. Algicidal activity all pairs. Ulva reduced wild M. polykrikoides 92%, S. latissima reduced A. catenella 73-95%, Pseudo-nitzschia 69-75%. Sugar kelp lessened saxitoxin and domoic acid accumulation in shellfish.

name: Floating Solar Energy in Inland and Coastal Waters
lead_organizer: Rafael Almeida, Indiana University
co_organizers: Simone Cardoso, Federal University of Juiz de Fora
description: Floating solar photovoltaics (FPV) are expanding rapidly worldwide as a low-carbon energy solution. This session invites talks that explore ecological, biogeochemical, and water quality responses to FPV systems.

presentations.title: TRACKING THE RISE OF FLOATING SOLAR ENERGY ON GLOBAL AQUATIC ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Global overview of FPV development. Remote sensing-derived database of 3,000+ FPV systems characterizing types of water bodies, project sizes, construction patterns, regional trajectories. Outlines major ecological and biogeochemical questions: shading, altered thermal regimes, hydrological changes.

presentations.title: AQUATIC GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS OF FLOATING SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAIC SYSTEMS (FPV)
presentations.abstract: Monthly monitoring Feb 2025 onward in shallow stormwater retention pond with 70% FPV coverage. CH4 ebullitive and diffusive emissions higher in open water than FPV (reduced turbulence, bird faeces). Pond was a CO2 source on average. Surface DO slightly higher in open water due to reduced water-atmosphere mixing.

presentations.title: Floating photovoltaics restructure microbial communities through sustained light reduction and oxygen limitation
presentations.abstract: Two-year whole-ecosystem manipulation in experimental ponds. FPV coverage drives persistent hypoxia and light limitation, restructuring microbial communities. Strongly suppressed oxygenic photosynthesis by planktonic cyanobacteria; enriched benthic cyanobacteria and anoxygenic phototrophs. Methanotrophs expanded by order of magnitude in 2024. Metabolic regime shift toward alternative stable state.

presentations.title: GLOBAL PATTERNS OF PHYTOPLANKTON CHANGE ACROSS GRADIENTS OF FLOATING SOLAR ENERGY COVERAGE
presentations.abstract: Remote sensing assessment of FPV coverage relating to phytoplankton (NDCI proxy). ~500 installations mapped. Sentinel-2 MSI NDCI processed on Google Earth Engine. ΔNDCI generally small at low/moderate coverage but slightly negative at >70% coverage. Reductions stronger in high-chlorophyll systems.

presentations.title: The ecological effects of floating photovoltaic systems vary with panel coverage and lake trophic status: an experimental approach
presentations.affiliation: UFRN - Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte
presentations.abstract: Experimental tested 0%, 25%, 45%, 65% FPV coverage with nutrient enrichment. Increasing FPV reduced water temperature/evaporation. Zooplankton higher abundance at 45% FPV; macroinvertebrate richness/diversity declined with increasing FPV particularly in enriched mesocosms. GPP and respiration decreased with FPV; decomposition and CO2 affected only by nutrients.

presentations.title: THE IMPACT OF FLOATING SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAICS ON PRIMARY PRODUCTION IN A FRESHWATER LAKE
presentations.abstract: Three years of monitoring data from quarry lake in Netherlands. Oxygen levels under FPV systems significantly lower, corresponding to sharp decline in primary production in upper water layer. Reductions can have consequences for entire aquatic ecosystem.

name: Ecological Effects of Flow Alterations, Dam Removals, and Dam Renewals
lead_organizer: Jennifer Lento, Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
co_organizers: Philip Harrison, Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
description: Flow alteration by dams remains one of the largest threats to freshwater ecosystem health. This session aims to broaden our understanding of the ecological impacts of dams.

presentations.title: Restoring flow: dam removal as a tool for riverine habitat restoration and fish migration
presentations.abstract: Columbia Dam (NJ) removal 2018-2019 opened 20 miles of streams in Paulins Kill watershed for migratory fish (American Shad, eel, Sea Lamprey). Long-term monitoring 2016-2025 above and below dam. Migratory species documented in old impoundment; macroinvertebrate scores high indicating good water quality.

presentations.title: Effects of dam removal on microbial biodiversity and functioning within biofilms in two European climate zones
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research UFZ
presentations.abstract: Biodiversa+ project RESTOLINK testing effects of dams and dam removal on streams (2nd order) across European climate gradient. Microbial communities (biofilms): organic carbon and nitrate uptake, microbial biodiversity (16S sequencing) linked to small-scale hydromophology. Many but not all functions recover with restored hydromorphology.

presentations.title: DAM REMOVAL IN EUROPEAN RIVERS LEADS TO DIFFERENT EFFECTS ON MACROINVERTEBRATE BIODIVERSITY AND ASSOCIATED ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS
presentations.abstract: RESTOLINK project across European climate gradient. Macroinvertebrate community recovery patterns differed across latitudinal gradient. Macroinvertebrate community composition and biodiversity do not necessarily recover same way as ecosystem functions. Need comprehensive monitoring including ecosystem functionality proxies.

presentations.title: Assessing anadromous fish connectivity following the removal of a hydropower dam on the Skutik River, New Brunswick
presentations.abstract: Radio-telemetry to assess migration of anadromous blueback herring and alewife over 2 years through reconstructed riverbed at Salmon Falls following hydropower plant removal on Skutik/St. Croix River 2023. Quantified passage rates and travel times using time-to-event framework.

presentations.title: Assessing the impact of 100 years of sediment accumulation on NO3 storm response in a small artificial reservoir in New England
presentations.abstract: Centenarian dam in small urban reservoir in New England. 25 years water chemistry data. Storms have concentrating effect on NO3. Baseflow NO3 slightly increased from 0.16 to 0.20 mg/l 1998-2018, likely from population/land use changes. Wetland development around reservoir does not outweigh anthropogenic land use changes.

presentations.title: How does variable water flow shape the behavior, physiology, and growth of stream-dwelling Arctic charr?
presentations.abstract: Three field experiments (180 fish: 60 per experiment) on Arctic charr behavior, growth, swimming, metabolic rate. Fast vs slow current. Arctic charr grew faster in fast-running waters than slower waters. In slow waters: less drifting prey, emerged later from shelters, more mobile, swam slower. Slow-water fish developed lower standard metabolic rate.

name: Advancing the Global Ocean Biodiversity Atlas
lead_organizer: Peter Busumprah, Ocean Rock Base
co_organizers: Olusola Adeoye, Natures Cares Resources Centre
Opoku Mensah Abrampah, Africa Ocean Alliance
description: This session explores innovative approaches to developing and enhancing the Global Ocean Biodiversity Atlas through integration of diverse, high-quality datasets. Addresses UN Ocean Challenges 2 and 8 and contributes to UN Ocean Decade endorsed African Ocean Biodiversity Atlas project.

presentations.title: African Ocean Biodiversity Atlas for a Sustainable Ocean Economy
presentations.affiliation: Ocean Rock Base and Africa Ocean Alliance
presentations.abstract: UN Ocean Decade project supporting SDG 14. Comprehensive data repository cataloging marine species, GPS technology to map fishery species. Fisheries atlas with indigenous names of fish species developed with local fishermen. Implemented in Ghana, expanding to Cameroon, Nigeria, Sudan, Tunisia.

presentations.title: African Blue Carbon Biodiversity
presentations.affiliation: Methodist University College- Ghana/ Africa Ocean Alliance
presentations.abstract: African Blue Carbon Biodiversity combines coastal wetlands and seagrass beds, playing crucial role in carbon sequestration. Habitats store large amounts of blue carbon, supporting diverse marine and terrestrial species. Sustainable management essential for preserving biodiversity and climate change mitigation.

presentations.title: Harnessing Ocean Accounting and Law of the Sea for Sustainable Blue Carbon Ecosystems and Fisheries
presentations.abstract: Role of ocean accounting and Law of the Sea in sustainable management of blue carbon ecosystems and fisheries. Effective frameworks for quantifying and integrating ecosystems into national/international decision-making. Recent advancements in ocean accounting methodologies; legal instruments influencing blue carbon and fisheries management.

presentations.title: DEVELOPMENT OF THE SOUTH PACIFIC VULNERABLE MARINE ECOSYSTEM BIOREGIONALISATION
presentations.abstract: VME-specific bioregionalisation to inform management of SAIs on VMEs. Gradient forest models applied to estimate taxon compositional turnover; hierarchical classification approach. 7-group VME-specific bioregionalisation for western South Pacific Ocean. Two distinct spatial uncertainty estimates for spatial planning.

presentations.title: Ocean Financing for Enhanced Biodiversity Mapping: Strategies and Opportunities
presentations.abstract: Innovative role of ocean financing as vital resource for biodiversity mapping. Financial instruments support development of high-resolution mapping technologies, data collection, capacity-building. Case studies, frameworks for aligning financial resources with conservation objectives.

presentations.title: Enhancing Inclusivity through Community Engagement in Fisheries and Marine Biodiversity
presentations.abstract: Inclusive participation of local communities fosters sustainable resource management, conservation, equitable benefit-sharing. Involves fishers, indigenous groups, local stakeholders leveraging traditional knowledge. Empowering marginalized groups for social equity and long-term commitment.

name: Nitrogen Cycling Processes in Aquatic Ecosystems
lead_organizer: Lin Zhang, Texas A and M University Corpus Christi
co_organizers: Mark Altabet, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth
Pat Glibert, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science
Annie Bourbonnais, University of South Carolina
Darcy Perin, University of South Carolina
description: Aquatic ecosystems are driven by intricate nitrogen (N) cycling processes essential for maintaining health of these environments and the food webs they sustain.

presentations.title: Nitrogen dynamics of 'miniature oceans': Microbially mediated biogeochemistry in Palau's marine lakes
presentations.abstract: Marine lakes of Palau as natural model system for examining microbial nitrogen cycling using paired metagenomics and geochemical sampling. Identification of complete denitrifiers (Arcobacteraceae) in C-rich but N-poor lakes. Investigates links between microbial community assemblage, denitrification modularity, competition between denitrification and DNRA.

presentations.title: Drying-rewetting cycles at the banks of agricultural ditches boost N2O emissions depending on soil type and nitrogen content
presentations.abstract: Soil cores from ditch banks in clay and peat areas. Greater N2O emissions during drying (10.5 vs 0.7 mg/m2/day clay; 0.9 vs 0.2 peat). Strong positive relationship with TDN for clay (40x more N2O at highest TDN). Netherlands water level fluctuations: 500/16 tons N2O/year additional emissions for clay/peat.

presentations.title: Total microcystins reduce the activity of genes involved in nitrogen fixation and denitrification in lakes of the southcentral USA
presentations.abstract: 20 lakes in southcentral USA. Microcystins negatively associated with presence and activity of cellular pathways for nitrogen fixation, denitrification, P uptake. Effects on gene activity could be separated from NOX/environmental factors. Negative correlations with N fixation, dissimilatory nitrite reductase. Concentrations 0.15-0.50 µg/L still affected genes.

presentations.title: Unraveling Nitrogen Preference in Lake Erie Microcystis Blooms Using Stable Isotope Probing Metagenomics
presentations.abstract: Lake Erie western basin Microcystis HABs. SIP metagenomics tracks isotopically labeled N substrates. Ammonium incorporated by most taxa at highest rate. Urea/nitrate variable. Microcystis incorporated less N than other Cyanobacteria, suggesting disproportionate use for storage and microcystin production.

presentations.title: RAPID PHOSPHORUS REMOVAL PROMOTES A SUSTAINED DECREASE IN NITROGEN IN EUTROPHIC LAKES
presentations.abstract: 46 in-lake alum treatments. Alum decreased TP, also decreased TN and increased TN:TP. TN response mediated by depth — positive in shallow, not deep lakes. Effects persisted >8 years. Macrophyte cover increase amplified TN decrease. Benthic N-cycling drives water column TN response following P reduction.

presentations.title: From Enzymes to Redoxclines: Mechanistic and Ecosystem Controls on Dual Nitrate N and O Isotope Effects During Denitrification in Lakes
presentations.abstract: δ15N-δ18O systematics across pure cultures, communities, lacustrine RTZs, sediments. Lake Lugano (Switzerland) lithotrophic nitrate reduction model. Nitrate-reductase identity (Nar vs Nap) and metabolic lifestyle modulate N-O isotope effects. Sediments show attenuated isotope effects under high reactivity.

name: C, N, P, and Stoichiometry Tea
lead_organizer: Isabelle Andersen, Miami University
co_organizers: Andras Abonyi, MTA-ÖK Lendület Fluvial Ecology Research Group
Xavier Benito, Institute of Agrifood Research and Technology (IRTA)
Jacob Diamond, Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme, UNESCO
Estela Romero, Centre for Ecological Research and Forestry Applications (CREAF)
description: Ecological stoichiometry bridges physiology, community ecology, and biogeochemistry by exploring how relative availability and demand for elements like C, N, and P shape ecological interactions from organisms to ecosystems.

presentations.title: Nitrogen deposition reveals global patterns in plant and animal stoichiometry
presentations.abstract: StoichLife database with N and P content data for 5,443 species across 1,390 sites. Plant stoichiometry in terrestrial/freshwater more strongly associated with N deposition than animal stoichiometry. Latitudinal patterns more closely associated with species turnover than intraspecific variation.

presentations.title: Elemental allocation to molecular drivers of biogeochemistry in the Southern Ocean
presentations.abstract: Elemental measurements with metaproteomics in Southern Ocean. Iron availability influences elemental allocation. Manganese primarily allocated to photosynthesis in iron-replete; reallocated under low iron. ~50% biogenic copper in plastocyanin. N:P decoupled from ribosomal abundance.

presentations.title: HIGH STOICHIOMETRIC CARBON TO PHOSPHORUS RATIO INCREASES MITOCHONDRIAL PERFORMANCE AND THERMAL TOLERANCE OF COLD-ACCLIMATED DAPHNIA
presentations.abstract: Daphnia at 10°C, 20°C, 30°C with C:P 76, 222, 424. High C:P at warm end threatens aerobic capacity (corroborated by P supplementation). Cold-acclimated: high C:P enhanced respiratory rates. High C:P also increased thermal tolerance via CTmax.

presentations.title: Evaluating Nutrient Flux in Watersheds Impacted by High Density Greenhouse Land Use using Chemical and Molecular Tools
presentations.abstract: Ruthven Tributaries (Lake Erie). Chemically characterize P and N inputs. Process-based watershed model simulations to determine spatial/temporal variability of N:P and isotopic signatures from greenhouse sector. Correlate microbial taxa shifts with greenhouse-derived nutrient signatures.

presentations.title: WATER COLUMN MICROBIAL COMMUNITY RESPONDS TO NITROGEN REMOVAL-INDUCED OLIGOTROPHICATION IN SHALLOW LAKE MESOCOSMS
presentations.abstract: 12 limnocorrals at U Mississippi Field Station. N:P ratios 2.2, 16, 55, 110. After N elimination 2023: TN and Chl a lower, TP higher. Greater alpha diversity in 2023; MCC more similar between treatments.

name: Microbial Ecology Along the Inorganic to Organic Continuum
lead_organizer: Rachele Spezzano, Marine Biological Laboratory
co_organizers: Mona Norbisrath, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution
description: This session invites contributions that examine dynamic interactions between the inorganic carbon system, microbial communities, and organic matter across freshwater, coastal, and open-ocean environments.

presentations.title: Novel in situ sensor for marine inorganic carbon: applications from coral reefs, sediment porewater, to open ocean
presentations.abstract: Solid-state reagentless pH-AT sensor with rapid (<60 s) measurement. Sensor error 2.85 µmol/kg AT. Deployed in Kaneohe Bay, HI. Plans for seagrass porewater, shellfish hatcheries.

presentations.title: RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN PARTICULATE ORGANIC COMPOSITION, MICROBES, AND INORGANIC C, N, O CONCENTRATIONS OVER DEPTH IN OPEN-OCEAN EUPHOTIC ZONES
presentations.abstract: Non-Redfield stoichiometry in surface ocean POM. Higher C:N near-surface, lower C:N deeper. Variations in carbohydrate and amino acid content of POM. Deeper low-light euphotic zone microbial responses can decouple from in-situ primary production.

presentations.title: Microbial interactions and community ecology in lake carbon biogeochemistry
presentations.abstract: Two studies: lake methanotrophy field study and phytoplankton-bacteria lab study. Shotgun metagenomics with DO, nutrients, pH, CO2, CH4. Framework for microbial contributions emphasizing microbe-microbe interactions and intermediate metabolite exchange.

presentations.title: The impact of algal blooms on promoting in-situ N2O emissions: A case in Zhanjiang bay, China
presentations.abstract: Zhanjiang Bay 15N isotope incubation and qPCR. Denitrification and nitrification-denitrification produced N2O. In-situ N2O production 3x higher during bloom. Fresh algal POM creates anaerobic microenvironments.

presentations.title: COMPARING MICROBIAL ADAPTATIONS TO SEASONAL ANOXIA IN MARINE AND FRESHWATER ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Time series in coastal Baltic Sea and Lake Lunz. Decrease in heterotrophic production due to induced anoxia less pronounced at seasonally anoxic depth in marine. In freshwater: spring dark carbon fixation increased under induced anoxia at year-round oxic depth.

presentations.title: Catch and release: How microbial strategies and POC flux regulate carbon export
presentations.abstract: Depth-resolved water-column model coupling particle-associated bacterial attachment, detachment, growth, mortality. Carbon export efficiency highly sensitive to POC flux. Prolonged high flux can reduce carbon burial via near-surface free-living degraders.

name: Harmful Algal Bloom Mitigation and Its Consequences
description: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) induced by climate change and eutrophication threaten global water quality. For some regions, HABs are unavoidable, and their management consists mainly of bloom control, such as direct interventions to suppress or destroy HABs. However, interference in the bloom process might lead to negative consequences for the ecological community.
lead_organizer: Patch Thongthaisong, Laboratoire LEMAR, Institut Universitaire Européen de la Mer, Université de Bretagne Occidentale, France

presentations.title: BEYOND SIZE: EXPERIMENTAL LESSONS WITH MACROPHYTES FOR EFFECTIVE ALGAL BLOOM CONTROL
presentations.abstract: Algal blooms have caused water quality issues in freshwater bodies for decades and managing these blooms has been an uphill task for water resource management organizations, both public and private. In this talk, I will cover the use of aquatic macrophytes for small to large scale algal bloom mitigation, the lessons we learnt and the future utility of macrophytes in man-made reservoirs in tropical regions (funded by Public Utilities Board, Singapore). We assessed 8 species of macrophytes for their efficacy in shifting phytoplankton community dominance (from cyanobacteria to green algae) using smaller scaled mesocosms (100 L). Two species (L. adscendens and P. barbata) used in medium sized mesocosms (1,000 L), significantly reduced chlorophyll a concentrations and total nitrogen concentrations. Finally, we introduced these macrophytes to large mesocosms (100,000 L) and found that macrophyte treatments did not significantly reduce total nutrient, chlorophyll a concentrations and cyanobacterial dominance. These findings indicated that upscaling from smaller mesocosms can have issues such as slower plant growth, pests and water body suitability for growth.

presentations.title: Environmental And Public Health Impact Assessment Of Lanthanum (La) Based Phosphorus Binders
presentations.abstract: The abundance of endemic species in freshwater ecosystems highlights their extraordinary ecological role and susceptibility to environmental changes and anthropogenic pressure. Nutrient enrichment (eutrophication) in aquatic systems triggers the dominance of potentially toxin-producing cyanobacteria and thus prompts the progressive loss of biodiversity. Chemical phosphorus inactivation using iron-, aluminium-, and lanthanum (La)-based materials is a common approach to manage internal phosphorus load. We conducted laboratory assays to evaluate the effects on Daphnia magna of a new lanthanum-modified silicate clay. The commonly used lanthanum-modified bentonite and natural bentonite served as comparative benchmark materials. The tests show absence of acute toxicity even at doses 5 times higher than commonly used application dosages. Chronic assays with and without exposure to high particle concentrations demonstrate that indirect effects must be distinguished from direct toxicity.

presentations.title: Biological Response to Aluminum Sulfate Treatment in the Lake Kanasatka Watershed, New Hampshire, USA.
presentations.abstract: The University of New Hampshire's Lakes Lay Monitoring Program has tracked Lake Kanasatka's water quality for decades. In 2020, volunteers observed declining clarity and green coloration, signaling worsening conditions. Cyanobacteria blooms persisted annually, peaking in 2023 when blooms lasted 83 continuous days. In response, local and state partners implemented an aluminum sulfate treatment in 2024, with UNH monitoring water quality and plankton throughout. Post-treatment, Kanasatka's Daphnia populations remained small (D. ambigua) and sparse, while Wakondah retained abundant nutrients and larger Daphnia species (D. pulex). A shift in phytoplankton composition from cyanobacteria to diatoms and golden-brown algae dominance was observed in Lake Kanasatka, whereas Wakondah Pond remained cyanobacteria dominant. This coincided with a significant decrease in bioavailable phosphorus following treatment.

presentations.title: Using phytoplankton to understand ecosystem health in the Darling-Baaka River after large fish death events
presentations.abstract: As part of a river health monitoring program, the Darling Baaka River Health Project, phytoplankton and water quality data were examined for the presence of cyanobacterial blooms and general indicators of phytoplankton health metrics between April and December 2024. This is important as the area has been impacted by fish kills in both 2019/20 and in 2023. Based on phytoplankton biovolumes and NHMRC recreational water use guidelines, 4 of the 101 samples reached Red Alert status while 44 reached Amber alert levels. The potentially toxic species Dolichospermum circinale, Raphidiopsis raciborskii, Microcystis flos-aquae, Chrysosporum ovalisporum and Aphanizomenon gracile were present across the study. Various algal and trophic indices indicated poor to very poor conditions through this period.

presentations.title: OYSTER RESTORATION: A MULTI-PRONGED STRATEGY FOR HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOM MITIGATION IN TAMPA BAY, FLORIDA, USA
presentations.affiliation: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
presentations.abstract: Blooms of toxic dinoflagellate Pyrodinium bahamense have degraded environmental health in the Old Tampa Bay (OTB) segment of Tampa Bay, Florida due to their frequent recurrence since 2000. P. bahamense blooms and degraded water quality have been linked to loss in seagrass coverage in the area. These blooms can also produce potent neurotoxins (saxitoxins) that can bioaccumulate in grazers. To investigate whether restoration of filter-feeding bivalves might serve as a multi-pronged strategy for mitigating these toxic blooms, clearance rates and saxitoxin accumulation and depuration rates were examined in the laboratory and in a mesocosm during a bloom in OTB. Using those laboratory derived rates, we developed simulated hypothetical scenarios with varying oyster densities to quantify the potential benefits and limitations associated with bivalve-based HAB control strategy in Tampa Bay. Our results suggest that grazing by bivalves would be most effective as a mitigation tool during the bloom development phase.

name: Eco-Evolutionary Feed-Backs in Limnology and Oceanography
description: Eco-evolutionary dynamics are characterized by feed-backs in which ecological changes (e.g., shifts in temperature, resource availability, or predation pressure) act as selective forces, causing evolutionary changes in population traits.
lead_organizer: Alison Derry, Université du Québec à Montréal
co_organizers: Julien Beaulieu, Université du Québec à Montréal
Annabelle Fortin-Archambault, Université du Québec à Montréal
Jennifer Fisher, Université du Québec à Montréal

presentations.title: The role of morphological plasticity in the ecology and evolution of Acropora cervicornis, a foundational marine species
presentations.abstract: Phenotypic plasticity can buffer populations from environmental change, yet its long-term influence depends on whether there is genetic variation for plasticity and its relationship to selection. My lab has been working to understand the eco-evolutionary role of phenotypic plasticity in the coral Acropora cervicornis by capitalizing on its clonal reproduction in a restoration context. Using field transplants, we showed that intraspecific variation in morphological plasticity is dynamic, with neutral to adaptive fitness effects. We recently confirmed that plasticity arises through a balance of growth rate and fragmentation, the latter of which may be influenced by variation in skeletal deposition. We quantified the relationship between plasticity and thermal tolerance, finding evidence for a trade-off: genets with the greatest morphological plasticity exhibited the highest thermal stress and mortality in response to a subsequent marine heatwave.

presentations.title: ELEMENTAL IMBALANCES ALTER THE ECO-EVOLUTIONARY DYNAMICS OF RANGE EXPANSIONS IN A PROTIST MODEL SYSTEM
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Evolutionary Science of Montpellier
presentations.abstract: Identifying the eco-evolutionary processes driving range expansions is key to understanding and managing aquatic ecosystems as invasive species spread and climate change shifts species' ranges. This study examines how phosphorus limitation (C:P) of the protist Tetrahymena thermophila affects life-history trait evolution during a range expansion and patterns of expansion speed. P-limitation had a strong ecological impact: population growth rate, maximum densities, and expansion speed were higher in HP than LP 'ecology-only' units. In HP-selected populations, selection on dispersal was weak, and core-front trait differences were minimal. In contrast, expansion speed accelerated over time in LP landscapes, and core and front populations showed distinct traits, including a 'resource-efficient' dispersal phenotype (elongated body, directional movement).

presentations.title: RESOLVING NICHE PARTITIONING IN RHIZARIA THROUGH METABARCODING-INFORMED PHYLOGENETIC PLACEMENT
presentations.affiliation: Arizona State University | Bermuda Institute of Ocean Sciences
presentations.abstract: Rhizaria constitute a supergroup of protists that play a critical role in marine nutrient cycling and carbon export. Variations in their feeding and reproductive strategies, vertical distributions, and seasonality among molecular clades reflect historical competition that has shaped distinct niches. DNA metabarcoding was employed to examine interactions among rhizarian clades and hydrographic variables, including depth, season, density, fluorescence, and oxygen, within the upper 1000 meters at the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (BATS) site. The results indicate pronounced vertical and seasonal niche partitioning, ranging from deep clade-level divergences to recent splits and fine-scale differences among closely related taxa. The findings suggest an evolutionary trend favoring more versatile non-constitutive mixotrophs over strict heterotrophs.

presentations.title: The impact of size-selective harvesting on foodweb through the lens of intraspecific variation
presentations.abstract: Eco-evolutionary research showed that population demography and foodweb structure reciprocally shape each other. We conducted a whole ecosystem experiment where ~75% of invasive Brook Trout (S. fontinalis) populations were size-selectively harvested in 5 lakes for three years while also following control (4) and fishless (4). The harvesting treatment reduced by ~64% fish abundance and changed prey communities, but we did not find evidence of feedback on fish life-history traits. When looking at the 20-fold natural variation in fish abundance, we found that lower fish density increases prey density and quality which increased the resource allocation in egg mass production and reduced investment in growth. We also found that neither harvesting nor natural variation in fish density impacted energy pathways in the foodweb, but invasive fish presence shifted the energy pathway from pelagic to benthic secondary production.

presentations.title: A NEW METHOD FOR PARTITIONING THE ECOLOGICAL EFFECTS OF EVOLUTION IN SPECIES INTRODUCTIONS AND RANGE EXPANSIONS
presentations.abstract: Most studies investigating the ecological effects of evolution are mesocosm studies that focus on the ecological consequences of trait variation. In nature the ecological effects of a given species arise from interactions between its traits and its population structure. We derived a new quantitative method that estimates proportional contributions of trait variation, population size structure, and density to changes in ecosystem function across space and time. We illustrate the use of this method using data on nutrient recycling from a fish introduction experiment where traits and demographics change over time. We show that the overall contribution of the introduced fish varies through time, caused primarily by fluctuations in density in early stages of introduction and trait variation in later stages.

presentations.title: Geography, environment, and evolutionary history shape population divergence in African snakehead (Parachanna obscura) fish
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: African freshwater ecosystems are among the most species-rich worldwide, a diversity shaped by the region's complex geography, climatic variability, and topographic heterogeneity, which have repeatedly isolated populations and promoted deep genetic divergence. We investigated population structure, evolutionary history, and speciation processes in Parachanna obscura using whole-genome variation and complete mitochondrial sequences from 127 individuals sampled across 12 river basins in five West African countries. Our results revealed strong population divergence among river basins (FST > 0.15), except among populations from hydrologically connected rivers or geographically proximate systems. Furthermore, our results highlighted the existence of an uncharacterized cryptic species within the Parachanna obscura complex, emphasizing the need for integrative taxonomic reassessment.

name: Emerging Ideas and Technologies Transforming Aquatic Trait-Based Ecology
description: Trait-based ecology has rapidly advanced over the past two decades, driven by a surge of data syntheses and technological breakthroughs in measuring functional traits in aquatic organisms. Emerging tools such as in-situ imaging systems, autonomous acoustic devices, and various -omics methods, are expanding the frontiers of how we observe and quantify traits.
lead_organizer: Sarah Hasnain, Institut de la Mer de Villefranche
co_organizers: Marie-Pier Hebert, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières
Celia Symons, University of California, Irvine
Sierra Cagle, Texas A & M University at Galveston

presentations.title: Advances, challenges and promises of trait-based approaches in aquatic sciences
presentations.abstract: Trait-based approaches have been used successfully in the aquatic realm for the last two decades. Focusing on functional traits provides an elegant way to incorporate biodiversity into our conceptual and mathematical models, which helps elucidate the mechanisms of community assembly and explain species distributions along environmental gradients. Trait-based approaches can be used to solve many other fundamental and applied problems in aquatic sciences, but we need to identify key challenges and best ways to use such approaches. Here I provide examples of how traits can advance our understanding of community and ecosystem resilience and reorganization, predict patterns of carbon sequestration and harmful algal blooms (HABs) now and in the future. I will then discuss what challenges we need to overcome to make trait-based ecology more successful, such as more concerted efforts to identify and measure key traits in diverse taxa and identifying ways to effectively bridge observational, experimental and modeling studies.

presentations.title: DEPTH AND WATER COLUMN MIXING IMPACT MIXOTROPHIC ACTIVITY IN FRESHWATER PHYTOPLANKTON
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton, through photosynthesis, uses CO2 and inorganic nutrients for growth, but under certain conditions, some species consume other living organisms to reach their nutritional needs. Such organisms, called mixotrophs, represent a large proportion of phytoplankton. While widely studied in marine ecosystems, few have investigated their behavior in stratified lakes. We tracked the trophic modes of phytoplankton through July and August at five depths in two differentially stratified lake basins owing to different fetch. To detect bacterial consumption, phagotrophy was identified using Catalyzed Reporter Deposition-Fluorescence in Situ Hybridization (CARD-FISH) allowing observation of ingested bacteria by cells immediately fixed at the moment of sampling. Results showed a greater presence of cells expressing mixotrophy in the epilimnion, especially in the basin where the water column was less exposed to wind.

presentations.title: FIXED ACTION PATTERNS AND SELECTIVE PARTICLE HANDLING IN THE COPEPOD TEMORA TURBINATA
presentations.abstract: Copepods use rapid, coordinated motions of their mouthparts to extract suspended particles from the feeding current they generate. Using high-speed video (500–1000 fps) and a horizontal microscope, we examined how Temora turbinata handles individual algal cells, algal chains, microzooplankton, fecal pellets, microplastics, and other particles moving through the feeding current. Our analyses focused on identifying Fixed Action Patterns (FAPs), innate and stimulus-driven behavioral sequences that structure the complex kinematics of food capture, rejection, and grooming. Frame-by-frame observations revealed distinct FAPs associated with recognizing desirable versus undesirable particles, including behaviors that prevent ingestion of low-quality or harmful items and others that enhance capture of nutritious prey.

presentations.title: What a fish wants: Using life history traits and remote underwater videography to rethink wood-based stream restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand
presentations.abstract: Instream wood is increasingly discussed as both an essential feature of healthy freshwater systems and a valuable tool for fish habitat restoration worldwide. However, current understanding is largely derived from salmonid-dominated systems located in the Global North. Aotearoa New Zealand, a small island archipelago in the South Pacific, is home to a distinct assemblage of cryptic, nocturnal, and disproportionately threatened freshwater fish. Life history trait comparisons show that these species differ markedly from salmonids. This study used remote underwater videography to document native New Zealand fish behaviour in small, forested stream pools containing varying amounts of instream wood. Cameras were deployed overnight in paired wooded and non-wooded habitats to record species presence, activity, and habitat use alongside environmental measurements.

presentations.title: r/K-selected phytoplankton trait gradients in ecosystem models underscore the necessity of trait representation for understanding of ecosystem functioning
presentations.abstract: Amongst the plankton, highly diverse communities of species are common, and the associated variety of form and function amongst these organisms is astounding. Representation of such variation poses a significant challenge to modeling efforts. However, trait-based models offer opportunities to, in-part, overcome this challenge through use of generalized frameworks. Here, we discuss a self-organizing phytoplankton assemblage defined by an r/K-selected trait gradient which has been coupled with ecosystem models of varying complexity. Through further analysis of the bay model, it was shown that in absence of the trait-gradient assemblage (replaced by a single trait-type metapopulation highly optimized to conditions), the model predicted lower total phytoplankton biomass and higher trophic transfer efficiency.

name: Microbial Interactions in Aquatic Environments: Mechanisms, Impact, and Future Directions
description: Microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, archaea, fungi, microalgae, and protists, are central components of aquatic ecosystems. Their interactions with each other and with their environment drive critical ecological processes, such as nutrient cycling, organic matter decomposition, and energy flow.
lead_organizer: Shira Ninio, Israel Oceanographic & Limnological Research

presentations.title: Putting parasites into PEG: advancing our understanding of parasitism and disease in the seasonal succession of lake freshwater plankton
presentations.abstract: Since its conception in 1986, the Plankton Ecology Group (PEG) model for lake seasonal succession has offered a classic heuristic for the dynamics freshwater plankton undergo as they respond to abiotic changes and biotic interactions over the annual cycle. Notably, the PEG model provides a baseline for how planktonic communities operate in freshwater lakes. Capitalizing on recent growth in aquatic disease research, we aim to advance our understanding of parasitism in the PEG model. Our international collaboration is focused on two core questions: (1) How do parasites respond to seasonal changes in the lake environment and host populations? (2) To what extent does parasitism contribute to seasonal shifts in plankton communities, interactions, and ecosystem processes? Using a targeted literature synthesis and systematic map of the literature, we are characterizing the landscape of knowledge on freshwater plankton disease.

presentations.title: Marine fungi and the 'bypass theory': A new perspective on P transfer in oligotrophic oceans
presentations.abstract: The seminal CYCLOPS experiment in the early 2000s revealed unexpected ecosystem responses to PO43+ enrichment in an oligotrophic sea, including a decline in chlorophyll.a while an increase in copepods egg production occurred. These observations were interpreted by alternative P-flow that circumvent traditional phytoplankton-based food-web ('bypass theory'). We integrated the role of pelagic fungi in the phosphorus-cycling and trophic dynamics in the ultra-oligotrophic Eastern Mediterranean Sea. Results show that fungi are ubiquitous and contribute significantly to microbial biomass. PO43+ enrichment led to increased fungal abundance, while chlorophyll.a remained unchanged. These findings suggest additional phytoplankton-based pathway not considered in the CYCLOPS campaign, where fungi infect phytoplankton and transfer P-rich zoospores to zooplankton.

presentations.title: Anthropogenic and Natural Factors impacting Microbiological and Physicochemical Surface Water Quality along an urban tropical wetland
presentations.affiliation: BOKU UNIVERSITY, Department of Ecosystem Management, Climate and Biodiversity, Institute of Hydrobiology and Aquatic Ecosystem Management
presentations.abstract: Monitoring microbial water quality is essential for understanding pollution dynamics and their implications for public health, especially in developing countries where waterborne diseases remain widespread. This study assessed seasonal variations in microbiological indicators along the Lubigi wetland, a riverine tropical system receiving stormwater and wastewater from Kampala's urban infrastructure. For 17 months, water samples were collected from six sites during dry and wet seasons and analyzed for Escherichia coli, faecal coliforms, heterotrophic plate counts (HPC), Enterococcus, and Salmonella species. Results showed that nitrogen compounds, E. coli, faecal coliforms, Enterococcus, and Salmonella were predominantly associated with stormwater runoff, while phosphorus, organic matter, and HPC were linked to wastewater effluent.

presentations.title: BEYOND CO-OCCURRENCE: UNCOVERING CHAOTIC NETWORK DYNAMICS FROM ENVIRONMENTAL DNA TIME-SERIES
presentations.abstract: Ecological interactions are key to understanding how communities assemble, yet they remain difficult to untangle and are often assessed in compartmentalized groups (e.g., zooplankton, phytoplankton), masking integrated interaction patterns that emerge only at the full cross kingdom scale. In this study, we reconstructed monthly ecological networks from a five-year time series collected in a tropical reservoir. We applied Empirical Dynamic Modelling to metabarcoding data to infer time-varying cross-kingdom associations spanning decomposers (bacteria), primary producers (cyanobacteria and eukaryotic microalgae), and grazers/predators (protists and zooplankton). This nonlinear, state-dependent approach enabled the quantification of both community composition and network structure change over time, linked to wet-dry cycles and interannual climate anomalies such as El Niño and La Niña.

presentations.title: Exploring the unseen: chytrid fungi in Arctic and Antarctic microphytobenthic communities
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Inst. for Freshwater Ecol. & Inland Fish.
presentations.abstract: Fungal parasites have been recognized as critical and abundant components of every ecosystem. They have the potential to regulate host populations, mediate interspecific competition between hosts and other species, and thus affect biodiversity and food web structure. However, parasite diversity is still poorly known, particularly for fungal parasites in aquatic ecosystems. A few recent studies in polar regions indicate that parasitic species, in particular of the early fungal lineages, are highly abundant in both Antarctic and Arctic aquatic ecosystems. We show that fungal parasitic taxa are present in these habitats in high abundances, whereby their correlations with benthic diatoms indicate potential parasitic interactions. Moreover, we show that temperature and salinity are major drivers of fungal diversity, community composition, and interactions with potential hosts.

name: Science at the Source: Mountain Lakes as Natural Laboratories for Understanding Global Change
description: Mountain lakes sit at the high-elevation confluence of the atmosphere, cryosphere, and hydrosphere, where environmental change can be rapid. Much of the change is driven by elevation-dependent warming, thawing glaciers, orographically enhanced precipitation, and increased atmospheric deposition of acids, metals, contaminants, and nutrients.
lead_organizer: Steven Sadro, University of California, Davis
co_organizers: Isabella Oleksy, University of Colorado Boulder
Katrina Eyvindson, University of Western Ontario
Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada, Reno

presentations.title: GLOBAL CHANGE IMPACTS ON A MOUNTAIN WATERSHED: AN INVESTIGATION OF 40 YEARS OF BIOGEOCHEMICAL PATTERNS IN LAKES AND THEIR OUTFLOWS
presentations.abstract: Global change factors such as warming, weathering, and atmospheric deposition can reshape nutrient and biogeochemical pathways to and processes within aquatic ecosystems. Mountain aquatic systems respond rapidly to environmental changes and integrate signals from their surrounding catchments and airsheds, making them particularly sensitive to the effects of global change. Long-term monitoring and research conducted in the Loch Vale watershed in Rocky Mountain National Park since 1983 has revealed changes in long-term water chemistry and primary producer assemblages in response to global change. In 2013 we used a mass balance approach to explore trends in water chemistry to find that weathering product concentrations and fluxes were significantly correlated with summer air temperatures. Here, we revisit this conclusion with an additional 10 years of data, comparison with upstream and nearby lake biogeochemical patterns, and new multivariate modeling to update our evaluation of patterns and drivers of biogeochemistry.

presentations.title: PREDICTING NITRATE LEACHING FROM ALPINE AREAS
presentations.abstract: We investigated the effects of changes in atmospheric deposition of inorganic nitrogen (IN = NO3 + NH4) and climate change on NO3 leaching from N-saturated alpine catchments in the Tatra Mountains, Central Europe. Our long-term data provided a unique opportunity to assess and model the impacts of the sharp increase in IN deposition between the 1930s and 1980s, its largest global decline since the 1990s, and the recently accelerating warming on lake water NO3 concentrations from 1937 to 2024. The results show progressive N saturation and NO3 leaching with increasing IN deposition until the late 1980s. Subsequently, NO3 leaching decreased, but at a slower rate than IN deposition in the 1990s–2000s, and finally declined more steeply than IN deposition in the last two decades, probably due to increasing air temperature. The empirical model, including catchment characteristics, IN deposition and air temperature, explained 81% of the spatial and temporal variability of NO3 concentrations in all types of alpine Tatra lakes over almost a century.

presentations.title: ATMOSPHERIC AMMONIUM DOMINATES NITROGEN INPUTS TO ALPINE LAKES IN THE FRENCH ALPS
presentations.abstract: Alpine lakes are highly sensitive to shifts in nitrogen (N) inputs under accelerating global change. Atmospheric nitrate deposition in mountain regions has declined, reflecting a shift in anthropogenic N emissions from nitrous oxides (NOx) towards ammonia gaining prominence. Consequently, atmospheric ammonium deposition has been increasing in alpine lakes. We investigated N sources in 26 mountain lakes in the French Alps in September 2023, using stable isotopes of nitrate (d¹⁵N, d¹⁸O, D¹⁷O). We find that atmospheric nitrate deposition accounts for ~0–30 % of lake DIN pool and is inversely correlated with watershed vegetation coverage. Using the Bayesian mixing model MixSIAR we identified atmospheric ammonium as the main substrate for in situ nitrification in the studied sites. When added together, we find that atmospheric nitrate and ammonium contribute more than half of the DIN pool for 25 of the 26 studied lakes.

presentations.title: Tracing the sources of phosphorous in alpine lakes
presentations.abstract: Alpine lakes are increasingly impacted by global environmental changes. Specifically, changing essential nutrient (nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P)) inputs are of significant concern for the functioning of these oligotrophic ecosystems. Recent studies have shown that atmospheric transport of P can be an important mechanism for nutrient delivery to lake ecosystems and can lead to increasing N limitation of phytoplankton growth. Eight lakes in the French Alps were selected along a gradient of anthropogenic and environmental pressures. Sediment samples were taken in spring to trace the origin and fate of P in the lakes using oxygen isotopic ratios of phosphate (18Op). Measured d18Op significantly differed from the theoretical equilibrium d18Op values, indicating low recycling of P by the biota and suggesting that the isotopic variability of the source materials is probably preserved. Low internal recycling of phosphorus means that external local or regional P inputs can have a stronger influence on the lake's trophic status.

presentations.title: Aquatic biodiversity responses to Late Holocene climate change in subarctic lakes.
presentations.presenter: María de los Ángeles González Sagrario
presentations.affiliation: CONICET, National Council of Science and Technology of Argentina
presentations.abstract: Subarctic lakes are key sentinels of climate change, responding directly to temperature shifts and indirectly to climate-driven vegetation changes that alter their physical, chemical, and biological properties. Yet the relative influence of these drivers on aquatic invertebrates remains poorly resolved. Using a multiproxy paleolimnological approach, we analyzed a ~5700-year sediment record from a subarctic lake to assess how aquatic biodiversity responds to long-term cooling, shifting precipitation regimes, and associated vegetation changes. Chironomids were used as indicators of benthic diversity, whereas cladocerans of pelagic and littoral biodiversity. Both groups showed major compositional shifts from specialist or warm-temperate to generalist or intermediate-temperature taxa as the climate cooled from the Holocene Thermal Maximum to the Late Holocene.

presentations.title: ASSESSING SPATIOTEMPORAL PATTERNS OF WATER QUALITY IN YELLOWSTONE LAKE IN RELATION TO INVASIVE LAKE TROUT SUPPRESSION
presentations.abstract: The spread of invasive fish is a pressing issue that alters ecosystem processes in lakes. Managers often implement programs to suppress invasive fish, but the effects of these programs on water quality are rarely studied. Yellowstone Lake presents an opportunity to study how a large-scale program to suppress invasive Lake Trout (Salvelinus namaycush) alters water quality. Nearly 300,000 Lake Trout have been dispatched annually and returned to the depths of Yellowstone Lake since 2012, potentially altering nutrient cycling through carcass decomposition. We compiled historical data on water quality in Yellowstone Lake (1954-2022), measured current conditions (2023-2025), and used generalized mixed effects models to assess variation. Many water quality parameters (e.g., Secchi depth, chlorophyll a) differed after the Lake Trout introduction. Currently, nitrogen and chlorophyll a vary seasonally, with high concentrations after ice-off.

name: Bridging the Gap in Macrophyte Research Across Realms: From Ecological Concepts to Nature-Based Solutions in Marine and Fresh Waters
description: Macrophytes in freshwater and marine realms are foundation species that control a wide range of key ecosystem processes, functions and services. They form habitat for many organisms and provide key benefits, i.e., supporting biodiversity, retaining nutrients, increasing sedimentation, stabilizing sediments, sequestering carbon, regulating greenhouse gas emissions.
lead_organizer: Morgan Botrel, Université du Québec à Rimouski, Groupe de recherche interuniversitaire en limnologie (GRIL)
co_organizers: Fanny Noisette, Université du Québec à Rimouski
Christian Nozais, Université du Québec à Rimouski
Sabine Hilt, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries

presentations.title: Aquatic macrophytes as Nature-based Solutions: Challenges and opportunities across inland and marine waters
presentations.affiliation: Université du Québec à Rimouski, Groupe de recherche interuniversitaire en limnologie (GRIL)
presentations.abstract: Nature-based Solution (NbS) is growing in popularity as a path forward to address the twin crises of climate change and biodiversity loss. NbS involve working with nature to solve societal challenges that co-benefit humans and biodiversity. Macrophytes have been recognized as NbS, however the discrepancy between study and application of macrophytes as NbS across inland and coastal ecosystems represents an opportunity to learn from different scientific approaches. Here, we report on a recent initiative bringing together macrophyte specialists across marine and inland water ecosystems to: 1) evaluate and compare current knowledge on macrophytes as NbS across realms; 2) identify knowledge gaps and advances in their use as NbS; and, 3) synthesize challenges and opportunities for application across realms. Our literature synthesis revealed that most papers on macrophytes as NbS are marine-focussed, with emphasis on climate change mitigation and adaptation. Conversely, the literature on macrophytes as NbS in inland waters focuses on biodiversity and eutrophication mitigation.

presentations.title: UNTANGLING THE EFFECTS OF LIGHT AND NUTRIENT AVAILABILITY ON EELGRASS PHOTOPHYSIOLOGY
presentations.abstract: Light and nutrients, two major limiting factors for aquatic primary producers, have rarely been examined jointly in cold-temperate seagrass meadows, where short growing seasons largely determine long-term persistence. We investigated how ecologically realistic variations in these tightly coupled factors shape the photophysiology of eelgrass (Zostera marina), a widely distributed foundation species. In August 2024, we collected 48 eelgrass cores from Rimouski Bay (QC, Canada) and acclimated them for 7 days in a flow-through seawater system.
