Shoots displayed a marked shift in photophysiological responses near the species' reported photosynthetic saturation point (~200 µmol photons m-2 s-1). Below this point, shoots adjusted to optimize light capture, while exposure to above-saturating irradiance triggered photoprotection. Nutrient enrichment had minimal effect on eelgrass photophysiology.

presentations.title: THE INFLUENCE OF HETEROGENEITY OF VEGETATION ON THE EFFICACY OF NATURE-BASED SOLUTIONS: INSIGHTS FROM THE COASTAL DOMAIN
presentations.abstract: The presence of aquatic vegetation influences hydrodynamic conditions by altering turbulence generation, energy dissipation, and sediment transport and deposition. These flow-vegetation interactions have led to the use of some species being promoted as a nature-based solution to reduce coastal or riverbank erosion, and mitigate the effects of flooding in both freshwater and coastal environments. We present high-resolution field measurements of velocity and turbulence within a sparse canopy of Avicennia marina mangrove roots and trees, characterized by multiple vegetation length scales. We compare measurements of turbulent kinetic energy, a key predictor of sediment motion, to predictions from laboratory-derived models. Crucially, the model only worked well if predictions considered and parameterized appropriately the existence of multiple vegetation length scales.

presentations.title: Spatial and temporal trends of floating canopy kelp forests in British Columbia
presentations.abstract: Canopy-forming kelp forests are foundational ecosystems along the British Columbia coastline, yet their trends used to be poorly understood. The 2014-2016 North Pacific Ocean marine heatwave highlighted the need to study the patterns of kelp persistence and resilience at the local level. In this talk, we will present the data and results from an extensive floating canopy kelp forest mapping project in British Columbia, using remote sensing techniques. Here, we will summarize emerging patterns at different geographical subregions (Salish Sea, Broughton Archipelago, Western Vancouver Island, Haida Gwaii). In general, we observe that sheltered and low-energy coastlines concentrate warmer sea surface temperatures that can be detrimental to kelp. In contrast, cold waters combined with high currents and exposure are the best conditions for kelp to thrive.

presentations.title: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF MANAGEMENT EFFECTIVENESS OF INVASIVE AQUATIC PLANTS IN CANADA
presentations.abstract: Invasive aquatic plants can have major adverse ecological effects on the systems to which they are introduced. In Canada, invasive aquatic plant management is an essential component of protecting and restoring marine and freshwater systems; once these species are established, they can be difficult to eradicate or control. To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive systematic review to identify plant responses to different management techniques to determine technique effectiveness. Following Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE) guidelines, we identify and describe the available evidence for over 20 species of invasive plants from over 600 papers. We found gaps in the available evidence for several species (e.g., for Trapa natans and Hydrocharis morsus-ranae), and clusters of evidence that allow for further assessment of effectiveness (e.g., for chemical and non-chemical treatments of Phragmites australis or Myriophyllum spicatum).

name: Macrophyte Communities and Ecosystem Functioning in a Changing Freshwater World
description: Freshwater macrophytes—rooted and free-floating vascular plants inhabiting lakes, rivers, wetlands, and streams—play a foundational role in ecosystem functioning. They regulate nutrient cycles, stabilize sediments, structure food webs, and support biodiversity.
lead_organizer: Lars Iversen, McGill University
co_organizers: Alice Dalla Vecchia, University of Parma

presentations.title: QUANTIFYING THE ROLE OF MACROPHYTE LIFE FORMS FOR CARBON SEQUESTRATION IN CONSTRUCTED WETLANDS
presentations.abstract: Macrophyte communities perform an important function in the carbon cycle of inland waters by sequestering carbon in the sediment, but carbon sequestration as an ecosystem service of macrophyte communities is poorly understood. We measured organic carbon sequestration in the sediments of three constructed wetlands, one supplied by stormwater, one by agricultural run-off, and one by treated wastewater. Using a piston corer we specifically developed for dense macrophyte stands, we took 183 sediment cores from the three sites, which were taken along 40 transects covering all types of macrophyte life forms and site morphologies. The data indicate that emergent macrophytes may contribute more to carbon sequestration than submerged or free-floating macrophytes, highlighting the roles of productivity and leaf litter recalcitrance in carbon sequestration efficiency. However, high spatial heterogeneity and superimposed morphological properties (e.g. water depth, flow paths) affirm the need to conduct highly resolved sampling.

presentations.title: Respiration is increased by macrophyte structural complexity and epiphytic interactions in stream benthic communities
presentations.affiliation: Instituto de Ecología y Desarrollo Sustentable (INEDES; CONICET-UNLu)
presentations.abstract: Complexity of macrophyte architecture could influence metabolic reactivity in streams due to an effective streambed occupation of the macrophyte-epiphyton ensembles, which promotes a more efficient use of solute resources. Here, we assessed the influence of the macrophyte complexity and macrophyte-epiphytic interaction on the community-level respiration in a microcosm experiment. We compared the respiration of two macrophyte species with higher (Elodea ernstae) and lower (Stuckenia striata) architectural complexity. Respiratory activity was consistently higher in the species with more complex structure (E. ernstae) than in those with less complex structure (S. striata). In addition, the presence of epiphyton on macrophytes significantly increased the respiratory activity of E. ernstae, but not of S. striata.

presentations.title: Realm-specific adaptations undermine terrestrial predictions of leaf economics in freshwater plant communities
presentations.abstract: The leaf economic spectrum bridges plant demography with terrestrial biodiversity gradients, community ecology, and ecosystem functions, providing a framework for the mechanisms underlying ecosystem change. However, it is unclear whether this framework applies to aquatic plant communities. Here, we show that leaf phenotypes in freshwater plant communities are a product of unique selection from both general and realm-specific trait-environment relationships. Across 6953 European lake and river communities, high bicarbonate and phosphorus concentrations, and warm temperatures select for acquisitive leaf traits in emergent plant communities, aligning with terrestrial predictions. Conversely, acquisitive submerged plant communities are favoured by high bicarbonate and low temperature, independent of phosphorus.

presentations.title: Constancy of macrophyte assemblage and abundance in 3 protected Adirondack lakes over 8 decades – implications for management of local and regional stressors
presentations.abstract: Macrophytes are important primary producers and defining structural organisms in littoral zones. Species composition, diversity and biomass of macrophytes in temperate zone lakes have been altered by anthropogenic perturbations, including nutrient loading increases, sediment runoff, road salt, acidification and introduction of non-native macrophyte species. The Huntington Wildlife Forest (HWF), a 6,000 hectare research field station within the Adirondack Park, has been managed by the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry for almost 100 years. We repeated 1940 surveys 80 years later. The protected lakes had nearly identical species composition and relative abundance as in the historical surveys, suggesting resilience of macrophyte assemblages to climate change and acid deposition, but susceptibility to invasive species.

presentations.title: Revegetation of littoral zones in snowmaking reservoirs: field assessment of aquatic plant establishment and biodiversity responses
presentations.abstract: Alpine freshwater ecosystems are biodiversity hotspots providing key ecosystem services but face threats from climate change and human activities. Snowmaking reservoirs have rapidly expanded in alpine regions in response to declining snow cover and growing winter tourism. This study experimentally assessed the feasibility of littoral revegetation using coir macrophyte rolls as a Nature-based Solution in a high-elevation snowmaking reservoir in the French Alps. Four native plant species were introduced and monitored over two years. Helophytes showed high survival (>97%), clonal expansion, and flowering, while hydrophytes initially grew but their longer-term persistence appears difficult under the specific management regime of the reservoir.

presentations.title: Continental-wide functional responses of a native and an invasive macrophyte to local environmental conditions
presentations.abstract: Freshwater biodiversity and ecosystem functioning are threatened by invasive macrophytes, which degrade habitat structure and disrupt key ecological processes. Here, we present the first results from the project 'Predicting DIVErsity of INvasive aquatic plants', which investigates the mechanisms driving invasion performance in aquatic plants. We sampled 53 populations of the invasive Elodea nuttallii and 55 populations of the native Trapa natans (with invasive potential) across broad geographic and environmental gradients in Europe. For each population, we quantified leaf traits related to resource-use strategies and measured water and sediment variables. Using multivariate models, we describe trait-environment relationships, highlighting which conditions trigger a more performative response for these species.

name: Wildfires and Aquatic Systems: Implications for Hydrology, Biogeochemistry, and Ecosystem Resilience
description: Aquatic ecosystems are increasingly vulnerable to wildfires, driven by the burning of watersheds, deposition of ash, and the shading effects of smoke. As the size, frequency, and intensity of wildfires continue to rise globally, understanding their impacts on aquatic ecosystems remains an emerging area of research.
lead_organizer: Facundo Scordo, University of Nevada, Reno; INIBIOMA-CONICET
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada, Reno
Adrianne Smits, University of California Davis
Mary Jade Farruggia, University of Colorado Boulder
Steve Sadro, University of California Davis

presentations.title: From Burned Watersheds to Smoke Exposure: Long-Term Wildfire Impacts on North American Lakes
presentations.affiliation: Instituto de Investigaciones en Biodiversidad y Medioambiente (INIBIOMA CONICET-UNCo) - University of Nevada, Reno
presentations.abstract: We evaluated how wildfires influence 984,406 lakes in Canada and the United States through three pathways: direct watershed burning, smoke exposure, and atmospheric deposition of wildfire emissions. Our analysis of long-term burned area trends (1984–2024) shows a strong, significant increase (slope = +1,188 km² yr⁻¹, p < 0.01). Yet the number of lakes whose watersheds burned exhibits no significant trend (p = 0.20). However, the expanding burned area has a much clearer signal when viewed through smoke exposure: lakes experiencing >20 smoke days per year (2010–2024) show a strong, significant increase (slope = +38,934 lakes yr⁻¹, p < 0.01). Together, our findings show that wildfire emissions (especially smoke) create broader and more regularly increasing pressures on lakes than direct watershed burning.

presentations.title: Impacts of wildfire smoke on thermal regimes of Western US rivers
presentations.abstract: Wildfire frequency and intensity are increasing globally with climate change, generating extensive smoke plumes that expose entire regions to smoke. Local-scale studies indicate that wildfire smoke can cool rivers by reducing incoming shortwave radiation, but we lack regional-scale synthesis studies that relate large-scale patterns of wildfire smoke exposure to river temperatures. Analyzing ≈2000 river-years from >110 sites with long-term (2005-2022) nearly continuous water temperature data alongside satellite-derived metrics of wildfire smoke exposure, we show 1) the highest exposure of river sites to wildfire smoke in northern California and southern Oregon; 2) significant reduction in surface shortwave radiation fluxes at high smoke densities; 3) increasing smoke exposure was associated with small but significant reductions in river temperature; and 4) increases in smoke exposure are associated with advances in the day-of-year of maximum river temperature.

presentations.title: Why do lakes and rivers C pools respond so differently to wildfires across studies?
presentations.abstract: There is an apparent lack of consensus on the impact of wildfires on aquatic carbon (C), which limits our capacity to predict future trends in aquatic C cycling as wildfires become more frequent and widespread worldwide. We aim to understand the main drivers of contrasting C responses within lakes and rivers affected by wildfires. First, we found that barely half of wildfire-impact studies on aquatic systems included at least one C form, with dissolved organic carbon (DOC) being the most frequent. The response of lakes to wildfires appeared to vary depending on SOC, with DOC tending to increase in burned landscapes containing beyond 80 tons ha-1 SOC and to decrease when SOC <70 tons ha-1. However, there was no such relationship for streams.

presentations.title: Long-lasting water-quality shifts following forest fires in boreal lakes
presentations.abstract: Forest fires are a key natural disturbance in the boreal biome, and their frequency and severity are expected to increase with climate change. We used a paleolimnological approach to assess the multi-decadal effects of forest fires on dissolved organic carbon (DOC) dynamics and aquatic primary production in five lakes of northwestern Quebec. Sediment spectroscopy was used to track post-fire changes in DOC and sedimentary chlorophyll-a (Chl-a). Our results show marked shifts following major fires, including increases in Chl-a (+10–20%) and DOC (+5–15%), with altered conditions persisting ~40–80 years. However, post-fire responses varied among lakes, indicating strong watershed-specific controls on sensitivity to disturbance.

presentations.title: WILDFIRE SHIFTS IN WATER QUALITY SUSTAINED FOR THREE YEARS POST-FIRE IN NORTHERN MINNESOTA INLAND LAKES
presentations.abstract: Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity across many regions and therefore have the potential to alter environmental conditions within freshwater lakes. Few studies have focused on water quality changes in inland lakes following fire exposure. This study examined 30 inland lakes (15 control and 15 burned) in northern Minnesota between 2022 and 2025. We found that (1) Lakes receiving runoff from burned catchments had higher concentrations of total phosphorus (TP), total nitrogen (TN), total suspended solids (TSS), and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and decreased Secchi depths in both years when compared to the control lakes; (2) TP, TN, and DOC concentrations all decreased from 2022 to 2025, while water temperature and acid neutralizing capacity (ANC) increased.

presentations.title: TRACKING WILDFIRE-DERIVED CARBON AND IRON DEPOSITION IN COASTAL WATERS USING RAMAN MICROSCOPY
presentations.abstract: In June 2023, New York City and surrounding areas experienced severe air quality deterioration as smoke from one of Canada's most intense wildfire seasons reached the U.S. East Coast. Using Raman microspectroscopy, we quantified BC, iron oxide, and other particles in surface water samples collected from the Western and Great South Bays (Long Island, NY) during and after the arrival of wildfire smoke. BC concentrations peaked on June 8 (2.01×10⁶ ± 0.95×10⁶ part L⁻¹). Iron oxide was detected in all samples and follow the same pattern as BC particles with concentration peaks on June 8 (4.88×10⁶ ± 2.66×10⁶ part L⁻¹) and June 15 (6.91×10⁶ ± 3.57×10⁶ part L⁻¹). The results indicate approximately a one-day lag between atmospheric smoke arrival and deposition of BC and iron oxide particles into coastal waters.

name: Assessing the Ecological Footprint of Hydropower: Greenhouse Gases, Mercury, Water Quality, Aquatic Life and Energy Balance
description: Hydroelectricity is a renewable energy source that plays a central role in the global transition toward a low-carbon energy economy. Hydroelectric facilities can alter the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of aquatic environments. Their environmental footprints must be considered and require a comprehensive, multidisciplinary evaluation.
lead_organizer: François Bilodeau, Hydro-Quebec
co_organizers: Thibaud André-Alphonse, Université du Québec en Outaouais

presentations.title: METHYLMERCURY GENERATION AND DOWNRIVER TRANSPORT FROM A NEW RESERVOIR: COMPARISON TO PRE-FLOOD MODELS USING INTENSIVE LONG-TERM SAMPLING
presentations.abstract: Increases in methylmercury concentrations in newly formed reservoirs is a known global occurrence. As part of a new hydroelectric development, pre-flood models were developed using reservoir characteristics and baseline conditions to predict the effects of flooding on methylmercury concentrations including downstream transport. An intensive weekly water sampling program was developed to monitor changes in methylmercury concentrations within the reservoir, downstream in the river, and the large downriver estuary fiord; a total river distance of over 250 kilometres. The results from the first five years after flooding indicate close agreement with predicted concentrations from both riverine and estuary models.

presentations.title: MERCURY AND CARBON CYCLING AFFECTED BY A RUN-OF-RIVER HYDROPOWER PLANT DEVELOPMENT IN A PERMAFROST-RICH SUBARCTIC CANADIAN REGION
presentations.abstract: A first run-of-river (ROR) power plant built in Nunavik (QC, Canada) lies in a continuous permafrost zone, a substantial carbon (C) rich mercury (Hg) reservoir. Three months after river impoundment, MeHg concentrations and proportions in the surface organic layer of flooded soils were seven and four times higher, respectively. A similar increase was observed in surface waters of the newly created bay, where MeHg concentration and proportion were ∼10 and four times higher. Biological MeHg concentrations increased in low trophic level organisms associated with this flooded environment. However, these rises were limited to the small (<1 km2) newly created bay.

presentations.title: Hydroelectricity and Mercury in Quebec, Canada: Fish Consumption and the Evolution of Communication Strategies
presentations.abstract: The creation of hydroelectric reservoirs is known to temporarily increase mercury levels in fish. As part of its environmental monitoring program, Hydro-Québec implements a tailored risk management strategy to address this issue. Data indicate that mercury exposure in concerned communities remains generally low, enabling the development of fish consumption guidelines that highlight the nutritional and cultural benefits of this resource.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF RUN-OF-RIVER DAMS ON MULTITROPHIC AQUATIC BIODIVERSITY: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
presentations.abstract: Hydropower is portrayed as a clean and sustainable energy source. However, its ecological effects remain incompletely understood—particularly for run-of-river (RoR) dams. Using the ROSES protocol for systematic evidence synthesis, 899 peer-reviewed articles were screened, and 127 studies were retained. Results reveal a clear research bias toward fish and macroinvertebrate assemblages, with reported impacts including reduced habitat connectivity, decreased fish diversity and abundance, and shifts in functional traits toward more tolerant taxa.

presentations.title: Influence of drawdown intensity on aquatic food web structure across multiple freshwater ecosystem
presentations.affiliation: Institut des Sciences de la Forêt Tempérée - Université du Québec en Outaouais (ISFORT - UQO)
presentations.abstract: Dams alter riverine systems worldwide. We evaluated the changes in the trophic structure of aquatic food webs of 11 water bodies located in Eastern Canada impacted by multiple drawdown intensities. Using stable isotopes, we looked at the overall structure of the food web. We found that drawdown had a limited influence on isotopic niche. At community level, the overall structure of the food web was not influenced by drawdown intensity. At species level, medium intensity drawdown negatively affected the trophic position and the degree of benthic-pelagic coupling of species.

presentations.title: Transient dynamics of ecological and biogeochemical variables following impoundment in large boreal reservoirs
presentations.abstract: By using unique long-term time series (40 years of data) from Hydro-Québec boreal reservoirs, we examined the transient dynamics following impoundment. Following impoundment, most variables increased, peaked, and then decreased over time. Model predictions peaked between three- and 11-years post-impoundment and returned to pre-impoundment levels after about nine- to 40-years. Variables also followed a clear sequence in which GHG emissions (CO2, CH4) peaked first, immediately after impoundment, followed by increases in phosphorus and Chl-a. Total mercury in fish peaked a few years later.

name: Novel Stable Isotope Approaches to Solving Big and Small Questions in the Aquatic Sciences
description: The application of compound-specific isotope analysis (CSIA) of organic compounds has seen significant growth over the past three decades. CSIA is increasingly being used in the aquatic and environmental sciences to answer questions at the individual, community, food web, ecosystem, watershed, and basin scales.
lead_organizer: Kyra St Pierre, University of Ottawa
co_organizers: Jessica Garzke, University of British Columbia

presentations.title: AMINO ACID CARBON AND NITROGEN STABLE ISOTOPES DIFFERENTIATE LITTORAL AND PELAGIC FOOD WEB PATHWAYS
presentations.abstract: Analysis of amino acid-specific carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes are providing new insights into aquatic food web linkages. Here we present amino acid-specific carbon and nitrogen stable isotope measurements for littoral, pelagic, and profundal invertebrates from Lake Geneva (CH-FR). Essential amino acid d13C values revealed distinct energy channels for littoral and pelagic/profundal habitats. Using amino acid d15N, littoral invertebrates exhibited anomalously low trophic position values when using standard trophic fractionation assumptions. Our results indicate a low nitrogen trophic discrimination factor (TDF) for littoral consumers, suggesting low deamination flux. These patterns suggest low use of protein as an energy source in the littoral zone compared to pelagic/profundal habitats.

presentations.title: A NOVEL APPROACH USING CSIA FOR TRACING AMMONIA DYNAMICS IN AQUATIC ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Ammonia (NH₃/NH₄⁺) acts as a central form between organic matter degradation, nitrification, and primary production. Although stable nitrogen isotope analysis provides a useful tool for quantifying them, the δ¹⁵N measurement of NH₃/NH₄⁺ remains technically challenging. In this study, we developed a simple and rapid method for measuring the δ¹⁵N values of NH₃/NH₄⁺ in aqueous samples. This method uses isopropyl chloroformate as an acylating reagent to convert NH₃ to an isopropoxycarbonyl-NH₂ derivative in a one-step reaction at room temperature. The δ¹⁵N values can be measured with a standard deviation of 0.3–0.9‰.

presentations.title: NEW APPROACHES FOR MEASURING ISOTOPIC RATIOS OF NON-EXCHANGEABLE HYDROGEN IN ORGANIC MATTER
presentations.abstract: Non-exchangeable hydrogen isotope ratios (δ²Hn) in organic matter (OM) are increasingly used in ecological and biogeochemical studies. We present a simple offline preparation system ('Isobox') and a paired-equilibration protocol designed for δ²H IRMS measurements. The approach combines low-temperature water equilibration, rapid freezing, sublimation, and final dry-gas/oven treatment, and is tested on reference materials spanning proteins, amino acids, small organics, and polymers. To quantify fex independently, we also introduce a complementary liquid-state NMR method based on proton-exchange experiments. Early results suggest that Isobox-IRMS and NMR derived fex values are mutually consistent.

presentations.title: A compound‑specific method for measuring the stable carbon isotopic composition of amino acids: elimination of the effect of isotopic fractionation during derivatization
presentations.abstract: Compound-specific isotope analysis (CSIA) of amino acids has been employed as a powerful tool for estimating the trophic tendency and resource utilization of organisms in food webs. However, the polar functional groups of amino acids should be neutralized by derivatization before the isotope analysis. In the present study, we developed a new derivatization method to minimize these issues, which can reduce the isotopic fractionation in 13C/12C by following two sequential reactions for the acylation: the first is acylation, which introduces isotopic fractionation, and the second is replacement of the pivaloyl group with that of pivalic anhydride.

presentations.title: Diet nutrition shifts carbon isotope ratios of glucose: resource allocation between sugars and amino acids in organisms
presentations.abstract: Stable isotope analysis of individual amino acids has been used to identify the fate of organic matter in the trophic transfer and the resource use of organisms. Glucose is metabolically connected with major amino acids via biosynthesis and metabolic loading in consumer species. Here, we suggest experimental and analytical procedure of isotope analysis of monosaccharides (sugars), including glucose, reducing the artificial isotopic fractionation during derivatization. Furthermore, we present several results on carbon isotope ratios of monosaccharides from both controlled-feeding experiments and natural samples.

presentations.title: REVERSIBLE METABOLIC SWITCHING BETWEEN FATTY ACIDS AND AMINO ACIDS DEPENDING ON DEVELOPMENTAL STAGES IN A JELLFISH
presentations.abstract: Jellyfish undergo drastic morphological and physiological changes across their life cycle. A previous study has reported that moon jellyfish, Aurelia aurita polyp uses fatty acids (FAs) as the main energy source to minimize the excretion of nitrogenous waste (NH3) under overpopulation. Controlled feeding experiments were conducted for all stages of A. aurita, and isotopic discrimination of amino acids (AAs) and FAs was analyzed by CSIA. As results, FAs consumption predominated in the polyp and medusa stages, whereas AAs consumption increased during the strobila to ephyra stage. These findings indicate a reversible metabolic switching between FAs and AAs consumption in jellyfish.

name: Submarine and Lacustrine Groundwater Discharge (SGD and LGD): What Can We Learn from the Other?
description: Groundwater plays a critical role in the hydrology, biogeochemistry, and ecology of surface waters. The aim of this session is to bridge the gap between the scientific communities dealing with submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) and lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD).
lead_organizer: Jörg Lewandowski, Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries

presentations.title: SUBMARINE AND LACUSTRINE GROUNDWATER DISCHARGE – SIMILARITIES, DIFFERENCES, AND HOW QUANTIFYING TEMPORAL VARIABILITY CAN IMPROVE OUR UNDERSTANDING
presentations.abstract: Groundwater discharge in both marine and lacustrine settings varies due to geologic heterogeneity, hydraulic gradient, water temperature and salinity, and biological processes. Geologic heterogeneity presents the biggest challenge in most nearshore margins. Temporal variability, especially at scales of seconds to hours, is also poorly understood because most measurement methods integrate seepage over multiple minutes to a day. Automated devices capable of sub-minute temporal resolution reveal that what averages as groundwater discharge is largely bi-directional in most settings. In lacustrine settings, lake seiche influences seepage in a manner similar but generally smaller than tides. The episodic presence or absence of a thin layer of low-permeability sediments, as well as the presence and density of burrowing organisms, both create complex seepage responses in the highly dynamic margins of both marine and lacustrine settings.

presentations.title: INFLUENCE OF SUBTERRANEAN ESTUARY MATRIX SEDIMENT ON NUTRIENT REACTIVITY AND RESULTING FLUXES TO THE COAST
presentations.abstract: The composition of submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) is strongly influenced by reactions occurring within subterranean estuaries. Redox conditions within subterranean estuaries largely depend on residence and flushing times of both fresh and saline groundwater, which are affected by the permeability and heterogeneity of the beach matrix. We combined field surveys with numerical reactive transport modeling using SEAWAT-PHT3D. Field data from Panxón Beach (Ría de Vigo, NW Iberian Peninsula) reveals the presence of a highly permeable gravel layer at 1-2 m depth, formed from the burial of anthropogenic materials. Combined field and modeling results show that the gravel layer decreased groundwater transit times and increased internal oxygenation.

presentations.title: Where Land Meets Water: The Overlooked Role of Groundwater Seepage in Lake Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: This essay highlights the emerging role of groundwater as an overlooked yet significant phosphorus source to lakes. We explore the mechanisms by which groundwater transports nutrients, its potential ecological effects on nearshore environments, and the challenges in quantifying its contributions to nutrient budgets. Recent studies indicate that lacustrine groundwater discharge can significantly influence phosphorus availability, algal blooms, and macrophyte distribution in lakes. As global change intensifies hydrological extremes and land use changes, groundwater-driven nutrient transport may become increasingly relevant.

presentations.title: ARTIFICIAL POND CO2 EMISSIONS FROM MOUNTAINOUS LOWLANDS AND THEIR SEASONAL DEPENDENCE ON SURFACE AND SUBSURFACE HYDROLOGIC CONNECTIVITY
presentations.abstract: Ponds are increasingly recognized as hotspots of carbon emissions, yet the seasonal dynamics and hydrological drivers of these emissions are largely unknown. We quantified and determined the seasonal dynamics of CO2 fluxes from several hundred artificial ponds across a subtropical mountainous headwater catchment (the Xin'anjiang watershed). The results showed that ponds are consistently net sources of atmospheric CO2 across both hydrological periods, with emissions significantly elevated during the dry period. Notably, small ponds with higher perimeter-to-area ratios exhibited disproportionately higher CO2 accumulation and emissions, reflecting their stronger sensitivity to groundwater-derived CO2.

presentations.title: The role of lacustrine groundwater in sustaining Boreal Shield lake hydrology and mitigating the effects of climate change
presentations.abstract: The extent to which lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD) contributes to lake hydrological resilience has been investigated for relatively few lakes globally. Groundwater constitutes 24% of long-term mean interannual inflows to Lake Papineau (17% from stream baseflow and 7% from LGD), with LGD buffering the effects of reduced summer baseflow contributions. Results indicate that in the presence of mean ensemble increases in temperature (+4.2°C) and precipitation (+19%) for the 2070-2100 horizon, Lake Papineau is relatively resilient, with no fundamental, long-term alterations to hydrogeological regime.

name: Aquatic Food Webs – Advances in Trophic Connectivity Within and Across Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Aquatic food webs are dynamic networks of dietary nutrient and contaminant transfer that are critical for sustaining ecosystem function, biogeochemical cycles, and biodiversity. Recent advances in analytical methods, such as stable isotope and lipid/fatty acid analysis, environmental DNA, and network theory, provide new insights into the complexity and connectedness of trophic interactions.
lead_organizer: Martin Kainz, Danube University Krems | WasserCluster Lunz

presentations.title: TOWARDS BALANCING THE BRIGHT AND DARK SIDES OF TROPHIC CONNECTIVITY WITHIN AND BEYOND AQUATIC ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Aquatic food resources can serve as sources of both limiting nutrients and contaminants for a diversity of consumers within and beyond aquatic ecosystems. We highlight a selection of the bright, beneficial aspects of aquatic trophic connections with some of their dark sides. For instance, aquatic-derived nutrients omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 LC-PUFA) as well as aquatic-derived contaminants like methylmercury (MeHg) can both biomagnify through trophic connections within aquatic food webs. Yet, while n-3 LC-PUFA are used as the building blocks for brain development, MeHg acts as a neurotoxicant. Understanding the balance between these risks and benefits is critical for making informed management decisions.

presentations.title: Multi-trophic responses to climate change in freshwater food webs
presentations.abstract: Climate change is reshaping freshwater ecosystems, yet the extent to which its impacts differ across trophic levels remains poorly understood. We examined how fish and zooplankton communities respond to present and projected climate conditions by 2100 across 156 lakes in Québec, Canada. Fish and zooplankton exhibited distinct diversity patterns under contemporary conditions, yet their community compositions were significantly coupled. Fish functional traits responded more strongly to climatic gradients, with declining body size and increasing thermal tolerance under forecasted, warmer conditions. Ecological networks became more connected and homogenized under future climates as warm-water species colonize colder sites.

presentations.title: The Shifting Clock of Alpine Streams - Phenological and Food-Web Responses of Aquatic Insects
presentations.abstract: Alpine streams host exceptionally diverse and sensitive communities. Warming may alter emergence timing, favour eurythermal over cold-adapted taxa, and reduce the nutritional quality of subsidies by altering essential fatty acid content. We explored climate-driven phenological and trophic shifts in Alpine stream insects across five catchments in the south-central Swiss Alps. Adult emergence traps and larval monitoring, combined with fine-scale temperature records, captured changes in community structure and emergence patterns. Fatty acid profiles and stable isotopes assessed how nutritional quality and trophic roles varied with elevation, glacial influence, and season.

presentations.title: TROPHIC FLEXIBILITY OF TWO BATHYPELAGIC MYSIDACEANS IN THE ST. LAWRENCE SYSTEM (CANADA)
presentations.abstract: Boreomysis (Mysidacea) are non-migratory bathypelagic species living in deep waters. As forage species, they play a pivotal role in benthic–pelagic coupling. In the St. Lawrence system, two species occur: B. nobilis, confined to the Saguenay Fjord, and B. arctica, only present in the estuary and the gulf. To determine their diet, we employed a multi-marker approach by combining fatty acids and stable isotopes. Stable isotopes reveal that B. nobilis has a more carnivorous diet, while B. arctica has a more omnivorous diet. At the intraspecific level, B. nobilis also exhibited a broader trophic niche than B. arctica, despite its more restricted geographic distribution.

presentations.title: Biodiversity shifts mediate global change effects on trophic pyramids
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institude of Limnology & Oceangraphy Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Trophic structure is fundamental to understanding ecosystem functioning, with primary production and ecosystem size as key determinants that are strongly influenced by global change. Here, we first use model simulations to illustrate when and how adopting a community perspective leads to different predictions of how trophic structure changes with both factors. Compared to the ecosystem perspective, the community perspective predicts lower richness and higher top-heaviness. We then studied 188 natural lakes and found that the effects of these two determinants on top-heaviness were more pronounced when they negatively influenced richness.

presentations.title: EUTROPHICATION CAUSES FUNCTIONAL HOMOGENIZATION IN FISHPOND ZOOPLANKTON: IMPLICATIONS FOR CONSERVATION AND MANAGEMENT
presentations.abstract: Fishponds are hotspots of biodiversity but are increasingly threatened by eutrophication. This study investigated how hypereutrophication affects zooplankton assembly rules and functional diversity in nine managed fishponds in Lower Austria. We used trait-based analyses in combination with null models. Although species richness remained relatively stable, functional diversity significantly declined due to strong trait convergence. Nutrient enrichment favoured fewer zooplankton species with similar traits, reducing the ecosystem's functional complexity.

name: Aquatic Connectivity: Measure, Model, Manage
description: Aquatic connectivity—the ability of water, organisms, and ecological processes to move across freshwater and coastal systems—is essential for sustaining biodiversity, ecosystem functions, and ecological resilience. Yet barriers such as dams, culverts, and land-use change have fragmented these systems globally.
lead_organizer: Anthony Fontaine, Université du Québec en Outaouais
co_organizers: Baptiste Nelaton, Université du Québec en Outaouais
Katrine Turgeon, Université du Québec en Outaouais
Sarah Bertrand, Université du Québec en Outaouais

presentations.title: Translating Data into Conservation Action: Tools, Models, and Planning Frameworks to Support Freshwater Connectivity Restoration
presentations.abstract: Canada holds roughly 20 percent of the world's freshwater supply, with vast lakes, rivers, and wetlands. Fish and other aquatic species need to move freely within freshwater ecosystems. We have developed a suite of datasets, models, and tools to support fish passage and freshwater connectivity restoration across Canada. These include the Canadian Aquatic Barriers Database, public-facing data-collection tools, connectivity and barrier prioritization models, and a community-led watershed connectivity restoration planning framework. These products provide a toolbox for communities, practitioners, infrastructure managers, and regulators to confidently take meaningful action to restore freshwater connectivity.

presentations.title: The impacts of connectivity breakdown on aquatic communities: literature review
presentations.abstract: There is accumulating evidence that connectivity loss and habitat fragmentation have major impacts on biodiversity. Freshwater species appear to be disproportionately affected because they rely on continuous, linear water pathways and cannot reroute around barriers the way terrestrial animals often can. A systematic literature review according to PRISMA standards has been undertaken to answer the following question: 'What are the impacts of connectivity disruption on aquatic communities?' This review enabled the determination of the effects of connectivity disruption upstream and downstream of a disturbance, assessment of impacts by barrier type, development of a typology of movement barriers, and a summary of the metrics used to assess aquatic connectivity.

presentations.title: Ripples Across Boundaries: Aquatic–Terrestrial Connectivity in a Changing World
presentations.abstract: Within-ecosystem connectivity is now largely recognized as an essential component of any biodiversity conservation plan. The implications, however, of cross-ecosystem connectivity remains largely understudied in more applied contexts. One key consequence of sharing permeable boundaries is that perturbations can propagate to various degrees across aquatic-terrestrial ecosystems. In this talk I propose to briefly present a working framework moving from theory to empirical data and comparative analyses.

presentations.title: Beyond barriers: indirect effects of forest stream crossings on macroinvertebrates through fish community reorganization
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Temperate Forest Sciences (ISFORT), University of Quebec in Outaouais (UQO)
presentations.abstract: Forest headwater streams supporting diverse assemblages of benthic invertebrates and small-bodied fishes are densely intersected by forestry road networks. We sampled over 50 road-stream crossings in cold-water headwater streams of Québec (Canada), including closed- and open-bottom culverts, bridges, and unimpacted reference reaches. Across structures, macroinvertebrate responses were inconsistent: culverts did not cause systematic losses of local diversity. Fish assemblages, in contrast, showed clearer signals: crossing severity was associated with species- and size-dependent asymmetries. The best-supported model was the indirect route: crossing severity altered fish community structure, which in turn predicted macroinvertebrate abundance.

presentations.title: Impacts of Culvert Reconstruction on Emergent Insect Biomass, Community Structure, and Stoichiometry
presentations.abstract: Forest streams are critical to maintaining biodiversity and ecological functions in forested landscapes. To evaluate the influence of culverts and their repairs on aquatic-to-terrestrial fluxes, we analyzed emerging aquatic insects collected with floating emergence traps across sites with culverts in varying states of repair in the Rivière au Saumon watershed. Our findings indicate that, while biomass fluxes did not respond, changes in community structure were observed in response to culvert renovation status. Those effects were mainly driven by variations in sensitive taxa (EPT). Stoichiometric ratios in some sensitive taxa were also marginally affected following major culvert reconstruction.

presentations.title: Dam-ponds in headwaters: disrupting river continuity yet reducing concentrations and fluxes of pesticides and transformation products
presentations.abstract: Across countries, fluvial networks differ in how rivers alternate with lentic systems. In France and elsewhere, small ponds (<50 ha) punctuate headwater areas. This presentation summarises more than ten years of measurements of pesticide fluxes along pond–river continua. Our work shows that very small streams transport, from the headwater reaches, mixtures of pesticides and numerous transformation products (TPs). Passage through the pond leads to a clear reduction in contamination. This reduction is not due to simple dilution, since fluxes are reduced by 10 to 100% depending on the molecule.

name: Threats to (and from) Aquaculture and Fisheries in a Changing World
description: In a time of unprecedented global change, food and economic insecurity are pressing issues. The aquaculture and fisheries sector plays a role in addressing both food and economic insecurity but also represents threats to wild populations and aquatic ecosystems.
lead_organizer: Sofia Sabbagh, Université du Québec à Rimouski
co_organizers: Sandra Ann Binning, Université de Montréal

presentations.title: Effects of Climate Change on Recreational Fisheries and Foods: A Global Perspective
presentations.abstract: Recreational fisheries contribute substantially to the wellbeing of coastal and inland regions worldwide, but climate change threatens their sustainability. A recent vulnerability assessment of recreational fish from marine and freshwater environments used species traits and climate change projections to quantify and map vulnerability patterns across the globe. Over 20% of recreationally targeted fishes were found to be vulnerable to climate change with hotspots emerging in several key regions. Recent work suggests recreational harvest can bolster food systems in many parts of the world.

presentations.title: Environmental Effects and Habitat Considerations for Cage Aquaculture of Tilapia in Lake Victoria
presentations.abstract: Cage aquaculture of Nile tilapia in Lake Victoria is expanding rapidly. To evaluate these risks, we monitored water quality and fish communities over two years at paired cage and control stations across four locations spanning a gradient from eutrophic inner-gulf to oligotrophic offshore waters. Localized shifts in dissolved oxygen, pH, and silica occurred near cages, yet broader multivariate patterns were shaped chiefly by spatial differences and seasonal cycles, and no large-scale deterioration attributable to cages was detected. Fish biomass was higher adjacent to cages, suggesting that cages act as de facto refugia.

presentations.title: Understanding Longfin Smelt Habitat In The Bellingham Bay (WA, USA)
presentations.abstract: The Longfin smelt (Spirinchus thaleichthys), known as 'Hooligans' to the Lummi Nation, is an anadromous forage fish of cultural and ecological importance in the Salish Sea. We used a non-invasive approach combining Environmental DNA sampling with Quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction. Detection patterns were mapped and statistically significant clusters were identified using Hotspot (Getis-Ord Gi*) analysis. Results indicate that high chlorophyll-a, greater marine productivity, and suitable substrate conditions correspond to stronger hotspots.

presentations.title: THE SIMPLE LOOP TO SUSTAINABILITY – AQUAPONICS
presentations.abstract: Aquaponics enable the simultaneous production of fish and plants in sustainable, closed-loop, water-efficient systems. Our research facility consists of 12 simple aquaponic systems that are replicable for home growers. We explored varying fish densities, feed composition, plant diversity, and pH levels. We found no difference in plant growth at different fish densities, suggesting that a low fish density (0.5 kg m-3) suffices when plant production is the focus and a medium density (1.5 kg m-3) when fish production is desired as well. Higher fish density adversely affected water quality parameters.

presentations.title: Thirty years of brook charr culture reveal the long-term effects of domestication and warming on resident and anadromous ecotypes
presentations.abstract: Since 1993, ISMER's aquaculture station has maintained a breeding program of anadromous brook charr from the Laval strain. Data on crosses, reproduction, growth, and environmental conditions have been systematically recorded for each cohort and generation. The objective of this presentation is to expose the breeding program in detail and present the long-term effects of domestication and environmental warming that have emerged in the anadromous phenotype.

name: Ecological Change in Arctic Freshwaters – Community and Food Web Responses to Climate Warming and Shifting Landscapes
description: The rapid warming of Arctic regions has led to alterations of landscape vegetation, catchment hydrology and habitat change, which in turn cause gradual changes in the diversity and ecological processes of lakes and rivers.
lead_organizer: Willem Goedkoop, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
co_organizers: Jennifer Lento, University of New Brunswick

presentations.title: Freshwater biodiversity in a rapidly changing Arctic: An expert horizon scan of key research questions
presentations.abstract: Arctic freshwater biodiversity is rapidly changing due to climate warming, resource extraction, infrastructure development, and landscape transformation. Using a horizon scan survey, Arctic freshwater research experts identified 77 critical research questions with experts expressing clear preferences for 17 questions that should be regarded as the most important for research assessment in the near term. A key priority identified was the urgent need for long-term, harmonized monitoring programs among Arctic countries.

presentations.title: TRACKING MICROBIAL COMMUNITY ACTIVITY ASSOCIATED WITH ARCTIC PERMAFROST IN NORTHWESTERN TERRITORIES
presentations.abstract: Permafrost soils in high-latitude regions store approximately 25–50% of global soil carbon. Upon thaw, these communities become active, decomposing long-stored organic carbon and releasing greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and CH₄. The Mackenzie River Delta in the Northwest Territories is proximal to numerous permafrost slumps. In this study we apply genomic tools to characterize the microbial metabolisms in these systems, providing new perspectives on metabolic activities such as carbon, iron and nitrogen cycling.

presentations.title: Phenological shifts in Lake Stratification and Biogeochemistry: Insights from Jackfish Lake, Northwest Territories
presentations.abstract: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) are now appearing in northern Canadian lakes once thought too cold and nutrient-poor to support them. Jackfish Lake in Yellowknife, NWT, now experiences annual, toxin-producing blooms of Planktothrix agardhii. We compare thermal structure, nutrient dynamics, and phytoplankton phenology across four lakes. Prolonged summer stratification in Jackfish Lake drives elevated phosphorus release from its anoxic hypolimnion. Surface microcystin concentrations in Jackfish Lake routinely exceed recreational guidelines.

presentations.title: Climate change-induced landscape change causes severe oligotrophication and alters carbon chemistry of subarctic lakes in Scandinavia
presentations.abstract: We used data from research, long-term monitoring, and satellite imagery to link decadal changes in Total-P, DIN, and C water concentrations of nine subarctic lakes to the greening of their catchments. Total-P showed declining trends for all nine lakes, ranging 1.5–3.6 %/y over the last decades. P sequestration in catchments generally increased by 12–30%. Despite increases in terrestrial vegetation, TOC of lakes showed declining trends. Conversely, alkalinity (ICalk) showed consistent increasing trends.

presentations.title: Monitoring of fish communities and their preys in Faroese Lakes
presentations.abstract: How cold water lakes respond to warming and anthropogenic changes is of primary importance. Here we revisited three small lakes in the Faroe Islands and assess ecological stability looking at fish communities and their preys 20 years after the NORLAKE project. The invertebrate communities in the lakes have changed between 2000 and 2022, both in composition and densities. We detected a shift to a less diverse diet in BT, but not in AC. The overall number of fishes was higher now than in 2000, but the ratio between AC and BT in Leynavatn has changed, with BT now being more numerous than AC.

presentations.title: HARMONIZATION AND SYNTHESIS OF ARCTIC FRESHWATER BIODIVERSITY DATA FROM THE CIRCUMPOLAR REGION
presentations.affiliation: Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
presentations.abstract: The Circumpolar Biodiversity Monitoring Program (CBMP) is the cornerstone program of the Conservation of Arctic Flora and Fauna (CAFF) working group. CBMP-Freshwater worked with scientists from all Arctic countries to compile a large, aggregated database of biodiversity data and supporting abiotic data for lakes and rivers from across the circumpolar region. This presentation will summarize the key findings from the data synthesis, including spatial and temporal patterns in alpha and beta diversity across Arctic freshwaters and the predicted drivers of change.

name: Towards a Convergence of Current Knowledge and Application of Multiple Stressor Ecology Across Aquatic Habitats
description: Global change biology often involves 'ecological surprises' arising from unexpected responses to extreme or novel environmental changes. We seek presentations that will stimulate exchange of methodologies used to generate mechanistic insights into the cumulative impacts of multiple stressors.
lead_organizer: Rolf Vinebrooke, University of Alberta

presentations.title: Mapping threats to the world's freshwater biodiversity
presentations.abstract: Earth has entered an era of unparalleled human activities, resulting in dramatic biodiversity loss worldwide. Here, we use comprehensive data from the IUCN to map the impact of 45 threats to all assessed freshwater amphibians, reptiles, fish, mammals, dragonflies. Our results highlight the most acute overlap of threats occurring in Europe and the Permanent Maghreb, with pollution and agriculture as the major threats to freshwater biodiversity. We provide evidence that freshwater species are nearly universally more impacted than terrestrial ones.

presentations.title: Losing our breath: The causes and consequences of aquatic deoxygenation
presentations.abstract: Dissolved oxygen losses are occurring in many waterbodies globally. The causes can be grouped into reductions in solubility associated with warming temperatures, stronger and longer stratification that reduces deep-water ventilation, and increases in biological and chemical oxygen demand. Deoxygenation impacts are diverse and can include the initiation of regime shifts. The loss of dissolved oxygen can harm biodiversity, contribute to release of phosphorus and dissolved organic matter from lake sediments, and regulate other processes such as mercury methylation and methane production.

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL RESPONSES TO MULTIPLE STRESSORS IN A SALINE LAKE AND IMPLICATIONS FOR CONSERVATION
presentations.abstract: Saline lakes throughout the world are threatened by decreasing water levels and increasing salinity. At Mono Lake, California, stream diversions led to an elevation decline and doubling of salinity. Since 1981, periods with large snowmelt runoff, followed by periods with low runoff, have led to six episodes of strong year-round stratification. Adult Artemia abundance has large interannual variability, and a 42% decline in abundance-weighted fecundity has occurred. Recent high phytoplankton abundance during summer indicates a significant shift in the balance between growth and loss of phytoplankton.

presentations.title: INDIVIDUAL AND CUMULATIVE EFFECTS OF FRESHWATER SALINIZATION AND HEATWAVES ON ZOOPLANKTON STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton play a crucial role in freshwater food webs. We conducted a 6-wk mesocosm experiment to test how crustacean zooplankton community structure and function respond to heatwave (HW) pulses and chloride (Cl-) press disturbances. Community structure showed no individual or interactive effects of either stressor, although diversity increased under the combined stressors. Copepod biomass declined upon the first HW pulse only. Compositional changes suggest a shift toward tolerant taxa. Overall, HW and Cl- disturbances resulted in detectable but limited impacts on zooplankton community structure.

presentations.title: Transgenerational Plasticity and Maternal Effects in Daphnia magna Across Multiple Stressors and (Mis)Matching Environmental Conditions
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic activities are increasing the number and intensity of environmental stressors. Past environmental conditions can shape future ecological responses through parental effects. We conducted a factorial experiment using three genotypes of Daphnia magna, exposing mothers to elevated temperature, elevated salinity, or both combined. Offspring were then reared under all possible stressor combinations. We quantified key fitness traits and show strong stressor-specific adaptive transgenerational effects.

presentations.title: TRACKING LONG-TERM CHANGES IN FOOD WEB DYNAMICS LINKED TO PAST SEABIRD INPUTS AT CAPE ST. MARY'S, NEWFOUNDLAND
presentations.abstract: Cape St. Mary's Ecological Reserve hosts the third-largest and southernmost Northern Gannet colony in North America. This project integrates sub-fossil cladoceran analysis into the existing multi-proxy paleolimnological framework to examine how primary consumers responded to seabird-derived nutrient inputs. By implementing cladocerans as response variables, we can quantify the timing and magnitude of past aquatic community and food web changes in relation to a historically increasing seabird population.

name: Some like It Hot: Cyanobacteria Adaptations and Expansion Across Different Habitats and Conditions
description: Cyanobacteria have long been recognized for thriving in eutrophic aquatic ecosystems with elevated temperatures. However, an increasing number of studies have reported their prevalence in cold water and even in oligotrophic ecosystems.
lead_organizer: Naila Barbosa da Costa, Université TÉLUQ
co_organizers: Sophie Crevecoeur, Environment and Climate Change Canada
Simone Cardoso, Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora

presentations.title: ARE ALL CYANOTOXINS CREATED EQUAL? DIFFERENTIAL DRIVERS OF CYANOTOXINS IN LENTIC WATERBODIES
presentations.abstract: We investigate the temporal and spatial patterns of anatoxin, cylindrospermopsin, microcystin, and saxitoxin in 200 Midwest waterbodies. While the highest anatoxin, microcystin, and saxitoxin concentrations were in eutrophic and hypereutrophic waterbodies, the highest cylindrospermopsin was in oligotrophic waterbodies. Seasonal cyanotoxin peaks occurred outside of typical summer sampling periods. We also question the assumption that green means toxic, as none of our proxies for phytoplankton biomass were significant predictors of cyanotoxins.

presentations.title: Historical Cyanobacterial Trends in Minimally Impacted Northern Lakes
presentations.abstract: Increasing reports of cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms in northern, historically low-productivity lakes have prompted questions. We analyzed radiometrically dated sediment cores from four northern Minnesota lakes, integrating 16S SSU rRNA amplicons and mcyE abundance to reconstruct cyanobacterial composition over the past 150 years. Across lakes, cyanobacterial communities exhibit gradual but directional shifts through time, including increased representation of putative N-fixing and bloom-forming taxa.

presentations.title: SEDIMENT ARCHIVES REVEAL CYANOBACTERIAL EXPANSION INTO COLD, LOW-PHOSPHORUS FINGER LAKES IN NEW YORK
presentations.abstract: Until about a decade ago, only one of New York's Finger Lakes—warm, eutrophic Honeoye Lake—experienced recurrent cyanobacterial blooms. Here we contrast Honeoye with oligotrophic, phosphorus-poor but nitrogen-rich Skaneateles Lake. We analyzed dated sediment cores from both lakes to reconstruct ~150 years of phytoplankton and cyanobacterial history. Both lakes show early-20th-century increases in cyanobacterial genes and pronounced rises in cyanotoxin genes from ~1980 onward. Skaneateles shows large relative increases in toxin genes and detectable microcystins despite little change in chlorophyll-a.

presentations.title: RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN ICE COVER, NUTRIENTS AND PHYTOPLANKTON TAXA IN A SHALLOW EUTROPHIC LAKE
presentations.abstract: We analyzed how changes in ice phenology and nutrient concentrations affected phytoplankton composition and spring biomass of cyanobacteria and diatoms in Lake Võrtsjärv, Estonia. We found drastic changes in the ice phenology since the 1990's: ice-on date has been delayed by 20 days and full ice-cover lasted on average one month less. Total cyanobacteria biomass in spring and that of the two main cyanobacteria species Limnothrix planctonica and Limnothrix redekei were strongly and negatively correlated to ice cover duration.

presentations.title: SOME LIKE IT SALTY: HIDDEN SALINITY HOT ZONES FOR CYANOBACTERIAL TOXIN PRODUCTION
presentations.abstract: Field surveys of over 100 Canadian Prairie lakes revealed that cyanobacterial biomass and toxin risk do not increase monotonically with salinity. Instead, microcystin concentrations peaked at two conductivity 'hot zones' (around 1,000 and 10,000 μS cm⁻¹) before collapsing at extreme salinities. We ran controlled salinity-gradient experiments using two Microcystis aeruginosa strains. The toxin-producing strain showed a large primary peak in cellular toxin quota between ~500–1,500 μS cm⁻¹ and a smaller secondary peak near ~10,000 μS cm⁻¹.

presentations.title: Seasonal dynamics of toxigenic cyanobacteria in urban stormwater ponds in relation to multiple stressors including temperature, nutrients, and chloride
presentations.abstract: Stormwater Ponds (SWP) serve as important flood management infrastructure in urbanizing environments. We conducted a study of 15 SWP in Oshawa, Ontario over the peak growing season. Results from this work confirm the dynamic presence of cyanobacteria over the course of the field season, with peak abundance generally occurring in late summer. A statistically significant multiple regression model explained 50% of the variation in mcyE gene abundance when using chloride, nitrate, total phosphorus, temperature, and filamentous cyanobacteria as independent predictor variables.

name: Aquatic Ecosystems Facing the Effects of Emerging Contaminants, Energy Transition and Global Changes: Recent Data, Challenges and Perspectives.
description: Aquatic ecosystems encompass various habitat types where a wide array of animals live, but at risk once exposed to several anthropogenic contaminants and environmental stressors.
lead_organizer: Maikel Rosabal, UQAM

presentations.title: ALATERED WATER-LEVEL REGIME IN LAKE KINNERET: ECOLOGICAL IMPACTS AND REHABILITATION MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES
presentations.abstract: The water-level of Lake Kinneret naturally fluctuates within ca.1.5 m. Use of the lake as Israel's primary drinking-water source has caused large variability in the annual min., mean and max. water levels, increasing the multi-year range of fluctuations to 6 m, x4 the natural range. This altered water-level regime has impacted the lakeshore by changing the bottom substrate from mostly stony to sandy. These changes harmed fish reproduction, reduced drastically native benthic invertebrates, and benefited invasive species.

presentations.title: LANTHANUM AND ALUMINUM GEOCHEMICAL CYCLING IN EUTROPHIC LAKE UNDERGOING EXTENDED IN-LAKE REMEDIATION
presentations.abstract: Chemical amendments using lanthanum- and aluminum-based compounds have been widely applied to reduce internal phosphorus loading. Aluminum binding is strongly influenced by pH, whereas La stability is more dependent on redox dynamics. Intensive sampling of a eutrophic lake was conducted over six months. This data captures sporadic shifts in dissolved and colloidal La concentration, with a maximum of 0.1μg/L observed in May (31% colloidal La), and the maximum dissolved Al concentration of 80μg/L in July.

presentations.title: TOXICITY MECHANISM ASSESSMENT IN THE EPIBENTHIC CRUSTACEAN HYALELLA AZTECA EXPOSED TO INDIVIDUAL AND BINARY MIXTURES OF RARE EARTH ELEMENTS (LA, GD, Y) IN CONTAMINATED SEDIMENTS
presentations.abstract: Rare Earth Elements (REEs) are increasingly used in multiple industrial applications. The objective of this study is to characterize the interaction and the resulting effect as well as the proteomic responses of the crustacean Hyalella azteca exposed to Lanthanum (La), Gadolinium (Gd) and Yttrium, individually and in binary mixtures. The toxicity tests showed toxicity differences between the individual REEs (EC50Y < EC50Gd < EC50La) and mostly additive effects in the binary mixtures.

presentations.title: TOXICITY, BIOACCUMULATION AND REMOVAL OF GADOLINIUM FORMS USING THE FREE-FLOATING PLANTS LEMNA GIBBA AND PISTIA STRATIOTES
presentations.abstract: In this work, we studied the duckweed Lemna gibba and water lettuce Pistia stratiotes for toxicity characteristics and bioaccumulation of a commonly used a gadolinium-based contrast agent (GBCA) and ionic gadolinium (Gd). For ionic Gd, the highest non-toxic concentration was determined as 6.7 mg L-1. The bioconcentration factor was up to 1294, and up to 2.5 mg kg-1 dry mass-based Gd tissue concentration was reached by Lemna, while Pistia accumulated up to 6.4 g Gd kg-1. Gd removal efficiency from the medium was 95%.

presentations.title: PHYTOREMEDIATION AND TOXICOLOGICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF RARE EARTH ELEMENTS (CERIUM, NEODYMIUM, SAMARIUM) USING DUCKWEED LEMNA GIBBA
presentations.abstract: In this work we studied duckweed Lemna gibba for toxicological characteristics and for bioaccumulation of three ionic rare earth elements (Ce, Nd, Sm). The highest non-toxic concentration ranges for ionic Ce, Nd and Sm were determined as 0.8, 1.8 and 7.7 mg L-1 while the plants showed 50% inhibition of the relative growth rate at 2.0, 2.4 and 13.3 mg L-1 respectively. The removal efficiency from the medium was between 94-96%.

presentations.title: Dynamic patterns between development and environmental response in the Nordic region: Sedimentary stratification of anthropogenic metals in Finnish lakes
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Urban Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: In Lahti and its vicinity, 12 lakes were selected to compose a developing category gradient as forest, rural, suburban, and urban in their catchments. With the 210Pb dating technology, the 12 lakes had sediment cores with a continuous chronology covering approximately the last 100 years. According to multidimensional variations of eight anthropogenic non-degradable metals, the sediment sections were distinctly classified into the four development categories, especially Zn, and Cu, Pb, Cr, and Cd with significant urban characteristics.

name: Ecological Significance of Dissolved Organic Matter
lead_organizer: Jianjun WANG, Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
session_description: DOM molecular characterization across aquatic ecosystems; bridges chemical complexity with ecosystem biogeochemistry.

presentations.title: Chemogeography of dissolved organic matter across freshwater and marine ecosystems
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, CAS
presentations.abstract_summary: Introduces a chemogeography framework: rivers show watershed-driven molecular structure, oceans have horizontal/vertical turnover with high-latitude homogenization, lakes benefit from functional chemogeography combining intrinsic and extrinsic traits.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) consists of thousands of molecules whose spatial variation reflects the ecological and biogeochemical processes shaping carbon cycling. We introduce a framework for the chemogeography of DOM and demonstrate its utility across major aquatic domains. In rivers, molecular richness and composition show clear geographic structure driven by watershed characteristics, hydrology, and climatic factors. Moving to the global ocean, chemogeographic turnover reveals systematic horizontal and vertical gradients, with decreasing rates toward deep and high-latitude waters where DOM composition becomes increasingly homogenized. For lakes, we highlight how functional chemogeography, integrating intrinsic molecular traits with extrinsic traits such as environmental responses and transformation pathways, provides explanatory power for DOM persistence, ecosystem processes, and predictive modeling. Together, these examples show that chemogeography and its functional extension offer a scalable framework for linking molecular complexity with environmental drivers across ecosystems such as rivers, lakes, and oceans. This approach advances our ability to interpret and predict DOM dynamics under global environmental change.

presentations.title: Chemodiversity of dissolved organic matter in boreal inland waters and links to water history
presentations.abstract_summary: FT-ICR-MS on >400 sites in Eastern Canada: lakes have highest molecular richness; deuterium excess (water history) is the strongest driver; transformations highest in lakes.
presentations.abstract: Recent studies of DOM in inland waters have increasingly highlighted the importance of terrestrial-aquatic links and of hydrological connectivity in shaping both DOM concentration and composition. Here we present a study of large-scale patterns in DOM composition in boreal inland waters where we establish links to hydrologic, watershed and environmental factors. For this we used ultrahigh-resolution mass spectrometry to analyze the molecular composition of DOM from over 400 sites including lakes, reservoirs, and fluvial systems, encompassing broad geographic, climatic and environmental gradients in Eastern Canada. Rarefaction curves of DOM molecular richness, both overall and by system type, approach asymptotes, indicating good coverage of DOM diversity in our dataset. Lakes had the highest molecular richness and the most distinct DOM composition relative to that of reservoirs and fluvial systems. Redundancy analysis identified deuterium excess (d-excess), an index of water evaporation and an integrator of previous water history, as the strongest driver of DOM variation, with land cover features further contributing to these differences. The low molecular novelty and uniqueness that we observed across system types, combined with the prevalence of ubiquitous molecules, suggests that degradation processes dominate over the production of new DOM along the aquatic continuum. This is further supported by patterns in putative biochemical transformations, quantified by matching mass differences between peaks to known reactions. Transformation rates were highest in lakes and declined with increasing d-excess, suggesting that individual molecules undergo more transformations in evaporatively enriched systems than in other environments. Overall, these results offer new insights on how water history and landscape context shape DOM diversity and transformations across boreal inland waters.

presentations.title: [empty/withdrawn slot]
Molecular characterization, source identification and biogeochemical processes of DOM
presentations.affiliation: University of Science and Technology Beijing
presentations.abstract_summary: Optimized PPL-FT-ICR-MS for algal DOM, multi-proxy source apportionment model applied at Lake Erhai/Caohai; eutrophication weakens lake carbon sink; microplastic-DOM aliphatic and toxic-precursor.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays an essential role due to its high activities in freshwater systems, which exert significant influence on carbon cycling, nutrient dynamics, and migration of pollutants. However, due to the complexity of chemical composition, sources and biogeochemical processes of DOM, the understanding of their migration, transformation and fate within freshwater ecosystem remains limited. Specially in the context of global warming and eutrophication, the sources and fate of DOM will also undergo significant dynamic changes. Therefore, in this study the extraction and characterization strategy, source identification method and biogeochemical processes of DOM were systematically explored. Firstly, we optimized the extraction methods of organic matter from diverse sources, and thus identified their specific molecular fingerprint of organic matter in multiple medium. For example, the results showed that the optimized PPL solid-phase extraction at a 1:500 PPL/DOC ratio with dual ESI mode coupled with FT-ICR-MS enabled effective full-component molecular characterization of algae-derived DOM. And then based on this, we established a quantitative source apportionment model for aquatic DOM by integrating spectroscopic, molecular (FT-ICR-MS), and isotopic fingerprints. Refractory molecules were identified as the stable, source-diagnostic fraction of DOM, and then applied random forest importance ranking to quantify how optical and molecular parameters explain the variability of these signatures, allowing us to select the key tracers for model input and develop a new multi-proxy method for DOM source apportionment. This model has successfully applied in several lakes such as Lake Erhai and Caohai. Moreover, the biogeochemical processes including degradation, precipitation and environmental effect were also explored. Mineral adsorption exhibited distinct fractionation: terrestrial DOM (rich in aromatic compounds) was strongly adsorbed, while algal DOM (aliphatic-rich) showed weaker, reversible adsorption, thus eutrophication might potentially weaken carbon sink potential in lakes. Degradation experiments indicated that aliphatic compounds were readily bio-degraded, whereas aromatic, highly unsaturated compounds persisted, forming a refractory carbon sink. Furthermore, the molecular fingerprint and potential risk of anthropogenic microplastic-derived DOM (MP-DOM) were also explored. The results showed that MP-DOM was more aliphatic, oxygenated and lower aromaticity and they also showed higher potential for generating toxic disinfection by-products compared to natural organic matter with protein-like substances identified as key precursors. This research provides critical methodological advances for the characterization and source identification of DOM, and also provide theoretical insights for the precise management of lake organic pollution and proactive risk assessment and control of microplastics.

presentations.title: Depth-dependent DOM dynamics in the Saguenay Fjord
presentations.abstract_summary: Saguenay Fjord: humic fluorescence 80% in surface, 50% at depth; CRAM upstream, condensed aromatics at fjord bottom; stratification controls DOM composition.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is central to carbon cycling in coastal and estuarine systems, yet its dynamics in strongly stratified fjords remain poorly understood. We examined depth-dependent DOM composition in the Saguenay Fjord, a sill-bounded system influenced by freshwater from the Saguenay River and saline intrusions from the St. Lawrence Estuary. Using optical measurements and high-resolution mass spectrometry in both positive and negative ionization modes, we identified distinct molecular and optical signatures across depths and basins. DOM was largely allochthonous, with humic-like fluorescence dominating surface waters (80 ± 7%) and decreasing at depth (50 ± 8%). Molecular profiles revealed highly unsaturated carbon (31–33%), carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecules (19–20%), and condensed aromatics (18–19%), with CRAM enriched upstream and condensed aromatics near the fjord bottom. Nitrogenous compounds and increasing apparent oxygen utilization at depth indicated microbial and sediment-driven transformations. Strong stratification isolates deep waters, while surface mixing promotes transport. These findings highlight how terrestrial inputs, microbial activity, and water mass structure shape DOM composition, influencing carbon cycling and export to the St. Lawrence Estuary.

presentations.title: Thermal Rearrangement of DOM-Microbe Interactions Magnifies Climate Forcing of Northern Lakes
presentations.abstract_summary: 40-lake boreal-temperate gradient: warming shifts lakes from CO2-dominated to CH4-emitting systems via thermal reorganization of DOM-microbe coupling.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) represents one of Earth’s largest and most reactive carbon pools, with its molecular composition influencing its environmental persistence and ecosystem function. Anthropogenic warming, which is most pronounced in northern ecosystems, is rapidly altering the dynamics of DOM production, export, and processing in aquatic systems. Here, we present a large scale (1600 km) space-for-time substitution across a boreal-to-temperate gradient to test the hypothesis that warming fundamentally reworks the relationships between DOM composition, microbial community function, and carbon emissions. We sampled 40 lakes over all seasons, integrating molecular-level DOM characterization, shotgun metagenomics sequencing of microbial communities, in situ measurements of GHG fluxes, and assessments of lake metabolism. We found that warming moves lakes along a continuum from CO 2 -dominated systems to potent CH4 emitters, driven by a thermal reorganization of both DOM composition and microbial community structure. By linking high-resolution chemodiversity data with microbial taxonomy and ecosystem function, this research provides a mechanistic framework to predict how climate-driven shifts in ecosystem function and structure will alter the role of northern lakes in the global carbon cycle. These findings are critical for informing models of future atmospheric carbon loading and guiding climate mitigation and freshwater resource protection policy.

name: Novel Ways to Improve Mechanistic Understanding and Prediction of Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs) Across Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Harmful algal blooms are proliferating in many parts of the world. Main drivers include abiotic factors such as increasing nutrient concentrations and temperature, as well as biotic interactions.
lead_organizer: Elena Litchman, Michigan State University

presentations.title: Physical Drivers of Cyanotoxin Dynamics: Stratification and Wind Mixing in Subalpine Lakes of the Brooks Lake Watershed, Wyoming
presentations.abstract: This project investigates how lake stratification and wind-driven mixing influence cyanotoxin presence and distribution in the Brooks Lake watershed. Our results showed that stratification patterns were closely tied to toxin behavior. During stable summer conditions, cyanotoxins accumulated at depth; when wind events partially or fully mixed the water column, these deeper toxin pools were redistributed upward, producing short-term spikes at the surface.

presentations.title: Effects of Hydrologic Disturbance on Cyanobacteria Bloom Dynamics in a Shallow Eutrophic Lake
presentations.abstract: We investigated the impacts of hydrologic disturbance on cyanobacteria bloom dynamics in a shallow, eutrophic lake during the 2024 and 2025 ice free seasons. In summer 2024, the remnants of Hurricane Beryl resulted in stratification of the polymictic lake due to cold water intrusion. The 2025 season had a rainy spring into June, followed by an intense drought. This drought allowed blooms to intensify with little disturbance to cause a collapse.

presentations.title: DECIPHERING HOW PROXIMITY TO WASTEWATER INPUTS DRIVE HAB DEVELOPMENT ALONG AN URBAN-SUBURBAN GRADIENT WITHIN LONG ISLAND SOUND
presentations.abstract: Urban estuaries surrounding NYC tend to be chronically enriched by anthropogenic nitrogen inputs from wastewater. Here we describe observations from multi-year, interdisciplinary research testing how proximity to wastewater, particularly inputs enriched with DIN, influences the incidences of HABs in NY/CT estuaries. Multiple systems were surveyed for physical water quality, nutrients, HABs, chlorophyll a, toxin levels, and bacteria.

presentations.title: PREDICTING SHIFTS IN CYANOBACTERIAL BLOOM DOMINANCE IN WESTERN LAKE ERIE: INTEGRATING MODELS AND COMPETITION EXPERIMENTS
