presentations.abstract: In this study, we developed a resource competition model of cyanobacterial growth and calibrated it using nutrient and temperature traits measured from WLE strains. Dolichospermum dominated under low nitrogen concentrations while Microcystis outcompeted Dolichospermum at higher nitrogen concentrations. Temperature and phosphorus affected growth rates and total biomass respectively but played a smaller role in competition outcome.

presentations.title: LAKE SNOW AND ROCK SNOT: EXTRACELLULAR POLYSACCHARIDE 'BLOOMS' PRODUCED BY INVASIVE DIATOMS IN NUTRIENT-POOR NEW ZEALAND LAKES AND RIVERS
presentations.abstract: In 2004, novel algal blooms were noticed in relatively pristine lakes and rivers of the mountainous South Island, New Zealand. Invasive, non-native diatoms rapidly colonised nutrient-poor lakes and rivers, resulting in unusually high biomasses of extracellular polysaccharides. We found evidence of nitrogen fixation and enzymes that cleave phosphate from dissolved organic molecules within the polysaccharide matrices produced by L. intermedia and D. geminata.

presentations.title: NUTRIENT-DRIVEN CHANGES IN VITAMIN B12 PRODUCTION POTENTIAL AND DYNAMICS
presentations.abstract: Vitamin B12 is synthesized exclusively by certain bacteria and archaea, yet it is essential for ~50% of eukaryotic algae. We conducted an outdoor mesocosm experiment to investigate how warming and nutrient enrichment influence prokaryote community structure and vitamin B12 production potential. Nutrient enrichment significantly altered prokaryote community composition and increased diversity.

name: Water in Peatlands
description: Peatlands are wetlands that cover around 3% of continental surfaces but that store approximately 25% of the global soil carbon. Water in and above these soils include peat lakes, ponds, pools, streams and porewater.
lead_organizer: Julien Arsenault, Université du Québec à Montréal

presentations.title: Continuous measurements of stable carbon isotopes of dissolved CO2 in a peatland-dominated headwater stream show controls by photosynthesis and respiration
presentations.abstract: Peatland headwater streams are rich in organic carbon species and act as significant sources of CO2. Here, we present a novel monitoring setup that enables continuous measurements of the stable carbon isotope of dissolved CO2 to decipher short-term fluctuations and turnover processes. Measurements from July 3 to 20, 2025, in a peatland-dominated headwater stream (southern Germany) showed diurnal cycles of CO2 concentrations and δ13CCO2 values, with respiration and photosynthesis as the main drivers.

presentations.title: Tracking DOC from Organic Soil to Reservoir: Mechanisms, Monitoring, and Management Options
presentations.abstract: Increasing concentrations of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) challenges drinking water production. We conducted a multi-year investigation to quantify the magnitude and drivers of DOC production and export in a German headwater–reservoir system across patch, plot, and catchment scales. We evaluated potential mitigation measures aimed at reducing DOC export to the reservoir.

presentations.title: CENTENNIAL TRENDS IN ORGANIC CARBON CYCLING IN SPORADIC DISCONTINUOUS PERMAFROST PEATLAND LAKES
presentations.abstract: We used paleolimnological techniques to assess how permafrost thaw is altering dissolved organic carbon transport to lakes in the Taiga Plains ecoregion of the southern Northwest Territories. Two out of 23 lakes exhibited a transition from an epiphytic-dominated assemblage to one dominated by small benthic Fragilariaceae, potentially indicative of lake browning. The timing of the transition coincided with geochemical indicators of a wildfire event. The results suggest that lake responses to permafrost thaw are non-linear.

presentations.title: LATE HOLOCENE EVOLUTION OF PEATLAND PONDS AND LAKES IN WAPUSK NATIONAL PARK, WESTERN HUDSON BAY LOWLANDS, CANADA
presentations.abstract: The subarctic Hudson Bay Lowlands contain thousands of shallow ponds and lakes mostly formed by thermokarst processes. We took sediment cores from ponds and lakes in the three ecozones and investigated lake evolution based on paleolimnological analyses. Peat plateau and coastal fen sites showed a recent trend towards taxa tolerant to desiccation, potentially resulting from changes in vegetation or peatland colonization.

presentations.title: Road infrastructure as a driver of hydrological and ecological changes in boreal peatlands
presentations.abstract: This study assesses the impact of roads on groundwater flow and peatland ecosystems in the Côte-Nord region of northeastern Québec, Canada. Preliminary results show limited influence of roads on water table levels. However, road infrastructure facilitates the transfer of minerals and chemical elements via surface runoff, altering plant community structure, notably with the loss of Sphagnum mosses and lichens.

presentations.title: Assessing long-term impacts of wildfire on the aquatic communities and food webs of subtropical peatlands
presentations.abstract: In 2019–2020, two major wildfires burned over 60% of K'gari. This study investigates environmental conditions, macroinvertebrate assemblages, and food webs across burnt and unburnt Empodisma minus (wire rush) fens five years after the 2020 bushfires. Preliminary analysis shows that environmental conditions and macroinvertebrate assemblages are not significantly different across burnt and unburnt sites.

name: Autonomous and In Situ eDNA Technologies: Scaling Molecular Biodiversity Observations in Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Environmental DNA (eDNA) technologies are transforming aquatic ecosystem monitoring by enabling sensitive, non-invasive detection of biodiversity. As demand grows for scalable and high-resolution biological observations, autonomous and in situ eDNA sampling systems are becoming essential.
lead_organizer: Elizabeth Allan, University of Washington
co_organizers: Kevan Yamahara, Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute

presentations.title: FIDO: A new type of autonomous aquatic sampling instrument for 'omics studies
presentations.abstract: In collaboration with the USGS, we have designed a new type of robotic sampler called FIDO (Filtering Instrument for DNA Observations), which filters environmental water through standard 47mm filters and preserves the collected material for later analysis. FIDO can acquire 144 samples and operates from a simple web-interface via cell or satellite linkage. Laboratory testing confirms no significant differences between FIDO and traditional bench filtration methods when detecting target species.

presentations.title: Ascension: Field Applications of an eDNA Auto Sampler from Ocean Diagnostics
presentations.abstract: We present the utility of the Ascension eDNA Sampler, an autonomous, compact, tethered multi-sampler capable of collecting filtered eDNA samples down to 400m from the side of any small boat. Ascension integrates in-situ filtration, real-time depth, temperature, salinity, flow rate, and cumulative water volume data, enabling depth-resolved sampling in diverse environments.

presentations.title: AUTOMATED eDNA SAMPLING WITH SELF-PRESERVING FILTERS: LESSONS LEARNED FROM A U.S. GEOLOGICAL SURVEY READI-NET PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP
presentations.abstract: In this presentation, we outline a recently developed eDNA autosampler capable of collecting 8 self-preserving eDNA filters on a pre-programmed schedule. We will share key lessons learned from the public-private partnership between Smith-Root and the U.S. Geological Survey READI-NET project, which aims to integrate automated eDNA sampling into routine aquatic invasive species monitoring.

presentations.title: SMARTER, FASTER, DEEPER: SCALABLE SOLUTIONS FOR ROBUST EDNA COLLECTION FROM WATER
presentations.abstract: Here, we introduce novel devices for diverse waterborne eDNA collection applications, including high-speed open-water sampling, shore-based systems, vessel-integrated devices, and emerging deep-water and AUV applications. These tools expand spatial and volumetric coverage, remain user-friendly, minimize contamination, and enable non-specialist operation.

presentations.title: First Integration of an eDNA Sampler with a Self-Righting Solar-Powered USV Reveals eDNA as an Effective Tool at a Globally Recognized Ocean 'Hope Spot'
presentations.abstract: In September of 2024, we deployed a first-ever integrated solar-powered, self-righting uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) with an autonomous eDNA sampler in Shinnecock Bay, New York. The baywide eDNA survey was able to resolve spatial patterns for over 200 species, including 9 species of special concern, 5 endangered species, and distributions of 10 invasive species. eelgrass beds were hotspots of biodiversity across multiple trophic levels.

name: A 'Silver Bullet Assessment' of Nature-Based Solutions (and Other Measures) for Lakes
description: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are gaining momentum as sustainable, multi-benefit approaches to address the complex challenges facing lake ecosystems—from eutrophication and biodiversity loss to climate-driven hydrological shifts.
lead_organizer: Bryan Spears, UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology
co_organizers: Rowen Monks, Norwegian University of Life Sciences
Tallent Dadi, Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research

presentations.title: ADVANCES IN IN-LAKE AND CATCHMENT MEASURES FOR SUSTAINABLE LAKE RESTORATION
presentations.abstract: A structured literature review assessed recent innovations for lake restoration. Most innovations (55%) concerned in-lake measures, largely nature-based or multifunctional solutions enhancing circularity and biodiversity. External catchment measures comprised 40% of innovations, dominated by NbS reducing nutrient losses through improved land, crop, and forest management. Cost data and post-intervention monitoring were often insufficient.

presentations.title: CATCHING PHOSPHORUS AT INFLOWS FOR CLEANER LAKES AND CIRCULAR RECOVERY
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research GmbH – UFZ
presentations.abstract: We designed and tested the efficiency of a coagulant dosing system at a drinking water reservoir during a three-month continuous FeCl3 dosing in spring 2025. The coagulant dosing significantly improved phosphorus retention with removal of up to 95% and 65% for SRP and TP respectively. Residual Fe concentrations remained low. Our work demonstrates an effective phosphorus removal strategy for diffuse-loaded reservoirs and lakes.

presentations.title: HEAT-INDUCED MORPHOPHYSIOLOGICAL STRESS IN ALGAE UNDERMINES NbS
presentations.abstract: This study investigated the intraspecific response of the alga Scenedesmus obtusus to elevated temperatures. In a 28-day microcosm experiment, we exposed the alga to temperatures of 28°C and 31°C above an ambient baseline of 26°C. Density increased significantly from 26°C to 31°C. Furthermore, higher temperatures resulted in significantly smaller cell sizes (p<0.001), indicating cellular stress.

presentations.title: Digging for solutions: A circular pathway for sustainable lake restoration
presentations.abstract: Phosphorus is a finite and increasingly scarce resource yet it continues to accumulate in lake sediments as legacy pollution. Dredging P-rich sediments offers a dual opportunity: reducing internal loading while providing a secondary P source for agriculture. This presentation outlines a holistic workflow - from the development of a semi-automated, gentle dredger to the dewatering of sediment and evaluation of its fertilizer value in agricultural trials.

presentations.title: TAKING A LONG BREATH: RESTORING WATER QUALITY IN LAKE KRALINGSE PLAS, THE NETHERLANDS
presentations.abstract: Lake Kralingse Plas suffered from cyanobacterial blooms since the 1990s. Three interventions were implemented: dredging/sand capping (2009/10), hydrogen peroxide (2016), and lanthanum-modified bentonite addition (2021). The 3rd intervention lowered TP substantially to 0.02 (±0.01) mg P/L from 2021-2025. The lake's trophic state index declined from hypertrophic to mesotrophic.

presentations.title: BUILDING CONSENSUS ON WATER QUALITY INTERVENTIONS TO ADDRESS EUTROPHICATION
presentations.abstract: Despite efforts to address eutrophication issues, many lakes continue to show poor water quality. The prairie region of Canada is notable for high trophic status lakes. Using results spanning insights from expert surveys to interviews, we identified areas of consensus on priority water quality interventions. We bring tools bridging natural and social sciences to understand interventions to improve water quality in agricultural landscapes.

name: Integrative Approaches to Freshwater Monitoring: Emerging Technologies, Community Based Programs, and Indigenous Knowledge Systems
description: This session is about people, the environment, and respect for Nibi (Water). Indigenous knowledge holders and community-based groups have led the way in monitoring aquatic systems. The field of molecular biology and environmental sensing is undergoing rapid progress.
lead_organizer: Jack Greenhalgh, McGill University

presentations.title: From Genes to Satellites: Uncovering Microbial Drivers of Water Quality and Green House Gas Flux in Southeastern U.S. Reservoirs
presentations.affiliation: The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
presentations.abstract: Our research integrates field sampling with metagenomic sequencing, flow cytometry, high-throughput microscopy, and satellite remote sensing in key reservoirs of the southeastern U.S. Initial findings from Jordan Lake, NC reveal substantial spatial variability in microbial cell abundance, identifying 'hotspots' with microbial biomass double that of adjacent areas. Metagenomic analysis produced over 80 distinct microbial genomes including the assembled genome of the known toxin-producing cyanobacterium Raphidiopsis brookii.

presentations.title: HOW VEGETATION REMOVAL IMPACTS FRESHWATER SOUNDSCAPES: INSIGHTS FROM TWO ONTARIO LAKES USING SOUNDSCAPE ANALYSIS
presentations.abstract: This study analyzes broadband acoustic data (2 Hz–250 kHz) collected from Lake Scugog and Canal Lake to examine how vegetation removal influences soundscapes. Three methods of removal were used: aquatic thruster, weed sickle, and lake rake. Preliminary analyses show a slight increase in detected sounds after removal in both lakes. These results suggest that vegetation removal effects are subtle, variable across methods.

presentations.title: Environmental and predator control of mysid shrimp vertical distribution in Lake Superior assessed from uncrewed surface vessels
presentations.abstract: We use active hydroacoustic data from two autonomous Uncrewed Surface Vessels (USV) collected in the western arm of Lake Superior to assess the vertical distribution of mysids and fish through several diel vertical migration cycles. Surface light intensity and bathymetric depth significantly explained mysid depth both day and night. At night, mysid depth was further influenced by surface water temperature, fish depth, and fish biomass.

presentations.title: Can different molecular identification approaches to aquatic insects effectively supplement morphology-based biomonitoring in a multi-gradient river system in Japan?
presentations.abstract: In Japan's Fujikawa River Basin, the study applied DNA metabarcoding (DM) and species delimitation (SD) to supplement morpho-based biomonitoring in 25 stream sites. Based on Chironomid data, DM findings has 25 taxa while SD-based data has 52 MOTUs. Negative binomial GLM showed that most biodiversity indices based from molecular identification had contrasting response with Cl- and pH.

presentations.title: THE POTENTIAL OF UNDERWATER IMAGERY FOR THE CHARACTERIZATION OF NEOTROPICAL FRESHWATER FISH COMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: This research aims to evaluate the reliability of underwater videos for the characterization of neotropical freshwater fish communities. We compared community and trait data collected with underwater videos to data obtained from minnow traps and ex situ fish photographs. Fieldwork took place in the Stann Creek District of Belize, where the selected streams were sampled from November 2024 to May 2025.

presentations.title: Using open-source camera traps to detect Endangered Lake Chubsucker, Erimyzon sucetta, in the Old Ausable Channel, Ontario
presentations.affiliation: CIEE Living Data Project - University of Regina
presentations.abstract: In this study, we developed open-source camera traps with integrated temperature and dissolved oxygen sensors and deployed them in the Old Ausable Channel. We detected juvenile Lake Chubsucker at 14 of the 18 study sites, at temperatures ranging between 19.81 °C and 27.92 °C. Juvenile Lake Chubsucker and Common Carp tended not to be detected at the same sites.

name: AI in Aquatic Sciences: Advancing Ecology and Sustainability with Artificial Intelligence
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping many scientific fields, yet aquatic sciences have only begun to tap into AI's broader potential.
lead_organizer: Alexander Flecker, Cornell University
co_organizers: Maria Camila Mejía García, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

presentations.title: AI and the Emergence of Computational Sustainability
presentations.abstract: In this talk, I will introduce Computational Sustainability, an interdisciplinary field devoted to developing computational models and techniques that balance environmental, economic, and societal needs. I will illustrate its potential through diverse projects relevant to aquatic ecosystems, including biodiversity and wildlife conservation, strategic hydropower dam planning in the Amazon basin, organic carbon cycle modeling, and materials discovery for renewable energy.

presentations.title: KNOWLEDGE GUIDED MACHINE LEARNING IS RESHAPING HOW WE CONCEPTUALIZE LIMNOLOGICAL PROBLEMS
presentations.abstract: Knowledge guided machine learning (KGML) is a paradigm for co-advancing the sciences of limnology and artificial intelligence by combining domain expertise with modern deep-learning methods. Beyond improving the accuracy of lake predictions, KGML is beginning to reshape how we conceptualize problems, evaluate mechanisms, and generalize insights across ecosystems.

presentations.title: PROBABILISTIC DEEP LEARNING FORECASTS OF RIVER CHLOROPHYLL: OR, HOW I LEARNED TO STOP WORRYING AND LOVE THE UNCERTAINTY
presentations.abstract: I demonstrate how explicitly accounting for uncertainty in environmental drivers, observations, and model outputs can improve forecasts of riverine HABs. I developed a probabilistic deep learning framework that forecasts river chlorophyll concentrations 1 to 10 days in advance using long short-term memory neural networks combined with asymmetric Laplacian distributions to quantify uncertainty.

presentations.title: AI-Driven modeling of temporal patterns of greenhouse gas emissions in excavated fishponds
presentations.affiliation: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
presentations.abstract: Drawing on temporally resolved data from aquaculture systems in Brazil, we use machine learning to model the temporal variability in CO2, CH4 and N2O fluxes from excavated ponds. Techniques include Bayesian hierarchical models, model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) and conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs).

presentations.title: Smoke on Water: Using AI to analyze impacts of Wildfires on Lakes in California
presentations.abstract: This research uses AI and Machine Learning tools to disentangle the relationships between extreme events brought about by climate change on water quality on lakes in the state of California. The use of AI and ML allowed us to analyze the large amount of data in a discrete and informative way that offered impactful results.

presentations.title: Innovative Hybrid Modeling for Harmful Algal Bloom Research in Inland Waters
presentations.abstract: This study presents a novel hybrid adjustment framework that integrates Remote Sensing derived chlorophyll-a maps with hydrodynamic model simulations for Torment Lake, Nova Scotia. We develop a two-step approach: a retrieval model calibrated using observed Chl-a measurements, and a machine learning adjustment model trained to quantify and correct discrepancies.

name: Aquatic Primary Production Across Scales: Drivers, Dynamics, and Consequences
lead_organizer: Stuart Jones, Grand Valley State University
co_organizers: Paul Hanson, University of Wisconsin - Madison
Isabella Oleksy, University of Colorado Boulder
Chris Solomon, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
Kathleen Weathers, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
description: Primary production is the engine of aquatic ecosystems, fueling food webs, regulating biogeochemical cycles, and shaping ecosystem responses to environmental change. Yet, understanding how primary production varies across spatial and temporal scales—from microbial interactions in localized patches to global patterns in lakes, rivers, and oceans—remains a critical scientific challenge. This session will bring together limnologists, oceanographers, and interdisciplinary researchers to explore the drivers, dynamics, and consequences of aquatic primary production across freshwater and marine systems.

presentations.title: EXPLORING PRAIRIE WETLAND POND METABOLISM USING MULTIPLE APPROACHES
presentations.abstract: Wetlands are highly productive ecosystems that provide critical ecosystem services including carbon storage, hydrological buffering, biodiversity protection, and nutrient remediation. In the Prairie Pothole Region of North America, many wetlands have been extensively altered by agricultural activities, potentially diminishing these functions. Measures of ecosystem metabolism are useful as a tool to monitor food web functioning and biogeochemistry. Here, we paired three methods to quantify the rates of gross primary production (GPP), ecosystem respiration (ER), net ecosystem production (NEP), and community respiration in wetland pond habitats in the prairie region in Alberta, Canada. Across wetlands, rates of both GPP and ER were high compared to other aquatic ecosystems. Isotope (seasonal) and sensor-based (daily) estimates showed wetlands were heterotrophic 55 and 61% of the time, respectively. The correlation of GPP and ER varied in strength between ecosystems, suggesting inconsistent coupling between auto- and heterotrophs. Our incubations showed that aerobic respiration was greater in sediments than the water column, and highest in open-water areas rather than vegetated, littoral zones. Overall, the patterns of aquatic metabolism vary widely both within and across wetlands in the Prairie Pothole Region, however most ponds tend toward heterotrophy, and most sustain intense rates of photosynthesis and respiration that reflect the highly-productive food webs.

presentations.title: Understanding how model parametrization affects metabolism estimates using NEON streams
presentations.abstract: Streams and rivers play a critical role in the global carbon cycle, linking the land, sea and atmosphere. In addition to transport and evasion, streams also transform carbon through the processes of gross primary production (GPP) and respiration (ER), collectively known as metabolism. Metabolism is commonly estimated from daily changes in dissolved oxygen (DO), necessitating either constraining the abiotic rate of gas exchange (K600) using field-based tracer gas experiments, or using models such as streamMetabolizer to estimate GPP, ER and K600 as free parameters simultaneously. Here, we compare these alternative approaches at continental scales using National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) sites. The results suggest that in steep streams where K600 is relatively high (and variable in response to discharge), failure to strongly constrain K600 results in model equifinality and poor estimation of GPP, ER and K600. In contrast, free parameter fitting appears a viable approach in low gradient streams (where K600 is relatively low and less variable in response to discharge) and may actually improve K600 estimates give the difficulty of measuring such low rates directly using tracer gases. Similarly, in shaded streams where GPP and the resulting diel variation in DO is small, constraining K600 is more critical than in open streams where GPP and the resulting diel variation in DO is larger, and K600 can often be left as a free parameter. Understanding limitations and how best to parameterize streamMetabolizer across different types of streams will improve our estimations of metabolism, as well as gas exchange rates. These improved estimates will in turn allow a better understanding of how drivers such as light availability and stream discharge control rates of carbon transport and cycling at continental scales.

presentations.title: Network-scale estimation of river ecosystem metabolism using geostatistical modeling and satellite remote sensing
presentations.abstract: Rivers connect ecosystems across landscapes. Primary production and respiration (i.e. ecosystem metabolism) rates in rivers are susceptible to flow alterations, land use change, and climate variability. Because rivers connect disparate ecosystems and biomes, these disturbances can have far-reaching consequences on ecosystem processes. Daily ecosystem metabolism values can be estimated in rivers from diel oxygen time series on a site-by-site basis. We present a modeling framework to scale this understanding to entire river networks by linking satellite remote sensing indices to in-situ river ecosystem metabolism measurements. Our approach expands on existing geostatistical methods by using computationally efficient spatio-temporal statistical techniques to model variability across both space and time within river networks. We can use this framework to create long-term spatially explicit time series of ecosystem metabolism predictions and uncertainty across whole river basins. Furthermore, we can explicitly model how disturbances such as flow alterations, land use change, and point-source pollution affect ecosystem processes downstream and over time. As temporal, spatial, and spectral resolution of satellite products increases, we believe this is a crucial methodological development which will allow us to fully utilize the observational time series now available and develop the next generation of aquatic ecosystem models.

presentations.title: LAKE METABOLIC REGIMES: A NEW GLOBAL SYNTHESIS OF GPP AND ER PATTERNS AND DRIVERS
presentations.abstract: Why do some lakes share similar annual patterns in gross primary production (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (ER), while in other lakes these patterns differ in myriad ways? What determines a lake's metabolic regime – its characteristic pattern of GPP and ER over the course of a year? We address these questions by analyzing data from GLAMR, the Global LAke Metabolism Respository, a new database that brings together high-frequency data and estimates of lake metabolism from around the world. Time series clustering of >30,000 lake-days of data from >100 lakes reveals distinct metabolic types, which differ in the number and magnitude of annual peaks in GPP, the relationship between GPP and ER, and other ways. Regional and local drivers interact to shape these metabolic regimes, such that geographic proximity is a poor predictor of the similarity in metabolic regime between two lakes. Our results shed new light on the drivers of ecosystem metabolism in lakes, and help inform how we model these important ecosystem processes now and into the future.

presentations.title: PHYSICAL DRIVERS OF BENTHIC AND PELAGIC ALGAL BIOMASS DYNAMICS: A CONCEPTUAL EXPLORATION WITH THE PROCESS-BASED MODEL 'LAKE2D'
presentations.abstract: Basin morphometry affects lake-internal processes relevant for productivity, such as turbulent mixing, vertical light attenuation, sedimentation, and nutrient cycling. Yet, in empirical and computational studies of whole-lake primary production, lake morphometry is often reduced to a single 1-dimensional measure – lake mean depth. We developed the process-based model 'Lake2D' to ask: (1) How are pelagic and benthic algal dynamics affected by lake bathymetry and other physical drivers. (2) Can these dynamics be captured by a model using mean depth as the only morphometrical variable? The distinguishing feature of Lake2D is the reduction of lake bathymetry to a hypsographic bottom profile and a radially symmetric lake basin. We compare predictions for Lake2D and the corresponding 1D-model preserving only lake mean depth across a wide range of lake sizes, mixing conditions, water transparencies, and nutrient contents. Lake 2D predicts several qualitatively novel phenomena such as persistence of benthic algae even in the deepest lakes, the possibility of a benthic deep chlorophyll maximum, and shifts in the relative importance of benthic vs. pelagic algae with increasing lake size and depth. Quantitatively, the mean depth-based 1D-model underestimates benthic biomass and overestimates pelagic biomass, the net effect on total algal biomass being a 5-50% underestimate in shallow lakes and a 5-20% overestimate in many deeper lakes. Our analyses identify the light environment set by lake depth and pelagic nutrients, but also lake area, as main drivers of these differences.

presentations.title: Scale-up discrete measurements of primary production to global distribution via the phytoplankton absorption approach
presentations.abstract: One of the primary goals of satellite ocean color remote sensing is to obtain maps of phytoplankton primary production (NPP) over the global ocean, where traditionally this was based on chlorophyll concentration (Chl). Since phytoplankton absorption coefficient (aph) is a direct indicator of energy absorbed for photosynthesis, an absorption-based model (AbPM) has been developed for this purpose, and various studies have demonstrated its better performance compared to Chl-based approaches. However, while aph of the global ocean can be estimated from ocean color, the determination of the photosynthesis quantum yield (ϕ), a prerequisite for AbPM, was never reached. In this study, based on discrete in situ measurements of NPP from various parts of the ocean, a scheme is developed to estimate the maximum quantum yield (ϕm), where ϕ can be further inferred. Evaluation with independent data showing that the estimated ϕm is within ~10% of known values, suggesting confidence to obtain global ϕ. This result opens the way to estimate global NPP based on AbPM, as well as various regional specifics. Further, ways forward to improve NPP estimation based on AbPM are discussed.

name: Microbial-DOM Coupling in Inland Waters in the Light of Biogeochemical Cycles
lead_organizer: Paola Ayala-Borda, University of Lethbridge
session_description: Microbial-DOM interactions and biogeochemical cycles (C, N, P, Fe, S, Hg) in inland waters; bridges molecular DOM characterization with microbial omics.

presentations.title: One year along a river continuum: seasonal variation of DOM quality and microbial diversity from the Andes to the Pacific
presentations.abstract_summary: Rapel catchment Chile, 25 sites: spring protein-like FDOM in headwaters → humic-rich downstream; Flavobacterium and hgcl clade dominate.
presentations.abstract: Mountain-to-ocean river continuums offer natural laboratories to explore DOM-microbe relationships across changing environmental gradients. We present one year of data on DOM dynamics and microbial diversity in the Rapel catchment, Central Chile, a Mediterranean semi-arid system shaped by strong hydrological gradients and anthropogenic pressures, extending from Andean headwaters to the Pacific coast. Seasonal sampling was conducted at 25 sites covering the main sub-watersheds and tributaries. At each site, water samples were collected for the analysis of dissolved organic carbon concentration (DOC), DOM optical properties (CDOM and FDOM), and microbial community composition (16S rRNA gene metabarcoding). Across this Andes-to-ocean system, FDOM reveals pronounced seasonal and topographic transitions, with spring protein-like signatures dominating higher-elevation headwaters and progressively shifting toward humic-rich compositions in lower valley sections from summer into autumn-winter. These patterns co-vary with microbial communities dominated by Flavobacterium and the hgcl clade , reflecting hydrological controls and biogeochemical transitions along the longitudinal gradient. Coupled multivariate and network analyses identified the main drivers of these dynamics and disentangled key processes underlying ecosystem functioning and stability. This work presents an integrative view of the relationships between DOM processing and microbial ecology along a river continuum, highlighting the value of a holistic approach to understanding riverine biogeochemistry.

presentations.title: Distinct pathways for intracellular and extracellular phosphorus entrapment in biofilms
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research - UFZ
presentations.abstract_summary: Mesocosm full-factorial experiment: intracellular P entrapment responds strongly to light via algal-bacterial interactions; extracellular not driven by labile carbon.
presentations.abstract: Entrapment of phosphorus (P) by benthic biofilms refers to all processes which retain P either extra- or intracellularly thereby causing a temporary reduction of P loads. Extracellularly entrapped P is associated with polymeric substances the cells are embedded in, while intracellular entrapment involves cellular uptake. In a previous study on benthic stream biofilms we found the ratio between intracellular and extracellular P entrapment to be negatively correlated with light, labile DOM and SRP. To disentangle the specific role of biofilm energy sources on P entrapment pathways, we performed a full-factorial mesocosm experiment using artificial flumes in a streamside river-bypass design, manipulating light availability and labile carbon supply. We found that intracellular P responded strongly to light, leading to the highest absolute P entrapment under maximum light exposure. Furthermore, high β-glucosidase and leucine aminopeptidase activities found in those treatments suggest that algal-bacterial interactions contribute to intracellular P entrapment. Contrary to expectations, there was no decrease in the ratio of intra- to extracellular P under increased supply of labile carbon and light, indicating that extracellular P entrapment was not primarily driven by microbial energy sources. These findings pave the way for more function-oriented studies linking intra- and extracellular P entrapment and microbial activity to the role of biofilms in riverine P retention.

presentations.title: Links between bacterioplankton community structure and key properties of DOM in lakes across Canada
presentations.abstract_summary: LakePulse 393 lakes: terrestrial DOM-dominated lakes have flat rank abundance and simpler bacterioplankton morphology; autochthonous DOM lakes show steeper dominance and complex morphologies.
presentations.abstract: Bacterioplankton and dissolved organic matter (DOM) are fundamental components of aquatic ecosystem function yet unravelling how these two components interact across freshwater ecosystems and along environmental gradients remains a major challenge. Here we explore the potential links between two aspects of bacterioplankton structure, the rank abundance structure, derived from 16SrRNA sequencing, and the morphological structure, derived from a cytometric approach, and the optical and molecular structure of DOM. These links were explored across 393 lakes in the context of the pan-Canadian LakePulse project, the first standardized, national lake survey that covered wide environmental, climatic and human impact gradients at a continental scale. Our results suggest that lakes dominated by terrestrially derived DOM and associated optical and molecular components are characterized by bacterioplankton communities with flat rank abundance curves (i.e. no marked dominance) and with simpler morphological structures (i.e. oblate shapes dominated by low-DNA structure and single cytometric populations). The opposite pattern was found in lakes with a larger fraction of autochthonous derived DOM, where bacterioplankton communities have steeper rank abundances curves (i.e. more marked taxa dominance) with more complex morphological structures (i.e. more diffuse, prolate shapes with distinct cytometric populations and dominance of high-DNA fractions). Overall, key aspects of bacterioplankton and DOM structures appear to covary along broad freshwater environmental gradients.

presentations.title: Fungal functional ecology across a DOC gradient in Canadian lakes
presentations.abstract_summary: NSERC LakePulse 249 lakes: shotgun metagenomics shows microbial eukaryotes >50% of reads; fungal CAZymes structure with DOM chemistry from forested to agricultural land.
presentations.abstract: Aquatic fungi play critical roles in organic matter decomposition, yet their ecological roles remain under studied in the context of carbon and nutrient cycling in freshwater ecosystems. The objective of our study was to link fungal gene diversity to dissolved organic matter (DOM) across a land use gradient. We applied shotgun metagenomics and parallel measurements of organic matter and its chemical composition on pelagic surface water samples from 249 lakes across Canada. These lakes are part of the NSERC Lake Pulse Network, which covered broad environmental, climatic, and land use gradients, ranging from forested to agricultural watersheds. Microbial eukaryotes accounted for over 50% of the metagenomic sequencing reads, providing a unique opportunity to link fungal functional potential to organic matter composition at an unprecedented continental scale. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) ranged from 1 to > 100 mg/L and the DOM composition gradient varied from a dominance of terrestrially-like aromatic and humic compounds in forested watersheds to lakes dominated by autochthonously-like pools in agricultural lands. This gradient provided a framework to assess the diversity of fungal carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZymes) genes that are involved in the breakdown of complex carbohydrates and link it to DOC chemistry, color, nutrients, and chlorophyll levels. Our findings highlight strong spatial and environmental structuring of fungal functional profiles, emphasizing their important role in organic matter transformation and broader lake biogeochemistry. This is the first continental-scale study to examine fungal gene functions in lakes, offering novel insights into how aquatic fungi contribute to freshwater carbon cycling.

presentations.title: [empty/withdrawn slot]
Going with the flow: how microbes shuffle nutrient cycles through a treatment wetland
presentations.abstract_summary: Frank Lake treatment wetland (Alberta) metagenomics: N-, Fe-, S-, CH4-cycling genes follow redox gradient across basins; N-cycling drives all other elemental cycles.
presentations.abstract: Treatment wetlands mitigate the impacts of eutrophication derived from wastewater inputs by supporting microbial communities that oxidize and reduce pollutants. Because individual elements are processed under different redox conditions, multiple biogeochemical cycles can occur in parallel or sequentially along horizontal gradients, but their coordination remains unclear. Here, we tested whether element processing follows predictable patterns shaped by redox dynamics. Using metagenomics, we identified and quantified genes involved in nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), iron (Fe), sulfur (S), and methane (CH₄) cycling in surface sediments across three basins (1–3) of the Frank Lake treatment wetland (Alberta, Canada). Denitrification and anaerobic ammonium oxidation genes were most abundant near the effluent source, where Basin 1 removed the majority of NO₃⁻, NO₂⁻, and NH₄⁺. Genes associated with Fe and S cycling increased in Basins 1 and 2, while S- and CH₄-cycling genes were elevated in Basin 3. These shifts followed a predictable sequence tied to the redox gradient as electron acceptors were progressively depleted, and they aligned with changes in solute concentrations. High inorganic N loads in Basin 1 exerted strong control on microbial community function, with N-cycling genes correlating with all other elemental cycles along the gradient. Our results provide mechanistic insight into how Frank Lake processes wastewater pollutants and highlight the significant ecosystem service it provides to Alberta.

name: Sediment Derived Nutrients, Cyanobacteria and Climate Change
lead_organizer: Gertrud Nürnberg, Freshwater Research
description: As a sediment researcher, nutrient (P and N) specialist, or someone studying eutrophication and cyanobacteria proliferation in lakes world-wide, we invite you to participate in this special session. More and more knowledge has come to light that involves legacy nutrients in lake sediments in the proliferation of cyanobacteria.

presentations.title: Investigating the impact of sediment derived nutrients on cyanobacteria during climate change (Tutorial/Overview)
presentations.abstract: Legacy nutrients in lake sediments appear to be increasingly associated with cyanobacteria proliferation and dynamics, particularly under the accelerating pressures of climate change. Specifically, internal phosphorus loading is released from anoxic sediment surfaces via reduction processes at the sediment-water interface and via mineralization processes. This release varies with productivity and can fertilize a lake throughout the summer or later in the fall, depending on the lake's stratification regime. Internal load has been increasing due to climate change, which also increases disturbance events, water and sediment temperature, water column stability, and hypoxia among other lake characteristics. Thus, sediment-derived nutrients (especially of phosphorus, but also of nitrogen via mineralization processes) may give a boost to cyanobacteria proliferation during important seasons in conjunction with increased development and climate change. Different investigative approaches support the main hypothesis that the recent increase of cyanobacteria is partially fueled by internal loading.

presentations.title: LEGACY NUTRIENTS AND CLIMATE PRESSURES AS DRIVERS OF CYANOBACTERIA DOMINANCE: INSIGHTS FROM THREE DECADES OF PHYTOPLANKTON DATA
presentations.affiliation: FB Environmental Associates / University of New Hampshire
presentations.abstract: Legacy nutrient stores in lake sediments are increasingly recognized as a critical—but often under-quantified—driver of cyanobacteria bloom dynamics, particularly under the accelerating pressures of climate change. Warming surface waters, prolonged stratification, and more frequent drought or extreme storm events can intensify internal phosphorus loading and amplify cyanobacterial growth during ecologically sensitive periods. This presentation utilizes a three-decade phytoplankton record from over 150 New Hampshire lakes to examine shifts in phytoplankton community assemblages, with the hypotheses that (1) cyanobacteria have gained dominance relative to other major taxa, altering community diversity and seasonal succession that reinforces eutrophication, and (2) the transition to a cyanobacteria-dominated state under a changing climate is driven by biogeochemical and physical lake characteristics that augment internal phosphorus loading.

presentations.title: Short-term thermal stratification drives hypoxia, nutrient release and cyanobacterial dynamics in a shallow polymictic lake
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract: Many shallow lakes experience intermittent periods of thermal stratification during warm and low-wind conditions, yet the chemical and biological consequences of these events are understudied compared to deep lakes. To understand the role of short-term stratification events in hypoxia formation, sediment nutrient release and cyanobacterial growth, we studied 47-years of weekly monitoring data together with 21-years of high-frequency sensor measurements from the shallow Lake Müggelsee. The lake has undergone 87% and 79% reductions in external loading of TN and TP and the phytoplankton community is regularly N-limited in summer. Thermal stratification was episodic and rarely exceeded a consecutive period >10 days. However, frequent bottom-water hypoxia occurred which coincided with hypolimnetic enrichment of SRP and NH4+. High temporal resolution measurements of O2 and SRP demonstrate large and rapid fluctuations. The nature and timing of these fluctuations is consistent with internal wave activity. Horizontal transport from deeper lake regions dominates oxygen and nutrient dynamics across much of the lake's area. These nutrient pulses are of increased importance to cyanobacteria given the low external inputs. We argue that N2 fixing cyanobacteria are particularly disadvantaged by pulsed N dynamics which may explain the overall reductions in cyanobacterial biomass.

presentations.title: Exploring the role of oscillating sediment redox conditions on internal phosphorus loading in lake ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Climate change is expected to introduce intermittent thermal stratification and bottom water anoxia to previously well-mixed and oxygenated lakes, altering the reduction-oxidation (redox) conditions at the sediment-water interface and facilitating a cascade of biogeochemical processes that alter ecosystem structure and function. Frequent mixing with anoxic bottom waters, termed anoximixis, has been shown to facilitate internal phosphorus (P) loading and cyanobacterial blooms; however, while internal P loading has been well described, knowledge gaps remain in understanding how the frequency of anoximictic events creates oscillations between oxic and anoxic environments which in turn influences the rate of internal P loading and the potential for sediments to sequester or mobilize P. In this study, we paired high-resolution monitoring of lake oxy-thermal structure with laboratory incubations of sediment cores under oxic, anoxic, and oscillating conditions to directly measure the effects of anoximixis on internal P loading rates.

presentations.title: HIGH-FREQUENCY IN-SITU MONITORING REVEALS TEMPERATURE-DRIVEN PULSED INTERNAL PHOSPHORUS DYNAMICS IN A SHALLOW POLYMICTIC LAKE
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research – UFZ
presentations.abstract: Internal phosphorus (P) loading remains a key challenge for managing eutrophication in shallow lakes, yet the short-term interactions between temperature, oxygen, and algal activity are rarely resolved. Using sub-hourly, high-frequency in-situ measurements of soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP), dissolved oxygen (DO), chlorophyll-a, temperature, and other physico-chemical parameters, this study reveals temperature-driven pulsed P dynamics in a shallow polymictic lake over a full seasonal cycle. Based on surface temperature trends, three distinct thermal phases were identified: Rising (spring warming to 20 °C), High (≥ 20 °C stable summer conditions), and Decreasing (post-peak cooling below ~20 °C). During the High-temperature phase, an exponential SRP–DO relationship (R² = 0.73) indicated strong redox-mediated P release under hypoxia. In contrast, the Rising and Decreasing phases showed short-lived SRP peaks that typically preceded algal growth or coincided with brief mixing events that may have enhanced P availability, suggesting that physical disturbance and subsequent changes in phytoplankton activity jointly modulate short-term P dynamics.

name: From Immediate Shocks to Long-Term Shifts: Terrestrial Disturbances and Aquatic Ecosystem Responses
lead_organizer: Guillaume Grosbois, Université du Québec en Abitibi-Témiscamingue
co_organizers: Hélène Masclaux, Université de Bourgogne Franche-Comté
description: Freshwater ecosystems are essential components of global landscapes and are closely connected to their terrestrial surroundings through complex physicochemical, biological and ecological interactions. One of the strongest links between terrestrial and aquatic environments is the substantial transfer of organic matter and energy from land to lakes.

presentations.title: Darkening waters: climate-induced shifts in precipitation and DOM reduced phytoplankton but not zooplankton in dimictic boreal lakes
presentations.abstract: This study examines the extent to which temporal (1980 – 2019) increases in precipitation drove dissolved organic matter (DOM) loads and lake concentrations, and evaluates implications to physical, chemical and biological variables within dimictic boreal lakes at the IISD Experimental Lakes Area, Canada. Long-term increases in precipitation (c. +27%) were associated with increased DOM loads and lake concentrations (c. +9%). Increased DOM within dimictic lakes over time was associated with shallower thermocline depths (c. -17%) and euphotic depths (c. -13%), reduced mean light intensity in the water column (c. -20%), reduced depth-integrated phytoplankton biomass (c. -32%) but increased epilimnetic chlorophyll a concentration (c. + 27%), and we detected no significant temporal declines in crustacean zooplankton.

presentations.title: REGIONAL DIFFERENCES IN BROWNING-INDUCED ELEMENTAL IMBALANCES IN ZOOPLANKTON
presentations.abstract: Lake browning, the increase in water color, is a serious concern for aquatic ecology and ecosystem services. It is caused by increased inflow of terrestrial dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in tandem with nutrients, iron and other elements from the lake catchment, thereby altering the transport and availability of various elements in lakes. Drivers behind lake browning include climatic change, land-use change and recovery from acidification, which may be disproportionately important in different regional settings. To assess elementome wide shifts in browning lakes, we studied the elemental composition of water and zooplankton in 42 small lakes or ponds with inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The lakes were chosen from pristine areas to exclude the impact of land use, but are located in three regions expected to differ in their browning mechanisms: boreal Finland heavily affected by acidification, climate change impacted subarctic Finland, and permafrost thaw impacted Arctic Canada.

presentations.title: Freshwater browning : Effect on growth and metabolism of juvenile brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis)
presentations.affiliation: Institut national de la recherche scientifique
presentations.abstract: Freshwater browning from increasing chromophoric dissolved organic matter (cDOM) alters shortwave radiation and thus impacts food web dynamics. Yet, its direct physiological effects on fish remain poorly understood, albeit juvenile salmonids are highly sensitive to shortwave radiation. Juvenile brook trout (n = 108; 6.5 ± 1.2 g; 8.7 ± 0.6 cm) were reared for 64 days at 14 °C under 14L:10D cycles in nine tanks (3 Control: CG, 3 Low humic: LH, 3 High humic: HH; a₃₂₀ = 0.1, 20, 60 m⁻¹). Mass was measured throughout the experiment. Under the same conditions as during rearing, we estimated standard (SMR) and maximum metabolic rates using intermittent flow respirometry on 77 fish and subsequently calculated aerobic scope (AS, mg O₂ h⁻¹). No differences were observed between groups' final body mass and overall growth rate. However, Fulton's condition factor decreased with increasing cDOM.

presentations.title: LONG-TERM LIMNOLOGICAL EFFECTS OF SPRUCE BUDWORM DEFOLIATION NEAR SEPT-ÎLES, QUEBEC: A PALEOECOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVE
presentations.abstract: The eastern spruce budworm (SBW) is a species of moth native to North America whose larvae feed on balsam fir and spruce trees. Outbreaks occur every ~30-40 years, during which time larval numbers increase from approximately 5 to 20,000 per tree. These outbreaks cause mass loss of needles and repeated annual defoliation that can lead to widespread tree death. Though the terrestrial impacts of SBW have been rigorously studied, the effects of SBW on lake systems are poorly understood. This project aimed to reconstruct the long-term impacts of SBW outbreaks on lakes in the Sept-Îles region (Côte Nord, Quebec), an area that experienced severe and sustained SBW defoliation between 2007 and 2020, using paleolimnological techniques.

presentations.title: The influences of land disturbances on lake water quality and food webs in managed boreal forests: an overview
presentations.abstract: The boreal biome contains dense aquatic networks closely linked to surrounding forests. Here, I synthesize recent findings from eastern Canadian managed forests on how land disturbances affect lake ecosystems. Forest harvesting, especially clearcutting, degrades water quality by increasing organic matter and nutrient inputs. We showed that 20-m riparian buffers are often insufficient, particularly when affected by windthrow and ruts, allowing long-lasting water degradation. Clearcutting also elevates lake greenhouse gas emissions, with CO2 spikes in the first post-harvest year. Resulting nutrient loads can promote harmful algal blooms, which we found may dominate year-round, even under ice.

presentations.title: TRACING THE PATHWAYS FROM URBANIZATION TO ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONING IN STREAMS
presentations.abstract: Streams are tightly connected to surrounding landscapes, making them highly vulnerable to urban pressures. Yet the mechanisms through which urbanization alters ecosystem functioning remain insufficiently understood. We examined how impervious cover (IC) shapes abiotic conditions, macroinvertebrates communities, trophic structure, and organic matter decomposition across two comparable North American river systems spanning an IC gradient. Using a pathway analysis framework, we quantified direct and indirect effects of IC on stream functioning. IC directly degraded water quality and indirectly restructured macroinvertebrate assemblages and trophic niches. Despite declining macroinvertebrate diversity, decomposition rates increased with IC, a pattern that runs counter to expectations from biodiversity - ecosystem functioning theory.

name: Complexity in Space and Time: From Optical Properties to Ecosystem Processes
lead_organizer: Carina Seitz, University of Nevada Reno
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada Reno
Catherine O'Reilly, University of Minnesota Duluth
description: Inland water ecosystems and their watersheds are constantly reshaped by the complex interplay of their physical, chemical, and biological connections. In the face of accelerating environmental change, lake and river ecosystems are undergoing unprecedented transformations.

presentations.title: The nonpareil chlorophyll fluorescence measurement to study primary producers from cells to ecosystems and beyond
presentations.abstract: While chlorophyll fluorescence has no raison d'être, its measurement is incredibly powerful and unique in aquatic sciences. It allows the study of both the biomass of primary producers and their photosynthetic capacity or more broadly their photophysiology. With appropriate instruments and platforms, this can be done from single cells to ecosystem scale with applications ranging from picoseconds to years. After reviewing basic theory, in this tutorial, I will provide several vignettes to illustrate key applications of its use both from the literature and from our work.

presentations.title: Mapping optical complexity: Multi-scale limnodiversity of lakes and ponds across thawing permafrost landscapes
presentations.abstract: Arctic and Subarctic landscapes are undergoing rapid transformations due to climate warming and permafrost thaw, but the heterogeneity of their millions of small waterbodies poses a major challenge for understanding their collective importance to global biogeochemistry and feedbacks. To address this complexity, we developed a multi-scale remote sensing framework integrating PlanetScope, Sentinel-2, and Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) data, enabled by a deep learning model (Mask R-CNN), to automatically detect, delineate, and classify the optical properties of water bodies across a boreal forest-tundra permafrost gradient in northern Quebec (Nunavik, subarctic Canada). Our landscape-scale analysis revealed a region of exceptional aquatic abundance and diversity, mapping 335,281 water bodies, over 90% of which were smaller than 0.01 km².

presentations.title: SPATIAL AND VERTICAL COMPLEXITY OF OPTICAL PROPERTIES AND PARTICLE DYNAMICS IN LAKE TAHOE
presentations.affiliation: Centro Regional Universitario Bariloche-Universidad Nacional del Comahue
presentations.abstract: Lake Tahoe's clarity is influenced by sediment, nutrients, and biological processes, but uncertainties remain about variations in particle composition and optical properties across space, depth, and time. We performed an integrated assessment of optical and particle-size characteristics in Lake Tahoe (USA) over different seasons, using spectrophotometric absorption (CDOM, total, non-algal, and algal particulate matter), light attenuation (Kd, c), water-quality measures, and high-resolution particle-size distributions (LISST 200X) across three littoral and three pelagic sites. Our initial analyses reveal clear spatial and vertical differences in absorption and particle concentrations.

presentations.title: Reconstructing phytoplankton absorption spectra: a comparison of lakes with contrasting optical characteristics and latitudes
presentations.affiliation: Laboratoire d'Oceanographie de Villefranche, Sorbonne Université, CNRS
presentations.abstract: The optical properties of inland waters reflect the biological and physicochemical properties. Techniques to quantify these properties are advancing rapidly, yet the high optical diversity of limnic ecosystems demands a broader latitudinal coverage. Canada spans temperate to polar climates, with diverse hydrology and over a million lakes ranging from turbid and eutrophic to extremely clear. Uruguay, entirely situated in a subtropical climate, is dominated by shallow lakes and reservoirs with extreme optical complexity driven by cyanobacteria blooms, high sediment loads, and variable hydrology. In this work, we invert particulate absorption spectra into end-members representing phytoplankton groups and non-algal particulates across Canadian and Uruguayan waters.

presentations.title: LÉXPLORE: ADVANCING MULTIDIMENSIONAL OBSERVATIONS OF LAKE ECOSYSTEM PROCESSES
presentations.abstract: LéXPLORE is a state-of-the-art floating platform on Lake Geneva that enables high-frequency, multidimensional observations of lake processes. It integrates advanced in situ sensors, profiling systems and meteorological instruments to capture interactions across physical, chemical, and biological domains from surface to depth. Real-time open data on parameters, including temperature, oxygen, chlorophyll-a, waves, and water currents, support cross-disciplinary research on lake processes and their responses to environmental forcing. Since 2019, more than 70 projects have addressed topics from ecosystem functioning, physical mixing, carbon cycling, and pollution by microplastics.

name: Breaking the Flow: Biogeochemical Responses of Riverine Carbon and Nutrients to Anthropogenic Disturbances and Extreme Events
lead_organizer: João Miguel Merces Bega, University of São Paulo
description: Rivers and streams act as reactive conduits for carbon and nutrients transport from terrestrial landscapes to coastal systems. Increasing anthropogenic pressures and extreme events are affecting the natural capacity of catchments to sequester and transform carbon, remediate excess nutrients, and host key biogeochemical processes.

presentations.title: Global synthesis of river silicon dynamics shows long-term change, with seasonality and relationships to discharge linked to land use and land cover
presentations.abstract: The substantial role of land cover in altering nutrient availability in aquatic ecosystems has been widely documented. However, compared to changes in nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), changes in dissolved silicon (DSi) remain comparatively understudied, despite growing evidence that human activities alter riverine Si concentrations, fluxes, and seasonality. To address these uncertainties, our team has created the Global Aggregation of Stream Silica (GlASS) dataset, which includes stream nutrient (Si, N, P) chemistry, discharge and watershed characteristics from >300 rivers across all seven continents. We document long-term changes in annual river Si dynamics that differed across land use/cover types, with trends most apparent in high latitude and alpine systems.

presentations.title: THE RISE AND FALL OF AN ALPINE GEOHAZARD CASCADE FOR WATER QUALITY IN COASTAL BRITISH COLUMBIA, CANADA
presentations.abstract: In alpine watersheds globally, glacier retreat has resulted in the simultaneous expansion of meltwater-formed lakes and the destabilization of mountain slopes, the combination of which has potentially major yet rarely documented impacts on water quality in downstream ecosystems. On November 28th 2020, an 18 million m3 landslide hit the proglacial lake that feeds Elliot Creek in the Coast Mountains of British Columbia, Canada resulting in an instantaneous, 100-m high wave in the lake and an outburst flood. From 2017 to 2023, we combined near monthly samples of carbon, nutrients, and trace metals with discharge in the Southgate River and the adjacent, unimpacted Homathko River. Remarkably, dissolved constituents were largely unaffected by the event, while elevated fluxes of particulate parameters persisted during summer peak flows for only two years.

presentations.title: Land use and erosion effects on nutrient retention in tropical headwater streams
presentations.abstract: Headwater streams are tightly coupled to their surrounding landscapes and play a critical role in regulating nutrient fluxes from terrestrial to aquatic ecosystems. This study assessed the relative effects of anthropogenic land use, erosion, and elevation on the retention and transport of key nutrients in headwater streams of the Rwenzori Mountains, Uganda. Erosion emerged as the dominant control on nutrient dynamics, exerting a stronger influence than land use. Sites affected by high erosion showed reduced nutrient retention, likely driven by decreased algal biomass due to sedimentation and increased turbidity.

presentations.title: When Rivers Run Wild: Contrasting Carbon Pools and Turbidity Dynamics During Flood Events in Human-Influenced Rivers
presentations.abstract: Flooding events are expected to intensify with climate change, affecting carbon and sediment dynamics, with direct implications for drinking water treatment. Working with regional treatment facilities, we examined how hydrological variability shapes dissolved organic carbon (DOC), turbidity, and dissolved organic matter (DOM) quality in three rivers of the southern St. Lawrence basin (Québec, Canada). Most variables (DOC, humic-like components, turbidity) showed transport-limited responses, reflecting mobilization of terrestrial material during events, while protein-like components tended toward dilution.

presentations.title: Landcover and hydrology drive landscape C balance in pristine tropical headwaters
presentations.abstract: Landscape carbon (C) balance is central to understanding exchanges between terrestrial and aquatic C pools, yet limited paired observations of terrestrial and aquatic C fluxes hinder accurate assessments of landscape-scale C dynamics. Our study focuses on two long-term monitoring sites with paired high-frequency aquatic and terrestrial C flux measurements in two contrasting tropical headwater catchments: a fire-prone wet-dry savanna and a humid rainforest, both with perennial streamflow. The savanna catchment had a much larger reduction in its net landscape C balance relative to the rainforest catchment.

presentations.title: Effects of riparian forest restoration on in-stream carbon fluxes in tropical headwater catchments
presentations.abstract: In southeastern Brazil, the Atlantic Forest and Cerrado biomes have undergone extensive restoration efforts aimed at recovering ecosystems and biodiversity. Riparian revegetation is particularly crucial, as it helps maintain the structure and functioning of headwater streams that sustain larger river systems. Here, we evaluated how riparian forest restoration in tropical catchments influences in-stream gaseous carbon fluxes, specifically carbon dioxide and methane. Research was carried out in two contrasting watersheds: the Corumbataí River Basin and the Upper Paraíba Valley.

name: Connecting Habitats: Understanding Hydrological Connectivity Effects on Biological Systems Through Omics
lead_organizer: Jérôme Comte, INRS
description: Water bodies are interconnected within hydrological networks linking aquatic habitats to each other and to the terrestrial environment, enabling the movement of water, nutrients, organisms, and energy across the landscapes. Omics technologies are transforming our capacity to investigate connectivity by enabling detailed tracking of microbial communities and functions.

presentations.title: Understanding the long-term trajectory of antibiotic resistance gene variants in wastewater
presentations.abstract: Given global concerns about increasing antimicrobial resistance in human pathogens, it is critical that we understand how antibiotic resistance develops and spreads in urban environments. Within connected water systems, wastewater surveillance is one potentially useful method of tracking the diversity of antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) variants present in a community. To assess changes in wastewater ARG variants, both temporally and spatially, we performed CRISPR-enhanced metagenomics targeting ARGs on a 12-year time series of wastewater influents from two Milwaukee wastewater treatment plants. We find evidence of both seasonal and temporal changes in ARG variant composition in both treatment plants.

presentations.title: Tracking Ecological function and source identification using advance genomics in the western Lake Ontario watershed, Ontario Canada
presentations.abstract: Urbanized regions of watersheds feeding the Great Lakes can experience rapid shifts in their ecological condition due to anthropogenic influence. In collaboration with environmental government monitoring strategies, additional research applying 16S rRNA metabarcoding and metatranscriptomics was determined from sediment samples collected within a spatial gradient of 11 tributaries. In this study microbial bioindicators and functional traits were determined for a range impacted watersheds and land use.

presentations.title: FROM PEAT TO PONDS: LANDSCAPE HETEROGENEITY DRIVES METABOLIC NETWORKS AND GREENHOUSE GAS RELEASE FROM THAWING PERMAFROST
presentations.abstract: As permafrost landscapes degrade, they transform into a hydrological mosaic of dry palsas, collapsing thermokarst slumps, and water-saturated ponds. We investigated greenhouse gas (CO2, CH4, N2O) production potentials across several permafrost thaw gradients in sub-Arctic peatlands of Northern Norway, linking landscape-scale changes to genome-resolved metabolic networks. We show that the shift from oxic to anoxic conditions triggers a non-linear restructuring of the microbial network, where less efficient central metabolism drives high N2O and CH4 yields but suppressed CO2 production.

presentations.title: CHANGES IN LANDSCAPE CONNECTIVITY AND IMPACTS ON MICROBIAL DIVERSITY AND ARCTIC FRESHWATER ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONING
presentations.abstract: Most of the lakes on Earth are located in Arctic and sub-Arctic regions. Rapid climate warming in the Arctic is promoting both lake expansion and shrinkage depending on the location, altering landscape connectivity among aquatic ecosystems. Using metagenomics, we investigated how landscape connectivity influences the dispersal of bacteria and the genes they carry. We focus on two continuous permafrost regions in Canada: Bylot Island, Nunavut, where the number of lakes is increasing, and Ts'udé Nilįné Tuyeta protected area.

presentations.title: Unraveling the Role of Plasmids in Eco-Evolutionary Trajectories of Permafrost-Connected Thermokarst Ponds
presentations.abstract: With climate change, the thawing of permafrost leads to the formation of thermokarst ponds, which are recognized as sources of greenhouse gas emissions and can release metallic compounds. Mobile genetic elements such as plasmids, which are known to evolve rapidly, may facilitate microbial adaptation as communities transition from terrestrial to aquatic habitats. A multilayer plasmid network based on genetic similarity highlights potential horizontal gene transfers between soils and thermokarst samples, and the emergence of a distinct plasmidome in coalescent ponds.

presentations.title: MICROBIOME ADAPTATION AND BIOGEOCHEMICAL CAPACITIES IN THE DEEP ANOXIC ZONE OF THORES LAKE, NUNAVUT, CANADA
presentations.abstract: Microbiome communities often dominate the short, truncated food webs of Arctic lakes, where they play a central role in biogeochemical cycling. Here, we investigated the vertical variations in Thores proglacial Lake microbiome, located on the northern coast of Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada. The lake bottom (60m) includes a pocket of anoxic and trace elements enriched water. These sharp physicochemical gradients create different ecological niches supporting taxonomically and functionally distinct microbial and viral communities.

name: Species Diversity and Community Shifts of Freshwater Phytoplankton Along Environmental Gradients
lead_organizer: Man Xiao, Nanjing Institute of Geography & Limnology, CAS
description: Lakes and reservoirs function as sentinel ecosystems, integrating and amplifying signals of environmental change through shifts in their biological communities. Phytoplankton communities, in particular, exhibit high sensitivity to environmental gradients.

presentations.title: A framework for linking phytoplankton phenology, traits, and model formulation to improve bloom prediction
presentations.abstract: Whilst there is a diversity of approaches for modeling phytoplankton blooms in aquatic systems, it can be argued that their accuracy in predicting the onset and manifestation of a bloom is still lagging behind what is needed to support effective management. We outline a new framework that integrates trait theory and ecosystem modeling to improve bloom prediction. This framework builds on the concept that the phenology of blooms is determined by the dynamic interaction between the environment and traits within the phytoplankton community. A case study is described for the Hawkesbury River, Australia.

presentations.title: Weathering the Storm: Metabolic Flexibility Buffers Change in Phytoplankton Communities After Extreme Weather Events
presentations.abstract: Extreme weather events such as storms, floods, and heatwaves can cause environmental change in lakes at accelerated rates, resulting in cascading effects on biodiversity, biogeochemistry, and community composition. We sampled four remote temperate lakes biweekly across three consecutive years. Increasing frequency and severity of disturbance events resulted in lowered phytoplankton biomass, increased allochthonous organic matter, and altered phytoplankton phenology.

presentations.title: Short-term nutrient enrichment triggers rapid phytoplankton reorganization: insights from a large drinking water source reservoir
presentations.abstract: Nutrient-driven shifts in phytoplankton communities are a key driver of harmful algal blooms, yet conditions that promote cyanobacterial dominance are difficult to predict across freshwater ecosystems. We conducted an in-situ microcosm experiment in eutrophic Danjiangkou Reservoir – China's primary water source for the South-to-North Water Division Project. Phosphorus emerged as the primary limiting nutrient. Notably, Aphanocapsa, Chroococcus and Microcystis species accounted for >80% of the cell concentration at 0.05P.

presentations.title: Environmental drivers of cyanobacteria harmful algal blooms and community succession in a temperate Australian reservoir
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacteria harmful algal blooms (cyanoHABs) are a growing global concern in freshwater ecosystems, driven by climate change, anthropogenic eutrophication, and flow modification. This study investigated the environmental factors that influenced the dynamics of cyanoHABs in Pindari Dam, a temperate reservoir in inland northern New South Wales, Australia, over two years. Spring and autumn cyanoHABs were dominated by the potential toxin producer Dolichospermum circinale. Microcystis aeruginosa and Microcystis flos-aquae succeeded Dolichospermum circinale as the dominant cyanobacteria in summer.

presentations.title: LONG-TERM PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITY DYNAMICS IN A HYPEREUTROPHIC RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Acton Lake is a hypereutrophic reservoir whose nutrient dynamics are shaped by external watershed loading and internal loading from gizzard shad. Over the past 25 years, declining external nitrate loads, due to increased conservation tillage in the watershed, and increasing nutrient contributions from gizzard shad have decreased dissolved N:P supply resulting in more frequent, stronger periods of N limitation. Preliminary results show that the long-term total biovolume of potential N fixers has increased.

presentations.title: Assessing bloom conditions along a transect between two river inflows in Western Lake Erie 2021-2025
presentations.affiliation: Cooperative Institute for Great Lakes Research
presentations.abstract: Following improvement of the harmful algal bloom impairment in the 1970s, Lake Erie began experiencing re-eutrophication in the 1990s. Western Lake Erie (WLE) is subject to high nutrient input from the Maumee River (MR) from the southwest and large, nutrient-poor discharge from the Detroit River (DR) from the north. We explored how water quality and the phytoplankton community changed along a transect between these inputs.

name: Plastic Pollution from Freshwaters to Oceans: Linking Occurrence to Ecological Impacts
lead_organizer: Veronica Nava, University of Milano-Bicocca
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada, Reno
description: The role of aquatic ecosystems in the global plastic cycle is increasingly acknowledged. Yet, the links and differences between freshwater and marine systems, particularly in how plastics are transported and their impacts, remain poorly understood.

presentations.title: RIVERS AS RESERVOIRS: RIPARIAN STORAGE AND FRAGMENTATION OF MACROPLASTICS DRIVE MICROPLASTIC TRANSPORT ACROSS LAND USE GRADIENTS IN A MEDITERRANEAN CATCHMENT
presentations.abstract: Mismanaged plastic waste has risen exponentially in recent decades. This study investigates how plastic transport and storage vary across riparian and benthic stream compartments under contrasting land use pressures in the Tordera catchment, Spain. Thirteen sites spanning forested, agricultural, and urban areas were surveyed for MacP occurrence and MicP transport in the water column. Forested sites showed consistently lower abundances of MacP than urban ones. Retention of MacP occurred mainly in riparian hotspots (67%), rather than in the river channel (<15%).

presentations.title: SEASONAL VARIABILITY OF SMALL-SIZED MICROPLASTICS (>10 µM) IN THE OTTAWA RIVER
presentations.abstract: Microplastics (MPs), plastic particles less than 5 mm in size, are a global environmental threat. This project assesses the current status of small-sized MPs (> 10 µm) in the Ottawa River, the main source of drinking water in the City of Ottawa. MP samples were collected on filter discs using Ocean Diagnostics' automated depth sampler at two locations: Petrie Island Main Channel and Petrie Island Bay. Fragmented MPs were dominated by polypropylene, polyethylene, and polyamide.

presentations.title: Quantifying and Characterizing Microplastics in Winyah Bay and North Inlet Estuaries, SC
presentations.abstract: Microplastics (1 μm to 5 mm) accumulate in the bodies of marine organisms and negatively impact their health. This study quantified, characterized, and compared microplastics in a protected estuary (North Inlet Estuary, South Carolina) and an estuary impacted by anthropogenic activities (Winyah Bay, South Carolina). Results indicate a significant difference in plastic abundance between North Inlet and Winyah Bay (p=0.03) and in composition (p = 0.006). Fibers were the most abundant plastic type in both estuaries.

presentations.title: PLASTIC POLLUTION IN LAKE ONTARIO: INPUT, FATE, AND RISK TO ECOSYSTEMS AND PEOPLE
presentations.abstract: In the Great Lakes region of the US, plastic pollution rivals the oceans and is growing. The Lake Ontario Center for Microplastics and Human Health, a Center for Oceans and Human Health, brings together environmental and human health scientists to address this gap in knowledge with the overarching hypothesis that spatial and temporal environmental heterogeneity in the watershed and the lake will influence the input, transformation, fate, and impact of plastic pollution. Results to date indicate that environmental heterogeneity drives input, fate and impact of plastic pollution.

presentations.title: MICROPLASTICS RAPIDLY SINK AND BEACH IN A WHOLE-LAKE EXPERIMENT
presentations.abstract: Addressing the global problem of microplastic pollution requires a better understanding of their transport and fate in aquatic ecosystems. Here, we share an initial mass balance of microplastics within the first thirteen days of our whole-lake experiment. Within the first thirteen days, we demonstrate that microplastic fragments rapidly redistribute – exiting the water column and settling on the bottom and on the shorelines. At the 13-day sampling point, 4% of the plastic was in the water column, 23% on the shorelines, and 53% on deep bottom sediments.

presentations.title: Fate and recovery of polyamide microplastics in the sediments of an aquatic outdoor enclosure mesocosm experiment
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research - UFZ
presentations.abstract: Understanding microplastic exposure and effects in freshwater systems needs defined experiments under realistic and complex conditions with relevant particles. Polyamide microplastics (PA, 5-50 µm diameter) were applied in an outdoor enclosure mesocosm system in three different nominal concentrations and compared to control enclosures over a period of 12 weeks. Both image-based methods did not reveal changes in particle size distribution over time and achieved about 26% recovery in experimental samples.

name: Multiple Stressor Effects on Freshwater and Marine Ecosystems in a Changing Climate
description: The triple planetary crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution highlights the complexity of the effects of multiple stressors in aquatic ecosystems.
lead_organizer: Mechthild Schmitt-Jansen, Helmholtz-Centre for Environmental Research UFZ
co_organizers: Sabine Hilt, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
Peiyu Zang, Institute of Hydrobiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
