Juan Du, Yangtze River Fisheries Research Institute

presentations.title: CLIMATE OR LAND USE, WHAT ARE THE MOST IMPORTANT DRIVERS FOR DIFFERENT RUNOFF NUTRIENTS IN AN AGRICULTURAL WATERSHED?
presentations.abstract: To investigate nitrogen and phosphorus loading we used a 29-year nutrient dataset and climate data from PRISM. The most important driver of nutrient loading was some aspect of Precip. Total annual Precip was the most important predictor for TN load (RI=0.46) and NO3 load (RI=0.39). For TP and SRP the number of extreme rains in a year was the highest predictor.

presentations.title: Why ponds concentrate nutrients: the roles of internal features, land use, and climate
presentations.abstract: We examined 240 ponds across eight countries to assess how internal pond characteristics, surrounding land cover and livestock intensity, seasonal climatic variation and climate influence nutrient concentrations. Shallow ponds and short hydroperiods had higher TN and TP concentrations. Land use also played a significant role with agricultural intensity increasing nutrient concentration.

presentations.title: CLIMATE-LINKED CHANGES IN PHYSICAL AND BIOGEOCHEMICAL DRIVERS INTENSIFY HYPOXIA IN BOREAL LAKES
presentations.abstract: We analyzed ~55 years of data from four morphometrically different lakes at IISD-ELA. Mann-Kendall trend analyses showed a slight increase in mean hypolimnetic DO through time; however, indicators of oxygen depletion such as hypoxic volume, anoxic factor and areal hypolimnetic oxygen deficit also increased. Hypolimnetic DOC and particulate phosphorus increased over time.

presentations.title: TURNING UP THE HEAT AND THE NUTRIENTS: LINKING MICROBIAL DYNAMICS TO ECOSYSTEMS FUNCTIONING IN LAKE MICROCOSMS
presentations.affiliation: Institut national de la recherche scientifique (INRS)
presentations.abstract: We investigated how warming and nutrient enrichment affect microbial communities in microcosms using water from an oligotrophic and a eutrophic lake. Our preliminary results indicate that warming and nutrient enrichment act synergistically to reshape microbial composition and gene expression, promoting cyanobacterial dominance and increasing the metabolic activity of toxin producers.

presentations.title: SCORESBY SOUND, THE WORLD'S LARGEST FJORD SYSTEM, MAY LOSE KEY ECOLOGICAL SPECIES DUE TO GLOBAL CHANGE
presentations.abstract: Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida) is a key ecological species and the main forage fish in the Arctic. Ichthyoplankton and zooplankton surveys conducted in the fjord between 2022 and 2024 reveal a drastic decline in Arctic cod larvae abundance. Meanwhile, high abundances of the carnivorous copepod Paraeuchaeta glacialis were recorded. Our observations suggest that P. glacialis may prey on Arctic cod larvae.

name: Freshwater Springs: Hidden and Neglected Limnological Pearls
description: Freshwater springs are unique multiple ecotonal ecosystems harboring disproportionately high biological diversity. Despite this, springs are gravely threatened by unsustainable exploitation.
lead_organizer: Marco Cantonati, University of Bologna, BiGeA

presentations.title: TALKING ABOUT SPRINGS AT (ASLO-)SIL 20 YEARS LATER: HAS AWARENESS ABOUT THESE ECOSYSTEMS INCREASED AMONG LIMNOLOGISTS?
presentations.affiliation: Alma Mater Studiorum Università di Bologna - UniBO
presentations.abstract: In 2007 we organized a Special Session on springs at the SIL Congress in Montreal. Since then, >5 special sessions have been organized at major limnological meetings. The overall impression is that the global limnological community remains insufficiently aware and supportive of spring science and stewardship. Nevertheless, a growing global ecohydrogeological community is laying better foundations for deeper understanding.

presentations.title: TEMPERATURE VARIABILITY AFFECTS POPULATION FLUCTUATIONS AND RELATIVE ABUNDANCE OF FRESHWATER MACROINVERTEBRATES
presentations.abstract: In my talk I show that the coefficient of variation of the density of 57 freshwater non-emergent macroinvertebrate populations is significantly positively correlated with annual range in ambient water temperature. The relatively low population variabilities in thermally stable springs and springbrooks may also be the result of the relative constancy of other environmental factors.

presentations.title: INVASIVE MACROINVERTEBRATES IN BALKAN SPRING ECOSYSTEMS: A SYNTHESIS OF CURRENT KNOWLEDGE AND CASE‐STUDY INSIGHTS
presentations.affiliation: University of Niš, Faculty of Sciences and Mathematics
presentations.abstract: This study synthesizes knowledge on invasive macroinvertebrates in Balkan springs. Using two case-study species—Potamopyrgus antipodarum (in cold springs) and Melanoides tuberculata (in thermal springs)—we examined pathways through which invasive taxa affect native macroinvertebrates. Native gastropod assemblages differed between invaded and uninvaded springs.

presentations.title: Linking ecohydrogeology and conservation: defining strategic spring zones in the Emilia-Romagna Apennines (Italy)
presentations.abstract: Springs are keystone ecosystems hosting highly specialized communities. An ecohydrogeological framework was developed in two mountain regions of Northern Italy. Based on geological and hydrochemical characteristics, five main strategic zones were identified in the Emilia-Romagna Region. Building on almost 30 years of annual spring monitoring in the Adamello-Brenta Nature Park, a new long-term ecological research programme integrates Alpine and Apennine sites.

presentations.title: Should Springs Be Considered an Aquatic Biome? A Debate and Discussion
presentations.abstract: Springs are small but abundant ecosystems neglected in biome descriptions. Not fitting into existing classification, we debate if and how springs can be regarded as a global biome. Arguments in favor include springs being discrete ground and surface water linkages supporting unique assemblages, functioning as 'keystone ecosystems', and providing baseflow for most non-glacial rivers. Contrary points include their diverse, individualistic, ecotonal nature.

name: Exploring the Confluence of Data, Models, and Forecasts for Advancing Adaptive Management Strategies for Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Management of aquatic ecosystems often requires extrapolating beyond current conditions. Ecological models and forecasts are widely applied to provide managers with estimates of future aquatic ecosystem conditions.
lead_organizer: Cayelan Carey, Virginia Tech

presentations.title: Historical and cultural considerations for effective ocean forecasting: the American lobster fishery
presentations.abstract: Ecological forecasting is an emerging field for the ocean. Forecasting for the American lobster fishery has morphed from the 1970s to present in response to changes in science and technology. A multi-decadal review of news archives documents forecasts of lobster fishery collapse that were consistently dismissed as unreliable by industry. The history of forecasting in this fishery illustrates how forecasts happen in a social context.

presentations.title: LAKE HYPOXIA UNDER CLIMATE CHANGE: MODELING ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES IN MOEHNE RESERVOIR
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre For Environmental Research GmbH - UFZ
presentations.abstract: This study develops long-term lake ecosystem projections to anticipate oxygen dynamics under future environmental change. We apply an integrated workflow of climate projections with open-source lake physical and ecological modelling (GLM-AED2) to evaluate management strategies in the Moehne Reservoir. Simulations to 2100 test the effectiveness of nutrient input limits, aeration, vertical mixing, and selective withdrawal.

presentations.title: DEVELOPING SCENARIO-BASED, NEAR-TERM ITERATIVE FORECASTS TO INFORM WATER MANAGEMENT
presentations.abstract: We applied a near-term, iterative water quality forecasting system at Lake Alexandrina, Australia. Over ~2 years, forecasts accurately predicted lake level, water temperature, and salinity and outperformed null baseline models up to 10-30 days ahead. Alternative barrage management scenarios were particularly important during drier hydrological conditions and resulted in substantive changes to lake level and export of salt from the lake.

presentations.title: IDENTIFYING EFFECTIVE LAKE MANAGEMENT PATHWAYS USING TARGET-SEEKING OPTIMISATION
presentations.abstract: We designed a framework that combines the process-explicit lake ecosystem model PCLake+ with a differential evolution optimisation algorithm to identify management pathways based on stakeholder-identified targets and acceptable measures. We apply this approach to identify alternative pathways to desired futures as well as limits to achieving targets given environmental and socio-ecological constraints.

presentations.title: Using Statistical Tools and Near Real Time Data to Advance Harmful Algal Bloom Forecasts in Lake Erie
presentations.abstract: Since 2009, NOAA has been delivering cyanoHAB monitoring products and ecological forecasts for western Lake Erie. We developed evaluation metrics for forecasts using statistical and software tools (METplus) adapted from numerical weather forecasting. The developed evaluation metrics were used to test what types of model changes can deliver improvements to stakeholders.

name: Scaling up Freshwater Biodiversity Research Through Data Synthesis
description: While marine and terrestrial systems benefit from macroscale, multi-year community datasets, the freshwater realm has lagged behind due to fragmented monitoring efforts and the absence of standardized metadata formats.
lead_organizer: Celia Symons, University of California, Irvine
co_organizers: Rachel Pilla, Oak Ridge National Laboratory

presentations.title: PHYTOPLANKTON DIVERSITY IS STRONGLY RELATED TO MIXOTROPH PREVALENCE IN NORTH AMERICAN LAKES
presentations.abstract: We examined the influence of mixotroph prevalence on phytoplankton community diversity across more than 1500 North American lakes. Mixotroph prevalence was the most important predictor of diversity independent of lake geographic position or sampling date. Diversity was greatest at intermediate mixotroph prevalence, where we predicted ecological niche partitioning to be highest.

presentations.title: DECODING FRESHWATER BACTERIOPLANKTON STRUCTURE IN SOUTH AMERICA: CONTINENTAL PATTERNS ALONG CLIMATIC, TOPOGRAPHIC, AND LIMNOLOGICAL GRADIENTS
presentations.abstract: We analyzed bacterioplankton communities across a continental gradient of lentic systems. Bacterioplankton community composition differed significantly among ecoregions revealing a clear continental-scale biogeography modulated by broad-scale climatic conditions, topography and local limnological drivers.

presentations.title: Linking paleoecological and limnological databases to facilitate watershed- to continental-scale environmental change research
presentations.abstract: Here, we match data from LAGOS with the Neotoma Paleoecology Database. Through a series of rules, we matched ~59% of Neotoma US lacustrine sites to LAGOS lakes. For these ~3,600 matching sites, we integrated paleoecological data from Neotoma with contextual and environmental data from LAGOS. This integration enables future research into topics such as the effects of climate or invasive species on inland water bodies.

presentations.title: LAKE TROPHIC STATE MEDIATES PLANKTON FUNCTIONAL GROUP SIZE DISTRIBUTIONS ACROSS CANADA LAKES
presentations.abstract: We tested whether biomass-size relationships differed among functional feeding trait groups and by lake trophic states. We analyzed plankton biomass-size relationships in >500 Canadian lakes from the Lake Pulse dataset. Community size analyses showed that autotrophs and mixotrophs had significantly different biomass-size relationships that also differed among lake trophic states.

presentations.title: Long-term changes in freshwater zooplankton and phytoplankton biomass, biodiversity, and composition in lakes recovering from acidification
presentations.abstract: Here, we use a multi-decade dataset of water chemistry and planktonic biota in Adirondack State Park lakes. Our results show that some attributes such as dissolved organic carbon concentration, acid neutralizing capacity, and pH have increased, while other attributes such as nitrate, sulfate, aluminum, and calcium have declined over time. Aquatic biodiversity metrics for both phytoplankton and zooplankton have increased over time, but total biomass has remained constant or declined.

presentations.title: OPEN ACCESS LONG-TERM DATA OF PLANKTON COMMUNITIES, PRODUCTION, FOOD WEB STRUCTURE AND FORCING FACTORS ENABLE TRAIT-BASED DIVERSITY AND FOOD WEB RESEARCH
presentations.abstract: Lake Constance is a well-studied temperate lake making it suitable as a model system. The data set comprises 12-20 years of almost weekly microscopic counting of all plankton organisms, providing a high taxonomical and size resolution. The data set is extensively used for theory building in ecology, to develop concepts in population and community ecology, and to better understand pelagic ecosystems.

name: Remote Sensing of Inland Water Responses to Extreme Climatic Events: Local to Global Perspectives
description: The frequency and intensity of extreme climate events are increasing globally. Remote sensing provides a unique opportunity to detect, monitor and understand the impacts of these extreme events.
lead_organizer: Monica Pinardi, Institute for Electromagnetic Sensing of the Environment, National Research Council
co_organizers: Mariano Bresciani, Institute for Electromagnetic Sensing of the Environment, National Research Council

presentations.title: MITIGATING CLIMATE-DRIVEN ANOXIC EVENTS IN THE ORBETELLO LAGOON (TUSCANY, ITALY) BY EARLY DETECTION OF BIOMASS ACCUMULATION THROUGH SENTINEL-2 DATA
presentations.abstract: In this study, we explore and evaluate the potential of Sentinel-2 imagery for assessing benthic coverage and its evolution in the Orbetello lagoon, using a physics-based model inversion approach (SwamPy). We observe that dystrophic crises were consistently preceded by extensive macroalgal coverage during the colder months, highlighting the role of biomass as an early indicator of anoxic events.

presentations.title: Advancing SDG 6.3.2 Monitoring with Earth Observation: Early Development and Results of an Ambient Water Quality Indicator
presentations.abstract: Using the growing capabilities of Earth Observation, we developed a fully EO-based indicator for SDG 6.3.2 Level 2. The first version was implemented at Lake Tanganyika. We present an enhanced version, produced with the upgraded ESA Lakes_cci LWQ product, that adds aCDOM and phycocyanin and has been tested in 4 additional lakes.

presentations.title: Climate-driven biophysical responses in lakes revealed by long-term satellite observations
presentations.abstract: The Lakes_cci project provides harmonised satellite observations of key Lake Essential Climate Variables. The dataset delivers a 30-year time series with daily temporal and 1 km spatial resolution for more than 2,000 large lakes worldwide. This study highlights the contribution of the long-term Lakes_cci dataset across scales.

presentations.title: Remote sensing observed impacts of climate and human activities on water quantity and quality in reservoirs
presentations.abstract: This study takes Lake Qadisiyah in Iraq as a case to investigate how climate and human activities can impact the water quantity and quality. We expanded the same analysis to 20 reservoirs globally. We found that 45% of reservoirs' water level changes are mainly associated with droughts in the catchment, 30% of the reservoirs' Chl-a variations were associated with temperature, and 50% of the reservoirs' turbidity changes were related to precipitation.

presentations.title: INVESTIGATING CHANGES IN LAKE ICE COVER USING THE CCI LAKES GAP-FILLED PRODUCT
presentations.abstract: This study will showcase the new gap-filled version of the CCI Lakes Lake Ice Cover product. The gap-filled product removes cloud cover in the baseline CCI LIC product and replaces it with predicted observations of ice and water using a 3D convolutional neural network. The product is used to determine global trends in lake ice phenology across the 2000-2024 period, for more than 1300 lakes.

presentations.title: Primary production in the Baltic Sea – results of satellite remote sensing
presentations.abstract: In the context of the Baltic Sea, the SatBałtyk system, launched in 2015, allows for daily monitoring of PP. The average daily value of PP in the Baltic Sea showed seasonal variability, from about 5 mgC m-2day-1 in winter to more than 700 mgC m-2day-1 in July. The annual value of total primary production during the analysis period ranged from 37 to 45 million tons of coal per year.

name: Aquatic Pollution in an Era of Climate Change and Anthropogenic Stress
description: While the impacts of pollutants on aquatic organisms have been extensively studied, recent years have introduced a range of emerging environmental stressors that increasingly affect aquatic populations.
lead_organizer: Peleg Astrahan, IOLR

presentations.title: Impacts of Crude Oil on Bacteria Affect Metamorphosis in Marine Invertebrate Larvae
presentations.affiliation: UNIVERSIDAD DE LAS PALMAS DE GRAN CANARIA
presentations.abstract: In this study, we investigated the impact of acute exposure to sublethal, environmentally relevant concentrations of dispersed crude oil on competent planktonic larvae of the polychaete Hydroides elegans. Acute exposure to crude oil (1–5 µL L⁻¹) caused a significant reduction (up to eight-fold) in the metamorphic success of H. elegans larvae. The effects of oil were mediated through alterations of bacterial communities that trigger metamorphosis.

presentations.title: Marine Assets Face Disproportionate Risk from Offshore Hydrocarbon Spills: An Integrated Oil-Spill Modeling Assessment in the Eastern Mediterranean
presentations.abstract: We developed an integrated modeling framework that couples OpenOil weathering with OceanDrift Lagrangian transport to assess the potential impacts of medium-scale offshore hydrocarbon releases. Using Israel's Eastern Mediterranean Exclusive Economic Zone as a testbed, we simulated 144 spill scenarios. Results show that spill location is the dominant driver of impact severity. We recommend that pre-licensing, spatially explicit spill-risk evaluations be adopted as a standard requirement for offshore energy planning.

presentations.title: Effects of different bivalve species on plankton community and water quality in eutrophic waters
presentations.affiliation: Department of Ecology and Institute of Hydrobiology, Jinan University
presentations.abstract: Outdoor experiments were carried out in mesocosms with a small bivalve Corbicula fluminea, with a medium bivalve Cristaria plicata, with a large bivalve Sinanodonta woodiana, and without bivalve as controls. Compared with the bivalve-free control, the small, medium and large bivalves all reduced phytoplankton biomass with species-specific patterns. The large bivalve enhanced the biomass ratio of zooplankton to phytoplankton.

presentations.title: The synergistic effects of chronic gas condensate pollution and warming on the survival, performance and reproduction of the mussel Brachidontes pharaonis
presentations.abstract: This study is the first to examine the long-term impacts of chronic gas condensate pollution and seawater warming (+3.1 °C) on a sentinel bivalve species, Brachidontes pharaonis. While overall survival was high, physiological performance was notably affected: respiration and clearance rates declined significantly under gas condensate exposure. When combined with warming, these stressors produced synergistic negative effects.

presentations.title: Sediments as 'Pollutant Buses': Transport of Contaminants to Environmental Hotspots
presentations.abstract: Hydrophobic pollutants are common in aquatic environments. Our most recent study conducted at Lake Kinneret, Israel, revealed that the predominant pollutants in this environment originate from petrochemical sources or incomplete organic combustion pathways. We show that polluted sediments are not distributed homogenously in the lakebed but tend to accumulate in hotspots. We present a pilot application of Ozone Nanobubbles (NBO3) treatment, resulting in up to 99% oxidation rate of aromatic pollutants.

name: Headwaters as Windows of Opportunity: Connecting Disciplines and Processes to Understand Watershed Functions in a Rapidly Changing World
description: Headwater streams are fundamental links between terrestrial and aquatic systems. Despite their small size, headwaters make up the majority of river networks by length and disproportionately influence downstream flow.
lead_organizer: Audrey Campeau, Université de Montréal
co_organizers: Marcus Wallin, Swedish University of Agriculture

presentations.title: Sentinels of change: What headwater nitrate C-Q hysteresis reveals about watershed function in a rapidly changing world
presentations.abstract: Intact headwater streams are powerful sentinels of climate change. We test this idea using a network of 30 intact headwater streams spanning snow-dominated to rain-dominated temperate forests over four decades. We show that NO3- export regimes reorganize nonlinearly in response to relatively small shifts in climate and water balance.

presentations.title: IMPACTS OF THERMAL VARIABILITY IN MOUNTAIN STREAMS ON MULTITROPHIC METABOLIC RATES
presentations.abstract: In this study, we analyze in situ estimation of oxygen consumption rates of different fluvial ecosystem compartments in six mountain streams in the Deva-Cares and Sella catchments (Spain). Our preliminary results find that metabolic rate is more sensitive to increasing temperatures in thermally variable streams.

presentations.title: GLOBAL SYNTHESIS OF THE MAGNITUDES AND DRIVERS OF MOUNTAIN STREAM CO2 AND CH4 EMISSIONS
presentations.abstract: Mountain streams are an important source of uncertainty in global inland water carbon budgets. Here, we present preliminary results from a global synthesis of magnitudes and drivers of mountain stream CO2 and methane emissions. With data extracted from over 30 studies of mountain streams, we expect high CO2 and CH4 emissions in streams below the treeline and with decreasing catchment glacial cover.

presentations.title: SMALL STREAMS, BIG IMPACT: UNRAVELLING FISH BETA DIVERSITY IN NEW ZEALAND USING A NATIONAL-SCALE EDNA DATABASE
presentations.abstract: To understand if small streams host distinct fish assemblages, we analysed fish beta diversity across stream sizes using a publicly available eDNA database. Our results indicate that low order streams host more unique fish assemblages than medium or high order streams, despite having lower species richness.

presentations.title: HYPORHEIC PROCESSES ACROSS HEADWATERS OF A BOREAL STREAM NETWORK: PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CONTROLS OVER METHANE AND CARBON DIOXIDE CYCLING
presentations.abstract: Here we evaluate how local- and catchment-scale physical and chemical conditions shape patterns of hyporheic CH4 and CO2 concentrations across five headwater streams in the Krycklan Catchment Study, Sweden. Hyporheic CH4 concentrations varied ~1000-fold across sites and sampling campaigns, were ~60 times higher than in corresponding surface waters, and were inversely related to hyporheic dissolved oxygen.

presentations.title: Headwater stream macroinvertebrate community responses to novel riparian buffer design under forestry clear cutting
presentations.abstract: In this project, we investigated the effectiveness of different buffer alternatives at preserving biodiversity. Using harvest trials, we performed a BACI study, where we assessed macroinvertebrate community changes 1 year before and 1-3 years after harvest under four different buffer alternatives. Minimal differences in invertebrate richness and abundance between unharvested controls and buffered sites implied that all buffers mitigated the impact of forestry on aquatic biodiversity in the short term.

name: Stable Isotope Solutions to Aquatic Ecology Problems
description: Stable isotope techniques have become essential tools for disentangling ecological and biogeochemical processes in aquatic systems.
lead_organizer: Alexander Frank, University of Bayreuth
co_organizers: Johannes A.C. Barth, University of Erlangen-Nuremberg

presentations.title: AN INTERDISCIPLINARY APPROACH TO RIVER ECOSYSTEM MONITORING USING WATER-ASSOCIATED STABLE AND RADIOGENIC ISOTOPES IN NORTHEAST GEORGIA, USA
presentations.abstract: We used an interdisciplinary approach to monitoring river systems that incorporates water-associated isotope ratios in the Middle and North Oconee Rivers in Georgia during 2024. River isotopes could provide an interdisciplinary framework for evaluating river ecosystem health with less effort compared to traditional methods.

presentations.title: Isotopic models of CH4 oxidation in lakes
presentations.abstract: Methane emissions from aquatic ecosystems represent one of the largest yet least constrained natural sources of CH4. The objective of the paper is to offer some guidance on the type of isotopic model best suited to different experimental and environmental field conditions and to identify the adequate interpretation of the isotopic signal appropriate to each.

presentations.title: DETERMINING THE ROLE OF DISSOLVED ORGANIC MATTER AS A NUTRIENT RESOURCE IN FRESHWATER ECOSYSTEMS USING DUAL-LABELLED STABLE ISOTOPE PROBING
presentations.abstract: In two major UKRI research programmes, we have developed a novel stream experimental approach using dual-labelled stable isotope dosing at 1% enrichment in replicate mesocosms. Our 13C15N bulk data demonstrate three key principles, including that 15N-DON uptake occurs across all biotic groups at rates =/> inorganic 15N-DIN uptake. Our compound-specific isotope data reveal rapid (<2 h) uptake into protein biosynthesis.

presentations.title: Fatty acid hydrogen isotope ratios record large millenial-scale trophic changes on the southwest Greenland coast and their influence on carbon burial
presentations.abstract: We used the hydrogen isotope composition of short-chain fatty acids, extracted from a sediment core recovered on the southwest Greenland shelf, to reconstruct the prevalence of heterotrophy and the history of OC biodegradation over the past 12,000 years. Elevated hydrogen isotope ratios during the HTM imply increased heterotrophic OC biodegradation.

presentations.title: Stable isotope perspectives on nitrogen cycling along massively disturbed redox gradients during a Baltic Sea inflow event
presentations.abstract: During early spring 2024, an inflow of oxic, seawater from the North Sea disrupted the characteristically sharp redox gradients of the Baltic. We present data both from stratified basins and along the inflow front capturing the northward progression of redoxcline disruption.

presentations.title: SEEKING STABILITY: INHIBITORS FOR PRESERVING ISOTOPE RATIOS OF DISSOLVED GASES IN FRESHWATER SAMPLES
presentations.abstract: Mercury chloride is widely accepted as the best-performing preservative for samples but its use is restricted in some areas due to toxicity. To address this gap, we compared the time-dependent performance of silver nitrate, sodium azide, zinc chloride, benzalkonium chloride, and sterile-filtration. The findings provide practical guidance for aquatic ecologists to choose an effective and safe substitute for mercury chloride.

name: Urban Waters Under Pressure: Socio-Ecological Feedback and Anthropogenic Stressors in City Ponds, Streams, and Estuaries
description: Urban aquatic systems are hotspots of complex socio-ecological interactions facing mounting pressures from anthropogenic stressors.
lead_organizer: Maja Ilić, Institute of Zoology, University of Cologne
co_organizers: Kristien I. Brans, Vrije Universiteit Brussel
Zsófia Horváth, HUN-REN Centre for Ecological Research

presentations.title: UNCOVERING THE BIODIVERSITY OF GARDEN PONDS THROUGH CITIZEN SCIENCE
presentations.abstract: We worked with over 800 pond owners across Hungary in a large-scale citizen science project. Over 300 garden ponds were sampled using both conventional techniques and eDNA. We argue that small ponds should be recognised as integral to urban blue–green infrastructure.

presentations.title: Amphibian communities are structured by local management practices in garden ponds and spatial factors in public ponds
presentations.abstract: We assess differences in amphibian community composition between public and garden ponds. Species composition in garden ponds is primarily driven by local environmental factors, whereas in public ponds, spatial position plays a greater role in shaping community structure.

presentations.title: Fish and urban cover shape zooplankton communties in garden and urban ponds
presentations.abstract: Garden ponds hosted lower local and regional richness compared to urban ponds, but more than half of all zooplankton species were shared between the two pond types. Among local environmental variables, fish presence played an important role in shaping zooplankton communities in both urban and garden ponds.

presentations.title: In-lake Fountains May Increase Potentially Harmful Bioaerosols in Urban Airsheds
presentations.abstract: This research investigates the dispersal of potentially harmful waterborne bioaerosols from two urban ponds equipped with in-lake fountains. We used flow cytometry and 16S rRNA gene sequencing to evaluate microbial communities in both water and aerosol samples. Although no aerosolized cyanotoxins were detected, significant correlations were found between the bacterial taxa present in water and air samples.

presentations.title: The influence of development on urban freshwaters and implications for monitoring; the case of Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada
presentations.abstract: Here, we investigate urban lakes and wetlands in Halifax Regional Municipality. We establish a historical timeline through the analysis of biological indicators and water and soil quality parameters from 40 lakes. Chloride concentrations were significantly higher in deep-water samples than respective outlet samples, suggesting temporal sampling could be used to fingerprint road salt-impacted lakes.

presentations.title: Ancient urbanization, modern applications: A multiproxy paleolimnological assessment of Maya-occupied Lake Coba
presentations.abstract: We leverage a ~6800-year-old record from Lake Coba (Quintana Roo, MEX). The initial period of urban development was characterized by 400% increases in phosphorus from the previous agricultural period. These results indicate that primary producer responses to pollutant reduction in modern urban ecosystems might be significantly delayed.

name: Emerging Directions in Community-Based Water Monitoring, Participatory Science, and Transdisciplinary Engagements
description: Community-based water monitoring (CBWM) and participatory approaches have long played a role in increasing the scale and scope of data collection.
lead_organizer: Edward Millar, University of Windsor
co_organizers: Andrew Bramburger, Environment & Climate Change Canada

presentations.title: Michigan's Cooperative Lakes Monitoring Program: Lessons learned over 50 years of community science for research and conservation
presentations.abstract: For the past 51 years, community science volunteers have collected ecological data on lakes through the Cooperative Lakes Monitoring Program. We will provide a brief history of the program from its origin as a water transparency monitoring program to today, when volunteers can choose from a variety of water quality and habitat attributes to monitor.

presentations.title: UNEQUAL WATERS: HOW COMMUNITY DEMOGRAPHICS SHAPE WATER MONITORING EFFORTS AND LAKE ACCESS IN THE U.S.
presentations.abstract: Using the LAGOS-US HUMAN module, we explored the relationships between racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic demographics of lake communities, lake accessibility, and the sources of lake monitoring data. We found that boat launches are less likely to be present in marginalized communities, showing access inequality. Additionally, these lakes are less likely to be sampled by CBWM programs.

presentations.title: Strengthening Community-based Water Monitoring through DataStream's open data platform
presentations.abstract: DataStream is a free, open-access platform for sharing water and sediment quality data in a standardized format. Today, over 50 million water quality observations collected by more than 300 initiatives can be accessed on DataStream.

presentations.title: Lake Erie Rangers: community monitoring, local knowledge, and emerging methods in a transdisciplinary watershed program
presentations.abstract: The Lake Erie Rangers program (2024–2027) supports community engagement in systematic water quality and stewardship activities across the Lake Erie basin. Volunteers contribute frequent monitoring and related stewardship actions while data are shared via Water Rangers and to the Great Lakes DataStream, with nearly 10,000 datapoints from 160+ locations to date.

presentations.title: Under Thin Ice: A story of Extreme Citizen Science, Collaboration, Exploration, and Discovery
presentations.abstract: Here, we describe a novel twist on citizen science, wherein highly skilled volunteer ice-divers worked alongside researchers to collect samples from an otherwise inaccessible environment. During February 2024, we conducted complementary water column, sympagic, and benthic sampling in 4 bays in Lake of the Woods. Preliminary findings demonstrate that the ice-associated community is unique and highly important to year-round lake function.

presentations.title: A PARTICIPATORY SCIENCE NETWORK TO MONITOR CHLORIDE AND HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS IN RURAL MINNESOTA LAKES
presentations.abstract: Minnesota Sea Grant and the Natural Resources Research Institute are leading a community-based monitoring initiative targeting chloride contamination and harmful algal blooms. We are developing a participatory science network engaging trained volunteers across rural Minnesota lakes.

name: Global Examples and Perspectives for Improving Lake and Reservoir Water Quality
description: Lakes face increasing pressures from human activities and climate change. This session focuses on sharing global examples for improving lake and reservoir water quality.
lead_organizer: Danielle Wain, 7 Lakes Alliance
co_organizers: Brian Ginn, Lake Simcoe Region Conservation Authority

presentations.title: DECREASING WATER LEVELS IN LAKES AND RESERVOIRS PROMOTE INCREASING PHYTOPLANKTON LEVELS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
presentations.abstract: We conducted a systematic literature review to identify peer-reviewed studies that included waterbodies >5m deep that experienced a water level change. We found that phytoplankton and cyanobacteria were significantly more likely to increase if water level decreased, and conversely, were significantly more likely to decrease if water level increased.

presentations.title: DECOUPLED NUTRIENT LOADS AND LAKE MANAGEMENT
presentations.abstract: In Lake Simcoe (Ontario, Canada), we explored how changing precipitation patterns affects the supply of phosphorus and how quagga mussels have altered P dynamics. With these new dynamics, using a single metric, such as P loads, to set mitigation targets and track progress is not reliable as well-established ecological relationships may no longer be applicable.

presentations.title: THE RIVER STARTS AT THE DAM? FILLING DATA GAPS FOR A HEADWATER LAKE AND WATERSHED MANAGEMENT PLAN
presentations.affiliation: State University of New York at Oneonta
presentations.abstract: Otsego Lake (NY, USA) is a 16.4 km² glacial lake that forms the source of the 715-km-long Susquehanna River. While Otsego Lake water quality is generally good, the lake faces modern limnological challenges. The Otsego Lake community is collaborating with the state agencies to create a Nine Element Plan.

presentations.title: THE WATERS OF JÆREN, NORWAY – EFFORTS TO ACHIEVE ENVIRONMENTAL OBJECTIVES
presentations.abstract: The waters of the Jæren region suffer from excess nutrients inputs and eutrophication. This presentation highlights two cases: one lake where nutrient-reducing measures have been implemented for more than 40 years, and another lake where more recent approaches to achieve good status have been carried out.

presentations.title: Improving Ecological Health of a Hypertrophic Urban Lake in Estonia: A Dual Approach to Reducing Legacy Phosphorus
presentations.abstract: In our study of a small natural lake in Estonia, we aim to test two restoration methods - floating islands and aluminum mineral-based sediment treatments. Lake Põrmujärv is heavily polluted with year-round blooms of Planktothrix agardhii. In September 2025, a 32 m² floating island was installed.

presentations.title: A COMMUNITY OF PRACTICE (COP) ON LAKE, RESERVOIR AND POND RESTORATION
presentations.abstract: To tackle fragmentation and facilitate learning, we have launched a Global Community of Practice (CoP) on lake restoration under the umbrella of the uPcycle project. We'll inform attendees about the progress of this CoP and how it will be fruitful for learning and boosting restoration.

name: Coupled Elemental Cycles in River Systems: Emerging Patterns, Stoichiometric Shifts, and Anthropogenic Drivers
description: River systems are critical integrators of elemental fluxes across landscapes. Elemental cycles are increasingly disrupted by anthropogenic pressures.
lead_organizer: Joanna Carey, Babson College
co_organizers: Lienne Sethna, Science Museum of Minnesota

presentations.title: Infusing ecological stoichiometry into riverine biogeochemistry
presentations.abstract: This tutorial will review how different lenses of river studies have informed our understanding of flowing waters in global biogeochemical cycles. We employ the framework of ecological stoichiometry to investigate our understanding of coupled elemental cycles in a riverine ecosystem using a case study that employs high-frequency nitrogen and phosphorus sensors in agricultural streams.

presentations.title: HOW ELEMENTS ARE COUPLED IN FINE PARTICLES TRANSPORTED BY STREAMS AND RIVERS
presentations.abstract: To define the continental-scale patterns and controls of elemental coupling in stream particles, we used National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) wadeable streams. Our estimates show particles comprise 20% of organic C, 17% of N, and 76% of P. We found consistent particle C:N across streams pointing to tight coupling of C and N, but C and P were generally weakly coupled.

presentations.title: LAND USE INFLUENCES NUTRIENT REGIMES AND THE TIMING OF NUTRIENT DEPLETION IN RIVERS
presentations.abstract: We found that only six distinct regimes described the seasonal patterns of Si, N, and P across nearly 350 rivers spanning 18 countries. Coherence among all three nutrients was most common in less-impacted sites, whereas anthropogenically-impacted sites tended to exhibit little-to-no coherence among solutes.

presentations.title: Are there stoichiometric patterns in environments with different land use intensities?
presentations.abstract: In the Paraná 3 Basin, water quality was monitored across 12 streams over 18 sampling campaigns. So far, no clear relationship has been observed between the N:P ratio and either regional agricultural land use or accumulated precipitation. Variations in nitrogen and phosphorus concentrations in group A streams were similar to those observed in groups B and C.

presentations.title: Same stressor, different city: Can we consistently predict watershed and socio-ecological drivers of urban stream carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus?
presentations.abstract: We collected grab samples during baseflow conditions from 100 sites on four occasions over one year in four cities. Sociodemographic factors in addition to more commonly assessed watershed characteristics predicted city-specific stream C, N, and P patterns. However, the direction and strength of relationships between urban predictors and stream C, N, and P varied among cities.

presentations.title: INFLUENCE OF SEASONS AND BACKGROUND GEOLOGY ON THE AQUATIC GEOCHEMISTRY OF CRITICAL MINERALS
presentations.abstract: This research investigates variations in critical mineral concentrations across four seasons and the transition of background geology in four river systems in Southeastern Canada. We collected water samples along the Otonabee, Trent, and Ottawa Rivers over four seasons. We report the concentrations of 55 elements, reflecting the heterogeneous water chemistry of rivers draining the Canadian Shield.

name: Mesocosm-Based Approaches for Tackling Grand Challenges in Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Mesocosm experiments have become an essential approach for addressing grand challenges in aquatic sciences.
lead_organizer: Cihelio Alves Amorim, WasserCluster Lunz - Biologische Station GmbH
co_organizers: Gabriela Ágreda-López, IMDEA Water Research Institute
Gülce Yalcin, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries

presentations.title: AQUANAVI: A NEW NAVIGATION TOOL FOR AQUATIC MESOCOSM-BASED RESEARCH TO ADDRESS GRAND CHALLENGES AND THEIR MITIGATION
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inlands Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract: The AQUACOSM-RI consortium comprises over 60 state-of-the-art mesocosm facilities at 28 host institutions across Europe. Within the AQUANAVI project, we created an interactive atlas of aquatic mesocosm-based experimental research information. Expert knowledge is integrated into a single, accessible platform incorporating Open Knowledge Maps' AI-driven visual discovery tools.

presentations.title: SMALL STREAMS, BIG EXPERIMENTS: WHAT REALISTIC FLUVIAL MESOCOSMS CAN – AND CANNOT – DO
presentations.abstract: Here, I present a unique outdoor fluvial mesocosm facility consisting of twelve 15-m flow-through channels built within the Krycklan Catchment Study in northern Sweden. The system delivers natural stream water mimicking boreal headwaters. We revealed strong individual and interactive stressor effects on algal biomass, whole-stream metabolism and microbial processing of carbon.

presentations.title: Biogeochemical responses to ocean alkalinity enhancement in coastal sediment mesocosms
presentations.abstract: Using a controlled flow-through mesocosm system, we applied a gradient of NaOH-based alkalinity additions to quantify how short-term shifts in pH and carbonate speciation influence sediment biogeochemistry. We observed consistent changes in water-column TA, DIC, and pH that altered sediment oxygen demand and dissolved inorganic nitrogen fluxes.

presentations.title: Exploring Whole Lake Analogues: Sediment Microbial Diversity and Functional Response to Quaternary Ammonium Compounds using in-Lake Mesocosms
presentations.abstract: This study used open-bottom mesocosms deployed in Lake 375 at the IISD-Experimental Lakes Area to examine the effects of a gradient of BAC concentrations on sediment microbial communities over a three-month period. We combined qPCR and 16S rRNA metatranscriptomic sequencing to assess changes in community diversity and functional gene expression.

presentations.title: DIFFERENT TYPES OF NETWORK FRAGMENTATION DRIVE DISTINCT BIODIVERSITY RESPONSES IN EXPERIMENTAL METACOMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: In this study, by conducting an outdoor mesocosm experiment as a proxy of pond networks, we evaluated the impact that different types of fragmentation have on eukaryotic metacommunities diversity. Communities that increased its isolation due to Strong fragmentation type showed local diversity decreases.

presentations.title: Hydrological connectivity of deep lakes promotes local phytoplankton diversity while homogenizing metacommunity after an extreme deep-mixing event
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract: Using a large in-situ mesocosm facility, we experimentally tested how lake-to-lake connectivity shapes phytoplankton community responses to an extreme storm event. Mixing in the initial enclosure triggered the dominance of a single taxon (Planktothrix rubescens). Connectivity allowed the disturbance effect to be transmitted downstream, but also reduced phytoplankton peak biomass.

name: Salinization of Inland Waters: Impacts on Food Webs, Water Quality, and Biogeochemical Cycles
description: Climate change, sea-level rise, hydrological alterations, and pollution are accelerating global salinization of inland waters.
lead_organizer: Matthew Bogard, University of Lethbridge

presentations.title: JOINTLY ADVANCING OUR UNDERSTANDING OF SALINIZATION IMPACTS ON INLAND WATERS
presentations.abstract: In April 2026, we will convene a small international workshop bringing together hydrologists, microbiologists, and ecologists. Our goals are to develop a global map of inland waters that are already salt-rich or at heightened risk of salinization, and to synthesize the major ecological and biogeochemical challenges across different regions.

presentations.title: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF SPATIAL ENVIRONMENTAL CONTEXT ON THE TOXICITY OF ROAD DE-ICERS TO ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: To investigate the influence of environmental context on salt toxicity, we conducted concurrent mesocosm experiments in a soft and hard water lake, exposing plankton communities to a gradient of 10 Cl- concentrations for both rock salt and Thawrox (TR). For dominant species and groups, 71% showed significant differences between de-icers; among these, 80% exhibited biomass reductions under TR.

presentations.title: Changes in Zooplankton Community Structure, Function, and Diversity in Response to Salinity Gradients and Salinity–Heatwave Stress in Two Different Mesocosm Experiments
presentations.abstract: We conducted two different mesocosm experiments. The gradient experiment included 16 salinities (0.5 to 50 g/L). Increasing salinity resulted in significant, nonlinear declines in zooplankton richness, biomass, size, and RUE. Community composition showed threshold responses: rotifers replaced cladocerans and copepods. The heatwave treatment further intensified these patterns.

presentations.title: Impacts of salinization on invertebrate community composition in 34 coastal urban lakes
presentations.abstract: We analysed larval chironomid community composition and diversity in surface-sediments from 34 Halifax lakes over a chloride gradient. Threshold indicator taxa analysis identified 78.5 mg Cl–/L as the value at which most assemblage change occurred. Shannon diversity and rarefied richness were significantly lower in lakes with Cl– concentrations above 78.5 mg Cl–/L.

presentations.title: INFLUENCE OF HIGH CALCIUM ON CHLORIDE TOXICITY IN ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: To investigate whether high Ca2+ ameliorates Cl- toxicity on zooplankton communities, we conducted a 6-week mesocosm experiment to test how Ca2+ modifies Cl- toxicity. Early results show that crustacean biomass decreased as Cl- increased, however there was no evidence of an effect of Ca2+.

presentations.title: Physiological responses and population growth of green algae across a salt gradient
presentations.abstract: Here we present a lab-based growth experiment examining effects of 10 salt treatments on two species of phytoplankton and one species of periphyton. While C. vulgaris was resilient to salt treatments, both chlorophyll and FvFm declined with higher chloride concentrations for S. quadricauda and S. pratensis.

name: Reducing the Uncertainties in Methane Emissions from Aquatic Environments
description: Freshwater, brackish, and marine environments significantly contribute to global methane emissions; however, the large variability in reported values remains a primary source of uncertainty.
lead_organizer: Mina Bizic, TU Berlin
co_organizers: Paul del Giorgio, Université du Québec à Montréal
Yves Prairie, Université du Québec à Montréal

presentations.title: Methane and carbon dioxide emissions from thermokarst lakes of the Northern Hemisphere
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: By synthesizing >3000 observations of CH₄ and CO₂ fluxes across all major permafrost regions, thermokarst lakes globally emit 206 ± 0.7 Tg C yr⁻¹, equivalent to 1.44 ± 0.01 Pg CO₂-eq yr⁻¹. CH₄ contributes 53% of the radiative forcing despite being only 10% of total emission in carbon mass.

presentations.title: Oxic Methane production by algae metabolism in freshwater
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Recent discovered methane production under oxic conditions challenges the classic biological CH4 production. Algae oxic CH4 production may have long been underestimated. Further controlled light and temperature experiments revealed that CH4 production rates were significantly higher under warm conditions than cold conditions. AOMP process was entirely light-driven.

presentations.title: Methane on the storm: A large-scale enclosure experiment shows disruption of the methane cycle by deep mixing during an experimental storm event
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract: To investigate how storm-induced deep-mixing alters CH4 production, we conducted a large-scale experiment over 8 weeks in the IGB LakeLab. After stratification was naturally re-established within days, mixed and control enclosures followed similar temporal patterns. These results show that storm-induced deep mixing of lakes can reshape CH4 dynamics.

presentations.title: REMARKABLY CONSISTENT SEASONAL PATTERNS OF METHANE EMISSIONS REVEALED BY LONG-TERM EDDY-FLUX MEASUREMENTS IN A SMALL TEMPERATE LAKE
presentations.affiliation: GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences
presentations.abstract: Here, we used 9-years of eddy covariance measurements of methane emissions from a small mesotrophic lake in Germany. We found a remarkably recurrent seasonal pattern of methane emissions, with emissions ramping up over the course of the stratified summer period leading to pronounced peaks each year during fall turnover.

presentations.title: Which Gases Produce Bubbles? Evaluating Gas Partitioning in Bubbles Across Reservoirs
presentations.abstract: Using a sediment probing technique, we collected > 300 bubble samples from intentionally disturbed sediments from 16 reservoirs across Canada. We found that gas partitioning within bubbles was highly variable, with both N₂ and CH₄ concentrations covering nearly the full range of relative contributions. Our findings challenge a core assumption used in most ebullition models.

presentations.title: Within-season changes in methane oxidation rates in a lake undergoing enrichment
presentations.abstract: During the summer of 2025, we experimentally enriched a lake to induce a bloom and investigated how net oxidation rates varied across the water column. The results showed higher variability in oxidation rates throughout the summer in the enriched lake than in the reference lake and higher overall rates in the enriched lake.

name: Trophic Ecology and Biogeochemistry in Aquatic Food Webs: Integrating Novel Techniques to Disentangle Ecosystem Dynamics
description: Understanding trophic interactions, nutrient cycling, and energy flow is central to food web ecology. This session showcases novel and advanced techniques in trophic ecology.
lead_organizer: Rita García Seoane, Instituto Español de Oceanografía (IEO-CSIC)
co_organizers: Maja Ilić, Institute of Zoology, University of Cologne
Grégoire Saboret, Department of Ocean Sciences, UC Santa Cruz

presentations.title: Linking phytoplankton biosynthesis of essential fatty acids to consumer bioconversion and gene expression in boreal lakes
presentations.abstract: In this field study, we measured LC-PUFA biosynthesis in 12 boreal lakes along a trophic gradient. Biosynthesis of LC-PUFA phytoplankton varied between 1.0 and 400 pg C (mg C)-1 h-1. Only a fourth of the 643 boreal and subarctic lakes met the biosynthesis level necessary to reduce required bioconversion efforts.

presentations.title: EFFICIENT TRANSFER OF PLANKTONIC FATTY ACIDS IN THE RAPIDLY WARMING AND SALINE RED SEA
presentations.abstract: We conducted a monthly time-series analysis of phytoplankton and zooplankton FA quality in the warm, saline, oligotrophic and rapidly warming Red Sea. Both phytoplankton and zooplankton exhibited high FA quality, suggesting a strong potential to sustain the nutritional needs of higher trophic levels.

presentations.title: Zooplankton reliance on autochthonous and allochthonous resources across mountain lakes assessed with essential amino acid δ13C analysis
presentations.abstract: Here, we show terrestrial plants, benthic algae, and POM have distinct essential amino acid carbon isotope fingerprints across eight freshwater habitats in California's eastern Sierra Nevada Mountains. Autochthonous resources accounted for the majority (76–93%) of AAESS assimilated by zooplankton.

presentations.title: Resource quality and quantity exert distinct influences on trophic interactions and food web pyramids across varying water nutrient levels
presentations.affiliation: Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, China
presentations.abstract: This study explored how resource quality and quantity influenced trophic interactions and food web pyramids under varying water nutrient levels. Nutrient enrichment significantly boosted phytoplankton biomass leading to a bottom-heavy biomass pyramid. However, this increase was accompanied by a notable reduction in ω3 LC-PUFA in primary producers.

presentations.title: An enhanced view into fish life histories and marine planktonic food webs provided by adding sulfur isotopes to the traditional isotope toolkit
presentations.abstract: We will present stable isotope results on zooplankton species from the South Atlantic Bight and northeastern Gulf of Mexico, which indicate the utility of 34S data in identifying benthic contributions to marine food webs in coastal environments. S isotopes also provide additional constraints upon consumers occupying similar niches.

presentations.title: MODELLING TROPHIC DYNAMICS DURING THE RESERVOIR TROPHIC SURGE: A MECHANISTIC FRAMEWORK
presentations.abstract: We developed a quantitative framework to model the trophic upsurge phenomenon. We built a five-level multitrophic model representing the dynamics of phosphorus, phytoplankton, zooplankton, fish, and piscivores. Preliminary results show that the model successfully simulates the magnitude and timing of the P-pulse and the corresponding staggered peaks in biomass.

name: Bridging the Gap Between Microbial Community Biodiversity, Ecosystem Function, and Ecological Restoration
description: This session aligns various research from natural environments; beginning with microbial diversity and evolution through time in freshwater systems and moves into the effects of pollution on microbial diversity and sustainable ecosystem management.
lead_organizer: Jackie Lemaire, University of Wisconsin Madison
co_organizers: Katherine McMahon, University of Wisconsin – Madison
Augustina Nnenna Okereke, Nigerian Institute for Oceanography and Marine Research

presentations.title: MICROCYSTIS BLOOMS ARE DRIVERS OF BACTERIAL BIODIVERSITY AND FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY IN WESTERN LAKE ERIE
presentations.abstract: Using 16S and metagenomic datasets from western Lake Erie, we found that the bacterial community diversity was shaped by both seasonality and Microcystis bloom conditions. A consistent seasonal successional pattern in the bacterial community was observed across years, with a distinct bloom community.

presentations.title: TOPIC ANALYSIS ENABLES DISCOVERY OF ECOLOGICALLY COHERENT SUBCOMMUNITIES OF PROKARYOTES AND PHYTOPLANKTON IN THE LAURENTIAN GREAT LAKES
presentations.abstract: We applied Latent Dirichlet Allocation to an eight-year, cross-domain time-series from the Laurentian Great Lakes. LDA decomposed communities into distinct subcommunities that followed coherent spatial and temporal patterns. These results show how topic modeling can resolve ecological structure across microbial domains.

presentations.title: EXPLORING CYANOBACTERIAL POPULATIONS THROUGH GENE VARIATION IN NATURAL ENVIRONMENTS
presentations.abstract: Using 125 curated Cyanobacterial genomes recovered from 464 metagenomes spanning 20 years, we have the unique opportunity to investigate evolutionary differences. Preliminary results indicate a majority of these variable genes are involved with prokaryotic host defense.

presentations.title: REVISITING THE MECHANISMS OF ADAPTATION AFTER 200 GENERATIONS OF SIMULTANEOUS OCEAN WARMING AND ACIDIFICATION IN A WIDESPREAD MARINE COPEPOD
presentations.affiliation: University of Vermont / University of Connecticut
presentations.abstract: By experimentally evolving A. tonsa for over 200 generations under OWA conditions, we elucidate how microbiome dynamics are shaped by long-term exposure to future environmental regimes. Our preliminary data presents how non-additive responses to thermal and pH stress can result in distinct microbiome configurations.

presentations.title: Metabolic activity and diversification of rare-biosphere prokaryotes in oceanic Oxygen Minimum Zones
presentations.abstract: To close this knowledge gap, we implemented a strategy for selecting redox-active populations using Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (RAP-FACS). Multiple high-quality MAGs from taxa never before reported in OMZs showed lineages with limited genomic representation. Phylogenomic analysis provided unprecedented resolution of the enigmatic Marine Group III archaea.

presentations.title: Protein-based functional signatures reveal global patterns of ocean microbial metabolism
presentations.abstract: To address this, we analyzed 1,379 marine metagenomes using a sensitive clustering strategy that groups protein sequences into Operational Protein Units. We identified ten OMSs that collectively capture key metabolic capacities, each exhibiting specific spatial patterns and functional traits.

name: Trait-Based Plankton Ecology and Environmental Change
description: Planktonic primary producers form the basis of aquatic food webs. Trait‑based frameworks promise to clarify how particular trait combinations confer competitive advantages under shifting environmental conditions.
lead_organizer: Sabine Wollrab, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
co_organizers: Philippe Pondaven, Université de Bretagne Occidentale

presentations.title: Do phytoplankton form cliques in the Great Lakes? It seems so, and perhaps we can use them to track stressors.
presentations.abstract: Using two decades of phytoplankton monitoring data from the Laurentian Great Lakes, we used co-occurrence network analysis to identify phytoplankton associations, or cliques. These analyses identified five stable phytoplankton cliques which differed in their responses to environmental parameters.

presentations.title: SPECIES IDENTITY CONTROLS THE EFFECT OF DIVERSITY ON BLOOM FORMATION IN AN ARTIFICIAL FRESHWATER PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITY
presentations.abstract: Our results show that biodiversity effects varied with nitrate availability and grazing. Further, biomass accumulation was mainly determined by one species, suggesting that bloom formation is more dependent on a species identity effect than on diversity alone.

presentations.title: Changes in phytoplankton life strategies along a temperature gradient
presentations.abstract: Here, we use empirically determined thermal performance curves for main taxonomic phytoplankton groups in freshwater and marine habitats as the basis to theoretically derive shifts in the three life-strategy quantities along a temperature gradient. Under warm conditions, all phytoplankton groups tend to have high µmax and K.

presentations.title: Phytoplankton nutritional quality dependance on growth phase and environmental conditions
presentations.abstract: Eight different species from four groups (diatoms, chlorophytes, cyanobacteria and cryptophytes) were grown in batch cultures under 12 different non-factorial treatments. Our results show that the growth phase, rather than environmental treatments, is often the most determining factor for phytoplankton nutritional quality.

presentations.title: Effect of marine phytoplankton diversity on biomass production, resource use and community dynamics in a new co-culturing microcosm design
presentations.abstract: For this purpose, we used specifically designed microcosms where dialysis bags allowed us to monitor the physiology and the growth of the different taxa individually. Results indicate that initial diversity has an effect on the growth and on the biomass production at both species and community level.

presentations.title: Trait-based phytoplankton community ecology in an urban estuary
presentations.abstract: Using a published time series spanning over two decades, we test whether functional traits explain phytoplankton community dynamics in San Francisco Bay. We highlight key combinations of environmental conditions hypothesized to drive the dominance of different taxonomic groups.

name: The Overlooked Bloom: Benthic Cyanobacteria and Their Toxins in Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Benthic cyanobacteria are receiving increased attention from water authorities and aquatic science due to their ability to produce potent neurotoxins.
lead_organizer: Sven Meissner, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)

presentations.title: FROM OVERLOOKED TO IN FOCUS: BENTHIC CYANOBACTERIA – CHALLENGES, ADVANCES AND WHAT COMES NEXT
presentations.abstract: Working with substrate-attached taxa presents distinct challenges including their patchy distribution, variability at millimetre- to river-scales, benthic growth form, and typically filamentous nature. Over the past two decades, advances across disciplines have improved our understanding of some benthic genera, notably Microcoleus/Phormidium.

presentations.title: TRACKING ANATOXIN-PRODUCING CYANOBACTERIA IN SWITZERLAND: A MOLECULAR APPROACH ENABLED BY CITIZEN-SCIENCE SAMPLING
presentations.abstract: To improve our monitoring scheme, we developed molecular markers targeting genes within the anatoxin biosynthetic operon. We started a citizen science project, yielding approximately 35 samples from rivers and lakes throughout Switzerland. Among these samples, 29 contained filamentous cyanobacteria, and 16 tested positive for anatoxin-related genes.

presentations.title: Long-term persistence and functional interactions of toxigenic and non-toxigenic Microcoleus in freshwater benthic mats
presentations.abstract: We analyzed Microcoleus-dominated mat samples collected over five years. Metagenomic analyses revealed two persistent Microcoleus subspecies: the toxigenic Microcoleus sp. Wq-II and the non-toxigenic Wq-I. The streamlined genome of Wq-I may reflect metabolic dependency within its consortium, consistent with the Black Queen Hypothesis.

presentations.title: Prevalence of benthic cyanobacteria and cyanotoxin potential in periphyton along lake shorelines
presentations.affiliation: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
presentations.abstract: We characterized the benthic microbial communities along shorelines of Lake Ontario and two Finger Lakes via 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Benthic cyanobacteria were ubiquitous but varied across sites. Cyanotoxin encoding genes were quantifiable in most samples tested. Our observations show that periphyton may be a source of exposure to cyanotoxins.

presentations.title: BLOOMS OF TOXIC BENTHIC CYANOBACTERIA IN A TEMPERATE MESOTROPHIC LAKE – NOT OVERLOOKED ANYMORE
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract: Since 2017, anatoxin-producing benthic cyanobacteria have been causing dog fatalities in the mesotrophic Lake Tegel in Berlin. Our project DIVATOX aims at generating a model to predict toxic benthic blooms in lakes. Lake monitoring has revealed that local blooms of benthic cyanobacteria occur during spring and autumn.

name: Ecosystem Processes in a Changing World: Honoring the Career of Mike Pace
description: Dr. Michael Pace has made substantial and lasting contributions to our understanding of freshwater, estuarine and marine ecosystems through his work on food web dynamics, carbon cycling, ecosystem metabolism, resilience, and long-term ecological change. His research, which often integrates whole-ecosystem experiments, comparative studies, and long-term observations, has helped to advance our understanding of how aquatic ecosystems respond to natural and human-driven change.
lead_organizer: Grace Wilkinson, University of Wisconsin - Madison
co_organizers: Jonathan Walter, University of California Davis

presentations.title: A PILLAR OF ECOSYSTEM SCIENCE
presentations.abstract: Mike Pace's contributions to science use all four pillars of ecosystem science: long-term observations, cross-ecosystem comparisons, whole-ecosystem experiments, and theories. His work strengthened all four pillars. By combining traditional approaches in creative ways, he generated new ideas about aquatic ecosystems for 5 decades. By example, Mike showed that leadership is the essential fifth pillar of ecosystem science. Mike's analyses of lake ecosystems were motivated by theory and strengthened by principles of experimental design. Lakes were distributed on gradients, and most of the measurements were made by Mike and his team. Thus they obtained a wide range of near-independent predictor variates measured by consistent methods and avoided the nonsense correlations and feedback circularities that plague happenstance datasets.

presentations.title: Resilience of a dystrophic lake during five whole-lake fertilization experiments
presentations.abstract: Lakes globally are undergoing directional changes in nutrients and staining because of climate change and shifting human resource use, including both eutrophication and brownification. The consequences of these directional changes and their interactions for lake resilience to blooms is not well known, even though nutrients and light are important controls on phytoplankton biomass. Methods to measure resilience of stochastic multistable systems are applied here to five separate whole-lake nutrient additions that we conducted in Tuesday Lake, Michigan, USA. Tuesday Lake is a small, deep, dystrophic lake where staining varies interannually due to variability in precipitation and winter conditions. We found that resilience of Tuesday Lake also varied from year to year during our experiments, allowing us to partition factors influencing lake resilience to blooms and identify when critical transitions occurred.

presentations.title: A REVERSAL IN THE DIRECTION OF LONG-TERM CHANGE IN THE DOC CONCENTRATION OF THE HUDSON RIVER ESTUARY
presentations.abstract: Mike Pace has made major contributions to our understanding of both the Hudson River Estuary and the sources and roles of dissolved organic carbon in aquatic ecosystems. We show new evidence that the increase in DOC concentration observed in the Hudson between the late 1980s and early 2000s – an early and influential example of the 'browning' of aquatic ecosystems – has reversed course, declining by 2020 to levels similar to those seen in the late 1980s. We evaluate a series of hypotheses to explain this change, including changes in non-point watershed inputs, point-source pollution, internal loads, and internal processing.

presentations.title: What would Michael say? The restoration of eutrophic Great Lakes ecosystems
presentations.abstract: The Great Lakes are some of the most impacted ecosystems on the planet, with stressors ranging from industrialization, invasive species, management decisions, climate change, and of course nutrient loading. Nearshore zones, chiefly associated with urban or agricultural dominated watersheds often have serious localized ecosystem impacts associated with eutrophication. Here I will discuss the issues and difficulties associated with 3 very different Areas of Concern studied by Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) within Lake Ontario (Toronto, Bay of Quinte, Hamilton), which while having very similar total phosphorus levels, have completely different ecosystem responses, and as such, have different aims with respect to eutrophication.

presentations.title: CHEMICAL CONTEXT MATTERS: CATION-DRIVEN CHANGES IN ORGANIC CARBON DYNAMICS
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) represents the primary pool of reduced carbon in lakes and reservoirs, making it a central subject of limnological research. While the discipline has traditionally focused on carbon fluxes and pools, little attention has been paid to the chemical environment in which DOC is dissolved, particularly the influence of solvent properties such as cation concentration, alkalinity, and pH. This presentation synthesizes decades of collaborative research with Mike Pace and demonstrates how variations in cation and water chemistry markedly modulate DOC dynamics. In alkaline systems, changes in DOC optical properties enhance photobleaching and accelerate microbial biodegradation. In addition, high cation concentrations promote DOC coagulation into particulates, affecting both carbon sedimentation and long-term storage.

presentations.title: Advancing fundamental and applied understanding of aquatic systems through synthesis science
presentations.abstract: Synthesis science leverages often disparate existing datasets to facilitate new insights, even into questions that were unanticipated when the original studies were initiated. Across aquatic science and allied disciplines, synthesis science has been used to expand the spatial and temporal scales of research, to explore the generality of key ideas and understand exceptions to broad ecological patterns, and to make new discoveries underpinned by novel combinations of datasets well beyond the feasibility of individual research teams to collect. Mike Pace's career spans the rise of synthesis science as a major research approach in aquatic science, and despite being arguably best known for his work with whole-ecosystem manipulation experiments, Mike has been an important practitioner of synthesis science.

name: The Waters We Share: Challenges and Successes in Outreach
description: Many scientists recognize the importance and value of strong science communication skills and around the world researchers, departments, and institutions are conducting impactful outreach programs. When done effectively, aquatic science communication can foster understanding, inspire action, and support informed decision-making at all levels of society.
lead_organizer: Emily King, COSEE China, State Key Laboratory of Marine Environmental Science, Xiamen University
co_organizers: Laura Falkenberg, University of South Australia, UniSA STEM
Vera Shi, State Key Laboratory of Marine Environmental Science, Xiamen University

presentations.title: A Sensor-Driven Communication Platform: Developing the Tahoe Environmental Observatory Network for Real-Time Environmental Outreach
presentations.affiliation: Centro Regional Universitario Bariloche-Universidad Nacional del Comahue
presentations.abstract: High-frequency environmental sensor networks produce valuable data for understanding watershed and lake processes, but these datasets often remain inaccessible to non-specialists due to technical, linguistic, and cultural barriers. The Tahoe Environmental Observatory Network (TEON) was established to address this challenge and provide comprehensive public information about Lake Tahoe Basin conditions. TEON integrates data from over 30 terrestrial, atmospheric, and aquatic sensors and consolidates continuous and manual data in a cloud system with basic quality checks and clear visual displays.

presentations.title: AN INNOVATIVE DIGITAL AND HANDS-ON EDUCATION TOOL FOR ADVANCING FLOODPLAIN AND WETLAND LITERACY IN THE DANUBE BASIN
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) Berlin
presentations.abstract: River floodplains and wetlands are critically threatened worldwide, despite providing essential ecosystem services. Their restoration depends not only on scientific expertise but also on public understanding of their ecological and societal importance. To address this gap, the EU Restore4Life project developed the Living Floodplain: Learn, Explore, Restore4Life Toolbox, an innovative hybrid educational framework that translates wetland science into intuitive and emotionally engaging learning experiences. The toolbox was developed through a three-phase process. All components converge in an interactive platform presenting ten awareness-raising topics visualised along the Danube River.

presentations.title: FOREL: A RESEARCH VESSEL CONNECTING PEOPLE, SCIENCE AND THE ARCTIC IN A CHANGING CLIMATE
presentations.abstract: The FOREL research platform, named in honor of the Swiss founder of limnology, François-Alphonse Forel, is a 28-m high-tech sailing vessel designed and operated for research across the land-air-ocean continuum in the coastal polar regions. Forel's founding concept of limnology was to integrate not only geophysics, geology, biogeochemistry and biology, but also to include the human dimension. This inclusive vision figures prominently in the FOREL outreach program, which centers on climate change issues, and includes youth-oriented activities at the home port of Lorient (France), mini-comics in multiple languages, podcasts, YouTube videos and schoolchild-focused activities on the vessel during visits to Arctic Inuit communities.

presentations.title: FROM POND TO POST: USING INSTAGRAM TO TEACH AND COMMUNICATE PLANKTON ECOLOGY IN AN UNDERGRADUATE COURSE
presentations.abstract: Although social media is ubiquitous among students and faculty, many faculty hesitate to use it in teaching due to concerns about privacy, sensitive public content, academic integrity, grading, and measuring effectiveness. Despite the downsides, social media can be a powerful science communication tool in the natural sciences. I will present on the use of Instagram in an undergraduate aquatic ecology course (LSM4260 Plankton Ecology) designed to engage the public about plankton communities in Singapore's ponds. Students sampled and identified plankton in various ponds, then created a single Instagram post using images/illustrations and hashtags to attract public attention.

presentations.title: OVERCOMING BARRIERS THAT LIMIT THE INCLUSION, PARTICIPATION, AND IMPACT OF AQUATIC RESEARCH IN PUBLICATIONS
presentations.abstract: Equity, diversity, and inclusion are increasingly recognized as essential to improving the quality, transparency, and relevance of scientific publishing in aquatic sciences. Yet structural barriers, such as inequitable access to funding, biases in peer review, and limited visibility for researchers from underrepresented communities, continue to influence who participates in science and whose work is disseminated. In this presentation, drawing on my experience as Editor-in-Chief, I examine how scholarly journals can help address these challenges by implementing open practices, policies, and initiatives that promote fairer participation across the research ecosystem.

presentations.title: Failures and Successes in Community Engagement: Reflections from 30 Years of Practice
presentations.abstract: Effective community engagement is increasingly recognized as essential for broadening participation in science and countering growing anti-science narratives. Many scientists enter this work without training, institutional support, or clear models for assessing success. I synthesize the lessons I have learned over 30 years of developing and implementing aquatic science outreach initiatives, with the goal of providing practical guidance on ways to be successful and advice on avoiding some of the pitfalls I encountered. My early experiences in community engagement were ad hoc efforts, often characterized by well-intentioned but underperforming activities.

name: Curating Limnology with Kindness: Honoring Jim Cotner
description: Microbial limnologist, Dr. Jim Cotner, has built a remarkable career with major contributions to the freshwater science over a range of subjects (from genes to ecosystems) and sub-disciplines (from microbial ecology to biogeochemistry). For over four decades, Jim has explored how microbes shape aquatic environments through their composition and metabolism.
lead_organizer: Ed Hall, Colorado State University
co_organizers: Bopaiah Biddanda, Grand Valley State University

presentations.title: Curating Cotner: An EEB perspective on Jim's contributions to freshwater science and scientists
presentations.abstract: Jim Cotner has been my neighbor, collaborator and friend throughout my career as faculty at the University of Minnesota. Reflecting on the past 23 years, my talks describes diverse examples of Jim's contributions, large and small, to freshwater science and scientists. My talk is organized around three areas. First, I highlight Jim's early contributions to longstanding questions, and how this work remains highly relevant to present day limnology. Second, I describe our ongoing work to connect controls over physical, chemical and biological conditions that regulate carbon, oxygen, and nutrient regimes.

presentations.title: Low RQ, High Impact: Methanotrophic Controls on Lake Carbon Cycling
presentations.abstract: Freshwater lakes are dynamic biogeochemical reactors that transform and emit substantial amounts of carbon dioxide and methane. The balance between methane production and its aerobic oxidation depends critically on oxygen availability. Because methanotrophy is both highly oxygen-demanding and characterized by a low respiratory quotient (RQ), it can be a major but understated sink for dissolved oxygen - especially in lakes with persistent stratification. As climate change intensifies and lengthens stratification, oxygen renewal to deep waters is reduced, creating conditions where methane accumulates and oxygen becomes increasingly scarce.

presentations.title: THE FATE OF METHANE IN PONDS: DRIVERS AND CONTROLS OF PRODUCTION, OXIDATION, AND EMISSIONS
presentations.abstract: Ponds are increasingly recognized as disproportionately large contributors to freshwater and global carbon cycling, notably releasing large amounts of methane (CH₄) relative to their global surface area. In this study, we measured CH4 dynamics and emissions in 15 ponds spanning four different ecoregions across New York State (USA). We used an isotopic mass-balance approach to quantify CH₄ oxidation rates and partition total CH₄ production into its major pathways: storage, oxidation, and emissions.

presentations.title: Sunlight-driven conversion of dissolved organic sulfur to sulfate and methanesulfonic acid
