presentations.abstract: The dissolved organic sulfur (DOS) pool is one of the most photoreactive components of dissolved organic matter, yet the role of photochemistry in the aquatic sulfur cycle remains poorly quantified. We have shown that sunlight converts a wide range of DOS compounds to sulfate and low-molecular-weight S products, and that triplet-sensitized one-electron oxidation followed by sulfite-to-sulfate conversion may represent a general mechanism.

presentations.title: DOM PHOTODEGRADATION FLAVORS FRESHWATER WITH FORMS OF ELEMENTS FAVORED BY FLORA AND FAUNA
presentations.abstract: Cotner and Heath (1990) showed that photodegradation of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in freshwaters may supply iron and phosphorus to microbes. Using metatranscriptomics and analysis of DOM composition, we tested Cotner and Heath's ideas in arctic freshwaters. Significant differences in gene expression between the sunlight-exposed vs. dark control DOM suggested that sunlight changed the chemical forms and availability of iron and phosphorus.

name: A Decade of Insights with the Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship
description: This session celebrates ten years of the ASLO Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship (RCEF), a transformative initiative empowering early career researchers (ECRs) in scientific publishing. Established in 2017 through a generous endowment by Dale and Ross Cole in honor of Raelyn Cole, former managing editor of Limnology & Oceanography, the RCEF has become a platform for ECRs wishing to advance equity, open access, and mentorship in scientific publishing.
lead_organizer: Frank Akamagwuna, University of Alabama
co_organizers: Paul F Kemp, University of Hawai'i

presentations.title: Introduction by Dale Cole & Susanne Menden-Deuer
presentations.affiliation: Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography
presentations.abstract: Dale Cole & Susanne Menden-Deuer will give introductory remarks.

presentations.title: A SEAT AT THE EDITORIAL TABLE: EARLY-CAREER EDITORS AS PARTNERS, NOT TRAINEES
presentations.abstract: Early-career researchers (ECRs) are central to evolving norms around open science, equity, and reproducibility in publishing. In 2016, Limnology and Oceanography Letters and ASLO launched the Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship (RCEF), a two-year program designed to give Fellows a sustained 'seat at the table' as partners in society publishing. We will (1) summarize the fellowship model and its society–publisher partnership; (2) present indicators of impact including recent editorial fellowships and early-career editorial boards; and (3) position the RCEF along a spectrum that ranges from one-way 'apprenticeship' initiatives to genuine power-sharing with ECRs.

presentations.title: Open Access Publishing as a Way to Increase Your Work's Impact
presentations.abstract: In the 'Publish or Perish' context of academia, publishing is perhaps the most valuable currency of a researcher. The increased uptake of Open Access (OA) publishing in the past decade has transformed the aquatic sciences publishing landscape. In this presentation I will (1) introduce attendees to the different types of OA publications (gold, diamond, and green) and copyright licenses; (2) briefly touch upon the benefits, pitfalls, and potential improvements to OA publishing; (3) contextualise OA and related topics as perceived by previously surveyed ASLO members.

presentations.title: TEACHING BEYOND THE PUBLISH OR PERISH MODEL
presentations.abstract: Peer-reviewed scientific publishing is a keystone of the scientific method and is one of the most important metrics by which success is measured in academia. To address this gap in training, two ASLO Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellows (Peck & Franco-Santos) designed a course on science publishing piloted by Peck at the University of Rhode Island Graduate School of Oceanography.

presentations.title: RETHINKING LAY SUMMARIES: BOTH JARGON AND READABILITY MATTER FOR ACCESSIBLE WRITING
presentations.abstract: Scientific publishing seeks to communicate research broadly, yet accessibility remains a challenge. Journals increasingly request Lay Summaries to help make findings understandable to non-specialists, but these are often no more effective than traditional Abstracts due to persistent jargon and low readability. In this study, conducted under the Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship, we analysed Lay Summaries across multiple journals and found most scored poorly on jargon and readability metrics, limiting their effectiveness.

presentations.title: HOW GOOD THINGS HAPPEN: THE STORY OF THE L&O LETTERS EARLY CAREER PUBLICATION HONOR
presentations.abstract: Inequities abound in academia. Chief among these are differences in publishing resources, particularly for early career researchers (ECRs) and those from the Global South. To address this issue in limnology and oceanography, we created the L&O Letters Early Career Publication Honor. Initiated in 2019, the honor provides OA fee waivers for ECR-led publications based on need and potential impact of the research.

name: Sharing Experiences Among Early-Career Researchers
description: The future of aquatic science will be built on the connections we make today. This special session is a platform for early-career researchers (ECRs) to share and explore meaningful strategies for collaboration, an important tool to boost career development.
lead_organizer: Benjamin Misteli, WasserCluster Lunz
co_organizers: Bruno Cremella, Laboratoire d'Océanographie de Villefranche
Brittany Schieler, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography
Adina Paytan, University of California Santa Cruz
Susanne Menden-Deuer, University of Rhode Island

presentations.title: SHARING EXPERIENCES AMONG EARLY-CAREER RESEARCHERS IN AQUATIC SCIENCE: UNLEASHING THE POWER OF COLLABORATION
presentations.abstract: Early-career researchers (ECRs) are already shaping the future of aquatic science. This tutorial talk opens session EP010, organised by ECRs for ECRs, and shows how collaboration and society programs can accelerate both science and careers. We introduce the early-career and student structures within the Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography (ASLO) and the International Society of Limnology (SIL), and outline concrete ways to get involved.

presentations.title: AQUACOSM-ECR NETWORK: CONNECTING AQUATIC MESOCOSM EARLY CAREER RESEARCHERS GLOBALLY
presentations.abstract: We will briefly introduce the AQUACOSM-ECR network, a community of early-career researchers (ECRs) engaged in mesocosm-based research and, more broadly, aquatic sciences. The network was inspired based on experiences through the AQUACOSM-plus project and our aim is to continue to promote knowledge transfer and collaboration amongst ECRs.

presentations.title: GLOBAL LAKE ECOLOGICAL OBSERVATORY NETWORK (GLEON) STUDENT ASSOCIATION INITIATIVES TO PROMOTE STUDENT INVOLVEMENT IN GLOBAL COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH
presentations.abstract: The Global Lake Ecological Observatory Network (GLEON) is an international grassroots network of researchers interested in conducting team science to advance our understanding of freshwater ecosystems in a changing environment. GLEON provides a unique learning experience for students and other early-career researchers (ECRs) from a wide range of backgrounds and disciplines. The GLEON Student Association (GSA) addresses student needs, promotes student well-being, provides training opportunities, and ensures student perspectives in decision-making.

presentations.title: BRIDGING THE ACADEMIC METABOLIC RIFT: FROM COLLABORATION TO SOLIDARITY
presentations.abstract: The modern academic landscape, with its hyper-competitive funding environment, pervasive job insecurity, and intense publication pressure has created precarious realities for early career researchers trying to build a sustainable career. Loosely drawing on the metabolic rift theory developed by John Bellamy Foster, we chart the similarities between the disruption of metabolism and carbon cycling of aquatic systems and academic society and explore how international collaboration can be leveraged not merely as a scientific tool but also as a pathway towards international solidarity.

presentations.title: EARLY CAREER REFLECTIONS FROM WORKING AT A PUI
presentations.abstract: In August 2024, I began my career as a faculty member at a primarily undergraduate institution (PUI), teaching and conducting research across two programs. Over the past two years, I have experienced moments of deep joy while also navigating the challenges that come from trying to balance teaching, research, and service expectations. In this presentation, I will share honest reflections noting both successes and the missteps from the beginning of my career at a PUI.

presentations.title: Advancing Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion in Limnology: Community Perspectives, Emerging Trends, and Pathways for Progress
presentations.abstract: Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) are increasingly recognized as essential to the quality and impact of science, yet evidence on how EDI is experienced within the limnology community remains limited. The International Society of Limnology (SIL) EDI Task Force and the Developing Economies Committee designed an anonymous global survey to explore experiences and perceptions of EDI among limnologists within and beyond SIL.

name: How to: Compiling Knowledge to Reduce Barriers for First-Timers
description: Students and early career professionals (jointly referred to as ECRs) in aquatic sciences often learn how to perform the many intricate activities necessary for the craft by doing them. The Limnology and Oceanography Bulletin is a great vehicle for sharing knowledge with peers, especially first-timers.
lead_organizer: Rita Franco-Santos, Oceans Institute, University of Western Australia
co_organizers: Laura Falkenberg, UniSA STEM, University of South Australia

presentations.title: PROMOTING SKILL DEVELOPMENT IN THE SUSTAINABLE BLUE ECONOMY THROUGH THE DESIGN AND DELIVERY OF NON-CREDIT MICRO-CREDENTIAL COURSES
presentations.abstract: The blue economy is a rapidly growing sector, offering a wide variety of career pathways that demand both technical and professional skills. We designed the Leadership for the Sustainable Blue Economy Certificate Program, with courses including Introduction to the Sustainable Blue Economy: Concepts, Challenges, and Opportunities, Communicating Ocean Science: Stakeholder Engagement and Impact, Indigenous Knowledge and Leadership in Blue Economy Futures and Modeling the Future Ocean: Climate Data for a Sustainable Blue Economy.

presentations.title: IMPROVING LEARNING AND SCIENCE OUTCOMES IN THE RESERVOIR OBSERVER STUDENT SCIENTISTS (ROSS) PROGRAM THROUGH A DATA QUALITY ASSESSMENT EXERCISE
presentations.abstract: The Reservoir Observer Student Scientists (ROSS) program engages high school students in year-round water quality monitoring to detect and understand cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cyanoHABs). The ROSS program has been running continuously since 2017 and includes high school students from Minnesota and Missouri, USA. Results show that students not only developed procedural knowledge and data literacy, but also produced scientifically valid data comparable to professional standards.

presentations.title: Don't Get Eaten, Stranded, or Soaked: Your Fieldwork Safety Checklist for the Middle of Nowhere
presentations.abstract: Got a remote field project that's equal parts exciting and intimidating? This session is your essential pre-trip briefing, designed specifically for students and ECRs gearing up for their first major field campaign. We'll move beyond theoretical risk assessments and tackle the real-world 'how-to' of staying safe, sane, and productive when you're miles from the nearest help or cell signal.

presentations.title: HOW TO WRITE WITH CLARITY AND INSIGHT: LESSONS AND PRACTICAL TIPS FROM DEVELOPING BOOK REVIEWS
presentations.abstract: Strong writing skills are essential for career development and progression in the aquatic sciences, yet many of us receive little formal training in communication, especially beyond technical audiences. Writing for general readerships, through outlets such as the Limnology and Oceanography Bulletin, offers valuable opportunities to practice and refine this skill. Drawing on my experience as Editor of the Bulletin, I will share insights as to what works and what does not both for Book Reviews, and writing more generally.

presentations.title: How to Leverage Membership in Scientific Societies for Career Development – the ASLO Example
presentations.abstract: Scientific societies provide the framework for professionals to contribute individually and collectively to advancing their fields. In this presentation I reflect on my journey with the Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography (ASLO) and what I learnt along the way to draw examples of how students and early career professionals can leverage their membership in a scientific society to propel their career development.

presentations.title: HOW TO OVERCOME THE MID-CAREER BLUES: INSIGHTS FROM TWO 'MIDDLE AGED' AQUATIC SCIENTISTS
presentations.abstract: Your persistence and dedication have paid off and you have attained what you always coveted - tenure at an academic institution you enjoy, a permanent job at a government agency, or stability in your consulting career. The exciting thing about the midcareer stage is that your next goal really can be whatever you want it to be. In this session, the authors will provide some examples of their own soul-searching, help frame discussion for how to manage the uncertainty of the mid-career stage.

name: Ecological Stoichiometry: Honoring Jim Elser
description: This session will focus on key areas of the scientific legacy produced by the long and fruitful career of Jim Elser to honor his upcoming retirement. Beginning with his work on the relative availability of key nutrients in temperate lake ecosystems, Jim ultimately took ecological stoichiometry into a wide range of aquatic ecosystems around the globe.
lead_organizer: Paul Frost, Trent University

presentations.title: FROM ELEMENT RATIOS OF PLANKTON TO GLOBAL PHOSPHORUS POLICY
presentations.abstract: Jim and Monica Elser were essential to success of the first whole-ecosystem experiment on trophic cascades at the U. Notre Dame Environmental Research Center on the Wisconsin-Michigan border in 1984-1986. Jim noticed that shifts between micro- and macro-grazers were followed by changes in N:P supply ratio to phytoplankton. Ecosystem stoichiometry was born. Jim was a leader in publicizing the importance of phosphorus for national security and global economy.

presentations.title: Follow the elements: how ecological stoichiometry changed limnology, astrobiology, and the careers of many
presentations.abstract: The field of ecological stoichiometry is firmly rooted in limnology. This talk will reflect on Jim Elser's role in co-leading the NASA Astrobiology Institute team based at Arizona State University (2009-2016). Limnological studies from Argentina to Mexico to Yellowstone provided empirical evidence for the biological constraints of microbial life.

presentations.title: Stoic? No, it is stoichiometry
presentations.abstract: In this talk, I will revisit my early collaborative research with Professor James J. Elser and his distinctive, 'stoic' approach to science, and then outline future perspectives that build on this foundation. In his pioneering studies, Dr. Elser observed that changes in zooplankton community composition were accompanied by shifts in the nutrient limiting phytoplankton growth—from nitrogen to phosphorus.

presentations.title: THE WOODSTOICH WORKSHOPS – HOW FIVE DAYS OF PEACE AND STOICHIOMETRY CAN SHAPE SCIENTIFIC CAREERS
presentations.abstract: Scientific legacies are not only determined by research papers and novel discoveries. They are also built through the careers of the following generations of scientists who start their paths through academia inspired by scientific mentors and role models. The series of meanwhile five 'Woodstoich' workshops were a transformative experience for several generations of early career researchers.

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL STOICHIOMETRY OF FUNGI: OUT OF JIM ELSER'S COMFORT ZONE AND YET ON HIS RADAR
presentations.abstract: Fungi are peculiar organisms. Much neglected throughout the history of biology, their astounding diversity and functions in ecosystems are increasingly gaining center stage in ecological inquiry. If ecological stoichiometry encapsulates fundamental principles of the existence of life, an intriguing question is to what extent fungal decomposers conform to the stoichiometric patterns known for other organisms.

presentations.title: FROM FLATHEAD LAKE TO WATERMELON SNOW: JIM ELSER'S TENURE AT THE FLATHEAD LAKE BIOLOGICAL STATION
presentations.abstract: From Flathead Lake's long-term stoichiometry to astrobiology, environmental sensors, wastewater treatment, and watermelon snow. Come hear a retrospective about Jim Elser's tenure as the Director of the University of Montana's Flathead Lake Biological Station.

name: Two-Eyed Seeing: Indigenous Knowledge and Western Science
description: There are a growing number of research programs in many parts of the world that are working in partnership with indigenous knowledge holders to improve understanding and design more salient solutions for the protection and sustainable future of water and water resources.
lead_organizer: Roxane Maranger, Université de Montréal
co_organizers: Katrine Turgeon, Université du Québec en Outaouais

presentations.title: BLENDING WESTERN SCIENCE AND INDIGENOUS PERSPECTIVES: INSIGHTS FROM 30 YEARS ON THE CANADIAN PRAIRIES
presentations.abstract: Canada has failed to uphold its treaties with Indigenous peoples. Additional historical injustices include residential schools, the pass system, governmental legislation to actively eliminate Indigenous culture, and federal policies to sequester natural resources. This paper summarizes the abundant mistakes, and occasional successes, of that approach in studying freshwaters in western Canada – homeland of the Cree, Saulteaux, Lakota, Nakota, Dakota and Metis peoples.

presentations.title: INDIGENOUS ECOLOGICAL ECONOMICS - CREATING SPACE FOR HOLISTIC, CUSTOMARY APPROACHES TO FRESHWATER VALUATION.
presentations.affiliation: Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka
presentations.abstract: Freshwater valuation requires a layered approach honouring measurable, relational and prioritised water value dimensions. We introduce Indigenous Ecological Economics as an interdisciplinary approach that centres Indigenous epistemologies and weaves ecological integrity, and social justice into how we value and govern lake freshwater ecosystems. Lake Tarawera, New Zealand is a case study.

presentations.title: A decision tool for fish habitat compensation in Eeyou Istchee
presentations.abstract: In Eeyou Istchee (Cree territory), waterways and aquatic biodiversity are integral to overall ecosystem health and Cree wellbeing. To better plan fish habitat compensation, decision tools can help effectively allocate resources and set priorities. In this project, we used participatory research with the Eeyouch, inspired by the two-eyed seeing approach.

presentations.title: INDIGENOUS AUSTRALIAN PLANT USE AND SPECIES-SPECIFIC ALGAL SUPPRESSION BY STEPHANIA JAPONICA LEACHATE
presentations.abstract: For over 65,000 years prior to British colonisation of Australia in 1788, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples sustained freshwater systems through seasonal traditional ecological knowledge and deeply embedded place-based cultural practices. This study presents the first experimental evaluation of the vine, Stephania japonica, a culturally significant plant traditionally used by Kombumerri People, for its capacity to suppress growth of six freshwater eukaryotic and cyanobacterial algal species.

presentations.title: THE NUNATSIAVUT RIVERS PROJECT: BRIDGING KNOWLEDGE SYSTEMS TO SUPPORT RESILIENT RIVER MONITORING AND COASTAL ECOSYSTEMS IN NUNATSIAVUT
presentations.affiliation: Memorial University of Newfoundland and Labrador
presentations.abstract: The Nunatsiavut Rivers Project emerged from the Inuit-led Nunatsiavut Sea Ice Observers Program (NSIOP), which promotes Inuit knowledge of the sea-ice season. Labrador Inuit have a strong connection and reliance on river ecosystems for travel routes, cultural practices, and subsistence activities.

presentations.title: EELGRASS ECOSYSTEM COLLAPSE AND SOCIAL-ECOLOGICAL REGIME SHIFT DRIVEN BY HYDROPOWER DEVELOPMENT AND CLIMATE CHANGE
presentations.abstract: Global declines in coastal habitats and wildlife have devastating consequences for Indigenous Peoples. In some places, hydropower development has environmental impacts that contribute significantly to the coastal habitat loss. Here, we follow a detection and attribution framework to understand the collapse and limited recovery of a social-ecological system including eelgrass (Zostera marina, shikaapaashkw), geese (Branta spp., nisk and iyiwaapuwaau), and Cree (Eeyou) in subarctic eastern James Bay, Canada (Eeyou Istchee).

name: Amplifying Voices in Aquatic Sciences: Aquatic Confluence
lead_organizer: Pascal Bodmer, Cornell University
co_organizers: Bianca M. Rodríguez-Cardona, International Institute of Tropical Forestry
Mina Bizic, Technical University of Berlin
Members of the Early Career Committee (ECC), ASLO
session_description: ASLO ECC virtual session for early career researchers from underrepresented groups, presenting via pre-recorded talks.

presentations.title: Future-proofing on using OMIC approaches in South East Asia: A Case analysis of using eDNA in Biomonitoring Philippines Inland Waters
presentations.abstract_summary: Bibliometric review of 308 SE Asia phytoplankton/HAB papers reveals geographic and methodological gaps; eDNA metabarcoding underutilized in freshwater Philippines.
presentations.abstract: The spread of nonnative freshwater phytoplankton, biological invasions, and harmful algal blooms (HABs) is becoming a significant risk to aquatic ecosystems, especially in tropical areas where monitoring capacity is still inconsistent and environmental change occurs quickly. The occurrence, causes, and ecological effects of these events in Southeast Asia are still poorly understood, even though they are frequently reported in temperate settings. The region's freshwater systems, including the Philippines, are particularly vunerable to eutrophication, climate variability, and increasing anthropogenic pressures. However, monitoring efforts are still primarily reliant on time-consuming conventional microscopy-based taxonomy and physicochemical assessments in aquatic ecosystems. The study presents a regional-scale bibliometric analysis and systematic review of freshwater phytoplankton, HABs, and molecular biomonitoring research across Southeast Asia, with a focused assessment of the Philippines. This process yielded a final dataset of 308 publications, excluding irrelevant data sets from the search query. The result from the analysis highlights significant differences in geographic coverage and the underutilization of omics-based tools for inland water monitoring; it also offers the first thorough regional overview of research patterns and methodological gaps in freshwater phytoplankton and HAB studies in Southeast Asia on using eDNA metabarcoding. There is an imbalance in research output across Southeast Asia, with Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore leading contributions, whereas the Philippines accounts for only 7 publications (~2.3%), and representation from Vietnam and Laos remains minimal, with no recorded studies from Cambodia and Brunei. Furthermore, thematic patterns on methodology on molecular approaches reveal approximately 60–70% of studies employ eDNA, metabarcoding, or next-generation sequencing. While conventional approaches comprise 25–35%, integrative studies combining molecular and ecological workflows remain scarce (<10%). Thematically, research is dominated by biodiversity assessment and biomonitoring, whereas HAB-focused studies constitute less than 10% and favor marine environments, which puts emphasis on critical gaps in freshwater and phytoplankton-specific molecular applications of eDNA metabarcoding. Southeast Asia is transitioning toward omics-based biomonitoring, but the application of these approaches to freshwater phytoplankton and HAB research remains limited. The Philippines represents a critical gap despite high ecological vulnerability. Addressing these gaps through the integration of eDNA metabarcoding, development of phytoplankton reference databases, and establishment of long-term monitoring frameworks will be essential for advancing freshwater ecosystem management and mitigating HAB risks in the region

presentations.title: From model to validation and beyond: Assessing spatial-temporal impacts of changing winter conditions on Lake Ecosystems
presentations.abstract_summary: Validates light/temperature lake-ice models with global observational data; assesses ice-cover impacts on subsequent ice-off water quality.
presentations.abstract: Using simple models of light and temperature, recent work has highlighted the importance of light flux and ice-cover duration, with profound and underappreciated implications for global lakes. This finding is critical because historically lake scientists have paid less attention to ice cover period. As a follow-up to the recent work, we used observational data to validate the theoretical assumptions made in the previous study. Specifically, we utilized global lake ice cover, solar radiation, thermoregimes, and other relevant datasets. Modeled historical and future lake ice cover data were used to quantify spatial and temporal impacts from changing winter conditions. Additionally, we explored relevant remotely sensed water quality data during ice off season to assess how ice cover period affects subsequent ice-off lake water environmental dynamics. Using the observational and modeled data specified above, we aim to contribute to ongoing efforts to address the knowledge gap in assessing changes in winter conditions and projecting future impacts on lake ecosystem functions, such as aquatic primary production.

presentations.title: Social aspects in the transfer of pejerrey (Odontesthes bonariensis) floating cage aquaculture to the tourism-fishery sector in Pampas lakes
presentations.abstract_summary: Participatory workshops show pejerrey floating-cage aquaculture is transferable in Pampas lakes; cultural attachment to silverside drives adoption.
presentations.abstract: The relationship between recreational fishermen and Pampean Lakes is deeply linked to the regional economy and tourism, where fishing stands as the main tourist attraction. These lakes are eutrophic environments where communities of phytoplankton, zooplankton, and fish with high biomass converge. They are also centers of productive and subsistence activities for surrounding communities, constituting part of their identity. The pejerrey ( Odontesthes bonariensis ) is the emblematic species of the region and the primary target of sport fishing. Between 2017 and 2022, technological transfer of pejerrey farming in floating cages was carried out in the San Lorenzo, Vitel, La Salada de Monasterio, Chis Chis, Blanca Grande, and Gómez lakes. The objective was to evaluate the aquaculture transfer experiences from the adopter's perspective. Participatory workshops and semi-structured interviews (n=14) were conducted. The results showed that the farming technique is transferable and presents no operational drawbacks, except for those related to the procurement of materials rather than the design and functionality itself. Adopters have a positive acceptance regarding the application and operation of the model. They also link it as a tool to raise awareness and promote the sustainable use of the lakes. This work revealed that the profound cultural embeddedness and affection of the participants for the silverside were the primary motivation for their involvement in the execution of the proposed farming.

presentations.title: Land use overrides stream order effects on dissolved organic matter and ecosystem metabolism in Afrotropical-savanna rivers
presentations.abstract_summary: In the Mara River, livestock density shapes DOM composition more than stream order; ecosystem respiration still tracks the river continuum concept.
presentations.abstract: In the lower savanna river landscape, large mammalian herbivores frequently interact with rivers during feeding and watering. These interactions can influence river functioning, particularly through the input of organic matter, but studies focusing on organic matter composition and ecosystem metabolism in Afrotropical savanna rivers are still limited. In this study, focusing on the Mara River, we assessed the effects of livestock density and stream order on dissolved organic matter (DOM) composition and ecosystem metabolism. Our findings show that land use, specifically livestock density, plays a significant role in shaping DOM composition, which in turn affects DOM quality and ecosystem metabolism. Although land use significantly influenced DOM composition, certain ecosystem metabolism parameters, such as ecosystem respiration (ER), still followed longitudinal patterns consistent with the river continuum concept. Neither stream order nor livestock density had a significant effect on the ratio of gross primary production to ecosystem respiration (GPP:ER).

presentations.title: Exploring uncharted waters: The role of artificial aquatic ecosystems in freshwater science
presentations.abstract_summary: Argues for recognizing artificial aquatic ecosystems (AAEs) as valid components of the modern hydroscape with biogeochemical and policy importance.
presentations.abstract: Artificial aquatic ecosystems (AAEs) are human-made environments in managed landscapes that encompass a spectrum from straightened streams to newly constructed ponds. Research on AAEs is now expanding into diverse environmental science fields as we grapple with ongoing pressures threatening freshwater ecosystems. These novel water environments represent the modern hydroscape, are the first line of defense in freshwater pollution, and are designed to handle extreme conditions. Yet AAEs remain sidelined in the traditional study of freshwaters, limiting their recognition in catchment and atmospheric processes. This talk will challenge the entrenched idea that human-made waters have limited ecological value and call attention to how recognizing AAE’s in fundamental research will improve freshwater resource management in an increasingly human-impacted future. We advocate for increased recognition of AAEs in freshwater science on four key points: 1) their ubiquity across human-impacted landscapes; 2) their contributions to biogeochemical cycles and ecosystem services; 3) as sources of insights to fundamental questions on pressures facing freshwater ecosystems; and 4) their lack of inclusion in policy. We call for a paradigm shift from viewing AAEs as low in the hierarchy of natural sciences to recognising them as critical components of the modern hydroscape that offer opportunities for interdisciplinary research and improvement of water resources.

presentations.title: Thematic and geographic biases in global phytoplankton-nutrient research and their ecological consequences
presentations.abstract_summary: Structural Topic Model on 8,861 papers (1942-2024) shows USA/China dominate phytoplankton-nutrient research; Latin America, Africa, S. Asia remain underrepresented.
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton drive nutrient dynamics in aquatic ecosystems; however, current knowledge remains fragmented due to uneven evidence. Scientific attention is concentrated in high-income countries, leaving developing regions underrepresented. This imbalance limits the generality and transferability of ecological theories and obscures ecosystem responses to stressors such as climate change and eutrophication. To quantify these biases, we applied a Structural Topic Model (STM), a machine learning method, to 8,861 articles published between 1942 and 2024. We characterized temporal trends and geographic distribution of marine and freshwater phytoplankton–nutrient research. Our results reveal a pronounced geographic skew: the United States and China dominate research output, whereas Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and South Asia remain underrepresented, with foundational topics still underexplored. Thematically, research has shifted from fundamental topics, such as biogeochemical cycles and community ecology, toward applied themes, including watershed management. These disparities reveal critical gaps across underrepresented regions. Limited ecological information in these areas may lead to biased assumptions that compromise predictions of ecosystem functioning and responses to environmental change. By demonstrating how thematic and geographic patterns structure scientific knowledge, this study highlights the need for more inclusive global collaboration to ensure that ecological knowledge truly reflects global biodiversity patterns.

presentations.title: Resolving Diel Fecal Pellet Flux with in situ Imaging and a Migration-Sinking Model
presentations.affiliation: University of Rhode Island Graduate School of Oceanography
presentations.abstract_summary: EXPORTS campaign in NE Pacific combines UVP5 imaging and GelCam to resolve diel patterns in fecal pellet flux by morphology (long, tabular, ellipsoid).
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton fecal pellets are a major pathway for vertical carbon export in the ocean, and their flux depends on pellet type, sinking behavior, and the vertical distribution of their producers. To examine how these processes vary over the diel cycle, we combined in situ imaging with a simple migration sinking model during the EXPORTS campaign in the subarctic Northeast Pacific. Hundreds of Underwater Vision Profiler (UVP5) casts resolved depth dependent distributions of particles and zooplankton throughout the water column, while upward facing camera systems (GelCam) on a surface tethered sediment trap array captured time series observations of sinking particles at discrete depths. Together, these complementary approaches resolved hourly patterns in the abundance and flux of three morphologically distinct fecal pellet types: long, tabular, and ellipsoid. These measurements were compared with the distributions of likely producers, including crustacea, salps, and appendicularia. The imaging data revealed distinct diel patterns among pellet types, reflecting differences in producer behavior and pellet transport. A simple model linking vertical migration, pellet production, sinking, and attenuation reproduced the main temporal patterns observed for migrating groups and helped interpret the timing of pellet flux at depth. Together, these results show that short term variability in fecal pellet export emerges from the interaction between zooplankton movement and pellet properties.

name: Aquatic Invasion Ecology
lead_organizer: Pascal Bodmer, Cornell University

presentations.title: Trophic interactions between stream macroinvertebrates and the invasive diatom Didymosphenia geminata
presentations.affiliation: Science Museum of Minnesota, St. Croix Watershed Research Station
presentations.abstract_summary: North Shore Lake Superior streams: Chironomidae and Baetidae consume invasive didymo, indicating it can be a primary energy pathway in invaded cold-water systems.
presentations.abstract: Didymosphenia geminata (“didymo”) is an invasive, stalk-forming diatom that can form thick mucilage mats that alter physical benthic habitat and nutrient dynamics in cold, low nutrient streams. Although didymo mats can dominate primary producer biomass, it remains unclear whether stream macroinvertebrates are able, or willing to use didymo as a food resource. We investigated macroinvertebrate–didymo trophic interactions streams with didymo mats on the North Shore of Lake Superior using a combination of contemporaneously-collected periphyton diatom community structure and macroinvertebrate gut-contents. Our results show that several macroinvertebrate taxa, including taxa from collector-gatherers and grazer functional groups consume didymo when mats are present, with increasing didymo cells in periods of peak didymo density. Chironomidae and Baetidae showed the highest consumption of didymo, whereas Heptageniidae and Leptophlebiidae exhibited little to no consumption. These findings indicate that didymo can be a primary energy pathway within invaded streams. Understanding whether macroinvertebrates can incorporate didymo into their diets provides insight into how nuisance blooms reshape trophic structure and energy flow in cold-water ecosystems, informing both ecological impact assessments and management strategies for affected trout streams.

presentations.title: Habitat and landscape gradients shaping invasive Corbicula fluminea distribution
presentations.abstract_summary: Upper Savannah River basin: Corbicula presence linked negatively to forested high-gradient streams, positively to developed land use and upstream reservoirs.
presentations.abstract: Threats and damage caused by invasive freshwater bivalves continue to grow throughout North America and globally. The range of Corbicula fluminea continues to expand since first introduced in the Pacific Northwest in the 1930’s. Despite the breadth of its introduced range, mechanisms of local dispersal between waterbodies are not fully understood. This is further complicated by the generalist nature of C. fluminea , which is successful in both lentic and lotic systems. In a recent study in the upper Savannah River basin of South Carolina and Georgia, USA, we documented Corbicula presence in 20 of 50 sites across five HUC10 watersheds. We used an information theoretic approach (AICc) to evaluate competing hypotheses of habitat and land use as correlates of Corbicula presence. The best model (91% AICc weight) contained habitat variables associated with forested landscapes, including significant negative relationships with % riffle and % cobble at a site. The second-best model (4% AICc weight) included significant and positive relationships with % developed landscape surrounding a site, and with the presence of a reservoir upstream in the watershed. Both models also included significant positive relationships with stream width or other modeled reach habitat characteristics. We found the reduced presence of Corbicula in higher gradient forested streams (i.e., higher riffle % and cobble %) consistent with general assumptions of their habitat use. Additionally, we found the positive correlations of % developed land use at a site, and presence of upstream reservoirs intriguing as both variables may be informative for human or wildlife mediated dispersal. While our dataset is limited in scope, it points to patterns that could be useful in guiding future tests of conceptual models of invasive dispersal.

presentations.title: Spreading to the north: environmental drivers of Bythotrephes invasion from temperate to boreal lakes
presentations.abstract_summary: Temperate-zone alkaline carbonate-rich water and boreal-zone humic darkness are different environmental barriers to Bythotrephes invasion across Canadian ecozones.
presentations.abstract: The invasive zooplankton Bythotrephes cederstroemii has transformed lake ecosystems across North America, yet environmental factors controlling invasion success remain unclear in the most recently invaded northern ecozones. We compared environmental conditions between invaded and uninvaded lakes across temperate, mixed, and boreal ecozones in Canada to identify zone-specific environmental factors that facilitate or constrain invasion. We compared water chemistry, dissolved organic carbon concentration, and light-attenuation variables across ecozones and assessed their influence on lake invasion status. Our results demonstrate that Bythotrephes faces different environmental barriers across ecozones, with invasion success and constraints driven by distinct mechanisms in each zone. In the temperate zone, uninvaded systems exhibited high conductivity, pH, and dissolved inorganic carbon concentration compared to invaded lakes, indicating that alkaline, carbonate-rich water creates a strong barrier to invasion in southern Canada. In the boreal zone, uninvaded lakes had significantly darker colour and shallower euphotic zone because of high dissolved organic carbon concentration than invaded lakes, suggesting that high concentrations of terrestrial humic substances constrain invasion in northern lakes. Mixed zone lakes did not show any significant water chemistry patterns. These findings highlight the need for ecozone-tailored management strategies that account for the distinct environmental filters.

presentations.title: Competition between the invasive Mesocyclops pehpeiensis and the native Mesocyclops longisetus
presentations.abstract_summary: Used Neutral Red dye to distinguish morphologically similar copepods; invasive M. pehpeiensis is the superior competitor with higher growth rate.
presentations.abstract: Exotic species often outcompete native taxa, and thus establish their populations in non-native habitats. Mesocyclops pehpeiensis (Cyclopoida, Copepoda), originally from Asia, is now widely distributed in 4 continents and 12 countries including Mexico. Twelve species of Mesocyclops have been reported from Mexico. Here we tested competitive interactions between M . pehpeiensis and Mesocyclops longisetus . One of the challenges in achieving this is the ability to distinguish between these two morphologically similar copepods. We tested the dye, Neutral Red (hydrochloride salt of phenazine) to daily stain one of the species, during the entire study. We conducted acute toxicity tests to determine the tolerance levels of the copepods and their prey ( Brachionus calyciflorus and Moina macrocopa ) to the dye. Life tables were also conducted on the invasive species with and without the dye. We also conducted life table experiments of M. pehpeiensis and M. longisetus alone and together (1:1 ratio), where the invasive species was stained daily. We compared the survivorship, egg ratio and egg hatching time of the copepods. Our acute toxicity tests indicated that the micro-crustaceans were more tolerant; mortality was observed at concentrations of 40-125 mg/L of Neutral Red. B. calyciflorus was more sensitive; mortality was observed between 3-7 mg/L. We observed that M. pehpeiensis had a higher growth rate than M. longisetus. Our results indicate that the invasive species is indeed the superior competitor to other species of Mesocyclops and hence widely spread in Mexico.

presentations.title: Predicted and observed effects of northern snakehead (Channa argus) on the food web of a large freshwater marsh in the early stages of invasion
presentations.affiliation: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
presentations.abstract_summary: Bashakill Wildlife Management Area: gut contents and stable isotope analyses show northern snakehead at the invasion front not yet altering fish diet composition.
presentations.abstract: Northern snakehead ( Channa argus) is a piscivorous species of fish non-native to North America. They have generated widespread concern due to their highly piscivorous nature and ability to become a top predator in invaded systems, but more work is needed to quantify early invasion effects on food webs. The Bashakill Wildlife Management Area in the Delaware River Basin and Catskills region of New York State was selected as a study site, due to its position at the invasion front. Northern snakehead has not established throughout the large site (4047 m 2 ), making it an ideal location to characterize changes northern snakehead invasion may bring to food webs in initial stages of invasion. This study analyzed fish gut contents as well as stable isotope ratios of D 15 N and D 13 C from fish, invertebrates, and basal resources to compare food webs at sites with and without northern snakehead present. Gut contents showed no difference in diet composition of piscivorous fish between sites with and without snakehead presence. Diet estimations based on stable isotope modelling showed no differences in diets of piscivorous fish between invaded and non-invaded sites, indicating that northern snakeheads at the invasion front are not currently significantly altering fish diet composition or other food web interactions. Whole ecosystem modelling is predicted to show no current deleterious effects by northern snakehead on the food web of the marsh. This study has the potential to be the first in a series of studies characterizing northern snakehead invasion effects throughout stages of invasion.

presentations.title: An Atlantic invader in the Mediterranean: multi-scale drivers, dynamics and impacts of the blue crab (Callinectes sapidus)
presentations.abstract_summary: Northern Italy: GBIF data, fisheries monitoring, and direct sampling characterize blue crab invasion drivers, abundance dynamics, and small-scale fisheries impacts.
presentations.abstract: The Atlantic blue crab, Callinectes sapidus, is native to the Atlantic coast of the Americas. However, it has recently spread in the Mediterranean becoming one of the most recent threats to these ecosystems and fisheries. During the last two years, research in our unit has focused on the drivers and effects of blue crab invasion in coastal and inland waters of Northern Italy. Using data from open sources (like Global Biodiversity Information Facility), fisheries monitoring and direct field sampling, we first illustrate the large-scale drivers influencing blue crab occurrences across the Mediterranean Sea. We then present local-scale drivers of its abundance within specific coastal lagoons, discussing its population increase in relation to associated changes in small-scale fisheries. Finally, we speculate on its potential effects in freshwater habitats, a critical frontier where data are not yet available for the invaded area. This work provides timely insights for conservation, fisheries management, and invasive species governance.

name: Coastal Ecosystems
lead_organizer: Osvaldo Iván Ulloa Quijada, Universidad de Concepción Chile

presentations.title: The advective mechanisms and foraging implications of patchy zooplankton seascapes
presentations.abstract_summary: Hydrodynamic models of plankton aggregation seascapes in Gulf of St. Lawrence; correlations with North Atlantic right whale distribution and ecosystem productivity.
presentations.abstract: Plankton are organisms that drift in the water, carried by currents. As they transport them, currents create “aggregation seascapes” where plankton is more or less concentrated. Since plankton form the basis of marine food webs, these aggregation zones should therefore constitute important feeding areas. However, this link remains poorly studied. In addition, many planktonic organisms can migrate vertically, exposing themselves to currents of varying intensity and direction depending on their position. The objective of my project is to simulate aggregation seascapes using hydrodynamic models of currents and observations of the vertical distributions of plankton groups, and to use these results to study the distribution of other species that feed on them. First, I will show their correlation with the distribution of North Atlantic right whales in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Gulf of Maine, indicating areas of interest for reducing the risk of fatal accidents related to human activities. Next, I will present the initial results of a study on the link between current-driven aggregation patterns and ecosystem productivity in the Mecatina Basin, northeast of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Finally, I will explore the importance of spatio-temporal scales in understanding these aggregation phenomena.

presentations.title: Ecosystem structure and biodiversity losses in coastal wetlands in the eastern Mediterranean, Türkiye
presentations.abstract_summary: Survey of 28 Turkish Mediterranean wetlands shows eutrophication, salinisation, and 70% Kentish plover decline driven by hydrological alteration.
presentations.abstract: Coastal wetlands are globally important blue carbon ecosystems and biodiversity hotspots, yet they are being degraded at unprecedented rates due to land reclamation, hydrological modification and climate change. To assess ecosystem structure, function and anthropogenic pressures along the Turkish Mediterranean coast, we surveyed 28 coastal wetlands and lagoons between 2022–2023. This effort was complemented by catchment analyses, paleoecological sampling, and evaluation of long-term demographic data for key shorebird species at selected sites. Our ecosystem assessments highlight the prominent influence of eutrophication and salinisation, strongly modulated by the degree of hydrological connectivity between wetlands and the sea. Historical aerial imagery since the 1950s reveals dramatic changes in land cover and hydrology, while fluctuations in diatom assemblages preserved in lagoon sediments indicate substantial ecological responses to recent hydrological alterations. Although saltmarshes have experienced widespread degradation, carbon stocks demonstrate that these ecosystems may still function as significant carbon sinks. Long-term monitoring of a representative coastal breeding shorebird, the Kentish plover Charadrius alexandrinus, in Lake Tuzla of the Çukurova Delta shows a severe 70% reduction in population size over 25 years. Population viability analysis (PVA) based on local demographic parameters suggests that this population was likely already a demographic sink in the 1990s, indicating low resilience within coastal wetland biodiversity under intense anthropogenic pressures.

presentations.title: Impact of climate change on seagrass dynamics in the Chesapeake Bay
presentations.abstract_summary: Widgeon grass maintains 70% higher photosynthesis than eelgrass under elevated pH; bicarbonate-use efficiency favors widgeon grass dominance under climate change.
presentations.abstract: Seagrass meadows are foundational habitats in Chesapeake Bay but are increasingly threatened by sediment loading, eutrophication, and climate-driven shifts in temperature and salinity (Arnold et al., 2017; Lefcheck et al., 2017). Eelgrass ( Zostera marina ) and Widgeon grass ( Ruppia maritima ) are dominant ecosystem engineers in polyhaline regions, yet the interactive effects of climate stressors (Temperature and Salinity) on their metabolic performance remain poorly understood. This study evaluated oxygenic photosynthetic responses across gradients of salinity (10–30 PSU) and pH (6.1–10) at 20°C temperature. Results showed that widgeon grass maintained approximately 70% higher photosynthesis rates than eelgrass under elevated pH (>8.5) and moderate salinities (15–25 PSU), reflecting greater efficiency in exploiting bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) as a carbon source. The maximum photosynthetic rates and half-saturation constants for both species were incorporated into the Grasslight model (a bio-optical model). These measurements predicted that widgeon grass could sustain maximum leaf area index under warmer, lower-salinity conditions (15-25 PSU) where eelgrass declined. These findings align with recent field observations of widgeon grass expansion and eelgrass retreat in the Bay, indicating that differences in bicarbonate-use efficiency are likely to shape future competition and distribution patterns. While ocean acidification may partially counterbalance this trend by stimulating eelgrass photosynthesis, the overall trajectory suggests a shift toward widgeon grass dominance under future climate scenarios.

presentations.title: A biomonitoring toolbox for coastal aquatic ecosystems in the vicinity of ports
presentations.abstract_summary: EcoZone research chair: 6 years of urban-port coastal limnology in Sept-Îles, Québec, Saguenay, Qikiqtarjuaq, Pointe-à-Pitre.
presentations.abstract: Coastal ecosystems are among the most highly impacted environments on the planet. They are also very dynamic and diverse systems that are challenging to monitor. Nevertheless, it is vital to gain a deeper understanding of how they function and how they are changing to mitigate the effects of current rapid planetary changes on the services they provide to large human populations. Urban-port areas apply a wide range of pressures on coastal environments. These anthropogenic hotspots are vital to economies worldwide and depend on the persistence of ecosystem services. In 2020, Université Laval initiated the EcoZone research chair in partnership with the Port of Sept-Îles and the Northern Institute for Research in Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety, to study the urban-port environment of Sept-Îles, the largest mineral port in North America, with the goal of assessing the state of its coastal ecosystem and better understanding the ecological impacts of urban and port activities in the context of global change. The EcoZone research Chair undertook a series of projects in coastal limnology and oceanography in the Sept-Îles region and near other ports (Québec, Saguenay, Qikiqtarjuaq, Pointe-à-Pitre) to explore diverse elements of the aquatic environment, including assessing the current state and long-term variations in coastal lakes and ponds, rivers, intertidal zones and near-shore regions, along environmental gradients of anthropogenic impacts. Here, we present an overview of the results from the past six years of our team’s research in the vicinity of ports.

presentations.title: [empty/withdrawn slot]
Eelgrass meadows as blue-carbon ecosystems: carbon sink capacity in subarctic meadows
presentations.abstract_summary: Saint-Lawrence subarctic seagrass beds: above-ground 0.07-0.13 kgC/m², sediment 0.13-0.52 kgC/m²; lower than high-latitude meadows.
presentations.abstract: Seagrass meadows are highly efficient blue-carbon ecosystems, converting CO₂ into organic carbon through primary production. Part of this carbon is stored short term in plant biomass, while a substantial fraction is sequestered long term in sediments. Yet global estimates of blue-carbon capacity rely mostly on temperate and tropical regions, whereas sub-Arctic environments remain under-documented. In summer 2025, five seagrass beds located in diverse habitats across the Saint-Lawrence system were sampled to quantify organic carbon stored in above- and below-ground biomass and sequestered in sediments. Carbon sink capacities varied greatly among sites, likely reflecting differences between intertidal and subtidal habitats. Organic carbon stored in above-ground biomass ranged from 0.07 to 0.13 kgC m⁻² across meadows, values comparable to other temperate eelgrass systems. Sediment organic carbon content ranged from 0.13 to 0.52 kgC m⁻², with the highest concentrations in the upper 10 cm. These sequestration capacities is lower than the range reported for high-latitude meadows. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of sub-Arctic seagrass beds as contributors to coastal carbon budgets and highlight their potential role in nature-based climate solutions. Documenting their sequestration capacity is crucial for conservation and management, especially because the degradation of seagrass meadows could release stored carbon back into the atmosphere and weaken their climate-regulation services.

name: Community Ecology
lead_organizer: Michele Burford, Griffith University

presentations.title: Spatial extent affects estimates of process contributions to pond metacommunity assembly
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract_summary: Joint species distribution models on 170 European ponds: environment dominates regional scale, species interactions dominate semi-continental, both at local scale.
presentations.abstract: Metacommunities are defined as local communities linked with the regional diversity pool via dispersal. The contributing local assembly processes environmental filtering, dispersal limitation and species interactions can be estimated by joint species distribution models (jSDM). However, the three processes may have differently strong contributions at varying spatial extents. We collected empirical data on pond metacommunities, encompassing presence/absence data of fishes, amphibians, zooplankton and benthic macroinvertebrates, in 170 ponds from 30 pondscapes in six European countries. We run jSDMs at three spatial extents, namely the semi-continental (all countries), the regional (countries separated) and the local (ponds in 1-2 pondscapes per country) extents. The pure and shared contributions of space to metacommunity assembly were minor in all models, while environment and species associations contributed strongly. The strongest pure contribution of environment was found for the regional scale, while species interactions were a strong contributor at the semi-continental scale, but also co-contributed with environment at the local scale. Important environmental predictors were pond hydroperiod, trophic state and coverage by macrophytes. Negative species associations at the local scale can plausibly be interpreted as predator-prey or competitive interactions, but positive associations dominate at all spatial extents. The contribution of the three community assembly processes differed among sites and species, suggesting a strong internal structure of pond metacommunities.

presentations.title: Weaving trait co-occurrence networks from local to landscape scales
presentations.abstract_summary: Trait co-occurrence network approach across 56 Swedish lakes and 36 rivers: lakes driven by environment, rivers by geography.
presentations.abstract: Functional composition of communities arises from the interaction between local environment and species traits, reflecting the interplay between local filters and species performance. Yet, trait-based approaches often overlook regional heterogeneity, which is defined by geographic or environmental distances between communities. This limits our ability to disentangle the role of local or regional drivers for functional assembly and hinders our understanding of both global change impacts and community functioning dynamics. To address this, we expanded a functional network approach, shifting the focus from species–trait associations to trait–trait co-occurrences, enabling us to evaluate how network structure evolves from local to regional scales while integrating spatial and environmental gradients. We developed this approach using simulated and empirical metacommunities from 56 Swedish lakes (20 years) and 36 rivers (11 years). We progressively merged communities by spatial proximity, environmental similarity, or random selection, constructing trait co-occurrence networks at each step and calculating several network indices to track structural shifts across scales (e.g., edge density, graph strength). Our results revealed scale dependency in metacommunity functional structure by showing that lake functional assembly was primarily driven by environment, while river functionality was mostly driven by geographical proximity. By bridging local and regional perspectives from a metacommunity standpoint, our method expands current understanding of trait-functional assembly.

presentations.title: 30 Years of Plankton Monitoring in Lake Champlain
presentations.abstract_summary: Long-term Lake Champlain monitoring (1992-present): zebra mussels, alewife, Bythotrephes, Cercopagis sequentially altered zooplankton; phytoplankton shifts since 1970.
presentations.abstract: The Lake Champlain Basin Program has conducted Long-Term Monitoring in Lake Champlain since the mid-1990s. This includes water quality monitoring and biological monitoring focused on planktonic communities. Long-term records (1992-present) for native zooplankton in Lake Champlain illustrate the impact of invasive species on community structure over the past three decades. Zooplankton exhibited shifts in composition associated with invasive species, including a decline in rotifer and Mysid abundance in the mid-1990s, following invasion of zebra mussels ( Dreissena polymorpha ). More recent community alterations can be attributed to invasion of the Alewife ( Alosa pseudoharengus ) in 2006-08, Spiny Waterflea ( Bythotrephes longimanus ) in 2014 and Fishhook waterflea ( Cercopagis pengoi ) in 2018. These patterns represent major changes in community structure with potential implications for the Lake’s food web dynamics. In addition, altered Diel Vertical Migration (DVM) behavior was observed in Lake Champlain following the Spiny Waterflea and Fishhook waterflea invasions. We also detected a decline in Mysis diluviana abundance following the zebra mussel invasion in Lake Champlain along with changes in population size structure over the past 3 decades. In addition, we compared phytoplankton community composition in Lake Champlain from 1970 to present demonstrating long-term shifts in composition of cyanobacteria and other taxa. Patterns in Lake Champlain’s pelagic plankton communities illustrate the threat that invasive species and/or altered thermal regimes may pose to the ecological integrity of freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: A Framework for Trait Inclusion in Fourth Corner Models: Zooplankton in Ontario Lakes
presentations.abstract_summary: 45 Ontario lakes: RLQ + fourth-corner shows fishing pressure shifts feeding strategy (filter vs raptorial), not body size; rotifers important to include.
presentations.abstract: Characterizing zooplankton communities through functional traits offers a powerful complement to taxonomic approaches, yet no standardized framework guides the inclusion in ecological models. We develop and demonstrate a generalizable framework to evaluate trait inclusion in fourth corner RLQ models, using data from 45 lakes across Ontario, Canada. Taxonomic abundance, functional traits, and environmental variables were integrated to test how environmental and anthropogenic factors structure zooplankton communities. Bayesian regression provided quantitative support for including traits, after which RLQ and fourth corner analyses were applied. While ecoregion did not differ based on environmental variables alone, RLQ identified distinct community gradients along axes of nutrient productivity and lake depth. Fishing pressure was associated with shifts in feeding strategy rather than body size, with filter-feeders associated with low pressure lakes and raptorial feeders with high pressure lakes. Rotifers, often excluded from such analyses, comprised a substantial proportion of observed communities highlighting the importance of their inclusion. We recommend broader adoption of trait-based approaches across zooplankton and other taxa, as they reveal community patterns not captured by environmental gradients and taxonomy alone.

presentations.title: Environmental disequilibrium in Canadian freshwater bioindicator communities
presentations.abstract_summary: CABIN data on 100 Canadian watersheds: eastern bioindicator communities show environmental disequilibrium; challenges reliability of bioindicator-based assessment.
presentations.abstract: Freshwater monitoring programs worldwide rely on tracking shifts in the abundances of macroinvertebrate bioindicator species, whose populations are thought to reflect freshwater ecosystem health. However, extensive evidence has demonstrated that ecological communities frequently exhibit environmental disequilibrium, where lagged responses to environmental change result in communities composed of species that are mismatched to the observed environment. Here, we use the Canadian Aquatic Biomonitoring Network (CABIN) data, which provides long-term hydrological, chemical, nutrient, and macroinvertebrate measurements, to investigate freshwater macroinvertebrate communities across 100 Canadian watersheds for environmental disequilibrium. Our preliminary results reveal spatial patterns: bioindicator communities in eastern Canadian watersheds are exhibiting environmental disequilibrium, whereas northern and western communities appear closer to environmental equilibrium. Further, using Latent Variable Models, we find that environmental disequilibrium significantly alters the relationships between macroinvertebrate bioindicator taxa and local water chemistry, challenging the reliability of bioindicator-based environmental assessments. Our findings highlight the need for adaptive strategies that incorporate community-environment mismatches, providing insights for more reliable ecosystem monitoring under ongoing environmental change.

presentations.title: Environmental filtering dominates zooplankton community assembly in ponds
presentations.abstract_summary: 52 Ankara ponds: trait-based analyses show strong environmental filtering with multi-filtering scenario; functional convergence in feeding, habitat, stoichiometric traits.
presentations.abstract: Ponds are biodiversity hotspots and ideal ecosystems for studying community assembly of different organisms due to being numerous, having small size, discrete boundaries and being in a network. Zooplankton, rapidly respond to environmental change and provide functional links within food webs. However, the drivers shaping zooplankton functional diversity in small waterbodies remain understudied. We examined zooplankton functional traits, community-weighted means, and standardized functional diversity indices across 52 ponds in Ankara, Türkiye. Using trait-based metrics and null-model standardized effect sizes, we assessed whether zooplankton communities are structured by habitat filtering or by limiting similarity. We found clear functional convergence, demonstrating strong environmental filtering. Several traits including feeding strategies, habitat preferences, and stoichiometric categories showed significant convergence relative to null expectations. In contrast; species richness, functional dispersion, and body size did not respond to single environmental variables, indicating that no single factor drives community assembly. The results point to the combined influence of multiple co-occurring stressors producing a multi-filtering scenario. Overall, zooplankton communities in these ponds are shaped by synergistic habitat filters rather than trait divergence, highlighting their vulnerability to land and water use. Understanding how multiple stressors jointly structure pond communities is essential for designing conservation strategies for these overlooked ecosystems.

name: Fish and Fisheries
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Isaac Armstrong, Queen's University Canada

presentations.title: UNDERSTANDING 25 YEARS OF CHANGE IN THE EAGLE LAKE FISHERY: RECENT SHIFTS AND IMPLICATIONS FOR THE FUTURE OF CALIFORNIA'S MOST PLANTED HATCHERY TROUT
presentations.abstract: Eagle Lake, California, supports a distinctive assemblage of native fish and is the home range of the endemic Eagle Lake Rainbow Trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss aquilarium), a highly valued trophy species and one of the most widely planted hatchery trout in the western United States. Despite its cultural and recreational significance, the trout are unable to maintain self-sustaining populations since the 1950s due to the degradation of natural spawning habitat, rendering it fully dependent on annual hatchery production. About 180,000 fish are stocked each year, yet long-term, systematic monitoring of in-lake conditions has been limited. Over the past 25 years, a series of independent studies—using seine and gill-net surveys, creel data, water-quality monitoring, invertebrate sampling, and stable-isotope analysis—have provided a fragmented but valuable record of ecological change. Synthesizing these efforts reveals notable shifts, including altered summer habitat use and a transition in adult trout diets from strong piscivory to increased reliance on invertebrate prey.

presentations.title: Changes in Minnesota fish communities indexed through mean temperature of the catch
presentations.abstract: Fish communities are responding to warming water temperatures through shifts in distribution, phenology, and community composition. Climate change has altered species abundances, yet detecting community-level responses is challenging due to natural variability, the influence of multiple drivers with time lags, indirect and nonlinear effects and the lack of long-term data with historical baselines. To address this, we use the Mean Temperature of the Catch (MTC), which integrates each species' preferred thermal niche weighted by its relative abundance, to track temperature-related changes in lake fish communities. Using hierarchical generalized additive models, we assessed temporal trends in MTC from long-term Minnesota DNR gill-net and trap-net fisheries surveys across hundreds of lakes relative to changes in lake water temperatures from 1950-2024. We also calculated MTC using angler creel surveys to evaluate whether angler catch rates reflect similar thermal shifts. MTC from fisheries-independent surveys increased over time and was strongly associated with warming, though patterns varied across lakes, with some systems showing asynchronous responses. In contrast, MTC from angler catches increased more slowly, potentially indicating hyperstability in angler-reported data.

presentations.title: NO EVIDENCE OF A MARINE RESOURCE LIMITATION IN ARCTIC CHAR AT THEIR SOUTHERN RANGE EXTENT
presentations.abstract: Climate change threatens southern anadromous Arctic char Salvelinus alpinus, potentially through indirect impacts of warming temperatures and decreased genetic diversity. Char's resilience to warming and shifting prey depends on its ability to utilize available marine food resources and allocate energy to storage before their late summer river migration. To assess possible climate impacts in the marine environment, we investigated the diets and energy reserves of Arctic char at six sites along a latitudinal gradient spanning ~53˚N to 59˚N in Labrador, a region approaching the southern limit of their anadromous range. We quantified diet breadth using stable carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur isotopes and evaluated energy reserves through lipid composition measured in the muscle tissue of 246 char. Contrary to expectations, char showed no latitudinal trend in isotopic dietary breadth (IDB), condition, or energy reserves. Across all sites, Postville Char had the smallest IDB and the highest energy stores. Our findings suggest that under existing climate warming, available marine resources are not limiting to Arctic char anadromy.

presentations.title: ENVIRONMENTAL GRADIENT SHAPING PARASITE DISTRIBUTION AND EYE SIZE VARIATION IN EUROPEAN PERCH (PERCA FLUVIATILIS) IN LAKE BALATON
presentations.abstract: Lake Balaton, Central Europe's largest lake, exhibits a strong west–east environmental gradient due to its multiple western inflows, single eastern outflow, and four different basins leading to differences in turbidity, chemical composition, among other parameters. This phenomenon may influence the distribution, growth, production and morphology of visual predator fish like the native European perch (Perca fluviatilis), which inhabit areas with varying water transparency. We seek to reveal the potential effects of light conditions on their relative eye size. During morphometric examinations of the perch, we also observed black spots appearing on the fish. The pigmentation is caused by the metacercariae of trematodes (Apophallus spp.). Our aim is to examine infection patterns of this ectoparasite in perch populations of the lake. Assessment was based on digital photographs of fish collected along the lake's northern and southern shores, including the western and eastern ends. Parasites showed non-random distribution, suggesting localized ecological or physiological constraints. Higher infection intensities were observed in the clearer eastern basin, likely related to water transparency and final hosts (diving birds). On the other hand perch inhabiting more turbid waters exhibited relatively larger eyes, indicating morphological plasticity.

presentations.title: IDENTIFYING IMPERILED TRANSBOUNDARY MIGRATORY FRESHWATER FISHES FOR CONSERVATION UNDER THE CONVENTION ON MIGRATORY SPECIES (CMS)
presentations.abstract: Freshwater migratory fishes are in decline worldwide, and numerous threats such as dams and habitat loss threaten these freshwater fish populations. Many of these migratory freshwater fishes migrate across international borders, and the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) is the only intergovernmental convention specifically designed to facilitate international conservation of migratory animals. However, over 60 nations are not party to CMS, hindering the convention's ability to conserve many transboundary migratory freshwater fishes. We identified 392 transboundary migratory freshwater fishes across the globe's 254 international river basins that are classified by the IUCN Red List as 'Near Threatened', 'Vulnerable', 'Endangered', 'Critically Endangered', 'Data Deficient', or 'Least Concern' with a 'Declining' population trend. Additionally, we used a scoring criterion that evaluated which imperiled transboundary migratory freshwater fishes should be prioritized by CMS. Overall, we found that nations that are not party to CMS have more imperiled transboundary migratory freshwater fish populations than nations that are party to CMS. Additionally, southeast Asia, eastern Europe, and South America are hotspots for imperiled transboundary migratory freshwater fishes.

presentations.title: The importance of understanding processes that shape intraspecific diversity for conservation
presentations.abstract: The world's biodiversity is facing accelerating, and unprecedented, decline. This can be clearly seen in aquatic ecosystems which have been altered, fragmented, and simplified because of anthropogenic influences. However, even though biodiversity has been defined as diversity, within species, among species and among communities and ecosystems, the concept of biodiversity is usually understood as quite static construct. The focus is commonly on species rather than on intraspecific (within-species) diversity. Furthermore, the focus has emphasized describing patterns rather than the processes which generate and maintain biodiversity over time. This focus can be seen among scientists, studying biodiversity, among policymakers and is reflected in the public's general lack of understanding / misunderstanding of biodiversity concepts. Focusing on species as the unit of diversity in a static way carries great conservation risk as it does not account for individual- and population level processes and their interactions. It furthermore ignores evolutionary distinctiveness of populations, that may be evolutionary and ecologically different. Now populations are being lost at higher rate than species, and the loss of populations has a great impact on the survival of species, it is crucial that we put the focus on intraspecific diversity in research, conservation planning and management.

name: Zooplankton Ecology and Physiology
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Nandini Sarma, FES Iztacala, UNAM

presentations.title: DEVELOPMENTAL PLASTICITY, NOT ADAPTATION TO OCEAN WARMING, DETERMINES A COPEPOD RESPONSE TO MARINE HEATWAVES
presentations.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHW), thermal events during which temperatures exceed the 90th percentile of 30-year historical mean for more than five days are increasing in frequency, intensity, and duration. MHW can have adverse effects on ectotherms since such high temperatures are often physiologically stressful. Organisms can cope with MHW via phenotypic plasticity or genetic adaptation to warming, but the relative roles of these adaptive mechanisms is poorly understood. We tested how evolutionary thermal adaptation and developmental thermal plasticity shaped the response of the copepod, Acartia tonsa, to future MHW by measuring the responses of warm-adapted (reared at 22°C for >150 generations) and warm-acclimated (22°C for two generations) copepods to MHW temperatures of 27.5°C and 30.8°C. Adult breeding pairs were exposed to MHW conditions for 7.5 days during which we measured survival, egg production rate (EPR), and egg hatching success (HS). Our preliminary results did not reveal greater survival, EPR, HS, nor transgenerational benefits in the adapted treatment compared to the acclimated treatment. This suggests that evolutionary adaptation to elevated temperatures does not provide additional benefits beyond those of developmental plasticity during future MHW.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF MICROPLASTICS AND NATURAL PARTICLES ON THE AQUATIC INVERTEBRATE DAPHNIA MAGNA UNDER DIFFERENT DIETARY QUALITY SCENARIOS
presentations.abstract: Natural and synthetic particles co-occur in the aquatic environment. However, little information is available about the effects of natural particles on freshwater animals and how these effects differ from those of synthetic particles, especially under the scenarios of decreasing dietary quality and increasing cyanobacteria in the aquatic environment. Therefore, this study evaluated apical and molecular effects of polypropylene (PP) microplastics (MPs) and three natural non-food particles (i.e., kaolin, peat, and sediment) on the freshwater invertebrate Daphnia magna fed either a green alga or a mixture of green alga and cyanobacterium. After the 21-d chronic exposure of 10 mg/L PP when using the green alga Acutodesmus sp. as diet, the size of D. magna was significantly reduced, and the molting time was significantly extended compared with the control. However, the chronic effects of PP were masked when the cyanobacterium Pseudanabaena sp. was added to their diet. The natural particles kaolin, peat, and sediment posed insignificant effects on D. magna regardless of dietary quality. The expression of molting-related genes (e.g., ecr-a) and oxidative stress-related genes (e.g., sod2) was significantly upregulated in D. magna with the exposure of both natural and synthetic particles. The predicted no-effect concentration of PP was derived as 0.025 mg/L, raising concerns relating to their toxicity and risks in the contaminated aquatic environment.

presentations.title: A HIGH-RESOLUTION PHYSIOLOGICAL TIME-SERIES UNCOVERS STRONG BUT VARIABLE SEASONAL ACCLIMATION OF COPEPOD THERMAL LIMITS
presentations.abstract: Community responses to warming are affected by both intra-specific variation in thermal tolerance and variation in acclimation capacity across community members. These factors, however, are often overlooked, leading to uncertainties about how climate change affects biodiversity. In temperate regions, communities are exposed to large seasonal temperature fluctuations, providing an opportunity to examine community-wide effects of acclimation under natural conditions. Using a weekly physiological time series, we examined seasonal variation in upper thermal limits for the entire community of calanoid copepods in Lake Champlain, a large and highly seasonal lake in North America.
