Thermal limits varied substantially between species, with winter-dominant species having lower thermal limits than summer-dominant species. Our high-resolution temporal data also revealed substantial but variable acclimation capacities across community members. Over the course of our collections, we also recorded two novel species occurrences in Lake Champlain, both of which were notable for their high upper thermal limits.

presentations.title: Demographic responses of brachionid rotifers (Brachionidae) to interspecific allelochemicals
presentations.abstract: Many species of planktonic rotifers especially members of Brachionidae coexist in trophic eutrophic waterbodies. Their relative abundances in nature vary depending on the season. Though, both, abiotic (temp., pH) and biotic (competition, predation) factors influence interspecific interactions, the role of allelochemicals in influencing the abundances of rotifers within Brachionidae is less documented. In this work we evaluated the demographic responses of each rotifer species (Brachionus angularis, Brachionus calyciflorus, Brachionus havanaensis and Plationus patulus) separately (controls) and in the presence of conditioned-medium (treatments) using Chlorella vulgaris at 1 million cells/ml) as algal food. Cohort life table data showed that survivorship and reproduction of the test rotifers in controls were higher compared to those cultured on conditioned-medium. P. patulus was most adversely affected due to allelochemicals from B. angularis, B. calyciflorus and B. havanaensis. On the other hand, B. havanaensis was least affected by the conditioned medium from the rest of rotifer species.

presentations.title: Population growth of Cordylophora caspia (Cnidaria) from River Tuxpan (Mexico) on rotifer or copepod diets
presentations.abstract: Rivers are among the entry points of invasive species into inland waters. Studies on two rivers in the State of Veracruz (Mexico), La Antigua and River Tuxpan indicate the presence of some non-native invertebrates such as Mesocyclops pehpeiensis (Cyclopoida), Notholca cf. lieppeterseni (Rotifera) and Cordylophora caspia (Cnidaria). Epicontinental rivers also show high abundances of Kellicottia bostoniensis and Daphnia cf. curvirostris, species not native to Mexican waters. Cordylophora caspia is a voracious hydrozoan predator with a high preference for cyclopoid and harpacticoid copepods than rotifer prey. Here we studied the population growth of C. caspia on Apocyclops panamensis (Cyclopoida, Copepoda), Nitokra lacustris (Harpacticoida, Copepoda) and Brachionus plicatilis (Monogononta, Rotifera) at three salinities of 10, 20, and 30 g/L of sea salt at 25°C. The results showed that C. caspia reached highest densities on diets of A. panamensis and Nitokra lacustris, and lowest on B. plicatilis. Population growth rates of Cordylophora were higher at salinities of 20 and 30 g/L than at 10 g/L.

presentations.title: Complementary Visual Morphology and Functional Traits Boost Automatic Macroinvertebrate Identification Through Multimodal Deep Learning
presentations.affiliation: Faculty of Sciences and Mathematics, University of Niš, Serbia
presentations.abstract: Deep learning and computer vision have been widely used to improve species monitoring in routine bioassessment of aquatic ecosystems. However, a major limitation remains the lack of specimens, especially for rare taxa, which leads to imbalanced training datasets and consequently a decline in model accuracy. This study aimed to improve the automated identification of aquatic macroinvertebrates by developing a multimodal convolutional neural network (mCNN) that integrates both visual and ecological characteristics of taxa for classification. For this purpose, a database was constructed, comprising images of larvae from 200 macroinvertebrate taxa collected across 56 sites within the South Morava River Basin, Serbia. In addition, a dataset of eight ecological traits per selected taxon was compiled based on field observations requiring no taxonomic expertise. Two classification models were trained: the first (M1) utilized image data only, while the second (M2) integrated visual data (specimen images) with ecological traits through a parallel multilayer perceptron (MLP) and weighted concatenation approach. The multimodal model (M2) achieved an accuracy of 99%, while the image-based model (M1) reached a substantially lower accuracy of 94%.

name: Ecology, Management, and Conservation of Temporary Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Global climate change is expected to exacerbate the drying out of temporary freshwater ecosystems worldwide.
lead_organizer: Luciana Barbosa, Federal University of Paraiba
co_organizers: Elizabeth Meyer, Institute for Evolution & Biodiversity
Elizabeth Walsh, University of Texas at El Paso

presentations.title: Biodiversity values of temporary wetlands in southern Australia: documenting the unseen and neglected
presentations.abstract: This study aimed to document the biodiversity values of remaining wetlands on private land in the Basalt Plains region of Victoria, Australia. We conducted annual vegetation surveys in wetlands. More than 100 species were detected with a high degree of segregation among wetlands. The results support the contention that there is a diversity of wetlands in this landscape.

presentations.title: Understanding and conservation of biodiversity - what can we learn from Icelandic freshwater systems?
presentations.abstract: Icelandic freshwater systems have many unique features that contribute to research and understanding of biological diversity. Here, we will present Icelandic freshwater systems in the context of the Global Biodiversity Framework and combine it with the current environmental issues, resource use, management and conservation of freshwaters in Iceland.

presentations.title: CHARACTERIZING THE ROLE OF HYDROLOGICAL PROCESSES ON POND WATER BALANCES OVER SPACE AND TIME IN THE WHOOPING CRANE SUMMER RANGE
presentations.abstract: Since 2022, we have obtained seasonal measurements of water isotope compositions and chemistry, and hourly depth logs at 63 ponds across the core nesting areas. Results show nest locations in 2022 clustered in areas where ponds are strongly connected to groundwater. Paleolimnological evidence indicates pond desiccation has been a rare occurrence since 1800.

presentations.title: SEASONAL DYNAMICS OF MONOGONONT ROTIFERS IN TEMPORARY ROCK POOLS IN BRAZILIAN SEMIARID REGION
presentations.abstract: This study analyzed the rotifer assemblages in semi-arid rock pools throughout the hydrological cycle. Ten genera belonging to eight families were identified. The wet phase exhibited more homogeneous assemblages, whereas the dry phase revealed greater heterogeneity.

presentations.title: THE FATE OF AQUATIC INVERTEBRATE COMMUNITIES OCCURRING IN TEMPORARY CHIHUAHUAN DESERT HABITATS IN RESPONSE TO INCREASING HEAT AND DROUGHT
presentations.abstract: To determine how heat and drought changes impact inhabitants of temporary aquatic habitats, we sampled rock pools and playas in the Chihuahuan Desert. Species richness recovered from water-filled habitats did not change in rock pools but decreased in playas. Predicted climate change may lead to simplified aquatic communities and altered ecosystem function.

presentations.title: CLONAL VARIATION IN INDUCED DAPHNIA RESPONSES TO MULTIPLE PREDATORS WITH CONTRASTING HUNTING STRATEGIES
presentations.abstract: This study examines Daphnia responses to three genera of invertebrate predators with distinct hunting strategies: Chaoborus, Notonecta, and Enallagma. Fourteen clonal isofemale lines of D. pulex were isolated from seven forest ponds and exposed to chemical cues from each predator.

name: Community Ecology
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Michele Burford, Griffith University

presentations.title: Does Global Marine Zooplankton Trait Variation Support Niche-Centrality?
presentations.abstract: Understanding the drivers of spatial patterns of species' abundance is central to biogeography. The niche-centrality hypothesis posits that species peak in abundance at the center of their ecological niche, and decline towards the edges as conditions become less favourable. Although evidence for niche-centrality for abundance is mixed, genetic variation consistently decreases with increasing distance from the niche center. However, patterns in trait variation have been rarely tested. While niche-centrality predicts trait variation should be lower at the edges, environmental filtering at these edges could promote novel trait expression through plasticity or adaptation, leading to greater trait variation at the periphery. Using a large database of in-situ individual images of marine zooplankton from over 3,000 sites across the world's oceans, we assessed whether zooplankton morphological traits followed patterns expected under niche centrality or stress-induced variation. Niche estimates for major zooplankton taxa were derived from concentration-based species distribution models, using shape-constrained generalized additive models. For the most abundant taxa, Copepoda and Rhizaria, we quantified variation in 12 traits related to size, shape, and transparency. We examined associations between variation in these traits and distance from the niche center. For copepods, trait variation generally decreased with abundance, supporting the niche-centrality hypothesis. In contrast, for single-celled Rhizarians, trait variation sometimes increased with distance from the niche center, suggesting stress-induced variation. Our results show that morphological trait variation in marine zooplankton follows contrasting global patterns, shaped by context-dependent eco-evolutionary processes.

presentations.title: BETA DIVERSITY IN ATLANTIC FOREST HEADWATER FISHES: DISPERSAL BARRIERS OR LOCAL ENVIRONMENTAL FILTERS?
presentations.affiliation: Universidade do Vale do Itajaí - UNIVALI
presentations.abstract: Coastal river basins in the Atlantic Forest of southern Brazil are historically isolated between mountains and the sea. Along with coastal human expansion, this isolation limits stream fish dispersal. We assessed spatial patterns of beta diversity, the mechanisms driving it, and the effects of environmental and spatial drivers over species composition in streams. The study was carried out in the Itajaí-Mirim River Basin (SC, Brazil; 170 km; 1,677.2 km²; 1,260–25 m altitude range). We sampled 40 1st–3rd order streams using 50-m blocked reaches and 3-pass electrofishing and measured limnological parameters. Beta diversity (species-matrix variance) was partitioned into LCBD, turnover, and richness variation. LCBD drivers were tested with a beta-GLM. Partial-RDA and variance partitioning was used to assess environmental and spatial drivers influence over species composition. We recorded 24 species (11 families; 5 orders). Beta diversity was low (BDTotal = 0.43), with no stream showing above-average LCBD, unlike typical tropical basins. Sites with higher temperature and lower DO tended to show higher LCBD – those sites had low richness (2 spp.), low abundance (11–46 ind.), and higher altitude. Species turnover explained 53% and richness variation, 47% of beta diversity. Species composition was weakly (non-significantly) explained by both environmental (0.069) and spatial (0.035) drivers. The low variation and weak turnover contribution may reflect dispersal restrictions from land-use changes and pollution, or historical isolation in high-gradient headwaters, yet to be tested.

presentations.title: BEHAVIOURAL TACTICS ACROSS THERMAL GRADIENTS ALIGN WITH PARTIAL MORPHOLOGICAL DIVERGENCE IN BROOK CHARR
presentations.abstract: Cold-water fishes must balance foraging needs with thermal and oxygen constraints, a challenge that is intensifying under climate change. In stratified lakes, brook charr (Salvelinus fontinalis) face strong vertical gradients, forcing them to decide when to enter warm surface waters or remain in cooler depths. Using high-resolution acoustic telemetry, we quantified fine-scale thermal habitat use, vertical forays, and diel patterns in a wild population across the summer period. As surface temperatures rose, brook charr reduced both the number and duration of epilimnetic forays, while hypolimnion use, not limited by oxygen availability, increased. Epilimnetic forays peaked at dusk and varied with moonlight, whereas hypolimnetic use peaked at dawn and dusk and was unaffected by lunar phase. Diel patterns shifted seasonally, with surface use restricted to twilight during warm months. Multivariate analyses revealed two repeatable behavioural tactics: a 'warm' tactic with frequent surface forays and a 'cool' tactic linked to deeper, colder habitats. These tactics corresponded with subtle morphological differences, particularly among males. Our findings show that brook charr exhibit consistent foraging behavioural tactics shaped by thermal constraints, suggesting that warming lakes may enhance phenotypic diversification linked to foraging and thermal ecology of lacustrine brook charr.

presentations.title: Daily Phytoplankton Dynamics During a Wet Spring-Summer and Subsequent Late-Summer Drought in a Hypereutrophic Reservoir
presentations.abstract: Within eutrophic waterbodies in the Midwestern United States, primary consequences of climate change–rising global temperatures and changes in precipitation patterns–may promote cyanobacteria persistence and proliferation outside their expected phenology, disrupting ecosystem function and stability. However, altering frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation events (hereafter, 'storms'), may further influence and mediate phytoplankton dynamics. Storms often provide simultaneous yet contrasting, environmental conditions that can affect major taxonomic groups of phytoplankton and within-group taxa, differently. To capture storm influence on lake condition and phytoplankton dynamics in the Midwest, a daily 250 day water collection effort in Acton Lake–a hypereutrophic Southwestern Ohio reservoir–was performed throughout the growing season and its shoulder seasons. Preliminary analyses for the first half of the study identified an intense multiday spring storm that resulted in severe regional flooding. On this day, total phytoplankton concentration declined from 51.04 μg/L to 11.30 μg/L, with concentrations below 10 μg/L for sixteen consecutive days following, reaching a minimum of 2.91 μg/L. Cyanobacteria comprised approximately 20-30% of the community during this period; pre-storm composition was dominated by diatoms (60-75% diatoms, <2% cyanobacteria). Further analyses will assess phytoplankton dynamics and lake condition for all storms captured throughout the study in addition to other climatic events (i.e. summer surface temperature maxima and late season drought).

presentations.title: How blooms of inedible producers and a dilution effect among grazers interact along enrichment gradients
presentations.abstract: In lake communities, heterogeneity within trophic levels can collide, potentially shaping both the size of algal blooms and epidemics of disease in grazers. To illustrate, consider two forms of complete resistance, inedibility and immunity. Specifically, imagine that a neutrally inedible producer competes for nutrients with an edible one that is consumed by susceptible and completely immune grazer-hosts. The immune host can control epidemics of virulent parasites in its competitor via the 'host regulation' of dilution. These two forms of resistance create four major different outcomes along enrichment gradients.

presentations.title: Water quality assessment of the Lake Xaltocan (Mexico City, Mexico) using seasonal plankton collections
presentations.abstract: Lake Xaltocan, part of Lake Xochimilco, is a shallow (<1 m depth) high altitude (2240 m above sea level) waterbody in Mexico City (Mexico). Lake Xochimilco is the type locality of the axolotl, Ambystoma mexicanum. Other endangered species found in this lake include the fish Chirostoma humboldtianum, and the amphipod Cambarellus montezumae. We collected monthly plankton (zooplankton and phytoplankton) samples from Lake Xaltocan for one year (December 2022 to November 2023) and evaluated the water quality. Along with plankton, physical and chemical parameters including temperature, depth, Secchi transparency, pH, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, alkalinity, Chlorophyll a and NO3-N and PO4-P levels were measured. The average temperature of the lake was 19°C. It is alkaline, with an annual mean alkalinity of 226.3 mg/L of CaCO3. pH ranged from 7.2 to 9.0, and conductivity varied from 326 to 1216 µS cm-1. Nitrate (1.7-19.6 mg L-1) and phosphate (1.5 - 7.8 mg L-1) concentrations indicated eutrophic conditions, consistent with chlorophyll a values (33 - 186 µg L-1). The phytoplankton community was dominated by chlorophytes and diatoms. The zooplankton community comprised 36 species. The rotifer family Brachionidae was dominant throughout the year. The trophic state index of rotifers (TSIrot) ranged from 77 – 92, indicating the Lake Xaltocan is hypertrophic.

name: Aquatic Invasion Ecology (Posters)
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Pascal Bodmer, Cornell Univeristy

presentations.title: ATTACHMENT OF ZOOPLANKTON TO RECREATIONAL AND WILDLIFE DISPERSAL VECTORS IN A REMOTE NATIONAL PARK
presentations.abstract: Isle Royale National Park is among the most remote and protected areas in the contiguous United States. Its relative isolation and restricted land use furthers the perception that its 200 inland freshwater lakes are immune to biological invasions. Yet even in wilderness settings, human recreation and wildlife movements may facilitate the overland transport of aquatic organisms. We tested this potential by quantifying the diversity and abundance of planktonic-stage rotifers and crustacean zooplankton attached to three pieces of recreational equipment (canoe, water filter, t-shirt) and three animal integuments (beaver, loon, moose) exposed to Lake Superior at Isle Royale. Mixed-effects models revealed significant effects of vector type on zooplankton attachment densities (p < 0.001), with consistently higher total estimated marginal mean densities on animal vectors (1601-2842 individuals m-2) compared to human (417-969). While total attachment density generally scaled proportionately with log-transformed ambient density (p = 0.043), smaller rotifers (Polyarthra and Keratella) and smaller crustaceans (Bosmina and Eubosmina) were overrepresented in attachment samples (mean = 46%, 30%, 27%, 24%, respectively) compared to ambient conditions (30%, 22%, 23%, 18%). These results suggest that attachment potential is not only based on vector type and environmental community densities but also on organism body size, highlighting the importance for management plans to consider both vector characteristics and biotic context when assessing invasion risk.

presentations.title: LAKE ERIE PHYTOPLANKTON AND NON-INDIGENOUS SPECIES HISTORIES REVEALED THROUGH aeDNA
presentations.abstract: Lake Erie, the most nutrient-enriched of the Great Lakes, has recurring harmful algal blooms (HABs) that impact both ecosystem and human health. Monitoring has improved HAB detection and forecasting. However, these records extend back only a few decades, leaving significant temporal gaps, which limit our understanding of how ecosystems have responded to past disturbances. We investigate ancient environmental DNA (aeDNA) from age-modeled sediments to reconstruct the dynamics of microbial and eukaryotic communities in western Lake Erie from 1865 to the present. We generated amplicons of the 18S rRNA gene to determine taxonomic inventories, and using CONISS, we found a significant change at ~1976 CE from a green alga-dominated to a diatom-dominated assemblage, suggesting a major ecological shift. This coincided with the establishment of the Clean Water Act and the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of 1972, which resulted in improved water quality in Lake Erie. This policy mediated water quality change potentially initiated the shift in the aeDNA reconstructed phytoplankton community. The shift to diatoms is dominated by non-indigenous genera (Actinocyclus and Skeletonema), which we hypothesize are likely overrepresented in our dataset because not all common Great Lakes diatoms have genetic vouchers. We also found dreissenids in our amplicon data, showing the utility of aeDNA in the detection of non-indigenous species. Collectively, our data show that aeDNA provides a more robust record of long-term ecological changes in the Great Lakes driven by disturbances and recovery.

presentations.title: STIRRING THINGS UP: DISPERSAL RATES OF ORGANISMS ON RECREATIONAL WATERCRAFT AMONG VARIOUS WATERBODIES
presentations.affiliation: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
presentations.abstract: Recreational watercraft transport organisms from a wide variety of taxa with different natural dispersal capabilities. Empirical data from previous studies on organisms transported over land via internal or external parts of watercraft have been limited to short time periods and few waterbodies and sampling sites, leaving a large uncertainty for dispersal rates of less common taxa. ESF-NYS OPRHP Watercraft Inspection Stewards collected water samples from bilges and other parts of watercraft at over 20 boat launches across upstate New York. Samples from the summers of 2019, 2023, and 2025 were filtered using a 50-micron mesh and organisms were identified, counted, and photographed under a dissecting microscope. Results were matched to corresponding boat steward inspections and survey data to analyze relative importance of factors including intended boater activity on the water, macrophytes removed during watercraft inspection, direction (launching or retrieving), spread prevention measures taken by the boater, and travel history. Preliminary statistics show an average of 133 zooplankton per liter of bilge and other water sampled on boats and suggest that boat launch location and direction are important predictors of the number of zooplankton transported. Approximately one third of water samples contained sediment and more benthic and macrophyte-associated organisms than pelagic ones. These results imply that benthic and epiphytic invertebrates, which naturally disperse shorter distances, are being transported by watercraft at a higher rate than previously expected.

presentations.title: Habitat-Driven Trade-offs in Pontederia crassipes and the Balance of Ecosystem Services and Disservices in Coastal Wetlands
presentations.abstract: Human activities have shaped wetlands of high ecological and economic value, but biological invasions have become one of the most damaging pressures. Free-floating invasive alien plants such as Pontederia crassipes disrupt hydrological stability, alter nutrient dynamics, and threaten coastal ecosystems. Modelling is an essential tool for mapping invasion patterns and designing effective management strategies. In this study, data from in situ decomposition experiments and ex situ mesocosm assays along a salinity gradient were incorporated into a model representing two seasons across aquatic continuums in the Ria de Aveiro. The results highlight the substantial effort required to control P. crassipes in a coastal system influenced by variable salinity. They also emphasize the need for an integrated and collaborative management strategy involving universities, policymakers, and local communities. This includes mechanical removal, biomass valorization, and coordinated actions to mitigate ecological impacts and preserve this sensitive wetland area. Our findings offer a scientific basis for planning sustainable control measures in coastal environments

name: Coastal Ecosystems (Posters)
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Osvaldo Iván Ulloa Quijada, Universidad de Concepción Chile

presentations.title: Response of the Littoral Epilithic Communities to Climate Change: an in-situ Warming Experiment Design
presentations.affiliation: Middle East Technical University - Institute of Marine Sciences
presentations.abstract: Global warming alters aquatic ecosystem structure and functioning, and it essential to understand how aquatic communities respond to thermal stress for better mitigation measures. Epilithic assemblages of the littoral rocky-shore communities play a key role in nearshore primary production and energy flow, making their thermal responses particularly relevant to coastal ecosystem functioning. In this study, we developed a novel in situ heated settlement system that enables dynamic warming of natural substrates under real coastal conditions. The setup contains 16 travertine rock plates (37.5 × 32 × 3 cm): 8 heated and 8 non-heated, with 2 of the non-heated plates serving as reference controls. All the heated and the reference plates are equipped with digital temperature sensors linked to an Arduino based automation system that maintains an adjustable temperature offset above ambient seawater. Heating is delivered to substrate through 75 W/m electrical cables embedded beneath the plates. Each plate is topped with 4 × 4 × 1 cm travertine stone units to standardize epilithic sampling. This field-based methodology provides a controlled yet ecologically realistic platform for testing how sustained or dynamically modulated warming influences biofilm formation, larval settlement, and community structure under future climate-driven temperature regimes. The results of one month trial of this system in coastal Eastern Mediterranean sea will be discussed in this presentation.

presentations.title: SPATIAL VARIABILITY OF AUTUMN DIATOM BLOOMS IN THE SOUTHERN BALTIC DERIVED FROM IN SITU MEASUREMENTS OF MARINE PARTICLE SIZE DISTRIBUTION
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton is a key component of the marine food web and plays an important role in shaping the ecosystem of the Baltic Sea. This study focuses on detecting the autumn bloom in the southern Baltic. Microscopic analysis of water samples from several locations confirmed that the bloom was caused mainly by one diatom species, Coscinodiscus granii. By combining measured cell sizes with particle size distribution (PSD) data, we identified equivalent spherical diameters between 47.4 and 188.0 μm, with clear peaks at 78.4–92.6 and 92.6–109 μm. These size ranges gave the bloom a distinct PSD signal that allowed us to separate C. granii from the total suspended particulate matter (SPM). Field measurements in 2012 and 2014 showed strong spatial changes: concentrations ranged from almost zero to 0.2 μL L⁻¹ in 2012 and from 0.3 to 0.9 μL L⁻¹ in 2014, while its share in total SPM varied locally from a few percent to about 50%. These results highlight how patchy and dynamic autumn diatom blooms can be. They also show that these methods can be useful for tracking dominant species during such events and may also help identify other seasonal particles, such as spring pollen.

presentations.title: Challenges in Estimating Net Ecosystem Production in Arctic Coastal Lagoons
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at El Paso
presentations.abstract: The Arctic is warming faster than the global average, yet the metabolism of Arctic coastal ecosystems remains poorly constrained. In Elson Lagoon, an estuary near Utqiaġvik, Alaska, continuous, year-round dissolved oxygen (DO) measurements during 2022–2023 were used to estimate net ecosystem production (NEP) and assess seasonal variation in metabolism. Metabolic rates were inferred from diel DO curves under the assumption that photosynthesis occurs during daylight and respiration dominates during dark conditions. However, multiple physical processes complicated NEP estimation. Preliminary data show that cold-water influxes from the ocean, wind-driven currents, and vertical mixing events introduced DO independently of biological activity. During periods of ice cover that impede atmosphere exchange, DO correlated with water velocity instead of following traditional diel cycling. For example, currents from the north increased DO, while currents from the east decreased DO. In contrast, during the open water period, air temperature became a stronger predictor of DO change, while other mixing patterns introduced variability. Physical influences obscure diel signals, highlighting challenges in separating biological from physical drivers. Our results demonstrate that NEP estimation in Arctic lagoons requires careful consideration of physical water movement, stratification and ice-cover dynamics. Understanding these interactions is critical for predicting how primary production and respiration respond to rapid warming and for improving carbon cycling models in Arctic lagoons.

presentations.title: Ocean Deoxygenation: A Case Study in the Easter South Pacific
presentations.abstract: The Easter South Pacific (ESP) is an ideal natural laboratory for examining the physical, ecological, and biogeochemical consequences of ocean deoxygenation (OD) driven by global warming. This premise forms the basis for an integrated study through the Millennium Nucleus DEOXS. Using modeling tools, ocean observations, and experimental work, this project studies changes in the distribution and intensity of the oxygen minimum zone in the southeastern coastal upwelling region and how the exacerbated hypoxia caused by ocean deoxygenation (OD) can impact the biodiversity and ecophysiology of zooplankton and the biogeochemical processes associated with the carbon and nitrogen cycles and the ocean-atmosphere exchange of greenhouse gases in the upwelling zone. This is an innovative approach to addressing a highly relevant problem (OD) that is generating significant concern worldwide and is very likely to impact on the productivity and health of highly productive upwelling systems in the eastern boundary, which support a large fishing industry and the well-being of several developed and developing countries.

presentations.title: Coastal Antarctic waters represent a strong carbon sink when phytoplankton biomass is high: insights from satellite ocean color
presentations.abstract: While the Southern Ocean is usually considered a sink for atmospheric CO2, disagreements remain about the magnitude of surface ocean carbon uptake and even the sign of the flux. Ice-covered regions and highly productive Antarctic coastal waters are often overlooked. Spatial and temporal gaps in Southern Ocean datasets may be ameliorated by incorporating satellite ocean color data. In this work we estimate average CO2 uptake versus outgassing conditions for the Southern Ocean by coupling ship-based pCO2 data with satellite ocean color data, with an emphasis on the coastal Antarctic waters with the highest biological productivity. In these productive waters, the air-sea carbon flux and Chl-a concentration are tightly coupled at monthly time scales. Approximately 15% of the Southern Ocean south of 55oS latitude is characterized by high phytoplankton biomass, defined here as Chl-a > 1 mg m-3; months and locations with this high biomass are associated with surface ocean carbon uptake (ΔpCO2 < 0) rather than outgassing. Results highlight the contrast between the offshore open-ocean Southern Ocean waters with lower phytoplankton biomass and coastal waters where biology is a major driver of air-sea carbon flux. These findings have two different implications for future coastal Antarctic waters in light of sea ice decline: areas with drastically less seasonal sea ice may become CO2 sources for more of the year as productivity decreases, yet previously ice-covered areas may become more productive and experience greater surface ocean carbon uptake in the future.

presentations.title: SEASONAL BIOGEOCHEMICAL DYNAMICS IN A MANAGED MOSQUITO IMPOUNDMENT IN THE INDIAN RIVER LAGOON
presentations.abstract: Wetlands throughout the Indian River Lagoon have been extensively modified for mosquito control. Managed mosquito impoundments are diked wetlands equipped with pumping systems that add lagoon water into the wetland and use outflow structures to control water depth. During the summer, this infrastructure maintains elevated water levels to submerge exposed sediments where mosquitoes typically lay their eggs. This seasonal management protocol, known as Rotational Impoundment Management, may influence the system's biogeochemistry; for example, winter water drawdowns can expose organic matter and promote nutrient efflux. To investigate these potential impacts, long-term monitoring was conducted in an actively managed mosquito impoundment to identify seasonal nutrient concentrations, physicochemical parameters, and soil characteristics. Results show increased inorganic nitrogen and dissolved oxygen both inside and outside of the impoundment in the cooler season compared to the summer, suggesting physicochemical conditions—often closely linked to hydrological changes—play a central role in driving nutrient dynamics.

presentations.title: Trait-Mediated Metacommunity Internal Structure: Insights from Waterbirds Assemblies in a Dynamic Estuarine System
presentations.abstract: Understanding how ecological processes shape species assemblages in dynamic environments is central to community ecology. Estuarine waterbirds offer a compelling system for metacommunity analysis due to their high mobility, functional diversity, and sensitivity to environmental variation. We investigated the internal structure of a waterbird metacommunity using Paranaguá Estuarine Complex (PEC), a World Heritage site in subtropical Brazil, as a compelling model system. We employed joint species distribution models (JSDMs) to partition the variation in species occurrence among environmental predictors, spatial autocorrelation, and species co-distribution. Our analyses included 32 waterbird species grouped into functional foraging guilds, incorporating field data, land cover variables, and spatial coordinates from 36 transects sampled monthly over one year. Our results indicate that environmental filtering and species co-distribution were the primary forces shaping community composition, with minimal spatial effects. This likely reflects the limited spatial scale and high waterbird dispersal capacity in the study area. Environmental variables, particularly salinity and air temperature, differentially influenced species across foraging guilds.

name: Community Ecology (Posters)
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Michele Burford, Griffith University

presentations.title: The wood turtle as a vector of nutrient transfert across terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Animals are important vectors in the transfer of nutrients across ecosystems. Their ability to move allows them to transport nutrients across barriers, such as waterways, and against natural gradients (gravity). In recent years, increased human activity has contributed to environmental degradation, leading to the loss or decline of several vector species. The loss of these nutrient transfers could have unexpected consequences for recipient ecosystems. Therefore, we aim to assess the potential ecological importance of a threatened semi-aquatic turtle species (the wood turtle, Glyptemys insculpta). Various key biotic and functional parameters, such as aquatic invertebrate community structure, water physicochemistry, and decomposition, were measured in the field to identify any differences between stream sites with and without turtles. In addition, nitrogen and phosphorus measurements were made from food, water, and feces from turtles in captivity to estimate individual wood turtle's nutrient contribution to their aquatic environment. By combining those data, we hope to assess the potential impact of the disappearance of this species on aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: Long-term monitoring of the restoration effects of sediment sluicing operations on the benthic macroinvertebrate community below the dams
presentations.affiliation: Central Research Institute of Electric Power Industry
presentations.abstract: The natural sediment regime has been impaired by the construction of dam reservoirs worldwide and they occasionally made severe impacts on riverine ecosystems due to lack of sediment. Meanwhile, dam managers have struggled to address reservoir sedimentation, which hinders operations for water use and flood control. Therefore, sediment control measures that remove sediment from reservoirs and return it below the dam are expected to balance sediment levels upstream and downstream of dams. In the summer of 2017, two dams on the Mimi River in Japan began collaborating on a sediment sluicing operation to manage sedimentation. This operation allows sediment from upstream to pass downstream during floods. Since 2015, we have monitored the benthic macroinvertebrates downstream of the dams to study the restoration effects. The taxa richness of benthic macroinvertebrate community increased shortly after dam operation began at one dam, confirming the restoration effect. At the other dam, no significant changes were observed in the community for a few years after dam operation began, but a restoration effect was subsequently observed. Results of our study show that sediment supply due to sluicing operations is essential for restoring river ecosystems below dams.

name: Fish and Fisheries (Posters)
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Isaac Armstrong, Queen's University Canada

presentations.title: LONG-TERM DYNAMICS OF LARVAL BLUEGILL ABUNDANCE AND SIZE IN A EUTROPHIC RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Shifts in environmental conditions can impact fish distributions, phenology, community composition, and population abundance. Here, we use 18 years of larval fish data to investigate bluegill (Lepomis macrochirus) hatch seasonality, abundance, and survival rate in a hypereutrophic reservoir. Along with gizzard shad (Dorosoma cepedianum), bluegill is one of the most abundant and ecologically important fish species in midwestern reservoirs. Larval bluegill were collected weekly via tows at two offshore sites in Acton Lake (USA) (April - August, 2007 - 2024) to quantify larval abundance and size. For determining the age of collected fish, estimated bluegill growth rates were used, allowing us to predict hatch dates and assess long-term trends. We found that larval bluegill density in the reservoir is increasing over time (18 years), and a preliminary analysis on a subset of years suggests that both the yearly date of peak abundance and peak hatch may be occurring earlier in the summer compared to the beginning of our study.

presentations.title: Don't Change That Channel: Hydraulic Risk and Fish Protection Screen Effectiveness at Australian Irrigation Water Diversions.
presentations.abstract: Water diversion practices negatively impact Australian freshwater fish populations by altering river hydraulic conditions in front of intake structures, resulting in high rates of removal from river channels. Fish protection screens mitigate these effects by modifying the velocities experienced by fish in front of pumps. However, there are few field-based studies that have captured the true extent of these effects, and how they shift post screen installation. This study implemented an Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler to measure and compare the occurrence, magnitude and extent of peak pump directed flow velocities near multiple water diversions under inactive, active and post screen installation conditions. Kriging interpolation found that active pumps increased effective approach velocities by up to 84%, within an area up to ≈165 m2. Screen implementation was found to reduce effective approach velocities by up to ≈54% and reduce the fish entrainment risk area by up to ≈78 m2.

presentations.title: Long-term change in zooplankton phenology: implications for anadromous fish recruitment in the Hudson River estuary
presentations.abstract: Rivers encompass a critical stage in the anadromous fish life cycle, as year-class strength is linked to juvenile survival and growth. Rivers are also undergoing significant changes from the effects of climate change and human alterations. Our ability to predict how these changes will affect year-class strength hinges on our understanding of the processes and drivers of juvenile population variability. One commonly hypothesized driver of variability is degree of overlap between prey production and critical juvenile growth periods, i.e., the match-mismatch hypothesis. In the Hudson River, New York, USA, zooplankton are a primary food source for numerous anadromous juveniles. To better understand anadromous population variability in the Hudson River, we investigate the relationship between zooplankton phenology and anadromous year-class strength in the context of the match-mismatch hypothesis using three decades of fish and zooplankton abundance data.

presentations.title: Ecosystem-scale assessment of migratory fish aqueous and sedimentary eDNA dynamics
presentations.abstract: Migratory fish are increasingly difficult to monitor across space and time, especially when movement occurs rapidly or falls outside of routine sampling windows. To improve detection of recent habitat use, we conducted an ecosystem-scale in situ manipulation experiment to quantify aqueous and sedimentary fish eDNA accumulation, transport, and persistence following the temporary introduction of a facultative migratory species, brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis). Target eDNA was detected within 24 hours of introduction in both water and sediments, with complete non-detection occurring within four months of removal, months earlier than persistence times reported from smaller-scale studies. These findings suggest that hydrodynamic and sedimentary processes in natural systems may impair eDNA detection relative to the simpler conditions of mesocosm experiments, highlighting the importance of scale-dependent processes when applying eDNA for migratory species. Nonetheless, sedDNA captured recent presence well beyond the temporal window of aqueous eDNA alone, suggesting that sediment samples – strategically collected from areas of recent habitat use – may provide an efficient and reliable tool to assess transient occupancy without requiring frequent water sampling or more intensive monitoring efforts.

name: Zooplankton Ecology and Physiology
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Nandini Sarma, FES Iztacala, UNAM

presentations.title: FORMATION OF POPULATION GENETIC STRUCTURE AND MAINTENANCE OF HAPLOTYPE COEXISTENCE IN OBLIGATE PARTHENOGENETIC DAPHNIA CF. PULEX IN A SMALL POND
presentations.abstract: How the population genetic structure changes during colonization in a novel habitat has been a main topic in ecology. Lakes, as semi-closed systems, have been effective model environments for studying it. However, genetic changes during early colonization remain poorly understood because early-stage populations are rarely observed. Using a paleolimnological approach with diapausing eggs, we revealed the long-term dynamics of an obligate parthenogenetic Daphnia cf. pulex population in Lake Fukami-ike, Japan. Furthermore, we examined the mechanisms underlying haplotype coexistence. Paleolimnological analyses revealed that the D. cf. pulex population established and persisted with one predominant haplotype and limited genetic diversity. In recent years, genetically distant haplotypes from a predominant one appeared but did not replace the predominant one. We tried to understand how these lineages coexist, focusing on the Storage effect. Laboratory experiments showed the recently appeared haplotype tended to produce diapausing eggs in broader environmental conditions than the predominant one.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF NUTRIENT LIMITATION ON MICROALGAL COMPOSITION AND NUTRITIONAL QUALITY TO A COPEPOD CONSUMER
presentations.abstract: Nutrient limitation structures the taxonomic composition, abundance, and physiology of producers, and consequently the prey abundance and quality available to consumers. While some types of marine microalgae are strictly autotrophic, others are able to ingest particles in a form of mixotrophy. It has been proposed that mixotrophs have more stable nutrient stoichiometry under variable/limiting nutrient conditions, which could make them a particularly valuable nutritional resource. We reared microalgal taxa under nutrient replete and nutrient limiting conditions and measured particle ingestion and biochemical composition. The chlorophyte Dunaliella sp. unexpectedly exhibited mixotrophy and maintained stable stoichiometry under low-nutrient conditions. Pyramimonas parkeae, Heterocapsa triquetra, Rhodomonas salina and Thalassiosira weissflogii exhibited more variable nutrient stoichiometry. These algal strains were tested as prey for the copepod Centropages typicus through multi-day feeding experiments with adult females. At high food levels (>400 ugC/L), most prey reared under nutrient-limited and -replete conditions supported similar levels of egg production by C. typicus. However, egg production decreased in copepods fed nutrient-limited diatoms (T. weissflogii) and increased in those fed nutrient-limited R. salina.

presentations.title: COMPARING TWO METRICS OF THERMAL TOLERANCE TO QUANTIFY THE EFFECTS OF STARVATION ON THERMAL LIMITS IN A COMMON COPEPOD
presentations.abstract: Several techniques are used to quantify thermal limits in aquatic species. The Critical Thermal maximum (CTmax) is a common technique that uses a loss of response to stimulus as an endpoint under rapid, acute temperature ramping. In contrast, other studies use mortality under exposure to a constant temperature to quantify the thermal limit. Due to the shorter duration of thermal stress, CTmax gives a higher thermal limit than most mortality-based metrics. Thermal limits are often reported using only a single method per study; therefore, a more robust understanding of the relationship between thermal tolerance techniques is needed. We measure the thermal tolerance of a common coastal copepod, Acartia tonsa, using CTmax and Lethal Temperature 50 (LT50, the temperature at which mortality is 50% after 24 hours of exposure) under food replete and starvation conditions. We found that CTmax was ~ 35.5°C for both treatments and unaffected by starvation. LT50, however, was significantly affected by starvation with starved individuals seeing an LT50 of 25.8°C compared to 30.5°C for the food replete treatment.

presentations.title: DRIVERS OF ZOOPLANKTON BODY SIZE IN PONDS ACROSS BROAD SPATIAL SCALES
presentations.abstract: Body size is a fundamental trait influencing ecological functions, trophic dynamics and organismal fitness across ecosystems. However, the environmental drivers shaping body size patterns in pond ecosystems across broad spatial scales remain poorly defined. We assessed how latitude, food availability and predation influence individual body size in cladocerans and copepods, as well as the size structure of the entire zooplankton community. Zooplankton was sampled using standardized protocols in 141 ponds across four European countries and Uruguay. Our findings indicate that latitude and predation are major selective forces shaping crustacean individual body size in ponds. Individual mean body size increased with latitude for both taxa, supporting the temperature-size rule, while fish presence was associated with smaller body sizes. In contrast, the entire zooplankton community size structure was mainly shaped by local factors and did not significantly differ along the climatic gradient. Steeper size spectra with increasing chlorophyll‑a concentrations reflected dominance of small-sized zooplankton.

presentations.title: BIODIVERSITY OF CRUSTACEAN ZOOPLANKTON IN THE ST. LOUIS RIVER ESTUARY OF WESTERN LAKE SUPERIOR
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton communities are indicators of environmental stressors such as climate, invasive species introduction, and other anthropogenic influences on water quality. The St. Louis River estuary on the Western tip of Lake Superior is important ecologically as the largest US tributary into Lake Superior. Industrially, it is also the location of the most active Great Lakes cargo shipping port and is the largest receiver of inter-lake ballast water, the vector by which numerous aquatic invasive species (AIS) have become established in the region. In 2008, ballast water exchange was fully implemented for vessels travelling internationally into the Great Lakes as a means of reducing movement of AIS from other locations. We sampled in 2007/2008 to establish a baseline of zooplankton biodiversity in the estuary and resampled the same locations in 2024/2025 to assess differences before and after ballast water policy changes.

presentations.title: SEASONAL POPULATION DYNAMICS OF ZOOPLANKTON AND THEIR PARASITE COMMUNITIES IN LAKES OF SOUTHERN ALBERTA
presentations.abstract: Parasite epidemics within zooplankton hosts can shape aquatic food web structure and functioning, potentially affecting higher trophic levels. Identifying the controls and consequences of epidemics can thus enhance our understanding of the ecology of aquatic systems. The parasite populations and communities in zooplankton are thought to be shaped by complex controls related to seasonal changes in the biotic and abiotic environment, including nutrient availability, mixing and resuspension of parasite infective stages, temperature-dependent release and viability of free-living parasite stages, and host population dynamics. These controls not only affect the parasites themselves, but also how they are transmitted from host to host. Here, we explored the seasonal patterns of zooplankton-parasite community dynamics in four eutrophic lentic ecosystems (lake, reservoir and open water wetland ecosystems) in a heavily agriculturalized and effluent-impacted aquatic network in southern Alberta, Canada.

name: Zooplankton Ecology and Physiology (Posters)
description: Thematic session.
lead_organizer: Nandini Sarma, FES Iztacala, UNAM

presentations.title: BODY SIZE AND GEOMETRY PREDICT ZOOPLANKTON SURVIVAL TO AIR EXPOSURE
presentations.abstract: Dormant life stages of freshwater zooplankton are typically resistant to environmental exposure, and this facilitates overland dispersal. However, environmental exposure and overland dispersal are less well understood for active life stages. To characterize empirically the longevity of active life stages out of water, survival time to air exposure was measured in the laboratory for eight cladoceran species using heartbeat cessation to signify survival time. Survival time increased with body dry weight with an allometric scaling exponent near 2/3 for a multispecies model with six bivalved species. The 2/3 scaling exponent is consistent with Euclidean geometry and points to water loss across the surface of a spherical body as the cause.

presentations.title: ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITY COMPOSITION IN WAQUOIT BAY, A SHALLOW, TEMPERATE ESTUARY
presentations.abstract: We sought to characterize the zooplankton community within Waquoit Bay, a shallow, tidally-mixed estuary on the south shore of Cape Cod, Massachusetts. As a National Estuarine Research Reserve, Waquoit Bay has been the site of diverse research studies and a long-term water quality monitoring program that is supported by volunteers. We collected mesozooplankton via net tows from four stations within the Bay at four monthly intervals between March and July 2025. Consistent with previous observations, the community was dominated by calanoid copepods, including Acartia spp, Eurytemora affinis, and Centropages hamatus. Zooplankton abundance was highest in March and decreased over the summer.

presentations.title: ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITY DISTRIBUTION AND COMPOSITION IN RELATION TO SUBSURFACE PRODUCTIVITY IN AN ARCTIC MARGINAL SEA
presentations.abstract: The significant climate change-associated loss of sea ice in the Arctic Ocean and its marginal seas is supporting increased phytoplankton primary productivity due to reduced obstruction of sunlight by sea ice cover. Subsurface phytoplankton productivity during the late open water season has been recently estimated to contribute a substantial portion of total primary productivity in the Chukchi Sea. We present the results of taxonomic classification and caloric value quantification of zooplankton communities in the Hanna Shoal and Barrow Canyon region of the NE Chukchi shelf in summer 2017.

presentations.title: Zooplankton in Transition: Biodiversity and Turnover Patterns in the Chilean Oxygen Minimum Zone under contrasting ENSO states
presentations.abstract: Las Zonas de Mínimo Oxígeno (ZMO) son regiones oceánicas críticas donde la baja disponibilidad de oxígeno limita la biodiversidad y altera el funcionamiento de la red trófica. Estos sistemas son altamente sensibles a la variabilidad climática, como los fenómenos de El Niño y La Niña. Durante las campañas oceanográficas realizadas en 2023 (condiciones de El Niño) y 2024 (La Niña/condiciones neutrales), se evaluó la diversidad del zooplancton a través de gradientes de oxígeno en la ZMO chilena utilizando ARNr 18S y metabarcoding COI. Los principales grupos detectados fueron Copepoda, Euteleostemi y Thaliacea. Subeucalanus subtenuis dominó durante El Niño, mientras que Pseudosagitta maxima prevaleció bajo condiciones neutrales/de La Niña. La riqueza de especies fue mayor en las capas oxigenadas y alcanzó un mínimo en el núcleo de la ZMO.

presentations.title: MULTIGENERATIONAL EFFECTS OF L-BMAA ON THE LIFE TABLE TRAITS OF CERIODAPHNIA DUBIA (CLADOCERA)
presentations.abstract: Secondary metabolites produced by CyanoHABs (Cyanobacterial Harmful Algal Blooms) in inland aquatic systems are often toxic to various members of the zooplankton community. This study aimed to evaluate the multigenerational effects of L-BMAA on the survival and fecundity of Ceriodaphnia dubia, exposed to three concentrations (12.5, 25, and 50% of the LC50) and a toxin-free control. Cladocerans were exposed for five consecutive generations. The results showed a progressive decline in all life-table variables across generations. Higher concentrations markedly reduced survival, especially in later generations, suggesting accumulation and generational transfer of the toxin.

presentations.title: THE EFFECTS OF GUT MICROBIOME ON FUNGAL INFECTION IN DAPHNIA DENTIFERA
presentations.abstract: The host-associated gut microbiome communities are involved in a wide range of processes within the host. To understand the effects of the gut microbiome in host-parasite exposure, a series of laboratory experiments were conducted with the parthenogenetic species Daphnia dentifera and the pathogenic fungus Astrolozyma monospora (formerly known as Metschnikowia bicuspidata). A transmission assay was performed in which two genotypes of Daphnia (Clear-1 and IL-16) were exposed to the fungus after either being raised in the presence (microbiome-reduced) or absence (control) of antibiotics. We observed that infection rate between the two treatments indicated that 'microbiome-reduced' Daphnia were less susceptible to the fungus.

presentations.title: WHERE THE WIND BLOWS: THE ZOOPLANKTON WILL BE
presentations.abstract: Strong winds, high precipitation, and energetic storms are most common during spring months in temperate regions and are becoming more extreme and more frequent as the climate changes. We hypothesize that weather events during spring and early summer months will change the horizontal and vertical distribution of zooplankton taxa, especially for larger species and larger-sized individuals. To test our hypotheses, we sampled vertical temperature, dissolved oxygen, and chlorophyll-a. Zooplankton were also collected weekly from three sites in Escanaba Lake, Boulder Junction, WI, USA. Early season weather events led to larger zooplankton species and larger-sized individuals accumulating on downwind shorelines.

presentations.title: THERMAL CONSTRAINTS AND PREDATION RISK SHAPE SPATIO-TEMPORAL DYNAMICS OF ZOOPLANKTON TAXA IN STRATIFIED LAKES
presentations.abstract: Predation risk and thermal structure jointly shape the spatio-temporal dynamics of fish and zooplankton in stratified lakes. Using in situ imagery (Underwater Vision Profiler) and acoustic telemetry of brook charr, we examined how 3D fine scale habitat variability, thermal barriers, and behavioral differences modulate predator prey relationships. During summer, zooplankton communities exhibited pronounced within lake heterogeneity, both in terms of contrasting species dominance and of strong variation in size spectra that matched differences typically observed among distinct lakes. As the lake cooled, fish redistributed across depths, initiating shifts in zooplankton size structure and composition that pointed to a cascading effect of predator movements.

presentations.title: The One Piece in the Biological Pump: Krill as Model Organisms for Spatial Variability in Zooplankton-Mediated Carbon Export
presentations.abstract: Krill (euphausiids) are a dominant zooplankton group and serve as model organisms for understanding zooplankton-mediated carbon export. This study examines spatial differences in euphausiid-mediated carbon export between the northwest Atlantic and northeast Pacific, two regions with distinct hydrographic conditions, community compositions, and proportions of resident and vertically migrating taxa. Zooplankton samples were collected with diel MOCNESS tows during NSF Ocean Acidification cruises in 2011 (Atlantic) and 2012 (Pacific). Preliminary results suggest that differences in euphausiid assemblages, particularly in the relative abundance of migratory (e.g. Euphausia sp.) versus resident (e.g. Stylocheiron sp.) taxa, drive distinct patterns of midwater carbon flux in each region.

presentations.title: SPECIES CO-OCCURRENCE PATTERNS OF ZOOPLANKTON IN A NEOTROPICAL FLOODPLAIN
presentations.abstract: In tropical floodplains such as the Pantanal, hydrological variation is a major driver of zooplankton distribution and species co-occurrence patterns. We investigated how seasonal shifts between flood and drought phases structure positive and negative species associations, and whether environmental variables mediate these patterns. Co-occurrence patterns were estimated using probabilistic models, and their relationships with environmental gradients were assessed through multivariate analyses and latent-variable models. Overall, positive associations predominated, indicating that many species respond similarly to environmental conditions. During the flood, positive co-occurrences were concentrated among functionally similar species, consistent with environmental filtering.

name: Ecosystem Processes in a Changing World: Honoring Mike Pace (Posters)
description: Dr. Michael Pace has made substantial and lasting contributions to our understanding of freshwater, estuarine and marine ecosystems through his work on food web dynamics, carbon cycling, ecosystem metabolism, resilience, and long-term ecological change.
lead_organizer: Grace Wilkinson, University of Wisconsin - Madison
co_organizers: Jonathan Walter, University of California Davis

presentations.title: In the middle of it all: metalimnion production, methane, and the scientific legacy of Mike Pace
presentations.abstract: Stratified lakes hide some of their most surprising ecology in the metalimnion, a dynamic layer shaped by steep gradients of light, oxygen, and nutrients. We conducted a series of whole-lake enrichment and shading experiments to assess how eutrophication affects seasonal methane storage. Bloom-driven changes in oxygen and light availability within the metalimnion strongly regulated the balance between methanogenesis and methanotrophy. Even during years with early ice-off, when oxygenation suppressed methane accumulation, surface cyanobacterial blooms rapidly reduced light and oxygen in the metalimnion, increasing whole-lake methane storage.

presentations.title: THREE WAYS TO STUDY LAKES
presentations.abstract: Limnologists employ many approaches for studying lakes, and different approaches can shape our understanding of these ecosystems and the subsequent questions we ask. In this talk, we pay tribute to Mike Pace and his use OF, and thoughtfulness to the issue of how different approaches, perspectives, and frames of reference can promote limnological understanding. Conceptual strategies for ecosystem science have been elegantly described as a table supported by the four legs of theory, long-term study, comparisons, and ecosystem experiments. A practical complement to this metaphor that addresses measurements strategies in lakes is 'the empiricist's stool' held up by the three sturdy legs of traditional limnological profiling, high frequency buoys, and spatial sampling.

name: The Waters We Share (Posters)
description: Many scientists recognize the importance and value of strong science communication skills and around the world researchers, departments, and institutions are conducting impactful outreach programs.
lead_organizer: Emily King, COSEE China, State Key Laboratory of Marine Environmental Science, Xiamen University
co_organizers: Laura Falkenberg, University of South Australia, UniSA STEM
Vera Shi, State Key Laboratory of Marine Environmental Science, Xiamen University

presentations.title: FROM THE FIELD TO THE LAB: STRATEGIES AND SUCCESSES FROM THE CONNECTING OPPORTUNITIES FOR RESEARCH EXPERIENCES (CORE) PROGRAM
presentations.abstract: Through an NSF-funded grant, the Science Museum of Minnesota's Kitty Andersen Youth Science Center and the St. Croix Watershed Research Station developed the Connecting Opportunities for Research Experiences (CORE) program. Rooted in watershed and lake sediment research, CORE provided youth with hands-on field, lab, and mentorship experiences that made aquatic and geoscience research accessible, relevant, and personally meaningful.

presentations.title: waterbodies: exploring sound media to broaden outreach on federally funded aquatic science
presentations.abstract: Nearly half of North American adults listened to a podcast in 2025 according to national surveys. The Cooperative Science and Monitoring Initiative (CSMI) is a US-Canada binational effort under the 2012 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement to coordinate science and monitoring activities in one of the Great Lakes each year. With support from the Great Lakes Research Consortium, and in collaboration with ESF's Digital Storytelling Studio, I developed waterbodies, a podcast designed to share research through sound.

presentations.title: CARING FOR OUR SURROUNDINGS TO CARE FOR THE WORLD: A RESEARCH EXPERIENCE WITH REAL IMPACT
presentations.abstract: Developing scientific literacy in schools is essential for empowering young people to understand complex environmental challenges and engage in evidence-based decision making. This project presents a hands-on research experience implemented at 'Colégio Nossa Senhora Medianeira,' a Jesuit institution recognized for its commitment to caring for our common home. Students collaborated with university scientists to investigate and design solutions for a local aquatic ecosystem.

name: Curating Limnology with Kindness: Honoring Jim Cotner
description: Microbial limnologist, Dr. Jim Cotner, has built a remarkable career with major contributions to the freshwater science over a range of subjects (from genes to ecosystems) and sub-disciplines (from microbial ecology to biogeochemistry).
lead_organizer: Ed Hall, Colorado State University
co_organizers: Bopaiah Biddanda, Grand Valley State University

presentations.title: AQUATIC STOICHIOMETRY ACROSS SCALES AND THE JOY OF ARGUING WITH JIM COTNER
presentations.abstract: Evaluating the fluxes of carbon as well as nutrients through the freshwater pipe suggests that elemental stoichiometry at the landscape level is not only regulated by what enters the pipe, but how elements are processed in different aquatic compartments. Furthermore, different landscapes have different baselines that need to be considered when understanding loss and transformation.

presentations.title: Are Daphnia from uninvaded lakes naive to chemical cues from the invasive predator Bythotrephes longimanus (spiny waterflea)?
presentations.abstract: Aquatic prey use chemical cues released from predators (kairomones) and/or alarm cues (ACs) from injured conspecifics to gauge predation risk and to alter their behavior or developmental traits to minimize their vulnerability to predation. Daphnia from lakes with established populations of the invasive zooplankton predator Bythotrephes longimanus (spiny waterflea) have been shown to display light-avoidance behavior (negative phototaxis) in response to Bythotrephes kairomones. Findings supported our hypothesis that Daphnia from invaded lake populations would show significantly more negatively phototactic responses to Bythotrephes cues than would Daphnia from the uninvaded lakes.

presentations.title: Zooplankton are big bacteria: zooplankton C:N:P ratios driven by taxonomic variation across seasons.
presentations.abstract: Jim Cotner is known for many things, one of which was to shed important light on the factors influencing C:N:P stoichiometry in bacteria in culture and in the wild, including assessments of the strength of stoichiometric homeostasis in bacteria, the range of variation in C:N:P ratios among microbial taxa, and the associations (or lack thereof) of bacteria C:N:P with growth rate. This talk will highlight how (just like bacteria?) variations in bulk zooplankton C:N:P ratios in Flathead Lake are also driven by taxon-specific differences in elemental composition.

presentations.title: Especially N, but also P: internal nutrient loading in lakes, and a short walk on Cotner's 'salty' side
presentations.abstract: Despite the session title, Jim Cotner's contributions extend beyond the freshwater sciences. In the 1990s, Jim was measuring nutrient dynamics in Baffin Bay, a shallow, hypersaline lagoon in south Texas. 'Internal nutrient loading' is typically used to describe redox-associated bioavailable P release from aquatic sediments, especially lakes. Bioavailable N fluxes (not denitrified) were dominated by chemically reduced forms (NH4 and urea) known to enhance cyanobacterial biomass and toxin production.

presentations.title: SO, WHAT THE HELL IS THE REDFIELD RATIO ANYWAYS?
presentations.abstract: The Redfield Ratio has become a 'constant' in ecology but has been misused as a species-specific optimum or an indicator of the nutrient limitation. New data from global ocean surveys and ecosystem experiments have revealed a modified convergence around 141:22:1, which has renewed our interest in Redfield and its meaning. We consider Redfield an emergent property of Earth's oceans that can tell us something fundamental about eco-evolutionary constraints on life balancing its energetic and elemental demands.

presentations.title: The Stoichiometric Trait Distribution of the Southern Indian Ocean Microbiome
presentations.abstract: It is currently challenging to link the changes in carbon:nitrogen:phosphorus (C:N:P) stoichiometry of the marine microbiome with the natural variations in environment that govern it. We collected samples across a wide environmental gradient in the southern Indian Ocean. We used Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy to analyze biomass C:N:P of individual microbes and applied a probability density function to create distributions for each stoichiometric trait (C:N, N:P, and C:P).

name: Curating Limnology with Kindness: Honoring Jim Cotner
description: Microbial limnologist, Dr. Jim Cotner, has built a remarkable career with major contributions to the freshwater science over a range of subjects (from genes to ecosystems) and sub-disciplines (from microbial ecology to biogeochemistry).
lead_organizer: Ed Hall, Colorado State University
co_organizers: Bopaiah Biddanda, Grand Valley State University

presentations.title: Finding Balance : How principles of ecological stoichiometry have shaped my career
presentations.abstract: In 2007, I arrived at the University of Minnesota as an 18-year-old kid, ready to embark on my scientific career. Little did I know that my first ever experience as a student in the College of Biological Sciences (an orientation program called Nature of Life) would alter the course of my career and life forever. As part of the Cotner lab, the fundamentals of ecological stoichiometry were (literally) tattooed onto my skin, but what I will be most forever grateful for will be the things I learned from Jim about being a scientist as a whole person.

presentations.title: Limited by Phosphorus, Driven by Rain: Carbon Loss in a Disturbed Tropical River
presentations.affiliation: Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora
presentations.abstract: Hydrological seasonality plays a pivotal role in shaping the composition and reactivity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in tropical river systems. In the Doce River Basin, a highly impacted river (specially iron taillings), experimental incubations revealed that rainy-season conditions enhance DOM concentrations and promote greater carbon fluxes, particularly of labile DOM. Moreover, there are evidences that the iron taillings may be removing P from the water to the sediment impacting carbon cycling.

presentations.title: Assessing Seasonal Changes in Nutrients Limitations Between Different Land Use Classifications of Minnesota Lakes
presentations.abstract: Seasonal shifts in nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) availability regulate lake primary production, yet how nutrient limitation evolves within a growing season across contrasting land-use types remains poorly understood. We conducted nutrient-addition bioassays from May through September across nine Minnesota lakes spanning metropolitan (Twin Cities) and forested (Itasca State Park) landscapes.

presentations.title: Life-Element Tangos: Cotner-Inspired Water Stories along Trophic and Redox Gradients in the Laurentian Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Understanding the abundance, distribution, and reactivity of organisms, organic matter, and inorganic resources across environmental, trophic, and redox gradients is a major focus of ecology. A continuum of Cotner-inspired studies on the Laurentian Great Lakes basin reveals such relationships along trophic and redox gradients in lake water and their sediments having significance to issues ranging from aquatic carbon and nutrient recycling to biosphere's oxygenation.

presentations.title: Centering Microbial Biomass in Aquatic Biogeochemical Cycles - Jim Cotner Showed Us Why the Matter in Small Things Matters
presentations.abstract: Throughout his career, which has spanned five decades to date, a central theme of Jim's work has been the exchange of chemical elements between microbial biomass and inorganic and organic forms in water. He applied this theme to diverse geographic settings and to various scales of biological complexity from subcellular structures and individual bacterial cells, chemostat cultures of strains and communities, and entire lake ecosystems.

presentations.title: WHAT'S OLD IS NEW AGAIN: A TROPHIC GRADIENT REDUX IN LIGHT OF THE GROWTH RATE HYPOTHESIS
presentations.abstract: Biddanda et al. (2001) helped us understand how dissolved and particulate pools of nutrients change as systems become more productive and here, we revisit those changes and confirm the key tenets, i.e., that oligotrophic systems are dominated by the microbial pool (<1.2 µm particle size) and there is a progressive shift of nutrients and carbon into larger seston in eutrophic systems.

name: Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship (Posters)
description: This session celebrates ten years of the ASLO Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship (RCEF), a transformative initiative empowering early career researchers (ECRs) in scientific publishing.
lead_organizer: Frank Akamagwuna, University of Alabama
co_organizers: Paul F Kemp, University of Hawai'i

presentations.title: More than a manuscript: career achievements boosted by the L&O Letters Early Career Publication Honor
presentations.affiliation: Centre for Nuclear Energy in Agriculture (CENA) in the University of São Paulo (USP)
presentations.abstract: As an awardee of the L&O Letters Early Career Publication Honor in 2022, I was able to fully enjoy all the benefits from the award. The peer-review process, in particular, was very pivotal for my development as a researcher. The award goes beyond providing a platform for a simple manuscript submission at L&O Letters. It helped me build my confidence as an early career researcher, representing my third paper published in an international journal.

presentations.title: CREDIT WHERE CREDIT IS DUE: RECOMMENDATIONS FOR INCLUSIVE AND ETHICAL AUTHORSHIP PRACTICES
presentations.abstract: Authorship is central to the career advancement of many limnologists, especially those in research positions. However, the processes used to assign authorship and authorship order are not always clear, ethical, or equitable. We developed the concept of authorship climate (perceptions of fairness related to procedures, communication practices, and outcomes of authorship decisions) and measured it using a survey of early-career scientists from the fields of non-medical biology, psychology, economics, and physics.

presentations.title: Navigating the Rise of AI in Scientific Writing: Insights from Early-Career Aquatic Scientists
presentations.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into scientific publishing is transforming how research is written, reviewed, and disseminated. As part of the ASLO Raelyn Cole Editorial Fellowship, we launched a global survey to explore how researchers, especially those in the aquatic sciences, engage with AI-powered tools in scientific writing and peer review.

presentations.title: What Makes a Good Data Repository? Insights from Aquatic Scientists
presentations.abstract: As journals increasingly mandate public data deposition, researchers in the aquatic sciences deserve information about best practices for data sharing. There are many options for databases that host these publicly available data repositories. This project seeks to answer these questions by surveying authors in the aquatic sciences from multiple career stages about their experience making data publicly available and summarizing the needs of the community moving forward.

presentations.title: Differences between suggested and non-suggested reviewer recommendations vary by author region across the ASLO journals
presentations.abstract: Peer reviewers are expected to provide objective evaluations of manuscripts. Many journals request that authors suggest appropriate, impartial reviewers during manuscript submission, but implicit bias may lead authors to (knowingly or not) suggest reviewers that will assess their work favorably. We examined 12,039 reviewer recommendations for the first round of review of 5,829 manuscripts submitted to Limnology & Oceanography, Limnology & Oceanography: Methods, and Limnology & Oceanography Letters. Suggested reviewers provided more favorable recommendations.

name: Sharing Experiences Among Early-Career Researchers
description: The future of aquatic science will be built on the connections we make today. This special session is a platform for early-career researchers (ECRs) to share and explore meaningful strategies for collaboration.
lead_organizer: Benjamin Misteli, WasserCluster Lunz
co_organizers: Bruno Cremella, Laboratoire d'Océanographie de Villefranche
Brittany Schieler, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography
Adina Paytan, University of California Santa Cruz
Susanne Menden-Deuer, University of Rhode Island

presentations.title: GO HABS GO!: THE CHALLENGES AND BENEFITS OF INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATION IN MICROBIAL ECOLOGY
presentations.affiliation: Southern California Coastal Water Research Project
presentations.abstract: Collaborations in the field of aquatic microbial ecology are highly advantageous to expand study areas as well as share resources for highly specialized analyses. As part of the ASLO 'Limnology and Oceanography Research Exchange' (LOREX) program, a collaborative project between researchers at Portland State University and McGill University examined the dynamics and potential indicators of harmful cyanobacteria blooms in high elevation lakes by using community-level DNA sequencing.

presentations.title: Making a limited time-frame work for initiation of long-distance research collaborations
presentations.abstract: Face-to-face interaction can benefit the establishment of new research collaborations, especially the early stages of relationship development with new colleagues. However, extended periods of travel are not possible for many individuals due to time constraints. I'll discuss how this limitation influenced my experience as part of ASLO's Limnology and Oceanography Research Exchange Program (LOREX), which was my first independently initiated international research endeavor.

presentations.title: THE SCIENCE OF FELLOWSHIP: LEARNING FROM AND LEANING ON COMMUNITY
presentations.abstract: My ASLO LOREX international research exchange stretched way beyond just an advancement in my dissertation research and laboratory skills- it was a journey fueled by creativity, collaboration and cross-cultural encounters. This past summer, I ventured to the North of Sweden to study arctic lakes in collaboration with Dr. Anne-Kristin Bergstrom. I used these chambers to study the effects of permafrost thaw on algal responses in a region that is rapidly warming at an alarming rate, Abisko National Park.

presentations.title: LOREX 2025: GETTING MY FEET WET IN SWEDEN'S SUBARCTIC LAKES
presentations.abstract: The Limnology and Oceanography Research Exchange (LOREX) program was an incredible international research experience that offered many opportunities for growth in a supportive, low-pressure environment. My exchange project involved new systems (freshwater lakes), new taxa (macrozoobenthos), new sites (Swedish subarctic tundra), and the chance to familiarize myself with a new technique (δ2H analysis).

presentations.title: TWO IS BETTER THAN ONE: LESSONS LEARNED FROM PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTING A FULL-SUMMER FIELD CAMPAIGN WITH ANOTHER PHD STUDENT
presentations.abstract: International collaborations are rich with opportunity. They offer the chance to connect with new colleagues, test research ideas in unfamiliar settings, and experience lab cultures that are different from what you're used to at home. The research I conducted in Abisko, Sweden wouldn't have been possible without my collaborators at Umeå University. The two of us teamed up and designed a sampling campaign that worked for us both, and we spent the summer collecting data side-by-side.

presentations.title: The importance of stepping out of your comfort zone: Lessons learned from conducting research abroad
presentations.abstract: Conducting research abroad offers early-career scientists invaluable growth opportunities - but also distinct logistical, cultural, and professional challenges. This presentation shares key lessons learned from completing a research project at a foreign institution, focusing on preparation, adaptability, and cross-cultural collaboration. Three core lessons frame the discussion: prepare thoroughly, stay flexible, and engage with curiosity.

name: Sharing Experiences Among ECRs (Posters)
