description: The future of aquatic science will be built on the connections we make today. This special session is a platform for early-career researchers (ECRs) to share and explore meaningful strategies for collaboration.
lead_organizer: Benjamin Misteli, WasserCluster Lunz
co_organizers: Bruno Cremella, Laboratoire d'Océanographie de Villefranche
Brittany Schieler, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography
Adina Paytan, University of California Santa Cruz
Susanne Menden-Deuer, University of Rhode Island

presentations.title: Antrelle's Declassified LOREX Survival Guide: the realities of adapting - AGAIN, through the LOREX UNICORN lens
presentations.abstract: Life is all about having a backup plan for the backup plan, which is no different in graduate school. In Summer 2023, I had the opportunity to participate in my first LOREX exchange, which research-wise didn't go so well. This talk will highlight the never-ending cycle of adapting on the fly in dissertation research and international collaborative science.

presentations.title: FIELD NOTES FROM SWEDEN: PERSPECTIVES ON INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATION THROUGH ASLO'S LOREX PROGRAM
presentations.abstract: Science is an increasingly cooperative endeavor, and opportunities to engage in collaborative research benefit early career researchers in numerous measurable and intangible ways. During the summer of 2025, I participated in the ASLO LOREX program, where I traveled to northern Sweden to investigate methane and carbon dioxide dynamics in boreal headwater streams in the Krycklan Catchment Study.

presentations.title: MIDDLE OF NOWHERE TO MONTRÉAL: INSIGHTS INTO MY LOREX EXPERIENCE
presentations.abstract: Last year, I participated in the ASLO Limnology and Oceanography Research Exchange (LOREX) program, and completed my exchange in Dr. Jean-François Lapierre's lab at the Université de Montréal from July through August 2025. In this poster, I'll highlight my experience in travelling internationally, moving samples across a border crossing, being welcomed into the lab, and learning a new lab technique where most SOPs are written in a language I don't speak!

presentations.title: From Pharmaceuticals to Friendships: What I Gained Through International Collaboration
presentations.abstract: My LOREX exchange in Sweden reminded me that research is only one part of what makes a scientific experience meaningful. I spent the summer working with Dr. Tomas Brodin's group at Umeå University and SLU, running experiments on how pharmaceuticals influence the behavior and physiology of damselfly larvae.

presentations.title: International and Citizen Collaboration Reveals Unexpected Biodiversity of Sea Slugs
presentations.abstract: DNA barcoding and large-scale surveys incorporating citizen science reveal a striking underestimation of marine biodiversity. Sea slugs are a hyperdiverse gastropod group whose similar morphology masks genetically distinct lineages. This combined effort yielded over 30 undescribed taxa, especially from the South Pacific, resurrected forgotten species, and at least three new candidate genera.

presentations.title: Collaborate early and often: Key advice for building your scientific network
presentations.affiliation: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
presentations.abstract: Building your network is one of the most valuable things you can do early in your career, but it is also one that comes without much instruction. My experience participating in ASLO's Graduate Research Exchange Program (LOREX) was transformative in the sense that I was collaborating with other researchers on my own for the first time.

presentations.title: BUILDING BRIDGES TO BROADEN PARTICIPATION: LEVERAGING C-COMP STRUCTURES AND RESOURCES TO CREATE OPPORTUNITIES TO 'TRY ON' RESEARCH CAREERS IN THE OCEAN SCIENCES
presentations.abstract: Improving the transition to graduate school is a top priority recognized by the National Academy of Sciences for broadening participation in the STEM workforce. At the crucial point between undergraduate and graduate education, we established the Bridge-to-PhD Fellowship Program (B2P) to provide diverse cohorts of Fellows opportunities to explore research interests, gain knowledge and skills, and experience interdisciplinary research.

presentations.title: Macrophyte Mondays: A network for students and early-career researchers
presentations.abstract: Students and early-career researchers (ECRs) studying macrophytes often find themselves isolated within their institutions, lacking local peers with similar research interests. To address this, we established Macrophyte Mondays, a global online network that connects undergraduates, master's students, PhD students, and postdocs with a shared passion for macrophyte research.

presentations.title: LOREX: Laying Down the Foundation for International Collaboration
presentations.abstract: ASLO's Limnology and Oceanography Research Exchange (LOREX) program has given me a chance to grow and learn about the intricacies and complexities of collaborative international research. Navigating collaborations is hard enough as graduate student, but throw in 'international' and it's a whole other ball game.

name: How to (Posters)
description: Students and early career professionals (jointly referred to as ECRs) in aquatic sciences often learn how to perform the many intricate activities necessary for the craft by doing them.
lead_organizer: Rita Franco-Santos, Oceans Institute, University of Western Australia
co_organizers: Laura Falkenberg, UniSA STEM, University of South Australia

presentations.title: HOW TO BE A CREATIVE SCIENTIST FROM DAY ONE
presentations.abstract: The transition from students who mainly absorb information to scientists capable of generating new knowledge typically occurs during doctoral training. This transformation often comes with frustration and may lead early-career researchers to abandon their scientific vocations. Creativity is an evolved cognitive mechanism that enables abstraction, synthesis, and the resolution of novel problems.

presentations.title: Open Data for the Uninitiated: How to find and use open data to support research in the aquatic sciences
presentations.abstract: Open data—free or low-cost data that can be used and re-used for any purpose—is an increasingly useful tool in the aquatic sciences. These shared data lower the cost of research, prevent unnecessary duplication across groups, lower the barrier of entry for incoming researchers.

presentations.title: Designing Interdisciplinary Courses for Equitable and Sustainable Leadership in the Expanding Blue Economy
presentations.abstract: As the Blue Economy expands, preparing a new generation of professionals to integrate diverse disciplines into the ocean sector is a key challenge. This project focuses on developing four stackable micro-credential courses on the Sustainable Blue Economy (SBE), designed to meet Canada's growing need for a skilled workforce in this rapidly evolving sector.

presentations.title: How to support a thriving community of students, researchers, and professionals in the water sciences
presentations.abstract: Early career researchers may finish their degrees still seeking opportunities to develop skills, learn best practices, and grow their career. The Consortium of Universities for the Advancement of Hydrologic Sciences, Inc. (CUAHSI) provides opportunities and infrastructure designed to lower barriers and equip water professionals with high quality resources and practical skills.

presentations.title: How to collaborate with artists to increase the reach of your science.
presentations.abstract: Artists can be valuable allies in science. In particular, working with an illustrator, animator, or graphic designer can be a great way to increase the impact of your work and engage with a broader audience. To help demystify the process, I'll share what I learned from working with a professional science communicator to design the cover art for the Bulletin's May 2025 Issue.

name: Ecological Stoichiometry: Honoring Jim Elser
description: This session will focus on key areas of the scientific legacy produced by the long and fruitful career of Jim Elser to honor his upcoming retirement.
lead_organizer: Paul Frost, Trent University

presentations.title: The 'Elser Elementaries' and their impact on Phosphorus, Past and Future
presentations.abstract: I had the pleasure of first meeting Jim Elser when he invited me to contribute to the second sustainable phosphorus summit in Tempe, Arizona in 2011. We immediately clicked, saw eye to eye, and motivated one another to push forward our understanding of the phosphorus sustainability challenge. Jim and I continued to interact through the following years, including coming together to write the book 'Phosphorus, Past and Future'.

presentations.title: Handprint on the P landscape
presentations.abstract: A lover of all elements, Jim has made his mark on phosphorus, as well as my career trajectory and love of phosphorus. As a master's student at Arizona State University, I had the privilege to help with the organization of the 2nd Sustainable Phosphorus Summit. Together with Elena Bennett, we published the 1st global phosphorus footprint paper, highlighting how animal product consumption is a key driver of anthropogenic impacts on global P cycling.

presentations.title: RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN NUTRIENT SUPPLY, PERIPHYTON STOICHIOMETRY, AND NUTRIENT UPTAKE RATIOS IN STREAM ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Research on nutrient spiraling in stream ecosystems has traditionally examined individual elements in isolation. Ecological Stoichiometry (ES) theory predicts that elemental cycles should be coupled and constrained by the relatively narrow range of C:N:P ratios in biomass. Using data from the STOICH database, we evaluated relationships among nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) availability, benthic periphyton stoichiometry, and nutrient uptake ratios across diverse stream ecosystems.

presentations.title: Ecological Stoichiometry From Bricks to Big Data: Continuing Jim Elser's Legacy of Teaching Through Undergraduate Education and Research
presentations.abstract: Jim Elser is well-known for his pioneering research on ecological stoichiometry theory, but that theory may not have gained as much traction as it did had Jim not dedicated so much of his time and energy to clearly and elegantly explaining his ideas to others and supporting the next generation of stoichiometry scientists. In this talk, I will discuss how Jim's approach has motivated my undergraduate-driven research program at a small liberal arts college.

presentations.title: Mathematical biology in the age of stoichiometric thinking: Jim's enduring influence on nutrient-based models
presentations.abstract: Mathematical ecology has long relied on systems of differential equations, from Lotka's foundational predator–prey models to modern food-web theory, to capture how interacting species shape one another's dynamics. Yet over the last several decades, this landscape has been profoundly reshaped by the recognition that populations are not only limited by their interactions, but also by elements that make growth possible.

presentations.title: SOME THINGS WE LEARNED FROM JIM ELSER
presentations.abstract: I personally learned a lot from Jim Elser, far more than can be distilled in a single talk. As many of his past students and collaborators will also attest, working with Jim influences not just how you do science, but how you think about science. This presentation will include short reflections and brief presentations by myself and other past mentees on science (and non-science) things that we learned from Jim Elser.

name: Ecological Stoichiometry: Honoring Jim Elser (Posters)
description: This session will focus on key areas of the scientific legacy produced by the long and fruitful career of Jim Elser to honor his upcoming retirement.
lead_organizer: Paul Frost, Trent University

presentations.title: Stoichiometric imbalance of carbon-nitrogen-phosphorus ratios in thermokarst lakes across the Northern Hemisphere
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Elemental stoichiometry of carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) has important impacts on lake biogeochemistry and ecosystem functioning. Here, we present the first global synthesis of C:N:P stoichiometry in thermokarst lakes across the circumpolar Arctic and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, uncovering a systematic and pervasive nutrient imbalance. Thermokarst lakes exhibit exceptionally high dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations but are severely phosphorus-deficient.

presentations.title: ECOSYSTEM STOICHIOMETRY RECONSIDERED: INTEGRATING NUTRIENT SUPPLY, DEMAND, AND FUNCTION
presentations.abstract: Ecological stoichiometry has emerged as a powerful framework to interrogate ecological processes at lower levels of biological organization (e.g., organism or community). Yet, its application at the ecosystem level is less well resolved. Here, we argue that a stoichiometric perspective much to offer in the advancement of ecosystem studies.

presentations.title: Limits on limitation: re-embracing ecoenzymatic stoichiometry as the microbial economy of resource investment
presentations.abstract: Microbial metabolism drives global biogeochemical cycles through the decomposition of organic matter and assimilation of carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P). Ecoenzymatic stoichiometry (EES) may be construed as a portfolio of investment in available resources or a reflection of elemental (co-)limitation.

presentations.title: Do trophic interactions change growth limitation patterns of phytoplankton in experimental plankton communities?
presentations.abstract: Freshwater phytoplankton is often limited by phosphorus (P) or nitrogen (N), depending on their availability and ratio. In this study, an experimental phytoplankton community was grown under N- or P-limiting conditions, followed by factorial additions of N, P, or both to determine limitation responses.

presentations.title: Revisiting and scrutinizing the Growth Rate Rule: Evolution of growth-stoichiometry coupling
presentations.abstract: In nature, there are fundamental Rules of Life that can aid in developing predictive frameworks. One potential candidate of such a rule is based on the well-known Growth Rate Hypothesis (GRH; based on fundamental work by Jim Elser and colleagues in the past 2-3 decades). Here, we focus solely on the findings of a recent evolution experiment with C. reinhardtii.

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL STOICHIOMETRY IN THE THIRD DOMAIN AND BEYOND: EFFECTS OF PLASMIDS AND VIRUSES ON GROWTH AND ELEMENTAL CYCLING OF A CRENARCHAEL HOST, SULFOLOBUS ICELANDICUS
presentations.abstract: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) play key roles in mediating biogeochemical cycles through diverse interactions with cellular organisms. To this end, we conducted factorial growth curve bioassay experiments using a model heterotrophic thermoacidiphilic crenarchael host (Sulfolobus icelandicus), nonconjunctive plasmid, and nonlytic virus system.

name: Two-Eyed Seeing (Posters)
description: There are a growing number of research programs in many parts of the world that are working in partnership with indigenous knowledge holders to improve understanding and design more salient solutions for the protection and sustainable future of water and water resources.
lead_organizer: Roxane Maranger, Université de Montréal
co_organizers: Katrine Turgeon, Université du Québec en Outaouais

presentations.title: REIMAGINING AQUATIC SPECIES MONITORING: AN EMERGING PROJECT TO FOSTER A PARTICIPATORY APPROACH TO INCLUSIVITY AND SHARED KNOWLEDGE
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems face growing pressures from species whose spread and impacts are reshaping aquatic communities, yet monitoring programs often overlook local concerns and Indigenous knowledge. Drawing on years of collaboration with communities seeking broader monitoring, our goal is to co-design a national list of aquatic species for monitoring through an inclusive, real-time Delphi survey.

presentations.title: INTEGRATING INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE AND WINTER LIMNOLOGY TO SUSTAIN ARCTIC FRESHWATER FOOD SYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Arctic freshwater ecosystems are undergoing rapid transformation as winters warm, snow deepens, and under-ice conditions shift in ways that fundamentally alter food webs and northern livelihoods. Through the pan-Arctic FROST program (Arctic Freshwater Food Systems: Influence of Warming Winters and Increased Snow Cover), co-designed with Inuit and Sámi partners, we integrate Indigenous knowledge and Western science.

presentations.title: Nurturing Ocean Connection Through Culture and Knowledge
presentations.abstract: Science offers essential knowledge to address climate and biodiversity crises, yet data alone struggle to motivate broad public engagement. Cultural practices, values, stories, and shared meanings shape how people relate to the natural world. The CCUNESCO UN Ocean Decade Working Group mobilizes the nexus of science, culture, and society to reconnect Canadians to the ocean by weaving multiple ways of knowing, including Western science, Indigenous knowledge systems, and local experiential expertise.

name: Ecology, Management, and Conservation of Temporary Aquatic Ecosystems
description: Continuation of SS001A. Global climate change is expected to exacerbate the drying out of temporary freshwater ecosystems worldwide.
lead_organizer: Luciana Barbosa, Federal University of Paraiba
co_organizers: Elizabeth Meyer, Institute for Evolution & Biodiversity
Elizabeth Walsh, University of Texas at El Paso

presentations.title: Dry rivers: Where different interests meet - Lessons from a karst stream system
presentations.abstract: Karst streams are a particular type of running waters with flow intermittency. There is still a need to monitor the specific properties of karst streams in order to classify these systems. This paper informs exemplarily how researchers, citizens and water managers can act jointly to the benefit of nature and humans.

presentations.title: LAND USE IMPACT ON ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES AND THEIR RESTING STAGES IN A LARGE RIVER FLOODPLAIN
presentations.abstract: We examined the effects of land use intensification on floodplain zooplankton in Lake St. Pierre floodplain. We found that land use at the local scale had little influence on zooplankton during flooding, with land use at a larger scale having a stronger impact. Natural wetland soils showed a higher number of hatchlings compared to agricultural soils.

presentations.title: MOUNDING, A CONSERVATION TOOL OR AN ECOLOGICAL TRAP?
presentations.abstract: This project aims to determine whether mounding can create suitable habitats for vernal pool-dependent amphibian communities. Preliminary results suggest that mounding-created pools seem to provide a suitable habitat for anurans, especially compared to other silvicultural practices. However, they appear unsuitable for salamanders.

presentations.title: State-and-Transition Models for Tropical Coastal Floodplains
presentations.abstract: We used an expert-elicitation process to develop an archetype model describing expressions of coastal floodplain wetlands under reference conditions. This archetype formed the foundation for a STM that incorporated both reference and modified states, including those shaped by feral ungulates, livestock grazing, weed invasion, altered inundation regimes and restoration actions.

presentations.title: TROPHIC PLASTICITY AS AN INVASION MECHANISM OF NON-NATIVE FISH SPECIES IN A NEOTROPICAL RIVER BASIN
presentations.abstract: Here we compare the individual trophic specialization of the non-native fish Knodus moenkhausii and the native Deuterodon cf. taeniatus. The native species increased specialization in sites with higher average natural shelter. In sites with greater human influence, the non-native species increased generalization.

presentations.title: HYDROLOGICAL MECHANISMS AND WETLANDS IN HYBRID POPLAR PLANTATIONS
presentations.abstract: The goal of this study was to characterize the hydrological processes that lead to the formation and persistence of potential wetlands. Results show that young plantations have significantly longer hydroperiods than deciduous forests and older plantations, largely due to fine-scale topographic features.

name: Ecology, Management, and Conservation of Temporary Aquatic Ecosystems
lead_organizer: Luciana Barbosa, Federal University of Paraiba
co_organizers: Elizabeth Meyer, Institute for Evolution & Biodiversity
Elizabeth Walsh, University of Texas at El Paso

presentations.title: Linking sublethal copper toxicity exposure to respiration response in monogonont rotifers
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at El Paso
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic metal contamination challenges freshwater ecosystems, and trace concentrations can impair physiological functions of organisms. Rotifers are valuable models for assessing heavy metal toxicity in aquatic habitats. We evaluated whether long-term habitat history influences tolerance to copper sulfate exposure by comparing two populations each of Epiphanes brachionus and E. chihuahuaensis, isolated from polluted and non-polluted temporary environments.

presentations.title: Reproductive behavior patterns in rotifer populations across different hydroperiod habitats
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at El Paso
presentations.abstract: Reproduction is critical for organisms inhabiting ephemeral aquatic habitats, where desiccation risk favors rapid and successful mating. Monogonont rotifers rely on sexual reproduction to produce resting eggs that withstand harsh conditions.

name: Gassy Waters: Advances in Understanding and Measuring Gas Fluxes Across the Aquatic Continuum
lead_organizer: Konstantinos-Marios Vaziourakis, Uppsala University
co_organizers: Marco dos Santos, Energy Planning Program/COPPE/UFRJ
Ulisse Cardini, Genoa Marine Center - Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn
Jorge Machado Damazio, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
Todd Kana, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science
Abigail Lewis, Smithsonian Environmental Research Center

presentations.title: Forces behind the flux: using machine learning to model small GHG datasets from restored wetlands of southern Ontario
presentations.abstract: Wetlands are the single largest source of methane to the atmosphere; we used Random Forest modeling on 7 restored Ontario wetlands sampled 6 times to find DO, pH, nutrients are best predictors of CH4/N2O/CO2 emissions.

presentations.title: BlueMinerva: a platform for autonomous carbon flux, hydrochemical, and bathymetric measurements in low-flow waterbodies
presentations.abstract: Autonomous BlueMinerva platform deployed at Dagow Lake (Germany) and Stordalen mire (Sweden) for spatially-resolved CO2/CH4 flux mapping; identified emission hotspots and validated low-cost sensors against high-end.

presentations.title: Novel drone-based measurement of greenhouse gas emissions from constructed wetland ponds
presentations.abstract: UAV-based mass-balance flux measurements over constructed wetland ponds, compared with chamber data, for CO2/CH4/N2O. Among the first UAV flux measurements in dense macrophyte stands.

presentations.title: Improving upscaling of greenhouse gas emissions from ditches through spatial surveys and high-frequency monitoring
presentations.abstract: 129-ditch national survey + BERTHA automated floating chamber high-frequency monitoring; ditch GHG emissions linked to local DO, sediment, vegetation, flow rather than land use; daytime sampling underestimates daily fluxes.

presentations.title: Methane ebullition dynamics in boreal aquatic environments using a high-resolution monitoring approach
presentations.abstract: 50 automated inverted funnels deployed 4 months in 4 boreal hydropower reservoirs + 2 lakes in Quebec Côte-Nord; sediment temperature and pressure are best CH4 ebullition predictors; synchronicity correlates with magnitude.

presentations.title: Dry flux CO2 emissions are partially offset by vegetation
presentations.abstract: Globally aligned campaign across 164 dry inland sites in 5 climatic regions; vegetated dry zones show 25% lower CO2 fluxes than barren; estimates 10% global suppression of dry-flux CO2 by new vegetation. Dry fluxes are 15% of total inland CO2.

title: Gassy Waters: Advances in Understanding and Measuring Gas Fluxes Across the Aquatic Continuum

co_organizers.name: Ulisse Cardini
co_organizers.affiliation: Genoa Marine Center - Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn

co_organizers.name: Jorge Machado Damazio
co_organizers.affiliation: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro

co_organizers.name: Todd Kana
co_organizers.affiliation: University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science

presentations.title: Carbon Evasion, Burial, and Offset Potential in Small Constructed Agricultural Reservoirs
presentations.abstract: Small, constructed reservoirs in in the northern Great Plains can disproportionately emit and sequester carbon relative to their surface area, and depending on the balance of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to carbon burial rates, have the potential to be used as carbon offsets. Here, we evaluate six years of measured GHG fluxes, including diffusive CO2, CH4, and N2O, and ebullitive CH4 fluxes, as well as carbon burial rates from a total of 121 small constructed agricultural reservoirs. Despite contrasting hydrological conditions (wet and dry) over the study period, the proportion of reservoirs emitting CO2 (~50%), CH4 (diffusive and ebullitive, 100%) and N2O (~25%) remained relatively consistent among years. Carbon burial rates averaged 3.0 g m-2 day-1 over several years. Together, these results suggest that when considering carbon evasion to burial (E:B) ratios by accounting for C atoms only, the sites were net carbon sinks (E:B = 0.3). When GHG fluxes were instead expressed by their Global Warming Potential, the mean evasion to burial ratio (E:B = 1.3), suggesting that, overall, the sites functioned as net carbon sources, though this average was skewed by a subset of sites with very high CH4 emissions. In fact, most sites (60-78% annually) acted as net sinks, indicating potential for use as carbon offsets. Although CH4 (diffusion + ebullition) dominate total GHG evasion (94.3%), reservoirs with low CH4 fluxes, such as those characterized with elevated salinity, may be suitable for offset initiatives.

presentations.title: Seasonal greenhouse gas dynamics and annual net carbon fluxes of temperate artificial ponds
presentations.abstract: Artificial ponds contribute to the anthropogenic carbon (C) cycling by emitting significant amounts of greenhouse gases (GHG) while accumulating C in their sediments. However, the global GHG emissions from these systems are highly uncertain, and the extent to which artificial ponds are net C sinks or sources remains an open question. In this study, we sampled eight artificial ponds in Central New York monthly from April to October to explore seasonal dynamics of carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) fluxes, and annual sediment C accumulation. We also installed temperature sensors to monitor stratification dynamics continuously. Seasonally, fluxes spanned over one, two, and three orders of magnitude for diffusive CO2, CH4, and ebullitive CH4, respectively. The GHG fluxes were within the range observed for other artificial ponds, with generally higher ebullitive than diffusive CH4 fluxes. Unexpectedly, seasonal trends in CH4 fluxes were weak, with only one pond showing the highest fluxes mid-summer. The relative contributions of flux pathways to overall GHG emissions, expressed in CO2 equivalents, were highly variable among ponds. Four ponds were dominated by diffusive CO2 emissions, two ponds by CH4 ebullition, one pond by diffusive CH4 emissions, and one pond had roughly equal contributions from diffusive CO2 and CH4 ebullition. Taking into account C sequestration in sediments, only one pond was a net C sink, while the rest were net C sources. By better understanding seasonal GHG fluxes and inter-pond variability, our study will help constrain the anthropogenic C budget.

presentations.title: DIEL AND SEASONAL GREENHOUSE FLUXES AND ORGANIC CARBON BURIAL IN AUSTRALIAN AGRICULTURAL PONDS
presentations.abstract: There are 1,694,671 documented agricultural ponds, or man-made basins of water in rural environments, in Australia. These ponds are capable of producing high water-air greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes and burying large amounts of carbon in their sediments. Although there has been a number of studies on water-air GHG fluxes from agricultural ponds in Australia, they either studied ponds in a single climate zone, sampled during only one season, or measured fluxes during daylight hours only, and no studies included carbon burial. We conducted 24-hour floating chamber incubations and collected sediment cores from 33 agricultural ponds across the tropical, subtropical, temperate, and arid/semi-arid climate zones of Australia during summer and winter to calculate their net CO2, CH4 and N2O fluxes. These fluxes were then scaled up to all 1.69 million agricultural ponds. CO2 and CH4 fluxes were greater during summer than winter. There was an uptake of N2O in summer and an efflux in winter. During both seasons, CO2 and CH4 fluxes were greater during the day than at night and N2O was released during the day and uptaken at night. Annual carbon burial was higher in arid/semi-arid ponds than in tropical, subtropical, and temperate ponds. This presentation will provide an estimate of the total organic carbon burial, total GHG flux (CO2-eq), and net carbon flux (CO2-eq) from all agricultural ponds in Australia.

presentations.title: Dissolved methane concentrations and fluxes from cage fish farms in lakes Kivu and Muhazi, Rwanda
presentations.affiliation: IHE Delft Institute for Water Education
presentations.abstract: Lakes are substantial methane sources, but global estimates are hindered by uneven distribution of studies, with African systems being underrepresented relative to temperate and boreal regions. At the same time, human activities are increasing in open waters. Cage aquaculture is one example of a prominent investment to improve food security and livelihood benefits, but the associated waste may also have an impact on methane dynamics, which has not been studied. This study examined methane concentration and fluxes in tilapia cage farming in Lake Kivu, a deep lake (485 m) shared by Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Lake Muhazi, a shallow lake (15 m) in the Eastern Province in Rwanda. Samples were collected in sites with and without cages. Surface water methane concentrations were determined using the headspace technique. Methane fluxes samples were collected every 15 minutes for an hour using static floating chambers. Vertical profiles of the water column and water quality were measured to understand their influence on methane dynamics in the two lakes. Results showed that the presence of cages plays an important role in methane concentration and fluxes over the other factors. Generally, methane concentrations and fluxes were higher in the shallow Lake Muhazi than in the deep Lake Kivu. In Lake Kivu, methane fluxes (FCH4) varied between 0 - 60.8 mg/m2/h in sites with cages, and 0 - 6.2 mg/m2/h in sites without cages. In Lake Muhazi, the FCH4 varied between 0.1 - 90.0 mg/m2/h in sites with cages, and 0.01 - 2.84 mg/m2/h in sites without cages. Cages located in a bay exhibited higher concentrations and fluxes than cages in open water.

presentations.title: AGRICULTURAL DITCHES AS SOURCES OF ATMOSPHERIC GREENHOUSE GAS (CO2, CH4 AND N2O) EMISSIONS – A SPATIAL ASSESSMENT ACROSS SWEDEN
presentations.abstract: Agricultural ditches are identified as emission hotspots of greenhouse gases (GHG) such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O). Although excess nutrient loading from fertilizer application is believed to be key in driving these emissions, the empirical evidence is scarce, with few field-based representative studies covering ranges in e.g. nutrient loading, soil type, climate. Here we present data on dissolved concentrations and atmospheric fluxes of CO2, CH4 and N2O collected in ditches of 28 agricultural catchments across Sweden. The sampling was made in synoptic campaigns covering three different seasons (spring, autumn and winter). Results showed that dissolved ditch concentrations of all three GHGs and their respective atmospheric fluxes were highly variable across sites and exhibited gas specific seasonal patterns. Fluxes were largely driven by air-water GHG concentration gradients with relatively low influence by physical forcing (i.e. gas transfer velocity). Overall, dissolved inorganic nitrogen and total organic carbon were identified as key influencing factors for concentrations N2O and CO2 respectively, whereas no clear drivers for CH4 were observed. Our study highlights the need for representative field-based studies that capture the magnitude and spatial control on GHG emissions from agricultural ditches. Such data are vital to understand how these emissions might respond to different nutrient mitigation strategies.

presentations.title: Natural ponds have higher summertime carbon flux rates than artificial ponds in New York, USA
presentations.abstract: Ponds are globally abundant, forming naturally or being constructed by humans for a myriad of purposes. Both natural and artificial ponds are hotspots for carbon cycling, with similar flux pathways for greenhouse gas production and emissions as well as carbon sequestration in sediments. There are limited comparisons of carbon flux rates between natural and artificial ponds, which hampers our ability to constrain both natural and anthropogenic carbon budgets. In this study, we compared summertime carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, methane (CH4) emissions, and carbon burial rates between 16 natural and 28 artificial ponds in New York State. We found that natural ponds had higher fluxes of CO2, diffusive CH4, and ebullitive CH4 compared to artificial ponds. Based on preliminary data from a subset of ponds, we also suspect higher rates of sediment carbon burial in natural ponds. Our results indicate that despite similar carbon flux pathways, temperate natural and artificial ponds have unique traits and may require different scaling factors to predict carbon fluxes from natural versus artificial ponds.

title: Gassy Waters: Advances in Understanding and Measuring Gas Fluxes Across the Aquatic Continuum

presentations.title: Distinct nitrous oxide (N2O) dynamics across enclosed bay and open coast under the typhoon event
presentations.abstract: Under the influence of global climate change, both the frequency and intensity of typhoons are increasing. This study investigates the impacts of typhoons on nitrous oxide (N2O) dynamics in diverse marine environments by integrating analyses of the 15N stable isotope labeling technique, nitrogen isotopes (delta15Nbulk-N2O), oxygen isotopes (delta18O-N2O), intramolecular 15N site preference (SP), and ancillary biogeochemical parameters. We conducted time-series sampling during Typhoon Chaba and Typhoon Yagi in a relatively enclosed bay and a more open coastal region off western Guangdong. Our results demonstrated that typhoon-driven degradation significantly enhances in-situ N2O production in bay waters, while subsequent typhoon-induced algal bloom senescence further amplifies sedimentary N2O generation. Typhoon events induce a 'first massive release, then rapid production' pattern of N2O in the bay environment, acting as a strong but short-lived atmospheric N2O source. Strikingly, the open coastal region behaves oppositely: post-typhoon mixing shifts the dominant nitrogen cycling process from nitrification to denitrification, accompanied by intensive N2O reduction. This shift is attributed to typhoon-induced organic matter degradation, which created abundant suboxic microenvironments and facilitated enhanced denitrification. Furthermore, extreme wind forcing promoted substantial atmospheric N2O influx into the WGCW through intensified air-sea exchange; however, relatively stable N2O concentrations are maintained in open waters. These observations suggest a negative feedback mechanism whereby open-water typhoon events may partially offset global warming through denitrification-mediated N2O consumption, representing an intense but previously overlooked atmospheric N2O sink.

presentations.title: Temporal variability in methane and nitrous oxide concentrations in a salt marsh creek
presentations.abstract: Salt marshes sequester carbon but also emit the greenhouse gases methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O). Most measurements of CH4 and N2O exchange between salt marshes and the atmosphere focus on the vegetated marsh platform, with less attention given to the many creeks and channels that drain these ecosystems. Salt marsh creeks drain groundwater from the marsh interior and often have sediments rich in organic material, likely resulting in high dissolved CH4 and N2O concentrations. Dynamics of CH4 and N2O in these creeks and channels are also likely to be highly variable over time. This temporal variability may be cyclical, associated with seasonal patterns like temperature and vegetation growth and dieback and over shorter diel and tidal cycles that can influence the direction of water flow, salinity, and dissolved oxygen concentration. Temporal variability in CH4 and N2O dynamics in salt marsh creeks can also be driven by stochastic events like droughts and storms that influence nutrient loading and hydrology. Deciphering the influence of these many controls on temporal variability is necessary to better understand the balance between carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas emissions in salt marsh ecosystems. Here, we use a two-year, weekly dataset of dissolved CH4 and N2O measurements from a salt marsh creek to identify controls on temporal variability on dissolved gas concentrations. We discuss our findings in the broader context of CH4 and N2O exchange between salt marshes and the atmosphere.

presentations.title: BIOTURBATION BY BENTHIC MACROFAUNA COMPLICATES METHANE EBULLITION IN THE BALTIC SEA
presentations.abstract: Methane ebullition, the release of methane (CH4) from sediments via bubbles, can be a major CH4 pathway from coastal sediments to the atmosphere. Our study examines how bioturbation, the alteration of sediment matrices by animal activity, affects CH4 ebullition in the Baltic Sea. We performed a controlled microcosm experiment using azoic Baltic Sea sediment and added three widespread macrofaunal genera - Macoma (bivalve), Monoporeia (amphipod), and Marenzelleria (polychaete) - representing distinct bioturbation modes. Over 21 days, we measured ebullitive CH4 fluxes across five treatments (Con, Mac, Mon, Mar, and All). At the end of the experiment, pore water chemistry (CH4 and SO42-), delta C-CH4 isotopic ratios of bubbles and pore water, and bioturbation intensity were measured. All fauna treatments showed higher CH4 ebullition than the control (Con), with the strongest increase in the treatment with all three species present (All). Our results suggest that bioturbation mechanically mobilizes trapped gas, enhancing bubble release. This indicates that benthic macrofauna can significantly increase sediment-to-atmosphere CH4 fluxes, underscoring their potential influence on coastal CH4 dynamics. Understanding how bioturbation regulates GHG emissions is crucial for refining coastal CH4 budgets.

presentations.title: SMALL BUT MIGHTY: MUD SNAILS REGULATE GAS EXCHANGE BETWEEN TIDAL FLATS AND THE ATMOSPHERE
presentations.abstract: Salt marshes and tidal flats accumulate and transform large quantities of carbon. Animals living in these ecosystems might have an important role in carbon cycling, particularly when found in high densities. One such animal is the eastern mud snail (Ilyanassa obsoleta), a common benthic invertebrate living in dense patches (>1000 ind m-2) in intertidal regions throughout the North Atlantic coast. In this study we investigate whether and how I. obsoleta influences carbon cycling in coastal Delaware with a focus on carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). To test if snails do influence carbon cycling, we measured exchange of CO2 and CH4 between exposed tidal flats and the atmosphere in locations with and without snails present, also considering the role of snail density. After finding differences in sediment-atmosphere gas exchange from tidal flats with and without snails present, we developed two lab experiments to determine the mechanisms underlying these observations. In the first experiment we constructed tidal flat mesocosms with varying sediment types to investigate how snail addition influenced rates of sediment-atmosphere gas exchange over time. In the second, we incubated mud snails of varying sizes to quantify rates of CO2 and CH4 by individual snails and scrubbed the shells of some snails to isolate the effect of the shell biofilm in snail CO2 and CH4 production.

presentations.title: RESOLVING THE SPATIOTEMPORAL VARIABILITY OF METHANE SOURCES AND SINKS IN A VEGETATED TIDAL WETLAND
presentations.abstract: Vegetated tidal wetlands are key components of the coastal carbon cycle, acting as long-term carbon sinks while simultaneously serving as sources of methane. Current approaches predominantly focus on estimating the vertical methane release to the atmosphere, however horizontal methane export via tidal creeks could also play a significant role in the vegetated tidal wetland methane budget. The aim of this paper is to predict the spatiotemporal variability of methane sources and sinks and estimate the relative contribution of vertical release and horizontal export of methane from a low disturbance subtropical vegetated tidal wetland in southern Moreton Bay, Australia. To achieve this, a 2-dimensional hydrodynamic model was coupled with a biogeochemical model to simulate methane dynamics over a full year. The modelling work was supported by an extensive field campaign that spanned different tidal phases and seasons including both groundwater and surface water samples. Through testing different model structures in their ability to capture observed methane levels, we found that groundwater methane inputs were the dominant source of methane to the tidal creek. The magnitude of horizontal methane export from the wetland was comparable to that of atmospheric methane release from the inundated wetland areas. The significant contribution of lateral exchange suggests that the spatial bounds of tidal wetland methane budgets need to be expanded, with significant emissions occurring far from their wetland source.

presentations.title: AN INTEGRATED HIGH-FREQUENCY AND EX-SITU CLOSED-CORE APPROACH FOR HIGH-RESOLUTION CO2, CH4, AND N2O FLUX MEASUREMENTS
presentations.abstract: Accurately quantifying greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics in natural aquatic ecosystems remains challenging due to spatial heterogeneity, diel variability, and rapidly changing adverse weather and sea conditions. These factors, combined with hazardous field environments and safety considerations during sampling, limit the effectiveness of in situ incubation techniques and low-frequency discrete sampling. Furthermore, manual sampling is labor-intensive, prone to human-induced handling errors, and often incapable of capturing short-lived fluxes, resulting in substantial uncertainty in local-scale GHG flux assessments. To address these complex challenges, we developed an ex-situ closed-core incubation system integrated with cavity ring-down spectroscopy to obtain continuous, real-time, high-frequency measurements of CO2, CH4, and N2O across the sediment-water-gas continuum. This configuration can collect data at a temporal frequency of 1 Hz. Using intact seagrass and bare sediment cores as a case study, the system maintains natural sediment structure and vegetation integrity while allowing natural light penetration and controlled temperature simulation. High-frequency measurements revealed continuous net GHG emissions, exhibiting species- and sediment-specific variability as well as diurnal metabolic fluctuations that conventional discrete sampling methods struggled to clearly recognize. In conclusion, this innovative method establishes a promising high-resolution monitoring approach for GHG exchanges across the sediment-water-gas continuum in various aquatic environments.

title: Gassy Waters: Advances in Understanding and Measuring Gas Fluxes Across the Aquatic Continuum

presentations.title: Combined effects of climatic scenarios and pesticide pressure on freshwater GHG emissions
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are sensitive to environmental pressures. With the projected climatic changes, both overall water temperatures and the occurrence of heatwaves are expected to increase in the coming decades. Simultaneously, freshwater ecosystems are under pressure from pesticides. However, the combined effects of these pressures on ecosystem functioning are often not well researched. This study assessed the combined effect of three climatic scenarios (ambient, 4 C warming and the occurrence of 8 C heatwaves) and the insecticide azadirachtin (control, 30 and 300 ug/L) on GHG emissions from freshwater mesocosms. The experiment (n=4 for chemical control treatments and n=3 for chemical treatments) ran for a period of 6 weeks in early fall. Diffusive CO2 and CH4 emissions were measured on a weekly basis. Preliminary results show that all mesocosms shifted from net CO2 uptake to CO2 emissions over the experimental period and CH4 emissions increased over time. Pesticide treatment significantly affected both CO2 and CH4 emissions, with higher emissions in the 300 ug/L pesticide treatment. Additionally, temperature treatment significantly affected CH4 emissions, with higher values in the warmed and heatwave treatment compared to ambient temperature. This effect interacted with pesticide treatment, as highest CH4 emissions were recorded in the 300 ug/L pesticide treatment subjected to heatwaves. These results indicate that both pesticides and temperature changes affect freshwater GHG emissions and that these pressures can interactively affect emissions in complex ways.

presentations.title: WARMING AND NUTRIENTS SHIFT PONDS FROM POSSIBLE SINKS TO CERTAIN SOURCES OF GREENHOUSE GASES
presentations.abstract: Shallow lakes and ponds are globally the most abundant freshwater body. These biogeochemical hotspots both sequester carbon in their sediments and emit greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. Burial rates of carbon are reportedly high, and whilst emission rates of carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) are known to be large, they are also highly uncertain. Thus, the overall balance between burial and emission, and how that is altered by climate change and eutrophication remains unclear. Here, we present data from a highly standardized survey of pond characteristics, water chemistry, ecological status and seasonal estimates of GHG from over 240 ponds in Europe and Uruguay, combined with data from a long running climate change experiment in Denmark. Our analyses reveal that patterns in the emission of both CO2 and CH4 show extremely large variability between ponds. Notwithstanding the large amount of unexplained variation in emissions, the combination of data from natural systems, rain-fed fish-ponds and the experimental mesocosm system demonstrate the overriding impact of nutrient enrichment and temperature in controlling GHG emissions. In addition, the long running mesocosm experiment shows that, whilst C burial increased with nutrient enrichment, it was overwhelmingly offset by elevated CH4 emission, particularly at higher temperatures. In summary, warming and nutrient enrichment combined to alter ponds from a condition where they have the potential to be net carbon sinks into a state where emissions are so large they are certain to be sources of carbon to the atmosphere.

presentations.title: Large-scale assessment of oxic methane production in lakes using an isotopic mass balance approach
presentations.abstract: Widespread methane (CH4) supersaturation in lake surface water is a key contributor to natural greenhouse gas emissions. Oxic CH4 production (OMP) has recently been recognized as a potential CH4 source, challenging the long-held view that surface CH4 originates solely from anoxic sediments. Yet most studies are limited to individual systems, leaving broader-scale dynamics uncertain. Here, we apply surface-CH4 mass balance approaches incorporating CH4 isotopes across 260 lakes spanning diverse landscapes. OMP accounts for 32% of total surface CH4 sources on average, at a rate of 1.2 mmol m-2 d-1, comparable to air-water diffusive CH4 emissions. Our results provide insight into cyanobacterial photosynthesis as an important contributor to OMP in nutrient-rich lakes at the continental scale. Moreover, OMP exhibits a higher temperature sensitivity than any other surface CH4 processes, overall indicating its importance for future CH4 emissions under eutrophication and climate change.

presentations.title: Opposing response of CO2 and CH4 fluxes following thermokarst erosion along tundra-lake interfaces in the western Canadian Arctic
presentations.abstract: Erosion from ice-rich permafrost thaw (thermokarst) alters tundra vegetation, soil moisture, and laterally transports organic matter into lakes. These changes affect carbon and nitrogen cycling and fluxes of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous oxide (N2O) in tundra and lakes. Tundra and lakes are rarely examined together to understand their joint response to widespread thermokarst erosion. Our goal was to quantify growing season CO2, CH4, and N2O fluxes and the underlying abiotic and biotic controls along the tundra-lake interface in the presence of thermokarst erosion. We sampled weekly gas fluxes (June - August 2022, 2023) along three transects of mineral upland tundra with an eroding slope and adjacent lake north of Inuvik, NT, Canada. We observed an opposing impact of thermokarst erosion on net CO2 (FCO2) and net CH4 fluxes (FCH4). Eroding tundra consumed more CO2 (i.e., more negative FCO2) compared to stable tundra (mean -64.0 ± 79.7 vs -26.7 ± 84.2 mg C m-2 h-1), driven by increased photosynthetic activity in vegetated tundra. We observed CH4 uptake in stable tundra (mean -0.024 ± 0.027 mg C m-2 h-1) while eroding tundra FCH4 was near neutral. In adjoining lakes, FCO2 did not differ between eroding lake shores and stable lake shores. In contrast, FCH4 was significantly higher from eroding lake shores compared to stable lake shores (2.56 ± 5.65 vs 1.05 ± 3.61 mg C m-2 h-1). N2O fluxes were negligible. The diverging responses of tundra and lake CO2 and CH4 fluxes underscore the complex effects of erosion at the tundra-lake interface.

presentations.title: Impact of water level changes on greenhouse gas dynamics in river-floodplains under climate change
presentations.abstract: Hydrologically active river-floodplains, which form composite mosaics of connected and disconnected side arms are biogeochemical hot-spots for carbon transformations and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). Yet, we still have limited information on how GHG emissions respond to hydrological changes, especially in temperate floodplains. Although, these systems are sensitive to climate change, particularly declining water levels, the consequences on future river-floodplain GHG fluxes remain unclear. The main objective of this study was to assess the impact of water level changes on CO2 and CH4 fluxes from floodplain waters with varying connectivity during an exceptionally dry hydrological year, lacking regular spring flooding. The study was conducted March - November 2025 in three temperate river-floodplains (Poland). We used automated flux chambers (AFC) equipped with sensors continuously logging CO2 and CH4, allowing to determine GHG emissions with high temporal resolution across lotic to lentic gradients. Our results demonstrate high spatio-temporal variability of GHG fluxes. We show that water level fluctuations had opposite effects on GHG dynamics, depending on the hydrological connectivity with the main channel. Reduced water levels, together with elevated air temperatures, significantly enhanced GHG emissions from river-floodplain side arms. Thus, changes in hydrological patterns should be considered in the context of climate change, which in the future may intensify GHG emissions from river-floodplain systems.

presentations.title: NITROUS OXIDE EMISSIONS AND MICROBIAL FUNCTIONAL RESPONSES IN AN AGRICULTURAL WATERWAY FOLLOWING NITROGEN FERTILIZATION
presentations.abstract: In Canada, the agriculture sector is responsible for approximately 10% of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, accounting for 54MT of carbon dioxide (CO2), as well as 31% of methane (CH4) and 75% of national nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions. However, these estimates may underestimate the indirect GHG emissions from agriculturally impacted waterways. Our study investigates an area of intensive agricultural land use in Southwestern Ontario, Canada, where over 3000km of agricultural drainage ditches collect runoff directly from agricultural fields, providing direct routes to the Great Lakes. These drainage waterways are foci for nutrient transformation and biogeochemical hotspots with enhanced N2O emissions. Previous work identified a 2.5-fold increase from pre-fertilization to post-fertilization N2O emissions. In this study we seek to link N2O emissions in the drainage ditches to microbial community function. A high-intensity, short-duration sampling effort was conducted following urea-ammonium-nitrate fertilizer application, and a combination of molecular genomics and gas measurements were used to capture the functional response of the microbiome. We hypothesize that there will be an upregulation in denitrification and nitrification functions immediately following fertilization, which will subside as the N within the system is utilized by the microbes and they turn to other available energy sources. This upregulation will correspond with an increased N2O flux. This information can be used to help inform future policies related to GHG budgets in Canada, as well as globally.

title: Gassy Waters: Advances in Understanding and Measuring Gas Fluxes Across the Aquatic Continuum

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF BIOTURBATION MODE AND INTENSITY OF BENTHIC MACROFAUNA ON DIFFUSIVE METHANE FLUXES IN COASTAL SEDIMENTS.
presentations.abstract: Coastal ecosystems contribute over half of marine methane (CH 4 ) emissions despite covering a small fraction of ocean area. In marine sediments, CH 4 is microbially produced and can escape via diffusion into the overlying water column. However, the biological controls of CH 4 diffusion in the presence of bioturbating macrofauna remain poorly quantified. Macrofauna alter sediment structure and redox conditions through particle reworking and burrow ventilation (bioirrigation), possibly enhancing CH 4 fluxes by increasing porosity and providing escape pathways. To investigate species-specific effects of bioturbation on CH 4 diffusion, we conducted a controlled microcosm experiment with Baltic Sea sediments. We manipulated faunal composition using equal densities of Macoma balthica , Monoporeia spp., and Marenzelleria spp., which represent different bioturbation modes. Bioturbation intensity was quantified via luminophore profiles (particle reworking) and sodium bromide (NaBr) tracer dilution (bioirrigation), and these were related to measured diffusive CH 4 fluxes. While our diffusive fluxes varied among treatments, the highest was observed in the Marenzelleria treatment, a known bioirrigator. We now aim to link our measured fluxes to NaBr profiles to confirm that bioirrigation substantially enhanced CH 4 transport. These results will help to elucidate the role of macrofaunal bioturbation mode and intensity as a regulator of CH 4 diffusive fluxes, and improve our understanding of the importance of benthic macrofaunal functional traits in mediating coastal greenhouse gas emissions.

presentations.title: Insights from monthly measurements and high-frequency monitoring of CO2 and CH4 fluxes in Lake Chavoley, a eutrophic lake with high greenhouse gas emissions
presentations.affiliation: CARRTEL - INRAE (French National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment)
presentations.abstract: Lake Chavoley (Ain, France) is a small eutrophic to dystrophic natural lake characterized by currently low anthropogenic pressure, but it nevertheless acts as a significant hotspot for carbon emissions (CO 2 and CH 4 ), particularly regarding CH 4 ebullition events during destratification periods. To investigate the spatiotemporal variability of these GHG fluxes, we implemented a hybrid monitoring strategy combining monthly sampling with high-frequency sensing from March 2023 to December 2025. In addition to monthly water chemistry characterization and continuous monitoring of the oxythermal regime, gas fluxes were quantified using multiple approaches. Diffusive CO 2 and CH 4 fluxes were assessed via i) the gradient method, based on monthly determination of dissolved gas concentration in surface water, and ii) continuous surface water and air pCO 2 measurements with low-cost sensors. Both diffusive and ebullitive GHG fluxes were determined by manual floating chamber (monthly) and low-cost automatic floating chamber (continuous). To capture total fluxes with better representativity, the setup was supplemented by a series of 10 static mini-chambers (monthly surveys). Furthermore, to resolve spatial variability, an autonomous surface vehicle (HARLE) coupled with an echosounder and a laser spectrometer embedded probe Sub-Ocean was deployed for high-resolution CH 4 bubble mapping. Data analysis is currently ongoing. This communication will present the seasonal dynamics of fluxes observed during the 2023-2025 cycle, highlighting the critical discrepancies between monthly and high-frequency monitoring for flux estimation.

presentations.title: Evaluation of methods for the analysis of oxygen and carbon dioxide in environmental samples across terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Quantifying the concentrations of both carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and oxygen (O 2 ) is essential in studies of biogeochemical cycles, but selecting the right methodology can be challenging due to the range of available instruments and their differing capabilities. Some analyzers are designed to measure via air sample injection, while others focus on the dissolved phase. While several studies examine the abilities of specific analyzers, comparison of multiple analyzers and environmental sample types is lacking. Here, we examined the performance of various analyzers across a broad range of environments, including lake water, sediment, soil and leaf litter. Widely used analyzers were evaluated, included O 2 optode sensors, membrane inlet mass spectrometry (MIMS), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) analyzer, cavity ringdown spectroscopy (CRDS), and gas chromatography (GC). We also present a new aquatic sample handling technique that enables the simultaneous determination of both O 2 and CO 2 . Among all tested instruments, MIMS emerged as the most versatile since it was the only analyzer that successfully measured both CO 2 and O 2 in both solid and liquid samples across both high and low gas concentrations. Both MIMS and optode sensors performed comparably for O 2 . For CO 2 , MIMS had the highest reproducibility, with the lowest coefficient of variation across all analyzers. Overall, this study offers practical guidance for selecting an appropriate gas analyzer. It emphasizes the importance of employing flexible methods that can accurately measure respiration across a wide range of environmental samples.

presentations.title: CARBON DYNAMICS IN TROPICAL WETLANDS: INSIGHTS FROM A CASE STUDY IN THE AMAZON
presentations.abstract: Inland waters are disproportionately biogeochemically active in relation to their area. Aquatic habitats in the lowland Amazon emit large quantities of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ). However, information on CH 4 and CO 2 fluxes and concentrations from these aquatic habitats, which include open water environments (lakes and river channels), seasonally flooded forests, and areas dominated by emergent and floating herbaceous plants, is sparse. Seasonally flooded forests that constitute 80% of the surface area of ​​aquatic environments in the lowland Amazon basin are particularly understudied. I will synthesize our findings from a multi-year investigation, where we measured dissolved CO 2 and CH 4 concentrations and fluxes between the water and atmosphere and ecological data within flooded forests, herbaceous plants, and at open water areas in a floodplain system located in the central Amazon basin. I will discuss these results, pointing to some mechanisms that are associated with the variability in gas fluxes and concentrations, and will briefly discuss the implications of these results for the regional CH 4 and CO 2 evasion in the Amazon basin.

presentations.title: REAL-TIME MEASUREMENT OF GREENHOUSE GASES IN AND NEAR AQUEOUS ENVIRONMENTS
presentations.abstract: Bodies of water may act as both sources and sinks of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), methane (CH 4 ), nitrous oxide (N 2 O) and others. This respiration process may depend on several factors, including microbial respiration, stratification and mixing, temperature, organic matter decomposition, nutrient enrichment, vegetation, and more. It is important to understand the interplay between these factors and the net greenhouse gas respiration for all types of surface water. We have constructed a portable, battery powered quadrupole mass spectrometer with a custom differentially pumped inlet section that allows for real-time part per billion gas analysis at ambient air pressure. For this study, relative concentrations of greenhouse gases are measured in the ambient, near surface region of pond water in addition to gas concentrations in sealed air volumes in equilibrium with the pond water surface. While some small lakes and ponds emit greenhouse gases in consistent, predictable amounts, others are highly variable. It may be possible to model pond and other water body respiration if sufficient data is available. The study of dissolved greenhouse gases in bodies of water is also important for understanding the role of bodies of water in the global carbon cycle. Understanding dissolved greenhouse gases is crucial for analyzing the complex feedback loops between water bodies and the atmosphere. Here, we have used polymer membrane (PDMS) inlet technology with the portable mass spectrometer to measure real-time relative greenhouse gas concentrations below the water surface and compare these concentrations with gas concentrations just above the water surface.

presentations.title: WATER, SOIL, AND TREES: SOURCES OF VARIABILITY IN GREENHOUSE GAS FLUXES IN A FLOODPLAIN FOREST
presentations.abstract: Forests can act as substantial sinks of CO 2 but are neither strong sources nor sinks of the more potent greenhouse gases CH 4 and N 2 O. However, permanent water bodies and fluctuating groundwater levels, as found in floodplain forests, can substantially affect the balance between sources and sinks of CH 4 and N 2 O. Therefore, increasing our knowledge of their flux dynamics is crucial for improving estimates of the terrestrial greenhouse gas budget. In our study, we thus measured monthly fluxes of CH 4 , CO 2 , and N 2 O from the individual floodplain forest components (streams, lakes, adjacent soils, and tree stems) to quantify their contribution to the ecosystem-scale greenhouse gas budget of the floodplain forest quantified continuously throughout the entire year using an eddy covariance system. Measurements in water bodies included both diffusive fluxes from the water surface using floating chambers and ebullitive fluxes using bubble traps. Soil and stem fluxes were measured with the chamber method in transects in the forest leading away from the water bodies. We found that ecosystem-scale CH 4 and N 2 O fluxes measured by the eddy covariance system were largely driven by emissions from water bodies but episodes of elevated groundwater levels increased the relative contribution of emissions from terrestrial parts of the ecosystem.

presentations.title: Regional-scale upscaling of agricultural stream greenhouse gases fluxes: a first-order estimate and clues of geographical control mechanisms
presentations.abstract: Low-order agricultural streams have the potential to be a significant source of greenhouse gases (GHG) due to their integration into agricultural land, which exposes them to significant amounts of organic matter as well as inputs of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) from fertilizer use. However, their altered hydrology and the variability in agricultural practices from surrounding fields cause considerable uncertainty regarding their capacity to act as downstream transport or processing points for organic carbon (OC). Here, we produce a first-order estimate of the fluxes of CO 2 and CH 4 to the atmosphere and the export of OC downstream in agricultural ditches from three agriculture-dominated regions in southern Québec (Pike River, Milles-Îles, lac St-Pierre). Using geospatial analysis, we develop a detailed portrait of the hydrological network across these regions, including a hierarchization of the stream network, identification of intermittent streams, drainage density assessment and qualification of the vegetated riparian strips with association with crop-type on land. Combining these estimates with empirical measurements will enable identifying emerging spatial controls in the composition and magnitude of stream GHG emissions across the agricultural landscape of Québec.

presentations.title: SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL PATTERNS OF STREAM N2O IN THE YAHARA WATERSHED
presentations.abstract: Nitrogen (N) inputs from agricultural landscapes can affect both water quality and greenhouse gas emissions in streams. Of particular concern is N₂O, both because it is a potent greenhouse gas and because streams account for a substantial fraction of global aquatic emissions of this gas. Despite this significance, the factors shaping spatial and temporal variability of N₂O in streams remain unclear. Since June 2024, we measured CH₄, CO₂, and N₂O concentrations along with NO₃⁻, NO₂⁻, NH₄⁺, and TN in eight stream sites in an agriculturally-dominated watershed in Wisconsin, USA to better understand patterns and drivers of spatial and temporal variability of N₂O. N₂O concentrations varied substantially within sites, yet many sites display broadly consistent temporal patterns. While temporal coherence may be indicative of larger climatic controls at play, correlations with different N forms and N₂O were positive at some sites and negative at others, suggesting that factors in addition to nutrient loads affect N₂O concentrations among sites. Generalized additive models identified non-linear relationships between N₂O saturation and N forms that differed between periods of high flow and temperature-dependent baseflow conditions. Subsequent piecewise linear analyses provided evidence for potential thresholds at which relationships with N forms shift above specific concentrations These findings suggest that the mechanisms driving N₂O production vary seasonally.

presentations.title: SPATIAL PATTERNS OF GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS IN A FLOODPLAIN SYSTEM – THE UPPER DANUBE CASE STUDY
presentations.affiliation: The University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences BOKU, Vienna
presentations.abstract: This study investigated the spatial and temporal dynamics based on floodplain network connectivity of carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) emissions within a dynamic floodplain of the National Park DonauAuen in Austria – a last free-flowing floodplain stretch of the upper Danube. It focuses on the roles of hydrological connectivity, network properties, organic matter (OM) characteristics, and environmental drivers during a spring period, with no typical flood event. CO2 fluxes exhibited spatial patterns, with sites intermediately connected to the main channel having the highest emissions, showing a link between nutrient-rich channel water inputs and groundwater influence. CH4 fluxes lacked spatial but displayed temporal dynamics, increasing substantially within the spring season. CH4 hotspots were prominent in the disconnected sites. Statistical analysis confirmed a variety of environmental drivers: CO2 was positively related to protein-like dissolved OM, temperature, and groundwater proxies, while CH4 was associated with humic-like OM, temperature, and dissolved organic carbon (DOC), confirming the dependence of methanogenesis on bioavailable substrates. Overall, CO2 and CH4 emissions are governed by a complex interplay of connectivity, temporal variability, and OM quality. This work demonstrates that changes in floodplain hydrology substantially influence their role as significant and variable sources of greenhouse gases, underscoring the necessity of integrating these systems into regional carbon budgets, climate and restoration strategies.

presentations.title: NITROUS OXIDE CYCLING IN THE BAY OF BENGAL USING STABLE ISOTOPES AND ISOTOPOMERS
presentations.abstract: Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) is a greenhouse gas 270 more potent than carbon dioxide and a stratospheric ozone depleting substance. The quantification of N 2 O production and consumption rates is crucial to understand N 2 O cycling and thereby predicting its fluxes into the atmosphere. The low oxygen conditions in the Bay of Bengal favor the production of nitrous oxide by different biogeochemical processes, i.e., nitrification, and partial denitrification. Previous research has indicated considerable accumulation of N 2 O due to partial denitrification in the Bay of Bengal; however, the spatial and seasonal variability of N 2 O distribution in this area remains poorly understood. N 2 O samples were collected at 12 stations in the low-O 2 region the Bay of Bengal during June-August 2025. We measured N 2 O concentrations, stable isotopes and isotopomers as well as production and consumption rates. N 2 O production and consumption rates were measured using 15 N-labeled incubations. Loligo spot sensors were employed to monitor oxygen concentrations at each time points of the incubation experiments. This presentation will discuss N 2 O transformations, production and consumption rates and fluxes to the atmosphere in the Bay of Bengal during the southwest monsoon.

presentations.title: ASSESSING ISLAND SALT MARSH CARBON DYNAMICS: INSIGHTS UNDER CONSTRAINED SEDIMENT SUPPLIES
presentations.abstract: Island salt marshes are critical coastal buffer zones that offer a host of ecosystem functions including carbon burial. Increasing rates of sea level rise and anthropogenic pressures, including tidal restrictions, threaten marsh geomorphic stability and potentially increase lateral carbon export, devaluing salt marshes as carbon sinks. Island marshes serve as model ecosystems to which fluvial delivery can be constrained, allowing for exploration of underlying mechanisms controlling stability, thus serving to improve regional and global models of salt marsh dynamics and allowing for more accurate valuation of these blue carbon ecosystems. Over the next two years, this study will use a suite of analyses including short-lived radionuclides to create age-depth models, pore water source characterization to create a hydrodynamic mixing model, and headspace gas sampling to assess salt marsh vulnerability to drowning. We will thereby quantify carbon storage and fluxes across time and anthropogenic gradients, and aid in local coastal management and restoration decision-making to protect and improve salt marsh function on Block Island, Rhode Island, US. We expect that increasing tidal restrictions, which limit sulfate availability, will lead to greater lateral carbon flux, decreasing marsh stability, and potentially devalue the marshes as carbon sinks. Using UV-Vis spectrophotometry to assess exported carbon lability, we then seek to answer the question: if exported carbon is recalcitrant, does it create an alternative avenue for long term storage?

presentations.title: ADVANCING AQUATIC GREENHOUSE GAS MODELLING WITH WET: INSIGHTS FROM A TEMPORARILY STRATIFYING LAKE
presentations.abstract: Greenhouse gas emissions from inland and coastal waters are linked to eutrophication, mixing regimes, and ecosystem metabolism. Reproducing and forecasting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and methane (CH₄) dynamics therefore requires models that integrate physical, biogeochemical, and ecological processes across the water column and the benthic domain. The process-based Water Ecosystems Tool (WET) builds on extensive water-quality and nutrient-cycling applications. With WET v2.4, the carbon module is expanded to explicitly represent CO₂ and CH₄ production, oxidation, transport, and emission through both diffusive and ebullitive pathways. We evaluated these new capabilities using a 5-year dataset from the 5-m deep, hypereutrophic Lake Ormstrup, Denmark, spanning hourly temperature and dissolved oxygen profiles, weekly nutrients and CO 2 and CH 4 concentrations, and continuous ebullitive CH 4 emissions. Coupled to the water column model GOTM, GOTM-WET accurately reproduced frequent, short-lived summer stratification events and the resulting anoxia in the hypolimnion, captured bottom-water accumulation of phosphate, ammonia, and greenhouse gases during anoxia, as well as their rapid release during mixing events. Overall, WET v2.4 shows promising performance in simulating seasonal CO 2 and CH 4 emissions as well as the changes in water quality and the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles. With demonstrated global applicability for water-quality modelling, WET provides a robust platform for advancing prediction and attribution of aquatic greenhouse gas fluxes.

presentations.title: Water column methane dynamics in deep boreal glacial lakes
presentations.abstract: Large, glacial lakes are abundant throughout western boreal Canada, but we have a limited understanding of their greenhouse gas dynamics. We often assume these lakes are negligible sources of methane (CH 4 ) due to their typically organic-poor sediments and deep, oxygenated water columns that promote CH 4 consumption. But as the north warms, oxygen concentrations are expected to decrease as water temperatures increase, potentially altering CH 4 production and consumption. In collaboration with the Kaska Dane Nan Yḗ Dāh Land Guardians, we measured depth-resolved, monthly water temperature, chemistry, and dissolved CH 4 concentrations at the center of five lakes (20-55 m deep) in Kaska ancestral territory (British Columbia and Yukon, Canada). Oxygen levels varied between 5 and 110% saturation, with the lowest concentrations occurring in bottom waters at the end of the stratification period in August. Dissolved CH 4 concentrations ranged from 0.02-1.5 µM and were decoupled from oxygen concentrations. We observed the highest concentrations of CH 4 near the thermocline on most sampling occasions. This suggests CH 4 is either produced in the oxic water column or is transported laterally from external sources. Stable carbon isotope results will provide insights into CH 4 production and consumption pathways. This project is part of a long-term monitoring project, with additional sampling campaigns planned through 2029. In future field seasons, we will deploy automated floating chambers to link water column CH 4 dynamics to fluxes. Our ultimate goal is to monitor the impacts of regional warming on lake health, while also exploring how these changes influence CH 4 dynamics.

presentations.title: Multivariate analysis of 50 lakes in Kangerlussuaq (West Greenland) to elucidate drivers of methane cycling
presentations.abstract: As part of the CLIMET consortium, we investigate the drivers of methane (CH₄) cycling in 50 lakes in Greenland, with yet unquantified impacts on regional carbon dynamics. In West Greenland’s Kangerlussuaq region, hundreds of lakes provide a natural laboratory for identifying environmental controls on CH₄ processing. We present preliminary findings from a survey of 50 lakes spanning gradients in depth, altitude, and distance from the Greenland Ice Sheet. Our approach links potential drivers such as nutrients, micro-elements, dissolved organic matter (DOM), and key chemical properties, to CH₄-cycling responses using multivariate analysis. Because CH₄ cycling cannot be measured directly, we use complementary indicators: whole-lake CH₄ concentrations, top–bottom CH₄ gradients, and δ¹³C signatures in both waters and sediments. Together, these proxies provide insight into CH₄ production, oxidation, and transport. Measurements reveal strong spatial variability in temperature, dissolved oxygen, nutrients, DOM, and elemental composition. When combined with lake morphometry and water chemistry, these patterns help identify the dominant environmental controls on CH₄ cycling. Establishing this baseline is essential for predicting how Greenland’s lakes may respond to future changes in methane dynamics.

presentations.title: GREENHOUSE GAS DYNAMICS AND DISSOLVED ORGANIC MATTER IN THE DAM-IMPACTED OTONABEE RIVER
presentations.abstract: Dissolved greenhouse gas (GHG) in streams and rivers are altered by various anthropogenic activities including dams, urbanization, and agricultural farming. In order to explore these anthropogenic effects, we measured GHGs (i.e., CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O) and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in the Otonabee River watershed, a river flowing through Peterborough, Ontario. Preliminary results revealed lower levels of dissolved GHG in the dammed upstream reach compared to the downstream free-flowing reach. CO 2 and CH 4 were higher in the tributaries and ponds, which may have contributed to elevated levels downstream. Unlike CO 2 and CH 4 , highest dissolved N 2 O was found along the downstream river compared to upstream river, tributaries, and ponds. DOC concentrations were relatively stable across sites, but elevated levels in tributaries and ponds may be responsible for enhanced microbial activity fueling GHG gas production. These patterns indicate that tributaries and ponds act as biogeochemical hotspots, amplifying carbon and nitrogen cycling within the watershed. Such localized variability underscores the need for targeted management strategies to mitigate GHG emissions from small river systems, which collectively influence regional carbon budgets and climate feedback.

title: Temporal Trajectories in Aquatic C Cycling on a Changing Planet

presentations.title: Centennial-scale carbon burial dynamics in lakes across Canada
presentations.abstract: Organic carbon burial in lake sediments has emerged as an important component of the global C balance, similar in magnitude as the soil and oceanic C sinks; this process is particularly active in the water-rich landscapes such as the boreal biome.
