There is evidence that OC burial in lakes across the Northern Hemisphere has increased since 1900 and accelerated since 1950-1960, yet the magnitude of this trend appears to vary considerably within and between regions. Despite the identification of several potential factors behind these changes in OC burial, the temporal patterns of this burial and their underlying causes remain poorly understood. Here we present a continental scale study of temporally-resolved OC burial rates of lakes across Canada, employing consistent field and laboratory methods that yield a highly robust and uniform dataset. The study involves 106 lakes located across the major ecozones of Canada, spanning a wide range of limnological, watershed and climatic properties. We observed a widespread increase in OC burial rates across lakes in the early 1900s, which accelerated after the mid-1900s. To determine potential factors associated with the increase in OC burial rates at the continental scale, we evaluated the relationship between changes in OC burial rates and temporal changes in drivers, including sedimentary Chl a, as a proxy of lake primary production, historical land-use in the watershed, and climatic variables. Preliminary results suggest major differences in the magnitude of this increase and in the drivers involved in this increase among ecozones.

presentations.title: ASSESSING HUMAN IMPACTS AND NUTRIENT CYCLING IN A PROTECTED TROPICAL WETLAND (LAKE LOKTAK, NORTHEAST INDIA)
presentations.abstract: Lake Loktak, the largest lake in Northeast India, is vital to surrounding communities, providing food, drinking water, and livelihoods for over 250,000 people. It also hosts a wide range of unique and rare biodiversity, including the critically endangered Sangai deer, with only ~260 remaining in the wild. Despite its ecological and socioeconomic significance, the lake is increasingly threatened by human and climatic stressors, including pollution, overfishing, and changes to its hydrological regime. Three sediment cores dated using 210Pb and 137Cs provide a ~150-year timeline of aquatic C dynamics and catchment drivers. Multi-proxy analyses - including C and N isotopes, C/N ratios, XRF, algal pigments, and diatoms - are used to reconstruct historical changes in pollution, organic matter origin, productivity, and C sources, cycling, and accumulation. Organic carbon accumulation rates increase abruptly following the construction of the Ithai dam in 1983, representing a substantial disruption to the hydrological regime, further compounded by increased harmful nutrient and pesticide inputs over this period. This provides the first integrated paleoenvironmental assessment of how anthropogenic stressors have, at different spatial and temporal scales, altered the hydro-ecological functioning and carbon pathways in Lake Loktak.

presentations.title: From holocene steadiness to industrial-era increases: shifting patterns of carbon accumulation in boreal and temperate lakes
presentations.abstract: Lakes play an important role in the continental carbon cycle, burying large amounts of terrestrial organic matter in their sediments. Although recent increases in carbon accumulation rates (CAR) have been linked to anthropogenic climate and land-use change, the extent to which modern CAR exceeds naturally varying Holocene trends remains unclear. This uncertainty reflects the lack of datasets combining long-term and recent CAR records with consistent sediment properties across broad spatial scales. Here, we quantify temporal change in CAR from the pre-modern Holocene (-8,000 BCE-1850 CE) to the industrial-era (post-1850) across boreal and temperate lakes using a novel bulk density-organic matter (BD-%OM) model. Our model improves predictive accuracy (R2 = 0.96) compared to previous approaches and captures variability across a wide range of OM. Change in CAR over time remained low and stable across all cores pre-1850, whereas post-1850 values rose on average (~20 ± 7 % above baseline), although nearly one-third of post-1850 layers decreased, highlighting the variability in response. The strongest increases occurred in deeper, low-elevation northern lakes with low pre-1850 CAR. Overall, our results suggest that post-industrial human activities have pushed lake carbon burial beyond Holocene baselines, increasing accumulation rates through sediment records, and variability both within and across sediment cores. This shows that anthropogenic influence has reshaped carbon storage in inland waters, with implications for predicting future carbon dynamics.

presentations.title: BALANCING THE ORGANIC CARBON BUDGET IN LAKE SUPERIOR: LOSS PROCESSES ARE MUCH LOWER THAN PREVIOUS ESTIMATES
presentations.abstract: Lake Superior (USA/Canada) is the largest lake on the planet by surface area and is one of the lowest productivity of the five Laurentian Great Lakes, but it plays an important role in global biogeochemical cycles. There is an increasing recognition that inland lakes play an outsized role in global carbon (C) cycling, including being important locations of C accumulation, burial, and greenhouse gas emissions. Despite this, Lake Superior's C budget is poorly constrained. Twenty years ago, Urban et al. (2005) published a comprehensive C budget for Lake Superior, which has served as the model for the past two decades. While Urban et al. (2005) represented a major step forward in estimating Lake Superior's C budget, most of the data included in the estimate came from a spatially-constrained study conducted near the Keweenaw Peninsula that likely does not represent the whole lake. Urban et al. demonstrated that the budget was significantly imbalanced and hypothesized that there is a major source of organic carbon (OC) to Lake Superior that is currently not accounted for. In this talk, we will update current loss estimates from the Lake Superior OC pool, including respiration and OC accumulation and burial, using newer published and unpublished data that will show these loss processes are much lower than previously estimated. Spatially explicit analysis of the heterogeneity of these loss processes across the lake will more precisely estimate OC accumulation and burial in Lake Superior sediments.

presentations.title: VARIABLE CARBON–NUTRIENT DYNAMICS IN SUB-ARCTIC LAKES ACROSS A LAND-USE GRADIENT IN A RAPIDLY WARMING REGION
presentations.abstract: Arctic lake sediments are among the largest global carbon stocks, and widespread increases in carbon burial rates have been documented across the region over the last century. Although these increases are broadly attributed to climate change and atmospheric nitrogen deposition, our understanding of carbon burial across the Arctic does not reflect landscape heterogeneity and is poorly constrained. In particular, the interactive effects of anthropogenic land-use and climate change on Arctic carbon burial remain largely unexplored. To assess the relative controls of land-use and climatic drivers on carbon burial, we quantified organic carbon burial and dual 13C & 15N natural abundance over the past 200 years in Arctic lakes that span a gradient of agricultural management. We paired these records with instrumental climate data extending back to 1875 to characterize changes in temperature and hydroclimate. Preliminary results show clear divergence in sediment nutrients and carbon burial rates at endmembers of the land-use gradient. However, variability in sediment across lakes with moderate agricultural influence demonstrates the importance of lake-specific and watershed drivers when quantifying the control of regional and global drivers on carbon burial. As the Arctic experiences unprecedented warming and agricultural activity is predicted to increase, understanding the interaction of climate change and land-use on carbon burial in Arctic lakes is critical for constraining the global carbon cycle.

presentations.title: Centennial trends of carbon sources and sinks in perialpine lakes revealed by sediment archives and process-based modeling
presentations.abstract: Lakes play a dual role in the global carbon cycle, acting both as sources of GHG and as long-term sedimentary carbon sinks. Yet these two fluxes are rarely assessed together over centennial scales, largely due to the scarcity of monitoring data. Here we combine sediment archives with process-based models to reconstruct carbon flux trajectories since 1850 CE in four large perialpine lakes that underwent eutrophication followed by reoligotrophication. Using high-resolution paleolimnological approaches, we show that organic carbon burial has more than doubled since the late 19th century, with no sign of decline despite major reductions in nutrient inputs. This persistent increase is attributed to both the maintenance of relatively high lake primary productivity and a shift toward the decline of deep-water oxygen conditions that increased: respiration rates are now up to four times higher than in pre-eutrophication conditions, reinforcing hypoxia and enhancing carbon preservation. To assess emissions, we calibrated a 1D thermal (GLM) model using multi-decadal monitoring data from the OLA observatory (RMSE < 1.5 C). Simulations show altered mixing and water-column warming, enabling the reconstruction of past GHG fluxes. These model-based estimates are curently validated through monthly field campaigns in 2025 and 2026. Together, these results suggest that reoligotrophic perialpine lakes may act as increasingly efficient long-term carbon sinks, raising the question of whether cumulative burial can partially or fully offset GHG emissions over decadal-to-centennial timescales.

title: Temporal Trajectories in Aquatic C Cycling on a Changing Planet

presentations.title: Multiscale diversity in dissolved organic matter across the Earth's lakes
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is one of the largest and most reactive pools of carbon on Earth, with widespread importance for climate regulation and the biogeochemical cycles that support life. Despite the importance of DOM, we know little about how its molecular composition varies seasonally and across large spatial gradients. DOM consists of millions of distinct organic compounds, each with a unique function that should reflect its sources and its exposure to microbial and photochemical processing. Therefore, DOM composition and function may exhibit clear seasonal shifts associated with transitions from summer to winter and from rainy to dry seasons. Here, we assessed monthly variation in DOM molecular composition using ultra-high-resolution mass spectrometry during a year of coordinated global sampling in 67 lakes spanning all major climatic zones. We discovered seasonal changes in the diversity of molecular formulae and their functional traits, as well as compositional differences among seasons. These seasonal changes were more pronounced outside of the tropics and were influenced by both trophic state and lake mixing regime. We also identified clear anthropogenic signatures in seasonal DOM composition associated with diverse environmental contaminants and we linked seasonal variation in DOM to both in-lake and catchment-level environmental characteristics. Together, our study highlights the dynamics of DOM at multiple scales and the underlying processes that can scale our theoretical understanding of chemical diversity across freshwaters globally.

presentations.title: ENHANCED MOBILIZATION OF DISSOLVED ORGANIC MATTER (DOM) IN HUMID BOREAL FORESTS IS LINKED TO REDUCED SOIL DEGRADATION IN WARMER WINTERS
presentations.abstract: Terrestrial to aquatic fluxes, important components of landscape C balance, are hypothesized to increase with climate change in boreal forests. By monitoring soil solution flux along a humid boreal forest climate transect for four years we observe increased DOM mobilization in years with warmer winters and reduced in snowpack duration. These trends may be due to decreased organic matter degradation with reduced snowpack insulation and thus lower loss to respiration, but increased loss via DOM flux over winter. To assess this hypothesis, we evaluate the seasonal flux and composition of soil DOM across this transect. Increases in annual dissolved organic carbon and nitrogen (DON) fluxes were attributed to greater melt period fluxes in the winter/spring (W/S). Elevated W/S fluxes were associated with lower C:N, %DON as amino acid-N, total lignin content and higher Ad/Al in years with warmer winters - more closely reflecting autumn soil DOM composition. In colder winters with longer snowpack duration, Ad/Al was lower and more consistent with bulk soil composition and the release of soil lignin-cellulose. Thus warming-enhanced mobilization of DOM in these forests is likely attributed to reductions in the degradation of C-rich plant-derived polymers from soil in warmer winters.

presentations.title: Hydrological Seasonality and Connectivity Drives DOM Composition in a Tropical Urban Reservoir
presentations.affiliation: Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais - Instituto de Ciências Biológicas
presentations.abstract: The dynamics of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in tropical aquatic systems are strongly shaped by hydrological seasonality and watershed input. We evaluated optical indices of chromophoric and fluorescent organic matter (CDOM and FDOM) across five reservoir sites and seven tributaries during bimonthly campaigns over one year. Tributaries showed marked spatial variability but weak seasonality: some streams had BIX > 1 and low HIX, indicating degraded, microbially derived DOM, whereas others, with higher HIX and lower FI and BIX, were dominated by allochthonous, humic-rich material. The downstream reach of the reservoir exhibited BIX > 1 and SR values similar to the reservoir, reflecting microbial activity and influence of the outflow. In contrast, the reservoir showed limited spatial variation but marked seasonality. During the rainy season, higher HIX and larger molecular size indicated stronger allochthonous inputs, whereas in the dry season, DOM became more autochthonous, with FI around 1.5, higher BIX, lower HIX, and lower SUVa254. DOC ranged from 1.1 to 25.7 mg L-1 in the reservoir and up to 92.1mg L-1 in tributaries.

presentations.title: Interactions between environmental predictors modulate dissolved organic carbon concentrations natural lakes
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) represents a major fraction of carbon in lakes, which, in turn, make up a significant proportion of the global carbon budget. We currently lack comprehensive and generalisable knowledge about how the environment affects DOC patterns, despite increasing scientific interest and research. For example, we know how DOC concentration ([DOC]) varies with some commonly measured environmental variables (e.g. lake area, precipitation), yet these relationships are often non-generalisable, suggesting that simple linear correlations are not sufficient for explaining [DOC] patterns. We address this gap by assembling a comprehensive global dataset comprising DOC measurements from natural lakes, which we compare against spatially and temporally accurate environmental predictors. Using a curated dataset comprising 18,851 data points from 1,202 studies/databases, we tested every permutation of environmental predictor pairs to identify useful predictors as well as their interactions using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM). We found that the global mean [DOC] in natural lakes is 8.21 ± 5.52 mg/L.

presentations.title: Unequal acceleration of lake browning following changes in legislation linked with DOC terrestrial dominance and water residence time
presentations.abstract: Recovery from acidification has driven widespread 'browning', i.e. increase in dissolved organic carbon (DOC) across northern hemisphere lakes over the last decades, but trends vary considerably in both strength and direction depending on the magnitude and trajectories of changes in NOx and SO2 emissions and lake and catchment properties. Building from long-term time-series of lake DOC for a hundred lakes in Eastern Canada, we compare long-term rates of changes in DOC and linked them with lake catchment properties and DOC composition as a proxy of source. Lake browning rates varied between 0 and 0.1 mg L-1y-1 when terrestrial DOC represented between 20% and 50%, and increased exponentially up to 0.6 mg L-1y-1 as the proportion of terrestrial DOC approached 80% of total, which only occurred in lakes with short WRT (<0.2y). Browning rates accelerated in recent years and this response was particularly strong in small lakes with low WRT dominated by terrestrial DOC, while high WRT lakes dominated by internal DOC production showed a muted response.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF CHANGING CLIMATE ON DISSOLVED ORGANIC MATTER EXPORT FROM A FORESTED RESERVOIR WATERSHED
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays a critical role in aquatic ecosystem functioning. Aquatic DOM dynamics are driven by both in-stream and terrestrial processes, which are both increasingly altered by climate change. Under warming and changing hydrology scenarios, DOM release from terrestrial ecosystems into freshwaters could either increase or decrease, which has large consequences for freshwater functioning. Using the Regional Hydro-Ecologic Simulation System (RHESSys) modeling framework, we explored the effects of changing climate on DOM export from a forested catchment into a drinking water reservoir in Virginia, USA. We configured and calibrated the ecohydrological catchment model with monitoring data and then tested how downscaled climate scenarios altered terrestrial export of DOM into the reservoir, and subsequent export of DOM from the reservoir downstream. Our coupled modeling approach allowed us to quantify how much DOM processing could be attributed to the terrestrial landscape, hydrological coupling, and reservoir water column.

title: Temporal Trajectories in Aquatic C Cycling on a Changing Planet

presentations.title: Progressive Early Diagenetic Alteration of Lake Izabal Sedimentary Organic Matter Revealed by Stepwise Py-GC-MS and Bulk Geochemistry
presentations.abstract: Understanding early diagenetic transformations of organic matter (OM) in lacustrine sediments is critical for evaluating carbon preservation and biogeochemical feedbacks in tropical lake systems. Here, we integrate temperature-resolved Py–GC–MS (300–700 °C) with TOC, TN, δ¹³Corg, δ¹⁵N, and major-element ratios from the core of Lake Izabal (Guatemala) to characterize depth-dependent structural evolution of sedimentary OM. Shallow sediments (0–3 cm; post-2000) exhibit molecular signatures dominated by poorly altered, highly degradable biopolymers. Low-temperature pyrolysis (300 °C) yields only minor amounts of simple compounds, while 400–500 °C pyrolysates contain abundant carbohydrate-derived products such as furfural and other oxygenated compounds, indicating substantial preservation of polysaccharide- and protein-like precursors. High-temperature stages (600–700 °C) generate limited chain-scission and aromatic condensation products, demonstrating that shallow OM retains largely intact macromolecular structures with minimal early diagenetic reworking. In contrast, deeper sediments (>6 cm; pre-1987) show clear evidence of diagenetically altered, low-molecular-weight residues and emergent humified structures. At 300 °C, NAOCs, low-molecular-weight hydrogenated PAHs, and residual sterane structures (e.g., androstane) are abundant, indicating substantial microbial modification and structural rearrangement prior to pyrolysis. At 600–700 °C, yields of AOCs, ANCs, and sulfur-aromatic compounds decrease relative to shallow sediments, reflecting the progressive transformation of labile biopolymers into more condensed, aromatized, and humified macromolecular networks during burial. These temperature-dependent patterns define a continuous early diagenetic trajectory from labile biomacromolecules to structurally reorganized, humified OM. Bulk geochemical indicators corroborate this depth-resolved evolution. Declines in TOC–TN and lighter δ¹³Corg in shallow sediments reflect preferential loss of isotopically light, reactive carbon. In deeper intervals, increasing Al₂O₃/(Al₂O₃ + CaO + Na₂O + K₂O) and decreasing Ca/Al and Mg/Al ratios indicate progressive clay enrichment and diminished carbonate dilution, consistent with sustained diagenetic overprinting. Together, these multi-proxy datasets reveal that Lake Izabal sediments capture a clear molecular-scale continuum of early diagenetic alteration, tracking OM transformation from labile biopolymers to humified, structurally stable macromolecules. This framework provides new insights into carbon preservation mechanisms in tropical lacustrine environments and highlights the value of temperature-resolved pyrolysis for resolving fine-scale diagenetic pathways.

presentations.title: Drivers of Mangrove Blue Carbon Stocks: Insights from an Understudied Lagoon Ecosystem in Malaysia
presentations.affiliation: Shahjalal University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Mangrove ecosystems are well-known for their capacity to sequester CO 2 and store blue carbon. Malaysia has the sixth-largest mangrove coverage in the world, yet data on blue carbon storage and its drivers remain limited, especially in lagoonal settings, where restricted exchange and long sediment residence can favor persistent soil carbon. This study quantified above- and below-ground biomass (AGB, BGB) and 0-50 cm soil organic carbon (SOC) in mangrove stands fringing Setiu Lagoon, Malaysia, across an undisturbed site (A) and an aquaculture-influenced site (B) dominated by Rhizophora mucronata and Bruguiera gymnorrhiza . Biomass was estimated with species-specific allometries and converted to carbon using measured tissue %C; soils were analyzed by dry combustion after carbonate removal. Mean biomass carbon was higher at Site A than Site B (AGB: 39.17 vs 36.53 Mg C ha -1 ; BGB: 21.36 vs 16.48 Mg C ha -1 ). SOC averaged 163.21 Mg C ha -1 , about threefold greater than tree-biomass carbon, indicating that soils are the dominant, longer-lived carbon pool in this lagoon context. Ecosystem stocks correspond to approximately 736-884 Mg CO 2 e ha -1 . Variation in total carbon aligned with contrasts in organic matter and bulk density, consistent with hydrogeomorphic control on storage capacity. These findings support prioritizing protection and restoration of relatively undisturbed lagoon-fringing mangroves, and routine tracking of soil properties, especially organic matter and bulk density, to maximize carbon benefits.

presentations.title: Carbon on the Move: Wetlands as Gateways Between Land and Water in the Lake Erie Watershed
presentations.abstract: Wetlands are crucial carbon sinks, storing significant amounts of carbon in sediments and vegetation. However, hydrological connections between wetlands and streamflow can mobilize this stored carbon, transporting it as dissolved organic carbon and dissolved inorganic carbon to streams and lakes. These carbon forms may then be emitted as greenhouse gases or sequestered in aquatic sediments. Whether wetlands act as net carbon sources or sinks depends largely on their geomorphology and hydrologic connectivity. Here, we present results on carbon flows from wetlands to streams within the Canadian Lake Erie Basin using the SPARROW (Spatially Referenced Regressions On Watershed Attributes) model. This parsimonious modeling framework provides a sound mechanistic foundation while remaining within the realm of statistical parameter estimation based on datasets for land use, soils, hydrology, and water quality. SPARROW has the capacity to characterize carbon fate and transport within a spatially explicit watershed context. We employed Bayesian inference techniques to calibrate transport parameters and quantify model uncertainty. We analyzed how DOC loads vary across the hydrologic network, with a particular focus on the influence of wetland configuration and connectivity in shaping carbon mobilization and storage. Two critical ad hoc components include the development of probabilistic formulations to represent prior knowledge of SPARROW parameters and the uncertainty associated with calibration data.

presentations.title: Anthropogenic impact on synchronous variation between sediment organic and inorganic carbon in karst lakes of subtropical China
presentations.abstract: Inorganic carbon cycling in Karst regions is a vital component in the assessment of land carbon sink. However, the dissolution of carbonate rocks and the catchment export has been strongly modulated by catchment development, causing a significant change in the carbon burial patterns in inland waters. To date evaluation of lake carbon burial has predominantly focused on sediment organic carbon, therefore there is a general lack of systematic analysis on the quantification of inorganic carbon burial as well as their synchronous changes with that of organic carbon burial. This study will conduct lake monitoring and sediment surveys in combination with stable isotopic methods for lakes in Southwest China. Firstly, seasonal and comparative analyses of carbon isotope signals will be applied for the samples collected from surface waters, sediment traps and surface sediments. Through the construction and application of isotopic mixing models, we will further track the variation in the sources and composition of inorganic carbon and quantify the relative contribution derived from processes such as catchment export and mineralization. Furthermore, multiple-proxy analyses of lake sediments will be conducted to identify the synchronous pattern in the temporal variations of sediment inorganic and organic burial rates over the last hundred to thousand years. Finally, the temporal patterns, driving factors and key processes of lake carbon burial at different stages of catchment degradation and lake eutrophication. Overall, the proposed analyses on long-term pattern and transfer pathway in lake carbon burial can contribute to evaluating the impact of catchment development on lake carbon burial in Karst regions, and provide scientific evidence for refining the numerical assessment of land carbon balance.

presentations.title: Scales of Variability in Marine Aggregate Carbon Flux
presentations.abstract: Marine aggregates represent a central conduit linking microbial activity and the export of photosynthetically fixed carbon from surface waters to the deep ocean, yet the community is still challenged by a scarcity of in situ observations. There is a dire need for sustained observations, particularly in the vast open ocean, to better predict marine carbon turnover, sequestration, and budgeting. To address this gap, we have combined optical measures of particle flux determined by an Underwater Vision Profiler 5 HD (UVP), with carbon flux recorded by Particle Interceptor Traps (PITs) in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG). This study incorporates 5 years (2020 to 2025) of particulate flux from Hawaii Ocean Time-series (HOT) cruises at Station ALOHA (22.75 ° N, 158.00° W) and 2 highly productive NPSG mesoscale diazotroph blooms. Significant findings include – (1) significant sub-daily variability in carbon export with (2) increases in marine aggregate biovolume observed during annual summer export pulse events and (3) variable particle export fates including suspension between mesopelagic isopycnals during eddy induced phytoplankton blooms. This novel dataset reveals the variability of carbon export across seasonal, interannual, and episodic scales in the oligotrophic NPSG. The work also highlights the strong potential for optical measurements of flux to greatly expand our catalog of oceanic flux measures.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF LANDSCAPE GREENING ON LAKE BROWNING IN THE EASTERN HUDSON BAY REGION, CANADA, OVER THE PAST 40 YEARS
presentations.abstract: Climate warming is expected to increase dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations in boreal-Arctic lakes, leading to lake browning, a key driver of aquatic ecosystem functioning. However, the extent to which this trend has already occurred in remote northern environments remains unclear. Here, we investigate whether climate change and associated shifts in vegetation cover (i.e., landscape greening) have driven lake browning in the eastern Hudson Bay region of Quebec, Canada, over the past four decades. We analysed water chemistry data collected in 1995 and 2021–2022 from 55 lakes spanning a 1082-km latitudinal gradient, together with 40 years of satellite imagery-derived lake surface colour and catchment-vegetation indices. Between 1995 and 2021-2022, DOC increased in 33 lakes and total nitrogen (TN) in 48 lakes, with mean increases of DOC and TN of 10.4% and 57.8%, respectively, across all lakes. Over the same period, satellite observations revealed browning trends in 32 lakes, indicated by declining lake surface green reflectance, and a greening trend in the catchments of 51 lakes, indicated by positive Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) trends. Lake surface green reflectance and NDVI were negatively correlated in 48 lakes, suggesting that catchment greening is contributing to darker lake waters. Our initial results provide a first detailed assessment of lake browning trends in the eastern Hudson Bay region, highlighting how ongoing climate change is reshaping terrestrial-aquatic carbon cycling and water quality in northern lakes.

presentations.title: CARBON SEQUESTRATION IN NEW YORK'S NATURAL PONDS: QUANTIFYING RATES AND IDENTIFYING ENVIRONMENTAL DRIVERS OF CARBON BURIAL
presentations.abstract: Recent studies suggest that carbon sequestration in small lakes and ponds may be as great or greater than that of forests, grasslands, and oceans. Ponds may have a particularly outsized role in carbon burial relative to their size considering that burial rates in ponds can be orders of magnitude higher in lakes (e.g., 60-17,000 g C m-2 yr-1 in artificial ponds). In this study, we examine contemporary and historical rates and drivers of carbon burial in natural ponds throughout New York State. We surveyed 16 natural ponds across four ecoregions of New York State. We sampled each pond for environmental variables and collected a sediment core from the deepest part of each pond. We are combining loss on ignition (LOI) data with 210Pb isotope dating to determine carbon burial rates from the mid-19th century until present for each pond. Our preliminary results from 8 ponds show that burial rates range from 25 to 450 g OC m-2 yr-1. We are exploring how land use, pond morphometry, and other environmental variables impact carbon burial. We plan to relate changes in historical burial rates to changes in land cover within pond catchment areas using historical aerial imagery and records. Ultimately, this study will expand our understanding of how globally abundant small and shallow water bodies contribute to carbon sequestration.

presentations.title: SEDIMENTARY MANGANESE FLUXES AND THEIR INFLUENCE ON SOUTHERN OCEAN CARBON EXPORT UNDER CHANGING CONDITIONS
presentations.abstract: Using the global ocean biogeochemical model NEMO PISCES-BYONIC, we quantify how external dissolved manganese (dMn) sources including sediment supply from shallow continental margins, atmospheric dust, and hydrothermal vents control primary production and carbon export in the Southern Ocean. Across a suite of control and sensitivity simulations, sediment-derived Mn, enhanced under low oxygen conditions, emerges as the dominant source sustaining surface dMn and supporting phytoplankton productivity. Removing sedimentary Mn inputs reduces annual carbon export by 16 percent (from 1.73 to 1.45 Pg C), while primary production declines only 4 percent (from 4.93 to 4.73 Pg C), indicating that Mn limitation disproportionately affects carbon export efficiency. In contrast, removing dust or hydrothermal Mn sources has negligible effects. These findings reveal how changes in sedimentary Mn supply and oxygenation can alter ecosystem productivity and carbon export over time, providing insight into the Southern Ocean’s potential response to ongoing and future environmental change.

title: Physical Limnology: Dynamics, Drivers, and Change in Inland Waters

presentations.title: Oxygen trends in seasonally ice-covered lakes
presentations.abstract: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is an essential resource in ice-covered lakes, regulating water quality and biodiversity, including the survival of economically important fish species. Most of the world's lakes seasonally freeze, often resulting in oxygen depletion as ice cover inhibits water column ventilation and snow cover limits photosynthesis while respiration continues. Widespread shortening of ice cover duration in a warmer world might improve winter oxygenation by decreasing the duration of under-ice oxygen depletion, but this hypothesis remained untested. Here we performed a systematic analysis of 6.6 million physical and chemical observations from 19645 lakes in the Northern Hemisphere during 1960-2022. Contrary to expectations, under-ice DOvw trends ranged from significantly negative in small lakes (surface area <10 ha) (-0.14 ± 0.05 mg L-1 decade-1) to significantly positive in large lakes (>=10000 ha) (0.11 ± 0.03 mg L-1 decade-1). This divergence with lake size emerged partly because ice cover periods have shortened 2.2 times faster in large lakes compared to small lakes.

presentations.title: RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN WEATHER, LAKE STABILITY AND OXYGEN OF A POND IN THE LAURENTIAN GREAT LAKES REGION
presentations.abstract: Climate change affects many aspects of lake ecosystems, including increasing thermal stability and reducing dissolved oxygen concentration. This study investigates how weather impacts thermal stability and oxygen in a dimictic, urban pond in the Laurentian Great Lakes region. Weather time series data was compared to hourly water temperature and dissolved oxygen data using 18 HOBO Pendant Temperature/Light 64K loggers and five HOBO Dissolved Oxygen loggers. We assessed the relationships between calculated Schmidt stability, oxygen variance in the water column, and several weather variables using wavelet coherence analysis. During stratified periods, surface air temperature was highly coherent with Schmidt stability. Our results suggest that for dimictic ponds in the Laurentian Great Lakes region, thermal stability will increase from rising air temperatures regardless of related changes in weather and climate, exacerbating urban pond hypoxia and anoxia issues.

presentations.title: CONTRASTING COLD WEATHER PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CONDITIONS OF CLOSED AND OPEN URBAN PONDS
presentations.abstract: Urban ponds, whether connected to or isolated from channelized drainage networks, provide ecosystem services to the landscape. We present two winters' temperature, salinity, and other water quality data of adjacent open and closed ponds, demonstrating the stark difference between pond type. Open pond salinity was significantly higher than the closed pond in both winters; however, the lack of ice in 2024 limited salinity-based stratification of the water column. The forebay of the open pond remained stratified due to road salt inputs for the entirety of the 2025 winter. Results demonstrate that winter phenology and hydrogeomorphology are important controls on urban pond ecosystem dynamics.

presentations.title: Hydrodynamic Controls on Hypoxia and Hydrogen Sulfide Emissions in a Shrinking Endorheic Lake
presentations.abstract: The Salton Sea, California's largest lake, faces severe environmental challenges driven by hypereutrophication and a long-term, accelerating decline in water levels. To examine how physical changes influence water quality in the Salton Sea, we collected high-resolution measurements of nitrate, oxygen, temperature, pressure, hydrogen sulfide (H2S), and meteorological conditions from 2024-2025. Stratification remained strong in the Salton Sea throughout the deployment period, with buoyancy frequencies on the order of 0.1 rad/s, that often hindered deep-water reoxygenation. As a result, deeper areas (10 m) remained hypoxic 90% of the time. Wind-driven mixing reoxygenates shallow waters, but it cannot offset oxygen demand, leading to frequent bottom hypoxia at the 2 m isobath. On longer (weekly) timescales, inferred lateral advection of deep hypoxic waters and subsequent mixing in shallow areas coincide with low-frequency episodes of hydrogen sulfide emissions.

presentations.title: LAKE RAVN MONITORING PROJECT: UNDERSTANDING ECOSYSTEM PROCESSES THROUGH MACHINE LEARNING
presentations.abstract: Computational limnology has become a dynamic field of research over the past few decades, with rapid advancements in computational power and modelling techniques. However, these models carry inherent uncertainties, simplifications, and errors. To address this, we are initiating a long-term monitoring scheme at Lake Ravn in Denmark, where three buoys will be deployed with high-frequency, depth-discrete, sensors for temperature and oxygen, along with fluorometers for chlorophyll-a monitoring. By integrating these high-frequency data with global datasets, we will employ data-driven models to refine our understanding of underlying physical processes. Our goal is to leverage machine learning to infer scientific insights and improve the parameterization of hydrodynamic and water quality equations.

presentations.title: THE PHYSICO-CHEMISTRY AND NUTRIENT DYNAMICS OF IMO RIVER IN SOUTHEASTERN, NIGERIA.
presentations.affiliation: Federal University Of Technology Owerri Nigeria
presentations.abstract: The anthropogenic and recreational activities such as Laundry, bathing, swimming, boating, sand mining, cow skin processing, etc, have been implicated as the major contributors to the overall pollution status and biogenic salts fluctuations of the water body. Water samples were collected from six ecologically distinct stations over a 12 months period. The samples were analyzed using standard laboratory methods as described by Wetzel and Likens. The results obtained were subjected to Two-way ANOVA. Most of the results fall within W.H.O permissible Standards, except for dissolved oxygen and total phosphorus that slightly deviated. The cationic order was: Na>k>Ca>Mg, with PEARSALL's index of 6.96mg/L. The Water Quality index recorded ranged from 68.5 to 96.3 which ranked the water body at grades C and D in the Water Quality Rating Scale.

title: Physical Limnology: Dynamics, Drivers, and Change in Inland Waters

presentations.title: Combined data analysis and numerical modeling reveal the role of inflow hysteresis and density currents in subtropical reservoir water quality during floods
presentations.abstract: A large fraction of the annual particulate and dissolved loads entering reservoirs is mobilized during short-term flood events. The fate of substances delivered from the watershed during these events depends on hysteresis in the concentration-discharge (C-Q) relationship and on density-current driven transport within the reservoir. Paso Severino Reservoir, the main drinking-water source in Uruguay, is a long and narrow reservoir in a rural subtropical catchment. This study investigates how flood-driven hydrodynamic and thermal processes affect the distribution of turbidity and colored dissolved organic matter in this reservoir, combining monitoring data with numerical modeling. A 3D hydro-thermodynamic numerical model was calibrated and validated with high-frequency temperature measurements and vertical profiles for the period 2022-2024. By linking C-Q hysteresis at the inflow with density-current structure and transport pathways, we aim to improve process-based interpretation of routine water-quality monitoring in drinking-water reservoirs.

presentations.title: Deepwater Warm Intrusions in the World's Deepest Temperate Lakes
presentations.abstract: Deep temperate lakes not only contain more than half of the world's fresh liquid surface water, but they also present a century-long puzzle: why is their deep water so well ventilated? Two prominent examples are the world's deepest lake, Lake Baikal in Siberia (1,642 m), and the world's deepest fjord-type lake, Quesnel Lake in British Columbia (524 m). There appears to be a scientific bias toward emphasizing rapid, openwater, wintertime, deepwater-cooling-events. Yet what remains greatly overlooked is that prior to the rapid wintertime cooling events, there is relatively rapid late-fall warming observed at depths of ~300-800 m that may provide an additional pathway of communication between surface and deep water. Here we utilize datasets, each spanning more than two-decades, from Lake Baikal (2000-2025) and from Quesnel Lake (2003-2025), to investigate the behavior of deepwater (~300-800m).

presentations.title: HYDRODYNAMIC MODELLING OF GREAT SLAVE LAKE USING NEMO
presentations.abstract: The subarctic Mackenzie River Basin is experiencing unprecedented climate warming, up to four times the global average, with significant impacts on regional hydrology and ecosystems. Great Slave Lake, an integral part of the basin, the second-largest lake entirely within Canadian borders, and the deepest in North America. This study aims to further our understanding of the lake's physical processes through numerical modeling. Numerical modeling of Great Slave Lake has been limited by insufficient bathymetric data. Collaborating with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, we developed the first complete bathymetric map by integrating historical naval charts with additional sounding data. This enabled creation of a high-resolution simulation domain for the Nucleus for European Modeling of the Ocean (NEMO) model, adapted for freshwater lake applications. Model validation shows NEMO robustly simulates lake processes, showing strong agreement with observed temperature profiles, and ice cover seasonality.

presentations.title: Equatorial dimictic crater lakes in western Uganda
presentations.abstract: To understand the ecological functioning of lakes, little is more crucial than knowing their mixing regime. We used 276 profiles of temperature, conductivity and dissolved oxygen from 60 crater lakes in equatorial western Uganda to classify these lakes according to mixing regime. Most lakes are small (29 ha on average), but together they cover a spectacularly large depth range (Zmax 1.4 to 220 m). We classified 4 lakes as continuous warm polymictic, 12 as discontinuous warm polymictic, and 11 lakes mix completely once or twice each year. We classify these as equatorial dimictic, because they undergo deep mixing during both dry seasons separated by long periods of stable stratification during the two rain seasons. The 33 remaining lakes do not usually mix completely and are thus meromictic. The main factor controlling these lakes' mixing regime is their relative depth (Zr).

presentations.title: DOES UPWELLING DRIVE GLOEOTRICHIA BLOOMS IN OLIGOTROPHIC LAKES?
presentations.abstract: Gloeotrichia echinulata is a large colonial cyanobacteria that can produces nuisance blooms in otherwise clear lakes. Since 2005, there has been a citizen science Gloeotrichia monitoring program in the Belgrade Lakes where volunteers estimate the density of colonies several times per week using a visual density scale. In this study, we attempt to create a process-based model for Gloeotrichia blooms using this citizen science data, meteorological data, and stratification data from a data buoy and a 1D lake model. Initial results indicate that periods of upwelling might correspond with spikes in Gloeotrichia population. Determining if the two phenomena are correlated could help create a forecasting system for Gloeotrichia blooms.

presentations.title: Physical Drivers of Early-Life Survival: A Modeling Study of Lake Erie Walleye
presentations.abstract: Waves and currents can strongly influence early life stages of fish by generating bed stress that dislodges eggs. In this study, we model these impacts for Walleye (Sander vitreus), which support over a billion-dollar fishery in Lake Erie. We simulated ice cover, water temperature and currents using the hydrodynamic model AEM3D and significant wave heights, periods and stresses using the spectral wave model SWAN. Egg survival, during the incubation period, was defined from published observations, where storm events that exceeded a mean-hourly critical shear velocity of 0.02 m/s resulted in dislodgment and an hourly mortality rate 2.5% egg. The results show that the timing of spring storm events and the associated wave-induced bed stress, relative to the egg incubation period, is a major driver of interannual variability in Walleye recruitment.

title: Physical Limnology: Dynamics, Drivers, and Change in Inland Waters

presentations.title: Direct numerical simulations of turbidity currents: impacts of rheology and sediment Schmidt number
presentations.abstract: Turbidity currents are sediment-laden, gravity-driven flows that shape lakebeds and influence the transport of sediment and contaminants in natural waters. Many numerical studies rely on a constant-viscosity assumption, which overlooks the rheological effects that arise at high sediment concentrations and under shear-rate dependent conditions. Using three-dimensional direct numerical simulations based on a lattice Boltzmann approach, we examine how non-Newtonian rheology and the sediment Schmidt number together affect the evolution of turbidity currents. The simulations indicate that rheology alters front velocity, the distribution of velocity and shear, the buoyancy field, and the overall energetics of the current. The DNS results also point to an important role for the sediment Schmidt number: when viscosity varies in space, a Schmidt number of order one produces propagation speeds closest to experimental observations.

presentations.title: SEDIMENT RESUSPENSION IN LAKES BY INTERNAL SOLITARY WAVES
presentations.abstract: Internal solitary waves drive sediment resuspension in lakes and the coastal ocean. This, in turn, enhances the nutrient circulation of lakes. However, the mechanism driving this resuspension remains to be clarified, as well as how the mechanism is modified in the presence of bathymetry. This presentation will discuss recent numerical and experimental work describing the mechanism of sediment resuspension, how the properties of the sediment determine whether sediment will be ejected into the water column, and how the transport of sediment has led to bedform generation. The instability has been shown to be convective in nature, such that velocity field oscillations in front of the wave lead to a greater instability amplification in the lee of the wave.

presentations.title: Settling and dispersion of Lagrangian particles in the presence of stratified Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and turbulence
presentations.abstract: Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) billows are common mixing events in lakes, estuaries, and coastal oceans, yet their influence on particle settling remains poorly understood despite its importance for sediment transport, biogeochemical cycling, and particle-based interventions. Using direct numerical simulations coupled with Lagrangian particle tracking, we examine how KH billows forming at the base of a mixed layer alter the settling and dispersion of heavy particles (20-100 micrometers) relative to their classical Stokes settling. Particles released just above the shear layer show size-dependent behavior. Particles larger than 40 micrometers settle more slowly because they become trapped within billow cores and preferentially sample upward-moving fluid. Small particles (~20 micrometers) experience strongly enhanced settling, up to seven times their Stokes velocity.

presentations.title: HOW THE VELOCITIES OF CONVECTIVE SEDIMENTATION SCALE WITH SEDIMENT CONCENTRATION AND CONCENTRATION AND PARTICLE SIZE: IMPLICATIONS FOR MARINE CARBON DIOXIDE REMOVAL.
presentations.abstract: When a river flows into a cold lake, suspended sediment in the buoyant surface plume often settles at rates that an order of magnitude larger than the Stokes settling velocity. This is likely due to convective sedimentation - however previous experiments have not systematically explored the influence of particle sizes and sediment concentrations in order to test various scaling relationship. Using a set of laboratory experiments we vary both the sediment concentration and particle size by an order of magnitude, and we find that in all experiment the sediment sinks in finger-like plumes at velocities significantly larger than the Stokes settling velocity. The scaling of convective sedimentation is also highly relevant for the efficacy of ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE).

presentations.title: Particle Aggregation in a Deep Oligotrophic Lake
presentations.abstract: Aggregation of suspended particulate matter (SPM) is of concern in freshwater bodies due to its impacts on water quality, ecology, and physics. We present novel in situ observations of SPM in deep, ultra-oligotrophic Lake Tahoe during autumn 2024 using digital holography. Particle size, geometry, and composition consistently change near the deep chlorophyll-a maximum (DCM), with aggregates on the order of 1 mm constituting the majority of observed SPM below the DCM. Mean particle diameter increases from 70 micrometers in the epilimnion to 300 micrometers below the DCM, while dimensionless particle solidity decreases from 1.0 to 0.8, indicating the formation of loosely-bound fractal-like aggregates.

presentations.title: The effect of hydrodynamics on zooplankton feeding
presentations.abstract: The interaction between hydrodynamics and cladoceran feeding is poorly understood, despite the fact that they are amongst the most common freshwater zooplankton in lakes. We examined the effect of vorticity (w) on Daphnia magna feeding using a horizontally oriented rotating cylinder in which we determined algal (Chlorella and Scenedesmus) clearance rates (CR) and recorded the swimming response of the Daphnia. The CR of D. magna followed the unimodal trend, with higher CR on the small, spherical Chlorella than on larger, elongated, and colonial Scenedesmus. The normal hop-sink swimming behavior of the Daphnia was affected by increasing w; hop frequency decreased, displacement increased, and ultimately there was a loss of vertical orientation. Lake hydrodynamics affect Daphnia feeding through changes in feeding currents, cleaning behaviors and the loss of orientation.

title: Physical Limnology: Dynamics, Drivers, and Change in Inland Waters

presentations.title: Effects of the long-term climate change and selective discharge schemes on the thermal stratification of a large deep reservoir, Xin'anjiang Reservoir, China
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography & Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The effects of global warming on water temperature and thermocline parameters, such as thermocline depth, thickness, and strength were assessed. A catchment model coupled with a reservoir thermal model with meteorological input calculated by a downscaled General Circulation Model (GCM) projection under three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) was applied to Xin’anjiang Reservoir located in East China. The sensitivity of thermal structure to meteorological parameter (air temperature and precipitation) variations were examined with reservoir thermal model. Water temperature in each layer increased (decreased) with the rising (decline) of air temperature, especially the surface water temperature. There was a significant negative (positive) correlation between thermocline depth (strength) and air temperature during the period of stratification weakness. Additionally, water temperature of the reservoir is sensitive to precipitation variation with the reservoir operation involvement. The most sensitive phenomenon of water temperature to precipitation change occurred in the middle layer (depth = 30m). The thermocline depth and thickness increased with decreases of hydraulic residence time which was caused by precipitation increases. According to the simulation experiments driven by RCP outputs, mean water temperature in each water layer in the future (2096-2100) has a strong response to air temperature increasing, which is projected to increase by 0.11-0.62 °C for RCP2.6, 0.76-1.19 °C for RCP4.5, and 1.50-2.35 °C for RCP8.5, comparing to baseline (2012-2016). However, mean water temperature in each water layer from 2096 to 2100 has a slight decrease caused by precipitation change, which is decreased by 0.03-0.25 °C for RCP2.6, 0.07-0.40 °C for RCP4.5, and 0.04-0.29 °C for RCP8.5, comparing to 2012-2016. Combined, under the effects of air temperature rising and precipitation change, the temperature of each water layer increases in different patterns under three RCP scenarios, with the maximum increase of water temperature being at the depth of 40 m for RCP2.6 and 5 m for RCP8.5. This phenomenon is concerned with the differences of seasonal distribution of air temperature increasing among three RCP scenarios. The mean thermocline depth in the future (2096-2100) will be decreased significantly, while the mean thermocline thickness will be slightly increased. On multiyear timescale, the impacts of air temperature change are stronger than those induced by precipitation variation. However, the effects of hydraulic residence time change caused by precipitation change (especially rainstorm) should be considered in the management of deep reservoirs.

presentations.title: ASSESSING THE PAST TO HELP PREDICT THE FUTURE: TRACKING PERMAFROST THAW DISTURBANCE CYCLES OVER THE HOLOCENE USING LAKE SEDIMENTS
presentations.abstract: The Canadian Arctic is warming at a rate approximately twice the global average. As a result of these warming temperatures, permafrost is thawing at an increasingly rapid rate. Thawing of ice rich permafrost can cause the formation of landscape disturbances, including retrogressive thaw slumps. Retrogressive thaw slumps are rotational landslide features which exhibit cyclical stages of active and inactive growth, termed polycyclicity. It has been hypothesized that initial thaw slump onset results in the most substantial changes to the physical, chemical and biological environment of the adjacent lake, but this then acts as a form of ecological memory which moderates how a lake responds to subsequent slumping events. Background disturbance regimes must be known to understand future sensitivity of lakes to retrogressive thaw slumping. Paleolimnological techniques provide a long-term record through the sediment core, establishing a record of environmental conditions and changes over long timescales, spanning the Holocene. This project will use sediment cores spanning the complete history of several lakes in the Mackenzie Delta uplands. The cores taken will allow for a sediment profile extending to the early Holocene coinciding with the Holocene Climate Optimum, a period of warm climate conditions thought to be the most significant period of thermokarst initiation in the region. By inferring historical trends, this research will contribute to a more accurate understanding of the responses of lakes to permafrost thaw across the Mackenzie Delta.

presentations.title: Assessing soil erosion in a tropical urban reservoir through an environmental fragility index
presentations.abstract: The augmented production and transport of fine sediments resulting from human-induced landscape alterations pose a significant threat to freshwater ecosystems, including reservoirs and their associated functioning and services. To support watershed management regarding the likelihood of soil erosion and reservoir sedimentation, we used an environmental fragility index (EFI) for an urban reservoir (the Ibirité “Lagoon”) in southeastern Brazil. The EFI was derived from measured geoclimatic controls on sediment production (rainfall, geology, soil texture, and terrain) and anthropogenic pressures, mainly land-use and land-cover aspects in the reservoir and associated hydrographic basin. We validated the EFI using instream physical habitat metrics related to fine sediment presence through the bed relative bed stability index (LRBS). The EFI showed strong and significant relations with sediment-related physical habitat metric (R2=0.72), reinforcing its effectiveness in identifying and mapping sediment-source areas across the catchment. The present methodology has potential for application in the management, recovery, and preservation of reservoirs and streams in tropical river basins.

presentations.title: Experiments Using Wave Energy to Reduce Surface Water Temperature and Their Potential
presentations.abstract: As global warming progresses, the water temperature of Lake Biwa has risen, and full-lake circulation failed to occur for two consecutive years starting in 2019. By using wave-powered pumps, it becomes possible during winter to supply cold, oxygen-rich water to the oxygen-depleted bottom layer, thereby restoring dissolved oxygen concentrations near the lake bed. In summer, transporting cold water from deep aquifers to the surface can help cool surface waters that have become excessively heated by solar radiation. To examine these possibilities, we developed a wave-powered pump that uses surface waves generated by winds blowing across Lake Biwa to move water vertically. We conducted multiple field tests and obtained highly favorable results.

presentations.title: What is the impact of floating leaf macrophytes on the thermal stratification of shallow lakes?
presentations.affiliation: Ecole nationale des ponts et chaussées | Institut Polytechnique de Paris
presentations.abstract: In the context of global change, the disruption of N and P biogeochemical cycles is a major driver of freshwater eutrophication. In shallow lakes, rooted floating-leaved macrophytes, such as water lilies, play a key role in eutrophication processes. Moreover, they contribute in biodiversity conservation. Understanding the physical functioning of shallow lakes is thus essential to grasp their ecological dynamics. This study aims to develop a process-based model of water temperature and lake level dynamics for a large, shallow lake, Lake Grand-Lieu, using the General Lake Model (GLM), a one-dimensional vertical (1DV) model widely used by the scientific community. Lake Grand-Lieu (western France) gets partially covered in water lilies from spring to autumn. The main goal of this study is to establish whether a 1DV model is able to simulate the thermal behaviour of the lake areas, with and without water lilies. A comprehensive dataset is available at an open water station and at one covered by water lilies. The addressed questions are: how to take into account the processes involved in the water balance, the surface heat transfer and the mixing? The derived equations are described. Two set-ups are presented, respectively for the areas with and without water lilies. Key parameters are identified through a sensitivity analysis and calibrated using the CMA-ES algorithm. The resulting models successfully reproduce the water level dynamics, temperature profiles and daily thermal stratification patterns, for both open-water areas and areas covered by water lilies.

presentations.title: The role of wind-driven upwelling and downwelling events in structuring Lake Trout habitat usage in Lake Ontario
presentations.abstract: The near-shore water temperatures in Lake Ontario are constantly changing in summer due to the influence of wind-driven movements of the thermal stratification and can swing between 20 o C to 4 o C and back over a few days. Lake Trout are known to prefer waters that are less than 12 o C, so would be expected to modify their habitat usage in response to the downwelling of warm waters. This study focused on a section 200-kilometer-long sections of the Canadian shoreline of Lake Ontario, using 17 acoustic telemetry receivers recording Lake Trout positions between April to October 2023. These receivers also recorded benthic water temperature, so that we could determine when downwelling events warmed waters at 20 m depth from typical values of 8-12 o C to as warm as 22 o C. The downwelling events were coherent over horizontal scales of 30-60 km, and lasted for several days, and correlated with strong easterly wind events. After the wind event, the downwelling moved slowly in an anticlockwise direction around Lake Ontario as a Kelvin water. Lake Trout we always absent when downwelling events occurred, and were only ever detected when water temperatures were below 12 °C. Our results thus showed a strong connection between the physics of the wind impulse and the biological distributions of Lake Trout. The finding underlines that it is important to consider internal wave dynamics when further investigating fish habitats and sustainable fisheries management

presentations.title: PONDS AND SMALL LAKES ARE NEITHER DIMICTIC NOR POLYMICTIC: PROPOSING TELOMIXIS, A SEASONAL MIXING REGIME FOR THE SMALLEST LENTIC WATERBODIES
presentations.affiliation: State University of New York at New Paltz
presentations.abstract: Dimictic lakes have four distinct thermal mixing and stratification seasons: summer stratification, fall mixing, winter inverse stratification, and spring mixing. Summer stratification sets up rapidly following the spring mixed period; similarly, it can rapidly break down, culminating in a distinct turnover (mixing) event followed by a thermally mixed period. However, temperate ponds, small lakes, and shallow lakes, despite experiencing the same weather patterns and climate as larger lakes, have relatively low water volume that can accelerate mixing or stratification. These smaller and shallower waterbodies have distinctly different annual mixing dynamics compared to lakes. This study examines the mixing dynamics of mostly temperate, small, shallow, and summertime stratified waterbodies. We show that, in contrast to most lakes, smaller waterbodies have long and distinctive shoulder seasons in the fall and spring, characterized by repeated mixing and restratification, which can occur for days to months, before sustained stratified or isothermal conditions. We propose that these waterbodies require a new category for their mixing regime as they are neither dimictic nor polymictic. We are proposing that small waterbodies are ‘telomictic’ with telo- from the Greek root for ‘end’ to emphasize that both ends of summer stratification are marked by intermittent mixing. Describing small waterbody mixing regimes is an important update to established paradigms for lakes, and indicates that transition periods in spring and fall have the potential for high biogeochemical and ecological activity.

presentations.title: Dynamics of Thermal Stratification and Anoxia in a Tropical Urban Reservoir: The Role of Macrophyte Proliferation
presentations.abstract: High-frequency temperature (T) and dissolved oxygen (DO) data (Dec 2024 – Aug 2025) were used to investigate the limnological dynamics of a shallow tropical urban reservoir frequently affected by macrophyte blooms. We calculated the mixing layer depth (Z MIX ), the anoxic layer depth (Z ANOX ), and the Anoxia Factor (AF) to assess the reservoir's oxygenation status. The reservoir exhibited persistent, shallow thermal stratification, with a mean Z MIX of 0.40m. This shallow mixing resulted in severe hypolimnetic anoxia, with a mean AF of 55.9%, indicating that over half of the hypolimnion was anoxic throughout the study period. The Z ANOX showed high variability, ranging from 0.25 m (surface anoxia events) to 8.0m (fully oxygenated). A key finding was the temporal change associated with the proliferation of aquatic macrophytes, which dominated the study area from July 2025 onwards. Comparing the pre-macrophyte period (Dec-Jun) to the macrophyte-dominated period (Jul-Aug), the mean AF significantly decreased from 58.6% to 45.2%. This 22.8% reduction in the Anoxia Factor suggests that the presence of macrophytes may have a mitigating effect on hypolimnetic anoxia, possibly by increasing primary production and oxygen release into the water column, or by stabilizing the water column and reducing sediment oxygen demand. These results highlight the complex interplay between physical processes, oxygen dynamics, and macrophyte presence in shallow tropical urban aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: Evaluating Climate-Driven Phytoplankton Dynamics in a Drinking Water Reservoir Using Three-Dimensional Hydrodynamic and Water Quality Modeling
presentations.abstract: Lake Mead, a large reservoir in the desert southwestern United States, serves as a critical drinking and irrigation water source for over 25 million people across three states and Mexico. Since 2000, the lake has experienced a significant loss in volume (~70%) due to prolonged regional drought. Historically, Lake Mead has been phosphorus-limited, with the majority of phosphorus inputs originating from recycled, highly treated wastewater from a nearby urban area. Lake Mead last experienced a major algal bloom in 2001, after which phosphorus loading into the waterbody was greatly reduced; however, the continued effects of projected future climate change and ongoing drought on the algal communities are not well understood. In this ongoing study, we use the three-dimensional hydrodynamic and water quality model AEM3D to examine how surface water temperature (0–5 m) influences phytoplankton biomass and community structure, with a focus on potential ecological memory under extreme hydrologic conditions. Following initial model parameter optimization using historical data, we are analyzing relationships among temperature, nutrients, chlorophyll a , and phytoplankton composition by comparing historically warmer and cooler years. Planned analyses will use correlations, time series methods, diversity metrics, and machine learning to assess and quantify how surface temperature and hydrologic changes affect phytoplankton dynamics and elucidate key drivers of harmful algal blooms in Lake Mead.

presentations.title: RISING AIR TEMPERATURES AND SLOWING WIND SPEED DELAY FALL OVERTURN IN LAKE SIMCOE, ONTARIO
presentations.abstract: Previous studies have shown lakes in North America experience delayed fall overturn due to global warming. We studied this trend in Lake Simcoe, Ontario using bi-weekly vertical temperature profiles collected from 1980 to 2024. We analyzed air temperature and wind speed data above the lake collected from satellites to investigate the cause of this delay. Through the analysis of water column stability, the historical trend showed the day of fall overturn is getting later, with the duration of summer stratification lasting longer. This delaying fall overturn was found to be caused by a combination of slowing wind speeds and warmer air temperatures using multilinear regression (R 2 = 0.24). Lengthened summer stratification and delayed fall overturn have an impact on species living in the lake. Cold-water species, such as lake trout, are greatly affected as they must wait longer for the lake to be replenished with dissolved oxygen at depth in the fall.

presentations.title: Propagation characteristics of intrusive sediment-laden flows with applications to marine carbon dioxide removal
presentations.abstract: We are facing unprecedented global warming driven by excess atmospheric CO₂. Mitigation not only requires carbon emission reductions but also the implementation of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) strategies. Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement (OAE) is a promising CDR strategy, utilizing alkaline minerals to accelerate the ocean's natural carbon uptake. However, the efficacy of OAE depends on keeping these particles within the ocean's surface mixed layer long enough to sufficiently react with atmospheric CO₂. The release of alkaline slurries into the ocean generates "intrusive sediment-laden flows," where the hydrodynamics are governed by a complex competition between buoyancy-driven surface spreading and gravity-driven particle settling. This research utilizes two-dimensional numerical simulations to investigate these flow dynamics, specifically examining how varying particle concentrations and diameters influence the instability and dispersion of the sediment-laden flow. Results reveal that particle dynamics significantly alter the flow evolution. While buoyancy initially drives the mixture to spread across the surface, sedimentation of particles rapidly triggers Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities, manifesting as vertical plumes that transport material downward. We found that higher particle concentrations and larger diameters can accelerate this settling process, leading to one or two orders of magnitude faster effective settling speed, compared to the Stokes settling speed of an individual particle, thereby reducing the surface residence time required for carbon sequestration. Intermediate particle concentrations and diameters were found to be optimal, providing a good balance between entrained area and surface residence time of the sediment-laden flow. These findings offer critical fluid mechanics insights for optimizing OAE deployment strategies to ensure efficient CO₂ removal.

presentations.title: Hydrodynamic Responses in a Reservoir Under Extreme Hydroclimatic Variability
presentations.abstract: Understanding the spatial and temporal dynamics of reservoir systems is essential for effective water management under increasing climate variability. In semi-arid regions, reservoirs are shaped by pronounced hydroclimatic fluctuations, multi-year droughts, and high evaporation rates, which drive large water-level variations that reshape circulation, heat exchange, and stratification dynamics. Yet, the physical functioning of such highly variable systems remains poorly constrained. Here, we applied the three-dimensional Delft3D model to simulate hydrodynamic processes in a tropical semi-arid reservoir subject to extreme hydroclimatic variability. The model reproduced seasonal and diel changes in stratification and mixing, capturing strong thermal stability during the rainy season and enhanced mixing driven by wind forcing and large water-level changes during the dry period. Results show that variations in heat fluxes and water level strongly control the onset, strength, and breakdown of stratification. By explicitly resolving the response of reservoir hydrodynamics to extreme hydroclimatic forcing, this study improves understanding of semi-arid reservoirs and enhances predictive capability. The framework provides a basis for future coupling with water-quality processes and supports scenario analyses for adaptive management under increasing climate variability.

presentations.title: Mesoscale and Submesoscale Features Formed by Horizontal Density Gradients in an Ice-Covered Lake
presentations.abstract: Basin-scale rotating features have been identified multiple times in ice-covered lakes and in enclosed ocean basins such as fjords. These circulation features arise when horizontal density gradients are balanced by the Earth’s rotation (geostrophic balance). Despite repeated observations, little is known about how these gyres form, evolve, dissipate, and influence mixing and water quality. Here, we investigate the full life cycle of a basin-scale gyre in a 5-km-wide square ice-covered lake using a high-resolution numerical model. The large-eddy simulation uses 2-m horizontal and 0.2-m vertical resolution, for a total of more than 300 million grid cells, made possible by a GPU-accelerated code. Under a lateral buoyancy flux, a lake-wide gyre emerges within one month. The imposed buoyancy gradient injects potential energy into the system, which is subsequently converted into kinetic energy sustaining the circulation. Gyre energy is lost through drag beneath the ice cover and through the shedding of submesoscale features along its periphery. The simulation compares well with mooring observations from a similar ice-covered lake, indicating the model captures the key physical processes. A passive tracer released at a single point reveals that the gyre induces strongly non-uniform tracer concentrations, demonstrating that such features can generate significant spatial variability in water quality even in relatively small lakes.

presentations.title: The Mystery of the Lake Biwa Underwater Ruins: Why Haven't They Been Buried?
presentations.abstract: The underwater archaeological site off Tsuzuraozaki in Lake Biwa was discovered by fishermen about a hundred years ago and is known for its remarkable ancient artifacts. The oldest items are dated to approximately 9,000 years ago. Since the sedimentation rate in Lake Biwa is said to be about 1 mm per year, roughly 9 meters of sediment should have accumulated over the past 9,000 years. Yet these ancient artifacts remain unburied, and the reason for this has long remained unclear. From 2023 onward, we installed an ADCP on the lake bottom for two years and measured the vertical distribution of current velocity. The results revealed the presence of 24-hour internal Poincaré waves and 2–3-day internal Kelvin waves, both of which dominate during stratified periods. Our observations suggest that these strong oscillatory currents may be blowing away fine particles on the lake floor, preventing sediment from accumulating over the artifacts.

presentations.title: Physical drivers of circulation and scalar transport in a large shallow subtropical reservoir
presentations.affiliation: Facultad de Ingeniería de la Universidad de la República
presentations.abstract: The Rincón del Bonete reservoir is a large shallow subtropical reservoir in Uruguay, with a complex hydrodynamic system where large-scale circulation is influenced by the interaction between atmospheric forcing, hydraulic management, and intricate bathymetry. This study aims to characterize the circulation dynamics, transport mechanisms, thermal stratification cycles, and mixing regimes of this water body. We employed a 3D baroclinic numerical model that integrates hydrodynamic, thermal and sediment dynamics, in situ measurements and satellite image processing. Examination of the thermal structure indicates a regime sensitive to synoptic events, with spatial heterogeneity in stratification stability driven by differential heating and cooling. Density currents between a shallow area and the main channel were identified both in the observations and in the model. Shear flux was observed within a lateral constriction located in the center of the reservoir, which may act as a hydraulic control influencing mass exchange between sub-basins. Regarding scalar transport, sediment dynamics appear to be influenced both by river-flood–driven advection and, according to preliminary results, by wind-wave–induced bed shear stress in extensive shallow areas under low-water-level conditions. While fully coupled wave-sediment modeling is ongoing, this work provides insights into how the interplay between hydro-thermodynamic drivers and basin morphology helps establish the physical template regulating residence times and scalar pathways in the reservoir.

presentations.title: Predicting temperature variation in large polymictic basins: a machine learning approach
presentations.abstract: Polymictic lakes experience frequent mixing and rapid temperature fluctuations that are difficult to predict. This challenge is particularly evident in two large, shallow, and wind-driven systems: the southern basin of Lake Winnipeg and western basin of Lake Erie. Understanding temperature variability in these water bodies is important, as short-term thermal shifts could potentially cause dissolved oxygen variation and affect fish habitat. In this study, we analyzed four-year temperature data from both basins and applied a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict temperature dynamics in both basins. Both basins mix on a near-daily basis and exhibit only short, intermittent episodes of weak thermal stratification, and for ~85 % of the time, the water is well mixed with temperature difference from surface to bottom of less than 1 °C. The LSTM model effectively captured the surface thermal dynamics with RMSE of ~1 to 1.5 °C, reproducing rapid daily temperature fluctuations and short-term warming and cooling events that are typical in polymictic basins. Predicting bottom temperatures proved more challenging possibly due to occasional stratification and local turbulence near the lakebed, yet the model still captured the main trends and seasonal variations. These results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning approaches for forecasting temperature variation in polymictic systems. Improved short-term thermal predictions can support lake management and provide new methods for ecological risk assessment in highly dynamic basins.

title: Sustaining Safe Drinking Water and Healthy Aquatic Ecosystems in the Asia-Pacific (2nd AP-GLEON)

co_organizers.name: Man Xiao
co_organizers.affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Lake Science and Environment, Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences

presentations.title: Factors Affecting Cyanobacterial and Dinoflagellate Algal Blooms in Sediment Microalgae Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: The composition of the microalgae community in the sediments has an important impact on the succession of phytoplankton and the algal bloom in the surface water body. Phosphorus is one element that has shown great promise as an influential and inhibitory agent for eliminating the kinds of toxic blooms tending to destroy aquatic ecosystems' stability. In this study, sediment cores from the shallow reservior in China were investigated. Through the sequencing of 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA, cyanobacteria and dinoflagellate blooms were found to occur at an elevated frequency in the reservoirs on Jiulong River and the Three Gorges River reservoirs. The algal community structures in these reservoir sediments primarily comprised of chlorophyta, cryptophyta, dinoflagellates, and cyanobacteria. Correlation analyses indicated positive relationships between total phosphorus (TP), diatoms, cryptophyta, and cyanobacteria. However, dinoflagellates were negatively correlated with soluble active phosphorus (SRP), which indicated that cyanobacteria and dinoflagellates' proliferation are closely associated with the content and form of phosphorus. When the relationships between the RUE (resource use efficiency) approach and the cyanophyta and dinophyta community were explored, the higher proportion of cyanophyta exhibited a strong positive relationship with RUEP. The environmental variables also appeared to be closely connected with variations of cyanophya and dinophyata community compositions in co-occurrence/exclusion patterns of the whole network. Further analysis suggests that these community taxa play essential roles in the migration and transformation of the related proliferation of algae. The results of this study suggest that the sediment algae community is essential, diverse, and comparable to neighboring surface planktonic populations.

title: The Next Frontier in Aquatic Sciences: Linking Remote Sensing, Data Science, Modeling, and Open Science to Better Understand Aquatic Ecosystems

presentations.title: Toward Robust Foundation Models for Scientific Systems: An Application to Lake Sciences
