presentations.title: Delineating the response of fish size spectra to 30 years of environmental change in Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario, Canada
presentations.abstract: Fish feeding regimes are closely linked to body mass, which is shaped by ontogenetic dietary shifts, energy demands, predator–prey interactions, and metabolic scaling. These processes operate across biological levels, making body mass a valuable indicator of energy transfer within food webs. This study examined how fish size spectra have responded to three decades of environmental change in Hamilton Harbour, Lake Ontario. Segmented regression models quantified relationships between log-transformed body mass and log frequency of occurrence, yielding statistical indices capturing interannual variation across species, trophic guilds, and the broader fish community. Planktivores and invertivores comprised more than half of total abundance, while piscivores consistently accounted for less than 20%, indicative of a pyramid-shaped food web. The dominant planktivore, alewife, showed a long-term decline, marked by fewer individuals at the modal body size and a widening body-size distribution. Brown bullhead and common carp exhibited a shift toward fewer but larger individuals, alongside increases in smaller size classes below the modal size. Invertivores such as pumpkinseed, round goby, and white perch also displayed declining abundance, with modal body size shifting downward. Among piscivores, walleye trended toward larger body sizes and increasingly left-skewed distributions, potentially reflecting size-selective mortality or growth constraints. Overall, body-size patterns and abundance trends highlight persistent ecological impairment and continued dominance by non-native, pollution-tolerant species in Hamilton Harbour.

presentations.title: CONSTRUCTING PLANKTONIC FOOD WEB INTERACTIONS ASSOCIATED WITH OYSTER REEF RESTORATION EFFORTS
presentations.abstract: Oyster reef restoration is increasingly recognized as a strategy to enhance coastal ecosystem resilience, yet the food web dynamics that underpin oyster reefs remain unresolved. In the Hampton River, Virginia—a tributary of the Chesapeake Bay where large-scale oyster reef restoration is underway, understanding plankton diversity associated with these efforts is essential as plankton form the base of trophic networks, regulate energy flow and biogeochemical cycling. We use 18S rRNA metabarcoding to characterize planktonic food web structure associated with a natural oyster reef and a nearby control site lacking reef structure during winter and spring. Our analyses reveal diverse plankton assemblages, including primary producers Diatomea, Dinoflagellata, and Cryptophyceae that likely contribute to reef-associated primary production and energy input. Microzooplankton grazers, including Ciliophora, Cercozoa, and Foraminifera, suggest active microbial grazing pathways and trophic transfer to higher consumers, whereas Copepoda indicates a key link between microbial food webs and metazoan consumers. We also detected parasitic protists such as Apicomplexa, which may influence host population dynamics, as well as decomposers, Ascomycota and Peronosporomycetes that likely contribute to organic matter turnover and nutrient regeneration. Our findings provide insight into the hidden complexity of planktonic food webs associated with oyster reefs and establishes a molecular baseline to track how restoration-driven changes in oyster abundance and habitat structure influence trophic dynamics and ecosystem health.

name: Drying Waters
lead_organizer: Rachel Stubbington, Nottingham Trent University
co_organizers: Ryan Burrows, University of Melbourne and Melbourne Water
Lena Fehlinger, GEA, Universitat de Vic UVic-UCC
Lenka Kuglerová, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
description: Temporary aquatic ecosystems—which sometimes dry out—are widespread and diverse in Earth's critical zone, and their extent is increasing in both space and time due to climate change and other human pressures.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF EXPERIMENTAL STREAM BED DRYING ON DECOMPOSITION AND CHLOROPHYLL-a ACCRUAL IN BOREAL HEADWATER STREAM
presentations.abstract: Boreal headwater streams face increasingly frequent and intense droughts because of climate change. I investigated key ecological functions along two boreal headwater streams under varying hydrological years and an experimental drought, and the importance of spatial complexity from streambed drying patterns. 20 sampling stations spread over two 1-km reaches in two streams in the Krycklan Catchment Study (northern Sweden). For 3 years (2023-2025), I collected data on leaf litter and cotton strip decomposition, chlorophyll-a accrual and macroinvertebrate communities. In 2025, a severe 2-week drought was imposed on one stream. Initial results show high flows and drought affect decomposition rates and chlorophyll-a accrual, with considerable spatial variability.

presentations.title: STABILITY OF COMMUNITY AND ECOSYSTEM PROCESSES IN SUBTROPICAL RURAL PONDS AFTER A MAJOR DROUGHT
presentations.abstract: This study evaluated how an extreme drought affected the ecological stability of biotic communities and ecosystem processes in 30 rural artificial ponds in Uruguay subjected to two contrasting land-use intensities (extensive vs. intensive livestock grazing). We sampled before and after a major drought in 2022-23. We examined shifts in water level and physico-chemical characteristics propagating through trophic webs, focusing on phytoplankton, zooplankton, plants, and fish assemblages, plus nutrient cycling and organic matter processing. Agricultural intensification modulates drought effects, affecting both community and ecosystem stability.

presentations.title: Drought, drying and human pressure impacts on the invertebrate communities of England's groundwater-fed rivers.
presentations.abstract: We used invertebrate time series (8–30-year) from groundwater-fed river sites in England, including temporary reaches. Drought characteristics and human pressures interact to influence invertebrate community responses. Increasing spatial extent of drying reduced sensitive taxa and community-wide recovery. Water abstraction, increased water temperature and poor water quality accentuated declines in pollution-sensitive taxa during drought and slowed recovery, particularly as drought severity increased. Communities recovered on average within 1-3 years after 83% of droughts, but those at 47% of sites experienced ≥1 long-term, drought-related compositional shift.

presentations.title: CITIZEN SCIENCE MONITORING OF DRYING TEMPORARY WETLANDS: INSIGHTS FROM FRESHWATER WATCH IN UGANDA AND KENYA
presentations.affiliation: Earthwatch / African Center for Aquatic Resaerch and Education
presentations.abstract: Building on the FreshWater Watch citizen science program, this study mobilized over 500 community volunteers in Uganda and Kenya to collect water quality samples in seasonal ponds, streams, and wetlands using simple kits for phosphate, nitrate, turbidity. Between 2023-2025 volunteers generated ~2500 measurements. Transitions to low water level and drying are associated with marked nutrient enrichment, visible algal blooms, and loss of perceived water safety, raising One Health concerns. Community observations combined with satellite indicators identified hotspots where drying, land use pressure, and high nutrient loads coincide.

presentations.title: The decline of nitrogen retention across the United States due to the loss of vulnerable wetlands under changing Clean Water Act protections
presentations.abstract: Ephemeral and intermittent wetlands provide disproportionately high nitrogen removal despite their small size. Recent Clean Water Act interpretation changes will remove federal protections. We simulated post-Sackett rollbacks across 2,000+ watersheds in the conterminous US using multi-decadal remote sensing (1985–2024) and a coupled hydrologic-biogeochemical model. Loss of small, seasonally drying wetlands significantly reduces landscape nitrogen retention. Watersheds with abundant temporary wetlands are especially sensitive. Prairie Pothole Region and Southern Coastal Plain show most significant projected declines.

presentations.title: PLANTS AS INDICATORS OF NUTRIENT PRESSURES IN DRY TEMPORARY STREAMS
presentations.abstract: Temporary streams in England are impacted by nutrient enrichment. Aquatic plants are routinely used to monitor nutrient pressures during wet phases, but die back during dry phases. We used dry-phase plant communities (persisting aquatic plus colonizing terrestrial taxa) to assess nutrient pressures across English temporary streams. We developed metrics for N, P and total nutrient pressures across alkalinity, altitude and shade gradients. Identified two metrics with strong responses across ~50 streams, two years and three surveyors: Ellenberg-N-based mean nutrient-tolerance score and a cover-weighted version.

name: Drying Waters (Posters)
lead_organizer: Rachel Stubbington, Nottingham Trent University
co_organizers: Ryan Burrows, University of Melbourne and Melbourne Water
Lena Fehlinger, GEA, Universitat de Vic UVic-UCC
Lenka Kuglerová, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
description: Temporary aquatic ecosystems—which sometimes dry out—are widespread and diverse in Earth's critical zone, and their extent is increasing in both space and time due to climate change and other human pressures.

presentations.title: Impact of regional hydrology on prairie pothole wetlands' chemistry, carbon cycling, and metabolism
presentations.abstract: The Prairie Pothole Region (PPR) is characterized by millions of shallow ponds providing carbon sequestration, nutrient remediation, and water storage. We examine latitudinal differences in hydrology, biogeochemistry, and metabolism of PPR wetlands in Alberta. Higher elevation wetlands in southern Alberta (more arid, shorter wetted periods) are more inflow-dominated. Longer evapoconcentration causes higher salinity and dissolved carbon in central/northern wetlands. Higher elevation wetlands are net autotrophic with productivity pulses; lower elevation are net heterotrophic.

presentations.title: EXPLORING IMPACTS OF RESTORATION ON AQUATIC EMISSIONS IN A PRAIRIE POTHOLE WETLAND
presentations.abstract: Hydrologic restoration of wetlands is common in the prairie pothole region. We explored carbon cycling and GHG production in Stirling Lake, Alberta — restored via once-annual pulse from an irrigation canal. Pre-flooding: CO2 dominated, negligible methane. Post-flooding: dominance varied by location and season. Methane was highest at high plant biomass sites and increased with seasonal warming. Average emissions were not anomalous compared to regional wetland averages.

presentations.title: HOW DO GENOMES OF TARDIGRADES WITH DIFFERENT DORMANCY STRATEGIES COMPARE?
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at El Paso
presentations.abstract: Tardigrades have evolved cryptobiosis and encystment dormancy. We sequenced the genome of an encysting tardigrade species Pseudobiotus kathmanae from the Chihuahuan Desert. Over 22,500 proteins identified with BRAKER3 and Omicsbox. Compared with six cryptobiotic tardigrade species using OrthoVenn3, we found 3,077 shared clusters; P. kathmanae had 1,322 unique clusters. Many proteins may play roles in desiccation response (UGT74E2) or DNA damage response (ADPRS).

name: Invasive Bivalves (Posters)
lead_organizer: Bastiaan Ibelings, University of Geneva
description: Molluscs are the second largest group of animals, and in freshwaters include some of the most threatened and most invasive species. Particularly Dreissena rostriformis bugensis and D. polymorpha have established themselves as important drivers of change.

presentations.title: SIZE MATTERS: LAKE MORPHOMETRY DETERMINES DREISSENA ECOSYSTEM IMPACTS
presentations.abstract: We assemble high-resolution datasets spanning Secchi depth, P, chlorophyll, phytoplankton/zooplankton biomass over five decades and 18 lakes invaded by dreissenids. In polymictic lakes impacts manifest earlier than in stratified lakes. Zebra-invaded lakes usually show partial recovery, interrupted by secondary quagga invasion. In Great Lakes, no ecosystem recovery observed even after 30 years. Lake size more important than other parameters; small-lake results cannot be directly applied to Great Lakes.

presentations.title: Quagga mussel colonisation in Lake Geneva
presentations.abstract: Quagga mussel was first detected in Lake Geneva in 2015. Standardised surveys 2022 and 2024 across 72 sites between 10-309 m depth. Quagga overwhelmingly dominated bivalve community: 98.7% of individuals 2022, 100% in 2024. Densities and biomass peaked between 10-30 m, declined sharply below 50 m, zero below 250 m. Shell lengths increased across all depths, indicating population maturation. 2025 littoral survey at 2 and 6 m confirmed dominance. Population well established, strongly influenced by depth and lake morphometry, likely still expanding.

presentations.title: 100 YEARS OF BENTHOS MONITORING ON LAKE SIMCOE: MULTI-STRESSOR INFLUENCES OF CLIMATE CHANGE, NUTRIENTS, AND INVASIVE DREISSENID MUSSELS
presentations.abstract: In 1926, Donald Rawson undertook one of the first benthos studies in Canada on Lake Simcoe. Using Rawson's studies as baseline, we followed changes: rise/fall of zebra mussels, current dominance by quagga mussels, invasion of deepwater (>20 m) habitats. Quagga mussels redirect energy from nearshore to profundal benthic environment. Consequences of 'deepwater shunt' remain to be understood.

name: Bridging the Fresh/Salty Divide (Posters)
lead_organizer: Jemma Fadum, Carnegie Institution for Science
co_organizers: Laura Falkenberg, University of South Australia
description: While the fields of limnology and oceanography are closely related, individuals working in inland and marine ecosystems rarely find themselves in conversation. We invite submissions across the Fresh/Salty divide.

presentations.title: IMPROVING FRESHWATER ALKALINITY MEASUREMENTS IN THE LAURENTIAN GREAT LAKES
presentations.abstract: Freshwater systems lack standardized alkalinity approaches. Surface water from western Lake Erie split into filtered/unfiltered, stored at 4°C, measured weekly for 6 weeks then monthly for 6 months. First 2 months: <1% Alk variation. Filtered samples consistently ~30 µmol kg-1 higher than unfiltered. Implications for model-derived carbonate parameters.

presentations.title: GREENHOUSE GAS PRODUCTION FROM MINERALIZATION OF RIVERINE ORGANIC MATTER UNDER FRESHWATER VS. MARINE CONDITIONS
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research - UFZ
presentations.abstract: Microcosm experiment with POM (algae, river sediment) added to sediment cores from freshwater weir and marine river mouth. CH4 dominant in freshwater after POM addition (3-5x higher than control); CO2 dominated under marine conditions. Total GHG flux from freshwater up to 14x higher despite slightly lower sediment OM content. Construction of impoundments in estuaries can increase GHG emissions.

presentations.title: Seawater-Groundwater Mixing Dynamics in a Groundwater-fed Estuary: Ría Celestún, Yucatán, Mexico
presentations.abstract: Ría Celestún groundwater-fed estuary. Transect and individual sample data from May 2024, December 2024, March 2025, plus ~24-hour cycle transducer data. Saline in summer, fresher in winter, intermediate in spring. Future work uses field data to train a model and predict overall temporal behavior.

presentations.title: HOW DOES SALINITY AFFECT THE PHOTOCHEMISTRY OF DISSOLVED ORGANIC MATTER: PRELIMINARY RESULTS
presentations.abstract: Sampled nearshore brown water and open lake clear water from Lake Superior. Sterile filtered aliquots amended with DOC-free sea salt (salinities 0, 5, 17, 35) irradiated. Nearshore samples showed increases in photobleaching with increased salt content; greater preferential loss of aromatic DOC. Clear water samples showed similar story at salinity 35. EEMS shows larger fluorescence losses in salty samples.

presentations.title: CHARACTERIZING ESTUARINE ZOOPLANKTON DYNAMICS IN CONNECTION TO A WARMING GULF OF MAINE
presentations.abstract: Weekly sampling Saco Bay, GoM. 2024-2025 time series. Zooplankton biovolume highest in summer (Evadne, Eurytemora 2024; Podon, Evadne 2025). Secondary smaller mid-fall peak with copepod nauplii in 2024. Winter 2025: high copepod nauplii and Pseudocalanus. Higher Secchi and warmer temperature correlated with increased diversity.

presentations.title: DETERMINING SEASONAL AND LONG-TERM SHIFTS IN COASTAL PHYTOPLANKTON ABUNDANCE AND BIOGEOCHEMISTRY IN CONNECTION TO A WARMING GULF OF MAINE
presentations.abstract: Weekly phytoplankton time series at mouth of Saco River Estuary since April 2024 with biogeochemical observations since 2001. Lowest biomass in winter; spring bloom; secondary fall peak. Diatoms dominated spring; mixed community summer/fall partly dinoflagellates. Higher water temperature in summer drove community shifts.

presentations.title: Transitions to and from Anoxia in a complex Estuary: a flickering switch in the Anthropocene
presentations.abstract: Examined deep and shallow basins in the Bras d'Or Lake, Cape Breton (Nova Scotia). Variety of oxic conditions reveal complex cause-and-effect: water temperature, salinity, exchange turnover, estuarine circulation, submarine groundwater discharge, ice cover, nutrients, OM inputs, extreme weather. Anthropogenic changes (aquaculture, forestry) play significant roles.

name: High Arctic Limnology (Posters)
lead_organizer: Frédéric Bouchard, Université de Sherbrooke
co_organizers: Isabelle Laurion, Institut national de la recherche scientifique
description: As climate change accelerates across the circumpolar North, High Arctic limnoscapes are emerging as key sentinel environments.

presentations.title: Contrasting permafrost degradation trajectories alter carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus redistribution in the Yellow River Source Area of Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
presentations.affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Compared thermokarst lakes and adjacent terrestrial habitats on Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Lake sediments had lower C content/ratios; higher P content. Sediment stocks driven by nutrient availability, MAP, water chemistry. Terrestrial plants had higher tissue C/N; aquatic plants achieved greater biomass and nutrient densities, particularly P. P stock low in terrestrial; rich in thermokarst lakes.

presentations.title: LIGHT-DRIVEN AND BIOTIC CONTROLS ON VOC PRODUCTION IN POLYGONAL ICE-WEDGE PONDS
presentations.affiliation: Institut National de la Recherche Scientifique
presentations.abstract: Investigating VOC production in active thermokarst vs stabilized ponds on Bylot Island. Microcosm experiments isolating pelagic and benthic biota under light/dark conditions. Predict higher VOC under light, shifts in actively eroding ponds. Volatilome shifts with darkness reflecting heterotrophic VOC production.

presentations.title: THERMOKARST LAKE DYNAMICS IN A RAPIDLY CHANGING HIGH ARCTIC LIMNOSCAPE
presentations.abstract: Multi-temporal high-resolution satellite imagery 2010-2023, NDWI, DSAS shoreline displacement, field surveys near Iqaluktuuttiaq (Cambridge Bay). Net movements -103 m to +81 m. Newly formed thermokarst ponds shallow, expanded rapidly. Stable isotopes show stronger evaporative enrichment in isolated ponds.

presentations.title: USE OF WATERSHED CLASSIFICATION TO INFORM COMMUNITY-BASED RIVER MONITORING IN NUNATSIAVUT
presentations.affiliation: Memorial University of Newfoundland and Labrador
presentations.abstract: Coastal ecosystems in Nunatsiavut/eastern Arctic. Identified watershed attributes; collaborated with community members for locally informed classification. Cluster analysis classifies coastal watersheds. Brings together Inuit Knowledge and scientific knowledge.

name: Lipid Biomarker Approaches (Posters)
lead_organizer: Benjamin Gwinneth, Université de Montréal
description: Lake sediments preserve an extraordinary archive of environmental change. Among the most rapidly advancing tools for accessing these archives are lipid biomarkers.

presentations.title: Evidence for highly variable land use but a stable climate in the southwest Maya lowlands
presentations.abstract: Lake sediment core from Laguna Itzan, cenote adjacent to ancient Maya population centre. Faecal stanols (population), PAHs (biomass burning), δ13C and δ2H of n-alkanes. Three periods of significant population decline associated with precipitation change (3300-2900, 1860-1670, 1220-1050 cal yr BP). Transition from Preclassic intense fire/C4 agriculture to Classic dense populations and reduced fire use. No evidence of extreme drought in δ2H.

name: Controlling Algal Blooms (Posters)
lead_organizer: Alan Wilson, Auburn University
co_organizers: H. Dail Laughinghouse, University of Florida
description: Algal blooms in freshwater and marine systems are often dominated by toxigenic cyanobacteria or dinoflagellates. This session brings together scientists, engineers, and water resource managers.

presentations.title: CYAN AND BEYOND: EXPLORING REMOTE SENSING AS A TOOL FOR HAB MANAGEMENT AND RESPONSE FOR STATE AGENCIES
presentations.abstract: Tested EPA CyAN data 2016-2024 in 29 Arkansas lakes. Cluster analysis: 18 rarely had blooms, 6 sometimes, 5 consistently seasonal. Lakes situated on gradients of elevation, area, depth, and increasing nutrient trends. Developed regressions of CyAN values vs phytoplankton abundance for uncertainty quantification. Spatial resolution coarse (300x300m); new satellites can increase resolution by orders of magnitude.

presentations.title: ASSESSING THE EFFICACY OF A PEROXIDE-BASED ALGAECIDE AGAINST A CYANOBACTERIAL COMMUNITY DOMINATED BY TOXIGENIC, DIAZOTROPHIC R. RACIBORSKII AND U. OVALISPORUM
presentations.affiliation: University of North Carolina--Chapel Hill Institute of Marine Sciences
presentations.abstract: Lake Mattamuskeet (NC) hyper-eutrophic, dominated by R. raciborskii and U. ovalisporum. Highest US cylindrospermopsin concentrations (6.6 µg/L). Lake Guard Oxy (LGO) at 0, 9, 18, 36 mg/L. H2O2 undetectable after 2 days. Cyanobacterial biomass declined sharply within 12 hours. Eukaryotes increased; cyanobacteria suppressed during 6-day Cubitainer experiment but rebounded by day 16 in mesocosms.

presentations.title: BEYOND THE BLOOM: LINKING SPATIAL DRIVERS AND SOCIAL PERCEPTIONS OF CYANOBACTERIA RISK IN LAKE WINNIPESAUKEE
presentations.affiliation: University of North Carolina Chapel Hill
presentations.abstract: GIS-based spatial analysis of land use, watershed characteristics, climate change and shoreline development relating to cyanobacteria bloom distribution in Lake Winnipesaukee. Long-term climate data (ice-in/out trends). Anthropologically informed textual analysis of local news, community reports for risk perception.

name: Dam Removals/Renewals
lead_organizer: Jennifer Lento, Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
co_organizers: Philip Harrison, Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
description: Flow alteration by dams remains one of the largest threats to freshwater ecosystem health.

presentations.title: Hypolimnial releases from large dams alter thermal regimes and downstream ecosystems and the need for management solutions
presentations.abstract: Severn River, Australia, downstream of Pindari Dam. Cold water pollution Spring through Autumn, detectable up to 150 km downstream. Up to 13°C colder than reference sites in summer. Changes in nutrients and phytoplankton observed. Plans for amelioration through reservoir management.

presentations.title: ALTERATION OF HYDROLOGICAL, THERMAL AND METABOLIC REGIMES BY HYDROPOWER DAMS IN MOUNTAIN STREAMS
presentations.abstract: Picos de Europa National Park (Northern Spain). Flow, water temperature and river metabolism continuously monitored 2023-2024 in 13 sections (control-impact design). Significant differences in temperature, flow and metabolism. Magnitude/direction varied highlighting uniqueness of each hydropower development.

presentations.title: QUANTIFYING STRUCTURAL AND TROPHIC RESPONSE TO HYDROPOWER OPERATIONS THROUGH STABLE ISOTOPES IN A LARGE RIVER IN ATLANTIC CANADA
presentations.abstract: Wolastoq, large river in Atlantic Canada. Sites upstream/downstream of hydropower dams. Stable isotopes (C, N, H) for aquatic community. Overall N enrichment and higher niche widths downstream of hydropower dams demonstrating community and resource shifts in areas with increased flow variation.

presentations.title: QUANTIFYING THE INTANGIBLE: LINKING FLOW VARIABILITY AND WELL-BEING TO WATER GOVERNANCE IN A LARGE REGULATED RIVER
presentations.affiliation: Environment and Climate Change Canada @ Canadian Rivers Institute, University of New Brunswick
presentations.abstract: DPSIR-FCM framework in regulated, transboundary Wolastoq. 39 socio-ecological nodes with 941 connections. 'Flow variability' (environmental stressor) and 'peace and tranquility' (social-cultural-spiritual state) critical bridges. Feedback loop where well-being promotes environmental stewardship.

presentations.title: DAM MANAGEMENT CAN AMPLIFY OR OFFSET CLIMATE-DRIVEN DECLINES IN CUTTHROAT TROUT PRODUCTION
presentations.abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian stock-recruitment model for 13 populations of Yellowstone Cutthroat Trout in Upper Snake River, WY. Strongest driver: interaction between timing of natural and managed peak spring flows; matched peaks reduce productivity, mismatched extend flood pulse. Water management can amplify or offset climate-driven declines.

presentations.title: USING A BIOECONOMIC MODEL TO INFORM STREAMFLOW MANAGEMENT FOR TROUT PRODUCTION AND ANGLING ECONOMIES
presentations.abstract: Snake River, WY. Anglers willing to pay $356 for higher chance of catching Cutthroat Trout. Bioeconomic model: Ricker stock-recruitment model + multinomial logit model of angler preferences. Increased managed summer mean flow benefits anglers and angling industry.

name: Dam Removals/Renewals (Posters)
lead_organizer: Jennifer Lento, Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
co_organizers: Philip Harrison, Canadian Rivers Institute and University of New Brunswick
description: Flow alteration by dams remains one of the largest threats to freshwater ecosystem health.

presentations.title: WERE THE LOG DRIVERS LIKE BEAVERS? ECOLOGICAL AND HYDROLOGICAL LEGACY OF SMALL DAMS IN A NATIONAL PARK
presentations.abstract: 28 log-driving and beaver dams in La Mauricie National Park. Log-driving dams older and more permeable but structural/hydrological differences small. Wetland characteristics varied by dam type, with Fraxinus nigra associated with log-driving dams.

presentations.title: Cumulative impacts of hydropower and multiple stressors on fish in riverine ecosystems
presentations.abstract: PRISMA-based review of HP-stressor interactions on freshwater fish. Combined effects of hydropower and stressors result in additive, synergistic, or antagonistic impacts. Climate change and agriculture identified as key drivers. Research unevenly distributed globally.

name: Global Ocean Biodiversity Atlas (Posters)
lead_organizer: Peter Busumprah, Ocean Rock Base
co_organizers: Olusola Adeoye, Natures Cares Resources Centre
Opoku Mensah Abrampah, Africa Ocean Alliance
description: This session explores innovative approaches to developing and enhancing the Global Ocean Biodiversity Atlas.

presentations.title: Meeting Mediterranean conservation targets through systematic conservation planning
presentations.abstract: Systematic conservation planning (SCP) generated 5 scenarios for MPAs in Balearic Sea. Protecting 30% (10% no-take, 20% demersal no-take) through 'Equitable' scenario costs 13% of annual fishing revenue. Regionally informed SCP key for accommodating human uses and biodiversity conservation.

presentations.title: Empowering Women: Community-Led Biodiversity Practices for a Sustainable Ocean Economy
presentations.abstract: Innovative women-led community techniques for enhancing marine biodiversity. Case studies of women's roles in marine resource conservation. Empowering women through education, leadership opportunities. Scalable solutions for ocean economy frameworks.

presentations.title: Jellyfish population dynamics studies as an asset to anticipate their potential response to global warming
presentations.affiliation: Specialized Research Station for Marine Ecosystems of IRAD / University of Douala
presentations.abstract: Sea surface temperature is one of the main drivers of Chimearus palmatus temporal abundance and size distribution along Kribi-Cameroon coastal region. Population dynamics studies useful tool to predict species response under future climate change.

presentations.title: Reinforcing International Maritime Law for Sustainable Ocean Biodiversity Conservation
presentations.abstract: Examines current legal landscape (UNCLOS), gaps and challenges in implementing sustainable practices. Advocates enhanced legal regime emphasizing ecosystem-based management, stricter regulations, equitable resource sharing. Innovative legal mechanisms: MPAs, cross-border cooperation, adaptive governance.

presentations.title: Challenges to assess the pelagic biodiversity and lifestyles in deep and ultra deep-water realms of the ocean
presentations.abstract: Deep-water realm largest ecosystem on earth, least known biodiversity. Reviews current sampling technology and methodologies for ultra-deep (>5000 m) hadal realms. Water pumps, in-situ fixation, autonomous landers, bait traps, eDNA sampling.

presentations.title: Ocean Accounting: A Critical Framework for Sustainable Fisheries and Biodiversity Conservation
presentations.abstract: Ocean accounting integrates economic, ecological, and social data for sustainable fisheries management and biodiversity preservation. Identifies critical areas for intervention and monitors progress towards sustainability goals.

name: Nitrogen Cycling (Posters)
lead_organizer: Lin Zhang, Texas A and M University Corpus Christi
co_organizers: Mark Altabet, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth
Pat Glibert, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science
Annie Bourbonnais, University of South Carolina
Darcy Perin, University of South Carolina
description: Aquatic ecosystems are driven by intricate nitrogen (N) cycling processes.

presentations.title: THE ROLE OF SUBMARINE GROUNDWATER DISCHARGE IN COASTAL NITROGEN LOSS PROCESSES
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Oceanology Polish Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: SGD-impacted vs non-impacted sites in Puck Bay (southern Baltic Sea). Sediment incubations with 15NO3-, 15NH4+. Denitrification rates higher than anammox. SGD-impacted sites have increased N removal potential.

presentations.title: INTERNAL NUTRIENT LOADING IN EUTROPHIC LAKES: SEDIMENT P FLUXES AND BIOAVAILABLE N RELEASE VS. REMOVAL PROCESSES
presentations.abstract: Two mid-sized eutrophic shallow lakes in Estonia. Denitrification dominant N removal pathway, stimulated by 15N-nitrate. DNRA detected; no anammox. N removal lower than NH4+urea effluxes. External N controls needed in addition to P.

presentations.title: LINKING MICROBIAL ACTIVITY TO NITROUS OXIDE EMISSIONS IN WETLAND ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Restored effluent treatment wetland in Alberta. Spatial variability in N2O concentrations and N2:N2O ratios. Sites shifted between sources/sinks. Anammox additional N2 source near effluent input even with oxygen. N2O production/consumption spatially decoupled.

presentations.title: Amino Acids and Dissolved Nitrogen Species: Concentration and Isotopic Patterns in Phytoplankton and Culture Media Across Growth Phases
presentations.affiliation: Texas A and M University Corpus Christi
presentations.abstract: 10 phytoplankton species across 6 taxonomic groups under controlled conditions. AA molar ratios consistent across growth phases; total proteaceous AA increased during stationary. β values (δ15N-Glu - δ15N-Phe) stable across taxa, supporting trophic position estimates.

presentations.title: TESTING MODIFICATIONS TO DIEL N2 FLUX MODELS ACROSS EXPERIMENTAL N:P GRADIENTS TO IMPROVE SIMULTANEOUS QUANTIFICATION OF DENITRIFICATION AND N2 FIXATION IN RIVERS
presentations.abstract: 6 experimental streams with N:P treatments 2:1, 17:1, 200:1. 30-hour N2, O2, Ar concentrations; 15NO3 and 15N2 tracer assays. N2 flux models highly sensitive to parameters and priors.

presentations.title: Investigating the role of estuarine restoration on sedimentary nitrogen cycling and nitrous oxide production in Elkhorn Slough, CA
presentations.abstract: Three marsh locations in Elkhorn Slough including restored wetland. 15N-labeled whole-core incubations. Yampah Marsh highest denitrification (230.6 µmol N/m2/h), Hester (restored) 83.7, North 11.8.

presentations.title: Unraveling Nitrogen Cycling in the 'Forgotten Sea': Cyanobacteria and Anthropogenic Impacts in the Persian/Arabian Gulf
presentations.abstract: PAG biogeochemistry. Multidisciplinary survey indicates ammonium dominant N form, microbial remineralization key driver. High Trichodesmium abundance suggests N fixation by cyanobacteria. No nutrient accumulation from anthropogenic inputs; high recycling rates.

presentations.title: WHERE DID ALL THE NITRATE GO? ISOTOPIC EVIDENCE FOR THE FATE OF NITRATE IN TWO WHOLE LAKE NUTRIENT ADDITION EXPERIMENTS AT THE EXPERIMENTAL LAKES AREA, CANADA
presentations.abstract: Nitrate and P added weekly to 2 lakes (polymictic, dimictic). Stable isotopes of nitrate followed from ice-off to fall overturn. 15N/14N and 18O/16O increased in residual nitrate; 15N/14N also increased in POM and DOM.

presentations.title: Tracking particulate organic matter source composition during pre and post freshwater influence in the northern oligotrophic water of Bay of Bengal
presentations.abstract: BoB study 20-17.5°N, July 2025 strong surface freshening (~24 PSU). δ13C-POM and δ15N-POM. SIAR model statistics to compare pre/during/post-freshening with literature endmember values.

name: Stoichiometry Tea
lead_organizer: Isabelle Andersen, Miami University
description: Ecological stoichiometry bridges physiology, community ecology, and biogeochemistry.

presentations.title: Drawing lines between nutrients, eDNA, and watershed dynamics to understand seasonal cyanobacteria blooms in Damariscotta Lake
presentations.abstract: Damariscotta Lake (Maine) experiences three seasonal blooms: curly Dolichospermum early summer, Planktothrix late summer, straight Dolichospermum early fall. Integrates taxon-specific eDNA, dissolved nutrients, physical measurements 2023-2025.

presentations.title: THE EFFECT OF WATER CALCIUM CONCENTRATION ON DAPHNIA SURVIVAL, GROWTH, REPRODUCTION, AND CALCIUM CONTENT OF EPHIPPIA
presentations.abstract: D. pulex response to 0.3-30 mg/L calcium. Strong survival effect — few survived at 0.3 mg/L. Neonates increased from <10 to >90 per individual with Ca. Maximum at 15 mg Ca/L. Juvenile growth less Ca-dependent. Calcium content of ephippia could reconstruct past lake calcium.

presentations.title: SYNERGISTIC EFFECTS OF NUTRIENT ENRICHMENT AND TEMPERATURE ON PHYTOPLANKTON ELEMENTAL STOICHIOMETRY IN A SHALLOW LAKE OF SUBTROPICAL CHINA
presentations.abstract: Lake Yilong, subtropical eutrophic shallow lake. Nitrogen enrichment increased cellular N 24%, lowered C:N. Elevated TN and warming reduced phytoplankton P 44%. Synergy elevated community C:P, N:P. Species composition shifted to cyanobacteria with high C:P, N:P along rising temperature/nutrient gradients.

presentations.title: Monthly variation in seston and zooplankton stoichiometry in two eutrophic reservoirs
presentations.abstract: Two Nebraska reservoirs (Holmes Lake, Yankee Hill). Daphniid stoichiometry (C:P 176±117) more variable than copepods (107±46). Copepods dominated spring (98-93%); branchiopods dominated late summer (74-75%).

presentations.title: TO WHAT EXTENT IS NUTRIENT RECYCLING INCOMPLETE IN AQUATIC ECOSYSTEMS?
presentations.abstract: Closed Ecological Systems with algae and Daphnia. Despite assumption of complete recycling, sediments accumulate and dissolved/particulate organics are exported. Aquatic communities may be Meta-Ecosystems with inputs/outputs rather than complete in themselves.

presentations.title: TEMPERATURE AND NUTRIENT GRADIENTS REVEAL DISTINCT STOICHIOMETRIC RESPONSES IN CARNIVORES AND DETRITIVORES
presentations.abstract: 2,800 km latitudinal gradient in Brazil, freshwater macroinvertebrates from tank bromeliads. Carnivores: %P increased with warmer temps; declining variability, contracted niche. Detritivores: algal N:P linked to higher %C and %N; expanded niche volumes.

name: Stoichiometry Tea
lead_organizer: Isabelle Andersen, Miami University
description: Ecological stoichiometry bridges physiology, community ecology, and biogeochemistry.

presentations.title: Linking Functional Responses and Effects with Stoichiometric Traits
presentations.abstract: Multidimensional analytical and visual stoichiometric diversity framework linking organismal responses to and effects on environmental change using stoichiometric traits (acquisition, assimilation, allocation, excretion). New applications to study functional responses to urbanization in benthic invertebrates.

presentations.title: Biogeochemical characteristics of summer snow in western U.S.A. mountain ranges
presentations.abstract: 100 snow fields in two mountain regions. Molar TN:TP in summer snow remarkably close to Redfield (16.8 ± 1SE). Particulate N:P 13.8 and 23.0. No response to N or P enrichment. Winter snow TN:TP 46.5. Redfield ratio at ecosystem level set by snow algae.

presentations.title: UNPACKING DRIVERS OF HETEROTROPHIC N2 FIXATION ACROSS AQUATIC REDOX GRADIENTS: A MATHEMATICAL MODEL WITH BIOENERGETIC AND STOICHIOMETRIC CONSTRAINTS
presentations.abstract: Generalized chemostat model for free-living heterotrophic diazotrophs. Energy acquisition and respiratory efficiency are major controls on N2 fixation. Predicted N2 fixation under both N-limiting and N-replete conditions. Under eutrophic energy-rich C source: rates on par with field N-limitation observations.

presentations.title: CASTING A WIDE ELEMENTAL NET: STUDYING THE STOICHIOMETRICAL DISTRIBUTION OF SEVERAL CHEMICAL ELEMENTS IN LAKE SAINT-PIERRE, QUEBEC
presentations.abstract: 30+ elements in Lake Saint-Pierre using Vallisneria americana as bioindicator. Field sampling, remote sensing, lab analyses, spatial modelling. Reveals unique/sensitive ecological zones, advances nutrient cycling understanding.

presentations.title: DEPTH AND SEASON SHAPE THE ELEMENTAL FINGERPRINT OF LAKE SESTON
presentations.abstract: Dimictic eutrophic temperate lake, weekly seston ionome at 1m intervals 0-9m, April-October 2024. Pre-stratification: enriched in Fe, Al, Mn. Late September: shifted to Ca and Sr.

presentations.title: Pairing Molecular Tools with C:N Stoichiometry in Lake Erie Tributaries
presentations.abstract: Sturgeon Creek (Ontario), one of the most nutrient-impacted in Ontario. High-frequency sampling 2024-2025: water chemistry, dissolved metals, dual nitrate isotopes, 16S rRNA, qPCR. Differentiates nutrient hotspots.

presentations.title: SILICON STOICHIOMETRY OF NEARSHORE BENTHIC ALGAE IN THE GREAT LAKES
presentations.abstract: Cladophora and diatom epiphytes from 8 nearshore sites across Great Lakes 2020-2025. Si content 0.3-15% dry mass (mean 5%); not strongly correlated with C, N, P. Si content decreased through summer.

presentations.title: JOINT EFFECTS OF FISH KAIROMONE AND PHOSPHORUS LIMITATION ON POPULATION DYNAMICS OF DAPHNIA PULEX
presentations.abstract: Daphnia pulex 30-day microcosms with different P supply and kairomone presence. High P: exponential growth; low P: slower growth. Kairomones shifted maximum population earlier. Combined P-limitation+kairomone greatly limited population growth.

presentations.title: VARIABLE STOICHIOMETRY OF ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES IN THE KAWARTHA HIGHLANDS
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton community elemental content across Kawartha Highland lakes. C:N:P differs among lakes from changes in taxonomic composition. Likely influences nutrient cycling.

presentations.title: STOICHIOMETRIC INSIGHTS FROM THE AQUATIC NITROGEN FIXATION RESEARCH COORDINATION NETWORK
presentations.abstract: 3 main products: math model of phototrophic diazotrophs with nitrogenase as cellular pool, math model of organoheterotrophic diazotrophs, synthesis on chemoautotrophic diazotrophs. Highlights metal importance, co-limitation potential, energetic linkages, microhabitat syntrophies.

presentations.title: The impact of regime shifts in seaweeds biomass on water chemistry in hypereutrophic intertidal ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Yatsu tidal flat (Japan): green algae bloom 1995-2017, suddenly shifted to red algae (Gracilaria) 2018. After regime shift: higher nutrients, lower DO/EC. Gracilaria higher PO43- uptake; Ulva higher NH4+ uptake.

presentations.title: NITROGEN FORM, CONCENTRATION, AND MICRONUTRIENT CONCENTRATION INFLUENCE PHYTOPLANKTON BIOMASS IN LAKES ALONG A EUTROPHICATION GRADIENT
presentations.abstract: 8 lakes with 17 fertilization treatments. Significant effects of N concentration, N form, micronutrient concentration. Dual N+P enrichment significant. Phytoplankton responses largely lake-specific, influenced by ambient TN:TP.

presentations.abstract: Mo'orea reef 16S + biogeochem; community differentiation tracks wave power; oceanic taxa in high-wave forereefs, reef taxa in low-wave backreefs.

presentations.title: SPATIOTEMPORAL VARIATION OF CYANOBACTERIA IN LAKE WINNEBAGO, WI: A LAKE ERIE ANALOG
presentations.abstract: Many shallow eutrophic lakes regularly experience toxin-producing cyanobacteria blooms. We asked how cyanobacteria abundance varied among-years and spatially in Lake Winnebago, Wisconsin, a 55,700-hectare eutrophic lake. Field measurements (2023-2025) included cyanobacteria biovolume, phycocyanin, and cyanotoxins, and multiple predictor variables including nutrient concentrations, turbidity, wind direction and speed. We also compiled cyanobacteria abundance data (CIcyano from 2016-2024) for Lake Winnebago derived from satellite measurements. We used General Additive Models (GAMs) to predict direct and indirect measures of cyanobacteria abundance from a suite of abiotic variables. Cyanobacteria blooms in Lake Winnebago were dominated by Microcystis, Aphanizomenon and Dolichospermum. Total microcystin (TM) values exceeded the US EPA standard for recreational water quality on many occasions and the MC-LR congener was most abundant, along with anabaenopeptins. GAM models with turbidity, TN, and DOsaturation as predictor variables explained >85% of the variation in phycocyanin fluorescence and TM. There was large inter-annual variation in mean lake-wide CIcyano and spatial variation, particularly along an east-west axis. Spatial variation in CIcyano was partially explained by wind direction. Unlike in Lake Erie, the interannual variation in cyanobacteria abundance was not related to the magnitude of discharge from the largest tributary.

presentations.title: Optimal day of virus addition to control Harmful Algal Blooms
presentations.abstract: Ongoing human-induced environmental changes in aquatic ecosystems alter the patterns, distribution, and intensity of Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs), which cause large-scale damages due to toxin production, food-web altered dynamics or hypoxia. To decrease these damages, the inoculation of autochthonous viruses constitutes an effective biological control to prevent or reduce HAB formation. The efficacy of this method, however, depends on the timing of the virus application. Here, we estimated the optimal time of virus application that minimizes bloom formation using a simple Host-Virus model for the dinoflagellate Heterocapsa circularisquama and its RNA virus. The model was applied and calibrated using published experimental and observational data from Lake Kamo (Japan) from 2009 to 2021. The timely application of the virus 27 days before the maximum yearly temperature reduces by approximately 85% of the peak dinoflagellates cell abundance in simulated scenarios. The non-linear responses of the viral infection to temperature shift the optimal application day, requiring earlier applications under conditions of environmental warming. Overall, our results highlight the importance of appropriate management for the viral control of HABs.

presentations.title: Eco-evolutionary dynamics of restoring anadromous alewives to a landlocked lake
presentations.abstract: Restoration efforts provide opportunities to study eco-evolutionary dynamics at the ecosystem scale. We evaluated the consequences of restoring anadromous alewives (river herring) into a lake with an established landlocked population. Following fishway construction and annual stocking of anadromous adults from a nearby lake, we quantified recruitment, abundance and growth of anadromous juveniles, as well as hybridization and introgression with the landlocked population. Anadromous juveniles were produced annually, and naturally returning anadromous adults were detected within five years. Over a decade, more than 27,000 anadromous adults ascended the fishway, with the majority identified as offspring of stocked anadromous parents. Anadromous juvenile abundance fluctuated but never exceeded 8% of total juvenile abundance. Anadromous juveniles in the restoration lake grew faster than those in the progenitor lake, though this advantage did not lead to higher abundance or returns. Parentage analyses revealed that stocking date influenced reproductive success, age- and day- of return. Hybridization with the landlocked fish appeared from the start of restoration and gradually increased in abundance. Some hybrids successfully returned as adults after recruitment to the ocean. Landlocked juvenile abundance declined, indicating potential demographic shifts during restoration. Overall, restoration reestablished the anadromous life history in the lake but also led to introgression, showing how restoration may mediate evolutionary and demographic processes.

presentations.title: Evolutionary Forces Shaping Microcystin Gene Retention and Loss Across Microcystis
presentations.abstract: Blooms of Microcystis, a globally distributed cyanobacterium, impair ecosystem function and drinking water security. Its broad distribution across major ecological gradients and its ≥30 diverse species make Microcystis an ideal system for studying eco-evolutionary dynamics. A trait likely shaped by these dynamics is the production of the hepatotoxin microcystin, encoded by the mcy gene cluster. Despite hypotheses that microcystin provides protection from ecological stressors, the mcy gene cluster has been lost in 13 species. We used large-scale genomic analyses to identify evolutionary drivers underlying the maintenance or loss of the mcy gene cluster. Using BLAST- and annotation-based approaches, we identified mcy genes in 542 Microcystis genomes and evaluated sequence diversity, synteny of the mcy cluster and flanking regions, and selection pressures acting on mcy genes across species. We found that the mcy gene sequence is highly conserved, despite deep evolutionary divergence across the genus. Regardless of whether species retained or lost the mcy cluster, consistent and distinct coding sequence insertions were observed in the flanking regions. Selection estimates showed strong purifying selection on mcy genes, suggesting a requirement for mcy maintenance, while some lineages exhibited relaxed selection, suggesting reduced requirement for mcy function and potential gene loss. Together, these findings reveal genomic patterns and evolutionary forces shaping mcy gain and loss in Microcystis and provide a foundation for linking these dynamics to ecological drivers.

presentations.title: Eco-evolutionary feedbacks in competitive systems: Rescue or murder?
presentations.affiliation: IGB Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: Understanding how species respond to changing environments is important for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. Environmental change affects both population densities and traits. Such trait change can result from rapid evolution, which can be beneficial (e.g. evolutionary rescue) or detrimental (e.g. evolutionary suicide). In a multi-species setting, predicting whether evolution aids or harms species persistence is even more challenging to predict. Using a theoretical model inspired by freshwater ciliate systems, we simulate the density and trait dynamics of one and two competing species, each with two potentially evolving traits: physiological optimum and competitive tolerance. Both species experience a decline in the quality of their abiotic environment that ultimately leads to their extinction. However, extinction timing depends on trait evolution. In the single-species system, evolution consistently delays species extinction, potentially resulting in evolutionary rescue. By contrast, in the two-species system, evolution can either delay or accelerate extinction. In particular, when evolution enhances the persistence of the competitor, it can result in evolutionary murder of the focal species. In both systems, we find that the effect sizes of eco-evo interactions depend strongly on the number of traits evolving and the shape of ecological and evolutionary trade-offs. Our study consequently sets the stage for exploring eco-evolutionary dynamics in more complex biotic settings, extending our understanding of species responses to abiotic and biotic changes.

presentations.title: Evolutionary rescue of freshwater copepods during historical lake acidification
presentations.abstract: The persistence of populations facing severe environmental disturbance can be enabled by natural selection on heritable phenotypic variation - a process known as evolutionary rescue. Few studies have investigated the combination of factors (demographic, genetic, and environmental) that facilitate the rescue of populations in complex natural settings, even though their interplay can cause uncertainty about the long-term outcome of evolutionary rescue. Here, we used copepod resting eggs of Leptodiaptomus minutus from three time periods of lake ecological history, spanning ≈ 200 generations (100 years) in two populations impacted by historical acidification. Whole genome sequencing of the resting eggs revealed significant allele frequency shifts associated with the acidification followed by pH recovery. We used a resurrection ecology approach to retrace adaptive shifts concomitant with environmental transitions. Copepods from the pre-acidification period showed sensitivity to acidity, while individuals from the acidification period were adapted to acidic pH. This tolerance was subsequently lost during pH recovery, implying an adaptive reversal. Demographic models indicated a decline during the acidification process followed by population recovery, suggesting that selection led to evolutionary rescue. This study fills a critical knowledge gap about the long-term implications of evolutionary rescue in the wild.

presentations.title: Comparative evidence of fish-induced size-selective predation in Southern Greenland ponds
presentations.abstract: Predators can drive strong impacts on prey communities, shaping patterns of composition, abundance, and size structure, and thereby altering the distribution of total biomass. Although predator-prey interactions are well understood, the ecological consequences of different predator community contexts remain difficult to address. Here, we investigated how predatory fish communities influence benthic macroinvertebrate communities in freshwater ecosystems. We conducted a comparative survey of benthic macroinvertebrates in 27 natural ponds/lakes in Southern Greenland that differ in the presence of three-spine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) and Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus). We found that both predators shifted prey communities from multiple taxa to chironomid dominance and reduced the overall body-size range, but they showed distinct effects on community composition and size structure. Fish predation exerted strong top-down control, with both fish species reducing abundance and suppressing the total biomass of local macroinvertebrates. Notably, the suppressive effect of stickleback predation on the total biomass of macroinvertebrate communities was mitigated by a compensatory increase in snail species Lymnaea vahlii. Overall, our results provide evidence for 1) size-selective predation and its ecosystem-level consequences, and 2) the contrasting effects among predatory fish species. Those findings can illuminate potential mechanisms of selective predation, and predator-prey and predator-predator interactions within complex food webs.

presentations.title: Stickleback populations in highly dynamic environments reveal the spatial and temporal repeatability of natural selection
presentations.abstract: The evolution of genotypic parallelism under shared environmental conditions provides strong evidence for the role of natural selection. However, analyses typically examine genomic signatures of selection long after the putative selection event and only assess the repeatability of responses across spatial population replicates, impeding our ability to attribute a particular response to a given selection pressure and to disentangle non-parallel responses from those that are due to stochastic phenomena and/or local selective pressures. As such, the consistency of natural selection over space and time is unknown, and the role of persistent local selection pressures is unclear. Here, we leverage the natural bar-built estuary system of Santa Cruz, California, to understand the repeatability of natural selection in space and time. By assessing selection at the genomic level in threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) in real-time, we gain insight into the patterns, dynamics, and targets of repeatable selection. Because we compare selection that is shared across locations (spatial repeatability) to selection that is shared across time (temporal repeatability), we can distinguish local from non-parallel selection. We find evidence for natural selection that is highly repeated over both space and time. Although repeatability was most common among fewer populations and/or time points, the number of instances above neutral expectations increased with greater spatial and temporal sharing. While the specific genomic targets vary over time, estuary-specific patterns of responses were broadly consistent between years, suggesting an important role for local selection. Together, our findings demonstrate that selection is more widespread and parallel than previously inferred from patterns of spatial repeatability alone. Our findings highlight the importance of examining the repeatability of selection over both space and time, and they help to explain the parallel and non-paral

presentations.title: Associations between ancestry, morphology, and diet inferred through experimentally-admixed populations in a natural lake
presentations.abstract: Eco-evolutionary dynamics is a developing field that allows us to understand how organisms can evolve over short timescales, impacting their environment, which can in turn impact their evolution. Within this field, there is a significant lack of empirical knowledge from field and whole-ecosystem studies, and laboratory results are rarely directly applicable to what happens for organisms in a natural environment. We investigate the relationship between morphology and diet, and whether ancestry contributes to observed diet only via morphology or whether there is a direct effect of ancestry on diet. We use seven evolutionarily divergent lineages of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) to create an admixed population during an ecological restoration experiment. Our source populations were selected to represent local extremes of the benthic-limnetic axis, based predominantly on body shape and depth. Both ecotypes were added to G lake in 2022, a small oligotrophic lake on the Kenai Peninsula in Alaska. In 2024, we measured morphological traits, diet, and traced the ancestry of each fish back to our source populations to create an ancestry/morphology/diet database. Fish demonstrated evidence of predominantly benthic dietary niches both in terms of their stable isotope signatures and their stomach contents. Morphological feeding traits were strongly related to ancestry, and morphology (body depth and gill rakers) was correlated to dietary niche. Results illustrate the importance of evolutionary ancestry in determining feeding traits, and the role of these feeding traits in determining dietary niche, all within a natural lake system. Our experiment provides a unique opportunity to study the ecological interactions (through dietary niche) of a evolutionarily variable population, that which is rarely observed in nature. This study contributes to ‘proof of concept’ for the developing field of eco-evolutionary dynamics.

presentations.title: RESPONSES OF PRIMARY PRODUCERS AND CONSUMERS TO ENVIRONMENTAL AND ECOLOGICAL CHANGES OVER THE PAST ~150 YEARS IN NORTHERN EXPERIMENTAL LAKES
presentations.abstract: Northern ecosystems are experiencing climate warming at an accelerated rate compared to temperate systems. In addition to climatic stressors, some lakes in southern Alaska are experiencing non-native northern pike invasions, mostly human assisted for game fishing. These introductions are resulting in losses of native fish, likely leading to cascading effects in food webs. To restore native biodiversity and gain insight into eco-evolutionary conservation efforts, nine lakes previously invaded by pike were treated with rotenone. Different combinations of three-spine stickleback ecotypes were then intentionally reintroduced into these fishless lakes to re-establish the food web. However, we have limited knowledge on the baseline ecological conditions of these lakes. To address this gap, we are conducting paleolimnological analyses of four lakes in this experimental system to understand how the primary producers and consumers have changed over the last ~150 years. We are studying the dynamics in chlorophyll a (+ diagenetic products) and zooplankton subfossil remains archived in the sediment cores. Our preliminary analyses of Hope Lake show clear changes in cladoceran assemblages with Daphnia taxa becoming more abundant during the pike invasion era and then returning to low abundances after the limnetic stickleback ecotype was reintroduced. Overall, our findings will provide evidence for northern ecosystem responses to multiple stressors over time, while advancing the study eco-evolutionary conservation efforts.

presentations.title: Intra-specific diversity of lacustrine stickleback: ecological consequences and rapid evolution
presentations.abstract: Most species show massive genetic and phenotypic variation within and among their component populations. This intra-specific diversity is expected to have important effects on population dynamics, community structure, and ecosystem services. Threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) provide a case in point. I will describe the intra-specific diversity of stickleback across their range; and then provide examples of how that diversity is evolving rapidly within natural and experimental systems in California, British Columbia, Alaska, and Quebec. Finally, I will outline ongoing experiments in natural systems that seek to understand the ecological consequences of intra-specific diversity and its rapid evolution in stickleback.

presentations.title: Experimental evidence that introduced predators cause trophic cascades in freshwater ponds
presentations.abstract: Predators can cause cascading trophic interactions in ecosystems, influencing their structure, species composition, functioning, and cross-boundary fluxes. However, experimental tests of such predator-mediated effects at whole-ecosystem scales are rare. Here, we demonstrate that the introduction of threespine stickleback into six freshwater ponds in Southern Greenland significantly altered ecosystem structure and functioning through cascading trophic interactions. Stickleback decreased prey biomass and increased primary producer biomass in both benthic and pelagic habitats, culminating in an increase in whole-pond primary productivity. Furthermore, stickleback reduced the abundance of emergent insects in riparian spider webs, thereby affecting cross-ecosystem fluxes. A complementary analysis of natural lakes and ponds in Southern Greenland provided further evidence that stickleback drives pelagic trophic cascades in natural ecosystems. Collectively, our results highlight the profound effects of predators’ trophic interactions on diverse aspects of aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: GENETIC ANALYSIS OF DEEP-SEA SHRIMP PLESIONIKA SEMILAEVIS REVEALS THE INFLUENCE OF OCEANOGRAPHIC FACTORS ON BIOGEOGRAPHIC PATTERNS IN THE WESTERN INDIAN OCEAN
presentations.abstract: Larval dispersal patterns and phylogeographic structure play a key role in defining biogeographic provinces and guiding biodiversity conservation in marine ecosystems. However, limited research from the Indian Ocean has restricted clear understanding of these biogeographic boundaries. In this study, Plesionika semilaevis (Spence Bate, 1888) specimens from the southeastern Arabian Sea were examined using morphological traits and partial mitochondrial COI sequences. Additional COI sequences from the Mozambique Channel were retrieved from GenBank for comparison. Maximum likelihood phylogenetic reconstruction revealed two distinct clades: one comprising Arabian Sea individuals and the other representing Mozambique Channel-Madagascar specimens. Intraspecific COI divergence ranged from 4.2-5.4%, exceeding typical interspecific thresholds. The haplotype network further indicated clear breaks in distribution, showing 20 segregating sites between the two regional groups. AMOVA results demonstrated pronounced genetic differentiation (ϕST = 0.99409; P < 0.001), supporting the presence of cryptic lineages. Overall, the findings suggest that P. semilaevis in the Indian Ocean consists of two evolutionarily separate clades. Oceanographic features-particularly the South Equatorial Current (SEC), Mozambique Channel eddies, the east-west SEC flow, equatorial counter-currents, and regional bathymetry-appear to govern connectivity, promote isolation, and drive the allopatric divergence observed between Arabian Sea and Mozambique Channel populations.

presentations.title: What drives biomass variation in independent brook trout populations? Environmental gradients across divergent stream populations
presentations.abstract: As biodiversity declines globally, understanding the factors that regulate population biomass is critical for predicting ecosystem responses to environmental change. Salmonids (e.g., salmon, char, trout) provide an ideal model for studying biomass dynamics because of their global distribution, well-characterized life histories, and sensitivity to environmental pressures. Previous salmonid biomass models have largely focused on physical habitat features, such as stream depth, width, and pool abundance, leaving chemical and biological drivers, including nutrients, DOC, pH, and prey availability, understudied. In this study, 25 streams in Cape Race, Newfoundland are being sampled for brook trout biomass and a combination of chemical, biological, and physical variables. These streams each contain independent brook trout populations that experience distinct environmental conditions, and preliminary data show nearly 30-fold variation in biomass across them. By integrating often-overlooked chemical and biological variables with commonly measured physical habitat features into multivariate models, this study aims to identify the key combinations of factors driving such biomass variation. Understanding these drivers will clarify mechanisms underlying biomass differences, reveal how environmental variation translates into energy flow, and improve predictions of salmonid responses to environmental change, while also highlighting how ecological gradients and population-level trait differences may interact to shape biomass outcomes.

presentations.title: DRAWING LINKS BETWEEN EPIGENETIC AND GENETIC DIFFERENTIATION IN CANADIAN ATLANTIC SALMON (SALMO SALAR) POPULATIONS.
presentations.abstract: Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is a key contributor to phenotypic plasticity in eukaryotes and is increasingly recognized as a driver of evolution. DNA methylation (DNAm) is the addition of a methyl group to cytosines and generally silences genomic regions. This process has been linked to genetic differentiation among closely related teleost species. These recent findings highlight a potential role of DNAm in rapid and flash evolution, where a species can adapt to a stressor phenotypically by epigenetic regulation, leading to genetic differentiation reflecting the local stressors by altering fitness. Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) are of great interest for studying epigenetic traits. Canada hosts 16 genetically distinct populations of Atlantic salmon, many of which are in decline. To combat these declines, many hatchery rearing programs have been implemented. This rearing has been shown to induce maladaptive predictive epigenetic changes that can reduce fitness upon reintroduction to the wild. Understanding DNAm patterns across wild populations is therefore essential for identifying epigenetic states that reflect local environmental pressures rather than hatchery-induced cues. This study aims to characterize DNAm variation across wild Canadian Atlantic salmon populations, identify epigenetic traits across their range, and explore links between DNAm differences and genetic structure. By producing a baseline of population-specific epigenetic signatures, this work will support efforts to integrate epigenetic information into conservation and management strategies.

presentations.title: BEYOND THE POPULATION: INDIVIDUAL HABITAT STATEGIES IN WALLEYE AND IMPLICAITONS FOR FUTURE MANAGEMENT AND CONSERVATION
presentations.abstract: Studies of organisms in ecosystems often simplify patterns to the population level, but recognizing individual variation in traits and behaviors can improve management and conservation strategies. In the Midwestern United States, Walleye (Sander vitreus) are an ecologically, economically, and culturally important species threatened by loss of critical lake habitat and typically managed at broad spatial scales. To better understand individual contributions to population-level habitat use, we tagged 176 Walleye with temperature-depth sensors in two north-temperate Wisconsin lakes and paired these data with measurements of lake temperature, light availability, and dissolved oxygen. We used tag temperatures to estimate energetic costs and depth to assess dissolved oxygen use and calculate water-column search volumes based on light and known reaction distances. Individuals in the deep, cold lake used a broader temperature range (15.5–21°C), producing more variable energetic costs than fish in the shallow, warm lake where temperature use was constrained (20–21°C). Light use also differed, some fish consistently occupied low-light habitats while others inhabited high-light habitats, yielding differences in potential search areas. Most fish preferentially selected for high dissolved oxygen levels (7-9 mg/L). Our results suggest within- and among-lake plasticity in walleye habitat use, highlighting how incorporating individual-level behavior can refine management priorities and support species resilience to climate change through targeted conservation.

presentations.title: Evaluating diatom resource responses between oligotrophic and coastal populations
presentations.abstract: Diatoms are major drivers of marine primary production, carbon, and nutrient cycling in coastal areas. Diatoms are also found in oligotrophic systems where they can form blooms and influence carbon export patterns. The same genera can occur in these vastly different environments, but the extent to which oligotrophic and coastal populations are tuned to different resource environments is uncertain. Here, we leverage resource amendment incubation experiments and lab studies of isolates from these regions to identify differential gene expression and growth characteristics between oligotrophic and coastal Pseudo-nitzschia , a widespread model pennate diatom genus. Incubation experiments included nitrate or phosphate addition to natural communities on the New England shelf and the oligotrophic western North Atlantic. For the oligotrophic site, Pseudo-nitzschia had the highest relative abundance under N addition, making up 22.4% of the diatom community, while at coastal sites, the genus was most abundant at 33.4% under P addition. Across sites, Pseudo-nitzschia exhibited distinct gene expression patterns after nutrient amendment, suggesting that adaptations to oligotrophic or coastal environments may impact their responses. With further study of these responses across regions, along with nutrient limitation experiments with coastal and oligotrophic isolates, we can better predict how diatoms may respond to future oligotrophic scenarios.
