presentations.title: Novel Instrumentation for Marine Planktonic Bioluminescence Measurements and its Potential as a Functional Trait
presentations.abstract: Mechanically stimulated bioluminescence (MSB) can be observed in most marine ecosystems across most major planktonic groups, e.g., dinoflagellates, copepods, euphausiids, appendicularians, ctenophores, jellyfish. First flash kinetics parameters (FFKPs) are species-specific and allow for diverse scientific applications such as in situ identification, monitoring changes in the water column community composition, and detecting invasive species. Here, we detail field, instrument design and data processing components developed for establishing a library of FFKPs of bioluminescent marine plankton. We introduce the novel Lab-CODEX, a laboratory or shipboard instrument for measuring individual bioluminescence events. Allowing measurements of single bioluminescence events following species isolations and identification from net tows, Lab-CODEX precisely describes FFKPs of the planktonic community. Following four oceanographic cruises in distinct marine systems (Gulf of Mexico; East Sound, WA; Trondheimsfjord, Norway; Sargasso Sea), our team has collected over 350 individual bioluminescent signals from 25 genera and 7 phyla, creating a working library of bioluminescence signatures. Through linear dimensionality reduction, clustering and network analyses, we assess the potential of using bioluminescence and FFKPs as functional traits for studying biodiversity and community assemblage. Links between bioluminescence signatures and other ecological traits, e.g., vertical migration, toxicity, predator-prey interactions, feeding mechanisms, and taxonomy are explored.

presentations.title: Phonotaxis response of fish larvae to anthropogenic sounds: Effect of body size and auditory specialization.
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic sounds can impact fish behavior, leading to the avoidance of noisy underwater habitats by some species. Previous studies on adult fish have shown that fish with auditory specializations have better hearing capacities and show negative phonotaxis (avoidance) to anthropogenic sounds. However, very few studies have been conducted on early life stages (e.g. larvae), and none were conducted in freshwater habitats. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of body size and auditory specializations on the phonotaxis response of freshwater fish larvae to anthropogenic sounds. A field experiment was conducted in the St.Lawrence River (Canada), whereby larvae were sampled using light traps positioned near vs. far from an artificial sound source mimicking a motorized engine. We assessed whether the sound treatment influenced the abundance, body size, and species composition of larval samples. We showed that species without auditory specializations are attracted to the sound treatment regardless of their body size, while auditory specialists (e.g. species with a Weberian apparatus) showed a size-dependent response. A meta-analysis of fish hearing capacities in early life stages revealed a similar interaction between body size and auditory specialization, with greater ontogenetic shifts in auditory specialists. These results suggest that the phonotaxis response of larval fish to anthropogenic sounds depends on sensory traits and body size, and that the response of early life stages may differ greatly from the one of adults.

presentations.title: From individual coloration to ecosystem functioning: quantification of astaxanthin pigmentation on microscope images as an indicator of copepod fitness
presentations.abstract: Color is a morphological property that can be assessed at the individual level and that impacts survival, growth and reproduction of organisms; as such it corresponds to the definition of a functional trait. In zooplankton ecology, color has usually been overlooked since it is admitted that organisms are mostly transparent to fit the water medium. Copepods – small sized crustaceans – represent a hub of matter and energy in aquatic food webs. We will first present results from a literature review demonstrating that pigmentation from astaxanthin molecules is a shared and advantageous trait for freshwater and marine copepods at global scale. Astaxanthin pigmentation appears to indicate an efficient metabolism, lead to a better survival under oxidative stress, and enhance reproduction and offspring quality for various copepod species. Secondly, with a focus on marine (sub)Arctic Calanus species, we will present a method for automatic quantification of a redness index from microscope individual images. By intercalibrating historical image datasets and segmenting red pixels with color deconvolution technics, we quantify redness accumulated in the antennas, the genital segment and the basis of pereiopod of Calanus. Such an index could be used to test the ecological and physiological hypotheses about astaxanthin accumulation, or to monitor the transfer of antioxidant pigments in aquatic ecosystems up to human consumption.

presentations.title: HEAT TOLERANCE IN DAPHNIA: EMERGING PATTERNS AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
presentations.abstract: Predicting how elevated temperatures will reshape populations, ecosystems, and evolutionary processes requires the identification of ecologically relevant traits. Zooplankton such as Daphnia are particularly promising models for such approaches due to their key role for pelagic food webs. Heat tolerance has emerged as a candidate trait that is likely to influence community composition and evolutionary trajectories of Daphnia in warming environments. For the past two decades, heat tolerance research has focused on two proxies: the critical thermal maximum measured along a temperature gradient (CTmax) and time until immobilization measured at a constant temperature (Timm). The quantification of these two proxies, however, varies considerably across different studies that employ various experimental setups. Despite recent developments such as video tracking, which enables a robust and reproducible quantification of CTmax and Timm, an in-depth understanding of the mechanism linking heat tolerance to fitness and population dynamics is still lacking. This specifically applies to physiological processes, potential trade-offs between heat tolerance and other fitness-related traits, and the role of heat tolerance in intra- and interspecific competition. We here emphasize the need for data synthesis and standardization, present our recent findings from heat tolerance experiments with different Daphnia species, and discuss future perspectives and potential challenges in heat tolerance research.

presentations.title: Lipidomics and stable isotopes reveal ecophysiological dynamics of polyunsaturated fatty acids in zooplankton and fish
presentations.abstract: Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) are key micronutrients in aquatic ecosystems and critical structural components of neuronal tissues. Most consumers cannot synthesize them de novo and therefore depend on dietary supply and subsequent, energetically costly bioconversion to meet their physiological requirements, while balancing the ecological trade-off between investment in neuronal function versus somatic growth and reproduction. To better understand this ecophysiological system, we investigated how dietary PUFA and temperature affect consumers’ capacity to metabolize and allocate physiologically required omega-3 PUFA to neuronal tissues. We combined compound-specific stable hydrogen isotope analysis to trace PUFA metabolism with lipidomics using MALDI-MS imaging to map their distribution in neuronal tissues of daphnids and common carp. Our results reveal distinct species- and temperature-dependent strategies for routing and remodeling PUFA, including differential prioritization of neuronal tissues under stressful conditions. We identify critical constraints in the ability of consumers to maintain neuronal PUFA composition under suboptimal dietary conditions and thermal stress, suggesting limits to compensatory metabolism when environmental change alters resource quality. Together, these findings demonstrate that interactions between diet quality and temperature can fundamentally shape PUFA metabolism and organ-specific allocation, with important implications for consumer fitness, trophic transfer, and ecosystem functioning in a warming and nutritionally changing world.

presentations.raw: Integrating multiomics and multilayer data to unveil the mechanistic underpinnings of marine ectotherms’ ability to acclimate and adapt to combined global change drivers (10603) Tutorial/Invited: Invi

presentations.title: Integrating multiomics and multilayer data to unveil the mechanistic underpinnings of marine ectotherms’ ability to acclimate and adapt to combined global change drivers
presentations.abstract: The physiological mechanisms underpinning aquatic ectotherms’ ability to tolerate and evolve under environmental changes have long been studied but remain largely unresolved due to our historical reliance on reductionist approaches. However, recent advances in omics approaches are enabling us to acquire a more comprehensive portrait of the way physiological systems function, evolve and will respond to future environmental challenges. Going further, integrating multiomics analyses with higher layers of the biological hierarchy of organisms, communities and ecosystems can provide more meaningful ecological insights. On one hand, we can gain an in-depth and unbiased characterisation of the physiological status of an organism, and on the other hand, a deeper understanding of the links between organisms’ biology and ecosystems’ functioning. In this talk, using a case study, we explore the potential and limitations of multiomics and multilayer approaches to investigate the implications of rapid environmental changes to unveil the mechanisms underpinning marine ectotherms’ ability to acclimate and adapt to combined global change drivers.

presentations.title: DECIPHERING TERRESTRIAL ECOLOGY FROM ANIMAL TRACES
presentations.abstract: Ichnology is the study of modern and ancient traces—such as burrows, tracks and trails—produced by animals. Fossilized traces, or trace fossils are keys to understanding how their producers interacted with the environment and how those behaviours evolved across geological time. For example, an assemblage of trace fossils from a given sedimentary rock will not only tell us about the types of animals that were present, but also about the depositional environment and physico-chemical stresses posed to the fauna based on their behavioural responses. In comparison to marine invertebrates, significantly less research has been devoted to the ichnology of terrestrial invertebrates. One way to facilitate research is to establish a better understanding of the traces produced by modern aquatic invertebrates of inland waters. Neoichnology strives to do just that by observing how animals respond to different environmental parameters and how they are reflected on the substrate. Besides assisting in future ichnological and sedimentological interpretations, a neoichnological study focusing on the behavioural groupings of non-marine invertebrates and their responses to the physico-chemical environment may enhance our understanding on the ecology of benthic life.

presentations.title: Understanding Lake Geneva blooms using high frequency image observations
presentations.abstract: In Lake Geneva, phytoplankton species bloom regularly despite longstanding efforts to reduce these proliferations via control of nutrient inputs. The most recent blooms, formed by potentially toxic cyanobacteria, mixotrophic chrysophytes, or slow-sinking filamentous green algae, have been remarkably short-lived (~ 1 week), yet were major threats to the multiple services supplied by the lake, including drinkable water, fisheries, and recreational activities. To understand what conditions (meteorological, hydrological, and/or biological) favor these blooms, we have been monitoring phytoplankton and zooplankton communities at the floating-laboratory platform LéXPLORE, using various imaging instruments (profiling or single-depth mode) operating at daily or sub-daily scales. We analyzed our observations with computer vision models, aiming at automatically recognizing blooming species alongside their predators (zooplankton or parasitic fungi). This approach allowed us to assess most rates affecting the onset, maintenance, and termination of phytoplankton blooms: growth, as monitored through cell cycle markers, losses via estimates of sinking speed, grazing, and parasitic infections, as well as advection and vertical migration. The imbalance between growth and loss processes resulted in predictable succession patterns characterizing the recurring spring blooms but also in the discovery of sudden and complex secondary blooms.

presentations.title: HABITAT DEGRADATION AND TRAIT-BASED ASSEMBLY IN NEOTROPICAL RIVER FISH COMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: The assembly of local communities is often viewed as a process involving the dispersal of species from a regional pool and their subsequent filtering by the abiotic environment and the ecological interactions. In freshwater ecosystems, this framework provides a powerful lens to understand how environmental gradients and habitat degradation shape fish assemblages. Yet, little is known about how anthropogenic disturbances modulate the balance between environmental filtering and biotic interactions in Neotropical rivers. Assuming that degradation acts as a strong environmental filter, we expect that highly impacted sites harbor assemblages composed of species with similar functional traits and, therefore, low functional diversity. We sampled 46 river sites along a gradient of habitat degradation and applied a null model to evaluate whether the observed functional diversity was higher (overdispersion) or lower (underdispersion) than expected by chance. We calculated the standardized effect size (SES) of functional diversity and related it to metrics of habitat degradation, proximity of residences, and fine sediment cover using linear models. Assemblages occurring in silt-rich reaches and near human residences tended to show underdispersion pattern, indicating that anthropogenic stressors act as strong environmental filters selecting species with similar ecological strategies. Our findings highlight that habitat degradation simplifies the functional structure of fish assemblages, promoting trait convergence and potentially reducing the resilience of Neotropical river ecosystems.

presentations.title: EXPERIMENTAL ECOLOGY IN AQUATIC SYSTEMS: BALANCING REALISM AND FEASIBILITY TO PREDICT RESPONSES TO GLOBAL CHANGE
presentations.abstract: Aquatic experimental ecology has been pivotal in revealing mechanisms that shape ecological dynamics, from species interactions to ecosystem responses. As global change accelerates, the field faces a pressing challenge: balancing experimental feasibility with ecological realism. We identify five priorities to strengthen predictive capacity in aquatic systems: embracing multidimensional ecological dynamics, moving beyond classical model organisms, incorporating environmental variability, fostering inclusive and interdisciplinary collaboration, and leveraging emerging technologies. These priorities intersect across spatial, temporal, and biological scales, demanding integrative approaches that couple mechanistic insight with ecological complexity. Examples from microcosm, mesocosm, and whole-ecosystem studies illustrate how experimental designs can better capture natural variability and community structure. By critically examining trade-offs in experimental ecology, we outline pathways to advance the field in a rapidly changing world. To operationalize these principles, we propose a global experiment and invite session participants to contribute.

presentations.title: The Effects of a Novel Aeration Device on the Survivability of Faecal Indicator Bacteria
presentations.abstract: Climate change is increasing the frequency of extreme precipitation events and of combined sewer overflows, releasing fecal bacteria into receiving waters. Coupled with an extended shorebird breeding season, many freshwater bodies are experiencing episodic, or in some cases persistent, high levels of coliforms, E. coli, and, creating a significant threat to human health and economic stability. The persistence of fecal bacteria in surface water can be linked to dissolved oxygen levels; greater aeration may reduce their survival, shortening episodes of elevated exposure risk. This research explores a novel aeration device that can boost the levels of dissolved oxygen (DO) within a contaminated water body, thereby reducing the growth or persistence of fecal bacteria. Ten field microcosms (110 L drums) were assembled; five were treated with the device, and all were periodically monitored for DO. Microcosms were seeded with municipal wastewater 4 times over a month-long establishment period. Thereafter, water and sediment samples were collected multiple times from each microcosm to measure bacterial abundance (E. coli, total fecal coliforms, Enterococcus) to determine the loss over time. Enterolet and Colilert Quanti-Tray tests (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc.) were used. Samples were also plated on selective media for colony counts. Still, results were inconclusive, perhaps due to power failures of the aeration device in the field and the observed use of the microcosms by birds. The experiment is being repeated under more controlled laboratory conditions.

presentations.title: Resolving potential Phage–Host Interactions in Cyanobacterial Blooms Through Daily Metagenomics
presentations.affiliation: CENTRE ALPIN DE RECHERCHE SUR LES RÉSEAUX TROPHIQUES ET ÉCOSYSTÈMES LIMNIQUES
presentations.abstract: (nicolas.tromas@inrae.fr) Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CHABs) are increasing in frequency worldwide and pose major threats to water quality and public health. Understanding, predicting, and ultimately mitigating these blooms remains challenging because bloom dynamics are shaped not only by environmental conditions but also by complex biological interactions—particularly those between cyanobacteria and their phages. Phages are potential ecological drivers that can modulate cyanobacterial abundance, alter population structure, and influence the trajectory of blooms, yet their roles in natural ecosystems remain poorly quantified. To address this gap, we conducted an unprecedented daily sampling campaign during the 2019 cyanobacterial bloom in Petit Lac Saint François (Québec). We integrated high-resolution shotgun metagenomics to track fine-scale temporal dynamics of cyanobacterial hosts and their associated phages. This dense temporal framework allowed us to examine ecological processes across multiple biological scales—genus, species, and strain—and to reveal how rapidly cyanobacterial populations respond to phage pressure in situ. We complemented these data with high-resolution cyanotoxin quantifications to evaluate the relationships between phage dynamics and extracellular toxin release resulting from host cell lysis. Together, this unique dataset uncovered signatures of phage impact on cyanobacterial population structure, including rapid, phage-linked shifts in strain composition that reflect strong ecological interactions occurring on day-to-day timescales.

presentations.title: Tales of Lake Erie viruses using TALE/GALE
presentations.abstract: Publicly available sequencing data is often an underused resource for broad questions within ecology. The efforts of multiple research groups can be ethically combined to investigate larger questions within complex environments where species interactions, biogeochemical cycling, and anthropogenetic inputs, and other factors, heavily influence the environment’s dynamics. At the microbial level large lake ecology holds many untold stories, and we can explore these (and validate other findings) by amalgamating previous sequencing efforts spanning a single environment temporally and spatially. We have combined past sequencing projects of Lake Erie into two subsections, the metagenomes and metatranscriptomes. Metagenomes provide information on species genomic potential, relatedness, and when possible whole species genomes. Metatranscriptomes provide information on the expression of genes, therefore, what processes are being carried out by microbes in their environment and confirms the usage of “genomic potential” within metagenomes. We have called the metagenome section Genomes Assembled from Lake Erie (GALE), and the metatranscriptome section Metatranscriptomes Assembled from Lake Erie (TALE). This presentation will provide a look at Lake Erie viruses using TALE/GALE: showcasing diversity and ecological tales.

presentations.title: Salinity driven niche partitioning of aquatic viruses in the temperate mesotidal Elbe Estuary
presentations.affiliation: The Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: (julia.golebiowska@igb-berlin.de) Viruses are a vital part of the aquatic food web and hold a profound role in carbon and energy cycling at different trophic levels. Despite rising interest in aquatic viruses, very few studies were conducted in estuaries, where freshwater and marine communities meet along the salinity gradient. We present a paired analysis of metagenomics and metatranscriptomics data focusing on the viral fraction derived from seasonal sampling between May 2021 and November 2022 in one of Europe’s largest estuaries, the temperate mesotidal Elbe downstream of the city of Hamburg. Our results reveal a sharp delineation of viral communities along specific salinity niches and provide evidence for their adaptation. This implicates viruses as a structural component of microbial and phytoplankton ecology across the estuary. We provide a detailed overview of the spatiotemporal distribution of viruses including taxonomy and hosts, which emphasizes the role of giant viruses (Megaviricetes) in waters of lower salinity and RNA viruses in marine environments. We identify, besides salinity, total dissolved phosphate, and temperature as the main drivers of estuarine viral communities. We find a broad spectrum of metabolic pathways, potentially alternated by viruses via Auxiliary Metabolism Genes (AMGs). These included the underlying carbon processes like photosynthesis or methane metabolism, but also xenobiotics and antibiotics metabolism in this anthropogenically alternated estuary. This is the first detailed molecular study of viruses in the Elbe Estuary, shedding light on viral communities and their ecological roles in controlling microbial populations at the base of the estuarine food web.

presentations.title: Transcriptional stress response of the marine picoeukaryotic alga Ostreococcus lucimarinus during infection by related viruses under phosphate limitation.
presentations.abstract: Prasinophytes are green algae that are abundant in open ocean spring blooms and mesotrophic marine ecosystems. Here, we examined host-virus dynamics between the picoprasinophyte Ostreococcus lucimarinus and prasinoviruses OlV1 and OlV7, which are closely related but have distinct infection parameters (latent periods and burst sizes) and responses to micronutrient limitation. Additionally, OlV1 encodes a high-affinity phosphate transporter that is lacking in OlV7. We studied O. lucimarinus diel growth and transcriptional activity in replicate axenic or virus-infected (OlV1 or OlV7) cultures under replete (2.31±0.07 d-1) and phosphate-deplete (1.20±0.02 d-1). In uninfected controls, 23% of host genes were differentially expressed between replete and phosphate-deplete conditions at the initial time point, decreasing to 10% differentially expressed 12 hours into the light regime (³1.5-fold expression, q£0.01). With respect to viral infection dynamics, OlV1 exhibited shorter latent periods than OlV7 in replete conditions, like previous observations of infections in iron replete vs. deplete hosts. Despite high expression of the OlV1 high-affinity phosphate transporter, OlV7 appeared to lyse a greater proportion of host cells regardless of phosphate condition. More comprehensive evaluation of individual gene responses seen in hosts under the various conditions and time points is ongoing, as is evaluation of viral genes expression. Collectively, these findings bring nuanced data to host-viral dynamics relevant to natural ecosystems under predicted desertification of the open ocean.

presentations.title: INFLUENCE OF NUTRIENT LIMITATION AND MIXOTROPHY ON ALLELOCHEMICAL INTERACTIONS OF THE HARMFUL DINOFLAGELLATE ALEXANDRIUM CATENELLA
presentations.abstract: The effects of nutrient starvation and mixotrophy on the growth characteristics and the allelochemical potency of the harmful dinoflagellate Alexandrium catenella were investigated in laboratory experiments. Treatments with reduced nitrate (-N) or reduced phosphate (-P) were compared to nutrient-replete conditions (+NP) in A. catenella cultures growing purely phototrophically (without prey) or mixotrophically with the chlorophyte Ostreococcus tauri as food source. Both dissolved nutrient and prey supply affected dinoflagellate growth. Compared to purely phototrophic growth, mixotrophy in A. catenella resulted in significantly higher growth rates irrespective of nutrient supply, except for P-limited conditions. Nutrient depletion (N or P) reduced A. catenella growth. Subsequent bioassays with the rotifer Brachionus plicatilis showed a strong immobilization effect of the cell-free A. catenella supernatants that differed with nutrient and prey availability. Supernatants from nutrient-limited cultures growing mixotrophically led to a significantly stronger immobilization of the rotifer compared to those of phototrophic cultures. In contrast, allelochemicals released by A. catenella grown under nutrient-replete conditions (+NP) had a significantly stronger immobilization effect under phototrophic growth. These results indicate that differences in the allelochemical efficacy of A. catenella may vary depending on resource availability and that the potentially reduced production of allelochemicals during nutrient deficiency can be mitigated by the consumption of prey.

presentations.title: NITROGEN AVAILABILITY SHAPES EVOLUTION OF PHAGE RESISTANCE IN NITROGEN FIXING CYANOBACTERIA
presentations.abstract: Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria drive aquatic nitrogen and carbon cycling and can form harmful blooms, especially when dissolved nitrogen is scarce. Cyanophages can regulate blooms but also select for rapid evolution of resistance. In this study, we asked how resistance interacts with nitrogen availability and fixation. We studied resistance evolution in the nitrogen-fixing Nostoc sp. PCC7120 and Cylindrospermopsis raciborskii under nitrogen-replete versus nitrogen-starved conditions. Under nitrogen-replete conditions, resistance often carried a fitness cost, including reduced nitrogen fixation and poorer survival during nitrogen starvation. Yet under nitrogen limitation, resistant strains can evolve alternative resistance mechanisms that preserved heterocyst function and maintained fixation, enabling persistence in nutrient-limited systems. Resistance arose more slowly under nitrogen starvation than in nitrogen-rich environments. Whole-genome sequencing of 92 resistant isolates revealed nitrogen-dependent mutational signatures: mutations in glycosyltransferase and other cell surface-related genes were common, particularly under nitrogen-limited conditions, while resistance acquired in nitrogen-replete environments often affected regulatory genes involved in heterocyst development. Phylogenetic analyses suggest many resistance-associated loci are accessory genes shaped by lateral gene transfer. Overall, nitrogen availability shapes the tempo and genetic basis of cyanophage resistance and the magnitude of associated tradeoffs, with implications for bloom-forming diazotrophs.

presentations.title: EXPERIMENTAL INSIGHTS INTO BOTTOM-UP AND TOP-DOWN REGULATION OF FRESHWATER BACTERIOPLANKTON DIVERSITY AND METABOLISM
presentations.affiliation: Institut de Recherche pour le Développement
presentations.abstract: Microcosm experiments were performed to assess the interactive effects of nutrient enrichment and top-down controls (viruses and grazers) on freshwater bacterial community dynamics. Nutrient enrichment promoted the proliferation of high nucleic acid (HNA) bacterial cells, which showed elevated bacterial growth efficiency—indicating high carbon incorporation and metabolic activity. However, rapid HNA growth increased susceptibility to viral lytic infection, leading to their decline later in the experiment. In treatments containing viruses alone or together with flagellates, viral lysis selectively removed active HNA cells, indirectly benefiting low nucleic acid (LNA) cells that likely utilized lysis products for growth. Changes in bacterial physiological states were mirrored in community structure, assessed through 16S rRNA gene sequencing (Illumina MiSeq). Diversity indices (Chao and Shannon) indicated highest species richness in microcosms containing both viruses and grazers, suggesting that simultaneous top-down control maintained bacterial diversity by preventing dominance of specific taxa. Overall, nutrient enrichment stimulated bacterial metabolism, while viral and grazer pressures regulated dominant populations. These findings highlight that interactions between resource availability and top-down controls jointly stabilize bacterial community structure and function in freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: Sick and sinking: Are chytrid parasite infections changing Asterionella’s potential for carbon export?
presentations.abstract: Diatoms are major drivers of carbon export in aquatic systems because their large, dense cells sink rapidly. Asterionella formosa, a dominant diatom in temperate lakes, can contribute substantially to carbon fluxes to sediments during its spring bloom. However, both the timing and magnitude of this bloom are strongly influenced by chytrid parasites. Although these fungal parasites can collapse blooms by infecting diatom cells, their effects on Asterionella’s sinking rates, aggregation dynamics, and carbon content remain poorly understood. Chytrid infections may enhance carbon export by promoting aggregation and accelerating colony sinking, yet simultaneously reduce export by depleting infected cells of carbon before they settle. The net balance of these opposing mechanisms is currently unknown. We aim to experimentally quantify how chytrid infection modifies the sinking behavior and carbon content of Asterionella. Through controlled laboratory experiments, we will measure sinking velocity, aggregate formation, and carbon content in infected and uninfected colonies. Our results will improve understanding of how parasitism shapes carbon cycling in lake ecosystems.

presentations.title: CARBON CUISINE: DISSOLVED ORGANIC MATTER COMPOSITION AS A DRIVER FOR MICROBIAL COMMUNITY SUCCESSION IN FRESHWATERS
presentations.abstract: The decomposition of dissolved organic matter (DOM) by freshwater bacteria underpins the functioning of aquatic food webs and plays a critical role in the global carbon cycle. Climate change, including hydrological intensification and changes in vegetation cover, is predicted to alter the composition and concentration of DOM that enters northern freshwaters, with uncertain consequences for resident microbial communities. Here we asked how a model, six-species bacterial community responds when exposed to chemically diverse freshwater DOM substrates that are representative of projected future compositional shifts in organic matter. Using full-length 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing for species-level identification, paired with total community cell counts measured using flow cytometry, we characterized how microbial community succession varied among DOM sources and with different levels of species diversity over fourteen weeks. Preliminary analyses suggest that cell abundances varied with DOM source, time, and species diversity. Characterizing the response of a model microbial community to diverse DOM sources identifies new ways in which bacterial communities may respond to the impacts of climate change.

presentations.title: Phosphate-Solubilizing Fungi Reduce Algal Blooms: Implications for eutrophication process
presentations.abstract: (estervieiragbio@gmail.com) Phosphate-solubilizing fungi are promising biological agents for mitigating algae blooms in aquatic environments. This study evaluated the interaction between Trichoderma asperellum, a known phosphate-solubilizing fungus, and the microalga Chlorella sp. Phosphatase production by T. asperellum was tested in minimal medium (37.13 µg/mol p-nitrophenol mL-1 h-1). Following this assessment, one aliquot was subsequently added to the algae culture. The experiment was conducted in 1.5 L of BG11 medium under three conditions: negative control (water + algae), algal control (BG11 + Chlorella), and fungal treatment (BG11 + Chlorella + T. asperellum, inoculated on day 0). Growth was monitored for six days using spectrophotometric absorbance at 665 nm. Microalgal biomass was accurately quantified on Day 6 via chlorophyll a extraction. The algal control showed a gradual absorbance increase from 0.069 (24 h) to 0.210 (144 h). The fungal treatment presented similar values at the early stages (0.059 at 24 h and 0.062 at 48 h) but remained lower than the algal control at the end of the experiment (0.094 at 144 h). Chlorophyll a extraction on day 6 indicated higher pigment content in the algal control (1340 µg/L) compared to the fungal treatment (626 µg/L), confirming reduced pigment presence in the presence of the fungus. The fungal treatment resulted in a severe inhibition of microalgal growth, confirmed by a 53.3 % reduction in Chlorophyll. The findings highlight the potential of phosphate-solubilizing fungi as biological tools relevant to nutrient management and eutrophication studies.

presentations.title: METABOLIC EXCHANGE AND CRYPTIC MICROCYSTIN DEGRADATION IN MICROCYSTIS ASSOCIATED HETEROTROPHIC BACTERIA
presentations.abstract: Harmful algal blooms dominated by the cyanobacterium Microcystis are an ecological and public health concern largely due to their potential to produce the hepatotoxin microcystin. Microcystis colonies host diverse heterotrophic bacteria that influence bloom dynamics through nutrient cycling and, in some cases, microcystin degradation. The mlrA-D operon is currently the only described mechanism for degradation of microcystin; however, microcystin degradation has been observed in heterotrophic bacteria lacking the operon. We reconstructed genome scale metabolic models for twenty heterotrophs isolated from harmful algal blooms to predict metabolic exchange with Microcystis and screened for mlr genes. Cryptic (non-mlr) microcystin degradation by Acidovorax sp. has previously been reported; here, we confirmed that an Acidovorax culture isolated from the 2023 western Lake Erie bloom can also degrade microcystin and that its genome lacks mlr genes. We evaluated microcystin degradation by Acidovorax in growth experiments with BG11 media supplemented with microcystin as the only carbon source. Acidovorax growth was observed and microcystin degradation was validated by ELISA, reducing microcystin levels by 56.5% over 48 hours. We coupled these degradation assays with transcriptomic analyses to identify upregulated genes associated with this cryptic degradation pathway. This project aims to broaden our understanding of microcystin degradation mechanisms within the Microcystis-associated bacterial community and enable further identification of microcystin-degrading bacteria.

presentations.title: Coastal giant viruses and their interactions with hosts in China
presentations.abstract: Giant viruses, including marseilleviruses, are a group of double-stranded DNA viruses within the Nucleocytoviricota phylum that have a complex biology, which has never been described in other viruses. Here, we isolated some new marseilleviruses infecting Acanthamoeba castellanii, from mangroves, namely, Shenzhenvirus, Futianvirus, Dashavirus, and Xiwanvirus. Genomic analyses revealed that the four marseilleviruses carried different translation-associated protein gene sets. Shenzhenvirus is the first reported marseillevirus, to our best knowledge, lacking viral peptide chain release factor 3 (vRF3), while viral peptide chain release factor 1 (vRF1) is absent in Futianvirus. The in-silico tertiary structures revealed the conserved nucleotide-binding sites of vRF3 with GDP and vRF1 with mRNA and indicated their conserved roles during the termination step of protein biosynthesis. The protein interactome analyses revealed the interactions between vRF3 and eukaryotic RF1 (eRF1) or vRF1 and eukaryotic RF3 (eRF3) in A. castellanii. Combining the interface of the in-silico cellular-viral RF3·RF1 complex, we suggest that the viral homologs imitate the cellular termination protein complex to terminate host protein biosynthesis. Our results reveal that diverse marseilleviruses employ different strategies to hijack the amoeba translation system at the termination step by imitating cellular translation factors.

presentations.title: Depth discrete viral diversity and potential metabolic impacts across the Laurentian Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Viruses are the most abundant biological entities on earth and have important effects on microbial populations and biogeochemical cycling. Despite significant advances in understanding the diversity of viruses in natural environments, the ecological impacts of freshwater viruses remain poorly understood, particularly in large, deep lakes. The Laurentian Great Lakes are a useful model for studying viral ecology across lake ecosystems as they encompass a wide range of environmental conditions and diverse microbial communities. We characterized viral diversity in all five Great Lakes across seasons, nutrient gradients, and depths. In epilimnion samples, viral communities differed by lake, suggesting local-scale infection dynamics predominate in this interconnected system. Large, eukaryote-infecting Megaviruses were particularly abundant in surface samples. In hypolimnion samples, environmental similarity was associated with similar viral communities despite limited mixing between physically distant communities. Viral communities showed overall similarity across the hypolimnia of the Great Lakes, but viral OTUs were more likely to be endemic to a specific lake in the hypolimnion than the epilimnion. The Great Lakes appeared to share more viral OTUs with global deep lakes than nearby shallow lakes. Viral genomes contained numerous genes to manipulate the metabolism of their hosts. For example, phages predicted to infect nitrite oxidizing Nitrospirota, which dominate the hypolimnion of the deepest Great Lakes, encoded carbon fixation and nitrogen assimilation genes. Together, these results demonstrate how physical processes, local environmental conditions, and host community structure interact to shape viral communities in deep lakes, with important consequences for biogeochemistry.

presentations.title: Metagenomic Characterization of Microbial Community Shifts Associated with Prymnesium Blooms in the Oder River
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: (sai.hariharan@igb-berlin.de) Harmful algal blooms in freshwater systems are closely linked to underlying microbial community dynamics, which shape bloom onset, severity, and ecological impact. Following the unprecedented toxic Prymnesium parvum bloom in the Oder River in 2022, microbial community dynamics within the river were investigated with molecular tools. The study focused on bacteria, cyanobacteria, fungi, and other eukaryotes to better understand how microbial spatio-temporal dynamics changed with HABs. Sampling was conducted across 16 spatially distributed sites, including tributaries and ecologically buffered floodplain sites (refugees), between June 2023 and September 2024. Using a combined Illumina and Nanopore sequencing approach, high-resolution taxonomic profiling was carried out. The dual-platform strategy captured both short-read accuracy and long-read continuity, which improved assembly quality and functional annotation, particularly for complex and low-abundance taxa. This effort also led to the development of a gene catalog to better characterize overall gene abundances. The comparisons reveal marked shifts in microbial diversity and community composition during bloom events, alongside distinct functional signatures within a hydrological context. An integrated metagenomic approach facilitated better identification of microbial taxa and functional genes associated with bloom events, offering potential indicators for early detection. Linking the microbial community shifts with functional responses across spatial gradients, results in deeper ecological understanding of bloom dynamics.

presentations.title: The first 100+ weeks from PhytoChop, a microbial observatory on the Choptank River (Chesapeake Bay)
presentations.affiliation: University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences
presentations.abstract: The PhytoChop Observatory was recently established on the Choptank River, a subestuary of the Chesapeake Bay, to advance an understanding of microbial interactions and their biogeochemical relevance. We are collecting weekly size-fractionated filters for DNA, first targeting 16S/18S rRNA and COI amplicon analyses. Here we will present the first ~125 weeks of amplicon data analysis (June 2023 to December 2025). Strong seasonal patterns emerge at all organizational levels. Warm-season prokaryotes are enriched in Cyanobacteria (Cyanobium and Synechococcus), Planctomycetota, and Nitrososphaeria (archaeal ammonia oxidizers), with the latter showing abrupt fall increases. Cold seasons favor Bacteroidota, Verrucomicrobia, and Pseudomonadota. Free-living fractions favor Actinomycetota, while particle-associated fractions are enriched in Planctomycetota. Unexpectedly, Synechococcus were also enriched in the larger size fraction, suggesting possible associations with particles such as chitinous surfaces and a greater contributions to benthic fluxes than previously assumed. This molecular approach also enables assessment of niche partitioning among ASVs within genera. While many genera exhibit single modes (e.g., Eurytemora prefers <10°C, Micromonas >25°C), others display multimodal distributions. Skeletonema, e.g., exhibits three temperature modes (9°C, 19°C, 26°C), suggesting three co-dominant species. Such analyses may reveal cryptic species and help inform predictions of community shifts under environmental change.

presentations.title: ASSESSING MICROBIAL DIVERSITY IN MANITOBA LAKES USING OXFORD NANOPORE SEQUENCING
presentations.abstract: Freshwater microbial communities play essential roles in nutrient cycling, productivity, and ecosystem stability, yet microbial diversity across many regions of the Canadian Prairies remains poorly characterized. To contribute baseline data for Manitoba’s surface waters, we collected over 50 surface water samples from 20 lakes during the summer of 2024. Water was collected in sterile 500-mL containers, filtered onto 0.22 µm Sterivex GP filters, and temporarily stored on ice or in local freezers before transfer to the laboratory, where filters were archived at −70 °C. DNA was extracted using the Qiagen DNeasy PowerSoil kit, quantified using a Qubit fluorometer, and processed for shotgun metagenomic sequencing using Oxford Nanopore barcoded library preparation, including negative controls for contamination monitoring. Here we present preliminary analyses characterizing taxonomic composition and relative abundance across sampling sites, identifying a core of common taxa that have also been identified in large metagenomic surveys like Canadian Lake Pulse. Using metagenomic binning, we reconstructed draft genomes for dozens of bacteria, including Harmful Algal Bloom associated cyanobacteria, which were highly abundant in some lakes. This project contributes to broader assessments of watershed-scale microbial diversity, including downstream connectivity and transport toward Hudson Bay.

presentations.title: Metabolic capabilities of marine fungi in Sargasso Sea
presentations.abstract: Contribution of marine fungi in biogeochemical cycles and utilization of organic matter in marine environments has recently attracted attention. Still, our understanding of their functional diversity is lacking. Therefore, we isolated several fungal strains from seawater sampled in Sargasso Sea (surface, 80, 200, and 300m). We identified them using a combination of morphological descriptions and their phylogenetic placement through at least two biomarkers. We used FF MicroPlateTM to assess their metabolic capabilities over a 7-day period. FF MicroPlateTM contains 95 carbon sources whose interactions with fungal strains can be used as a proxy to evaluate their metabolic affinities. Our results showed that most isolated fungal strains are affiliated with Cladosporium and Penicillium. Additionally, we showed that these strains are present in all depths. Moreover, metabolic capabilities of Cladosporium and Penicillium strains, in terms of their utilization rates of different carbon sources, were shown to be significantly different. Our results suggest that although both Cladosporium and Penicillium strains are saprophytic lineages, they might engage with the biogeochemical cycles differently, by utilizing different sources of carbon throughout the water column.

presentations.title: KNOWLEDGE GAPS IN SUBMERGED MACROPHYTE RESEARCH LIMIT AQUATIC ECOSYSTEM CONSERVATION AND RESTORATION
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland
presentations.abstract: Submerged macrophytes are vital for maintaining good ecological status in freshwater and coastal ecosystems by shaping biodiversity, nutrient cycling, sediment dynamics, and water quality. Yet macrophyte communities are declining worldwide. Drawing on freshwater, marine, and terrestrial plant research, I argue that effective conservation and restoration are hindered by major knowledge gaps across organism, community, and ecosystem levels. At the organism level, understanding of physiological adaptations, life-history traits, and phenology under multiple stressors remains limited. New genomic and transcriptomic tools could clarify genetic diversity, stress tolerance, and adaptive responses, but are still rarely applied to macrophytes, and the roles of pathogens, endophytes, and microbiomes remain poorly known. Freshwater plant research is geographically biased and lacks model species. At the community level, interactions such as facilitation, including boom-bust dynamics of invasive species, are insufficiently understood. At the ecosystem level, macrophytes are underrepresented in models despite their influence on phenomena like alternative stable states. Monitoring gaps—including short time series and limited use of remotely operated vehicles—further impede management. Bridging these gaps requires interdisciplinary research linking genomic and physiological insights with community and ecosystem processes. Strengthening submerged macrophyte research is essential to predict responses to global change, improve restoration, and enhance the resilience of aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: MULTIPLE STRESSOR INTERACTIONS DRIVE UNPREDICTABLE PHYSIOLOGICAL RESPONSES IN SUBMERGED MACROPHYTES
presentations.abstract: Submerged macrophytes are central to freshwater ecosystem functioning but are declining globally under multiple anthropogenic stressors. We systematically reviewed 12,858 publications and extracted effect sizes from 124 experiments to identify general patterns in physiological responses and interaction types. Additive effects dominated (50%), indicating that accumulated stressors generally cause negative, but not necessarily amplified, responses. Synergistic interactions were relatively infrequent (14%) despite theoretical expectations of prevalence, though the limited number of experiments testing more than two stressors suggests their frequency may be underestimated. Most studies examined combinations of nutrient enrichment, shading, toxic trace metals, warming, and emerging contaminants such as PFAS and microplastics, typically under simplified 2×2 factorial laboratory designs. Antagonistic interactions often reflected dominance of a single stressor or compensatory responses, whereas synergisms were most frequent with metals combined with co-stressors enhancing bioavailability. Geographic and taxonomic biases were evident, with reliance on a few species and short-term assays. To improve mechanistic understanding, we propose Stuckenia pectinata as a model organism due to its cosmopolitan distribution, experimental tractability, and newly available genomic resources, enabling integration of physiological, molecular, and microbiome approaches. Expanding stressor complexity, experimental duration, and taxonomic breadth will strengthen predictions of macrophyte responses and inform freshwater conservation under global change.

presentations.title: Global Ecological Roles and Model Networks of Submerged Aquatic Vegetation Using AI-Aided Analysis
presentations.abstract: Submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV), including freshwater macrophytes and marine seagrasses, is fundamental to global aquatic ecosystems, regulating carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles while providing key services such as water purification and carbon sequestration. Drawing on an AI-aided analysis of 219 ecosystems, we identified primary ecological functions of SAV: flow attenuation, sediment stabilization, nutrient retention, carbon storage, oxygen production, competition with other primary producers, food provision, and habitat refuge. This functional portfolio is strongly conserved across lakes and reservoirs, rivers and streams, palustrine wetlands, estuaries and brackish lagoons, and marine shelves (mean pairwise Bray–Curtis similarity = 0.924, range 0.883–0.958). In contrast, mechanistic understanding remains highly fragmented: process-based frameworks cluster by ecosystem type (modularity = 0.854), with only 5.7% reused beyond their original domain. Overall, these findings reveal both the similarity of SAV roles across ecosystems and the fragmented nature of process-based modeling, underlining the need for integrative strategies to connect ecological understanding and modeling efforts globally.

presentations.title: Effects of artificial heating on periphyton and submerged macrophytes in temperate lakes
presentations.abstract: Experiments investigating the impacts of climate warming on aquatic primary producers and their interactions have often been conducted in laboratories or mesocosms, with contradictory results. Meanwhile, evidence at the ecosystem level remains scarce. We investigated the impact of artificial heating in a unique system of lakes in Konin, Poland, which is warmed by ~2°C by a power plant, using nearby non-heated lakes as a reference. Periphyton substrates and pre-grown macrophytes (Myriophyllum spicatum, Chara rudis) were deployed at five depths for four weeks. To quantify environmental effects, we used generalised additive models including both fixed predictors and random effects. Periphyton biomass increased significantly with warming and light availability, while grazer abundance had no effect. Macrophyte survival was strongly determined by light, with both species showing reduced survival under shaded conditions. Importantly, temperature had no direct effect on macrophyte survival, whereas periphyton biomass showed a negative effect, indicating that warming influenced macrophytes indirectly through increased periphyton shading. Overall, our results show that warming enhances periphyton biomass and strengthens shading pressure on submerged vegetation. Thus, the primary mechanism by which climate warming threatens macrophytes in temperate lacustrine ecosystems is indirect through periphyton-driven light limitation rather than direct thermal stress.

presentations.title: Major loss in algal species over 150 years of data: is ocean heating driving species loss in a biodiversity hotspot and how can it inform effective restoration?
presentations.abstract: We are in the midst of a global biodiversity crisis, with global heating and extreme events reshaping entire communities. Key amongst our concerns is the loss of habitats which support biodiversity and enhance ecosystem function. In many coastal marine systems, seaweeds are not only the major primary producers but also form extensive habitats. Yet, data on the effects of ocean heating and marine heatwaves on these algal assemblages is restricted to a few well-studied regions. Here, we have assembled a database of algal species records from the temperate-tropical climatic transition zone along the southern coast of China spanning ~170 years. We found that up to 150 species of algae have potentially been lost from the waters of Hong Kong, possibly representing poleward range shifts of a large percentage (>60% of recorded species) of the algal community. We then used in situ physiological measurements and laboratory warming experiments to demonstrate that warming winter (not summer) water temperatures over the past 3 decades have shortened the winter growth season for forest-forming Sargassum spp. Therefore, to save these once extensive seaweed forests from local extirpation we have begun implementing pre-treatment of juveniles in an attempt to “heat harden” them to future proof restoration attempts. Higher survival of heat-treated juveniles after out-planting points to potential early success, but also provides information to improve outcomes in future up-scaling of seaweed forest restoration.

presentations.title: ROOTED IN THE FUTURE: AN ECR PERSPECTIVE OF AQUATIC PLANT RESEARCH
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: (antonellabio@gmail.com) Aquatic ecosystems face complex and interconnected challenges — from climate change and unprecedented biodiversity loss to pressing management questions. Now, more than ever, we must take a diversified approach and incorporate fresh perspectives to tackle these challenges. Fresh perspectives can emerge from the development of new technologies and methods, interdisciplinary approaches, and growing computational power, while remaining deeply rooted in overarching ecological principles, rigorous science, and the historical development of the field. Here, we explore how early career researchers (ECRs) in the aquatic plant community see the future of macrophyte research. Based on a recent survey of 147 ECRs, the discussion highlights the priority areas where the field can expand, innovate, and respond to global ecological demands. We present potential theoretical, technological, and methodological advances, weaving in our own perspectives. Finally, we discuss the challenges that ECRs face in research, as well as the importance and opportunities for developing professional and social networks that facilitate engagement, information exchange, knowledge generation, and foster lasting collaborations to advance aquatic plant science. Through this talk, we reflect on how ECRs are building a macrophyte science that critically engages with the past, while extending its roots into the future. Strategic collaboration with, and among, the next generation will be key to effectively addressing environmental challenges.

presentations.title: Competing stressed out engineers – Influence of engineer species competition on benthic invertebrate community structure
presentations.abstract: Dominant species interactions, such as ones among ecosystem engineers like eelgrass and mussels, shape community structure in ecosystems. Multiple stressors are likely to affect the direction and strength of these interactions: it is an area poorly understood while having a crucial role in understanding how restoration can be successful under global changes. To demystify the influence of interaction among ecosystem engineers on invertebrate communities affected by burial events related to storms, we conducted a factorial in situ experiment in Rimouski Bay (Québec) with forty eelgrass quadrats in which we implanted, or not, blue mussels, macroalgae debris and seashell ash. Every month, we collected eelgrass morphometrics and sediments physicochemical properties. To evaluate the effects of our treatments after a whole growing season, benthic invertebrates were sampled after fourteen weeks of exposure in September 2025. Our preliminary results show that seashell ash increase sediment pH, eelgrass density and colonization by amphipods and polychaetes, likely because seashell have influenced sediment chemical conditions. Mussel presence and macroalgae enrichment limited eelgrass length, potentially because of competition for space and light. Considering the important effects of our treatments on eelgrass, we expect to observe cascading effects of mussel and stressors presence on invertebrate community structures in our upcoming results.

presentations.title: REVISING LAKE THERMAL MIXING CLASSIFICATIONS: INSIGHTS FROM MOUNTAIN LAKES
presentations.abstract: Classic limnological theory categorizes lakes into discrete mixing types (e.g., dimictic, polymictic) based on seasonal patterns shaped by latitude, elevation, and morphometry. These classifications guide interpretation of seasonal dynamics, species distributions, and ecosystem functions, but they assume steady climatic forcing and predictable annual overturn. This assumption limits predictive capacity because it treats mixing regimes as fixed properties rather than outcomes of variable energy inputs and storage. Observations now show that climate driven changes in lake energetics can alter mixing behavior, and many lakes are either actively shifting from one regime to another (e.g., dimictic to monomictic), or simply never conformed to a single classification. High interannual variability in ice-off timing, long term trends in ice out timing, and within-year variation in surface heat budgets produce mixing patterns that are inconsistent from year to year and difficult to classify within the traditional framework. These dynamics are especially evident in mountain regions where snowpack accumulation and melt strongly structure the seasonal energy budget. Lakes in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California, which experience high variation in snowpack size and duration of ice cover, illustrate mechanisms that drive between-year shifts in mixing behavior. We use mountain lakes to highlight how interannual variation in snowpack can govern mixing regimes, and propose a revised conceptual model of lake mixing regimes that incorporates temporal variability and differing magnitudes of spring mixing.

presentations.title: Lake volume and elevation determine thermal sensitivity of mountain lakes to variation in snowpack and ice cover
presentations.abstract: Mountain lakes exhibit higher interannual variability in water temperature than other lakes. This is because snow, which comprises a large fraction of lake ice in these systems, can vary considerably from year to year, influencing the timing and duration of lake heat gain. The responsiveness of lake temperature and stratification strength to variation in snowpack and ice cover should depend on lake and watershed attributes that mediate lake heat budgets. We used six years (2019 - 2024) of continuous hourly temperature data collected from 14 lakes in the California Mountain Lake Network (CaMoLaN) of the Sierra Nevada, USA, to quantify each lake’s thermal sensitivity to variation in snowpack. Lake volume and elevation both mediated the influence of snowpack and variation in ice-off date on lake warming —in general, small, high elevation lakes, which comprise the majority of lakes in the Sierra Nevada, were more responsive than other lakes. Loss of snowpack associated with climate warming trends will have profound implications for temperature-dependent ecosystem functions in lakes in the Sierra Nevada and other mountain ranges around the world.

presentations.title: CLIMATE CHANGE REFUGIA IN WARMING MOUNTAIN LAKES
presentations.abstract: In response to global environmental change, mountain lakes present a duality: they may act as highly-susceptible sentinels of change while, simultaneously, providing climate-change refugia across the landscape. Research on climate-change refugia in aquatic systems often emphasizes cold water habitats located in high-elevation regions, but this concept remains understudied in lentic compared to lotic systems. Furthermore, the role of high-elevation refugia is uncertain as lakes experience loss of ice and rising temperatures, and associated biological responses remain unclear. Here, we describe ice and water temperature dynamics in small, remote lakes ranging from 76 to 955 m above sea level in the northern Appalachian Mountains, USA, and evaluate the role of elevation in supporting cold habitat conditions. We also examined zooplankton phenology and community composition responses across this elevational gradient. We found that ice persisted on average 8 days longer in high elevation (>500 m) lakes compared to lower elevation sites, and water temperatures warmed faster but maximum temperatures remained lower in high-elevation lakes. Zooplankton phenology was driven by water temperature across all sites, but taxa varied in response to lake conditions and high- and low-elevation lakes supported different zooplankton assemblages. These patterns suggest that subalpine mountain lakes with longer ice duration and cooler summer temperatures may serve as important climate-change refugia, even as they warm over time.

presentations.title: LAKE-STREAM LINKAGES INFLUENCE TEMPERATURES, RESIDENCE TIMES, NUTRIENT TRANSPORT AND BIOTIC RESPONSES IN MOUNTAIN WATERSHEDS
presentations.abstract: In Sawtooth Mountain watersheds (Idaho, USA) lakes represent up to 94% of the water surface area, whereas streams have 76-86% of the water margin with land. Consequently, in summer, lakes act as solar collectors, whereas streams collect groundwater and cool the system. Consequently, the pattern of lakes and streams within a watershed have multiple effects. In summer, lake outflows were dramatically warmer than stream inflows (mean del 6.4 C, max 12.5 C) and had far smaller diel fluctuations (3.7 vs 5.1 C). As water travels downstream from lakes, temperatures cooled as rapidly as 9 C per km, but cooling was usually insufficient to reduce temperatures to baseline conditions before another lake is encountered. Trout densities were 240% higher in a warm (17 C) outflow than in a cold inflow (7.5 C). Terminal lakes without upstream lakes had cold inflows that plunged into the metalimnia, delivering nutrients there and supporting deep chlorophyll maxima, whereas in lakes with warm inflows, water and nutrients flowed into the epilimnia resulting in shorter effective residence times. Plunging inflows aided the lakes in capturing nutrient loading during spring snowmelt and delivering it slowly over the summer into outflow streams. Consequently, watersheds with several lakes had higher late summer nutrient levels than those with few lakes. Consequently, understanding how climate warming will influence the physical, chemical, and biological responses of mountain lakes and streams will require a landscape analysis of the interactions of these two subsystems.

presentations.title: Global change influences productivity in a glacial Sockeye Salmon nursery lake.
presentations.abstract: Glacial recession is changing mountain lake environments, including salmon nursery lakes. The loss of glaciers and associated changes in these watersheds can have variable effects, and may cause both reductions or increases in the productivity of salmon nursery lakes. Meziadin Lake is a glacially influenced lake in northwestern British Columbia, and the largest Sockeye Salmon nursery lake in the Nass River watershed. We evaluate five years of coupled physiochemical, zooplankton, and hydroacoustic fish surveys to describe the trophic dynamics and productivity of Meziadin Lake, using a bioenergetics model to estimate production and consumption of zooplankton. Results indicate that Meziadin Lake exhibits distinct glacial-driven physicochemical and biological gradients across space and time. While total zooplankton prey appear underutilized by sockeye fry, Daphnia represent the keystone zooplankton prey and high rates of consumption to production of Daphnia may limit fry growth in some years. We compare our results to available historical data to describe some ways this mountain lake has responded to global change over the past half century. Finally, we investigate how future glacial loss may affect food availability for sockeye fry by simulating a series of bioenergetics models under warmer lake temperature scenarios. Our study has implications for understanding the trajectories of other mountain lakes and salmon habitat throughout the Pacific region, as well as inform salmon management and conservation strategies such as the designation of Indigenous Protected Areas.

presentations.title: As the crow flies or as the fish swims? Permeability of a mountain landscape to dispersal of aquatic organisms
presentations.abstract: Lakes are habitat islands in a terrestrial matrix. Aquatic organisms disperse among lakes over land by wind or phoresy, or through hydrologic networks. Which pathway is most important may depend on organismal traits and landscape, climatic and hydrologic features. We characterized geographic centrality for 9,099 lakes in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California as the average Euclidean distance to all neighboring lakes, and hydrologic centrality as the average distance via surface water flow paths. We then compared the structure of crustacean zooplankton communities and the population occupancy of amphibians, fish and fairy shrimp in 376 lakes with the both centrality metrics. We found distinct effects of geographic vs. hydrologic centrality on zooplankton diversity and the occupancy of aquatic taxa. Our results indicate that different groups of aquatic organisms follow distinct dispersal pathways to move among lakes in mountain landscapes.

presentations.title: Insights from the Sierra Nevada Range CA, USA: Drivers of zooplankton community structure in a highly variable environment.
presentations.abstract: Average air temperatures are warming and precipitation variability is increasing across the California Sierra Nevada to determine the role of spatial and temporal variation in environmental conditions in shaping mountain lake zooplankton communities, we sampled lakes across a range of 2,500 - 3500 meters over 13 years. Within the past 13 years, the lakes have experienced a climate regime consisting of typically dry years that have low precipitation interrupted by intermittent years with extremely high snowfall. We present these lakes as natural laboratories to explore ecosystem responses of zooplankton communities to high amplitude environmental variability. We observe increasing trends in nutrients and chlorophyll over time. Surface water temperature is associated with elevation and air temperature regardless of snowpack. Wet years tend to have lower chlorophyll, higher zooplankton abundance, and lower water transparency. We find shallow lakes to be more susceptible to hydroclimate variability, whereas deep lakes are buffered from annual variability. Zooplankton communities become more variable at higher elevation and temperature. Our findings reveal that the interplay between climate variability, lake depth, and trophic structure governs mountain lake zooplankton dynamics.

presentations.title: FISH REDUCE SECONDARY PRODUCTIVITY OF ZOOPLANKTON IN MOUNTAIN LAKES
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton secondary productivity is a crucial link in lake food webs, but is poorly quantified in mountain lakes, where steep environmental gradients and strong biotic pressures interact. Using a chitobiase-based assay, we measured zooplankton secondary production in twelve Yosemite National Park lakes spanning a broad elevational gradient, with half of the lakes containing fish and half naturally fishless. We found that zooplankton biomass and secondary production declined strongly with elevation (biomass p=0.02; productivity p=0.007), indicating possible resource and temperature limitations at alpine elevations. Although zooplankton biomass did not differ between fish and fishless lakes (p=0.31), lakes with introduced trout showed reduced zooplankton secondary productivity (p=0.006) and longer whole-lake biomass turnover times (p=0.02) relative to fishless lakes. This mismatch between biomass and productivity reveals that standing stock alone can mask significant functional differences in how zooplankton communities respond to predation and environmental factors. Our findings demonstrate that elevation and fish presence jointly suppress zooplankton productivity in Sierra Nevada mountain lakes, highlighting the importance of functional metrics for detecting changes in ecosystem processes that biomass alone cannot capture.

presentations.title: Seasonal trends in community structure of alpine lakes in the Wind River Range, WY
presentations.abstract: Climate change and anthropogenic disturbances will affect montane and high alpine ecosystems across the globe through shifting snow and ice phenology. The Wind River Range, Wyoming is home to more than 1,300 named alpine lakes. Warmer and earlier snow-free springs will result in earlier and longer growing seasons for aquatic residents including phytoplankton, zooplankton, and historically stocked trout (Salvelinus spp. & Oncorhynchus spp.). We aim to assess how shifts in the timing and duration of growing season will affect alpine communities by examining the mechanistic relationship between trout, zooplankton, and algal biomass across the ice-free season in a chain lake basin. In 2024, we sampled each lake six times from May to October for water column chemistry, zooplankton biomass and community structure, and trout growth metrics. Using a combination of satellite imagery and remotely sensed snowpack metrics we defined these sampling events in terms of days post ice-off to quantify the seasonal relationship among spring turnover, herbivore zooplankton (e.g. Daphnia spp.), and standing algal biomass. Preliminary results show an early season peak in algal biomass followed by a delayed increase in herbivore zooplankton biomass. Despite high predation by trout, herbivore zooplankton biomass remained high whereas algal biomass remained low for the remainder of the growing season. These observed dynamics present an opportunity to assess how future climate scenarios may affect the present balance between algal biomass and zooplankton community structure.

presentations.title: Anthropogenic transformation of zooplankton biodiversity in remote alpine lakes recorded by sedimentary DNA
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic stressors alter biodiversity through top-down, bottom-up, and multi-level effects on ecological communities. Sedimentary DNA provides novel long-term perspectives, clarifying how these impacts depart from historic variability. Mountain lakes represent a model system involving top-down predation from introduced fish, bottom-up fertilization from nutrient pollution, and multi-level consequences of warming. Here, we reconstruct zooplankton communities by applying 18S rRNA metabarcoding to sediment cores from seven lakes in Wyoming and compare recent decades with previous centuries. Fish introductions and their interactions with nitrogen deposition and warming created large shifts away from baseline zooplankton communities. Large copepods dominated pre-impact communities and still act as keystone species in fishless lakes today, revealing limited natural variability. In lakes with twentieth-century fish introductions, however, small-bodied Daphnia rapidly increased, followed by small copepods in recent decades. Sedimentary DNA provides essential context showing that top-down predation transformed communities, making them more susceptible to chronic nitrogen deposition and warming.

presentations.title: PLANKTON DIVERSITY PATTERNS IN RAPIDLY CHANGING HIGH ALPLINE LAKES
presentations.abstract: High alpine planktonic communities are expected to be strongly impacted by climate change, with many of the effects indirect and modulated by local factors. To investigate this, since 2017 we have annually sampled the zooplankton communities and abiotic parameters of 18 high alpine lakes in the Austrian Hohe Tauern national park. The lakes encompass wide ranges of size, altitude, depth, and age. While microclimate is a dominant driver of the annual temperature cycle, long-term trends are emerging, with earlier ice-out dates and higher summer temperatures. Zooplankton communities show high beta diversity, with some species only occurring in a single lake. Lakes in close geographic proximity are often very different from another, with only water bodies with direct physical connections having similar communities. However, when comparing the first and second 4-year periods of the study, a pattern of increasing similarity emerges. This has not been accompanied by increasing gamma diversity, suggesting exchange of species between lakes is a more important mechanism than new species establishing themselves. While high alpine lakes are typically oligotrophic, several of our lakes have deep chlorophyll maxima with remarkably high chlorophyll values, albeit with high interannual variability. With logistical restraints limiting sampling to one date per year, the degree of intra-annual variability in the chlorophyll and zooplankton data remains unexplored. These data provide a baseline to measure the impending changes in high alpine aquatic communities brought on by climate change.

presentations.title: PREDATOR COLONIZATIONS DRIVE THERMOPHILIZATION BUT NOT HOMOGENIZATION IN MOUNTAIN LAKE MACROINVERTEBRATES
presentations.abstract: Ecological communities are responding to rapid climate warming. Thermophilization and homogenization are increasingly documented as patterns of warming-driven biodiversity change, with recent work demonstrating that thermophilization does not necessarily lead to taxonomic homogenization. However, homogenization can occur among species (taxonomic homogenization) or their traits (functional homogenization), with a trend in one facet not necessarily implying a trend in the other. Despite this, little attention has been given to the dynamical links between thermophilization and functional homogenization. Using mountain lake macroinvertebrate samples separated by 20 years of climate warming and declining winter snowpack, we found that colonizations by macroinvertebrate predators drove significant thermophilization, with contemporary compositions reflecting historically lower elevation communities. However, predator colonizations contributed only slightly to taxonomic and functional homogenization, and overall homogenization was minimal for either measure. Because thermophilization was driven almost entirely by colonizations and led to only minimal changes in beta diversity, our results could reflect a state of transience or resilience in mountain lake responses to climate warming.
