presentations.title: SENSITIVITY OF LONG-TERM ECOLOGICAL DATA: AN ANALYSIS OF THE EFFECTS OF REDUCED SAMPLING FREQUENCY ON WATER QUALITY TRENDS IN A MOUNTAIN WATERSHED
presentations.abstract: Long-term ecological data are critical for understanding ecosystem responses to climate change and are stronger drivers of environmental policy and resource management than short-term studies. Such datasets are especially important for high-elevation systems, where warming is amplified and lakes are coupled with the cryosphere, yet these datasets are costly to maintain. As both ecosystems and monitoring programs face growing threats, there is a need to establish and maintain long-term monitoring programs that minimize costs while maximizing captured variation and abilities to make ecological inferences. Using a 30+ year aquatic biogeochemical record from the Loch Vale watershed in Rocky Mountain National Park, we evaluate how reduced sampling frequency affects trends and variability in long-term data. We statistically subsampled the historical weekly time series to fortnightly and monthly frequencies and assessed changes in estimated trends in major cations and in distributions and variability of nitrate fluxes annually and during snowmelt, baseflow, and winter. Preliminary results show that estimated trends in solutes indicative of weathering are largely preserved when sampling frequency is reduced, though inference strength can weaken. In contrast, nitrate concentrations and N flux estimates are sensitive to statistical downsampling, especially during hydrologically variable periods. These results highlight the need to collect long-term data at frequencies aligned with research goals and to guide adaptation of monitoring programs for personnel maintaining these datasets.

presentations.title: CHANGES IN PRIMARY PRODUCER PIGMENT COMPOSITION AND ASSOCIATED PALEOECOLOGICAL/CLIMATOLOGICAL DRIVERS IN LAKE CINILI, THE TAURUS MOUNTAINS, TURKIYE
presentations.abstract: Alpine Lake sediments may contain a record of past climatic changes unaffected by human activity. We conducted the first large-scale paleoecological sampling in Anatolian alpine lakes between 2019-2023, collecting 15 sediment cores. Here, we present multiproxy results from an 85 cm core in Lake Çinili (11 m deep at 2667 m a.s.l.) and reconstruct its paleoecological history. C-14 dating of pollen suggests the core is approximately 2200 years old, with a possibly high reservoir age. Pigment analysis identified a total of 13 pigments, with high cyanobacterial pigment levels between 2200 and 800 BP. Diatom contribution has increased over the past 450 years. CN and XRF analyses showed significant fluctuations in organic matter and terrestrial input over time, with an overall decline in allochthonous carbon. The Mn/Fe ratio indicated abrupt water level drops and potential droughts between 649 and 410 BP. The alloxanthin/diatoxanthin ratio also reflected changes in water level linked to precipitation shifts. Clustering of pigments identified four periods aligning with the Roman Climatic Optimum, Medieval Climate Anomaly, and Little Ice Age. Overall, Lake Çinili experienced notable changes in water level and primary producer composition over the last 2200 years, demonstrating that regional climate fluctuations significantly impact the lake ecosystem. Results suggest that climate fluctuations in the region have a pronounced effect on the Lake Çinili ecosystem and Alpine lakes in Anatolia may serve as a potential paleoecological record.

presentations.title: TESTING THE ECOSYSTEM SIZE AND PRODUCTIVE SPACE HYPOTHESES IN ALPINE LAKES
presentations.abstract: This study evaluates two competing hypotheses for what regulates the architecture of food webs in California mountain lakes: ecosystem size or productivity. We measured food chain length and six multidimensional isotopic niche space measures in 36 mountain lakes representing varying lake volume and productivity dynamics. We demonstrate a modicum of support for the ecosystem size hypothesis, but no support for the productive space hypothesis. Across lakes ranging vastly in volume (8,773 – 3,999,753 m3), food chain length, and all multidimensional isotopic space niche measures showed positive trends with ecosystem size. However, only three measures (trophic area, niche centroid distance, and δ13C range) scaled significantly. There were no significant relationships between lake productivity and any of the six community niche metrics. Aquatic insects supported fish consumers in all lakes. However, reliance of consumer fishes on terrestrial insects and periphyton increased significantly and non-linearly with lake size, while reliance on aquatic plants showed opposite trends. These results expand understanding of the biogeography of aquatic food webs, and contextualize how ecosystem size and productivity drive trophic links in mountain lakes specifically.

presentations.title: WARDENS, BARRIERS AND PERSISTENCE: MECHANISMS DRIVING ZOOPLANKTON SPECIES COMPOSITION OF HIGH ALPINE LAKES
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton species in high alpine lakes face harsh conditions in extreme environments, with low productivity and short ice-free periods. Due to warming in alpine regions these hostile environments are rapidly changing, with earlier ice out, increasing water temperatures, and potential changes in productivity and accessibility. This has the possibility to both create habitats more amenable to lowland zooplankton species and to provide more opportunities for lowland species to colonize these habitats, leading to alternate species composition in the lakes. Potential barriers to colonization (competitive exclusion, harsh environments), as well as the concept of species sorting within the zooplankton community of the lakes of the National Park Hohe Tauern, Austria, have been investigated, with the following hypotheses: 1. When large zooplankton species are already present in a lake, they can preclude invasion by new lowland species through competitive exclusion. 2. The hostile environment (low temperature and productivity, high turbidity) of some high alpine lakes is limiting the colonization success of invading species. 3. Species sorting occurs, in that the species or clones found in a lake are those best adapted to the habitat in which they were found. Based on the results of the long-term monitoring of 18 lakes of the National Park Hohe Tauern, Austria, model lakes were chosen and the water and species from these lakes used to run experiments in the lab under controlled conditions.

presentations.title: USING SUBARCTIC ATLIN LAKE AS A SPACE-FOR-TIME MODEL FOR DIMINISHING GLACIAL INPUTS TO LARGE MOUNTAIN LAKES
presentations.abstract: Glacier meltwaters are an important source of nutrients, labile carbon, and cold waters to aquatic organisms in downstream freshwater systems. Atlin Lake is a large (791 km2 area) subarctic lake in Yukon and British Columbia, Canada within the Traditional Territories of the Taku River Tlingit (TRTFN) and Carcross/Tagish First Nations (C/TFN). The southern end of Atlin Lake is fed by the Juneau Icefield and other glaciers of the Coast Mountains, while the northern end is glacier-free and fed by streams from forested boreal catchments. Importantly, the outflow occurs mid-lake, separating the southern and northern ends and supporting a natural space-for-time design within a single system that allows us to predict how the southern glacier-fed end of Atlin Lake will change over time. With the glaciers feeding Atlin Lake predicted to be 60% gone by 2100, questions remain about the impact of climate change on the function of Atlin Lake. We comprehensively sampled physical (e.g., temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH), chemical (e.g., nutrients, carbon), and biological (e.g., phytoplankton pigments and speciation, zooplankton speciation and isotopes) parameters, notably from both open-water (i.e., summer) and below-ice (i.e., winter) depth-profiling in the northern (80 m) and southern (270 m) ends of Atlin Lake. Preliminary pigment results indicate that the northern end of Atlin Lake is nearly twice as productive as the southern end. Therefore, working closely with TRTFN and C/TFN, we seek to answer the critical question of how Atlin Lake – and other glacier-fed alpine lakes globally – will adapt to climate change.

presentations.title: Warming-induced release of benthic nutrients in mountain lakes: an incubation experiment
presentations.abstract: Mountain lakes are generally extremely oligotrophic, which limits the production of aquatic biomass and gives them the crystal-clear waters that make them popular tourist destinations. Recently, stakeholders involved in the French Lacs Sentinelles network (https://www.lacs-sentinelles.org) have observed a proliferation of benthic algae in the littoral zones of high-altitude lakes. These observations echo recent studies documenting a proliferation of benthic algae in many oligotrophic lakes around the world, whether located in lowlands or in mountains1,2. Among the various hypotheses proposed to explain this phenomenon, the interaction between the pronounced warming of high-altitude lakes and nutrients’ cycling is to date the most likely explanation yet to be tested3,4. Here, we test whether the increasing temperature of littoral zones in mountain lakes can trigger the release of nutrients contained in sediments to the water column. In spring 2025, littoral sediment cores were collected before ice melt in two mountain lakes (one forested, one proglacial) in the French Alps and brought back to the lab. The cores were then either submitted to increasing temperatures in a ~2-week incubation experiment (n=4, treatment group) or kept cold (n=4, control group) and were analyzed for the chemical composition of the overlying water at regular intervals. Increasing temperature induced a significant release of sediment ammonium to the overlying water for the forested lake, but not for the proglacial lake. Both lakes exhibited similarly decreasing nitrate concentration with warming, but no significant evolution of phosphate was measured. Analysis of the temperature sensitivity (Q10) of sediment microbial respiration revealed a significant temperature influence for the forested lake (Q10=2) but not for the proglacial lake (Q10≤1). These preliminary results highlight the potential importance of temperature as a driver of nutrient cycling in littoral sediments of mountain lakes. 1.

presentations.title: THE MOUNTAIN FUTURES YOUTUBE CHANNEL: SHARING MOUNTAIN SCIENCE WITH A GLOBAL AUDIENCE
presentations.abstract: Mountain landscapes are critical to the well-being of billions of people, yet they are often remote and difficult to access which makes it hard for people to connect to them. Still, incredible research is happening in mountains, including in the lakes and rivers they support. Despite the rich and important potential for storytelling, the people doing mountain research often exist in relative anonymity for the public. In 2024, I launched the Mountain Futures YouTube channel with a simple goal: raising the global profile of mountain science and the people studying these critical ecosystems. With no filmmaking experience, it has been a lesson in learning by doing. Just over a year in, we’ve grown to 600 subscribers from around the world and our videos have been watched more than 90,000 times. In our view, this is just the beginning. For this poster presentation, I will share the premise behind the channel and the plan for how we will sustain and grow it into the future. I will also invite mountain researchers—particularly those studying mountain lakes, streams, and the cryosphere—to connect with our team and perhaps be featured in a future video. If nothing else, I hope this poster will encourage mountain limnologists to think outside of the science communication box and pursue new avenues to share their work.

presentations.title: The Effects of Rock Glacier Meltwater on Thermal Regimes and Nutrient Characteristics in Alpine Lakes in the Uinta Mountains, USA: Preliminary Findings
presentations.abstract: Climate-induced warming represents a significant threat to alpine lakes, including rock glacier lakes. Warming temperatures increase the melt rate of rock glaciers, increasing the relative hydrological contribution of meltwater to adjacent lakes and streams. Our research focuses on the following question: How have warming-induced meltwater contributions from adjacent rock glaciers impacted the thermal regime and nutrient characteristics of lakes in the Uinta Mountains, USA? To investigate this, we analyzed sedimentary chlorophyll a and changes in diatom community composition in a 210Pb-dated sediment core from Gail Lake, a rock-glacier adjacent lake in Uinta Mountains, to infer environmental changes over the last several centuries. Our research indicates that despite enhanced nitrate loading from meltwater, evidenced by the dominance of Asterionella formosa in the uppermost sediments, rock glacier lakes have not experienced concomitant increases in contemporary primary production. Moreover, we find that rock glacier lakes are predominantly characterized by low water clarity and a shallow mixed layer, evidenced by the presence of Discostella stelligera throughout these sediment cores. We suggest that while rock glacier meltwater increases the availability of nitrate, it simultaneously contributes to cold, turbid lake conditions that limit primary production. Our research advances understandings of the effects of rock glacier meltwaters on alpine lake ecosystems at a critical time, as warming increases the hydrological impact of rock glaciers on alpine catchments around the world.

presentations.title: ECOSYSTEM-ATMOSPHERE CO2 EXCHANGE IN SUB-ARCTIC LAKES; WHAT IS THE ROLE OF EMERGENT MACROPHYTES?
presentations.abstract: Northern lakes are important sources of carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere, yet global estimates of lake CO2 exchange remain uncertain. In particular, the contribution of emergent macrophyte vegetation to lakes’ greenhouse gas (GHG) exchange is poorly known. We hypothesized that in sub-arctic lakes, often poor in organic matter and nutrients, vegetated areas contribute substantially to lakes’ ecosystem-atmosphere net CO2 and GHG exchange. To test this hypothesis, we studied three lakes in the Atmosphere-Ecosystem Supersite in Pallas, Finland (68°00'N 24°09'E). The lakes had low organic carbon and nutrient concentrations but differed in catchment properties and sediment organic content. We measured ecosystem-atmosphere CO2 exchange for two years in open water and vegetated areas (Carex spp., Equisetum fluviatile and Nuphar lutea) with paired transparent and opaque chamber measurements using portable GHG analyzers. In addition, high-frequency water CO2 concentration and eddy covariance measurements were conducted in one lake. Macrophyte abundances were modeled using field and Sentinel-1 and 2-data. We observed net uptake of CO2 in the vegetated areas, ca. 100–500 g CO2 m2 y-1, which counters the effect of the CO2 emissions in the open water areas, ca. 100–200 g CO2 m2 y-1. On the other hand, macrophyte production can fuel heterotrophic respiration due to relocation of dead plant material. Accounting for the vegetated areas in lakes’ GHG exchange is essential and assuming that they behave like terrestrial wetlands is not a valid approach.

presentations.title: Managed hydrochory: A novel process-based restoration approach for submerged macrophytes in regulated rivers
presentations.abstract: Hydrochory, the dispersal of propagules by water, is a critical process for recovery and resilience of freshwater macrophytes. Dams and other instream barriers fragment river networks, alter flow, and reduce opportunities for propagule movement and settlement, limiting recolonisation and connectivity. Downstream of a large dam in the mid-Brisbane River, south-east Australia, severe flooding has caused extensive scouring and substantial loss of submerged macrophytes that the threatened Australian lungfish relies on for spawning, juvenile refuge, and food resources. The dam inhibits natural hydrochory of macrophyte propagules, therefore active restoration is required to reestablish macrophytes downstream of the dam. We trialled the world’s first process-based restoration of submerged macrophytes through managed hydrochory, manually releasing vegetative propagules of two native species, Vallisneria nana and Myriophyllum verrucosum, just below the dam. Three releases (~50 kg wet weight per release) occurred over three months across a 1.5 km river reach. Wooden stakes were installed and monitored to evaluate propagule retention and establishment relative to local hydrology. Stakes increased retention, with most propagules trapped within the first 300 m, although some travelled the full reach. Establishment of both species was greater in shallow, fast flowing areas. Our approach shows early success and demonstrates that managed hydrochory can provide an effective, low-cost method for restoring submerged macrophyte habitat in regulated rivers following major scouring events.

presentations.title: MODELLING AQUATIC BRYOPHYTES AND OTHER MACROPHYTES IN DETERIORATING RIVERS
presentations.abstract: Bryophytes are an integral and important part of aquatic vegetation and biodiversity especially in river rapids and riffles. We modelled aquatic macrophyte data, some 50 bryophyte and 150 tracheophyte taxa, in 295 river sites with standardized sampling to estimate ecological quality. Using RIVPACS type approach we recognized 11 distinct plant communities in natural or near natural state. Size and soil of catchment area and latitude could be used to characterize natural macrophyte communities in pools and riffles. Based on reference communities we estimated ecological quality of impacted sites utilizing two indices: taxonomic completeness (O/E-taxa) and percent model affinity (PMA). Bryophytes in rapids alone can be used in ecological classification of rivers, though most reliable results are achieved by studying all aquatic plants in both riffles and pools. To assess changes in biodiversity we further modelled how species frequencies change due to environmental loading and disturbance, with a larger data of 780 sites and 124 bryophyte taxa. We paid special attention to more common proper aquatics with high confidence interval in the model. Of these, four species have clearly lower frequency even in sites of good ecological status than in reference sites whereas three were more frequent. Sites in high ecological status naturally did not differ from refence sites. This indicates that the target of the European environmental policy, good ecological status of all water bodies, is not good enough to maintain aquatic biodiversity

presentations.title: A Trait-Based Framework for Aquatic Plants Life Forms: The Emergent–Floating–Submerged (EFS) Continuum
presentations.abstract: 1. Freshwater plants exhibit diverse life-form strategies that allow them to persist across environments ranging from temporary flooded wetlands to deep lakes. Existing frameworks for freshwater plants, such as emergent, floating, and submerged life-forms, rely on the categorical classifications of species into fixed groups. Although they are widely used to describe ecological and evolutionary patterns in plant communities, these categorical schemes remain inconsistent across studies, fail to capture mixed or plastic morphologies within species and do not provide a quantitative link between fluctuating freshwater environments and plant morphology and function. 2. Here we introduce a continuous trait-based framework—the Emergent–Floating–Submerged (EFS) continuum—to describe aquatic plants based on the proportional expression of three key leaf type dimensions. Using a dataset spanning 1,640 species worldwide, we show that the EFS continuum captures morphological variability that can be used to understand ecological and evolutionary plant adaptations. 3. We found that continuous EFS traits outperform classical categorical definitions in predicting trait–environment relationships, revealing life-form dependent community responses to water transparency, alkalinity, and nutrient enrichment in community assembly models. We also show that the EFS framework can be used to map the evolutionary transitions among aquatic life forms. Emergent leaf strategies represent the ancestral condition within aquatic lineages and the principal source of transitions to alternative life forms, particularly submerged strategies. Floating strategies were comparatively rare and exhibited few inferred transitions. Together, these findings demonstrate that life-form identity is more accurately represented as a continuous and evolutionarily dynamic spectrum rather than as fixed categories. 4. Synthesis: By integrating inter and intraspecific leaf variation within a unified quantitative framework,

presentations.title: EUPHORIA: CONTINENTAL-SCALE PHENOLOGY OF FRESHWATER MACROPHYTES AND LINKS TO ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONING
presentations.abstract: Phenology, the timing of seasonal life-cycle events, is a key but overlooked dimension of freshwater macrophyte ecology. Shifts in the onset, peak, and duration of growth stages can alter primary production, nutrient uptake, habitat provisioning, and species interactions, yet broad-scale assessments of macrophyte phenology are almost absent. Here we present the EUPHORIA (European Plant Phenology Research in Aquatic Systems) project, a continent-wide, collaborative network that quantified phenological traits of common native and non-native macrophytes across European lakes, rivers, and wetlands. From April to October 2025, more than 100 early-career researchers applied standardized protocols to track key events (growth, flowering , peak biomass, senescence) and linked them with climatic conditions, water depth and water quality (including nutrient availability) along latitudinal and climatic gradients. We will present first results on the spatial variation in phenological traits and on correlations between traits, temperature and light conditions across sites. These findings will contribute to a better understanding of freshwater plant responses to environmental change and improve predictions of macrophyte dynamics under future climate scenarios. By providing a continental scale assessment, EUPHORIA offers valuable insights for conservation and management strategies in European freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: INTEGRATED MODELLING OF CLADOPHORA, DREISSENIDS, PHOSPHORUS, AND PHYTOPLANKTON IN THE NEARSHORE OF LAKE ONTARIO
presentations.abstract: Cladophora glomerata has re-emerged as a dominant benthic macrophyte in the nearshores of the lower Great Lakes, leading to extensive fouling of local beaches with decaying organic material. These blooms are influenced by several factors, including nutrient loading, light availability, and the presence of dreissenid mussels, thus requiring a more granular approach to modelling its growth and impacts. We present a novel process-based model that couples dissolved and particulate phosphorus with three interacting biotic compartments – phytoplankton, dreissenid mussels, and Cladophora. While these submodels have been studied individually, the evaluation of the range of dynamics they can collectively produce has been limited. Our analysis presents the findings from a comprehensive sensitivity analysis that identifies key drivers and ecological thresholds that control macrophyte biomass, nutrient retention, and the balance between benthic and pelagic production. Our study clearly identifies and addresses several knowledge gaps and outstanding questions to improve our understanding of the nearshore system. We discuss how these results can guide monitoring design and data collection, and identify management levers for reducing nuisance blooms, ultimately contributing to the effective management of macrophyte proliferation in the nearshores of Lake Ontario.

presentations.title: Modeling Water Hyacinth Dynamics to Support Management in an Urban Tropical Reservoir
presentations.abstract: (joseneto.ufmg@gmail.com) Urban reservoirs receiving untreated sewage and subject to industrial pressures experience intense ecological stress. In southeastern Brazil, a fuel-production facility relies on one such reservoir, located in a region where surrounding cities have low wastewater treatment coverage. Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) was first recorded around 2009 and rapidly expanded to dominate the reservoir surface, creating major challenges for environmental quality. The main management strategy has been mechanical removal, but biomass control has remained ineffective. To support decision-making, we quantified hyacinth cover using satellite imagery and compiled monthly biomass removal data from 2009 to 2023. We then fitted a set of population-dynamics models with different levels of complexity to assess how the inclusion of seasonal growth variation and harvesting delays affected model performance. Models were evaluated against observed cover time series. The best-performing model included seasonal growth and no lag, with peak expansion occurring in late summer (March-April), under warm, high-irradiance, nutrient-rich conditions. We then explored removal scenarios aimed at maximizing biomass reduction under realistic operational constraints. This modeling framework provides a decision-support tool for managers of urban reservoirs exposed to multiple stressors and recurrent water hyacinth outbreaks.

presentations.title: The impacts of charophytes, dreissenids, nutrients, and weather on synchronous lake-wide algal blooms in lakes Simcoe and Scugog, Ontario, Canada
presentations.abstract: Lakes Simcoe and Scugog are part of the Trent-Severn Waterway, an economically and environmentally important navigation system in the Great Lakes Basin of Southern Ontario. Both experienced synchronous lake-wide algal blooms for several weeks during the summer of 2024. This was the first lake-wide bloom recorded for both lakes in recent memory. Prior to this event, algal blooms in each lake periodically occurred in local embayments. The lakes were sampled for chlorophyll-a (Chla), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), macrophytes, and macroinvertebrates during 2024 and 2025 (May-September). For the 2024 lake-wide algal bloom year, cyanobacteria was also identified using microscopy, and environmental DNA samples were collected to quantify microcystin synthetase E gene (mcyE) abundance. By employing a Bayesian structural equation model (BSEM) framework, we modelled the mechanisms of bloom formation across Chla, cyanobacterial, and Microcystis spp. biomass, and mcyE, using wind, TP, TN, invasive Dreissena spp., native Chara spp., and invasive Nitellopsis obtusa abundance. Our results show that while charophytes and Dreissena spp. may suppress broader metrics like Chla and cyanobacterial biomass, they are positively associated with more specific taxonomic and toxigenic metrics including Microcystis spp. biomass and mcyE production. These findings highlight a critical limitation of relying on Chla alone for bloom assessment and suggest that toxin risk may increase even as conventional biomass indicators decline.

presentations.title: Effects of Urban Multi-Stressor Pollution on Macrophyte and Filamentous Algae Dynamics in Stormwater Management Ponds (SWMPs)
presentations.abstract: Urban environmental stressors negatively impact freshwater ecosystems with nutrient loading and road salt contamination. SWMPs (urban flood control infrastructures) are especially vulnerable, causing them to shift from effective sinks to active sources of pollution. This research assesses the isolated and cumulative effects of nutrient loading and salinization on the Benthic Primary Producer Matrix (BPPM), an assemblage of submerged macrophytes and benthic algae, within 12 urban SWMPs in Durham Region, Ontario. The study objectives aimed to assess whether increased nutrient loading with nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) will result in a shift from macrophyte to algae dominance, and whether elevated chloride (Cl) concentrations will negatively impact native macrophyte resilience. SWMPs were selected to reflect a gradient of Cl and P concentrations. Monthly sampling (summer 2025) assessed water quality parameters (Cl, P, N, pH, dissolved oxygen, and conductivity). Biological assessments included macrophyte and filamentous algae percent cover, dry mass, and chlorophyll-a concentrations. It is predicted that less contaminated ponds will harbour communities of diverse native species, while highly polluted ponds will be dominated by filamentous green algae while favouring highly tolerant invasive macrophyte species. Preliminary results have revealed notable shifts in the BPPM across environmental gradients. These data are currently being modelled to assess the influence of nutrient and salinity gradients on macrophyte and algal community composition and structure.

presentations.title: Environmental filters and competitive dynamics Inform early-season control of Elodea nuttallii in an urban lowland river
presentations.abstract: Invasive aquatic macrophytes raise increasing concern for freshwater ecosystems, where they alter biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and water-related services. Among them, Elodea nuttallii (Planch.) H.St. John has rapidly expanded across many European waterbodies, yet its ecology in regulated lowland rivers remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates the environmental, climatic and biotic factors shaping the occurrence and distribution of E. nuttallii in an urban river system. Field surveys conducted in 2025 documented macrophyte assemblages and habitat conditions in the Po River, the longest Italian river, flowing through the city of Turin. The results show that most vegetated patches are dominated by E. nuttallii, which is strongly associated with depositional areas characterised by soft sediments. Although interspecific competition appears to limit its abundance during the seasonal biomass peak, Elodea extended vegetative season likely contributes to its persistence. These findings underscore the importance of substrate type and biotic interactions in governing the establishment and persistence of E. nuttallii in regulated lowland rivers. They further highlight the need for early- season and site-specific management interventions. Given the ecological and recreational significance of the Po River and its role as a dispersal corridor, understanding the invasion dynamics of E. nuttallii is critical for informing management strategies, particularly in light of its designation as an EU-priority alien invasive species.

presentations.title: iMAD: updating ecological-functional knowledge on macrophytes in Italy
presentations.abstract: The iMAD project (Italian MAcrophyte Database; funded by the National Biodiversity Future Center in the frame of the NextGenerationEU program) was developed to update and integrate knowledge on aquatic macrophytes in Italy. Its objectives included updating distribution data, collecting ecological information, and analyzing functional data (with particular emphasis on the leaf economics spectrum) for a range of common native and alien taxa. This allowed for a comparison of eco-functional niches between different key categories of macrophytes (e.g., native vs. alien, aquatic vs. amphibious), incorporating intraspecific variability in the analyses. The updated distribution dataset includes 289 macrophyte species, of which 60 are alien (21%), showing an increase of ten species compared to the previous systematic review published in 2018. Lombardy is the region with the highest regional richness (202 taxa). Ecological and functional analyses were conducted on 38 species, across 209 sites, yielding 1,175 leaf replicates and over 14,000 individual trait measurements. Among native species, Myriophyllum spicatum, Spirodela polyrhiza, Persicaria amphibia, and Potamogeton nodosus are the most represented; among non-native, Lemna minuta, Myriophyllum aquaticum, and Elodea spp. dominate. Functional traits such as specific leaf area (SLA) and leaf dry matter content (LDMC) reveal comparable mean values between native and alien species, though variability patterns differed. Notably, the functional space of alien taxa encompasses that of natives, suggesting greater ecological plasticity. Overall, iMAD successfully integrates distributional, ecological, and functional perspectives to offer a comprehensive resource for explaining macrophyte diversity and directing aquatic ecosystem management in Italy, and beyond.

presentations.title: WILDFIRES CONTRIBUTE TO ELEVATED TOTAL MERCURY CONCENTRATIONS BUT NOT INCREASED MERCURY METHYLATION IN NORTHERN FORESTED LAKES
presentations.abstract: In northern forested catchments of North America, wildfires represent a major disturbance that can lead to increased mercury transport and sustained shifts in lake water chemistry, which may create conditions conducive to mercury methylation in lake sediments. To evaluate the effects of wildfires on total mercury (THg) and methylmercury (MeHg) concentrations, we studied lakes within burned catchments (burned lakes) and within nearby catchments outside of the burn zone (control lakes) in response to two recent wildfires in northern Minnesota USA. The 2021 Greenwood Fire was a high severity fire that burned 108 km2 of Superior National Forest, whereas the 2025 Brimson Complex Fire was a low-moderate severity fire that burned a smaller area. We sampled 30 lakes (15 burned, 15 control) within the Greenwood Fire and 6 lakes (3 burned, 3 control) in the Brimson Complex Fire burn zones for monthly water chemistry and preliminary surface water THg and MeHg concentrations. For the Greenwood Fire, preliminary findings indicate that THg concentrations were significantly higher in burned lakes compared to control lakes but MeHg concentrations were similar. For the recent Brimson Complex Fire, preliminary samples indicate THg concentrations were not significantly different in burned lakes compared to control lakes, but highly variable concentrations were observed in control lakes. These findings indicate that wildfire characteristics (e.g., severity), time since fire, and local catchment and water quality characteristics influence Hg transport and cycling in lakes following wildfires.

presentations.title: Student-Led Research for Long-Term Watershed Recovery in the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Burn Scar Area in Northern New Mexico, USA
presentations.abstract: The 2022 Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon (HPCC) wildlife was the largest, most destructive fire in New Mexico history, burning approximately 140,000 hectares (342,000 acres). Subsequent intense precipitation events after the HPCC wildfire have led to multiple flooding and erosion issues in the burn scar area. Rapid watershed restoration interventions are critical to control post-fire flooding and erosion. Local watershed restoration structures were designed and placed in small drainages to reduce heightened risks of flash floods and debris flows that could threaten communities within and downstream of the burn scar area. These structures use local materials of various sizes of logs and rocks, built in drainages where water mainly flows after precipitation events. The design and placement of these structures integrate natural channel designs, along with Indigenous land-use principals, and ecological restoration techniques. These structures were placed in drainages to mimic natural processes to reduce erosion, flooding and improve water quality. Undergraduate students worked with local nonprofit organizations to build these structures. This undergraduate led research continues longer-term monitoring and assessment focused on the performance of these structures. By extending this research across various seasons and flow regimes, this project fills current knowledge gaps, and provides more comprehensive scientific understanding of longer-term structural performance. Findings may also equip stakeholders to support informed-decision making across regional and broader burn scar areas.

presentations.title: Impacts of Wildfire Emissions on Human Populations
presentations.abstract: Exposure to wildfire-derived emissions has emerged as an increasingly critical public health crisis as the frequency, intensity, and extent of wildfires have risen globally. We conducted a review of populations in North American cities (Canada, the United States, and Mexico) exposed to wildfire smoke, along with a review of the literature, to understand the influence of smoke exposure on human health. The percentage of cities (n=1,213) affected by smoke shows an increasing trend with more than 20 smoke-days from 4% in 2010 to 44% in 2024, peaking at 71% in 2023. In 2010, only one city experienced 60 smoke days, while in 2024, 82 cities experienced more than 60 smoke days, including eight cities with over 90 smoke days. These results underscore that smoke exposure is not only becoming more frequent across North American cities, but the length of time populations is exposed during smoke events is also increasing. While the physiological effects of wildfire emissions on some human organ systems (e.g., circulatory and respiratory) are well characterized, significant knowledge gaps remain in critical aspects. We present research gaps regarding understudied organ systems (digestive, lymphatic, muscular, skeletal), special populations (pediatric, geriatric, highly-exposed occupational groups), emissions particle sizes (≥ 10 µm), and key public health dimensions (emotional, physical, other). Clarifying these knowledge gaps is essential for informing evidence-based ecological and public health solutions to reduce the harmful impacts of wildfire emissions globally.

presentations.title: IMPOUNDMENT OF A NORTHERN HYDROELECTRIC RESERVOIR IN THE BOREAL REGION - THE ALBEDO EFFECT
presentations.abstract: Globally, hydropower is a leading source of renewable energy, however the hydroclimatic impact of the creation of hydroelectric reservoirs in northern regions is not well understood. The impoundment of hydroelectric reservoirs modifies the surface properties and the energy exchanges between the earth’s surface and the atmosphere. In warm regions, due to the low albedo of water, most of the solar radiation is absorbed, and impoundment results in a positive radiative forcing. However, in cold regions, due to the presence of ice cover during several months of the year and the high albedos of snow and thick ice, the forcing may be negative. The magnitude of the negative radiative forcing depends on the pre-impoundment environment, as the vegetation type influences the albedo increase due to snow cover. A case study of the Romaine hydroelectric complex (~51°N, ~63°W) is used to investigate the net radiative forcing resulting from reservoir impoundment. First through comparisons of in situ albedo measurements using a natural lake, Lac Bernard, and a primarily black spruce boreal forest site as proxies for post and pre-impoundment conditions. Preliminary results indicate an annual negative forcing due to increased reflection during the ice cover period and increased longwave emissions during the later part of the open water period. Second, the Canadian Small Lake Model, a 1D dynamic lake model, will be used to spatialize the analysis to the scale of the Romaine-2 reservoir and simulate the radiative forcing resulting from the impoundment under future climate conditions.

presentations.title: A global participatory project with hydropower companies to assess reservoir greenhouse gas emissions: Challenges, successes and preliminary results
presentations.abstract: Reservoir greenhouse gas (GHG) emission data are essential for improving our understanding of emission dynamics and strengthening predictive models. Yet, major data gaps remain, particularly across Africa, Asia and Europe. This participatory science project addresses these gaps by engaging private hydropower companies in the measurement and assessment of GHG emissions. Field kits, training and technical support were provided, while participating companies locally sourced basic materials, conducted sampling, and returned the collected samples. Through this collaboration, 20 reservoirs across South America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, managed by 14 companies, were sampled three times over a one-year period. This approach provides a cost-effective way to extend GHG monitoring into remote or understudied regions that are rarely included in traditional sampling programs. Samples for dissolved carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) were collected at key water column depths upstream and downstream of the dams, along with temperature profiles and Secchi disk measurements. Preliminary results show surface GHG concentrations varying by up to fourfold among systems and up to threefold within reservoirs with corresponding consequences on diffusive and degassing fluxes, highlighting the importance of broad spatial coverage. This presentation discusses the challenges and successes of this large-scale collaborative effort and presents global findings with selected case studies demonstrating the value of public-private partnerships for expanding GHG monitoring in reservoirs.

presentations.title: Better understanding methane degassing emissions from Canadian reservoirs
presentations.abstract: Methane degassing is an emission pathway specific to reservoir, as it is linked to the dam design (intake depth), and represents the sudden release of methane at and right after the dam. Existing empirical models, such as the G-res tool, already allows to predict certain pathway of emissions, including methane degassing, but has important uncertainties. According to measured and modeled emissions, this pathway is also predicted to be the most important contributor to worldwide emissions. Due to limited number of studies measuring deep concentration of methane in reservoirs, this emission pathway remains poorly constrained. As part of the Canadian GHG-CaRe project, we have measured methane concentration at the intake depth and downstream the dam to estimate methane degassing from 17 reservoirs in temperate and boreal climate. Those measurements allow us to investigate the dynamic leading to methane accumulation and degassing emissions. As we have also measured diffusive methane emissions, we also investigate the relationship between the two emissions pathways and their link to the water residence time of the reservoir. Methane degassing emissions from the sampled reservoirs range from 0.08 to 140 gCO2e/m2/yr, showing that Canadian reservoirs have generally low, but variable methane emissions through degassing. When comparing to the other emission pathways such as CO2 and methane diffusive emissions and methane bubbling emissions, degassing is neglectable in many Canadian reservoirs but can represents as much as 30% of the total emissions in some systems.

presentations.title: The reservoir effect: exploring consistently higher CH4 concentrations in Canadian reservoirs compared to lakes
presentations.abstract: Human-made reservoirs are known hotspots of methane (CH₄), often exhibiting higher concentrations and fluxes than natural lakes. Previous studies have compared these ecosystems and suggested that morphological and ecological differences may explain these patterns. However, such comparisons have relied largely on heterogeneous, literature-based datasets, limiting the strength of their conclusions. Here, we explored the CH₄ concentration patterns in 16 reservoirs and 15 natural lakes across Canada and assessed their relationships with physical, chemical, and hydrological parameters to identify the drivers of higher CH₄ concentrations in reservoirs. Dissolved CH₄ concentrations were strongly and negatively related to surface area in both waterbody types (R² > 0.7). Nonetheless, average CH₄ concentrations were 50% higher in reservoirs than in lakes. Beyond surface area; catchment slope, mean distance to shore, and reservoir soil carbon content were the primary variables explaining variability in CH₄ concentrations. Our findings suggest that the sedimentary matrix formed from flooded soils in reservoir bottoms can sustain higher sediment CH₄ fluxes than lake bottoms, ultimately contributing to the higher CH₄ concentrations observed in reservoirs.

presentations.title: The net carbon footprint of La Romaine Reservoir Complex – Québec, Canada
presentations.abstract: Reservoirs are sources of greenhouse gases (GHG) to the atmosphere. Significant efforts have been made to quantify these emissions and the main emission pathways, yet assessments of their carbon footprint remain limited. Although carbon footprints rely on a straightforward accounting of GHG sources and sinks, their estimation remains challenging due to high spatial and temporal variability of reservoir fluxes and the complexity of landscape-level balances. An often-overlooked aspect is the distinction between reservoir-induced emissions and pre-impoundment natural fluxes. Here we present the carbon footprint of a newly constructed hydroelectric complex in Northern Québec, Canada – the La Romaine Hydroelectric Complex - comprising four consecutive reservoirs ranking among the largest hydroelectric developments in North America. We present an approach that integrates the spatio-temporal variability of gas fluxes and quantifies the contribution of different emission pathways for carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). In addition, the cascade configuration must be considered when estimating emissions attributable to individual reservoirs. Across all four reservoirs and for both gases, diffusion represented the main emission pathway, while the contribution of ebullition and downstream emissions were modest, varying among reservoirs. The temporal dynamics of GHG emissions during the initial years following impoundment also varied among reservoirs and deviated from previously published patterns. Overall, net GHG emissions from these young boreal reservoirs are relatively low compared to those documented for reservoirs in other landscape types.

presentations.title: From Rivers to Reservoirs: Lessons Learned in Long-Term Environmental Monitoring
presentations.abstract: The Romaine hydroelectric complex, located on Quebec’s North Shore, represents a major infrastructure initiative where aquatic ecosystems are central to environmental monitoring. The 25-year monitoring program was designed to assess and manage impacts on rivers, reservoirs, and coastal zones, acknowledging the complexity and sensitivity of these environments. Extensive baseline studies established the initial condition of aquatic ecosystems prior to construction, providing a critical reference for tracking changes in biological communities and physical parameters such as thermal regime, ice cover, and shoreline erosion throughout construction and operation. To differentiate project-related effects from natural variability and climate change, systematic comparisons were made with reference environments, including the Puyjalon River for salmon and selected bays for eelgrass. This approach ensured accurate attribution of observed changes and maintained the relevance of mitigation strategies. Mitigation and compensation measures were continuously adapted based on monitoring outcomes. Initiatives to support salmonid populations included stocking, creation of spawning habitats, and population monitoring. Ecological flows were maintained to preserve salmon habitats, while fish communities were monitored in reservoirs and at river mouths to inform management decisions. A key lesson learned was the necessity of long-term monitoring. Effects on aquatic communities, particularly fish and habitat integrity, often emerge over extended periods and require multi-year observation for robust assessment. Methodological flexibility enabled the integration of new indicators, such as environmental DNA (eDNA) for fish population tracking, and the discontinuation of quantitative objectives that proved unsuitable. Transparency and communication were fundamental to project success. Openly sharing results, including unfavorable outcomes, fostered community trust and strengthened adaptive man

presentations.title: Assessing the Thermal Regime and Water Footprint of the Romaine-2 Reservoir Using the Canadian Small Lake Model
presentations.abstract: Hydroelectric reservoirs significantly alter surface-atmosphere interactions, yet their contribution to regional evaporation and overall water footprint remains poorly quantified. This study aims to evaluate the hydrothermal response and water footprint of the Romaine-2 reservoir in Québec, Canada, using the physically based Canadian Small Lake Model (CSLM). CSLM is a one-dimensional, physically based model designed to simulate lake thermodynamics, ice cover, and surface energy and mass fluxes. The model will be forced with observed meteorological data and compared with in-situ surface temperature observations to assess its ability to reproduce the reservoir’s seasonal energy and mass fluxes. Simulations will be performed for both pre-impoundment and post-impoundment conditions to quantify the impact of reservoir formation on surface energy exchange and evaporation. The water footprint will be estimated as the excess evaporation attributable to impoundment per unit of electricity produced. Future simulations under CMIP6 climate scenarios will be used to examine the potential sensitivity of the reservoir’s hydrothermal regime to projected climatic changes. This work will provide a physically consistent framework for quantifying reservoir-induced hydrothermal alterations and evaluating the climate sensitivity of hydroelectric systems in cold regions.

presentations.title: Three Decades of GHG Monitoring in Hydropower: Hydro-Québec’s Corporate Program
presentations.abstract: Hydro-Québec, one of the world’s largest hydroelectric producers, launched in 1993 a corporate program to measure and understand biogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from its reservoirs. This initiative combines regular field campaigns, automated monitoring systems in generating stations (SAGES), and academic partnerships, enabling the development of robust time series and advancing knowledge of the biogeochemical processes driving carbon dioxide and methane fluxes from hydroelectric reservoirs. These efforts have resulted in significant improvements in emission modeling and transparent, science-based reporting, supporting the integration of biogenic emissions into the corporate carbon budget in alignment with upcoming GHG Protocol requirements in 2026. With more than 350 presentations, 150 peer-reviewed publications, and numerous international collaborations, this program is likely among the most advanced in the hydropower sector. We share these insights to encourage and support similar efforts across the industry, recognizing that collective progress is essential for transparent and science-based GHG management. The presentation will outline objectives, methodologies, and key findings, highlighting the importance of long-term monitoring and innovation in positioning hydropower as a renewable energy source with a low carbon footprint.

presentations.title: Comparing atmospheric CO2 exchange from a lake and hydroelectric reservoir and forest in a boreal watershed
presentations.abstract: Canada’s boreal landscapes are important carbon sinks, but land use changes due to hydroelectricity in the region can impact their carbon cycling. Aspects of the aquatic boreal carbon cycle are uncertain and data on year-round, landscape-scale carbon exchange are rare, limiting our understanding of hydroelectricity's carbon impact. Here, we present CO2​ eddy flux data from the Romaine watershed in Québec. Parts of La Romaine were impounded for hydroelectricity starting in 2014. Since 2022, we have measured carbon fluxes at a cascade reservoir, a natural lake, and an evergreen forest in the watershed, collecting 3 years of overlapping flux data. Initial work has focused on the lake fluxes, which are low and showed a spurious correlation with the sensible heat. After correcting this, the lake has two CO2​​ emission pulses during the spring and fall mixing with small but positive summer emissions. Deep water O2​​ saturation also declines over the summer and winter stratification, suggesting that the CO2​​ pulses are related to the release of CO2​​ respired in the sediment or hypolimnion. Future work will focus on creating quality assured CO2​​ flux data at the other sites and analyzing them. Initial results show that the reservoir has higher fluxes and a pronounced spring CO2​​ peak, while the forest has growing season uptake that is variably balanced by respiration in the rest of the year. We will also investigate the controls on the fluxes by analyzing them in relation to auxiliary measurements and time series analysis. Finally, we will use a gap filling methodology to create annual CO2​​ budgets at the sites and compare their roles in the carbon cycle. Our study contributes to our understanding of the boreal carbon cycle and will help constrain the carbon effect of hydroelectricity.

presentations.title: EVALUATING THE INFLUENCE OF LAKE CHARACTERISTICS, CLIMATE FACTORS, AND THERMAL TOLERANCE ON NICHE BREADTH AND OVERLAP OF MINNESOTA FISH POPULATIONS
presentations.abstract: Species assemblages arise from a combination of functional/physiological diversity amongst species and environmental variability. Climate change and dynamic global changes, such as invasive species, threaten to exacerbate environmental extremes and redistribute resources within ecosystems. These changes in lake ecosystems may increase competition among coexisting fish species due to possible reductions in thermal habitat and prey availability. To quantify how species across thermal guilds use resources within aquatic environments and if niche partitioning can be predicted by biological, ecosystem, and landscape factors, we examined stable isotope ratios across 36 Minnesota lakes. We calculated trophic position, littoral reliance, and niche breadth (standard ellipse area) for 8 piscivorous fish species across 3 different thermal guilds (cold, cool, and warmwater) using stable isotope mixing models. Niche breadth was significantly different across lakes and species, but was more influenced by lake-year than by species. The proportion of niche overlap between two species was best predicted by species pair, lake-year, and fish physiological metrics. Cool-warmwater species combinations were the most frequent pairs exhibiting niche overlap across lakes. This study highlights the importance of fish physiology in predicting niche partitioning and resource usage within lakes. Results also display frequent competition between co-occurring piscivores with different thermal preferences, regardless of local lake conditions and watershed factors.

presentations.title: INTEGRATING APPROACH OF MICROSCOPY, EDNA AND AMINO ACID ISOTOPE ANALYSIS TO RESOLVE POM ORIGIN IN AN ARTIFICIAL ESTUARINE CHANNEL
presentations.abstract: This study integrates the results of eDNA-based molecular diversity, amino acid isotope analysis, and microscopic observations of phytoplankton to evaluate particulate organic matter (POM) origin in an artificial estuarine channel (Ara Waterway). Microscopy revealed a spring phytoplankton assemblage co-dominated by diatoms and dinoflagellates. eDNA results identified the same major groups, demonstrating strong agreement between molecular and morphological assessments. Elevated primary productivity corresponded with this spring bloom. Discriminant analysis based on amino acid carbon isotope ratios indicated that POM was distributed within the microalgae source cluster, confirming that POM was largely derived from autochthonous microalgal production in spring. Together, these datasets consistently link producer composition with POM origin. By combining molecular, isotopic, and microscopic approaches, this study provides an integrated understanding of primary production and POM cycling in a physically and biogeochemically changing estuarine environment. This multimodal framework highlights the valuable implications of using complementary tools to resolve organic matter sources and microbial ecosystem in estuarine environments.

presentations.title: SEASONAL TROPHIC SHIFT OF ORGANISMS IN AKKESHI-KO ESTUARY, VIEWED VIA COMPOUND-SPECIFIC ISOTOPE ANALYSIS OF AMINO ACIDS
presentations.abstract: Compound-specific isotope analysis of nitrogen within amino acids has been employed as a powerful tool for estimating resource utilization and trophic position of organisms in ecological food webs. Applying this tool to the complex brackish estuary, however, remains challenging because of the presence of multiple resources, including seagrasses, epiphytic algae, and terrestrial plants. In this study, we measured the d15N values of one trophic amino acid (glutamic acid) and two source amino acids (phenylalanine and methionine) in seven dominant consumer species collected from the brackish Akkeshi-ko estuary in Hokkaido, Japan, in spring and summer. By comparing the d15N values of consumers with those of the three major nitrogen sources, we can reveal seasonal changes in the basal resource contribution and trophic position of these consumers, enabling us to illustrate how the food web structure changes between seasons. Terrestrial nitrogen contribution has a strong seasonality with decreasing from spring to summer for several species, which leads to the trophic decline from spring to summer. This study highlights the ecological connectivity of the Akkeshi-ko estuary, encompassing both marine and terrestrial inputs, and demonstrates how resource flexibility facilitates the trophic plasticity of consumers in an estuary.

presentations.title: TRACING MICROBIAL TROPHIC STEPS THROUGH AMINO ACID STABLE ISOTOPES: IMPLICATIONS FOR ESTIMATING PACIFIC SALMON BIOMASS
presentations.abstract: Since energy is lost with each transfer between trophic levels, food chain length (FCL) strongly affects the biomass and survival of upper trophic level species. One of the biggest challenges in resolving FCL is accounting for steps through the microbial community. Stable isotope analysis of amino acids (SIA-AA) is increasingly applied in food web studies to estimate consumers’ trophic positions (TP), particularly the fractionation of glutamine (δ15NGlu) in metazaon consumers. More recently it has been demonstrated that alanine (δ15NAla) fractionates in both metazoan and protozoan trophic steps. Comparing TP estimates derived from δ15NAla (TPAla) and δ15NGlu (TPGlu) therefore allows separation of the microbial trophic step, revealing microbial contributions and improving FCL estimates. Here, we analysed SIA-AA in meso-predators from the eastern North Pacific open ocean, including Pacific salmon Oncorhynchus spp. We tested how TPAla and TPGlu affected biomass estimates using a custom mass balance model that estimated biomass based on a 10% trophic efficiency. Estimated TP and resulting biomass varied greatly depending on whether TPAla or TPGlu was used: δ15NAla resulted in TP ~1 unit higher than δ15NGlu, yielding Pacific salmon biomass estimates 3-9 x higher in BiomassTL-Glu than in BiomassTL-Ala. These results highlight how the hidden microbial trophic step, and consequent FCL underestimation, can affect ecosystem modelling and interpretation of Pacific salmon production.

presentations.title: SPATIAL AND ONTOGENETIC VARIABILITY IN THE TROPHIC DYNAMICS OF ANTARCTIC TOOTHFISH REVEALED BY AMINO ACIDSNITROGEN ISOTOPE ANALYSES
presentations.abstract: The Antarctic toothfish (Dissostichus mawsoni) is an apex predator linking benthic and pelagic ecosystems of the Southern Ocean. This study examined spatial and ontogenetic variability in the trophic dynamics of D. mawsoni and its diets collected from the Bellingshausen Sea and the East Weddell Sea. Bulk carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes analyses revealed clear predator–prey relationships, confirming that the Antarctic toothfish occupied the highest trophic level. Amino acid nitrogen stable isotopes analyses showed distinct differences in baseline nitrogen isotope ratios among research blocks within the East Weddell Sea, whereas no such variation was observed in the Bellingshausen Sea. This pattern likely reflects the greater spatial separation between research blocks, indicating that foraging areas in the East Weddell Sea are spatially separated. In the Bellingshausen Sea, toothfish showed a clear trophic shift around 100 centimeters, with larger individuals having significantly higher trophic positions than smaller ones, indicating a dietary shift rather than a gradual increase with size. Both toothfish and its diet exhibited higher trophic positions in the East Weddell Sea than in the Bellingshausen Sea, due to lower primary productivity and a productivity-driven lengthening of the food chain. In summary, the trophic dynamics of toothfish would be affected by its ontogenetic dietary shift as well as, the spatial heterogeneity of primary productivity in Southern Ocean.

presentations.title: SOURCE IDENTIFICATION AND APPORTIONMENT OF POLYCYCLIC AROMATIC HYDROCARBONS IN MARINE SEDIMENTS USING STABLE CARBON AND HYDROGEN ISOTOPES
presentations.abstract: This study presents an optimized pretreatment method for compound-specific isotope analysis (CSIA) of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in marine sediments and demonstrates its effectiveness using real environmental samples. High-performance thin-layer chromatography (HPTLC) was applied to remove matrix interference, enhance separation, and improve compound purity prior to isotope analysis. Among the tested mobile phases, hexane:dichloromethane (7:3, v/v) provided the most efficient purification while preserving stable isotope signatures. As a result, PAH purity increased from 66% in raw sediment extracts to 96% after cleanup, and no measurable isotopic fractionation occurred during the procedure, confirming the reliability of the method. The optimized workflow was applied to surface sediments from Pohang New Harbor, South Korea, a heavily industrialized coastal region. Dual-isotope CSIA of carbon and hydrogen was combined with molecular concentration and compositional data to identify and quantify pollution sources. Although molecular patterns indicated selective loss of low-molecular-weight PAHs during atmospheric and depositional transport, δ13C and δ2H values remained consistent, with coefficients of variation below 10%, demonstrating their strong conservative behavior across matrices. Dual-isotope plots, principal component analysis, and a Bayesian isotope mixing model revealed that coal-related sources overwhelmingly dominated the PAH burden, accounting for 74% of total contributions, while liquid fossil fuel combustion and mixed sources represented only minor proportions. Overall, this study demonstrates that integrating optimized pretreatment, dual-isotope CSIA, and mixing models enables precise source apportionment of PAHs in complex coastal environments and provides valuable insight for environmental assessment and pollution management.

presentations.title: Seasonal Changes in Food-Web Structure Driven by Selective Gate Opening of the Nakdong Estuarine Dam
presentations.abstract: In Nakdong estuarine dam where selective gate operations have recently been implemented, we investigated seasonal changes in food-web structures (May, August, September, December) by analyzing hydrochemical properties and stable isotopic signatures of biota (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) collected across terrestrial-marine interface. Firstly, spatio-temporal variations of hydrochemical properties (e.g., temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen) varied from 11.2 to 31.6 °C, 0.1 to 32.9 psu and 3.1 to 9.2 mg/L, respectively. The isotopic values of biota samples varied from -29.2 to -16.4 ‰ for δ¹³C, 8.1 to 12.0 ‰ for δ¹⁵N, indicating potentially spatio-temporal variations of the ecological interaction following increased precipitation. Under broaden brackish boundaries (September), δ¹³C values of collected fish samples showed significant 13C-enriched patterns, reflecting the preferential uptake of autochthonous sources assimilated via carbonate weathering. Based on foodweb structures calculated by isotopic values of biota (i.e., phytoplankton, zooplankton, benthic invertebrates, and fishes), 15N-enriched biota samples inhabiting brackish boundaries may represent the preferential formation of higher trophic positions. Moreover, the concurrent decreases in bottom-water pH and dissolved oxygen during winter indicate increased microbial respiration associated with organic matter degradation, which supports the formation of conditions favorable for denitrification and the resultant shift in the nitrogen isotopic baseline. These results suggest that dam gate operations may alter primary sources and food-web niches. Especially, these interactive factors may ultimately influence the discriminative determination of trophic positions under broaden brackish systems. In near future, further studies involved in compound level measurement; fatty acids) may be necessary for evaluating metabolic pathway of top predators during broaden brackish formation.

presentations.title: APPLYING CSIA TO ELUCIDATE THE ROLE OF GLACIAL MELTWATERS IN STRUCTURING FRESHWATER FOODWEBS IN SUB-ARCTIC ATLIN LAKE, BRITISH COLUMBIA/YUKON, CANADA.
presentations.abstract: Glacier retreat is among the most conspicuous consequences of climate change, with impacts for all trophic levels, whole ecosystem structure and their emergent properties. Despite this, we still understand little about how glacial retreat will affect food web structures and dynamics in northern lakes. Atlin Lake, situated in the Canadian sub-Arctic within the traditional territories of the Taku River Tlingit (TRTFN), is an excellent model system for understanding the impacts of glacial melt on lake ecosystems as its mid-lake outflow, the Atlin River, separates a southern, glacially influenced basin from the northern basin that has no direct glacial inputs. Notably, lake trout are known to have different phenotypes at each end of the lake, although the ecological mechanism underlying this variation remains unknown. Thus, we are currently developing an in-house methodology to apply compound-specific stable isotope analysis (CSIA) of amino acids (AA) and fatty acids (FA) at the University of Ottawa to accurately measure the stable isotope ratios of biota samples from the northern and southern regions of Atlin Lake. Knowledge of the food webs along the environmental gradients linked to glacial influence will allow us to understand how glacial-induced changes intrinsically or extrinsically affect phenotypes, influence the food web structure and the nutritional quality of the food web subsidies, with broader implications for forecasting the impacts of glacier retreat on the food webs of polar and alpine lakes. Key words | CSIA, freshwater food webs, glacial meltwater, sub-Arctic

presentations.title: Lacustrine groundwater discharge and groundwater-borne phosphorus import into Lake Arendsee: Changes over the last 15 years
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: Lake eutrophication is often associated with phosphorus (P) loads from surface inflows, direct sewage discharges, atmospheric deposition, surface runoff, bathers or waterfowl, and other visible nutrient sources. In the case of Lake Arendsee, a 50-metre-deep monomictic lake in Germany, previous research has shown that more than 50 % of the external P load is due to excessive P inputs from an 'invisible' source: groundwater. This study aims to assess changes in groundwater P concentrations and loads over the past 15 years. P concentrations in groundwater were determined using permanent wells, temporary piezometers, and private domestic wells. Lacustrine Groundwater Discharge (LGD) rates were determined based on temperature depth profiles and Darcy calculations, which allowed the total annual P load to be calculated. Similar spatial patterns were observed at different points in time, indicating the reliability of the method and the extraordinarily high P concentrations in the urban area. However, there were also some differences, resulting in a drastic reduction of P loads in recent years. These reductions may be due to lowered groundwater tables or improvements in the catchment area (e.g. sewer replacement). Ongoing research will clarify these open questions.

presentations.title: GROUNDWATER CONTROLS ON LAKE BIOGEOCHEMISTRY ACROSS A LAKE SIZE GRADIENT
presentations.abstract: Biogeochemical interactions between lakes and their groundwater sources remain understudied despite the fundamental role of groundwater inflows in controlling lake water chemistry and biodiversity. To better evaluate the contribution of groundwater to lentic water bodies, we monitored seven groundwater-fed lakes spanning a size gradient. Within our urban observatory, lake areas range from 2×103 to 1×106 m2, and volumes from 5×103 to 7×106 m3. Preliminary results showed that lake area increased with decreasing lake perimeter to surface area ratio (P/A; R2 = 0.96, p-value < 0.001). As P/A can be regarded as a proxy of lake–groundwater coupling, this suggests that groundwater exchange decreases with increasing lake size, and that smaller lakes are more strongly coupled with groundwater inputs. Annual averages of in situ dissolved oxygen (DO) increased with lake area (R2 = 0.93, p-value = 2.2e-03) and volume (R2 = 0.90, p-value = 4.5e-03), while temperature increased with decreasing lake area (R2 = 0.85, p-value = 9.3e-03) and volume (R2 = 0.63, p-value = 6.0e-02). This suggests that climatic impacts are more pronounced in smaller lakes, which consequently exhibit a higher susceptibility to eutrophication driven by enhanced respiration rates that are tightly associated to elevated water temperatures and oxygen depletion. The spread of our data confirmed that our lake size gradient is sufficiently broad, and adding more lakes would not significantly improve biogeochemical interpretations.

presentations.title: USE OF GEOPHYSICAL TECHNIQUES TO CHARACTERIZE GROUNDWATER SALT PLUMES DISCHARGING ALONG A HIGHLY URBANIZED SHORELINE
presentations.abstract: High de-icing salt applications in cold climates are driving rising chloride (Cl) concentrations in urban groundwater and surface waters, posing risks to water supplies and aquatic ecosystems. Although groundwater discharge is known to influence urban stream salinization, its contribution to lake salinization along urban shorelines remains unclear. This study assessed the utility of geophysical techniques for characterizing groundwater salt plumes along the highly urbanized northern Lake Ontario shoreline, Canada. Electromagnetic induction (EMI) surveys were conducted along 27 shoreline areas to identify locations with potentially elevated groundwater salinity. Two suspected hotspots, Sunnyside and Bluffer’s Park, were then investigated in detail using 3D electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), shallow (<2 m) groundwater and sediment sampling, and horizontal hydraulic gradient measurements. 3D ERT surveys revealed high groundwater salinity at Sunnyside, with Cl concentrations up to 2310 mg/L, while Bluffer’s Park showed lower Cl levels (up to 553 mg/L) but still contained groundwater salt plumes. Hydraulic gradient measurements suggest higher groundwater discharge at Bluffer’s Park, suggesting that Cl loads to the lake may be higher there despite lower concentrations. Overall, this study highlights the potential contribution of lacustrine groundwater discharge to lake salinization and demonstrates the value of rapid, non-invasive geophysical techniques for identifying and characterizing salt plumes along urban shorelines.

presentations.title: INFLUENCE OF HYDROGEOLOGICAL CONDITIONS ON LACUSTRINE GROUNDWATER DISCHARGE TO LARGE GLACIAL LAKES
presentations.abstract: The role of lacustrine groundwater discharge (LGD) in delivering pollutants to nearshore waters of large glacial lakes, including the Laurentian Great Lakes, is poorly characterized. LGD is challenging to quantify as it tends to be spatially and temporally heterogeneous. Building on previous work, the objective of this study was to compare the influence of hydrogeological conditions on spatial LGD patterns along the shorelines of large glacial lakes (Lake Ontario, Lake Huron, Lake Simcoe). For this study, boat surveys, during which radon-222 (222Rn) was continuously measured, were conducted along the northern urbanized Lake Ontario shoreline in summers 2024 and 2025. These results were compared with in-lake 222Rn survey data previously obtained for Lake Simcoe and Lake Huron. Overall, in-lake 222Rn concentrations were relatively low (≤ 35 Bq/m3) in Lake Ontario nearshore waters. Maximum in-lake 222Rn concentrations were lower than previously measured in Lake Simcoe and Lake Huron nearshore waters, suggesting lower summertime LGD along the surveyed Lake Ontario shoreline. These results may be due to shallow overburden thickness along most of the surveyed Lake Ontario shoreline compared to thicker quaternary thickness and tunnel channel aquifer features along parts of the Lake Simcoe and Lake Huron shorelines. Understanding the underlying hydrogeological controls is important for identifying a priori shoreline areas where LGD may be high and potentially influencing nearshore water quality trends.

presentations.title: SOURCES AND FATE OF CALCIUM, CARBON, AND SULFUR IN TEMPERATURE SUBTERRANEAN ESTUARIES: A MULTI-ISOTOPE APPROACH
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research and Greifswald University
presentations.abstract: Subterranean estuaries (STEs) are a critical interface for element transformation and transport between land and ocean. STEs are reactors characterized by steep biogeochemical gradients that control the distribution of chemical elements such as carbon, sulfur, and metals. System-internal transformations depend on the availability of dissolved and solid phase electron donors and acceptors, and the active microbial community structure, modulated by physically driven flow conditions. Water-mineral reactions (e.g., sulfide and carbonate corrosion) may have strong impacts on the element loads and the buffer capacity of solutes being part of the benthic-pelagic coupling. Stable multi-isotope partitioning allows for source, fate, and reaction identification. Here, we explore different STEs from the microtidal coast of the southern Baltic Sea and a high-energy beach from the southern North Sea. Using a combination of C, S, O, and Ca isotope analysis of dissolved phases with sediment solid phase composition and mineral microtextures, we explore the connections between regional element sources with local system-internal biogeochemical transformations in the STE. We find that the intensity in microbial reduction of seawater-derived sulfate and corresponding accumulation of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), is controlled by the availability of electron donors (organic matter versus methane) and the fixation in sulfides by Fe reactivity. Moreover, carbonates in coastal aquifers and overlying sediments act as further DIC and alkalinity source in the continuum between fresh and salt water.
