presentations.title: Biodiversity and lipids in nutrient-rich pond foodwebs: zooplankton functional diversity increases highly required lipids in fish
presentations.abstract: Aquatic ecosystems are poor in dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), yet zooplankton generally contain high contents of physiologically required PUFA. How zooplankton manage to obtain or convert dietary PUFA is currently debated. In this multi-seasonal study, we investigated planktonic food web biodiversity of eutrophic fishponds to test the hypotheses that increasing species richness of phytoplankton augments their dietary PUFA supply and increases PUFA in zooplankton, and subsequetly in fish. We further predicted that increasing eutrophic pond status requires zooplankton to endogenously convert dietary PUFA. This investigation revealed that phytoplankton PUFA predicted PUFA contents in herbivorous and carnivorous zooplankton. Rising phytoplankton richness in hypereutrophic ponds increased PUFA contents in copepods and Daphnia, whereas zooplankton PUFA decreased under eutrophic pond conditions. Across time (seasons) and space (nine ponds), dietary lipids increased zooplankton functional richness, which subsequently increased the omega-3 PUFA docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) in fish. Moreover, zooplankton functional richness and trait dissimilarity were positively correlated with DHA and arachidonic acid in fish. These results provide correlative evidence of zooplankton functional traits being crucial for supplying highly required dietary PUFA to fish across eutrophic ponds. Ongoing compound-specific stable isotopes analysis scrutinizes the innate ability of zooplankton to convert (trophic upgrading) dietary PUFA in eutrophic aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: How lake-to-lake connectivity shapes total phytoplankton dynamics along river-connected lake chains
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: Worldwide, freshwater ecosystems are impacted by anthropogenic forcing including global warming-induced alteration of hydrological regimes and land use changes. For river systems, these changes might have far-reaching consequences as nutrients received from the terrestrial surrounding upstream may unfold both short and long-term effects downstream. Thereby, river-connected lakes may modulate the spatial spread of eutrophication events throughout an aquatic network. However, studies on river-connected lake systems are scarce and limited by low temporal and spatial resolution. We investigated phytoplankton (Chlorophyll a) development along river-connected lake chains on a regional-scale by linking theoretical model investigations with empirical observations. The field study encompassed 19 lakes in NE-Germany, contrasting strongly river-connected lakes with those weakly connected. High temporal and spatial resolution were achieved by combining water constituent measurements and automated in-situ probes with spaceborne reflectance measurements. Our results suggest that - depending on flow regime, lake characteristics and residence time - similar point sources lead to profoundly different maximum intensity, spatial range and regional-scale magnitude of responses to eutrophication along lake chains. High flow regime leads to a stronger synchrony in Chlorophyll a dynamics from up- to downstream lakes. We also highlight the potential of combining in-situ measurements with remote sensing to improve regional lake monitoring.

presentations.title: BOTH RESOURCE PULSE QUALITY AND DYNAMIC DRIVE MACROINVERTEBRATE COMMUNITY RESPONSES IN FRESHWATER MESOCOSMS
presentations.abstract: Aquatic ecosystems worldwide are closely connected to riparian environments and are influenced by cross‑ecosystem resource inputs. When occurring as perturbation events, the composition and timing of such resource pulses can generate changes in receiving aquatic ecosystems, impacting ecological processes, trophic status, and food‑web structures. However, despite their variability in composition and temporal dynamics, our understanding of the cascading impacts of resource pulse variations remains limited. This presentation reports advances from a large experimental study in aquatic mesocosms conducted in 2022, focusing on how terrestrial resources of differing quality (animal versus plant based) and temporal dynamics (from low to high pulses) can restructure benthic consumers in freshwater lentic systems. Over 17 weeks, our experiment showed that an increase in resource pulse quality (from plant to animal based) was the dominant driver of macroinvertebrate communities, with total abundance and rapid colonizers increasing from recalcitrant to labile pulses, while pulse dynamics modified and sometimes reversed those effects. Moreover, our study suggested that more diverse pulses (mixtures of animal and plant inputs) tended to stabilize functional structure, whereas abrupt animal‑based pulses amplified fast energy transfer, favoring opportunistic predators and emergent insects, and plant‑based pulses promoted detritivore dominance and sensitivity to timing.

presentations.title: Evaluation of freshwater macroinvertebrate food web metrics of the k-core subgraph to detect spatiotemporal trends
presentations.abstract: Increased prevalence of cost-effective biomonitoring procedures like DNA metabarcoding have created opportunities to use heuristic food webs to track spatial and temporal trends in ecosystem structure and function. Food web metrics (e.g., network density, connectance, betweenness) help characterize functional responses of ecosystem level shifts in assemblage structure caused by high inter-annual turnover. To explore this, freshwater macroinvertebrate food webs were modeled annually at eight sites in the Peace-Athabasca Delta, Alberta, Canada from 2012–2022. Assemblages were identified by DNA metabarcoding, and food webs were modeled for each sample using a heuristic food web pipeline that infers interactions from functional traits. Metrics were calculated for the full assemblage and for the subset of taxa in the k-core, the most interconnected subgraph of the food web. Taxa from each functional feeding group appeared in the k-core of at least one sample, demonstrating that top predators and prey can be equally connected and influential in defining food web structure. Metrics for the full assemblage showed a significant negative trend over time, suggesting increasing simplification of the PAD food webs. By contrast, no significant trends were observed for connectance or betweenness when calculated for the k-core. These results highlight the potential importance of k-core taxa in maintaining system stability across a gradient of environmental conditions.

presentations.title: DO FISH FERTILIZE TREES? EXPLORING THE TRANSFER OF MARINE-DERIVED NITROGEN FROM ANADROMOUS FISH TO RIPARIAN FORESTS OF THE EAST COAST OF NORTH AMERICA
presentations.abstract: Anadromous fish are drivers of aquatic food web connectivity, linking marine and freshwater ecosystems. Their migrations have been demonstrated to enhance aquatic ecosystems with the transfer of marine-derived nutrients (MDN) such as carbon or nitrogen. Advances in analytical methods of stable isotope analysis have allowed marine-derived nitrogen to be detected in riparian vegetation. Softwood tree cores have been used as historical archives of salmon-derived nitrogen and salmon abundance on the West Coast of North America. However, these approaches have not been widely used in the mixedwood forests of the East Coast of North America, due to the predominately iteroparous nature of the anadromous fish and the relatively young age of forest stands. This study uses tree-core stable isotope analysis to test whether MDN can be detected in riparian forests of New Brunswick, Canada. Preliminary results suggest that marine-derived nitrogen can be identified in riparian forests on the East Coast, however, this requires further validation. Interpretation is complicated by isotopic fractionation, nitrogen translocation within tree rings, and broader ecosystem interactions. Ongoing work compares MDN uptake between hardwood and softwood through refined isotope methodology for mixedwood environments. These findings advance emerging tools for reconstructing connectivity across the aquatic-terrestrial boundary and have implications for ecosystem function and informing fisheries and habitat management.

presentations.title: Intra- and inter-individual variation in Cisco Coregonus artedi resource use across drowned river mouths in Lake Michigan
presentations.abstract: Cisco Coregonus artedi, an ecologically, economically, and culturally important native fish species within the Laurentian Great Lakes, experienced a population collapse in the mid-20th century due to overfishing and competition with non-native species. In recent years, cisco in Lake Michigan have begun to rebound, likely driven by changes in fish community composition, environmental conditions, and cisco foraging ecology. Specifically, cisco have shifted from primarily planktivory to higher rates of piscivory, including while occupying drowned river mouths (DRMs) during winter. While genetic differentiation among DRMs is currently limited, spatial variation in resource use among DRMs and site fidelity remain unknown but is hypothesized to be high. To examine intra- and inter-individual variation in cisco in Lake Michigan, we analyzed δ13C, δ15N, and δ34S stable isotopes of multiple tissues to characterize spatial variation in short- (liver), intermediate- (muscle), long-term (fin), and lifetime (eye lens) foraging ecology across multiple DRMs. Findings indicate high intra- and inter-individual variation in cisco foraging across DRMs potentially driven by differences in the composition and rates of fish consumption and suggests strong site fidelity. DRMs likely provide ample forage opportunities in the recovery of a proportion of the Lake Michigan cisco population. Management and conservation to enhance cisco population growth and expansion may benefit from explicit consideration of DRMs, including further assessment of harvest rates and habitat restoration and connectivity.

presentations.title: Insect-mediated biomass and essential nutrient fluxes in a river-floodplain network
presentations.abstract: Emergent aquatic insects contribute significantly to cross-ecosystem biomass and nutrient fluxes. Aquatic insects represent an important source of energy for riparian predators and are of high nutritional quality due to their high content of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA). We quantified the export of PUFA from a large, human-impacted German river, the Oder, and adjacent floodplain water bodies (FWB) via emergent aquatic insects and estimated insect-mediated PUFA fluxes across the aquatic-terrestrial interface. Insects were collected using emergence traps installed on groyne fields along the river and on adjacent FWB. In addition, terrestrial insect traps were deployed at different distances from the shore between river and FWB to assess cross-ecosystem biomass and PUFA fluxes. The total insect biomass and PUFA export was higher from the river than from adjacent FWB, whereas the export of physiologically important long-chain PUFA was higher from FWB than from the river. In contrast to total biomass, the biodiversity of aquatic insects emerging from the river groynes was significantly lower than that of insects emerging from the FWB due to a higher proportion of non-chironomid taxa, such as Ephemeroptera and Trichoptera, in the FWB. Aquatic insect biomass decreased with distance from the river shore and the majority of aquatic insects did not penetrate further than 50 m into the adjacent terrestrial habitat. Our data highlight the importance of FWB for trophic connectivity and as a source of essential nutrients in human-impacted riverine ecosystems.

presentations.title: PERIPHYTON AT THE PEAKS – ELEVATIONAL AND SEASONAL SHIFTS IN ALPINE STREAM PERIPHYTON
presentations.abstract: Many alpine streams are experiencing climate-driven shifts in their physical characteristics. Changes in abiotic factors like water temperature, flow, and light availability shape primary production in these systems. Benthic periphyton forms the base of alpine stream food webs, especially at high elevations where allochthonous inputs are minimal. Because algal turnover is rapid in alpine streams and closely tied to temperature, flow, and light - the quantity and quality of periphyton can change quickly. Shifts in primary production affect the quantity, nutritional quality and phenology of emergent aquatic insects (primary consumers), which are key prey for both aquatic and terrestrial secondary consumers. As a result, climate-induced changes in primary production may have far-reaching effects on alpine stream food webs. We quantified shifts in benthic primary production in five streams across Switzerland from April through October 2025. We collected chlorophyll-a and ash-free dry mass samples monthly from five sites along an elevation gradient within each stream. We categorized the periphyton community using fluorescence measurements and quantified fatty acid content. We observed seasonal and elevational trends in algal community composition and overall primary production at our sites. We aim to understand the effects of algal community composition and temperature on fatty acid content, and the impact of stream flow on overall biomass. This study offers a high-resolution analysis of temporal and spatial patterns of benthic periphyton in high-elevation streams.

presentations.title: DOES INUNDATING DIFFERENT TYPES OF FLOODPLAIN HABITAT LEAD TO DIFFERENT FOOD WEB RESPONSES? INSIGHTS FROM MICROCOSM AND MESOCOSM EXPERIMENTS
presentations.abstract: Floodplain inundation is critical for sustaining riverine food webs, yet habitat-specific responses remain poorly understood. We tested whether different floodplain habitats drive distinct food web processes using microcosm and mesocosm experiments in Australia’s Murray-Darling Basin. Sediment and leaf litter were collected from 24 habitats spanning redgum forests, blackbox forests, and lignum shrublands. In separate experiments, we simulated inundation and measured organic carbon and nutrient leaching, microbial and algal production, microinvertebrate emergence, and higher trophic responses. Redgum and blackbox habitats released more dissolved organic carbon and phosphorus than lignum. Microbial and primary production did not differ in short-term microcosms, but in five-week mesocosms, bacterial abundance was highest in redgum, while planktonic and benthic chlorophyll a peaked in lignum. Microinvertebrate emergence was greater in redgum and blackbox than lignum. Crayfish (Cherax destructor) survival was lower in redgum, though growth rates were similar across treatments. These findings suggest floodplain food webs respond differently to habitat inundation, but complex interactions between factors including resources, light, and oxygen may constrain scaling from local to basin levels.

presentations.title: IMPACTS OF MARINE HEATWAVES ON CARBON PRODUCTION AND TRANSFER DYNAMICS ON MICROBIAL FOOD WEBS
presentations.abstract: Marine microbial food webs regulate energy and carbon transfer in marine ecosystems, yet their responses to intensifying marine heatwaves (MHWs) remain poorly understood. In this study, impacts of MHWs on microbial food webs were investigated through seasonal dilution experiments using seawater filtered through a 200 um sieve in the South Sea of Korea during the 2024 MHWs events. We compared grazing processes, carbon production, and trophic transfer in MHW-affected versus non-affected regions across different seasons. Results indicated that MHWs played a season-dependent role. In spring, MHWs had positive effects by warming water temperatures to optimize diatom growth, driving rates up to 2.8 d-1. However, grazing failed to keep pace, resulting in marked trophic decoupling with a low grazing-to-growth ratio (< 0.5). This mismatch led to diatom biomass accumulation, reaching approximately 30 ug C L-1, which promoted a bloom exceeding grazer consumption capacity. In summer and fall, MHWs increased temperatures beyond thermal thresholds, suppressing microplankton. While temperature-tolerant microbial food webs thrived, cyanobacteria and heterotrophic bacteria (HB) sharply increased, replacing diatoms. Cyanobacteria exhibited rapid turnover where grazing rates exceeded growth. HB dominated bulk carbon production (30 ug C L-1) but showed reduced net transfer efficiency relative to non-MHW periods. Extreme heat likely imposed high metabolic costs and respiration rates on HB. Thus, while grazers consumed ~60% of bacterial production, energy was largely trapped within the microbial loop. These findings suggest MHWs induce a fundamental shift in food web structures, transitioning the primary energy pathway from microplankton- to picoplankton-based systems.

presentations.title: Urban impact on aquatic subsidy size structure cascade to riparian predator community
presentations.abstract: The export of emergent aquatic insects is a critical energy subsidy for terrestrial food webs. While urbanization is known to alter stream communities, its effects on the size structure of these insect subsidies and the subsequent consequences for riparian predators remain poorly understood. Yet, body size, a key dimension of subsidy quality, can strongly shape resource use by terrestrial predators, given their size-dependent foraging. Here, we investigated how impervious cover affects the body-size distribution of emergent insects and riparian spider communities along the entire length of two urban streams in Quebec, Canada. We demonstrate that urbanization does not significantly affect the total biomass exported to the terrestrial environment. However, it drastically alters subsidy quality. We observed a replacement of large-bodied taxa (e.g., Plecoptera, Trichoptera) by small dipterans (Chironomidae), leading to a size structure homogenization marked by reduced mean size and size range contraction. These qualitative alterations cascade to riparian consumers. Spider trophic reliance on aquatic subsidies increased with smaller prey size. Moreover, spider community structure was driven more by insect size traits than by land-use variables directly. Our results underscore that prey size homogenization is a key mechanism propagating anthropogenic disturbances from aquatic to terrestrial ecosystems.

presentations.title: GLOBAL META-ANALYSIS OF DRIVERS INFLUENCING THE STRENGTH OF MERCURY BIOMAGNIFICATION IN AQUATIC FOOD WEBS
presentations.abstract: Mercury (Hg) is a potent neurotoxin that accumulates in organisms and biomagnifies through aquatic food webs. Globally, elevated Hg concentrations in apex predators and commercial species has motivated extensive research into its biomagnification across diverse ecosystems. Understanding ecosystems at risk and mechanisms that enhance biomagnification guides research efforts, policies, and management of ecosystems. We conducted a global meta-analysis on 565 correlation coefficients (r) from 189 studies, derived from published trophic magnification slopes (log₁₀Hg vs stable nitrogen isotope (δ¹⁵N), a proxy of trophic position). Using r as a measure of Hg biomagnification strength across a wide range of freshwater and marine ecosystems, we quantified the influence of geography, biogeochemistry, climate, and ecology, and investigated underlying mechanisms. Hg biomagnification strength varied across continents and oceans and was higher in freshwater than marine ecosystems. Variables (total nitrogen and dissolved organic carbon) that explained the greatest variance in Hg biomagnification strength occurred in freshwater ecosystems, where higher latitudes were associated with stronger Hg biomagnification, identifying polar freshwater food webs as the most susceptible. Consistent effects of all variables across ecosystems indicated that shared mechanisms may drive Hg biomagnification worldwide. These findings provide a global framework to better understand Hg biomagnification across diverse aquatic systems.

presentations.title: Cyanobacteria disrupt aquatic-terrestrial linkages via dual pathways: toxicity versus nutritional quality
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms are well known for deteriorating freshwater ecosystems, but their indirect impacts on terrestrial systems remain poorly understood. These blooms can impair the aquatic stage of insects during their development through toxicity and/or food quality. This may potentially reduce insect emergence and disrupt their role in terrestrial including key ecosystem functions and services. To address this gap, we examined how cyanobacteria affect emerging insects via two pathways — nutritional stress and toxicity — and how these effects are mediated by adaptation. Larvae were collected from eutrophic and oligotrophic ponds and exposed to treatments targeting each pathway. For toxicity, larvae encountered microcystin-LR-producing Microcystis aeruginosa and dissolved toxins from the cell lysis of Microcystis aeruginosa. For nutritional stress, larvae were fed mixtures of nutrient-rich algae and nutrient-poor cyanobacteria. This design allowed us to disentangle the relative contributions of food quality and toxin exposure while accounting for population-level differences in prior exposure history. Results provide mechanistic insight into how blooms compromise insect emergence, with cascading consequences for cross-ecosystem nutrient fluxes and terrestrial ecosystem services.

presentations.title: Comparative analysis of the lipid profiles reveals nutritional quality and quantity variation across forage species in the St. Lawrence Estuary and Gulf
presentations.abstract: The St. Lawrence Estuary and Gulf situated in eastern Canada is the southernmost environment with a seasonal sea-ice cover. During the last decade, major environmental and ecosystemic changes have disrupted energy flow in terms of both energy quantity and nutritional quality from primary producers to top predators. The decrease in prey nutritional quality has been hypothesized to play a central role in the lack of recovery of several endangered marine mammal populations. Here, we determined the lipid content and lipid classes of six forage species from demersal and pelagic to anadromous habitats. We found that nutritional quality exhibits temporal variability but also varies significantly across sex and reproductive stage. We observed that lipids class composition changed in relation to the spawning season particularly for the triacylglycerols and phospholipids. We also observed changes related to fish habitats. These results will help identify key species and periods based on their nutritional profiles for predators and contribute to improving stock management in the current context of global change and the management of endangered species in the St. Lawrence ecosystem.

presentations.title: WHAT ROLE DOES RIPARIAN VEGETATION AND FISH PLAY IN ESKER LAKE BIODIVERSITY?
presentations.abstract: Eskers are geological formations created by glacier retreat, consisting of sand and gravel, and offering high-quality drinking water, and recreational resources in northern countries. Most esker lakes are fishless and isolated water bodies, characterized by an acidic pH and high-water transparency. Such characteristics play a decisive role in determining lake biological communities and predator-prey interactions. In this study, we assessed how riparian vegetation and the presence of fish influence the adult Odonate communities in Eastern Canadian esker lakes. Odonates are generally top predators in fishless lakes. Our experimental design included 12 esker lakes (6 fishless and 6 fish-bearing) and 6 clay-belt lakes (fish-bearing), which served as reference sites. Adult odonate species richness was higher in esker lakes (Clay: 14.3 ± 1.6; Esker (fishless): 18.0 ± 1.7; Esker: 17.3 ± 1.7), and each type harbored a distinct species composition, reflecting differences in environmental conditions. In esker lakes, the degree of peat development along the shoreline varies, associated with a decline of approximately 1.3 pH units. This variation, along with the presence of ericaceous shrubs or Typha, plays a key role in shaping the structure of riparian habitats for organisms associated with these lakes. Catch rates of Aeshna were roughly 70% higher in fishless lakes, consistent with reduced fish predation in these systems. The unique habitat structure of fishless esker lakes supports a distinctive biodiversity, highlighting the importance of their conservation.

presentations.title: Modelling the recovery potential of anadromous sockeye salmon in Coquitlam Lake
presentations.abstract: Habitat fragmentation by barriers prevents diadromous fishes from migrating between marine and freshwater habitats to complete their life cycles. Anadromous sockeye salmon (Onchorhynchus nerka), landlocked in Coquitlam Lake by the construction of the Coquitlam-Buntzen hydro system in British Columbia, Canada, have residualized into a freshwater-resident life cycle. Re-establishing anadromy in this population would restore a lost migratory life-history, recover ecosystem nutrient inputs and genetic diversity, and re-establish a culturally significant salmon run extirpated by hydropower development. However, prioritization of management actions to support this restoration has been challenging due to uncertainty about the relative benefits of different interventions across life-stage bottlenecks. In this case study, we implement the Cumulative Effects Model for Priority of Recovery Actions (CEMPRA) to estimate the recovery potential of anadromous sockeye salmon in Coquitlam Lake. By developing life cycle models for both anadromous and freshwater-resident sockeye salmon, defining stressor-response relationships for various management actions, and applying these across the system, our models predict how different recovery scenarios would shift the composition of the two contrasting life-history strategies. These results will provide a decision-support framework to guide evidence-based restoration planning for the Coquitlam system and demonstrate how cumulative effects modeling can improve restoration strategies for other salmon populations affected by fragmentation.

presentations.title: Connection is Key: Assessing Restoration Effects on Multifunctionality and Ecosystem services in River Floodplains of the Danube system
presentations.affiliation: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences
presentations.abstract: (bhargavinerikar@gmail.com) Rivers and floodplains offer a plethora of Ecosystem Services (ES) in their natural state. However, various human interventions have altered the connectivity that also drives the provisioning of these ES, which in turn affects the Multifunctionality of these aquatic ecosystems. The recent decades have seen various efforts aiming to restore connectivity of riverine ecosystems to bring back lost ecosystem functions and thus the ES offered. This research examines how ES supply varies for three sections in Austria at the rivers Danube, Morava and Traisen (2 tributaries of the Danube) - where connectivity within each section was restored. Based on when these measures were implemented, two time steps, 2012 and 2020, were chosen to assess the pre and post conditions. Based on the restoration approach taken, i.e. ‘The National Park Approach’ for Danube, ‘The Transformative Approach’ for Traisen and ‘The Transboundary approach’ for Morava, each section is assessed to determine ES provision, synergies, trade-offs and ultimately the multifunctionality of each system. Using various indictors to quantify ES, the results show substantial increase in ES scores in Traisen followed by Danube. The synergies and trade-offs between the nine chosen ES were also more pronounced in the Traisen, followed by Danube and Morava. The Regulating ES (particularly Phosphorous and Nitrogen retention) increased significantly in each of these sites, followed by Cultural ES. Overall, an increase in multifunctionality was observed as a result of restoring the connectivity in these rivers.

presentations.title: The application of the meta-ecosystem approach to analyse restoration efforts in large river ecosystems – the Upper Danube
presentations.abstract: Large river ecosystems, such as the Upper Danube, are highly fragmented due to extensive engineering measures for flood protection, navigation, and hydropower production. These modifications have led to the loss of riparian habitats and floodplains, resulting in significant declines in aquatic biodiversity. Despite these challenges, large rivers continue to provide critical ecosystem services and support various human uses. Over the past 25 years, local-scale restoration measures have been implemented in the Upper Danube to improve ecological conditions, particularly for fish populations and other organisms. This study applies the meta-ecosystem approach to assess the cumulative effects of these localized restoration efforts on a larger scale. The meta-ecosystem approach was applied to integrate local habitat conditions and spatial factors by using network properties. By considering the impacts of historical alterations and focusing on longitudinal and lateral connectivity integrated in a network framework, we evaluated how restoration measures influence ecosystem functions, biodiversity, and ecosystem services. Results demonstrated how network connectivity has decreased over the last 200 years, and how fish populations are distributed within the current river network, as well as the mobility patterns exhibited by different species. This approach offers a comprehensive framework for better understanding and guiding future restoration strategies in highly modified river systems.

presentations.title: Connectivity outweighs habitat quality for native fish assemblage resilience under salmonid invasion in Chilean Rivers
presentations.affiliation: Universidad Católica de la Santísima Concepción
presentations.abstract: The 3R framework emphasises that the ecosystem resilience of rivers relies on three key components: Resources (habitat quality), Recruitment (connectivity), and Refugia (hydrological variability). Although initially developed for assessing diverse faunal communities, the framework does not explicitly address biological invasions. In our study, we evaluated how these mechanisms influence the resilience of native fish assemblages in Chile's Biobio and Imperial River catchments, which are affected by salmonid invasions. We conducted sampling across 154 sites and assessed resilience capacity using community-weighted means (CWM) of functional traits linked to each mechanism, and mixed-effects models with connectivity (IIC) and land-use gradients (PCA) as predictors. Trout were detected in 38% of the sites, accounting for 92% of the non-native biomass. Recruitment emerged as the dominant factor, with connectivity being the key predictor of native species richness and functional composition. Paradoxically, high-quality native forests, when isolated, held fewer native species (2.9 on average) than degraded but well-connected sites. Trout biomass was three times higher in isolated, pristine regions and displaced late-maturing, large-bodied natives in low-connectivity zones. Our findings suggest that in invaded systems, connectivity promotes both higher native richness and lower invader biomass. Conservation prioritising habitat over connectivity may inadvertently reduce native fish resilience capacity.

presentations.title: The Impact of Land Use on Lotic-Lentic Connectivity in a Coastal Virginia Lake
presentations.abstract: Watershed land use has been shown to have important impacts on downstream aquatic ecosystems. Flow of dissolved and particulate nutrients and organic matter are well established as drivers of significant environmental issues such as eutrophication and hypoxia. Although the flow of pathogens has been investigated, little work has been done on the downstream flow of microbial communities more generally. In this study we investigated the impact of watershed land use on the downstream flow of bacterial and viral communities from streams into a small lake. Monthly for one year, we sampled three lotic stream sites feeding Lake Matoaka (Williamsburg, VA) and paired lentic sites where the streams discharged into the lake. One stream drained a fully forested watershed, another drained a landscape of lawns and parking lots, and the largest stream drained the most fully developed watershed of Williamsburg. Bacterial and viral diversity and abundance, geochemistry, and hydrological parameters were collected. Whereas geochemical and hydrological parameters differed in stream sites based on watershed type, the lake sites were similar. In contrast, both viral and bacterial diversity metrics showed downstream connectivity between lotic streams and their lentic sites in the lake. Bacterial communities were most persistent in the lake from the forested stream and viral communities were most persistent from the stream draining campus. These results further support the importance of watershed land use on downstream microbial ecology even in small watersheds in close geographic proximity.

presentations.title: ESTABLISHING LONG-TERM MONITORING FOR THE HURON MOUNTAIN STREAM-LAKE NETWORK
presentations.abstract: Long-term monitoring is central to ecosystem studies as global climate trends drive interdecadal alterations to ecosystem structure and function. The Huron Mountain region in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan contains a stream-lake network that is tributary to Lake Superior. In 2025, we established annual monitoring throughout the stream-lake network to enable analysis of long-term responses to climate change in a relatively remote and protected region of the continental USA, and to provide spatial context for field experiments. Routine sampling of lakes includes vertical profiles of water quality (temperature, dissolved oxygen, specific conductivity, salinity, pH, turbidity, chlorophyll), secchi depth, epilimnion zooplankton, and sample collection for chlorophyll, dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), and inorganic nutrients (NO3-&NO2-, NH4+, PO43-) in each lake layer. Tributary monitoring consists of discharge, water quality, and grab samples for DOC, TN, TP, and inorganic nutrients. Additionally, one lake has a continuous time series of vertical temperature data initiated in 2013, which will be analyzed for interannual variability in lake stratification. During 2025 sampling, we observed a range of lake transparency (Secchi depth 2.9 - 5.3 m) and DOC concentrations in lakes and streams (4 - 8 mg-C/L). In future studies, we intend to explore organic matter transformations between lakes and their outlet streams, including photodegradation of lake organic matter and consequences for downstream microbial assimilation and nutrient cycling.

presentations.title: Assessing the passability of river obstacles for american eel using drones, photogrammetry and eDNA in Centre-du-Québec, Québec
presentations.affiliation: Conseil des Abénakis d'Odanak - Bureau Environnement et Terre d'Odanak
presentations.abstract: American Eel (Anguilla rostrata) migrates through numerous anthropogenic barriers that alter habitat connectivity in rivers of central Quebec. We assessed obstacle passability in six rivers of the Ndakina territory using a combined approach integrating drone imaging, photogrammetry, and environmental DNA (eDNA). High resolution drone surveys provided multi angle coverage of dams and hydroelectric structures that are often difficult to access. Images were processed to produce precise 3D models, allowing measurements of slope, crawling path length, and hydraulic features relevant to eel passage. In parallel, eDNA samples were collected at 14 sites upstream and downstream of major obstacles to detect eel presence. Several structures, including major hydroelectric dams, were classified as non passable, while potential crawling routes were identified at other sites. eDNA detections supported observations derived from the geomorphological models and helped refine the spatial extent of accessible habitat. The integrated methods provide a robust framework for evaluating aquatic connectivity in poorly accessible systems. Management recommendations include installing eel ladders at priority structures, removing obsolete barriers, and conducting additional assessments to guide restoration planning.

presentations.title: Impact of ocean alkalinity enhancement on calcification rates of eastern oyster, periwinkle, quahog and blue mussel exposed to CO2-induced ocean acidification
presentations.abstract: CO2-induced ocean acidification has been shown to slow rates of calcification of marine mollusks. In fact, some mollusk aquaculturists have commenced adding Na2CO3 to aquaculture waters to mitigate the impacts of localized acidification on commercial mollusk growth. We have conducted controlled laboratory experiments investigating the effects of ocean alkalinity enhancement via dissolution of Ca(OH)2 and Na2CO3 on calcification rates of eastern oyster (Crassostrea virginica), periwinkle (Littorina littorea), quahog (Mercenaria mercenaria) and blue mussel (Mytilus edulis) exposed to seawater acidification caused by atmospheric pCO2 of 400, 1000, and 3000 ppm. Net rates of calcification determined by buoyant weighing of mollusk specimens reveal that both Ca(OH)2- and Na2CO3-addition mitigate the deleterious impacts of CO2-induced acidification on all four mollusk species. These trends likely result from the added alkalinity increasing the dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentration of the seawater, while simultaneously de-protonating the elevated HCO3- ions to yield elevated CO32- ions for biocalcification. In addition to mitigating the impacts of CO2-induced ocean acidification on commercial mollusks, ocean alkalinity enhancement also has the co-benefit of increasing the capacity of seawater to sequester atmospheric CO2 as DIC. These results show that alkaline mineral addition holds promise as both an effective and sustainable approach to mitigating the impacts of CO2-induced ocean acidification on wild and aquacultured marine mollusks.

presentations.title: Marine Heatwaves Through the Predator’s Eye: Defining Events for Migratory Species in a Dynamic Ocean
presentations.abstract: Marine heatwave studies often rely on standardized definitions, yet our recent work demonstrates that several critical methodological choices for characterizing these events substantially influence which heatwaves are detected and how their severity is measured. Building on these insights, we apply intentionally selected marine heatwave detection methods to evaluate how these extreme events intersect with habitats of highly migratory predators in the Northwest Atlantic Ocean. To ensure the focal heatwave events are ecologically relevant, we tailor detection methods to the dynamic habitats used by predators rather than relying solely on traditional metrics and fixed thresholds. Habitat for ecologically and economically important predators is represented using species distribution models trained with fisheries-dependent data, ensuring that results are directly relevant to associated fisheries. Our findings show that methodological choices fundamentally shape how we detect and interpret extreme events, and that integrating ecological relevance into marine heatwave methodology provides a stronger foundation for anticipating impacts on predators and the fisheries that depend on them. By tailoring the detection of extreme conditions to predator habitat, this work helps set the stage for forecasting meaningful impacts on predators and fisheries weeks to months ahead.

presentations.title: THERMAL NICHES OF BROOK TROUT (SALVELINUS FONTINALIS) AND FALLFISH (SEMOTILUS CORPORALIS) IN A BOREAL RIVER
presentations.affiliation: Institu national de la recherche scientifique
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are undergoing significant changes due to climate change, altering species distributions and potentially intensifying interactions between native and northward expanding species. In Quebec’s Jacques-Cartier River, the increasing presence of Fallfish (Semotilus corporalis) has raised concerns about its impact on native Brook Trout (Salvelinus fontinalis), a species of high natural, economic, and recreational importance in the region. This study explored whether Brook Trout and Fallfish share similar metabolic rates at different temperatures, and how their field metabolic rates (FMR) and average occupied relative temperature compare. Maximum and standard metabolic rates, as well as aerobic scopes of both species were measure at four different temperatures using an intermittent-flow respirometry protocol in a controlled environment. Our study fish were wild juveniles (1+ or 2+) caught in the Jacques-Cartier River. After the respirometry trial, the otolith and dorsal muscle were sampled from each individual for 18O and 13C analysis to determine the averaged experienced temperatures, respirated C, and FMR and how they compare in the first years of the fish’s life, using thermometry. Our hypothesis is that Brook Trout have a lower aerobic scope, are less energy-efficient at higher temperatures and have a lower average experience temperature than Fallfish. If this hypothesis is confirmed, it would indicate that the temperature increases in rivers would lead to an accelerated competition for thermal habitat between species and within species. It would also indicate that Brook Trout survival is more likely to depend on the presence of thermal refuges.

presentations.title: LINKING HISTORICAL CONTAMINATION TO FOOD WEB CHANGES IN SALMON NURSERY LAKES: INSIGHTS FROM BIOLOGICAL SUBFOSSIL, SEDIMENTARY DNA, AND GEOCHEMICAL RECORDS
presentations.abstract: Reconstructing long-term ecosystem dynamics is a critical step towards understanding how anthropogenic stressors have influenced aquatic food webs. Sockeye Salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka), a keystone species across much of the North Pacific Rim, are of vital ecological, cultural, and economic importance but have experienced substantial population variability over the past century. Salmon provide a critical link between marine and freshwater ecosystems by delivering essential nutrients to typically oligotrophic nursery lakes, enhancing primary production and supporting zooplankton communities—a key food source for juvenile Sockeye Salmon. To assess how historical contamination may have altered trophic dynamics underlying fluctuating salmon populations, we reconstructed ~200 years of habitat change (i.e. sediment geochemistry, including potentially toxic metals), primary production (i.e. hyperspectral chlorophyll a), and zooplankton community structure (i.e. subfossil cladocerans and sedimentary DNA) from five salmon nursery lakes in British Columbia, Canada. Substantial shifts in zooplankton assemblages were detected, reflecting changes in both planktonic and littoral food web structure, concomitant with widespread increases in potentially-toxic metal concentrations, suggesting recent intensification of contamination. Together, these multi-proxy records offer a high-resolution perspective on how pollutants shape food web dynamics, and provide valuable baseline information to support sustainable fisheries management.

presentations.title: TRACKING ECOSYSTEM CHANGE IN TROUT LAKES UNDER VARYING FISHING PRESSURES USING PALEOLIMNOLOGY
presentations.abstract: Brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) are key salmonid species targeted by recreational fisheries in Quebec, yet both face increasing vulnerability to interacting stressors, such as global warming, species introductions, overexploitation, and long-term environmental change. To support the development of a new fisheries management plan in Mont-Tremblant National Park, we assessed how these combined pressures have shaped trout habitat conditions over time and how protected-area status can buffer their effects. Using paleolimnology, we reconstructed past ecological conditions through cladoceran assemblages to track changes in trophic structure, habitat quality, and stressor interactions. To broaden interpretation, we compared these protected lakes with a nearby unprotected lake that hosts lake trout and additional competing species. This contrast provided insight into how different management strategies shape salmonid habitat conditions in lakes over time. Overall, our study demonstrates the value of paleolimnology in understanding multi-stressor dynamics under climate change and in guiding climate-adapted fisheries management for long-term conservation of salmonid populations.

presentations.title: ENHANCING THE SUSTAINABILITY OF AQUACULTURE: AN ASSESSMENT OF WATER QUALITY, BIODIVERSITY, AND ECOSYSTEM SERVICES OF CHALK STREAMS
presentations.abstract: Rivers are unique freshwater systems providing humans with essential goods and services. However, river water quality, quantity, and the habitats they support are increasingly stressed by human activities such as fish farming. Freshwater fish farming is dependent on good water quality and stable conditions, making chalk streams ideal environments for supporting it. The Itchen and Test are two iconic chalk streams in southern England, UK, with multiple fish farms, but there is little evidence on the impacts of these fish farms on chalk rivers. Studies on the effects of fish farming on river water quality predominantly use invertebrates as bioindicators, with pollution-tolerant species dominating downstream invertebrate communities. However, bacterial diversity has yet to be studied in response to salmonid farm effluent, despite their suitability as indicators. 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing of river biofilms was used to evaluate the effects of fish farming on the Itchen and Test, linking this to water physicochemical parameters. The data indicate that microbial biofilms were distinct upstream and downstream of the farms. There were higher nutrient concentrations downstream of most fish farms and declines in dissolved oxygen, suggesting reduced water quality. Additionally, the ecosystem services used and provided by these fish farms were characterised qualitatively through interviews with fish farmers. Q methodology was used to evaluate stakeholders’ perspectives on fish farms in these river catchments and understand the social impacts of this activity.

name: Ecological Change in Arctic Freshwaters – Community and Food Web Responses to Climate Warming and Shifting Landscapes
lead_organizer: Willem Goedkoop, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences
co_organizers: Jennifer Lento, University of New Brunswick

presentations.title: Permafrost Slumps Rewire Carbon Flow and Food Webs in Arctic Streams
presentations.abstract: Permafrost thaw slumps are rapidly transforming Arctic freshwater ecosystems by mobilizing and transporting large quantities of previously frozen sediments, nutrients, and organic carbon into watersheds. These inputs drastically alter the biogeochemistry and ecology of freshwater streams by reshaping food web dynamics and altering lower trophic community structure and function. Here, we review our recent and ongoing research in the Western Canadian Arctic investigating the consequences of thaw-slump material on aquatic carbon pathways and instream food webs, using complementary experimental and field-based methods and an extensive suite of traditional taxonomic, stable isotope, and genomic approaches. We found clear differences in microbial composition and functional potential between benthic habitat types from upstream and downstream of thaw slumps and that these effects propagated to observable differences in food web dynamics, and markedly long-term impacts to aquatic macroinvertebrate community structure. This ongoing research program reveals novel insights into altered instream ecological structure and function induced by long-term thaw slump impacts in a region with rapid expansion of permafrost thaw features.

presentations.title: LAKE TROUT BIOENERGETICS MODELS TO ASSESS CLIMATE CHANGE VULNERABILITY
presentations.abstract: Arctic and subarctic watersheds are warming rapidly, with unknown consequences for fishes and the human communities dependent on them. The Arctic-Yukon-Kuskokwim (AYK) region of Alaska, USA and Yukon Territory, Canada, lacks data assets of fish energy allocations and consumption patterns to assess how rapidly increasing water temperatures are affecting growth trajectories. Lake systems within national parks in this region harbor many fishes that are critical to the culture and food security of Alaska Native and First Nations Indigenous subsistence-dependent communities. Given the socioecological importance of Arctic fish, understanding how a changing climate will impact current and future habitat suitability, metabolism, and resiliency is a critical knowledge gap for national park managers responsible for protecting and restoring these valuable watersheds. In partnership with state and federal agencies and local communities, models incorporating historical and future-projected lake temperatures, observational phenological, morphological, and physiological data were used to project historical (2008-2023) and near-future growth potential of lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) across Alaska national parks. We used the highly-adaptable software, Fish Bioenergetics 4.0, to simulate energy budget responses specific to each lake system. By parameterizing bioenergetics models, we assess the differential impacts of a changing climate on migration timing, energetic condition, and mortality dynamics of lake trout.

presentations.title: Multi-decadal trends in Northern lakes show contrasting responses of phytoplankton and benthic macroinvertebrates to climate change.
presentations.abstract: Three decades of continuous monitoring of 110 lakes across Sweden revealed significant long-term changes in physicochemical habitat and biological assemblages comprising multiple trophic levels related to climate. The environmental variables that showed the strongest temporal patterns were increasing water temperatures and decreasing TP and TOC concentrations for lakes in the north and increasing pH and TOC for lakes in the south. Phytoplankton and benthic macroinvertebrate assemblages tracked climate changes, but trends differed regionally and among the three organism groups. The most pronounced trends in both magnitudes and rates of changed (slopes) occurred in the northernmost oligotrophic lakes, but responses differed: phytoplankton and profundal macroinvertebrates had negative, while littoral macroinvertebrates had positive slopes for richness and diversity, and total phytoplankton biovolume and littoral macroinvertebrate abundance had positive slopes. Spatiotemporal patterns of phytoplankton and littoral macroinvertebrates were largely correlated with temperature and nutrients but not profundal assemblages. For lakes in the south isolating climate-induced effects was confounded by post-acidification recovery, e.g. all three organism groups correlated with pH but not with water temperature. Phytoplankton and littoral macroinvertebrates generally showed the strongest trends related to climate and therefore should be considered as robust sentinels to gauge climate impacts directly and trophic-level effects indirectly in these climate-vulnerable ecosystems.

presentations.title: Examining zooplankton communities after the implementation of hypolimnetic aeration in Frame Lake, City of Yellowknife, Northwest Territories
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic disturbances in many urban subarctic lakes are raising the need to test management and rehabilitation strategies. Frame Lake, located in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, provides an opportunity to assess rehabilitation methods in a lake that has experienced eutrophication, winter anoxia, and the extirpation of fish communities. To address winter anoxia, a hypolimnetic aerator was installed in the north basin of the lake in July 2024. We used a before-after, control-impact (BACI) study to evaluate water quality and zooplankton communities before and after the implementation of aeration in Frame Lake and in two reference lakes. The goals were to: 1) Evaluate changes in zooplankton community metrics (abundance, richness, diversity, evenness) with aeration; and 2) To assess how water quality is related to variation in these metrics. While data collection is still ongoing, preliminary analysis using repeated measure ANOVAs do not indicate significant differences in water quality (including dissolved oxygen) or zooplankton community metrics. These results suggest that the aerator has not successfully increased oxygen levels in Frame Lake during the first year of operation, possibly due to excessive oxygen demand from lake sediments. However, our analyses demonstrated significant positive relationships between dissolved oxygen levels in our study lakes and zooplankton community metrics such as abundance and richness, indicating that should aeration increase oxygen levels during ice cover, zooplankton communities in Frame Lake are likely to respond positively.

presentations.title: Forecasting climate-driven shifts in Arctic char habitat and trophic dynamics in Lake Tasikallak, Nunavik, Canada.
presentations.affiliation: Institut national de la recherche scientifique
presentations.abstract: Rapid climate change in the Arctic is increasingly threatening lake ecosystems and indigenous livelihoods. Arctic char is a key species supporting food security and the well-being of local communities. In response to local concerns—including a massive fish kill in 2002—this project examines changes in Arctic char habitat quality in Lake Tasikallak near Kangiqsualujjuaq. We aim to determine how the characteristics of the watershed and the lake affect the winter habitat of Arctic char and how climate change is impacting the population. The process-based lake model MyLake, calibrated with multiyear data, will be paired with regional climate projections to estimate past, current, and future thermal structure, oxygen dynamics, and light availability—three variables fundamental to food-web functioning. Habitat modeling may help reconstruct the conditions that led to the 2002 fish kill and anticipate similar events. In addition, paleolimnological analyses will document past environmental changes and determine whether other fish-kill events occurred over the past. Existing evidence of rising water temperatures, reduced under-ice light from changing snow regimes, and possible oxygen declines suggests major food-web restructuring with consequences for lake trophic state and fish health. This study is part of the project FROST, a circumpolar initiative comparing 12 Arctic lakes to understand how changing winter conditions affect food webs, food security, and ice travel safety, supporting locally driven adaptation.

presentations.title: EXAMINING THE POTENTIAL ROLE OF TRIBUTARIES IN INITIATING CYANOBACTERIA BLOOMS IN A LARGE SUBARCTIC LAKE
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacteria blooms are an emerging water quality concern in high latitude lakes due to climate change. Frequent summer blooms have been observed since the early 2000s in Sambaa K’e (a.k.a., Trout Lake), a large, oligotrophic, subarctic lake. This is a concern for the Dene community of Sambaa K’e for whom the lake holds ecological, cultural, and spiritual significance and is the source waters for the municipal drinking water treatment plant. Several Sambaa K’e tributaries drain thawing discontinuous permafrost peatlands, and community members have indicated that blooms appear to originate where these tributaries enter the lake. Phytoplankton and water chemistry were analyzed from samples collected in July 2024 across the eight tributaries of Sambaa K’e. We also analyzed samples that were collected weekly from July-August 2024 in one of the small creeks (“Island Bay Creek”) that had been identified by community members as a common area to observe algal blooms, as well as a paired location in the bay where the creek drains into the lake. Three of the tributaries analyzed were dominated by bloom-forming cyanobacteria taxa that are capable of toxin production (Microcystis, Aphanocapsa). These tributaries were small, and impacted by thawing permafrost peatlands. Weekly samples analyzed from Island Bay Creek revealed a proliferation of Microcystis and Aphanocapsa cells as the summer progressed. These preliminary findings lend support to the hypothesis that fluvial seeding is a potentially important initiating mechanism for cyanobacteria blooms in Sambaa K’e.

presentations.title: PROBING THE REPOSITORY OF FRESHWATER MULTIPLE-STRESSOR EXPERIMENTS TO DETERMINE THE FREQUENCY OF COMMUNITY CO-TOLERANCE
presentations.abstract: Community co-tolerance is an often-cited and highly regarded concept that is used to inform management personnel and decision makers on how to approach mitigating multiple stressors. However, despite its conceptual links to the Hutchinsonian niche, co-tolerance remains largely theoretical, with limited empirical justification. Advancing this framework requires examining correlated species responses to multiple stressors in ecologically relevant systems. Recent work by Orr et al. (2024), who compiled a comprehensive database of 2,936 freshwater multiple-stressor experiments spanning diverse stressor types, taxa, and levels of biological organization, provides a powerful foundation for such analyses. Leveraging this dataset enables efficient identification of patterns that would be otherwise obscured by the logistical challenge of assembling studies individually. Here, we test whether co-tolerance patterns emerge across freshwater communities and evaluate whether there is a predominant correlated species response. Building on this resource, the next critical step is to focus on conservation-relevant taxa to better understand the stressor combinations most likely driving observed declines. By linking species-level response correlations to community-level stressor interactions, this study advances co-tolerance from theory toward an operational framework for predicting ecological surprises.

presentations.title: GENOTYPE-DEPENDENT EFFECTS OF SALINIZATION AND COPPER CONTAMINATION ON SHORT-TERM SURVIVAL IN DAPHNIA MAGNA
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic stressors are major drivers of ecological change in freshwater ecosystems, yet they rarely act alone. Their combined effects can differ from single-stressor outcomes, complicating predictions of organismal responses. This study examined how salinization and copper contamination interact to affect short-term survival in three Daphnia magna genotypes from distinct habitats (Finland, France, Belgium). Individuals were exposed for 24 hours on well plates to 12 salinity concentrations (0.33–16.5 g/L) crossed with 12 copper concentrations (0–1000 µg/L), totalling 144 treatments. Survival data and LC50 values were used to assess single and combined effects across genotypes. Tolerance varied substantially, with the French genotype showing greater sensitivity. Furthermore, copper toxicity was influenced by salinity intensity, although this relationship was genotype-dependent. These interactions may arise from chemical processes, such as the formation of less bioavailable copper–chloride complexes, or from biological mechanisms like cross-tolerance. Variation in tolerance underscores the role of genetic and evolutionary factors. As freshwater systems increasingly experience concurrent salinization and metal pollution, understanding genotype-specific responses to multiple stressors is vital for predicting ecosystem resilience under global change.

presentations.title: Interactive Effects of Temperature Regimes on Population Dynamics of Brachionus calyciflorus
presentations.abstract: In aquatic environments, temperatures fluctuate naturally due to daily cycles and weather variability, creating dynamic conditions for organisms. Such temperature fluctuation regimes are particularly likely to influence rotifers of the family Brachionidae living in the epilimnion. These fluctuations vary in amplitude, frequency, and mean temperature, together forming a temperature regime. With climate change expected to increase the frequency of extreme weather events, such fluctuations are likely to intensify, posing potential challenges for ecological processes and population stability. Understanding how organisms respond to temperature fluctuations is therefore essential for comprehending their reactions under realistic temperature conditions and predicting their future responses. We examined the effects of four temperature regimes, combining two mean temperatures, two amplitudes, and two frequencies, on the population dynamics of a clonal line of Brachionus calyciflorus. Populations were monitored daily over the course of one week. Our results indicate that the frequency of temperature fluctuations has a significant impact on rotifer populations. High mean temperatures increased population growth, while large-amplitude fluctuations at low frequency had the strongest negative effects. The responses also varied across life-history traits such as fecundity, indicating trait-specific sensitivities to thermal variability. Overall, our study highlights the importance of considering all components of a temperature regime, rather than focusing on single parameters in isolation.

presentations.title: Beyond exposure: Emergent generational consequences of multiple stressors
presentations.abstract: As aquatic systems face increasing anthropogenic change, their inhabitants often encounter multiple stressors simultaneously. How long an individual or combination of stressors persist in the environment varies, which can lead to exposure spanning multiple generations. There is increasing evidence that some stressors induce phenotypic changes across generations known as transgenerational plasticity (TGP). We evaluated potential TGP in host fitness and infection outcomes across four generations of the freshwater crustacean, Daphnia dentifera using two naturally co-occurring stressors: the fungal pathogen, Australozyma monospora, and the fungicide azoxystrobin, which commonly enters lakes as runoff. We compared lineages under continuous stressor exposure (CS) and those with varying azoxystrobin exposure histories (AEH) under continued pathogen pressure. We found that host fitness consistently varied across generations in both the CS and AEH lineages, but did not observe the same consistency in infection outcomes. Instead, infection risk differed only in the AEH lineages, which varied by generation and its interaction with azoxystrobin exposure history. Interestingly, we found evidence of great-grandmaternal effects of azoxystrobin, highlighting the potential for TGP research to uncover “hidden” impacts of anthropogenic stressors emerging many generations after exposure. As such stressors increasingly co-occur with natural enemies in aquatic systems, it is critical to elucidate how their timing and persistence influences population dynamics over larger timescales.

presentations.title: The Dose Dogma: Understanding the interactions of multiple exposure factors through salinity on freshwater zooplankton
presentations.abstract: Road salt is a global concern in freshwater ecosystems, and interacts with water hardness, nutrients, and food enrichment to modulate toxicity. Despite guidelines, thresholds may be too lenient as chronic guidelines are often exceeded in urban streams and lakes during the non-salting season, and significant declines in zooplankton abundance and species diversity are noted below guidelines. While guidelines exist, they were derived from continuous and simplified assays that generalize exposure profiles. Real environmental chloride exposure is a true form of multiple stressors ecology, though rarely assayed, thus reducing the interactions of exposure duration, time-variable concentrations, and frequency of changes in risk assessment. This research evaluated the impact of dynamic acute exposures observed in Toronto Harbour on endemic zooplankton. We modified chloride concentrations, durations, and repetition of exposure, assessing the impact of high chloride discharge events, simulating early spring melt and salt discharge, to nearshore environments. Logistic regression models support first-order toxicokinetic assumptions of net exposure, but reveal interspecies variation and dynamic responses to exposure factors. For instance, exposures split over two pulse periods reduced survivorship odds by 18-21%, across species. While exposure data rarely exists for contaminants, including chloride, collaboration among water monitors and ecotoxicologists is important to improve how risk is evaluated and to improve the protectiveness of current chloride water guidelines.

presentations.title: A life-history omnivore reduces the predictability of population dynamics: Experimental evidence from zooplankton
presentations.abstract: Understanding the factors determining community dynamics and their predictability is a long-standing key issue in community ecology. In particular, life-history omnivores, which are present in many systems, form complex networks of interactions—a combination of competition and intraguild predation—due to dietary shifts associated with development. Due to such characteristics, theoretical studies have suggested that they can complicate community dynamics, but empirical research supporting this theory remains insufficient. In this experimental study, we examined the effects of life-history omnivores on the predictability of community dynamics under both disturbed and undisturbed conditions using zooplankton—the primary consumers in freshwater ecosystems—as a model system. We hypothesized that for communities with life-history omnivores, in this case cyclopoid copepods, the predictability of dynamics should decrease and responses to disturbances should become more complex. Our results clearly demonstrated that in communities with cyclopoid copepods, there was a pronounced rise in the variability of community dynamics between replicates. Furthermore, even under disturbance by pesticide exposure, communities with cyclopoid copepods had more complex dynamics compared to those without them. These results support the notion that life-history omnivores function to reduce the predictability of community dynamics and emphasize the importance of focusing on them in community ecology.

presentations.title: ASSESSING RECENT CLIMATE WARMING AND LEGACY IMPACTS ON LAKES NEAR THE FARO MINE (YUKON, CANADA)
presentations.abstract: The Faro Mine in southeastern Yukon (Canada) was once the largest open-pit lead–zinc mine in the country and, for a time, the largest in the world. The mine operated intermittently from 1969 to 1998 on the traditional, unceded territory of the Kaska Dena, and has left behind one of Canada’s most extensive and costly remediation projects. A primary concern is the leaching of metals from approximately 70 million tonnes of tailings and 320 million tonnes of waste rock into fluvial systems, which could affect First Nations communities downstream. However, the local effects of the mine on surrounding lakes and ponds – particularly the spatial distribution of mining dust and associated ecological impacts – remain poorly understood. Recent climate warming in subarctic Canada is an additional stressor to these ecosystems, which are an important natural resource for the local First Nation community, but is also poorly understood in this locality. In partnership with the Tū Łídlīni (Ross River) Dena Council’s Lands Department, we developed a study to address these knowledge gaps. Here, we assess the current limnological conditions of nearby lakes and ponds and reconstruct long-term ecological trajectories using sedimentary proxies. Specifically, we examine sedimentary chlorophyll-a as an indicator of paleoproduction, diatom assemblages to infer past limnological conditions, and sedimentary metal concentrations as markers of aerial transport and deposition of mining dust. These data provide critical long-term environmental context to support the Tū Łídlīni Dena’s role in mine remediation and reclamation planning at the Faro Mine and helps to assess aquatic responses to recent climate warming in the region.

presentations.title: PREHISTORIC MAYA AND CULTURAL EUTROPHICATION: NUTRIENT INPUTS, HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS, AND HEAVY METAL POLLUTION DURING OCCUPATION AROUND TROPICAL CENOTE XCACH, YUCATAN, MEXICO
presentations.abstract: Widespread harmful algal blooms (HABs) and decreases in water quality in modern lakes are associated with recent land use and multiple human impacts. These HABs and pollution are typically managed with nutrient and pollution reductions along with other strategies. Little, however, is known about the occurrence of prehistoric HABs, water pollutants or the factors that triggered them. Here, we present a ~2000-year sediment record from Cenote Xcach, a small, hypereutrophic, tropical lake located in the Yucatan region of Mexico that is surrounded by multiple Prehistoric Maya structures. Nutrients, organic matter, heavy metals, photosynthetic pigments and cyanotoxins were measured throughout the sediment core providing a continuous record of material inputs from the landscape and responses by aquatic biota. Results show that nutrient inputs into Xcach began around 550 CE during the Maya Classic Period and maintained high concentrations until decreases began around 900 CE. During this same period photosynthetic pigments showed increases in total abundance of the primary producer community including diagnostic pigments for cyanobacteria, diatoms, and green algae. During this same period, cyanotoxins increased along with toxic levels of Hg capable of impacting aquatic biota and humans. Hg is rarely associated with the Yucatan area of the Maya and has no natural sources. As a result, the Hg in our core is believed to be from the use of cinnabar around the lake, which indicates Xcach would have been a potential trade route for this commonly used red pigment. From 900 CE to the present, nutrients and primary producers show a second period of increase corresponding to the modern hypereutrophic period developed in the last 50 years. Cenote Xcach provides a historic record of eutrophication and toxic pollution preceding modern human impacts and demonstrates that water quality oscillates through time between healthy and polluted water conditions.

presentations.title: AN INVESTIGATION OF REGIONAL STRESSORS IN THE PROTECTED LAKES OF BIGWIND LAKE PROVINCIAL PARK: A PALEOLIMNOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVE FOR PARK MANAGEMENT
presentations.affiliation: Paleoecological Environmental Assessment and Research Laboratory, Queen's University
presentations.abstract: Bigwind Lake Provincial Park in Ontario (Canada) has long been designated a ‘natural environment park’ but is slated to become fully operational with the construction of recreational facilities including campsites, cabins, trail systems and access roads. Although the remote lakes within the park have been historically protected from local development, they are not immune to regional anthropogenic stressors (e.g., acid deposition, climate change). Over the past few decades, there have been reports of taste and odour-causing chrysophyte blooms in some of these lakes. To provide context for recent and future changes requires knowledge of background (pre-industrial) environments. Although monitoring data exist for some of the lakes, they do not extend beyond a few decades. Paleolimnological approaches can provide a retrospective assessment of long-term environmental conditions in these minimally impacted lakes prior to the transition to a full-service park. Here, we examine biological proxies (diatoms, scaled chrysophytes, spectrally-inferred chlorophyll-a) preserved in dated sediment records of three park lakes, collected before the proposed development of recreational infrastructure. Our results indicate that whole lake primary production is increasing whilst total phosphorus is declining, and that the lakes were naturally slightly acidic but acidified further since the industrial era. Despite evidence of chemical recovery, our biological proxies have continued to diverge from their pre-industrial assemblages. These results can help inform future park management efforts.

presentations.title: Over a century of phytoplankton community trends show differing impacts of climate and eutrophication on lakes in Atlantic Canada
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic increases in temperature and nutrient loads are promoting cyanobacterial blooms in lakes and subsequent global increases in lake hypoxia. A lack of long-term monitoring data as well as the presence of cyanobacterial blooms and hypoxia in oligotrophic lakes make it difficult to understand the drivers of these threats and the rate at which they emerge. We measured pigment biomarkers in sediment cores to examine phytoplankton community trends over the past ~140-190 years in 6 lakes from the Wolastoq River watershed (New Brunswick, Canada) representing a range of trophic conditions. Eutrophic lakes had a ~2-fold increase in indicators of total phytoplankton biomass (pheophytin a, carotenes) that mostly occurred after 1990. Oligotrophic lakes (including a reference site, Ayers Lake) had lower total phytoplankton biomass that had a relative increase similar to eutrophic lakes in scale (1.4-2.0 fold) and timing (mostly after 1990). These trends align with shifts in major phytoplankton taxa after 1990 that differed depending on lake trophic status. Cyanobacteria indicators (echinenone) increased 1.7-2.0 fold in eutrophic lakes as other taxa showed small declines. In contrast, indicators of chlorophytes (lutein), diatoms and chrysophytes (diatoxanthin), and cryptophytes (alloxanthin) increased 1.3-2.0 fold in oligotrophic lakes. Our results suggest that region-wide increases in phytoplankton biomass reflect a variety of community responses to recent climate change, while community shifts toward cyanobacterial dominance are associated with eutrophic conditions.

presentations.title: LONG-TERM ECOLOGICAL CHANGES LINKED TO HISTORICAL MINING IN AN ACID-SENSITIVE LAKE ON THE ATIKAMEKSHENG ANISHNAWBEK FIRST NATION RESERVE (SUDBURY, ONTARIO)
presentations.abstract: Large-scale mining and smelting in Sudbury (Ontario) beginning in the 1880s led to metal contamination and acidification of nearby ecosystems. Environmental degradation was widespread and led to regulatory reforms in the 1970s, which greatly reduced emissions and allowed for some recovery. Paleolimnological surveys of regional lakes used biological indicators like diatoms and Cladocera to track environmental change, as their assemblages reflect acidification and chemical shifts. Unfortunately, many lakes on First Nation lands remain understudied, despite their ecological and cultural importance. This study examines a ~200-year history from Lake 10 on the Atikameksheng Anishnawbek First Nation Reserve using a paleoecotoxicological approach to determine how this isolated lake has responded to aerial acid and metal deposition. Results from our multi-proxy approach (e.g., sedimentary metals, dissolved organic carbon, chlorophyll-a, Cladocera, Chaoborus, and chironomids) showed that biological communities have yet to return to their pre-disturbance conditions. Ongoing ecological imbalances, such as low calcium and phosphorus levels or altered trophic and predation dynamics, may be limiting full biological recovery. Discussions with community members will allow for Western science findings to be evaluated alongside Indigenous Knowledge, resulting in a collaborative approach that strengthens lake management strategies and ultimately supports the protection and restoration of aquatic ecosystems on Traditional Lands.

presentations.title: Effective, sustainable monitoring is needed to safeguard lakes in the Peace-Athabasca Delta, Canada, from degradation by industrialization and climate change
presentations.abstract: The Peace-Athabasca Delta is recognized as a Ramsar Wetland of International Importance and is a major contributor to the UNESCO World Heritage status of Wood Buffalo National Park (WBNP). Despite protections afforded by these designations, international, federal and Indigenous governance bodies have issued urgent calls to implement long-term monitoring of lakes to safeguard the Delta’s freshwater resources from threats posed by major energy projects and climate change, and to inform stewardship decisions. Drawing on knowledge gained from 7 years of research (2015-2021), we offer action-oriented solutions to address key challenges that have long impeded establishment of an effective, sustainable lake monitoring program. Here we summarize insights from our research that generates information capable of detecting aquatic ecosystem degradation, identifying the probable cause(s), and evaluating the effectiveness stewardship decisions. Highlighted among our findings is that freshwater availability in the Delta during this interval is strongly influenced by broad-scale climate patterns. Spearheaded by a range of contemporary and paleolimnological methods, implementation of monitoring approaches that we propose is particularly timely to assess remediations that are currently under consideration by the federal Action Plan for WBNP to mitigate reduction of freshwater availability in the Delta that has occurred in recent decades.
