presentations.title: DEVELOPING NEW TOOLS TO RECONSTRUCT THE IMPACT OF MULTIPLE STRESSORS ON WALLEYE (SANDER VITREUS) FISHERIES
presentations.affiliation: Conservation Sciences Graduate Program, University of Minnesota
presentations.abstract: Lakes are experiencing multiple stressors that affect fisheries and their associated food webs. Walleye, which are critical cultural and economic resources for local communities, are vulnerable to habitat loss due to warming, changing nutrient conditions, and invasive species. Understanding walleye responses to historical environmental conditions can inform successful fisheries management under present and future conditions; however, retrospective fisheries data are scarce and sporadic. We employed a paleolimnological approach to reconstruct historical fish community composition in lakes over the past 200+ years, with an emphasis on walleye population resilience. For calibration, we used paired contemporary zooplankton and fish data in 205 lake-years in Minnesota (USA) to build a statistical model of co-occurrence patterns within and across zooplankton-fish communities, while accounting for environmental drivers. The results show a zooplankton-fish relationship we will leverage to build a predictive model of fish communities using fish surveys and preserved zooplankton remains in recently deposited surface sediments from 36 lakes. Ultimately, we will reconstruct historical fish communities from sediment cores in a subset of 17 lakes to understand how environmental conditions and fish communities have changed prior to present-day monitoring programs, what lake conditions are associated with fish community structure, where and when walleye populations were most resilient to change, and what lakes are most sensitive to future perturbations to guide management moving forward.

presentations.title: GLAHF-P2F DATABASE: LINKING ENVIRONMETAL DRIVERS AND FISH COMMUNITY DYNAMICS ACROSS THE GREAT LAKES
presentations.abstract: Environmental gradients and ecosystem change influence fish community composition, species interactions, and relationships between ecosystem productivity and fish biomass, all of which modify fisheries productivity and stability. Existing efforts to characterize factors driving fish community dynamics in the Great Lakes have generally focused on local and regional change; however, there is a need to conduct assessments of fisheries dynamics across temporal and spatial scales. Over the past decade, the Great Lakes Aquatic Habitat Framework (GLAHF) has facilitated management, research, and policy making by providing a consistent geographic framework to link, integrate, map, and track physical, chemical, and biological changes across the Great Lakes. However, data from long-term fish community surveys are fairly limited in GLAHF, making it difficult to identify cross-scale drivers of fish community dynamics in the Great Lakes. Recently, the GLFC-funded Phosphorus-to-Fish (P2F) project collated nearly 40 fish community surveys across the Great Lakes and calculated long-term trends in fish biomass. Our research is working to update key environmental layers and integrate the P2F database into GLAHF to identify cross-scale relationships between environmental conditions and fish community dynamics across the Great Lakes. Results will contribute to on-going GLAHF efforts to classify and assess habitats, conduct ecological forecasting, estimate habitat and fisheries effects of potential rehabilitation projects, and monitor and track rehabilitation activities across the Great Lakes.

presentations.title: Assessing fish-kill risk in inland rivers in a changing climate: linking ecophysiology and ecohydrology
presentations.abstract: Fish kills are common in freshwater, marine or estuarine environments and have been increasing globally. Large recurrent events cause substantial ecological, environmental, and social-economic impacts. Hypoxia is a major driver of fish mortality, and its effects are exacerbated when combined with heat stress, which simultaneously elevates metabolic oxygen demand and limits supply. As climate change intensifies heatwaves and droughts, fish kill events are expected to become more frequent and severe. Here we present a novel mechanistic fish habitat suitability model that can be used to assess fish kill risks based on metabolic responses to temperature and oxygen, combined with a cumulative thermal injury function which accounts for both the intensity and duration of heat stress. We applied the model to dryland refuge river waterholes in the Murray Darling Basin in Australia, where over a million fish died during a single event in summer 2018. Our approach integrates 1) physiological data of a key native species; 2) physiological models based on the Oxygen Limitation Hypothesis and thermal death time theory; and 3) ecohydrology model that simulates temperature and oxygen dynamics during drought based on meteorological conditions, in order to predict habitat conditions and thus fish kill risks over time. Our model also offers insights into differences in risk among size classes and temperature-acclimation histories. The model can serve as a tool to inform water management decisions and climate adaptation strategies.

presentations.title: Multiple stressors, one pattern: spatial shifts across aquatic communities in a neotropical coastal river
presentations.abstract: Aquatic communities change along environmental gradients, and patterns become more complex in ecosystems exposed to multiple stressors. The Guaraguaçu River Basin is a tropical coastal ecosystem in southern Brazil affected by pollution, biological invasions, drainage works, and land-use changes, which create a heterogeneous setting for ecological responses. We investigated whether multiple biological groups respond similarly or differently to spatial gradients shaped by multiple stressors. Samplings were conducted quarterly in 2024 at 22 sites distributed across five river zones that included the main channel, two tributaries, and an area influenced by wastewater discharge. Community composition was analyzed using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity, PCoA ordination and PERMANOVA to test spatial differences among zones. All groups showed significant spatial variation. Macrophytes presented the strongest structuring (R² = 0.333, P = 0.001), followed by zoobenthos (R² = 0.26, P = 0.001) and associated macroinvertebrates (R² = 0.224, P = 0.001). Zooplankton (R² = 0.205, P = 0.001) and fish (R² = 0.19, P = 0.001) showed weaker but significant patterns. Tributaries differed from the main channel, and changes in biological composition were evident in the wastewater-influenced zones, highlighting a clear spatial structuring across groups and shifts in biota along the spatial gradient shaped by multiple stressors. These findings reinforce the value of multi-taxa assessments for understanding and monitoring ecological dynamics in rivers exposed to human pressures.

presentations.title: Identifying priority areas for freshwater conservation and restoration in Switzerland
presentations.abstract: The global biodiversity crisis is particularly dramatic in freshwater ecosystems which have suffered exceptionally high species loss. High local endemism of fish in Swiss perialpine lakes and the number of imperiled species in the surrounding rivers makes them sensitive to multiple anthropogenic threats. This creates an urgent need to allocate limited resources strategically across conservation and restoration amid competing demands for land and resources. Spatial prioritization models can support such decisions, but conservation and restoration are rarely integrated, and restoration planning often fails to quantify how specific threats shape species distributions, and therefore which actions would most effectively support recovery. We present an interdisciplinary project involving scientists, government agencies, and NGOs that develops data-driven models integrating conservation and restoration in a heavily regulated watershed in Switzerland. We combined national observations of fishes with high-resolution environmental data to model habitat suitability and used a causal forest and explainable AI framework to estimate how individual threats (e.g., flow alteration, habitat fragmentation, pollution) constrain the distributions of 45 riverine fish species. We mapped these local causal effects as stressor-specific recovery potential and used them as features in a spatial restoration optimization explicitly linked to candidate actions (e.g., barrier removal, riparian revegetation, pollution abatement). In doing so, our approach moves beyond area-based habitat gains to identify spatial “leverage points” where feasible actions remove limiting threats and yield the greatest ecological benefits, directly connecting threat–species relationships, restoration actions, and expected recovery outcomes within a single quantitative planning framework.

presentations.title: Pathogens in a Polluted World: How Multiple Factors Shape Ecosystem processes via Host-Mediated Nutrient Cycling
presentations.abstract: Parasites represent nearly 40% of known diversity and can influence ecosystem processes, yet their contributions to biogeochemical fluxes are not well characterized. They can reshape nutrient pathways through disease-induced mortality or by modifying host traits such as feeding and excretion. Parasites can also drive evolutionary shifts in host tolerance that alter how infected hosts interact with their environment and, in turn, contribute to nutrient release. Furthermore, as ecosystems face mounting human pressures, parasite effects may further shift when combined with pollutants, generating unexpected outcomes. These complexities highlight the need to examine parasite contributions to nutrient cycling within multifactor frameworks rather than as isolated drivers. Using an amphibian–virus (FV3) model, we tested how pathogens, host susceptibility, and a freshwater pollutant (NaCl) interact to shape animal (host)-mediated nutrient cycling. FV3 alone did not alter NH₄ or SRP excretion. However, with NaCl, NH₄ excretion increased with viral load in both tolerant and susceptible hosts, while SRP increased in susceptible but decreased in tolerant hosts. These results show that animal-mediated nutrient dynamics, a key contributor to nutrient cycling, are sensitive to interactions among pathogens, host traits, and pollutants. As emerging diseases increasingly affect sensitive species and harvestable resources, such context-dependent patterns underscore the need for mechanistic, multi-stressor approaches to inform conservation and restoration of degraded aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: Zooplankton Community Response to Multiple Stressors Over 40 Years in Urban and Remote Boreal Lakes
presentations.abstract: The Ontario Ministry of Environment, Conservation and Parks (MECP) has been monitoring Sudbury area Boreal Shield lakes for over 40 years, with an initial goal of using physicochemical metrics and zooplankton community responses to track recovery from acidification in 11 lakes. In recent years, variation in recovery extent and trajectories among lakes has been detected, indicating potential influences of multiple emerging environmental threats. This study used these long-term monitoring records to evaluate changes in zooplankton diversity that have accompanied shifting lake water chemistry, changes in thermal and oxygen habitat, and their complex interactions. Preliminary results indicate both legacy and emerging stressors as important drivers of zooplankton community changes. Urban lakes were more severely impacted by metal smelter emissions, and concentrations of nickel and copper continue to exceed water quality guidelines. Calcium decline is widespread, but with larger decreases in the remote lakes. Lakes have shifted in thermal structure with decreases in epilimnion depth and expansion of the hypolimnion and cold-water habitat. Zooplankton communities in urban lakes have become more diverse, now more closely resembling communities in remote lakes. Redundancy analyses using chemistry or physical parameters explained 40% and 29% of total variance within zooplankton communities, respectively. These ordination plots also indicated that the magnitude of change within urban and remote lakes was similar, despite being impacted differently by the stressors analyzed herein.

presentations.title: A COMPARISON OF THE EFFECTS OF INCREASED TEMPERATURES AND NUTRIENT ENRICHMENT ON HIGH-LATITUDE AND HIGH-ELEVATION LAKES
presentations.abstract: Globally, human activities have profoundly altered lake ecosystems, with many becoming more eutrophic due to nutrient enrichment and warming temperatures. Nutrient enrichment may also be occurring at high-latitude and high-elevation lakes distant from direct human effects. The synergistic and relative impacts of different stressors on lake ecosystems remains poorly resolved, yet is critical for effective management. To explore differences in the effects of these two stressors, we selected lakes from two study areas, a high-latitude region near Yellowknife, Canada and a high-elevation region, the Uinta Mountains, USA, which, due to differences in geography, were hypothesized to be more influenced by warming temperatures and nutrient enrichment, respectively. We used a paleolimnological approach, analyzing sedimentary chl-a, biogenic silica, and diatoms to investigate the timing and magnitude of lake ecosystem changes compared to known climate and nutrient records. Generalized additive models revealed unprecedented algal production increases beginning in the 20th century in 16 of 17 lakes from both regions. The timing of changes and diatoms indicate that in the Yellowknife region, production was driven by warming. However, in the Uinta Mountains, atmospherically-delivered nutrients initiated production increases which were later exacerbated by warming. This research shows profound changes in remote lakes due to a combination of stressors related to distant human activities, signalling a serious threat to critical resources and challenges to timely and effective management.

presentations.title: Metal pollution from gold mining plays a role in functional, but not taxonomic, metacommunity structuring in subarctic lakes
presentations.abstract: Environmental change caused by anthropogenic stressors has the potential to alter how species are distributed and how communities are structured. By studying the influence of environmental conditions, biotic interactions and dispersal limitation, we can better understand the mechanisms behind these changes at the landscape scale. To further investigate these patterns, we applied joint species distribution models to a crustacean zooplankton metacommunity in subarctic lakes across a severe arsenic pollution gradient (1.3 to 1120 µg/L) near Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, Canada. Our models included a suite of abiotic and biotic variables as well as functional traits and phylogeny to evaluate their contributions to species responses. We found that abiotic (chloride concentration) and biotic (protist community) variables most strongly influenced zooplankton taxonomic structure. Surprisingly, arsenic and other metal concentrations played only a minimal role in shaping this metacommunity. We did, however, detect relationships between functional traits (body size, feeding guild) and metal concentrations (manganese and arsenic concentrations, respectively). While taxonomic composition responded primarily to local physico-chemical and biotic variables, functional traits captured a marked response to the pollutants in the region. Understanding what environmental gradients shape taxonomic and functional species distribution is essential for managing and restoring biodiversity and ecosystem function in anthropogenically impacted landscapes.

presentations.title: LONG-TERM RESPONSES TO RECENT ENVIRONMENTAL STRESSORS IN SASKATCHEWAN (CANADA) LAKES
presentations.affiliation: Paleoecological Environmental Assessment and Research Laboratory, Department of Biology, Queen's University
presentations.abstract: Our research is part of the Indigenous-led project Collective Climate Accountability and Adaptation Project (CCAAP), coordinated by the Clearwater River Dënë Nation in Saskatchewan. We reconstructed long-term changes in two Saskatchewan ecozones: the Prairies and the Boreal Plains. The Prairies ecozone is highly susceptible to climate variations and has experienced considerable agricultural impact. Meanwhile, the Boreal Plains is covered by different forests, grassland/cropland, and wetlands. Together with Indigenous partners, study lakes were selected along a latitudinal gradient with the overall aim of capturing transitions in vegetation, land use changes, and climate, all of which influence lake ecosystems. Given that direct monitoring data are not available for these lakes, a variety of paleolimnological indicators preserved in dated sediment cores were used to establish baseline conditions and examine spatial and temporal trends across ecozones. Here, we present multiple trophic level responses to environmental change focusing on primary consumers (Cladocera) and make comparisons to primary producers (diatoms). Our paleo-proxy records indicate that Prairie lakes were naturally high in nutrients but have responded to intensified agriculture at the turn of the 20th century. Biological indicators in lake records across ecozones registered responses to accelerated climate change in recent decades. With our partners, we will provide a more holistic assessment of how trophic levels responses have changed due to recent climate warming and other stressors.

presentations.title: Linking land-use gradients to aquatic ecosystem health: A paired geospatial modelling and monitoring approach in a Northern Plains River Basin
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are threatened by human activities on the surrounding landscape, yet managers rarely know which stressors matter most or where to intervene. We studied the North Saskatchewan River Basin, a watershed facing agricultural expansion, urbanization, flow regulation, and resource extraction. We compiled geospatial data for 63 anthropogenic and natural variables across 231 subwatersheds. Field-based aquatic ecosystem health (AEH) data on water quality and biological communities (bacteria, periphyton, benthic invertebrates, and fish) were collected from 98 stream sites. Causal pathways linking landscape factors to AEH indicators were evaluated using structural equation modelling. Agricultural and residential land use and road–stream crossings were key stressors affecting biota, mainly through indirect effects on nutrients, salinity, and habitat structure. We then developed candidate geospatial models to estimate watershed integrity using alternative cumulative effects modelling approaches (additive, multiplicative, and dominance) and validated them by testing their statistical relationships with field-derived AEH indicators. Dominance and multiplicative models best captured observed patterns in AEH indicators and were used to map priority subwatersheds for management. Our analysis pinpoints stressors and locations where mitigating actions should focus, underscores the need to pair water-quality and biological monitoring, and demonstrates how geospatial modelling with limited, targeted field monitoring can guide basin-scale freshwater management.

presentations.title: Millennial-scale biological responses to agriculture and extreme storm events in a eutrophic lake
presentations.abstract: Freshwater lakes are increasingly affected by anthropogenic disturbance and extreme weather events, yet long-term biological responses remain poorly understood. We investigated a eutrophic lake in Aotearoa New Zealand to examine how lake communities respond to extreme storm events (pulse disturbance) within a timeline of increasing anthropogenic intensification in the catchment (press disturbance). We used a paleolimnological, multi-method approach incorporating sedimentary DNA, pollen, trace metals, X-ray fluorescence, and hyperspectral core scanning. From this, we reconstructed a 1390-year sediment record that spanned pre-human settlement through subsistence to intensive agriculture. Within this trajectory, we identified four high-intensity storm events that occurred during distinct phases of human impact. We hypothesised that intensifying press disturbance would drive major biological change and amplify responses to press disturbance, resulting in reduced biological resistance to storm events. To test this, we examined sedimentary DNA from bacteria, phytoplankton, zooplankton, and macrophytes alongside fish to evaluate long-term trends and storm-specific responses. A pronounced decline in total fish abundance around 1950 CE coincided with increased cadmium flux, reflecting the onset of strong agricultural intensification. Under this heightened disturbance regime, we observed reduced resistance in lower trophic levels to storm events. This study demonstrates how press and pulse disturbances interact to shape the long-term trajectory of lake ecosystems.

presentations.title: Anthropogenic Stressors in the Saguenay Fjord: A Study of Spatial Distribution of Cumulative Exposure and Ecological Risk
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic activities are intensifying worldwide, leading to profound and ongoing impacts on marine ecosystems, including along the Canadian coastline. Understanding how anthropogenic stressors affect vulnerable coastal and marine ecosystems is essential because of the importance of these ecosystems in fisheries, economic activities, and the carbon cycle. The Saguenay Fjord, located in Quebec, eastern Canada, is a unique and hot spot for biodiversity subjected to numerous human-induced stressors concentrated within a limited area. These combined pressures have raised concerns about declining water quality, habitat degradation, and the overall status of the fjord’s ecosystem. This study applies geospatial modeling and statistical analysis to map the distribution, intensity and cumulative exposure of key anthropogenic stressors, including fishing, shipping, agricultural activities, wastewater treatment discharge, forestry operations, and coastal development, in the Saguenay Fjord, The generated maps show distinct geographical patterns of cumulative exposure, with the highest levels found close to more urbanized and populated areas where human activity is concentrated. This spatially explicit assessment identified zones at risk of environmental degradation. This study provides essential insights to support evidence-based management and conservation strategies for this fjord ecosystem. Keywords: Saguenay Fjord, Anthropogenic activities, Cumulative exposure.

presentations.title: MODELING THE INTERACTIONS OF FLOW AND TEMPERATURE TO REFINE ENVIRONMENTAL FLOWS IN MEDITERRANEAN STREAMS
presentations.affiliation: Southern California Coastal Water Research Project
presentations.abstract: As a changing climate and increasing streamflow modifications continue to alter numerous streams and threaten biota, improving the estimation of environmental flows is critical for protecting stream ecosystems. Flow alterations impact stream organisms not only directly, but also by altering physical habitat and water quality parameters, like temperature. Yet the influence of streamflow on water temperature and how this influence varies spatially is not well understood. Often, environmental flow studies are conducted at the reach-sale, limiting applications at larger spatial scales. Therefore, we developed watershed scale models of flow and water temperature to determine how environmental flows could be refined to consider the thermal limits of sensitive species. We took a functional flow approach, which breaks down the hydrograph into key seasonal components. We similarly developed functional thermal metrics. We leveraged existing continuous temperature data and daily flow models for two watersheds in California, USA. We expected that the duration and timing of maximum temperatures to be most strongly related to dry season baseflow and duration of lowest flows. We also expected that the relationships to vary with drainage area, shading and groundwater contribution. This approach can aid in prioritizing monitoring and conservation efforts by providing insights into where environmental flows should be adjusted to minimize thermal stress to key species.

presentations.title: LONG-TERM ECOLOGICAL IMPACTS OF ANTHROPOGENIC DISTURBANCES ON CACHE LAKE: A PALEOLIMNOLOGICAL STUDY OF FOOD WEB DYNAMICS IN ALGONQUIN PROVINCIAL PARK
presentations.affiliation: Paleoecological Environmental Assessment and Research Laboratory, Department of Biology, Queen's University
presentations.abstract: Algonquin Provincial Park (APP) is one of Canada’s oldest protected areas with thousands of lakes that are critical to regional biodiversity, including those that provide habitat for deep-water lake trout. Despite its protected status, many aquatic ecosystems within APP have experienced anthropogenic disturbances over the past century, including logging, infrastructure development, cottage expansion, and fish stocking. Cache Lake, centrally located in southern APP, has a well-documented history of anthropogenic influence including experimental nutrient fertilization in the 1940s, the highest fish-stocking intensity of any lake in APP, and the second-highest number of cottages in the park, each with the potential to significantly alter food web dynamics. Previous paleolimnological investigations assessing the long-term impacts of these historical stressors have found significant changes in diatom and Cladocera assemblages coinciding with the fertilization experiment with shifts towards planktonic and pelagic taxa indicating food-web restructuring. Here, we analyzed sedimentary records of subfossil chironomid and chaoborid assemblages from a dated sediment core collected from Cache Lake in 2015. These aquatic invertebrate groups are widely used as bioindicators in paleolimnology due to their sensitivity to changes in temperature, oxygen, and food web dynamics, particularly those linked to fish community structure. Assemblages show a pronounced response to the 1940s fertilization experiment, followed by indications of partial ecological recovery in recent decades.

presentations.title: Using diatom-based paleolimnological approaches to assess recent changes in nearshore environments of Lake Huron near the Bruce Power Generating Station
presentations.abstract: The Laurentian Great Lakes have been impacted by a broad range of environmental stressors, including the introduction of invasive species, climate warming, and watershed development of varying intensities. Lake Huron, the second largest of the Great Lakes, is the location of the Bruce Power Generating Station, on the eastern lake shore. Bruce Power has been operating since the mid-1970s and is one of the largest power generating facilities in the world. The power plant releases thermal effluent into Lake Huron, as lake water is drawn into the facility to be used for cooling, and then released to the lake at as much as ten degrees above ambient lake temperatures. We will present the results of a paleolimnological assessment of recent (last ~200 years) environmental changes in sediment cores taken from shallow, nearshore areas of Lake Huron at a range of distances up to ~75 km from Bruce Power, to investigate potential impacts of thermal effluent. Sedimentary diatoms are being analysed, as this indicator group can provide insights into several gradients of environmental change, including those that might be related to changing water temperatures or associated habitat shifts. Ultimately, this work will contribute to a better understanding of how multiple environmental stressors may be impacting the shallow nearshore areas of Lake Huron.

presentations.title: LANDSCAPE AND IN-LAKE DRIVERS REGULATE OXYGEN DEPLETION ACROSS HUNDREDS OF UPPER MIDWEST US LAKES
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic stressors including climate change, eutrophication, and invasive species indirectly threaten cool- and cold-water fish by reducing habitat and/or food resources. We aimed to quantify the magnitude of the impacts of these stressors on hypolimnetic oxygen in lakes in the Upper Midwest US and determine if lake characteristics (e.g., geographic position, morphometry) modulate the response to these stressors. In hundreds of lakes across Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin we quantified 1) TDO3, an oxythermal habitat variable, that is defined as the temperature at 3 mg/L of dissolved oxygen, and 2) the volumetric hypolimnetic oxygen depletion rate (VHOD). VHOD is the flux of dissolved oxygen out of hypolimnetic waters, largely through metabolic activity and is related to the habitat component of TDO3. We then assessed the impact of in-lake and landscape-scale characteristics on these metrics by comparing the relationships across multiple gradients including climate, productivity, land cover, and invasive species status. Preliminary random forest analysis on a subset of lakes from Minnesota suggests that lower VHOD is associated with higher water clarity, a greater proportion of forest cover in the watershed, a lower proportion of agriculture and wetland in the watershed, and a smaller lake surface area. Future analyses will incorporate VHOD and TDO3 into modeling efforts for lakes across all three states, and explore the role of invasive species (i.e., Dreissena polymorpha and Bythotrephes longimanus) on oxygen dynamics.

presentations.title: RISING FROM THE DEPTHS: ENVIRONMENTAL DRIVERS AND EMERGING RISKS SHAPING FRESHWATER BIODIVERSITY IN HISTORICALLY ACIDIFIED KILLARNEY PARK LAKES
presentations.abstract: The degree to which freshwater habitats recover from anthropogenic disturbances remains poorly understood, especially as it often co-occurs with multiple emerging environmental challenges. To investigate these dynamics, we assessed acidification recovery in Canadian Shield lakes facing multiple stressors linked with climate change and invasion. This effort involved a 45-lake survey in Killarney Provincial Park (Canada) in summer 2024 to provide data for comparison with historical surveys dating back to 1972-1973, when industrial acidification peaked. Despite the substantial chemical recovery in lake water pH, climate warming has generated warmer and shallower epilimnia. These physical changes, together with rapid lake browning linked to acidification recovery, are narrowing habitat availability. Biological recovery has followed a similar, albeit lagging, trajectory, with species diversity and richness rising markedly in lakes that experienced the greatest historical acidification. Consequently, lakes once dominated by the acid-tolerant copepod Leptodiaptomus minutus now exhibit more complex community structures, including the return of acid-sensitive taxa such as Daphnia mendotae and Tropocyclops extensus. Notably, some pH-recovered lakes are showing signs of biodiversity loss, potentially associated with the dispersal of the invasive predator Bythotrephes. Our findings highlight the importance of long-term monitoring for understanding how multiple stressors shape recovering ecosystems and for guiding conservation and management of protected areas.

presentations.title: Two centuries of change: tracking how benthic chironomid assemblages respond to multiple disturbances in Lower Rideau Lake (Ontario, Canada)
presentations.affiliation: Paleoecological Environmental Assessment and Research Laboratory, Queen's University
presentations.abstract: Lower Rideau Lake is a large polymictic basin in the Rideau Canal system that has experienced multiple catchment disturbances over the past two centuries. While early anthropogenic stressors such as canal construction, logging, increased settlement, and agriculture had pronounced impacts on the local environment, recent diatom- and cladoceran-based studies reveal that the most significant community shifts occurred within the last ~30 years. These trends are attributed to regional warming which can reduce ice coverage, intensify thermal stratification, limit vertical mixing, and decrease deep-water oxygen availability. While previous studies highlight changes in the pelagic zone, little is known about how benthic communities have responded to these environmental stressors. Chironomids are sensitive to shifts in temperature and dissolved oxygen concentrations, making them ideal indicators of past ecological changes in the benthic zone of Lower Rideau Lake. Using a dated sediment core collected in 2020, we track chironomid assemblage responses to environmental change over the past ~250 years. Complementing previous paleolimnological research, our work addresses the benthic response to multiple regional disturbances (e.g., canal construction, increased settlement, regional warming). By integrating the responses of organisms occupying different trophic levels, this research can help lake managers better predict and mitigate the impacts of environmental change in freshwater systems.

presentations.title: Long-term lake and catchment dynamics: using diatoms, sedimentary ancient DNA (SedaDNA), organic matter (OM) and XRF to investigate drivers of change at Rostherne Mere, Cheshire, UK
presentations.abstract: Sediment archives from lakes contain detailed records of ecosystem dynamics that can provide insight not only into long-term aquatic ecosystem trajectories but also into better mitigation strategies and restoration. Only a few UK lakes have yielded complete sedimentary records since the early Holocene, resulting in discontinuous and fragmented knowledge of long-term lake-catchment interactions. Rostherne Mere, Cheshire UK, is a rare example where a complete sediment sequence has been recovered. Rostherne Mere provides long-term preservation of biological and geochemical proxies due to the lake’s cold temperatures and seasonally anoxic conditions in the bottom waters due to chemical stratification. This study undertakes a multi-proxy approach using diatoms, Sedimentary ancient DNA and geochemistry (organic matter, XRF) across a continuous, long sediment record that spans the last 10,000 years, covering a wide range of lake states and long-term record of change. This multi-proxy sedimentary archive offers an exciting opportunity to elucidate the interactions between drivers of the local aquatic and regional terrestrial systems to determine stressors and provides a robust assessment of environmental change and sediment transport across the landscape on a decadal, centennial to multi-millennial scale. A complete record of the proxies covering the last 10,000 years at varying temporal resolutions, and the combination of all proxies, provides a detailed insight into Rostherne Mere throughout the Holocene to access the cumulative impact of multiple stressors across various scales.

presentations.title: Using freshwater zooplankton life-history parameters in a multiple stressor context to inform appropriate region and taxon-specific guidelines to protect aquatic ecosystems from road salt pollution
presentations.abstract: Mitigating the impacts of road salt pollution on aquatic ecosystems is a wicked problem and one that requires a better understanding of the sub-lethal impacts of chloride (Cl) that considers multiple stressors in a regional environmental context and species-specific responses. Regional spatial variability can be associated with differences in water chemistry (e.g., calcium - Ca) and taxonomically there exists a wide range of tolerances, even within genera and species. Further, although an understanding of the acute effects of Cl and Ca on individual taxa mortality is emerging, we know much less about chronic effects on life history parameters. We conducted a laboratory study with 3 species of Daphnia (catawba, pulex and pulicaria) at 3 calcium (Ca) concentrations (2.5. 15, 45 mg/L) exposed to a gradient of Cl spanning three orders of magnitude (0.4 – 4800 mg/L). We measured 4 key life history parameters; total neonate production, mean clutch size, day of first reproduction, and survival, over a period of 21 days. We used a generalized linear modelling approach to estimate EC50s for each species x calcium comparison for the suite of life history parameters. For almost all life history parameters, Ca influenced the response to Cl such that our lowest calcium concentrations consistently generated the lowest EC50 outcomes (i.e., the Cl associated with a 50% change) for individual taxa. Among species, we observed marked differences in both the pattern and magnitude of response for all parameters at concentrations well below current Canadian guidelines suggesting that populations may be impacted at even lower levels than those used to develop current water quality guidelines. Together these findings demonstrate the importance of considering sub-lethal, region and taxon-specific effects to develop appropriate targets for protecting aquatic ecosystems from Cl pollution.

lead_organizer: Naila Barbosa da Costa, Université TÉLUQ

presentations.title: GENOMIC CHARACTERIZATION OF CYANOBACTERIA STRAINS ISOLATED FROM BRAZILIAN RESERVOIRS FOCUSING ON GLYPHOSATE HERBICIDE RESISTANCE
presentations.affiliation: Federal University of Juiz de Fora
presentations.abstract: Glyphosate (N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine), the active component in many widely used glyphosate-based herbicides (HGBs), is applied to control weeds, especially in monocultures that use genetically modified seeds resistant to this active ingredient. Although glyphosate resistance mechanisms are well-established in some prokaryotes, the interaction between emerging contaminants, such as glyphosate, and cyanobacteria is an under-explored area of research. Thus, the objective of this study is to investigate the presence of genetic mechanisms of glyphosate resistance in cyanobacterial strains, particularly Raphidiopsis raciborskii strains. This species is strongly linked to harmful algal blooms (HABs) and the production of toxins that compromise water quality and public health. The strains were sequenced using Illumina and Nanopore platforms, and the gene clusters responsible for producing cyanotoxins (saxitoxin and microcystin) were characterized. We searched on the genomes for genes of interest, including EPSPS synthase, glyphosate oxidoreductase (GOX), C-P lyase, and YhhS using BLASTp analysis. All strains presented the EPSPS class II enzyme, which is commonly associated with glyphosate resistance. Additionally, we found coding sequences for an enzyme belonging to the FAD-dependent oxidoreductase class, which may act in glyphosate degradation. The C-P lyase gene cluster appears to be present exclusively in R. raciborskii. Based on these findings, we propose that cyanobacteria possess glyphosate resistance mechanisms and the ability to use glyphosate as a nutrient source.

presentations.title: Predicting cyantoxin concentrations in lakes and reservoirs using microbial information
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms and their toxins pose persistent challenges to freshwater ecosystems. Herein, we combined ecological, molecular, and machine-learning approaches to analyze genomic time-series data (10 years across eight lakes and reservoirs spanning a broad latitudinal gradient) and identify the drivers of cyanotoxin diversity. First, zero-inflated Joint Species Distribution Models (JSDMs) testing the relationship between toxin composition and abiotic drivers showed that seasonality was the strongest driver of both toxin presence and abundance, followed by ammonia and total phosphorus. Next, analyses of biotic drivers using topic models (Latent Dirichlet Allocation; LDA) characterized the seasonal succession of toxins, revealing that certain toxins appeared earlier in the season across lakes while others peaked in late summer. Microbial interaction networks (Sparse InversE Covariance estimation for Ecological Association and Statistical Inference; SpiecEasi) identified taxa most strongly associated with specific toxin variants (e.g., Microcystis with microcystins and Planktothrix with anabaenopeptin-B). Analysis of the main microbial carriers of cyanotoxin genes through metagenome co-assembly (Intra-Strain variation; InStrain) further showed that Microcystis was the dominant contributor to mcy genes in most lakes. Finally, Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) demonstrated that total microcystin concentrations were well predicted using either all observed cyanobacterial taxa or the top 500 non-cyanobacterial taxa. Taken together, integrating these layers, from species associations to single-nucleotide variants, provided a more complete picture of the ecological and evolutionary drivers of cyanotoxin production. As predictive models continue to evolve, incorporating high-resolution biotic data will be essential for developing robust tools to manage harmful algal blooms across freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: Functional microbial activity linked to cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms across interconnected systems of the Lake Erie watershed
presentations.abstract: Nutrient loading is a primary driver of cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cHABs). However, research focusing on abiotic drivers yields inconsistent bloom predictions, and there is increasing evidence that investigating the biogeochemical role of the broader aquatic microbial community (i.e., aquatic microbiome) in cHABs occurrence could help improve prediction. Here, we examined microbial processes in the Lake Erie watershed, from the upstream nutrient-rich Thames River to the downstream Lakes St. Clair and Erie, as a framework to assess shifts in microbial metabolisms and test microbiome’s influence on cHABs formation. Although upstream-downstream connectivity has been noted in genomic data, our meta-transcriptomic analysis revealed that the Thames River was more metabolically active and functionally distinct compared to Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie, with pronounced upregulation of Nitrogen-cycling functions. In contrast, Lake St. Clair and Lake Erie showed more moderate differentiation, suggesting transcriptional downregulation or lower metabolic specialization. These results collectively demonstrate that system-level structure strongly shapes microbial functional activity, with nutrient-cycling pathways driving major ecological differentiation at the transcriptional level. Linking these functional profiles with environmental gradients will further clarify how microbial activity influences bloom dynamics. This integration may ultimately improve predictions of cHAB persistence in Lake Erie and other affected systems.

presentations.title: RosHAB: From monitoring cyanobacterial blooms to constructing genomes of Quebec lakes microbiome
presentations.affiliation: Institut national de la recherche scientifique
presentations.abstract: In Quebec, 107 cyanobacteria harmful algal blooms (cHABs) per year on average have been reported between 2006 and 2016. With ongoing climate change and urbanization, the number of cHABs is expected to increase, stressing the need for a better surveillance of freshwater bodies. Although it is well established that nutrient loading drives the occurrence of cHABs, there is increasing evidence that the functional role and interactions among members of the whole aquatic microbiome may also contribute to cHABs. In this context, we have developed a pipeline for the Rapid on-site detection of Harmful Algal Blooms (RosHAB) using Oxford Nanopore Technologies via academic and governmental collaboration. During the summer 2025 (June-August), we have received water samples from more than 400 lakes across the province of Quebec through the community-based Lake Monitoring Program (RSVL) of the MELCCFP (Gov. Quebec). Water was analyzed for water chemistry and metagenomics. Extracted DNA has been sequenced on ONT P2 Solo sequencers. On-going MAG (metagenome assembled genomes) and genes-centric analyses will provide a detailed portrait of the spatial distribution of the aquatic microbiome (taxa and their genes) across Quebec lakes, and identify the main drivers of the lake microbiome biogeography including cyanobacteria in particular. As a whole, RosHAB will improve the efficiency of bloom surveillance by identifying cyanobacterial hotspots and lakes showing signs of bloom development.

presentations.title: Impact of simulated storm-induced deep-mixing on Planktothrix and microcystin dynamics in a large-scale lake enclosure experiment
presentations.abstract: /Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) (charlotte.schampera@uba.de) Planktothrix rubescens is a cyanobacterium that can form deep-water populations in cold, low-light metalimnion of clear-water lakes. Its ability to produce the toxin microcystin (MC) raises concerns about how climate-driven changes in lake mixing regimes may alter toxin dynamics. Increased frequencies and intensities of summer storms are expected to disrupt thermal stratification, modifying light, temperature and nutrient conditions that regulate Planktothrix biomass and toxin production. To assess these impacts, we conducted an enclosure experiment in the IGB LakeLab facility in Lake Stechlin, Germany, enabling ecosystem-scale manipulations under near-natural conditions. Six randomly selected enclosures were subjected to a deep-mixing event mimicking a severe summer storm while six additional enclosures served as stratified controls. The artificial storm greatly affected the vertical distribution of Planktothrix biomass throughout the six-week experiment, although the physical stratification of the mixed enclosures was re-established within days. Accordingly, MC concentrations diverged markedly between the deep-mixed and stratified enclosures, indicating that storm-induced physical disturbances can significantly modify toxin concentrations. Complementary agent-based model simulations support observed toxin dynamics and help disentangle the mechanisms driving MC variability. These results highlight the sensitivity of Planktothrix populations to climate-related mixing events and provide insight into toxin risks in stratified clear-water lakes under changing climate regimes.

presentations.title: Molecular monitoring of cyanotoxin in a tropical urban reservoir (Ibirité, Brazil): early warnings via mRNA
presentations.abstract: Urban reservoirs in tropical regions are under continuous pressure from eutrophication and contaminant inputs, and early detection of Harmful Algal Bloom remains challenging. This study aimed to evaluate the potential of early detection of cyanotoxin production in an urban eutrophic reservoir in Brazil by integrating molecular, chemical, and physicochemical indicators. A monthly monitoring was carried out from Feb-Sep/25 at a monitoring site in Ibirité Reservoir. Temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll a, solar radiation, phytoplankton, microcystin, and saxitoxin concentrations were analysed. Additionally, messenger RNA of stress-perception (pstS, ntcA, prxM) and cyanotoxin-production genes (mcyD, sxtA) were quantified using RT-qPCR. Microcystin and saxitoxin remained below established Brazilian recreational guidelines (1 and 3 ug/L, respectively), despite the consistent presence of potentially toxic cyanobacteria. Seasonal dynamics significantly influenced the environmental stress factors that drove gene expression. Key findings revealed strong correlations between stress-perception and cyanotoxin-production genes. Molecular responses suggest that gene expression has the potential to serve as early indicator of HAB and for the elucidation of environmental conditions that stimulate cyanotoxin production in the study area. The integration of molecular markers for stress and toxicity provides a powerful, proactive tool for monitoring and managing HAB, offering early warning capabilities beyond traditional chemical and cell-count methods for tropical water bodies.

presentations.title: PHENOLOGICAL GRADIENT CHANGES IN CYANOBACTERIA AND MICROALGAE OF PERUVIAN COASTAL LAGOONS DUE TO CLIMATE CHANGE
presentations.affiliation: Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos - UNMSM
presentations.abstract: In tropical region of South America, Peruvian coast at Pacific western has inland aquatic environments. Studied area was from north to south between 9°20S to 12°33S. They are exposed to annual fluctuating hydrological regime with flooding governed and gradual evaporation with desiccation periods during late summer and fall seasons. Observational approach during the last decade years evidenced the impact of climate change on the lagoon phenology. There is accelerating salinization process of eutrophic lagoons with saline crust formation where desiccation stressor is related to the aquatic to land continuum in coastal Pacific. Standard cyanobacterial and algal collections were done between 2010 and 2024 with physical chemical parameters as well as the morphospecies identification with sequences of their vegetative and reproductive stages. Some species move towards moist habitats of lagoon shores, wet soils or rock substrates according to the surrounding ecological gradient stressors (salinity, temperature, radiation, desiccation) becoming saline indicators species. The hypersaline species Pleurocapsa fuliginosa had an osmotic and hydric stress responses according to the precipitation of evaporitic minerals (gypsum, halite). During the autotrophic life cycle species, the resting stages formation as survival strategies (acinetes, cysts, aplanospores) and their dispersal ensure colonization under the global climate change.

presentations.title: Does one who see pigments, also see cells? Microscopy enumeration Vs. CHEMTAX estimation of phytoplankton in a tropical eutrophic reservoir
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms represent a global concern in lakes and reservoirs due to cyanotoxin production, which can cause severe illnesses to animals and humans or death. Phytoplankton characterization can be performed through microscopy, pigment analysis, and molecular biology. Specific pigments from different algal classes may be quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) integrated with the CHEMTAX program. This study aimed to compare the use of (i) traditional microscopy and (ii) CHEMTAX-based pigment analysis to assess phytoplankton composition in the urban eutrophic tropical Ibirité Reservoir (MG, Brazil). The algal matrices were optimized for freshwater taxa to estimate class-specific chlorophyll-a contributions evaluating their agreement and the potential of CHEMTAX to represent community structure. Preliminary results show that Cyanobacteria - characterized by zeaxanthin, myxoxanthophyll, and echinenone - dominated during the dry-season probably due to stratification. Meanwhile, chlorophytes and diatoms prevailed during mixing conditions, associated with chlorophyll b and fucoxanthin. CHEMTAX correlated well with microscopy but revealed additional picocyanobacterial signatures not visible under optical detection. Pigment-based inference was more efficient to detect structural shifts, supporting its use for early bloom warning and ecological assessment. Hence, the integration of microscopy and chemotaxonomy improves monitoring accuracy and provides valuable insight for managing eutrophic tropical systems under anthropogenic and climatic pressures.

presentations.title: Cyanobacteria in the cold: genomic analysis of high-latitude isolates reveals functional diversity yet little potential for toxin production
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacteria are among Earth’s oldest life forms, yet their evolution and adaptation to diverse habitats remain poorly understood. While many species thrive in warm, nutrient-rich waters and can form toxic blooms, others inhabit cold, oligotrophic environments, where their adaptive strategies are still unclear. Using Illumina and Nanopore sequencing, we analyzed the genomes of 99 cultures from the Polar Cyanobacteria Culture Collection (PCCC), comprising unicellular and filamentous strains from the Arctic, Antarctic, and subarctic regions. We searched for genes related to cold adaptation, toxin production, and biogeochemical functions to infer how they survive and contribute to polar ecosystem processes. All genomes contained genes linked to the carbon cycle, as expected for phototrophs, and some carried genes involved in nitrogen and sulfur cycling. A few strains carried cyanotoxin synthesis genes, yet none possessed complete biosynthetic clusters, suggesting no capacity to produce toxins. Ongoing analyses of cold-adaptation genes aim to clarify mechanisms enabling survival under freezing conditions. In addition to establishing the largest genomic database of polar freshwater cyanobacteria, this study provides insights into their ecological roles and adaptive strategies in both the Arctic and Antarctic. These polar ecosystems act as sentinels of climate change, underscoring the importance of understanding how they are changing over time.

presentations.title: Tracking the Rise and Toxicity of Harmful Algal (cyanobacteria) Blooms in the Sedimentary Record across six New York Finger Lakes
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial harmful blooms (HABs) have expanded in the New York Finger Lakes in recent years across a range of conditions including deep, low phosphorus, meso- and oligotrophic, raising questions about whether bloom-forming and toxin-producing cyanobacteria are novel invaders or long-standing community members responding to recent change. We conducted a six-lake paleolimnological comparison (Honeoye, Owasco, Cayuga, Seneca, Canandaigua, Skaneateles) to place the current trends in HABs in a long-term context. Duplicate ~60 cm gravity cores were collected in June 2025 at mid-lake sites approximately two-thirds of maximum depth, sectioned at 0.5 cm intervals and dated using ²¹⁰Pb to the past ~150 years. Total phytoplankton and cyanobacteria abundance, microcystin synthesis potential, and cyanotoxin presence were reconstructed using spectral approaches as proxies of total phytoplankton biomass, qPCR gene assays for cyanobacteria 16S and microcystin synthetase, and LC-MS analysis of toxin concentration. We also measured sediment total Hg concentrations, which in Cayuga and Seneca lakes track the operation of coal burning power plants from 1938 (Seneca) or 1955 (Cayuga) to the 2010’s, further corroborating the 210Pb dating. By comparing the timing and magnitude of changes in cyanobacterial and toxin signals among the lakes and relating these patterns to known histories of environmental and ecological change we can gain insights on whether recent HABs blooms reflect amplification of historically present cyanobacteria or functional community shifts toward more toxic assemblages.

presentations.title: Exploring the antioxidant ergothioneine in the cyanobacterial metabolic arsenal
presentations.affiliation: Centre of Nuclear Energy in Agriculture
presentations.abstract: in the University of São Paulo (USP) (rafaelbdextro@gmail.com) Ergothioneine (EGT) was first discovered in 1909, isolated from the ergot fungus (Claviceps purpurea), and later recognized for its antioxidant properties. Throughout the 20th century, EGT was mainly known as a compound found in fungi and plants, with its biosynthetic pathway remaining largely unknown. A significant discovery towards mass production of this compound came when the biosynthesis was confirmed in bacteria, including early evidence of production in cyanobacteria. However, the full genetic description of the ergothioneine biosynthesis cluster (EGT-BGC) remained elusive until more recent studies. The genetic basis for EGT production appears to vary between bacteria and cyanobacteria. Genomic advances, including high-quality assemblies of cyanobacterial strains, have revealed promising pathways for cyanobacterial EGT production. Based on gene phylogeny and sequence identity scores, several cyanobacterial strains, like Scytonema and Oscillatoria, confirm the genetic basis for ergothioneine production, with genes sharing 32-44% identity with known EGT-producers like Mycobacterium, Nocardia, and Methylobacterium. Phylogenetic analysis of the EGT cluster reveals a distinct separation between cyanobacteria and other EGT-producing bacteria, suggesting an evolutionary divergence in the biosynthetic pathways. These findings highlight cyanobacteria’s diverse metabolic capabilities and position them as a valuable model for biotechnology and ecological research, with potential for innovative applications in production systems.

presentations.title: CYANOBACTERIA BLOOM DYNAMICS IN A SOUTH CAROLINA RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Freshwater reservoirs in South Carolina (SC) often serve as primary drinking water sources and are heavily used for recreational purposes like swimming and boating. Understanding what causes harmful algal blooms in these reservoirs will help manage water quality moving forward. The aim of this project was to study cyanobacteria bloom dynamics in an urban SC reservoir, Goose Creek Reservoir, a shallow, 600-acre reservoir that serves as a source of drinking water and recreation for the surrounding community. In 2023-2025, we sampled monthly at three stations for temperature, D.O., pH, turbidity, phytoplankton biomass and community composition, nutrients, and algal toxins. Two cyanobacteria genera , Aphanizomenon sp. and Dolichospermum sp., bloomed often, but did not always produce algal toxins. Both these algal species had heterocysts, indicative of the ability for N-fixation. Akinetes were positively identified in the lake sediment and germination grow-out studies showed a significant increase in cyanobacteria biomass when compared to the control treatments. The results from this study indicated that cyanobacteria blooms in the reservoir are likely triggered by the germination of overwintering cells in the sediment, rather than nutrient inputs. Future work will look at the impact of wind, rain, and light dynamics on akinete germination in Goose Creek Reservoir.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF INCREASED TEMPERATURE AND ACIDIFICATION ON FRESHWATER NITRIFICATION RATES AND GENE EXPRESSION DURING A CYANOBACTERIAL HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOM
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cHABS) are a global threat to public health and aquatic ecosystem stability, and may worsen under climate change. Global temperature increases are causing surface water temperatures to rise, and elevated atmospheric CO2 is increasing dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) concentrations in lakes and oceans (“acidification”). These altered conditions may increase the severity and frequency of cHABs, including in Western Lake Erie (WLE), a eutrophic system that experiences an annual cHAB. Microcystis aeruginosa, the dominant cHAB species in WLE, produces a suite of hepatotoxins known as microcystins. As the biosynthesis of these toxins is influenced by the cellular carbon (C) to nitrogen (N) ratio (C:N), changes to environmental availability of both DIC and N substrate type (e.g., ammonium, nitrate, urea) could also change toxin production. Nitrification in particular is a critical N transformation that converts ammonium into nitrate, and has been shown to decrease under acidification in marine environments. In this study we tested how temperature (current vs high) and DIC (low vs high) affected natural WLE cHAB communities in terms of toxin production, C and N uptake and metabolism, and freshwater nitrification rates. We measured nitrification rates and toxin concentrations across treatments, and using metatranscriptomics, we also evaluated changes in gene expression, including carbon concentrating mechanisms (sbtA, bicA), N uptake and assimilation (nrt, amt, urt, gln, ntcA), and toxin production (mcy gene cluster).

presentations.title: ENVIRONMENTAL DNA REVEALS PATTERNS OF TOXIC CYANOBACTERIAL STRAINS IN MAINE LAKES
presentations.abstract: Climate change and nutrient enrichment are increasing the frequency, duration, and severity of harmful cyanobacterial blooms in freshwater ecosystems. These blooms can contain mixtures of toxic and non-toxic strains, yet the environmental factors that shape the distribution of toxin-producing genotypes remain poorly understood. To address this, we surveyed 50 lakes across Maine to assess the occurrence of toxic strains of three common microcystin-producing cyanobacteria: Dolichospermum, Microcystis, and Planktothrix. We used an environmental DNA (eDNA) approach combined with a triplex digital PCR assay targeting the mcyE gene from each taxon to quantify the presence and relative abundance of microcystin-producing strains. Across the surveyed lakes, we observed substantial variation in the number and type of toxic genotypes present. Some lakes contained multiple microcystin-producing taxa, while others showed evidence of only a single strain or none at all. These patterns suggest that local environmental conditions, watershed characteristics, or historical bloom dynamics may influence which toxic strains establish and persist. Integrating these results with long-term lake monitoring data will improve our understanding of why toxic strains occur or dominate in particular systems and support efforts to predict and manage harmful blooms under changing climate conditions.

presentations.title: Can High N Lead to Toxic Cyanobacteria Blooms in P-limited Lakes? Simulation Model to Explore Role of N in Toxin Production and Reduced Grazing Mortality
presentations.abstract: Until a decade ago, toxic cyanobacteria blooms had never been reported in the 10 oligotrophic and mesotrophic Finger Lakes of New York State. Now, all these lakes experience blooms of toxic Microcystis sp. each summer. Phosphorus inputs and concentrations remain low to moderate in all of the lakes, and our preliminary experiments show that the cyanobacteria grow very slowly. We hypothesize that the cyanobacteria proliferate despite slow growth because mortality is low. In our hypothesis, grazing mortality by zooplankton and benthic mussels is suppressed by toxins produced by the cyanobacteria. The toxins are N-rich, and we believe high N levels in the Finger Lakes may enable high toxin production by the cyanobacteria. We are exploring these hypotheses with a simulation model that predicts cyanobacteria biomass and toxicity as a function of growth, toxicity, and mortality terms. In the simplest version of our model, growth is a function of P availability, and mortality is a function of zooplankton biomass and concentration of toxins in the cyanobacteria. The toxin concentration, in turn, is a function of N availability. We hope to explore more complicated versions of the model that include grazing by mussels and the role of lake mixing and light availability on cyanobacteria growth in these lakes, many of which are quite deep and partially mixed. Our preliminary results to date confirm that blooms can occur despite P-limited growth rate due to little or no grazing loss because of the high toxin levels that are possible in N-rich lakes.

presentations.title: Towards a mechanistic understanding of platinum and palladium in mixtures in the aquatic invertebrate Chironomus riparius
presentations.abstract: (carle.alice@courrier.uqam.ca) Emissions of platinum (Pt) and palladium (Pd) are increasing due to growing industrial use, leading to accumulation in freshwater sediments where benthic organisms may be harmfully affected. Most ecotoxicological studies investigate single metal exposure in water, whereas little information from molecular to organismal levels exists on mixtures in sediments. We aimed to characterize the toxicological, metal-handling and proteomic responses of the insect Chironomus riparius exposed to Pt and Pd, individually and in mixtures. Standardized sediment toxicity tests were performed by fixing the concentration of one metal while increasing the other. Survival, growth and bioaccumulation were evaluated to determine the nature of Pd-Pt interactions. Subcellular measurements were performed to understand the metal distribution among detoxified and sensitive compartments. Protein alterations were evaluated using proteomics analysis on whole larvae to identify potential biomarkers of Pd- and Pt-induced toxicity. Toxicity tests showed significant antagonistic interactions at the highest mixture concentrations. Subcellular partitioning indicated that, in single-metal exposures, most Pt and Pd accumulated in detoxified compartment, with granules accounting for 54–68 % of total metal burden. Proteomics identified 719 proteins, among which 173 were significantly affected by individual exposures, while 209-223 proteins changed significantly in mixtures. This study will contribute to the development of relevant toxicity criteria for these metals for better protection of aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: PALEO-ECOTOXICOLOGICAL EVIDENCE OF CLADOCERAN ASSEMBLAGE CHANGES LINKED TO URANIUM MINE CONTAMINATION IN NORTHERN ONTARIO, CANADA
presentations.affiliation: Paleoecological Environmental Assessment and Research Laboratory
presentations.abstract: To reduce fossil fuel use, Canada is investing heavily in nuclear power, which requires mining and processing of uranium ore. While impacts to fish and their habitat are well documented in some regions, the full environmental and ecotoxicological impacts of uranium mining on aquatic ecosystems remain poorly understood, due largely to a lack of long-term monitoring data. Paleo-ecotoxicology, the science that relates long-term shifts in biological indicators with the history of metal(loid) exposure can be used to provide these missing datasets. Here we investigate the ecological impacts of uranium mining on Whiskey Lake, which received diluted uranium mining effluent from the Elliott Lake mining distict (N. Ontario) beginning ca. 1950s, causing the lake to acidify to pH 5.4 and become contaminated with radionuclides and metal(loid)s during peak production (ca. 1950-1970s). We report a shift in cladoceran assemblages (notably the loss of Eubosmina longispina) and a slight decline in whole-lake production inferred from sediment chlorophyll a (chl-a) concentrations. Following chemical improvements in the early 1980s, E. longispina returned and chl-a increased. Interestingly, when the lake reacidified to pH 5.0 in the early 1980s, E. longispina remained abundant, suggesting this taxon may be more sensitive to radionuclides/metal(loid)s, which concentrations remained below water quality guideline values at this time. This project lays the foundation for a broader investigation of uranium-affected lakes in N. Saskatchewan, in collaboration with the Clearwater River Dënë Nation.

presentations.title: Colloidal iron in the Arctic Ocean: Size distributions and concentrations in Baffin Bay and open ocean seawater
presentations.affiliation: CNRS – Université Laval – Sorbonne Université – International Research Laboratory Takuvik
presentations.abstract: Iron (Fe) is an essential but limiting micronutrient for marine primary production. At trace level in the ocean, its distribution depends on a complex speciation among various physicochemical forms that controls its behavior and bioavailability. Despite recent advances in marine geochemistry, significant uncertainties remain in the oceanic iron cycle, like mass balance estimates, probably because its colloidal fraction (cFe) is still poorly studied, defined, and characterized. As a result, the role of cFe in biogeochemical cycles is still not well constrained, particularly in the Arctic Ocean, where the cryosphere is a major source. In this region strongly affected by climate change, rapid ice melt and increased river inputs modify particle fluxes, which in turn influence iron species distribution and may alter iron and carbon cycle dynamics. This study investigates colloidal iron in the Arctic Ocean. Seawater samples from open ocean and Baffin Bay were collected. Colloidal fraction was separated using frontal ultrafiltration and tangential flow filtration. Size distributions were characterized using light scattering techniques and iron concentrations were quantified using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Analyses revealed site-specific colloidal populations, reflecting spatial variability in colloidal composition. Iron concentrations were higher in the colloidal than in the dissolved phase, highlighting cFe’s potential role in Arctic iron transport, bioavailability and biogeochemical cycling under rapidly changing polar conditions.

presentations.title: DIFFERENT CONCENTRATIONS OF ARTIFICAL MICROPLASTICS HAVE NO CLEAR IMPACT ON THE FATE, BEHAVIOUR OR EFFECTS OF OIL IN THE WATER COLUMN
presentations.abstract: Microplastics (MP) can absorb polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, affect sinking of oil after a spill and could affect hydrocarbon degrading microbes. To observe MP impacts on oil after a surface spill, a mesocosm experiment was conducted using coastal seawater seeded with 3 mm MP composed of 4 different plastic types at 5 different concentrations. After 4 d, crude oil was added to all enclosures which were sampled over 28 d. In all enclosures, regardless of the amount of MP added, similar patterns were observed. Dissolved hydrocarbon concentrations peaked early (0-3 d), before declining. Likewise, potential toxicity of seawater peaked between 1 and 3 d. Chlorophyll a and prokaryotic cell abundances also peaked around 3 d before decreasing, with larger variability in the phytoplankton compared to the prokaryotes. Even as abundances decreased, microbial community diversity increased over time. A shift to a hydrocarbon degrading community is indicated by increases in Cycloclasticus and Marivita. Differences in the behaviors of the 4 plastics types may have reduced the potential effects of the MP. One type of plastic sank prior to oil addition, while another tended to float ~10 cm below the surface. The other two types remained on the surface and mixed with the surface slick, but were not observed to sink during the experiment. Interactions between MP and oil spills may be complicated by type and size of MP as well as other environmental conditions such as temperature, salinity and mixing energy. The implications of MP remains an important unknown in oil spill response.

presentations.title: THE ROLE OF DISSOLVED OXYGEN IN DRIVING MICROPLASTIC SURFACE AGING BY PHOTOOXIDATION
presentations.abstract: As the main driver of plastic weathering, UV radiation has been shown to alter the surface chemistry of plastic—changing its functional groups, structural stability, and overall oxidation state over time. Oxidation relies heavily on oxygen including reactive oxygen species to initiate the progression of chemical reactions, which determine both the type and rate of polymer surface degradation. Despite the importance, there is a lack of mechanistic understanding of the overall role of oxygen in the plastic oxidation in marine environment. Such understanding may help clarify the pathways and chemical transformations that drive long term degradation of plastics in the ocean—thereby providing a clearer insight into fragmentation behavior after oxidation. In this work we aim to: (1) assess the development of oxygen containing functional groups with time, (2) identify the pathways of oxygen incorporation, (3) determine the vertical gradients of oxidative penetration in plastic polymers, and (4) understand how photo-weathering develops across the plastic surface. This experiment is still on going and the results will be presented.

presentations.title: INTERACTIVE IMPACTS OF TIRE-WEAR-PARTICLES AND DE-ICING ROAD SALTS ON DIATOM COMMUNITIES FROM HIGH MOUNTAIN STREAMS IN SPANISH NATIONAL PARKS
presentations.abstract: In the last 10 years, the number of visitors to Spanish National Parks has increased from 10 to 15 million per year. Given that the preferred transportation mode for visitors are vehicles, this might lead to stream pollution by tire wear particles (TWPs) as well as de-icing salts used to preserve safe driving conditions in winter. In this work, we evaluate if these road-related pollutants could potentially enter streams of high mountain National Parks and impact the abundance and composition of diatom communities. For this purpose, we collected water, sediment and periphyton samples in streams with and without road influence in three National Parks during spring and fall 2025. For each stream, shallow, illuminated and medium to high flow velocity transects were stablished and 10 rocks were selected, where an area of 100 cm2 was removed with hard-bristle brushes. The most frequent species belonged to the genera Gomphonema, Cymbella, Encyonema, Cocconeis and Nitzschia. Differences in community composition were analysed with permutational multivariate analysis of variance. Preliminary results show that, within seasons, diatom composition was statistically different in the three National Parks. The presence and concentration of road-related pollutants in water and sediment samples will be analysed and potential effects on diatom abundance and composition will be investigated. Although this is not directly related with road pollutants but with human impacts on protected areas, we report the presence of the invasive species Didymosphenia sp, in one of the National Parks.
