presentations.title: From prospective to field-based assessment: integrated ecotoxicological approaches to characterize pesticide transformation products in lentic small water bodies
presentations.abstract: Lentic small water bodies (LSWBs) located at the head of agricultural watersheds act as key interfaces for the accumulation, transformation and transfer of pesticides, often leading to the formation of transformation products (TPs). These TPs are considered contaminants of emerging concern due to their rapidly growing detection worldwide and the limited understanding of their ecological effects. Their ecotoxicological assessment still relies mainly on prospective, chemistry-based approaches, as field evidence of biological responses remains scarce. To partially address this issue, this presentation follows a methodological continuum from prospective to effective assessment to better characterize TPs related hazards in LSWBs. First, an environmental risk assessment was conducted along a gradient of agricultural intensity, comparing measured concentrations of pesticides and TPs to ecotoxicity thresholds to identify key contributors and spatial patterns of potential risk. Second, an active biomonitoring approach using caged Gammarus roeseli assessed in situ biological responses through integrative biomarkers. This combined framework links potential chemical risks with effective biological effects under realistic exposure conditions. Results show that several TPs strongly contribute to estimated risks, while biological responses reflect mixture toxicity, exposure gradients and local environmental conditions. Together these approaches improve the realism of ecotoxicological characterization and emphasize the central role of TPs in LSWBs under agricultural and climatic pressures.

presentations.title: AQUATIC HABITAT USE IS LINKED TO PESTICIDE CONTAMINATION OF FECES FROM AERIAL INSECTIVORES
presentations.abstract: Water bodies located in the agricultural landscape may face a substantial contamination by insecticides, herbicides, and fungicides. Emerging insects may act as vectors, transferring these pesticides from water bodies into terrestrial food webs when they leave the aquatic habitats as adults. We investigated the contamination of feces from various insectivorous organisms with different foraging modes and frequency of aquatic habitat use, quantified by habitat selection analyses based on high-resolution telemetry data. In total, we detected 16 current-use pesticide residues, two legacy compounds and six metabolites in the feces of three species which had a significant positive association to aquatic habitats: barn swallow (Hirundo rustica), Western house martin (Delichon urbicum), and the common noctule bat (Nyctalus noctula). In contrast, no substances were detected in feces of European starling (Sturnus vulgaris), a species that used rather terrestrial habitats and is known to feed on terrestrial insects. The fungicide prochloraz, used to combat fungal grain diseases, was the substance with the highest detection rate (69 % of all samples). While the direct ecotoxicological effects on the organisms are unclear, our study is one of the first ones to demonstrate the contamination pathway via emerging insects and to highlight that species-specific habitat use may strongly affect contamination pathways in aerial insectivores such as birds and bats.

presentations.title: HYDROCHEMICAL AND GEOSTATISTICAL ANALYSES TO EXPLORE CLIMATIC AND ENSO-LINKED VARIABILITY OF RIVERINE MICROPOLLUTANTS IN THE RIVER TOMEBAMBA, ECUADOR
presentations.abstract: The research focused on the River Tomebamba in Ecuador, which runs through the city of Cuenca. The analysed water samples were collected along the river at thirty sampling points during five sampling campaigns between 2023 and 2025. Concentrations of pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and other endocrine-disrupting compounds were evaluated together with hydrological and meteorological parameters. The results revealed strong spatial and temporal variability in pollutant concentrations. During dry periods, a total of 24 compounds had a risk quotient (RQ) value higher than 0.1, including estrogens and Bisphenol derivatives. Geostatistical analyses revealed that the spatial distribution of micropollutants is oriented along the main river axis, with the greatest heterogeneity observed near urban inflows and tributaries. The results also showed that increasingly irregular rainfall patterns and longer dry periods can increase the exposure to organic micropollutants in the Amazon Basin. The hydrological variability is strongly influenced by the macroregional effects of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation. Concentration patterns aligned with changes in discharge and precipitation indicate that the intensification of climatic extremes under ongoing climate change directly affects the temporal and spatial distribution of riverine contaminants. The study presents data-driven evidence that climatic and hydrological dynamics, combined with urban pressures, can jointly determine the spatiotemporal behaviour of micropollutants in the Ecuadorian watersheds of the Amazon Basin.

presentations.title: Exploring the impacts of contaminant combinations on phytoplankton communities in a managed SC reservoir
presentations.abstract: Freshwater sources are essential for society, impacting health, hygiene, and local economies. However, they are highly susceptible to human activities. In recent years, concerns about emerging contaminants have gained attention as we try to understand how excess inputs of both natural and synthetic chemicals damage aquatic ecosystems. Carbamazepine and diclofenac are among the most common pharmaceuticals found in global surface waters and adversely affect aquatic organisms across various trophic levels. Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), a type of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), has been associated with biomagnification and other harmful effects on aquatic life. 6ppd-quinone (6ppd-q), a byproduct of tire wear, was linked to a sudden die-off in coho salmon. Evidence suggests these contaminants can harm phytoplankton by reducing biomass and diversity, causing stress, and impairing photophysiology. However, much of this research uses phytoplankton cultures exposed to unrealistically high contaminant concentrations. This study explored how combinations of contaminants and nutrient stress affect phytoplankton, aiming to better understand their interactive effects at environmentally relevant concentrations. Whole water samples were exposed to contaminant combinations for 72h then analyzed for total biomass and photophysiological parameters. Preliminary results show that contaminants decrease biomass only under nutrient-rich conditions, highlighting that nutrient availability is a key factor influencing phytoplankton’s physiological responses to contaminant exposure.

presentations.title: MODELLING CONTAMINANT REMOBILIZATION DUE TO SEDIMENT RESUSPENSION
presentations.abstract: Numerous contaminants (PFAS, manganese, mercury, etc.) sorb to the surface of sediment, yet numerical models often ignore this important process when modelling transport. Sorption is a gradient-driven process, such that when contaminated sediment moves into relatively clean water, contaminants will desorb from the surface of sediment grains if they are sorbed reversibly. Disturbing lakebed sediment has the potential to reintroduce buried contaminants into the water column. We present a mathematical model for contaminant transport that accounts for exchange with an underlying sediment layer and reversible sorption. The system is described by two key dimensionless parameters; the ratio of the contaminant and sediment diffusivities, and the ratio of the sorption to settling timescales. Results from one-dimensional numerical simulations illustrate that the system is sensitive to how exchange between the water column and sediment layer is treated. We will discuss the bounds on the system behaviour that result from this exchange and from limiting values of the dimensionless parameters. The one-dimensional results will be compared to results from solving a 0D continuously stirred reactor problem. We will conclude with some preliminary results from higher dimensional simulations and a discussion of how we expect our findings to extend to three-dimensional and larger scale systems.

presentations.title: Tracking a century of ecological changes and human impacts using chironomid assemblages in lakes from the Wolastoq watershed
presentations.abstract: Over the last century, aquatic ecosystems have faced multiple human-driven stressors. Paleoecological studies using invertebrate bioindicators can help to understand long-term responses to cumulative impacts. This study evaluates chironomid assemblage responses to anthropogenic impacts in three lakes from the Wolastoq watershed in New Brunswick, Canada. Preliminary results shows that Ayers, the most pristine lake, has the highest richness (n=32) compared with Nictau and Unique (n=10). Ayers also shows a shift from deep-water taxa to littoral taxa, likely associated with climate changes that followed regional exposure to the insecticide DDT around 1960. Nictau shows a similar pattern but with lower overall diversity and a strong assemblage shift toward littoral taxa coincident with high sedimentary DDT and its metabolites. In contrast Unique, the most impacted site from decades of eutrophication, is dominated by taxa typical of productive environments. Unique shows a marked decline in chironomid abundance from the early 1990s to the present. Algal pigment data indicates that this loss of invertebrate biodiversity is likely associated with eutrophication. These three Wolastoq lakes show contrasting long-term responses to regional stressors, with assemblage changes reflecting impacts from legacy insecticides, eutrophication, and climate change.

name: Aquatic Ecosystems Facing the Effects of Emerging Contaminants, Energy Transition and Global Changes : Recent Data, Challenges and Perspectives.

presentations.title: RARE EARTH ELEMENTS DISTRIBUTION IN PORE WATER OF LAKE SEDIMENTS ALONG A PRODUCTIVITY GRADIENT
presentations.abstract: The recent extensive mining and use of rare earth elements (REE) has increased their influx into aquatic environments. This, among other issues, may be problematic for aquatic organisms exposed to REE. As such, a better understanding of the mechanisms controlling REE mobility is needed to accurately predict their fate in aquatic systems. The aim of this study is to better understand the processes responsible for REE mobility in lake sediment, using pore water as a sensitive indicator of the reactions occurring within it. In particular, we are focusing on REE interactions with dissolved and colloidal OM along a gradient of primary productivity and OM quality. We have determined the vertical distribution of REE and other analytes (pH, OM, metals) in the sediment and pore water of three temperate lakes: Tantaré (oligotrophic), Maskinongé (mesotrophic) and Swan (eutrophic). REE concentration profiles in the pore water showed similar features in all lakes, with a subsurface peak between 2 and 6 cm depth, coinciding with the production of porewater Fe and Mn. Yet, peak concentration spanned one order of magnitude amongst lakes. They were lower (max 0.35 µg/L) in the eutrophic Swan Lake, and higher (max 24 µg/L) in the oligotrophic lake Tantaré. This might suggest REE mobilisation to the porewater by complexation with dissolved OM, concurrent to their release along with Fe and Mn oxyhydroxides reductive dissolution. These preliminary results will be complemented by OM characterization and statistical analysis to better constrain controls on REE distribution in lakes.

presentations.title: Assessing the effect of environmental changes on shore-to-water distribution of rare earth elements and mercury in Nunavik aquatic systems (Canada)
presentations.abstract: Even far from major industrial hubs, Arctic regions continue to experience notable anthropogenic metal contamination via air and water. Addressing Inuit concerns over atmospheric mercury (Hg) deposition and rare earth (REE) mining contamination in Nunavik (northern Québec, Canada), our study evaluates spatial metal distributions across multiple environmental compartments under ongoing human and climate-driven shifts in hydrology, greening, and physicochemistry. Through water, soil, sediment, lichen, and berry sampling from 10×10m transects along the Kuururjuaq (n=24) and George River (n=20) watersheds and wetlands, paired with observations of riverbank greening (relative abundance, species) and topography (slope, soil type), we document the environmental fate of emerging trace metals in remote Inuit territories, ultimately reaching traditional food and water sources. Integrating atmospheric biomonitors, water chemistry, PARAFAC and isotope analyses, we correlated REE concentrations with the abundance of dissolved organic matter, thorium, iron, and aluminium, as well as water temperature across the watershed. Several contamination peaks and gradients were also detected near the local airport (barium, sodium, REEs) and garbage dumps (antimony, arsenic, chromium, lead), using lichens as biomonitors. Wild berries, however, presented very low content in Hg, indicating mixed biomonitoring results but positive implications for food safety. These data, alongside nutrient abundances from our 70+ element survey, will support the development of guidelines on contaminant risks.

presentations.title: Social License for Aquatic Science Research: How community-engaged research models can advance understanding of the effects of emerging contaminants, the energy transition, and global change
presentations.abstract: The concept of a social license to operate, the ongoing approval and acceptance from a group of community stakeholders to conduct activities, is a commonly applied framework in science policy and industry operations. However, the concept of a social license has been less applied in areas of basic research, where it is common to have research projects designed and carried out with minimal (or no) broader stakeholder engagement. As public trust in science has eroded over the past few years and many of the world's most pressing problems will require science-based solutions, the need for a broad social license between scientists and the public has never been greater. This talk will explore two case-studies of community-engaged research projects that aim to not only disseminate project findings to broad stakeholder groups, but to actively engage communities in the design and conduct of the research itself. The first case will explore community perspectives of the role of novel biotechnology in addressing issues of PFAS remediation and rare earth element mining. The second case will look at a co-developed research project to better understand how PFAS has contaminated culturally relevant foods in Minnesota’s Indigenous communities.

presentations.title: LETHAL AND SUBLETHAL EFFECTS OF LEAD AND CAFFEINE ON FRESHWATER ROTIFERS, PLATYIAS QUADRICORNIS AND BRACHIONUS ANGULARIS
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at El Paso
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic activities negatively impact biodiversity through the use of substances such as pharmaceuticals and heavy metals, which are now common in freshwater bodies. These pollutants can cause sublethal and lethal effects to aquatic organisms. Rotifers, key components of aquatic food webs, help transfer energy from microbes to higher trophic levels. Comparing populations of the same species from habitats with different pollutant levels allow investigation of adaptive responses to chronic contaminant exposure. We hypothesized that rotifers from polluted sites would show greater tolerance to the pollutants than those from unpolluted sites due to prior exposure. Freshwater rotifers, Platyias quadricornis and Brachionus angularis, from a pristine site at a remote state park (Laguna Prieta) were used as reference population, while the same species from a storm-fed retention pond (Feather Lake) were used as the polluted population. We tested two common contaminants, caffeine and lead. Preliminary acute toxicity tests showed that the Feather Lake population was more sensitive to caffeine than the population from the unpolluted site. For Brachionus angularis, 2697 mg/L of caffeine resulted in 50% mortality of the Laguna Prieta population, which is higher than reported LC50 values for other rotifer species. This opposite trend to our hypothesis may be due to chronic stress weakening the polluted-site rotifers or reduced genetic diversity. Lead exposure tests for both populations and the acute toxicity assays for the Feather Lake population are currently ongoing.

presentations.title: ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS DETERMINE THE IMPACT OF PLASTIC IN FRESHWATER LAKES
presentations.abstract: Plastic pollution and environmental heterogeneity are two of the most pressing issues facing aquatic ecosystems, however, there is little understanding of their interaction. In the Laurentian Great Lakes, storm intensity, water temperature, and water pH are shifting. At the same time, the input of plastic debris continues to rise. To evaluate the interactive effects of environmental conditions and plastic pollution on freshwater ecosystems, we are conducting a series of in vitro and in situ experiments. We hypothesized that the impacts of environmental change on plastic pollution would be polymer specific. Plastic debris used for our experiments was selected based on measured abundance in stormwater, the primary input pathway in the coastal zone of the Lakes. Post-consumer polypropylene (PP) wrappers and cellulose acetate (CA) cigarette butts, along with virgin polystyrene (PS) sheets were incubated using factorially designed in-lake mesocosms (“limnocorrals”) to test the impact of pH and temperature on biofilm characteristics, leaching, and toxicity to the model oligochaete Lumbriculus variegatus. Preliminary analyses suggest that biofilm formation and persistence varied by treatment and time. The acute toxicity of water from the mesocosms increased following plastic addition and decreased over time. Shifting pH and temperature appear to have significant impacts on both biological and chemical fate of plastics, suggesting an increased risk to organisms in the coastal zone and ultimately for ecosystem and human health.

presentations.title: Investigating the Influence of Aquatic Vegetation on Microplastic Retention in Riverine Sediments
presentations.abstract: Sediments in the water body can act as a long-term sink for plastic particles. Density and shape are factors that are believed to influence the movement of MPs, causing them to either remain suspended in the water column or sink to deeper regions. During this settling process, MPs can be intercepted and retained by aquatic plants along their circulation path. In marine research MPs have been shown to be attached to the periphytic biomass and epibiont communities such as algae that is growing on seagrasses. This research aims to investigate whether aquatic plants (macrophytes) in freshwater environments and the sediments found below can act as sinks for MPs in freshwater ecosystems by comparing sediment beds where plants are present and where plants are absent. Four locations in the Ottawa River have been sampled. Each of the four sampling locations includes a total of 10 sediment samples — five from unvegetated areas and five from vegetated areas. Additionally, five plant samples each composed of 2 individual plants were collected from the vegetated areas. Between 75 and 100 grams of sediment were used for the laboratory analysis of each sample. The samples were treated with hydrogen peroxide to break down organic material and then subjected to density separation. Preliminary analyses show that all examined plant samples collected contained MPs, suggesting that freshwater macrophyte beds may play a significant role in MP retention. This project will also examine whether this process varies among different species that are found in the Ottawa River.

presentations.title: SPF: Sun protection or phyto-frustration? Short-term impacts of sunscreen UV filters on freshwater phytoplankton
presentations.abstract: Commercially available sunscreens contain active ingredients that block ultraviolet radiation, known as UV filters (UVFs), as well as inactive ingredients that increase product stability and facilitate application. UVFs contaminate aquatic environments when sunscreen leaches into the water during recreational activities. As a result, UVF concentrations of 0.1–10 μg L-1 have been detected in freshwater and marine systems worldwide. While the effects of UVFs on marine organisms have been relatively well studied, far less is known about UVF effects on freshwater biota. Furthermore, most freshwater studies have focused on individual UVFs rather than examining the combined effects of mixtures of UVFs that are found within commercially available products. Understanding the sensitivity of freshwater primary producers to sunscreen products is essential for assessing ecological risk, as these primary producers sustain aquatic food webs and ecosystem functioning. We are investigating the responses of freshwater phytoplankton and periphyton to sunscreens containing common ultraviolet filters at environmentally relevant concentrations. Pilot data were collected from monocultures of the green alga Chlorella vulgaris exposed to a gradient of sunscreen solutions containing environmentally relevant UVF concentrations for 72 hours. Maximum photosynthetic yield (Fv/Fm) and cell density cell were surprisingly resilient to the UVF gradient, showing only a modest decrease in Fv/Fm. We are currently conducting an expanded study using the same protocol but with additional species of green algae and cyanobacteria, both phytoplankton and periphyton.

presentations.title: Investigating the effects of sediment resuspension on contaminant release in a coastal Texas bay due to storms, ship traffic, and dredging activities
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at Austin Marine Science Institute
presentations.abstract: Coastal sediments serve as repositories for various contaminants resulting from human activities. Although deep burial reduces their impact on marine life, sediment resuspension caused by natural events and human activities may release contaminants to the water column, which is a high concern to marine organisms and human health. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and mercury (Hg) are three commonly-found groups in marine sediments. Matagorda Bay, a shallow bay along the Texas coast with a history of contamination, is especially vulnerable to sediment resuspension and contaminant re-exposure due to ship traffic, dredging, heavy winds, and storm activity, which are expected to increase in frequency and intensity with climate change. The goal of this study is to evaluate the release of PAHs, PCBs, and trace metals from sediments to the water in Matagorda Bay due to resuspension. To do so, a Gust erosion system (UGEMS) was used to investigate the erodibility of sediments and release of adsorbed contaminants from Matagorda Bay sediment cores by simulating sediment resuspension under different shear stresses. Preliminary data shows that eroded sediment mass increased both as shear stress increased and along a spatial gradient from the inner bay to the coast. Although data analysis is still undergoing, it is hypothesized that the concentration of contaminants re-released into the overlying water will be greater at higher shear stresses. Results of PAHs, PCBs, and trace metals at different shear stresses and sites of the bay will be presented.

name: Ecological Significance of Dissolved Organic Matter
lead_organizer: Jianjun WANG, Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
co_organizers: Núria Catalán, Centre for Advanced Studies of Blanes, CSIC
session_description: There is a myriad of organic matter molecules in aquatic ecosystems that continuously undergo microbial and abiotic transformation, processes that critically influence carbon storage and climate feedback. Studies in the past two decades have made substantial progress in characterizing dissolved organic matter (DOM) across aquatic environments due to the advancements in ultrahigh-resolution mass spectrometry and statistical approaches.

presentations.title: If more UHR DOM data is the answer, what was the question?
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)
presentations.abstract_summary: Argues for hypothesis-driven FT-ICR-MS DOM studies under an Ecology of Molecules framework with three pathways (molecular keystones, chemodiversity-function, DOM-microbe networks); proposes decision criteria for when UHR molecular data resolves mechanistic uncertainty vs merely documents capability.
presentations.abstract: The rapid expansion of FT-ICR-MS applications has redefined the chemical resolution at which we interrogate dissolved organic matter (DOM), yielding molecular inventories of unprecedented breadth. Yet the predictive capacity of freshwater carbon-cycling models has not scaled commensurately. This gap exposes a central methodological tension: we routinely generate exquisitely detailed molecular atlases without equivalently rigorous articulation of the ecological questions that necessitate such resolution. What we require are mechanistic roadmaps—explicit links between molecular features, microbial strategies, and biogeochemical fluxes. Within the Ecology of Molecules framework, I delineate three mechanistic pathways through which molecular information can (and must) translate to ecosystem-level prediction. (1) Molecular keystones: discrete compounds or compound classes exerting disproportionate influence on reaction kinetics, microbial community assembly, or coupled nutrient cycles—functional analogs to keystone taxa in community ecology. (2) Chemodiversity–function relationships: empirical tests of whether molecular diversity and compositional redundancy regulate process rates, stability domains, or resilience to perturbation, paralleling biodiversity–ecosystem function theory. (3) DOM–microbe interaction networks: environmentally contingent coupling between molecular composition and microbial metabolic strategies across lakes, rivers, and wetlands, revealing bidirectional feedbacks between chemical architecture and microbial trait distributions. Through comparative analyses spanning contrasting hydrologic, thermal, and land-use regimes, I show that hypothesis-driven molecular approaches—interrogating explicit mechanisms such as photochemical lability, microbial selectivity, or hydrologic sorting—consistently outperform unconstrained molecular surveys. I systematically evaluate when bulk or optical metrics achieve equivalent explanatory power, and when molecular-level resolution is indispensable for forecasting DOM reactivity, transformation pathways, and persistence under environmental change. To advance predictive freshwater C-cycle models, I propose decision criteria for strategically deploying ultra-high-resolution mass spectrometry: conditions under which molecular data resolve mechanistic uncertainty versus those in which they merely document analytical capability. Without well-posed hypotheses, comprehensive characterization becomes descriptive accumulation rather than ecological inference. I conclude with a set of actionable frameworks for designing DOM studies that operationalize molecular information into ecological prediction—and with provocation for the community: How do we shift from expanding molecular inventories to constraining carbon fate? Under what circumstances has molecular resolution genuinely reframed ecosystem understanding, and when has it obscured the mechanistic narrative we seek to explain?

presentations.title: A Global Synthesis of Organic Matter Data
presentations.abstract_summary: CoreMS-aggregated >5000 FTICR-MS samples reveal coherent ecosystem-level OM groupings; PCA shows lakes/streams enriched in N:C and S:C, sediment/ice in H:C and P:C — providing a synthesized global resource.
presentations.abstract: Organic matter (OM) underpins ecosystem biogeochemistry across the globe. While research has focused on OM characterization within singular ecosystems, less attention has been given to cross-ecosystem patterns. Understanding the OM patterns across ecosystems may reveal broader constraints on OM contributions to broad scale biogeochemistry. We leveraged CoreMS and custom metadata management to aggregate >5000 FTICR-MS samples collected by a variety of labs from diverse locations and ecosystems across the globe. Our analyses indicate that ecosystems represent coherent groups despite the significant spatial distances, variation in collection methodologies, and differences in instruments. We observed significant multivariate differences across ecosystems that aligned with expectations (e.g., river OM diverged from sediment OM) but some patterns were unexpected (e.g., river OM was not divergent from soil OM). To investigate differences in OM chemistry, we used a principal component analysis (PCA) to evaluate OM properties enriched in each ecosystem. The PCA captured many significant multivariate differences and revealed potential OM properties associated with ecosystem types. For example, lakes and streams were associated with increased N:C and S:C ratios indicating potential nutrient loading while sediment and ice was affiliated with H:C and P:C ratios highlighting degradation. By integrating more ecosystems, we expect that this synthesized dataset will serve as an important resource to the scientific community to contextualize local information to global patterns.

presentations.title: Sediments act as major carbon storage and transformation in mangroves with different root structures
presentations.affiliation: National Pingtung University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract_summary: Compares Avicennia (pneumatophores), Rhizophora (supporting roots), and mixed mangrove stands in Taiwan; root morphology and seasonal anoxia jointly modulate sediment OM stability via an enzymatic-latch mechanism.
presentations.abstract: Mangroves play a vital role in carbon capturing, transforming and storage in coastalareas; however, their carbon storage and stability affected by environmental variables such as salinity, tidal change, and other biochemical factors. This study investigates how contrasting root morphologies— Avicennia marina (aerial pneumatophores), Rhizophora stylosa (supporting roots), and mixed-species stands—govern sediment carbon quantity and quality in the Haomeiliao mangrove forests in southwestern coastal areas of Taiwan. Field measurements were bi-monthly conducted across wet and dry seasons, including sediment organic carbon content, redox potential and dissolved organic matter (DOM) concentration and optical indices (fluorescence index, biological index) in porewater. Results show that, in generally, seasonal rainfall patterns induced persistent anoxia in sediments, which suppressed oxidative enzyme activity, indicating a hydrologically mediated “enzymatic latch” mechanism that declined decomposition rates of DOM and thus benefited carbon preservation and storage. Root morphology further modulated these processes: Rhizophora stands (supporting roots) showed constantly stable anoxic conditions with higher humic-like substances observed, whereas Avicennia stands (aerial roots) experienced greater redox variations, elevated enzyme activity, and higher carbon storage originated from stronger endogenous microbial and algal productions. Mixed forests displayed highest carbon concentration in the sediment , however, the humidification level of OM were lower (i.e., lower stability) of comparing to the pure Rhizophora forest. Our findings demonstrate that the interaction between root structural traits, sedimentary chemistry and seasonal rainfall patterns plays a critical role in regulating sediment carbon quality and quantity in mangrove ecosystems. Results provide critical knowledge for predicting the resilience of mangrove blue carbon under future climate-driven changes in precipitation, salinity, and species composition.

presentations.title: Compositional and hydrological drivers of DOM degradability across land-water continua of boreal watersheds
presentations.abstract_summary: Across 26 boreal/subarctic Quebec headwaters: bio- and photo-degradable DOM losses concentrate in different compartments (riparian vs streams/lakes); ~53% DOC lost from riparian to stream driven by protein-like depletion.
presentations.abstract: Recent studies showed efficient depletion and transformation of the terrestrial C pool from land to water, yet the strength and shape of this pattern vary geographically and the underlying drivers remain unclear. We assessed how DOM intrinsic degradability and watershed hydrology shape broad-scale DOM patterns by measuring biological and photochemical DOM degradability in terrestrial (upland, riparian) and aquatic (stream, lake) compartments of 26 headwaters across boreal and subarctic Quebec, Canada, spanning 48.9–59.1°N; 63.2–76.2°W. We linked degradability with DOM fluorescence and water stable isotopes (d-excess) as proxies of DOM composition and cumulative exposure to degradation processes, respectively. Fulvic-like and protein-like pools showed strong and preferential losses under photochemical and biological experiment, respectively. Reactivity potential also tended to decrease from land to water and with lower d-excess (denoting longer water transit times), indicating a progressive mineralization of bio- and photodegradable substances occurred during transit. However, the loss of biodegradability potential with rising d-excess was expressed mainly in riparian zones whereas photodegradability losses were concentrated in streams and lakes. Despite regional variation, DOC losses (x̄=53%) were greatest from riparian to stream, driven by protein-like depletion (x̄=85%). Thus, DOM intrinsic degradability and watershed hydrology jointly shape broad-scale DOM patterns with implication for C budgets as both aspects will likely respond to different facets of global change.

presentations.title: Accumulation of Ancient but Labile Dissolved Organic Matter in the Dead Sea
presentations.abstract_summary: Dead Sea DOC is ~10,000 years old yet remains biologically degradable when exposed to non-extreme microbial communities; redefines 'refractory' DOM as environmentally contingent rather than intrinsically stable.
presentations.abstract: The global reservoir of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) equals the amount of atmospheric carbon, yet the mechanisms allowing its long-term persistence in aquatic systems remain poorly resolved. The hypersaline Dead Sea offers an extreme model for testing how environmental constraints affect organic matter cycling and microbial utilization. We analyzed dissolved organic matter (DOM) from the Dead Sea, its tributary springs, and surrounding aquifers using 14 C dating and Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry. DOC concentrations in the Dead Sea were ~2000 µM, ~50-fold higher than in the deep ocean, with 14 C ages of ~10,000 years. Dead Sea DOM was molecularly almost undistinguishable from submarine and coastal springs, indicating that the DOM originates mainly from groundwater and sedimentary inputs rather than in situ production. Despite its age, molecular indices revealed features typical of labile material, and in incubation experiments with a productive North Sea microbial community, Dead Sea DOM was readily consumed. DOC decreased by 15% and 800 molecular formulas were lost within 3 years, demonstrating that it remains biologically degradable under non-extreme conditions. Accordingly, the long-term accumulation of DOC in the Dead Sea is not due to intrinsic molecular recalcitrance but to environmental inhibition of microbial degradation caused by extreme salinity and ionic toxicity, redefining the concept of “refractory” DOM as a relative property, determined by local environmental and ecological constraints rather than chemical stability alone.

presentations.title: Deciphering Labile and Refractory Organic Components in Natural Waters: Implications for Lake Carbon Cycling
presentations.affiliation: University of Science and Technology Beijing
presentations.abstract_summary: FT-ICR-MS plus optical spectroscopy across alpine lake, macrophyte lake, and urban river: molecular weight determines bio-incubation activity; phytoplankton-dominated lakes have substantially higher refractory DOM.
presentations.abstract: Photo-incubation and bio-incubation are key processes regulating the chemical composition and fate of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in inland surface waters. However, the reactivity and transformation mechanisms of different DOM components in inland natural waters remain inadequately characterized. In this study, three representative inland water bodies, an alpine lake dominated by phytoplankton, a macrophyte-dominated lake, and an urban river, were investigated using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) coupled with optical spectroscopy. Potential chemical reaction predictions were combined to elucidate the molecular transformation mechanism of DOM in photochemical and microbial incubation processes. Our results demonstrate that the critical role of intrinsic molecular properties of DOM, notably molecular weight, unsaturation, and humification degree, in regulating its reactivity and driving compositional shifts during biogeochemical processes. Molecular weight determined bio-incubation activity, while source-specific highly unsaturated and phenolic compounds modulated lacustrine DOM degradation patterns. Concurrently, complex biogeochemical processes drove compositional convergence of DOM across natural aquatic systems. Identification of refractory DOM (RDOM) revealed substantially higher RDOM content in phytoplankton-dominated lakes compared to macrophyte-dominated lakes and urban rivers. These findings elucidate the molecular drivers of DOM degradation in inland waters and provide a theoretical framework for identifying labile and refractory DOM, thereby enabling assessment of the carbon source-sink functions and cycling processes in diverse inland aquatic ecosystems.

name: Ecological Significance of Dissolved Organic Matter
lead_organizer: Jianjun WANG, Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, CAS
session_description: Third concurrent block of DOM session.

presentations.title: The NOSC-ΔG relationship in DOM: why it works, why it fails
presentations.abstract_summary: Quantum chemistry + Random Forest model predicts Gibbs free energy for >4000 DOM molecules; NOSC captures broad trends but fails within molecular formulae (>100 kJ/molC differences).
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) regulates carbon storage and microbial activity across aquatic ecosystems, yet we still lack a clear mechanistic link between its molecular composition and thermodynamic favourability and persistence. We combine quantum chemistry with a structure informed Random Forest model to predict the Gibbs free energy of oxidation per mole of carbon for more than 4000 environmentally relevant molecules, and apply these predictions to ultra high resolution mass spectrometry data from standard DOM reference materials. By revisiting the relationship between the nominal oxidation state of carbon (NOSC) and Gibbs free energy, we show that NOSC captures first order trends across broad DOM quality gradients but fails within individual molecular formulae and NOSC classes, where structurally similar molecules can differ by more than 100 kJ molC⁻¹ in predicted gibbs free energy. These results link DOM chemodiversity to thermodynamic constraints on microbial use and help to explain why DOM fractions with similar elemental composition can follow divergent degradation pathways across aquatic redox gradients due to underlying structural and thermodynamic diversity.

presentations.title: Environmental and Microbial Controls on DOM Across Aquatic Ecosystems
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, CAS
presentations.abstract_summary: 141 samples from glaciers, rivers, coast, ocean: universal lignin-like DOM pool grows from 65% glacier to 97% ocean; non-universal pool shaped by microbial communities.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is a key component of the global carbon cycle, yet its molecular evolution across major aquatic ecosystems remains unclear. We analyzed 141 samples from glaciers, mountain rivers, coastal waters, and the open ocean using FT-ICR MS, microbial 16S rRNA sequencing, and environmental measurements. DOM composition exhibited increasing homogenization and recalcitrance along the land-to-ocean continuum. The universal DOM pool, dominated by lignin-like molecules, increased from 65% in glaciers to 97% in the open ocean and was primarily regulated by environmental factors. In contrast, the non-universal DOM pool declined sharply and was strongly influenced by microbial communities, especially in glacier and open-ocean systems. These findings reveal distinct environmental and biological controls on DOM transformation and provide new insights into carbon cycling processes across connected aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: Longitudinal change of riverine DOM from source to sea and its photochemical and microbial transformation
presentations.abstract_summary: Elbe River source-to-sea: DOM shifts from aromatic O-rich to N-enriched low-MW; bacterial degradation > photochemistry in headwaters, then bacteria target autochthonous DOM downstream.
presentations.abstract: Transformations of organic matter along large rivers from their headwaters to the estuaries are ecologically important, yet field studies combining full river transect sampling with degradation experiments remain scarce. We investigated the Elbe River from headwaters in the Czech Republic to the North Sea and combined longitudinal sampling with degradation experiments to (1) track longitudinal changes in dissolved organic matter (DOM) composition, (2) test photochemical and microbial degradation of terrestrial DOM from deadwood leachate in headwaters, (3) assess bacterial DOM consumption in downstream river stretches, and (4) evaluate photodegradation of organic micropollutants along the entire river. DOM composition shifted longitudinally from allochthonous-dominated, aromatic, oxygen-rich, high-molecular-weight compounds in headwaters to more saturated, nitrogen-enriched, low-molecular-weight components in the estuary. We found that bacterial degradation of terrestrial DOM was higher than photochemical loss in headwaters. Further downstream, bacteria then preferentially consumed younger, autochthonous, oxygen-rich DOM. Additional flume experiments showed substantial photodegradation of organic micropollutants over the river stretch. This unique dataset clarifies the dynamic transformations and pronounced variability of DOM across the land–ocean continuum.

presentations.title: Hydrology and trophic status control lake DOM at continental scale
presentations.abstract_summary: 548 Canadian lakes across 5 basins: deuterium excess and TP are main drivers; Aliphatics tied to altitude, Aromatics to soil organic content.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is a key component of the lake biogeochemistry. Hydrology links variables influencing lake DOM at local and watershed scales, but its role at macroscales remains poorly understood. We studied the DOM concentration and composition from 548 lakes across the five major Canadian continental basins, using absorption spectroscopy and parallel factor analysis, and ultra‐high resolution mass spectroscopy, and linked these to deuterium excess, derived from stable water isotopes as a proxy for evaporation and regional hydrology. DOM concentration and composition varied greatly within and across basins, with strong correlations between molecular and optical properties. At a continental scale, d-excess and TP concentration were the main drivers of DOM concentration and composition. TP positively influenced DOM concentration, and specific DOM components, likely mediated by nutrient-driven effects on lake metabolism. DOM concentration declined with d-excess, but the relationships between individual DOM molecular classes and d-excess differed among DOM components and basins, resulting in regional differences in DOM composition along hydrologic gradients. The inferred source composition of DOM based on these patterns had subtle regional differences, with Aliphatics linked to average regional altitude, and Aromatics linked to average regional soil organic content. We conclude that differences in DOM processing along the hydrologic continuum is the main factor driving differences in DOM composition in lakes at a continental scale.

presentations.title: Urban infrastructure and seasonal hydrology alter DOM along coastal ecosystem gradients
presentations.abstract_summary: 100 Miami canal sites: tidal flooding causes shifts toward protein-like and lignin-like DOM, overriding seasonal patterns; stormwater shifts DOM toward microbial-like.
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations and dissolved organic matter (DOM) composition are shaped by multiple factors in urban waters. In coastal cities, interactions among tidal flooding, stormwater infrastructure, and freshwater inputs can create variable DOM pools, but the timing and seasonal dynamics of these hydrological and biogeochemical interactions remain unclear. We investigated how subtropical wet and dry seasonal variability and marine tidal flooding (high tide events) affect DOC concentrations and DOM composition across n = 100 canal sites in Miami (Florida, USA), and assessed how DOM varied with impervious ground, stormwater infrastructure, and septic density. Sites were sampled in wet and dry seasons during five synoptic events in 2021 and 2022 and analyzed for DOC concentrations and DOM characteristics using absorbance and fluorescence spectroscopy. DOC concentrations and DOM composition remained stable between the wet and dry seasons, which may be related to consistent hydrological conditions maintained through management strategies that reduce flooding. In contrast, marine tidal flooding events led to distinct shifts in DOM composition, characterized by increases in protein-like, tryptophan-like, and fresh lignin-like DOM and decreases in microbial- and terrestrial humic-like DOM. Marine intrusions can promote the transformation toward more labile DOM, overriding typical seasonal dynamics. Higher stormwater influence was associated with elevated dissolved oxygen and a shift in DOM composition toward fresher, microbial-like material. Results highlight the importance of considering hydrological water management and episodic marine intrusions when evaluating DOM dynamics in urban coastal ecosystems.

presentations.title: Influence of environmental factors on CuO-derived oxidation products of DOM
presentations.abstract_summary: Hudson/James Bay rivers: lignin phenols are biorefractory but photosensitive; fatty acid-like products show opposite behavior.
presentations.abstract: Thawing permafrost and increased river discharge are releasing carbon, including lignins into Arctic rivers and coastal waters. Hudson and James Bays, at the southern edge of the Canadian Arctic, rank among the fastest-warming regions globally, making it critical to examine how environmental changes affect the composition and fate of dissolved organic matter (DOM). Lignin phenols, derived from the breakdown of terrestrial vascular plants, are molecularly diverse compounds used as biomarkers to trace DOM transformation and watershed vegetation. They are extracted via alkaline CuO oxidation and quantified using liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry. This study investigates the bio- and photo resistance of lignin phenols and CuO-derived oxidation products in surface DOM from the Moose and Winisk River outflows into Hudson and James Bays. Short-term in situ incubations (3 days) revealed that lignin phenol concentrations decreased under light (0.3%) but increased with microorganisms (0.7%). Conversely, fatty acid-like products rose under light (+3.8%), indicating photoresistence, while lignin phenols were photosensitive. Microorganisms caused fatty acid-like products to vary by +4.1% and -3.5%, suggesting production or consumption. Overall, lignin phenols were biorefractory, while fatty acid-like compounds responded to microorganisms depending on their DOM source. These findings highlight that the chemical properties of lignin phenols and CuO-derived oxidation products can be altered by environmental factor such as light and microbial activities.

presentations.title: The relative importance of DOM source and mineral characteristics for adsorption
presentations.abstract: Adsorption of dissolved organic matter (DOM) onto minerals plays a critical role in carbon sequestration in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. It remains unclear if mineral properties or DOM composition are more relevant for predicting adsorption. We tested this by quantifying the maximum adsorption capacity (Qmax) of five minerals (podzol Bs horizon, agricultural subsoil, glacial stream sediment, kaolinite-dominated clay, synthetic goethite) and five DOM sources (humic lake, peat, leaf litter, algae, and pyrogenic organic matter) using a modified Langmuir model. Three minerals were also treated with sodium hypochlorite to remove pre-existing organic matter, enabling assessment of adsorption onto bare mineral surfaces. Qmax values spanned 31–28,630 mg C kg-1, exceeding previously reported ranges, and showing that both DOM composition and mineral properties variably control adsorption capacity. Even strongly adsorbing minerals such as goethite and clay showed a large variation across DOM sources, with highest adsorption for peat and lowest for algae. Likewise, DOM sources differed in their affinities for the mineral surfaces. Sodium hypochlorite treatment increased DOM adsorption, depending on material type and mineral characteristics, such as hydrous aluminum and iron phases. Overall, carbon adsorption onto minerals depends on both mineral and organic matter characteristics, suggesting that soil models that do not consider organic matter characteristics are limited in describing adsorption and predicting carbon sequestration potential in soils and aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: Greenhouse gases emissions via DOM photodegradation in tropical peatlands and eutrophic lakes, Indonesia
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) photodegradation is one of the major sources for greenhouse gases (GHGs; CO₂, CH₄, CO) from the aquatic ecosystems to the atmosphere. However, little is known about estimations of GHGs emissions via DOM photodegradation. Studies, especially in the tropical regions, remain limited despite the more intense solar radiation than other regions. In this study, to estimate rates and potentials of GHGs emissions via DOM photodegradation in the tropical aquatic ecosystems, we conducted the photodegradation experiments using Indonesian bog (River Sabanga) and eutrophic lake (Lake Rawa Besar) waters under an artificial sunlight simulator. In bog and lake waters, three GHGs emissions were observed under light. In bog water, CO2 rate and potential were the highest, followed by CO, with very low CH4. CH4 rate and potential in lake water were very low but CO2 and CO were high and not significantly different between them. CO₂ rate in bog water was significantly higher than in lake water, while no significant difference was observed for the CH4 and CO between the two waters. CH4 potential in lake water was significantly higher than bog water. Meanwhile, under dark, all GHGs emission rates were negligible except for CO2 in lake water. In Lake Rawa Besar, cyanobacterial blooms have been observed, suggesting CO2 release via DOM biodecomposition due to abundant bioavailable and low-molecular weight DOM. This study demonstrated that eutrophication is very important not only for water quality deterioration but also for GHGs emissions.

presentations.title: A Multi-Omics Approach to Quantifying Eddy-driven Dissolved Organic Carbon Export in an Oligotrophic Ocean
presentations.affiliation: Center for Chemical Currencies of a Microbial Planet
presentations.abstract: The dissolved organic carbon (DOC) pool, which is released and recycled by marine microbes, constitutes a major reservoir for carbon in the ocean. In the western subtropical North Atlantic, time-series data has shown the accumulation of DOC in the surface ocean in the summertime, which is then introduced to the ocean interior through deep convective mixing in the wintertime. However, ocean eddies have been shown to contribute to particulate organic carbon export and likely also transport dissolved organic carbon to the mesopelagic on sub-seasonal timescales throughout the year. Here, we use a multi-omics approach to observationally demonstrate how microbial community structure and DOC cycling vary across an ocean eddy and to estimate the contribution of eddy subduction to DOC export in the oligotrophic North Atlantic. Taxonomic information from metabarcoding data is complemented by metaproteomics, metatranscriptomics, and metabolomics to interrogate how the metabolic function of these communities varies across an eddy. We compare and interpret our findings with a coupled physical-biogeochemical model for the Bermuda Atlantic Time Series (BATS) region to evaluate whether observed patterns align with mechanistic predictions.

presentations.title: Interactive effects of nutrients, oxygen, and composition on estuarine DOM biodegradation
presentations.abstract: Biodegradation of dissolved organic matter (DOM) fuels aquatic biogeochemistry and is controlled by interacting environmental and chemical factors. We investigated how nutrients, oxygen, and DOM composition alter rates of biodegradation in the Chesapeake Bay, USA, an estuary impacted by nutrient pollution and hypoxia that receives considerable terrestrial and freshwater DOM. Building on previous work, we predicted that nutrient and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) additions would stimulate biodegradation under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, and DOM composition would strongly influence rates of biodegradation and humification. 4-day respirometry experiments using Chesapeake Bay water were conducted to monitor changes in DOC concentration, carbon dioxide (CO2) production, and DOM composition measured by optical properties. While nutrient additions did not alter total CO2 accumulation, nitrogen and phosphorus additions reduced the time to peak CO2 accumulation rates by ~2 hours, and algal-derived DOM led to ~50% more CO2 accumulation than soil-derived DOM. Total CO₂ accumulation was approximately 10% higher under aerobic than anaerobic conditions. This suggests DOM biodegradation can be supported by alternative electron acceptors supplied by nutrient additions. These results demonstrate that interactions between controlling factors may lead to unanticipated changes in DOM biodegradation under shifting environmental conditions.

presentations.title: DOM concentration and reactivity along the boreal aquatic network of La Romaine River, Québec, Canada
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) exported from terrestrial ecosystems to freshwaters plays a central role in the global carbon cycle, undergoing biological and photochemical degradation to CO₂ along the aquatic continuum. Hydrology, and in particular water residence time, is a major control on biological and photochemical reactivity at the watershed scale. Here, we investigate DOM dynamics throughout the aquatic network of a large boreal watershed by tracking DOM concentration and biological and photochemical reactivity. We sampled groundwater, lakes, streams and rivers from orders 1 to 8 (La Romaine River) within the watershed to assess how concentration and reactivity evolve along the continuum. Preliminary results show a net loss of ~40 % of DOC between order-1 and order-6 rivers, as well as a decrease in photochemical reactivity along the continuum, indicating progressive DOM removal, particularly in lakes. However, biological reactivity shows little change and localized increases in DOC concentration and reactivity also occur, pointing to DOM replenishment. Overall, our findings highlight water residence time as a major control on DOM concentration and reactivity in freshwaters, while demonstrating that lateral inputs can substantially modulate its influence at the watershed scale.

presentations.title: Quantitative and qualitative characterization of DOM excreted by Ephemera mayflies in stream ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Aquatic insects play an important role in the biogeochemical cycling of freshwater ecosystems, particularly through their release of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and related compounds. Among them, Ephemera mayflies are one of the key collector-gatherers that process fine particulate organic matter (FPOM). Recent studies have shown that Ephemera larvae convert ingested FPOM into dissolved organic matter (DOM), thereby contributing directly to stream DOC pools. We characterized the DOM excreted by Ephemera larvae using DOC analysis and excitation–emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectroscopy. Rearing experiments were conducted on E. orientalis and E. japonica in ultrapure and natural stream water under controlled laboratory conditions. Water samples collected over 10 days were analyzed for DOC and fluorescent DOM. Both species showed increases in DOC concentration and in the intensities of protein-like fluorescence peaks (Ex/Em ≈ 275/330 nm) and humic-like peaks (Ex/Em ≈ 350/425–440 nm; 275/450 nm), confirming that Ephemera larvae excrete DOM containing both labile and humified components. Moreover, E. japonica, which inhabits steep upstream reaches, excreted higher DOC concentrations and stronger fluorescent DOM signals than E. orientalis, a downstream species. These results indicate species-specific differences in DOM production and suggest that E. japonica may contribute disproportionately to DOM cycling in headwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: The risk of HABs in the Arctic assessed using the coexistence theory
presentations.abstract: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) are mass occurrences of toxic algae that threaten global water ecosystems. HABs are extensively observed in temperate and warm regions; however, due to global environmental change, i.e., nutrient supply and warming, the spread and bloom of toxic species could be favored also in the Arctic (Greenland). To investigate the future risk of HABs in the Arctic, we explored the potential of coexistence between arctic and boreal species—both HABs and non-HABs—including copepods as predator, and we measured resource-related traits (light requirement and consumption) across temperatures. We found species- and temperature-dependent responses to light, with boreal species showing photoinhibition, particularly under continuous light, and struggling with current arctic temperatures, while arctic HAB species were favored over non-HAB ones in warmer scenarios. This aligned with the competitive advantages observed in competition assays for the arctic species at low temperatures, which persist despite predation. Boreal species showed positive growths in projected future temperatures, suggesting a possible loss of competitive advantage by the arctic species. This study shows that determining resource-related traits and exploring biotic interactions (competition and predation) can help our understanding of the coexistence of arctic and boreal species and disentangle the complex interplay between abiotic and biotic factors, improving predictions of future risks of HABs in the Arctic.

presentations.title: Mechanistic modeling of cyanobacteria ecology and cyanotoxin production in Lake Mendota
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacteria harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs) and the produced cyanotoxins may lead to several problems such as animal deaths, human intoxications or drinking water supply interruptions. Mechanistic models are important tools to understand the environmental processes underlying toxin production and evaluating management options. We present a model of Microcystis and the toxin Microcystin (MC) in Lake Mendota for six years (2013 to 2018). The model simulates toxigenic and non-toxigenic Microcystis and other phytoplankton. Microcystis growth depends on phosphorus and nitrogen quota, light availability, and temperature. MC production is a function of temperature, nitrogen quota and light availability, and it benefits the toxigenic Microcystis. Intracellular MC may become extracellular due to grazing, excretion, or death. This model is based on a previously-developed code (Schampera & Hellweger, Ecological Modelling, 2025) and includes several extensions/improvements: (1) Representation of epilimnion and hypolimnion and sediment bed compartments and fluxes, (2) Dynamic simulation of grazing based on herbivore zooplankton concentration, (3) Simulation of additional non-Microcystis phytoplankton species and (4) Microcystis sediment bed overwintering and recruitment. The model can reproduce the observed seasonal patterns for 5 of 6 years. 2016 is not reproduced well, which may be due to the zebra mussel invasion that took place that year. The model is used to simulate management (nutrient load reduction) and climate change (higher temperature) scenarios.

presentations.title: TOXIC RELATIONSHIPS: PREDICTING DRIVERS OF LAKE MICROCYSTIN ACROSS THE U.S. AND INTO THE FUTURE
presentations.abstract: Toxic cyanobacteria blooms (cyanoHABs) are a major threat to lakes as they contaminate drinking water, harm aquatic organisms, and cause economic losses due to decreased recreation. Predicting cyanoHABs is difficult due to their complex drivers along with limited spatial data coverage. This challenge is further complicated by climate change. Luckily, new data and modeling approaches make it possible to build predictive models of cyanotoxins to understand local and regional trends in toxin production under a changing climate. We leverage the U.S. EPA’s National Lakes Assessment for 5,000 lakes, the LAGOS research platform, the CMIP6 climate model ensemble, and advances in machine learning to forecast bloom events based on multi-scaled chemical, physical, biological, climate, and human predictors. We present a set of gradient boosting models that predict microcystin presence in the present day and under future climate change scenarios. The present day model had 75% balanced accuracy and identified pH, nitrogen, turbidity, elevation, and chlorophyll-a as the most important predictors. We expect the second model to produce similar results with an emphasis on climate variables like air temperature, precipitation, runoff, and wind speed. With this framework, we can predict microcystin in lakes and describe which combinations of drivers lead to toxin production in cyanobacteria blooms. Our models can be extrapolated to lakes with limited data to enhance cyanoHAB prediction and management in understudied regions, aiding lake managers in their fight against cyanoHABs.

presentations.title: Resilience indicators as early warnings of harmful algal blooms in a large lake
presentations.abstract: Algal blooms can occur suddenly, seemingly without warning, and threaten ecosystem and public health. Providing advance warning of blooms can allow water treatment plants and other stakeholders time to prepare to mitigate algal toxins and give warnings to the public. Thus, developing methods to predict bloom onset is a topic of much interest to researchers and other stakeholders. Recently, efforts have been made to develop early warning signals of algal blooms by using measures of ecosystem resiliency, here defined as standard deviation, skew, kurtosis, and autocorrelation. Using five years of high-frequency monitoring data from seven locations in the western basin of Lake Erie, we test the feasibility and efficacy of resilience indicators as early warning signals of increases in chlorophyll. As an additional line of evidence, we test this same high-frequency data for usefulness as warnings of in-situ, low frequency, algal toxin (microcystin) concentration. We find that at least one metric provides an early warning signal of a shift in chlorophyll 85% of the time, and microcystin 90% of the time. However, agreement between metrics is low, and the time between the beginning of the early warning signal and the bloom is highly variable, indicating limited applicability for use as a forecasting method.

presentations.title: Whole-lake Manipulation of Resilience of Cyanobacteria to Nutrient Enrichment
presentations.abstract: Ecosystems worldwide are increasingly vulnerable to losses of resilience and abrupt state changes as climate pressures and resource demands intensify. Although resilience is central to ecosystem theory and management, identifying ecological thresholds and quantifying resilience in real ecosystems remains challenging. We conducted a multi-year series of whole-lake manipulations to evaluate whether resilience to cyanobacteria blooms can be predictably modified and measured. Specifically, we altered resilience to nutrient enrichment with the addition of a dye that attenuated light. Four treatments were applied, one in each year: ambient conditions, nutrient enrichment, dye addition, and combined enrichment and dye additions. We also monitored a nearby unmanipulated lake that served as a reference. High-frequency phycocyanin measurements were used to estimate stability landscapes and calculate the passage times between the low and high pigment states in each year of the experiment. Nutrient enrichment increased passage times out of the high pigment state, indicating longer periods of bloom conditions under enrichment. In contrast, enrichment in combination with shading reduced passage times out of the high pigment basin, suggesting lowered resilience of the bloom state. These experiments provide one of the first whole-ecosystem tests of theoretical predictions about resilience modification and highlight new tools for measuring and managing resilience in freshwater ecosystems facing intensifying environmental change.

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL RESEARCH ON AN ACADEMIC YEAR SCALE: LEVERAGING STUDENT RESEARCH PROJECTS INTO A MULTIYEAR SPATIAL ANALYSIS OF HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOMS
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cHABs), especially blooms that form surface aggregations and produce toxins, threaten the health of people, pets, and livestock. Toxic blooms are spatially and temporally heterogenous, leading to challenges in determining when and where it is advisable to recreate on hypereutrophic waterbodies. The ecosystem-scale research needed to understand cHABs is expensive and time-consuming, making it a challenging area of study at primarily undergraduate institutions (PUI). However, research on an environmental issue with a significant human health component is highly attractive to students with diverse interests and academic backgrounds (e.g. environmental science, health sciences, and molecular biology majors). By leveraging student funding opportunities, building interdisciplinary teams, and letting student interests guide project development, we have compiled a three-year data set of cyanobacterial toxin distribution across a 1000-acre lake. Student projects have mapped the rate of change in toxin concentration within a year, assessed the area of the lake with toxin concentrations considered harmful to pets and wildlife, and examined toxin distribution through the water column, while also conducting a twice annual spatial survey of toxin concentration. This presentation will describe the process of building an interdisciplinary team of undergraduates, share our conclusions from the spatial and temporal dataset, and discuss challenges and opportunities with engaging students in large-scale ecological research at a PUI.

presentations.title: A genomic dashboard for accessible analysis of microbial components in the context of Quebec lakes monitoring
presentations.abstract: Rapid on-site detection of Harmful Algal Blooms (RosHAB) represents the next generation of monitoring practices, incorporating an innovative, in-the-field applicable genomics workflow for real-time, reliable, accessible and cost-effective early detection of cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cHABs) outbreaks. In this context, we developed a unified graphical user interface (GUI) that streamlines bioinformatic workflows by integrating several third-party tools. The interface provides three analytical modes: (i) de novo assembly-based metagenomics for reconstructing metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs); (ii) read-mapping-based metagenomics for rapid taxonomic and toxigenic potential profiling; and (iii) isolate genome analysis using external pipelines. This integration replaces previously fragmented processes with an accessible, browser-based interface. Concurrently, the isolation of cyanobacterial strains and the reconstruction of MAGs from Quebec lakes will expand public genomic resources with region-specific cyanobacterial genomes, improving ecological interpretation and detection accuracy. Representative outputs, including MAGs generated via the mag-ont pipeline, metagenomic profiles from roshab-cli, and assembled isolate genomes produced through hybracter or autocycler — highlight the taxonomic and functional diversity captured by our workflows. Together, these components establish an accessible and reproducible framework for genomic monitoring of harmful algal blooms in lakes.

presentations.title: DETECTION OF HARMFUL ALGAL BLOOM TOXINS FOR EARLY WARNING IN NEW JERSEY AQUATIC ENVIRONMENTS
presentations.abstract: Harmful Algae Blooms (HAB) can devastate local waterways and environmental health through the production of organic toxins. Many New Jersey freshwater systems are monitored by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP), however, few studies have focused on coastal environments. In order to investigate HAB toxin distributions across NJ aquatic environments, fresh and coastal sites were chosen based on NJDEP monitoring maps. Surface water samples were collected in the summer of 2025, filtered through 0.2 um filters, and filtrate was further concentrated by C18 solid phase extraction. Twelve HAB toxins were analyzed using liquid chromatography triple quadrupole mass spectrometry, which serves as a useful tool for detecting low-concentration toxins. Overall toxin levels were low at most locations, except Metedeconk River, Greenwood Lake, and Weequahic Lake, in the early summer, but certain locations show development of HAB in late summer, suggesting detection of low-concentration toxins may provide an early warning for potential HAB development. NMDS ordination analysis indicates separation of HAB toxin patterns between freshwater and marine water, suggesting environmental factors determined HAB toxin production. In addition, rivers usually have a similar HAB toxin pattern as that in the coastal waters they discharge into, implying spatial connectivity of HAB toxins. The purpose of the research was to produce a useful baseline for future HAB research and improve understanding of spatial distribution of algal toxins in New Jersey Waters.

presentations.title: Development of a coupled hydrodynamic-biogeochemical-sediment model using a semi-enclosed canal as a testbed
presentations.abstract: Modeling biogeochemical cycles and harmful algal blooms (HABs) in shallow freshwater-coastal systems remain challenging as they involve a myriad of complex benthic-pelagic coupled biogeochemical processes. In addition, available data is highly limited to constrain model performance in simulating these processes. Here we present a coupled hydrodynamic-biogeochemical-sediment model for a canal linking Lake Okeechobee to St. Lucie estuary in Florida. The canal, however, is only occasionally open when the lake water is released into the estuary. Therefore, it is nearly isolated with low water movements most of the time, presenting it as an ideal testbed for observations, modeling, and even field experiments. The model simulates nutrients (N, P) cycles, phytoplankton blooms, and sediment diagenetic processes. Five phytoplankton groups including a species-specific Microcystis group has been included. A three-year (2018-2020) simulation has been completed and calibrated with available data. The results suggest that when there are no water discharges, the canal functions as an incubator with both phytoplankton blooms and biogeochemical processes are in quasi-equilibrium. In addition, there are significant downstream gradients of sediment nutrient fluxes due to sedimentation and accumulation of particulate organics in the upstream areas during the water releases. We expect this model to be applicable broadly to other inland water systems for understanding and managing water quality and harmful algal blooms.

presentations.title: MECHANISTIC MODELING OF CYANOTOXIN BIODEGRADATIN, PHOTOLYSIS AND SEDIMENTATION LOSS IN LAKES
presentations.abstract: Cyanotoxins, including the microcystin (MC) hepatotoxins, pose a significant human health risk. Mathematical models are critical tools for managing lake systems (e.g. evaluating nutrient reduction scenarios, climate change) and they support research (e.g. hypothesis testing). A number of mechanistic models have been developed that simulate production of MC by Microcystis considering the effects of temperature, light and nitrogen. However, loss of MC is still simulated via simple first-order decay, although there are several mechanisms, including biodegradation by planktonic bacteria and zooplankton (incl. their gut bacteria), photodegradation and adsorption/sedimentation that may exhibit non-linear kinetics. For example, MC-degrading bacteria (mlrA+) must first grow to sufficient numbers before they can impact the toxin concentration. Here, a model for MC loss considering biodegradation, photodegradation and sedimentation is presented. The model is applied to three systems (Dianchi Lake, San Juan Reservoir, Gongendo Reservoir) and can reproduce the main observed patterns, including the time-lag between the appearance of dissolved MC and MC-degrading bacteria. The model ranks the importance of loss processes: degradation by zooplankton > degradation by planktonic bacteria > sedimentation > outflow > photolysis. A model with first-order decay cannot reproduce the observed temporal pattern. Results of management (adding mlrA bacteria to the lake) and climate change (+3°C) simulations are presented.

presentations.title: DEVELOPING AN INTEGRATED AND COLLABORATIVE CYANOHABS SURVEILLANCE AND MONITORING PROGRAM ON LAKE SIMCOE (ONTARIO, CANADA)
presentations.abstract: Harmful algal blooms caused by cyanobacteria (CyanoHABs) are being reported more frequently in Ontario, and across the Great Lakes Region, threatening recreational uses and reputations of affected lakes, as well as their use as drinking water sources. Lake Simcoe, the largest lake in central Ontario, supplies drinking water to eight municipalities, and is one of the province’s most recreationally important lakes. The lake has a history of elevated phosphorus (P) and reports of algal scums (1970-80s); however, in-lake conditions have since improved and no lake-wide algal blooms were reported until 2024-5 when dense layers of cyanobacteria formed in the water column. Recognizing climate as a potential driver of algal blooms in low-nutrient lakes, we enhanced our lake science program in 2016 by incorporating monitoring components to detect conditions conducive to harmful algal blooms (HABs). Although some indicators (redox potential, hypolimentic dissolved oxygen, nutrients) have remained consistent over the last decade, our data also show an increase in surface water temperatures, chlorophyll a, and phycocyanin. As offshore and subsurface algal conditions may differ from what can be observed by shore-based monitoring, we partnered with a local municipality to develop a collaborative approach toward an early-warning system that alerts drinking water operators and recreational beach users of potential HABs. Our ultimate goal is to construct a predictive model for HAB formation and expand our collaboration to other municipalities and health units in the Lake Simcoe watershed.

presentations.title: Residence Time Rules: Linking Climate Change, River Metabolism, and Ecosystem Breakdown
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: (pusch@igb-berlin.de) Climate change alters precipitation, snowmelt, and evapotranspiration in many river basins worldwide, often reducing river discharge and slowing flow. Lower velocities and more frequent droughts increase water travel time in river systems. Longer residence times favour phytoplankton growth, and in long river systems even zooplankton may develop. Closer contact between river water and the benthic and hyporheic zones enhances fixed-phase biogeochemical processing. Hence, climate change increases both assimilative and dissimilative metabolic pathways. Which processes will dominate depends on water travel time, nutrient inputs, temperature, light, and channel form. Human impacts—such as canalisation, damming, and the addition of nutrients, organic matter, and other pollutants—further modify metabolic turnover and reduce ecological resilience, making rivers more sensitive to disturbances, excessive loading, and extreme weather. These changes diminish human usability by lowering water quality, raising treatment costs, impairing recreation, complicating navigation during low flows, and increasing risks from pathogens and toxin-producing algae. The Oder River (Czechia/Poland/Germany), which was affected by a toxic bloom of a brackish-water alga (Prymnesium parvum) causing a massive fish kill in 2022, is presented as a case study illustrating how water residence time has become the paramount factor governing river ecology and management in the Anthropocene.
