presentations.title: Geographical Study of Groundwater in Santomi Sinden and Suburban Areas in Tokyo (UNESCO Agricultural Heritage, July 2023)
presentations.abstract: Santomi Shinden was developed on the Musashino Plateau in 1692 by the 5th Shogun Tsunayoshi. It was a lean land of the Kanto loam layer. It is recorded that 11 wells were dug at that time because there was no river in this area. Shinji Yoshimura (1943) studied the shallow groundwater of these wells and considered the development of the village. Therefore, referring to Yoshimura's paper, we conducted a survey and research on the remaining shallow wells (shallow groundwater) at present. We examined 120 wells, mainly in Santomi Shinden. From there, 24 wells were selected. The survey was conducted once a month. This time, we report the results of two years from Augustt2022 to July2024. Based on the results of the water levels, the 24 sites surveyed were divided into four main areas. Water temperature, air temperature, electrical conductivity (EC), pH, RpH, depth from the top of the well to the surface (depth of the water surface), and depth to the bottom of the well (depth of the well bottom) were measured at the sites. The collected water was subjected to TOC and ion chromatography in the laboratory. The elevation of the well at the measurement point was read from a map of 1: 2500. October was the highest water elevation of the year, and March was the lowest. As for the depth of the water surface of the wells, two wells B 3-5 and B4-7 in area 1 were observed to be dry up from January to April. In the Minami-Nagai of area 4 of Tokorozawa City. fluctuating wells in shallow positions (-5～-６ｍ) were observed. C2-1 of area 2 showed similar fluctuations. From the change in pH, G5-1 of area 4 had a high coefficient of variation with a median value of 7.0 or more. As for the change in water temperature, there was a well C3-4 in area 2 that fluctuated at a higher temperature (19.0～21.0 ℃) than normal. presentations.title: DRIVERS OF LONG-TERM AND SEASONAL VARIABILITY OF REDOX CONDITIONS IN TROUT BOG LAKE, WI
presentations.abstract: Northern peatlands are important global carbon sinks and sources of greenhouse gases, particularly methane. Bog lakes formed from thawing peat are acidic and darkly stained by organic matter. Here we explore the role of anoxygenic phototrophic bacteria (AOPs) in modulating greenhouse gas production and emission from such systems. Due to thermal stratification, these systems develop steep redox gradients that favor anaerobic metabolism. Green sulfur bacteria (Chlorobium) use red light to oxidize reduced sulfur, iron, and humic compounds, fixing carbon and generating oxidized intermediates. Anaerobic respiratory organisms such as Geothrix consume these intermediates and regenerate reduced substrates (H2S, Fe2+, HS-), completing a cryptic redox loop. We hypothesize that this redox coupling retains electrons in the water column rather than allowing them to sink into deeper layers, effectively reducing methane production by methanogens. The vertical distribution of Chlorobium is a major driver of seasonal and long-term redox fluctuations in these lakes. Our long-term data show that water color in Trout Bog Lake has darkened since 1990, reducing the depth at which Chlorobium can grow. As light availability declines with browning, Chlorobium migrate upward in the water column, shifting redox gradients and potentially altering electron sequestration and methane production. Using multi-year redox profiles and 48-hour diurnal redox sampling on Trout Bog Lake, we characterize the temporal dynamics of these redox-driven processes and their implications for carbon cycling.

presentations.title: DRAINAGE-INDUCED CARBON EXPORT: IMPLICATIONS FOR PEATLAND CARBON BUDGETS
presentations.abstract: Dutch agriculture on peatlands depends on an extensive drainage network of ditches and subsurface pipes that maintains low water tables. While this enables current agricultural practices, it strongly alters peatland carbon dynamics. Drained peat soils emit large amounts of CO₂, and recent studies show that CH₄ emissions from drainage ditches also strongly contribute to the overall greenhouse gas emission. A major remaining uncertainty is the carbon lost from peatlands as dissolved and particulate carbon transported through drainage pipes into surface waters. We collected dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and total inorganic carbon (TIC) data from drainage pipes connected to a pump in two Dutch agricultural peat fields from 2020–2025. We quantified the carbon export from land to the aquatic system and assessed temporal patterns and links to precipitation events. Preliminary results show carbon export rates of 25 to 195 kgC ha-1 yr-1, strongly depending on yearly variations in precipitation. Considering that the C-loss to the atmosphere of these areas is approximately 4 t C ha-1 yr-1, this indicates that drainage-driven carbon transport is a relevant but understudied component of the peatland carbon budget. Understanding the quality and fate of this exported carbon is essential for evaluating its contribution to downstream CO₂ and CH₄ emissions. Further research on carbon transformations within the drainage network will improve estimates of total greenhouse gas emissions from drained peatland landscapes.

presentations.title: TRACE ELEMENTS IN PEAT BOG WATERS AS INDICATORS OF THE CHEMICAL REACTIVITY OF ATMOSPHERIC DUSTS FROM OPEN-PIT MINING ACTIVITIES
presentations.abstract: Open-pit mining is a globally significant source of dust and trace elements (TEs) to the atmosphere. The release of these TEs to aquatic ecosystems may be beneficial or detrimental, depending on the element, its concentration, and chemical speciation. Peat bog surface waters depend exclusively on atmospheric deposition. Further, the waters are acidic (pH ≤ 4) and rich in organic acids, two characteristics which promote mineral dissolution. In this study, dissolved TEs (<0.45 µm) in moss and peat porewaters were used as indicators of the chemical reactivity of atmospheric dusts. Waters were collected from bogs near open-pit bitumen mining activities and remote locations in Alberta, Canada. In both moss and peat porewaters, most TEs increase in concentration with proximity to industry, providing evidence of dust reactivity. These trends reflect the observed increase in dust deposition with proximity to mining reported in recent studies of snow, lichens, and Sphagnum mosses. Concentrations were greater in moss waters compared to the underlying peat porewaters. These differences are likely linked to dust deposition rates, with contemporary inputs (which affect moss water) being greater than in the past (as indicated by peat porewater). Bog waters provide a unique opportunity to explore the impacts of dust dissolution, today and in the past. Furthermore, moss and peat porewaters from age-dated peat cores could provide a chronological record of the impacts of TEs and other atmospheric contaminants on aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: EXAMINING ECOSYSTEM DRIVERS FOR SHIFTS IN THE SUMMER RANGING PATTERNS OF AN ENDANGERED KILLER WHALE POPULATION THROUGH IN SITU EDNA SAMPLING
presentations.abstract: Changes in distribution for top predators often indicates shifts in prey availability, habitat quality or large scale environmental drivers. In recent years, summer occurrences of the endangered Southern Resident killer whale population have decreased within the inshore waters of the Salish Sea (WA State, U.S.A and B.C., Canada), shifting towards increased occurrences in coastal waters around Swiftsure Bank (SB). Understanding the driving factors are key for supporting management and recovery planning for this endangered killer whale population. In September 2025, vessel surveys were conducted around SB using visual, acoustic, prey and eDNA sampling methods to detect killer whales, characterize prey communities and document predation. eDNA samples were filtered in situ using Ocean Diagnostics’ Ascension eDNA instrument to detect killer whale detections and characterize prey community composition. The Ascension was deployed at least once per survey day from a 16m vessel targeting multiple depths at each sampling station, using real-time data to monitor instrument performance and sample volumes. TaqMan allelic discrimination assays allowed the detection of killer whales and genetic discrimination among conspecific killer whale lineages. We share preliminary findings and discuss the feasibility of using a small, manually deployed in situ eDNA sampler for daily eDNA sampling deployments from a medium-sized research vessel platform in an adaptive sampling scheme.

presentations.title: Enhancing Biodiversity Monitoring with Nuclear and Mitochondrial eDNA: Insights from a Whole-Lake Experiment Using Active and Passive Sampling
presentations.abstract: Since its first application in 2008, the use of eDNA for biodiversity monitoring has increased significantly. However, the obtainable information from mitochondrial DNA alone is limited. To gain insight into the potential opportunities nuclear eDNA brings to biodiversity monitoring we designed a whole-lake manipulation experiment in a small lake in the Adirondack Park (Upstate New York). For our experiment, we utilized 3 strains of brook trout, a culturally and economically important species of fish, stocking them in varying but known quantities in three cages at the head of the lake. We made a series of configuration changes, releasing strains into and removing strains from the lake. We conducted systematic temporal sampling before each configuration change and spatial sampling at increasing distances toward the outlet. In addition to the sampling conducted manually, we employed a passive sampler at the outlet, changing the filters at every sampling event. Preliminary qPCR results suggest nuclear DNA was detected in similar quantities to mitochondrial DNA, and the passive sampler performed as well as the manual sampling did. We will now sequence genes on both the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes that distinguish between the strains, testing our ability to use mitochondrial eDNA for intraspecific monitoring and nuclear eDNA to estimate the abundance of brook trout stocked in the lake. In this context, our whole-lake manipulation experiment provides a testbed to test and demonstrate the potential to utilize both nuclear and mitochondrial eDNA in biodiversity monitoring efforts.

presentations.title: REMOTE GENOMICS: USING REAL-TIME DNA SEQUENCING FOR MARINE MICROBIAL MONITORING IN REMOTE ENVIRONMENTS
presentations.abstract: Exploring microbial genomics in field settings and remote environments has recently become feasible using real-time DNA sequencing technologies such as Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT). These techniques were successfully performed during experiments at the Ocean Sea-Ice Mesocosm (OSIM) at the Churchill Marine Observatory (CMO) while monitoring the effects of oil spills, and on the CCGS Amundsen during her 2025 cruise in the Queen Elizabeth Islands (QEI). During OSIM experiments in December 2024 and 2025, a GridION sequencing device was used to monitor the microbial community in sea-ice and seawater samples after an oil spill event. These were compared to an uncontaminated control pool and used to identify signs of hydrocarbon degradation in real-time. The proven accessibility of this method has significant benefits for environmental monitoring of contaminated areas, particularly the rapid turn-around times and ease of use which is amenable to Community Based Monitoring programs in remote regions like the Canadian Arctic. Additionally, on a research cruise to the QEI, MinION Mk1D sequencing devices were used onboard for active real-time monitoring of Arctic seawater and to allow for adaptive sample collection based on sequencing results. By having microbial community data accessible within 8 hours of sampling, sample collection can be modified based on genomic results to target specific depth profiles or sampling sites. These experiments have shown that ONT is highly accessible in terms of affordability and portability and has notable advantages for real-time data retrieval.

presentations.title: eRNA based Metatranscriptomics and Multi-Marker Metabarcoding Align on Eukaryotic Planktonic Community Responses but Differ in Taxonomic Resolution
presentations.abstract: While metatranscriptomics is being assessed as a tool to profile eukaryotic gene expression activity, it is simultaneously gaining attention as an amplification-free approach for community characterization that bypasses amplification-driven bias inherent to PCR-based metabarcoding. However, its high sequencing-depth requirements, coupled with more demanding library preparation and bioinformatic workflows compared to metabarcoding, have limited its routine use, highlighting the need to evaluate whether metabarcoding can capture similar ecological patterns and taxonomic diversity. Here, we evaluated how morphology, eRNA multi-marker metabarcoding (18S, mtCOI, 23S), and metatranscriptomics capture community responses to nutrient enrichment in artificial mesocosms. All molecular approaches detected significant community shifts in response to nutrient enrichment and showed broad agreement in the identity of dominant taxa at high taxonomic ranks. However, the methods diverged consistently at lower taxonomic levels and among rare taxa, reflecting both marker and reference-driven biases. These biases were further exhibited when metabarcoding failed to identify several abundant zooplankton that were detected by metatranscriptomics and morphological analysis. These results indicate that while broad-scale planktonic community patterns are robustly captured by both metabarcoding and metatranscriptomics, method-specific biases in taxon detection can influence ecological conclusions, underscoring that method choice remains a central determinant of biological interpretations.

presentations.title: Reading Heat Stress from Water: Toward Environmental RNA Biomarkers
presentations.abstract: Heat stress is an increasing threat to fishes, yet traditional monitoring approaches often detect impacts only after they occur. Environmental DNA (eDNA) based methods have transformed biodiversity monitoring, but capture presence, not physiological state. Recent work using RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) has shown that environmental RNA (eRNA) can recover differential gene expression patterns that mirror organismal RNA, demonstrating its potential to reflect real-time physiological responses. However, reliance on RNA-seq limits scalability for routine or field-based monitoring. Here, we build on this foundation by translating conserved heat stress gene expression signatures into a targeted, digital PCR (dPCR)-based biomarker panel. Using organismal RNA-seq data, we identified rapidly responding and conserved gene expression signatures of heat stress across Cypriniformes and confirmed these patterns in organismal tissue samples, enabling their detection from environmental samples without whole-transcriptome sequencing. By moving from RNA-seq to targeted dPCR, we establish a general framework for developing deployable eRNA biomarker panels across species and stressors. This approach uses simple water sampling and rapid PCR-based analysis, enabling routine processing by standard laboratories and integration into existing monitoring workflows, including programs built on distributed or citizen-based sample collection.

presentations.title: AN INNOVATIVE SOLAR-DRIVEN PUMPING AND SORPTION SYSTEM FOR IN-SITU PHOSPHORUS REMOVAL FROM A DRINKING WATER RESERVOIR HYPOLIMNION
presentations.affiliation: Biology Centre CAS, institute of Hydrobiology
presentations.abstract: Internal phosphorus loading from the hypolimnion is a significant challenge for managing eutrophication in drinking water reservoirs. Controlling this internal source is crucial for maintaining long-term water quality. This study presents an innovative, low-energy approach for in-situ phosphorus removal by actively targeting hypolimnetic water. An autonomous floating device was designed, constructed, and deployed for pilot testing. The device is equipped with a solar-driven pumping system that withdraws phosphorus-rich water from the hypolimnion. This water is pumped through a container holding a specialized sorption material, which effectively captures dissolved phosphorus. The treated water is then returned to the reservoir below the metalimnion layer to prevent stratification disruption and minimize nutrient mixing into the epilimnion. This method offers a dual benefit: improving water quality while creating a value-added product. The saturated sorption material is designed for recovery and potential reuse as an agricultural fertilizer, supporting a circular economy approach to nutrient management. This presentation will detail the technical construction of the solar-powered floating device, share initial experiences from the pilot operation, and present preliminary data on its phosphorus removal efficiency. This work is conducted as part of the EU project Fostering European lake restoration by nutrient removal, recovery, and reuse: integrated catchment and in-lake solutions (FERRO).

presentations.title: Carbon as a currency to detect regime shifts in wetlands and shallow lakes
presentations.abstract: One of the most promising approaches to mitigating anthropogenic climate change is the protection and restoration of wetlands, due to their ability to store large quantities of carbon (C). Although there is substantial evidence of wetlands acting as C sinks, they are dynamic systems whose function can shift rapidly with changes in nutrients, water levels, and temperatures. Phosphorus (P) enrichment and hydrologic variability can drive transitions from clear, macrophyte-dominated states to turbid, algae-dominated states, yet the implications of regime shifts for C cycling and greenhouse gas emissions remain poorly understood. To quantify the net C emissions from wetlands under these scenarios, we develop a process-based model that considers biogeochemical interactions affecting vegetation growth, and simulates primary production, decomposition, as well as CO2 and CH4 sequestration and export. To explore these scenarios in different wetland types, the model can be adjusted by modifying water levels and vegetation functional groups. Our first application parameterizes the model for the Mer Bleue bog complex (Ottawa, Canada), a nutrient-poor bog surrounded by marshes. We ask whether management actions aimed at reducing eutrophication align with or conflict with climate-mitigation goals. By explicitly integrating C cycling into the traditionally “P-centered” paradigm of wetland management, this work provides a framework for identifying thresholds and designing strategies that jointly maximize water-quality benefits and climate-regulation co-benefits.

presentations.title: Building the digital foundations for upscaling lake restoration
presentations.abstract: Effective upscaling of lake-restoration measures depends on coherent, accessible data systems that allow practitioners to test scenarios, compare options, and understand trade-offs, for example, between sustainable nutrient management and climate change mitigation. Without integrated digital tools, the transition from isolated pilot projects to basin- or national-scale required to meet Global Biodiversity Framework ambitions (including Target 2 and 7) will be limited. In addition, many countries lack data systems with which to assess restoration pathways. The EC FutureLakes and GEF uPcycle Lakes Projects are working to address this gap through the production of open data products to support lake restoration upscaling assessments at European and Global scales. The FutureLakes eLakes Portal provides an interoperable platform combining socio-economic, biodiversity, water-quality, and biophysical data to explore restoration pathways at European scale. The Global Phosphorus Dashboard complements this by integrating global-to-local phosphorus and nitrogen data with socio-economic and ecological information to identify sustainable nutrient pathways for lake basins globally. Together, these tools offer broad scope for evaluating investment opportunities through emerging nature markets, including biodiversity, nutrient, and climate markets. We will showcase these tools and provide demonstration analyses focussing on biodiversity and climate mitigation options using real lake restoration case studies from Europe and Latin America.

presentations.title: Biofilm eDNA as a Novel Method to Estimate Brook Trout Abundance in Headwater Streams
presentations.abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is increasingly utilised to monitor aquatic biodiversity, but provides information within a short temporal window, which may have limited value for assessing population abundance of mobile organisms. While conventional approaches sample waters, Biofilms are an underutilized matrix for sampling eDNA that may overcome these challenges: they can retain nucleic acids potentially acting as eDNA passive sampler of aquatic biodiversity. Here, we developed a novel method to estimate the abundance of brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) from eDNA in stream biofilms across 23 headwater streams in New Brunswick and northwestern Ontario. We compared the performance of biofilms with conventional water eDNA in estimating brook trout abundance via quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR). Brook trout biofilm eDNA copy number was positively correlated with fish biomass estimated from simultaneous electrofishing, but was not correlated with water eDNA. These results suggest biofilm-entrapped eDNA may be less susceptible to ambient variation, offering a more reliable proxy for local abundance. We propose that the biofilm eDNA approach offers promise as a powerful, integrative tool for aquatic biomonitoring, capable of delivering population and community data across trophic levels (i.e. from microbial community to fish) from a single sample.

presentations.title: Integrating environmental DNA into tribal resource management.
presentations.abstract: Pacific salmon (Oncorhynchus spp.) are a vital resource for Indigenous tribes on Washington’s Pacific Coast. In Washington State, the Pacific Coast treaty Indian tribes manage their fisheries within their usual and accustomed fishing grounds, waters which have provided for cultural and subsistence well-being since time immemorial. In recent decades, these same fisheries have experienced stark declines due to a myriad of environmental and anthropogenic stressors. To assist the tribal fisheries managers in understanding these shifting baselines, the Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission is working with member tribes to employ the use of environmental DNA (eDNA) to monitor the spatiotemporal occurrence of Pacific salmon, and to further understand freshwater habitat conditions. This initiative, known as the Coastal Watershed Assessment Project (CWAP), aims to monitor the spatiotemporal presence of Pacific salmon and to enhance understanding of freshwater habitat conditions. Through a multi-year endeavor, CWAP seeks to significantly augment species-level fish data available to treaty tribes. This data empowers tribes to 1) Prioritize habitat restoration initiatives, 2) Concentrate monitoring efforts in critical species-rich areas, 3) Identify barriers to anadromous migration, 4) Provide spatiotemporal distribution insights on salmonid populations, and 5) Detect invasive fish species within the region. With four years of study completed (and over 1200 sites sampled), preliminary case studies have been developed to demonstrate the integration of metabarcoding and qPCR assays into tribal fisheries management practices along the Washington Coast.

presentations.title: Microbial Community Structure in Lake Winnipeg
presentations.abstract: Lake Winnipeg is the central hydrological feature in Manitoba and is vulnerable to stressors imposed by human activities including excess nutrients like phosphate, leading to adverse events like Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs). Lake Winnipeg and its tributaries have deep cultural ties for Indigenous Peoples – the word “Winnipeg” itself is derived from the Cree word for “muddy waters”. As a provider of numerous ecosystem services, the deteriorating health of the lake directly impacts the livelihood of many communities. In this study we conducted Oxford Nanopore shotgun metagenomic sequencing to examine the ecology and biogeography of microbial communities using surface water samples collected across a network of stations spanning the north and south basins during spring, summer, and fall cruises aboard the M/V Namao between 2022-2025. Consistent with results from metagenomic surveys of other lakes (e.g. Canadian Lake Pulse), a core community of common microbes persisted across all samples, although clear differences in diversity and relative abundance of taxa were observed between the north and south basins and across seasons and years. Using metagenomic binning we reconstructed a draft genome for the dominant ecotype of Microcystis, a HAB-forming cyanobacterium, finding that it encoded the full microcystin toxin biosynthetic pathway. Our study contributes towards a long-term record of baseline microbial communities in Lake Winnipeg and future work will assess the utility of using microbes as functional indicators for overall health and response to stressors in lake ecosystems.

presentations.title: Understanding eDNA and eRNA Persistence Across Particle Sizes and Spatial Scales
presentations.abstract: Environmental nucleic acids (eNAs) are DNA and RNA that organisms release into aquatic environments as whole cells, fragments, organelles, vesicles, or free molecules. These materials enable non-invasive biodiversity monitoring, yet the physical states, persistence, and transport of eDNA and eRNA remain poorly resolved. We conducted two complementary experiments to test how particle state, degradation, and dilution influence the detection of both molecules. In a controlled microcosm experiment, we tracked eNAs across cellular (>1 µm), subcellular (0.2–1 µm), and free (<0.2 µm) fractions. eNAs occurred in multiple forms, and these forms shifted among particle sizes as degradation progressed. Small particles lost signal rapidly and often showed intermittent detection, whereas larger fractions retained eNAs longer and produced more consistent signals. In a 1000-L outdoor mesocosm experiment using connected ponds, we examined how serial dilution and hydrological transport shape detection at larger spatial scales. Both eDNA and eRNA remained detectable under strong dilution, supporting their use for identifying rare or low-abundance taxa. eRNA degraded within 24 hours and reflected metabolically active organisms, while eDNA persisted for nearly a month and, together with eRNA, was transported across connected habitats. These two-scale mechanistic insights clarify how molecular origin, degradation dynamics, and particle state shape eNA signals, improving interpretation across spatial scales and strengthening methodological practices for freshwater molecular monitoring.

presentations.title: Using sedimentary DNA to reconstruct natural and anthropogenic disturbances in freshwater lakes
presentations.abstract: Emerging molecular tools such as sedimentary DNA (sedDNA) are transforming our ability to reconstruct past and present biodiversity in freshwater ecosystems. This presentation demonstrates how sedDNA targeted quantitative PCR assays and metabarcoding can extend the temporal scope of monitoring by revealing historical fish and eukaryotic community dynamics from lake sediment cores. By combining species-specific assays with community-level metabarcoding, we reconstructed over a century of ecological change, documenting native fish presence, human-mediated introductions, and community shifts linked to natural disturbances. These molecular methods gave us much more detailed information over time than traditional surveys, which are important for environmental assessment and managing freshwater. Our work highlights how sedDNA integrates seamlessly into other knowledge sources, alongside Indigenous Knowledge within the surveyed region, to advance holistic, non-invasive monitoring of freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: eDNA metabarcoding identifies fish conservation priorities in deep-waters fjords of British Columbia
presentations.abstract: Connecting coastal temperate rainforests to the northeast Pacific Ocean, British Columbia (BC) fjords have been integral to First Nations culture for millennia, supporting traditional settlements, spiritual practices, and harvesting of diverse and abundant marine resources. However, post-colonial human activities have driven substantial fjord transformations through infrastructure development and overfishing, resulting in habitat loss and dramatic fish stock declines. Today, efforts combining First Nations Traditional Knowledge and Western science are ongoing to restore and protect these fragile ecosystems. However, significant gaps remain in our understanding of species occurrence, distribution, and habitat use within fjords, hindering the development of actions to manage these ecosystems. We sampled eDNA in five BC fjords to evaluate spatiotemporal patterns in fish assemblages. We consulted with First Nations and conservation groups to identify species of concern and determine effective approaches for sharing results to support local conservation initiatives. Using criteria derived from species life traits, we identified and mapped the distribution of 38 conservation priority species. Our results underscored the unique value of fjords as coastal habitat. The major outcomes of this study were communicated to fjord users, and eDNA data were integrated into an open-access Shiny web interface to support decision-making for conservation purposes. Examples of applications, such as data incorporation into Átl'ḵa7tsem / Howe Sound decision-support tools, will be discussed.

presentations.title: ROBOTIC 3D PROFILING TO STUDY HYPOLIMNETIC OXYGEN DYNAMICS WITH MARP-FG
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are important biological habitats and resources. They often require adequate management based on comprehensive waterbody monitoring. In lakes and reservoirs, conventional monitoring with crewed boats or stationary buoys has low spatial resolution that may fail to capture relevant limnological processes. Robotic monitoring can overcome this by obtaining data with high spatiotemporal resolution, independent of weather and without compromising data quality. This allows for studying horizontal heterogeneities in oxygen dynamics, which are rarely investigated due to lateral diffusion homogenizing the hypolimnion. However, spatial variability in sediment conditions can alter local oxygen availability in overlying waters. In this work, we present MARP-FG, a mobile robotic device that can autonomously record hydrochemical profiles. MARP-FG was applied during several sampling campaigns on a small artificial lake whose hypolimnion is supplied with oxygen during summer stratification. By obtaining a three-dimensional characterization of dissolved oxygen concentration, electric conductivity, and pH, we identified differences in local oxygen availability and sediment release dynamics before and during aeration. Such insights could help improve our understanding and the modeling of lake ecosystem functioning, as well as waterbody management.

presentations.title: UNRAVELING LAKE ERIE'S FALL TURNOVER: AUTONOMOUS UNDERWATER GLIDER CAPTURES SPATIAL BIOGEOCHEMICAL DYNAMICS
presentations.abstract: Lake Erie, the most productive of the Laurentian Great Lakes, attracts significant attention for its annual hypoxic events in its central basin. In this study, we utilized data from a three-week underwater autonomous glider (AUG) mission conducted from September to October 2021, with a flight path specifically designed to capture the summer-to-fall turnover in Lake Erie's central basin. The AUG repeatedly surveyed two transects east of Cleveland, Ohio, a ~30 km perpendicular nearshore-offshore and a ~50 km diagonal, yielding continuous 3D profiles of temperature, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll a, backscatter, and conductivity. We binned the data and summarized key variables, including offshore distance, to describe the limnological changes during this event. Before the turnover, the upper water column was homogeneous, with low backscatter, whereas the hypolimnion showed greater backscatter. Following turnover, material was resuspended, resulting in a significant increase in backscatter in shallow zones during the first week, then dispersed offshore by week two. This resuspension pulse aligned with stronger winds, a shift in wind direction, and a late-season chlorophyll a surge likely fueled by nutrients released from disturbed sediments. Statistical comparisons revealed significant spatial gradients in nearshore upper-water-column cooling, hypolimnetic warming, and offshore particulate entrainment. This study demonstrates AUGs’ unique capacity to resolve fine-scale, spatially explicit responses to lake overturns, insights unattainable with stationary sensors, while highlighting the need for space-time-aware analytics to leverage glider datasets for ecosystem process estimation fully.

presentations.title: Integrated Monitoring of Inland Waters in the State of Espírito Santo (Brazil)
presentations.abstract: The monitoring of inland water quality in the state of Espírito Santo is currently conducted by the State Water Resources Agency (AGERH) through the QualiRios Program, which evaluates physical, chemical, and microbiological parameters at approximately 100 sampling points distributed throughout the state's river basins. However, this approach has limitations in detecting subtle impacts resulting from land use and emerging contaminants. This project proposes the development of an integrated monitoring protocol that incorporates molecular and ecological tools to complement water quality assessment in the Santa Maria da Vitória River Basin, which is characterized by intensive agriculture. Methods based on environmental DNA will be applied to characterize aquatic biodiversity. Invertebrate communities and decomposition rates of organic matter will be evaluated as indicators of ecological integrity. Water and sediment samples will also be analyzed to detect residues of glyphosate, mancozeb, and chlorpyrifos, pesticides widely used in the study area. The project is expected to generate unprecedented information on the biodiversity and functioning of aquatic ecosystems in Espírito Santo by comparing regions with different levels of impact and integrating physical, chemical, biological, and molecular data. The results will provide scientific support for improving institutional monitoring and for the sustainable management of state water resources.

presentations.title: EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES FOR MEASUREMENT OF INLAND WATER CYANOBACTERIAL BLOOMS
presentations.abstract: Harmful cyanobacterial blooms are a significant concern for inland water ecosystems and public health. Tools for identifying and quantifying cyanobacteria are important for water managers and researchers attempting to understand bloom drivers and monitoring their dynamics. To fill this need, there has been an emergence of novel technologies and techniques for measuring these spatially and temporally dynamic systems. This research covers application of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), drones, aircraft and satellite remote sensing measurements for understanding inland water cyanobacterial blooms. Field campaigns were conducted in inland water bodies in California, United States and the Greater Cape Floristic Region, South Africa to measure blooms using these emerging technologies. We show the use of high spatial resolution data from AUVs and drones for quantifying the spatial variability of these blooms. We quantify the critical scale of variability, which is useful when designing sampling plans or specifying the spatial resolution of a satellite sensor necessary to resolve a bloom. We also utilize airborne and satellite imaging spectroscopy (“hyperspectral”) data to classify phytoplankton communities as well as cyanobacteria genera using novel approaches. These classifications are compared to in situ measurements of phytoplankton and cyanobacteria community composition determined from microscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography measurements of phytoplankton pigments. We discuss shortcomings of these techniques and opportunities for further research.

presentations.title: rLakeHabitat: A tool for generating bathymetric maps and quantifying physical aquatic habitats
presentations.abstract: Water level fluctuations can have profound effects on the availability and spatial configuration of aquatic habitats. These water level fluctuations modify the availability of shallow, nearshore littoral zones and shift the relative distribution of water volume within stratified habitats. The relative distribution of these habitats defines the physical structure of lakes and reservoirs, influencing key processes like oxygen dynamics, nutrient cycling, and ecosystem productivity. Quantifying how habitat extent varies with water level is essential for assessing ecological impacts of water level fluctuations and identifying hydrologic regimes that support biodiversity and productivity. Although bathymetry-based approaches are widely used to quantify the extent of specific habitat types, few open-source tools exist that enable users to quickly and easily generate bathymetric models and compute aquatic habitat metrics. To address this methodological gap, we developed the rLakeHabitat R package, a reproducible, flexible, and open-source tool designed to facilitate the creation of bathymetric models and quantify both littoral and pelagic habitat availability across water levels. Here, we demonstrate the functionality of the rLakeHabitat package by generating bathymetric maps for two Wyoming reservoirs and comparing changes in physical aquatic habitats across a range of water levels. This package will make bathymetry generation and habitat quantification more accessible, encouraging broader consideration of spatially explicit approaches in aquatic ecosystem management.

presentations.title: Using Earth Observations for Detecting Small Persistent Waterbodies
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: Small persistent surface waters such as ponds occur worldwide and are influenced by global change. They provide important ecosystem services, particularly for biodiversity, yet remain difficult to detect in global datasets. Existing products such as HydroLAKES (>100,000 m2) and the Global Water Bodies database (>2,000 m2) largely overlook small ponds. Using Sentinel-2 Surface Reflectance at 10 m resolution, we assessed the detection of 355 ponds in 7 European countries sampled within the Biodiversa+ TRANSPONDER and Horizon Europe PONDERFUL projects. We evaluated spectral indices commonly applied to lakes, including the Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), two variants (mNDWI1 and mNDWI2), the Sentinel Water Mask (SWM), the Automated Water Extraction Index (AWEI), and two single spectral bands (842 and 1610 nm). Statistical distribution consistency was assessed using skewness, to evaluate if the index is performing as expected, and kurtosis, to measure stability of the index across waterbodies. Positive kurtosis indicated higher consistency for NDWI, mNDWI1, SWM, and AWEI. Country-level analysis showed more negative NDWI values in Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Switzerland, and the UK, whereas Spain and Turkey were closer to zero. Spanish ponds alone showed negative kurtosis, likely due to their small average size (298 m2), highlighting spatial resolution limits. Although NDWI showed statistical consistency, its positive skewness reduced reliability, while SWM and AWEI achieved better classification performance.

presentations.title: WATERSHED WATCH: COMBINING EDNA AND COMMUNITY SCIENCE TO MONITOR AQUATIC SPECIES OF CONCERN
presentations.abstract: Climate change, habitat fragmentation, and human movement are increasing the spread of invasive species, harming biodiversity, ecosystem services, and public health. Traditional biodiversity monitoring is expensive, slow, and limited in coverage, leading to incomplete data. Here, we developed molecular tools- using environmental DNA (eDNA) technologies- to record the presence of invasive zoonotic mosquitoes in Ontario and Quebec regions of Canada and compare its diversity to traditional trapping methods. We tested six eDNA sampling methods at three locations across 30 freshwater waterbodies to identify protocols suitable for community scientists. All sampling methods recovered detectable mosquito eDNA, with passive eDNA samplers (PeDS) achieving the highest detection rate at 85%. Salt-preserved water samples (SALT) and traditional on-site filtration followed at 62% detection rate. SALT yielded the highest eDNA concentration per unit of water volume. The location of sampling (inlet, outlet, shoreline) within each water had no significant differences in detection rates. Community scientists successfully deployed PEDS and SALT, showing their high applicability. Our approach combines emerging eDNA technology and community science, enabling non-invasive, scalable monitoring of low-biomass organisms like mosquitoes. It can be used in volunteer lake monitoring programs to expand biodiversity knowledge and track species of concern, including invasive and rare taxa, offering a valuable tool for freshwater ecosystem surveillance.

presentations.title: CAN WATERSHED BIO- AND GEODIVERSITY INFORM THE HABITAT SUITABILITY OF SALMONIDS?
presentations.abstract: Brook trout (uinipeku-matemetu, Salvelinus fontinalis) and Atlantic salmon (ushashameku, Salmo salar) are both emblematic species of the province of Quebec for their popularity with recreational, commercial, and Indigenous food, ceremonial, and social fisheries. Anticosti Island, a recently named UNESCO World Heritage Site for its cultural significance and rich geological record, is a well-known destination for brook trout and Atlantic salmon fishing with populations of various health statuses. We developed a project to assess the links between river diversity and the various mechanisms underlying the ecophysiology and habitat preferences of Anticosti Island salmonids using fish otolith and water trace metal signatures, river morphology, and environmental DNA. In July 2025, 37 rivers and lakes across Anticosti island were sampled for environmental DNA, water chemistry, and river morphological characteristics.This data collection and future model development will be useful for future ecosystem restoration plans and conservation goals for native Brook trout and Atlantic salmon populations throughout the province of Québec.

presentations.title: EARLY DETECTION OF FRESHWATER EXOTIC INVASIVE MACROPHYTES THROUGH ENVIRONMENTAL DNA
presentations.abstract: Exotic invasive macrophytes are reshaping freshwater ecosystems, by changing community composition and altering key ecosystem functions and services. Early detection of exotic invasive macrophytes is essential for effective management, yet current monitoring approaches still rely heavily on traditional field surveys. These surveys are often costly and require specialized taxonomic expertise to identify species. As a result, sustainable solutions for detecting invasive macrophytes remain a major challenge for freshwater managers. Environmental DNA (eDNA) analyses are increasingly used for freshwater monitoring and provide a promising approach for tracking exotic invasive macrophytes. With this approach, water samples can be collected by non-scientists with minimal training and sent to a lab to detect the presence of selected species. We are developing an eDNA detection tool suitable for a large-scale exotic invasive macrophytes monitoring program. First, we used community metabarcoding sequencing to monitor both the presence of exotic invasive species and their potential impact on the local community. Then, we developed a targeted detection tool for Myriophyllum spicatum, a high-priority invasive macrophyte in Québec. Our preliminary results show positive detection of exotic invasive macrophytes through metabarcoding sequencing and successful discrimination of the invasive M. spicatum from other taxa through qPCR analysis. These tools can facilitate widespread, rapid, and cost-effective monitoring of exotic invasive macrophytes across Québec.

presentations.title: MANITOBA'S MESOSALINE MICROBES' METAGENOMIC MAPPING
presentations.abstract: Water has been described as the most precious resource in Manitoba, Canada, yet little is known about the microbial inhabitants of these waters. This is particularly true for the saline springs that are > 600 km from the closest marine ecosystem, where microbial communities are largely uncharacterized. No information on the composition, longevity or resilience after disruptions is available for these systems, which means that no framework exists for biodiversity conservation at the microbial level. With this work, we aim to use eDNA technologies to guide cultivation efforts to enrich for bacteria and archaea from these springs. To target anaerobic diversity, enrichment cultures were established in anoxic, moderately saline media (14.5 ppt) supplemented with several carbon sources for heterotrophs, and carbon dioxide for autotrophs, with a N2/CO2/H2 (88:7.5:4.25 vol/vol) headspace. Subsurface sediment from the springs was added as 10% v/v inoculum, and enrichments were incubated at room temperature, under circumneutral pH. After 13 days of incubation, metagenomic sequencing of cultures showed selection for new Desulfobacterota, Campylobacterota, Chloroflexota and Nanobdellota. This work established the first enrichment cultures for these organisms, with some described only at the order or family level, highlighting their unique genomic diversity. Future work entails characterizing these organisms to serve as anchor points for monitoring of the microbial communities in these springs, as the high degree of novelty may be indicative of endemic species in need of conservation.

presentations.title: MONITORING, UNDERSTANDING AND PROTECTING FRESHWATER BIODIVERSITY IN NATURAL, ARTIFICIAL AND MODIFIED WATERWAYS IN BOREAL FORESTS USING DNA METABARCODING
presentations.abstract: Man-made ditches, modified waterways, and small natural streams make up over 90 % of the total length of running waters in Sweden. Millions of kilometers of these small waterways are exposed to pressures from forestry, including insufficient riparian buffers along modified waterways and the cleaning of drainage ditches. Such practices pose major threats to aquatic biodiversity, yet we currently lack the capacity to predict biodiversity responses, as these systems are largely overlooked in monitoring programs. Using DNA metabarcoding targeting diatoms and bacteria sampled from multiple substrates at 56 sites across Sweden, we explored biodiversity patterns along a gradient from natural streams to man-made ditches, with and without recent forestry pressure. We can, for the first time, provide a snapshot of microbial biodiversity in these understudied systems. Our results suggest that recent forest harvesting surrounding waterways influences habitat conditions – especially light availability and temperature – more strongly than whether the system is natural or man-made. Interestingly, geographic region emerged as a stronger predictor of diatom community composition compared to both waterway type and recent forestry disturbance, suggesting that the biodiversity values of natural and man-made waterways may be more similar to each other than expected. Our ongoing work aims to develop a cost-efficient and scalable field and laboratory protocol and provide an eDNA-based diatom index tailored for small boreal forest waterways to assess their ecological status.

presentations.title: REASSESSING OUR NAMING PRACTICES FOR ORGANISMS IDENTIFIED FROM GENOMIC DATA
presentations.abstract: Nomenclature serves as the common language through which we communicate biodiversity. Using consistent and universal names allow unambiguous reference to organisms. This facilitates the critical connections between research in vastly different fields required for obtaining a holistic view of an organism. In the prokaryotes, a code of nomenclature that allows use of genomic data as types, SeqCode, has recently been developed. This means that prokaryotic genomes can now serve as anchor points for names ascribed to the biodiversity represented by them, including genomes derived from eDNA. However, with SeqCode development largely aiming for consistency with the International Code of Nomenclature of Prokaryotes that govern cultivated prokaryotes, many western practices in naming are inadvertently also being preserved. Thus, despite many microbial ecologists showing significant improvement in how we conduct research in collaboration with Indigenous communities, the naming of microorganisms does not yet reflect this progress. We are now at a pivotal point in the lifespan of the SeqCode to effect change in how we approach naming of prokaryotes, particularly organisms discovered from Indigenous lands. Here, we would like to extend a call to action to build a global network of Indigenous Peoples and researchers to develop guidelines for the naming of prokaryotes. Co-developed names will not only provide richness to the nomenclatural landscape but would show respect to the names and Indigenous knowledge gathered over generations by the guardians of this biodiversity.

presentations.title: SPATIAL REPRESENTATIVENESS OF EDNA SAMPLES IN A LARGE AND SHALLOW LAKE: IMPLICATIONS FOR MONITORING FISH ASSEMBLAGES
presentations.abstract: Representative sampling is a central goal in ecological research, biodiversity monitoring, and environmental management, yet accurately characterizing community structure in large, heterogeneous ecosystems remains challenging. We applied habitat-specific environmental DNA (eDNA) assays and real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR), to identify the optimal sampling effort and the spatial dependence of sampling representativeness for whole-lake level monitoring of fish assemblages in Lake Balaton, the largest shallow lake in Central Europe. Samples were collected in a spatially stratified systematic design to cover all habitat types and spatial and environmental gradients in the lake. Rarefaction and autosimilarity analyses showed that only a small proportion of samples was sufficient to capture taxonomic richness and to yield representative patterns of species composition and relative abundance. Detection of rare and traditionally underrepresented taxa, including benthic and large-bodied species, was consistently effective. Redundancy analysis identified the inshore–offshore gradient as the primary driver of community structure. Although latitude and mesohabitat type were statistically significant, their influence on assemblage structure at the whole-lake level was minimal. Overall, eDNA-based surveys offer a powerful and efficient tool for large-scale biomonitoring in Lake Balaton, requiring neither high sampling intensity nor fine spatial resolution to achieve representative assessments.

presentations.title: ADVANCEMENT IN EDNA FRESHWATER PHYTOPLANKTON RESEARCH AND BIOMONITORING – REFBAR PROJECT
presentations.affiliation: University of Belgrade, Institute of chemistry, technology and metallurgy
presentations.abstract: The quantity and quality of freshwater habitats in rivers, lakes, and wetlands are rapidly declining on a global scale. Almost half of all lakes in the European Union (EU) are below good ecological status. To improve the health of lakes, efficient biodiversity monitoring is essential. Phytoplankton, as a complex assemblage of different microalgal groups and cyanobacteria, responds to different pressures on lakes, and thus represents a key biological quality element required by the EU Water Framework Directive (WFD). The REFBAR project aims to improve the detection of freshwater plankton microalgae and cyanobacteria through a DNA-based method. The consortium includes three research institutions and three companies from Europe, as well as two academic institutions from South America. We will innovate a DNA extraction protocol for phytoplankton, design new 23S RNA primers suitable for long-read sequencing, develop a cost-effective portable genetic workflow, sequence DNA barcodes of phytoplankton specimens from culture collections (barcoding) and complex environmental samples (metabarcoding), and upgrade the Phytool reference library. Finally, an international expert team will be established to curate the Phytool barcode library. This project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under grant agreement No 101236590.

presentations.title: Identifying and Exploring the Persistence, Resistome and Mobilome of Campylobacter and Salmonella spp. and in Agricultural-Influenced Waterways of First Nation Communities in Manitoba
presentations.abstract: Campylobacteriosis and salmonellosis are the leading food and water-borne bacterial illnesses in Canada. The causative agents are Campylobacter especially Campylobacter jejuni and Campylobacter coli, and Salmonella spp. According to the government of Canada, Campylobacter spp. account for about 8% domestically acquired foodborne illnesses and about 14% hospitalizations from foodborne bacterial illnesses. Non-typhoidal Salmonella spp. account for approximately 5% domestically acquired foodborne illnesses and about 24% hospitalizations from foodborne bacterial illnesses. Agriculturally influenced environments, surrounding waterways, facilitate the transport of enteric pathogens, making them a sentinel location. FoodNet Canada, a federal program, has conducted assessments of these pathogens in sentinel sites across major regions in Canada; however, monitoring and screening of these pathogens in aquatic waterways of Manitoba remains unavailable. Using a combination of culture-dependent approaches and Oxford Nanopore whole-genome sequencing (WGS), we assess these pathogens and the water quality golden standard, thermotolerant E. coli, within agriculturally impacted waterways across three First Nation communities of Manitoba. Surface watersamples from 7 different sampling locations influenced by agricultural activities were collected during four different months from August to December 2025, which is the primary harvest period for most major crops in Manitoba. Genomic DNA was extracted from the three bacterial isolates of interest per sample location and prepared for WGS. Longer and more informative reads were generated, assembled and aligned against a reference genome for the respective bacterial pathogens, followed by a full genome annotation to identify antimicrobial resistance genes. Within this context, the complete resistome and mobilome of the isolates were characterised. Metadata and genetic information of all the isolates from the sample sites will be [MU1] integ

presentations.title: Sound:Wave – Passive Acoustic Monitoring of Recreational Boating in a Multi-Use Waterway
presentations.abstract: Recreational boating is increasingly recognized as a source of disturbance to freshwater ecosystems. Noise pollution and surface waves (wakes) are primary boat-induced stressors that can have immediate and cumulative impacts on waterways, biodiversity, and nearby users and residents. Navigation speed influences both underwater noise and wake height, highlighting the value of incorporating boat speed in monitoring programs. We present a practical, cost-effective, and fully autonomous method for estimating boat speed and traffic using open-source passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) devices in the Rideau River, eastern Ontario. Method validation was completed during experimental trials in September–October 2024 in the Eccolands Reach (Ottawa). A variety of recreational vessels were operated at known speeds (5-70 km/h), and passes were recorded at 48 kHz by two HydroMoths deployed parallel to the channel. Speed was automatically calculated from recorder spacing and the time interval between peak sound amplitudes (n = 67; RMSE = 10.2 km/h; MAE = 7.1 km/h). In August 2025, we surveyed the aquatic soundscapes at two sites in the Long Reach (Kars). Each HydroMoth recorded 20 minutes of 32-kHz audio per hour for one week (112 total hours). A machine-learning model was used to quantify boat traffic and estimates were compared with wake counts from do-it-yourself pressure gauges. This scalable approach demonstrates how PAM can simultaneously support boating management and ecological monitoring in recreational waterways.

presentations.title: FACTORS AFFECTING MICROBIAL COMMUNITY STRUCTURE IN SPLIT LAKE, MANITOBA
presentations.abstract: Split Lake is a large freshwater lake located on the lower Nelson River in northern Manitoba that was heavily negatively impacted by the 1976 Churchill River Diversion hydroelectric project, which diverted 75% of the water from the Churchill River into the Nelson. On the north shore of the Split Lake, lies Tatatskweyak Cree Nation, a community of the original Ininew people who have inhabited northern Manitoba for millennia and have been under boil water advisory since 2017. In partnership with the Tataskweyak Environmental Monitoring Agency, a group of tribal Members concerned for the health of the lake and people, we conducted a week-long sampling expedition to establish a baseline and understand the environmental factors influencing the lake’s microbial community. The study conducted in August 2024 encompassed 16 stations on Split Lake and Assean Lake, a nearby lake with minimal influence from hydroelectric development and the source of water for a new treatment plant. We used 16s SSU rRNA gene metabarcoding of aquatic eDNA to assess microbial community composition across the lake, which was strongly correlated with turbidity and dissolved oxygen level; six distinct microbial community clusters were identified. The dominant prokaryotic taxa were Actinobacteria hgcl clade and Cyanobium. Microcystin concentrations measured in lake waters were well below the Maximum Acceptable Concentration (MAC) set for Canadian federal drinking water standards. These results will inform community monitoring effects on the health of the lake.

presentations.title: DIFFERENCES IN MICROBIAL COMMUNITY STRUCTURE BETWEEN THE RED RIVER AND WINNIPEG RIVER IN MANITOBA, CANADA
presentations.abstract: Microbes play a dynamic role in nutrient and carbon cycling within riverine ecosystems so it is vital to understand their ecology and distributions in light of anthropogenic influences, particularly in systems heavily impacted by eutrophication like the Lake Winnipeg watershed. The two main inputs to Lake Winnipeg are the Red River, dominated by agricultural land use, and the Winnipeg River, which is primarily forested. While 70% of the water entering Lake Winnipeg comes from the Winnipeg River, 70% of the excess phosphorous comes from the Red. In 2002 we initiated an ongoing microbial community monitoring program in collaboration with local First Nations to conduct repeat seasonal sampling at 20+ sites in the Lake Winnipeg watershed including the Red, Assiniboine, La Salle, Seine, Brokenhead, and Winnipeg Rivers. Using Oxford Nanopore shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we conducted metagenomic binning to reconstruct draft genomes for the most abundant taxa in these rivers. As in other large metagenomic surveys like the Genome Resolved Open Watersheds database, we found a core of common taxa across river systems, but distinct compositions in each river. Significant seasonal and interannual variability were evident as well, indicating that ongoing monitoring is needed. Going forward we aim to include additional environmental parameters to gain a more complete understanding of the factors leading to changes in microbial community structure in this watershed.

presentations.title: Emerging methods for aquatic invasive species detection: Results of a global survey
presentations.abstract: Aquatic invasive species are among the most severe and rapidly intensifying threats to global freshwater biodiversity, driving more than half of documented freshwater species extinctions. Early detection of invasion fronts and effective monitoring of established populations are critical, yet freshwater environments present unique challenges: many invaders persist at low densities or remain cryptic, habitats are either highly fragmented (lakes and ponds) or extensively connected (rivers), and hydrological processes can redistribute organisms and their detectable signals. Recent technological innovations, including environmental DNA, drones, robotic samplers, passive acoustic sensors, underwater imaging, and machine-learning–based identification, offer transformative opportunities to improve surveillance. However, their effectiveness hinges on aligning method attributes with invasive species traits, behaviours, life-history strategies, and habitat use. In this talk, we present findings from a global survey of limnologists that explores how emerging detection methods are currently applied, perceived, and prioritized in the context of fundamental ecological characteristics of aquatic invaders. We highlight global patterns in perspectives, gaps between technological potential and real-world feasibility, and opportunities for strategically aligning species ecology with methodological innovation. Together, these insights help inform the synergistic deployment of emerging detection tools to enhance early-warning capacity and long-term monitoring of aquatic invasive species.

presentations.title: PASSIVE ACOUSTIC MONITORING OF BIOLOGICAL AND ANTHROPOGENIC SOUNDSCAPES IN THE RIDEAU RIVER SYSTEM.
presentations.abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring, well established in marine and terrestrial research, remains underused in freshwater ecosystem assessment. To demonstrate its potential, we conducted soundscape surveys in the Rideau River (Ottawa, Ontario) using low-cost, open-source HydroMoth hydrophones. Recorders were deployed for 8 days (06–13 August 2025) at two contrasting sites: a lower-disturbance no-wake zone adjacent to James Island and a higher-disturbance reach near W.A. Taylor Conservation Area, characterized by frequent boat traffic. Each unit recorded 20 minutes of 32-kHz audio every hour, producing 6,760 minutes of data. Machine-learning models were used to autonomously detect and classify acoustic events from biological and anthropogenic sources. Across sites, we compared diel patterns of biophony and anthropophony, quantified the contribution of boat noise to the overall soundscape, and examined how elevated noise conditions influence the occurrence of biological activity based on frequency and duration of detected events. Biological detections were greater at the lower-disturbance site, while boat noise contributed more strongly to the soundscape at the higher-disturbance site, revealing clear spatial and temporal differences in freshwater acoustic activity. The results illustrate how Passive Acoustic Monitoring, paired with machine-learning detection, captures meaningful differences in freshwater soundscapes and supports emerging applications of acoustic monitoring in freshwater environments.

name: AI in Aquatic Sciences: Advancing Ecology and Sustainability with Artificial Intelligence
lead_organizer: Alexander Flecker, Cornell University
co_organizers: Maria Camila Mejía García, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping many scientific fields, yet aquatic sciences have only begun to tap into AI's broader potential for innovation. AI enables the processing of vast datasets from sensor arrays and other big data sources, providing new insights into ecological processes, environmental change and sustainability solutions. For example, machine learning can automate species identification through image or bioacoustic recognition, as well as eDNA data, while deep learning enables high fidelity monitoring and forecasting of water quality, biogeochemistry, habitat change, and flow dynamics. Approaches such as AI-guided multi-objective optimization are increasingly supporting conservation planning within aquatic ecosystems—and offer substantial promise for scaling impact across the aquatic sciences.

presentations.title: An LMM-driven, context-aware AI framework enables efficient and scalable monitoring of aquaculture ponds across complex landscapes
presentations.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) are opening up new possibilities for image-based environmental monitoring by combining spatial context and reasoning in ways that conventional classifiers cannot. Waterbody identification represents a key application for managing freshwater landscapes. Yet, many targets, such small irregular aquaculture ponds, closely resemble natural water features and often require expert interpretation of high-resolution imagery, making them difficult to detect with traditional remote-sensing methods. Here, we introduce AISciVision-Aqua, a framework that integrates LMMs with visual retrieval-augmented reasoning and interactive tools to emulate expert analytical workflows when interpreting high-resolution imagery for aquaculture pond identification. We apply this framework to 5,000 labeled waterbodies in the Brazilian Amazon, where aquaculture has rapidly expanded and spatial inventories of ponds are lacking. AISciVision-Aqua improves pond detection, increasing accuracy from 0.78 to 0.91 relative to a supervised baseline, and performs especially well on the hardest cases (small, irregular ponds). Transparent reasoning transcripts further enable auditable, interpretable classification, providing users insights into the context driving target identification. Beyond aquaculture, this LMM-driven framework offers strong potential for any image-classification challenge where contextual understanding and expert interpretation are essential, including land-use mapping and infrastructure verification, such as identifying dams, irrigation and water-intake structures.

presentations.title: MAPPING SMALL WATERBODIES ACROSS THE CONTERMINOUS UNITED STATES FROM MULTI-SOURCE REMOTE SENSING WITH A NOVEL AI-AUGMENTED COMPUTATIONAL FRAMEWORK
presentations.abstract: Accurate mapping of small lakes and ponds (<0.1 km2) remains a challenge in global limnology, limiting our understanding of their critical role in biogeochemical cycles. While AI-enhanced remote sensing products have improved large-scale water detection, they often miss these small features due to resolution limitations and training data biases. To address this challenge, we developed the Automated Pond Object Mapper (AutoPOM), a novel machine learning framework that intelligently integrates optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite imagery by exploiting the spatial-temporal-spectral characteristics of small waterbodies. The framework begins with an adaptive segmentation that identifies prominent water signals and delineates their boundaries based on spatial proximity and spectral contrast. Building upon this, AutoPOM automates sample collection by harmonizing multiple land use land cover products, guided by AI-based class probabilities and spatial dependencies to represent ponds and key confused features. The classification robustness is further enhanced by incorporating semantic embeddings from the AlphaEarth foundation model into Random Forest classifiers. Implemented on the Google Earth Engine cloud platform, AutoPOM mapped 2.6 million waterbodies (>0.001 km2) across the Conterminous United States. This comprehensive inventory revealed widespread, previously hidden distribution hotspots of small waterbodies and established a power-law size distribution down to 0.001 km2, providing empirical foundations for quantifying and scaling their biogeochemical role.

presentations.title: Visual Characterization of the Invasive Zebra Mussel Across Morphs and Life Stages for Automated Detection
presentations.abstract: Zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha) are an invasive freshwater species that have affected ecosystems in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River since 1986, contributing to declines in native freshwater mussels and causing major biofouling impacts on infrastructure. Current detection and control methods depend on skilled labor, which limits scalability and increases costs. This project aimed to acquire high-quality image data for the development of an AI-based system for automated zebra mussel detection and, ultimately, population control. Because accurate visual recognition depends on reliable species characterization, we first identified the main visual features of zebra mussels that distinguish them from surrounding substrates. Under optimal visibility conditions, recognition accuracy reached 89% precision, although performance was influenced by lighting and turbidity. In the long term, this model is intended for deployment on an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) to support monitoring and control of invasive populations while minimizing disturbance to freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: Leveraging AI-powered optimization to balance freshwater biodiversity protection and countries' protection commitments under KMGBF 30by30
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems stand out for both their exceptional biodiversity and their high levels of threat: one quarter of all freshwater species are currently at risk of extinction. Protected areas (PAs) are intended to safeguard ecosystems from human pressures, yet their global coverage of rivers and lakes remains inefficient. As countries move toward achieving the 30by30 target of the UN Global Biodiversity Framework—protecting 30% of their territory by 2030—it is crucial to understand how PA expansion can more effectively encompass freshwater biodiversity. We use Mixed Integer Programming to identify spatial strategies that maximize protection for freshwater species (using fishes as a representative group) while ensuring the connectivity of proposed conservation areas, a key requirement for sustaining viable fish populations. Because much of the required protection is concentrated in the world's most biodiverse countries, we also evaluate how PA expansion affects the equity of protection commitments across nations. Our results provide a roadmap for countries aiming to better protect their rivers and lakes and highlight the need for conservation solutions that enhance freshwater protection without placing disproportionate burdens on a subset of countries.

presentations.title: AI-assisted Living Evidence Databases for understanding what works in conservation
presentations.abstract: For too long, crucial conservation decisions have been hampered by poor evidence use, harming nature and people. The Conservation Evidence project has worked for 20 years to change this, but gathering vast amounts of information is slow. Now, AI is transforming evidence synthesis (See https://rdcu.be/evkfj). In this piece, we call for the creation of Living Evidence Databases, offering a robust and dynamic alternative to static systematic reviews. This talk will describe the architecture and implementation of a complete, end-to-end pipeline for this purpose, developed initially for the conservation science domain. Designed to operate on local infrastructure using self-hosted models, the system ingests and normalizes documents from academic publishers, screens them for relevance using a multi-stage process, and extracts structured data according to a predefined schema. Key features include a hybrid retrieval model; a human-AI collaborative process for refining inclusion criteria from complex protocols, and the integration of an established, statistically-principled stopping rule to ensure efficiency. In a baseline evaluation against a prior large-scale manual review, the fully automated pipeline achieved 97% recall and identified a significant number of relevant studies not included in the original review, demonstrating its viability as a foundational tool for maintaining living evidence databases. We believe this work will fundamentally reshape how we use evidence to make smarter, faster, and more effective decisions in conservation, and beyond.

presentations.title: Minimizing tradeoffs among aquatic biodiversity, human nutrition, and renewable energy planning with AI-enabled decision making
presentations.abstract: Advancing aquatic ecosystem sustainability requires balancing multiple objectives that often conflict, such as biodiversity conservation and food and energy security. Yet reducing tradeoffs is challenging because these problems span large combinatorial decision spaces where the number of possible management choices expands rapidly with each added objective, exceeding the capacity of conventional analytical approaches. We examine two aquatic sustainability challenges that show how AI-enabled decision making can improve evaluation of complex tradeoffs. The first involves biodiversity and nutrition in global fisheries. Fisheries supply essential nutrients to billions of people, yet overexploitation drives biodiversity loss. Multi-objective optimization helps identify species combinations that meet nutrition while reducing overexploitation. The second concerns hydropower expansion under global Net Zero policy commitments. Hydropower supports decarbonization and grid stability but alters rivers and threatens biodiversity. Multi-objective optimization helps identify dam portfolios that meet renewable energy goals while reducing biodiversity impacts. We highlight that AI-enabled decision making can help identify species or dam portfolios that minimize tradeoffs, but implementation is constrained by the difficulty of encoding cultural and social considerations that influence decisions. AI provides a systematic way to understand mechanisms behind complex tradeoffs and guide potential solutions but cannot replace human judgment because many objectives fall outside what can be formalized.

name: AI in Aquatic Sciences: Advancing Ecology and Sustainability with Artificial Intelligence (Posters)
lead_organizer: Alexander Flecker, Cornell University
co_organizers: Maria Camila Mejía García, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping many scientific fields, yet aquatic sciences have only begun to tap into AI's broader potential for innovation. AI enables the processing of vast datasets from sensor arrays and other big data sources, providing new insights into ecological processes, environmental change and sustainability solutions.

presentations.title: AI AND THE EVOLVING LANDSCAPE OF AQUATIC SCIENCES: SESSION OVERVIEW
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping science and the world at large. Yet aquatic sciences have only begun to tap into AI's broader potential for innovation in substantive ways. This session highlights the transformative potential of AI, including machine learning, in advancing large-scale data acquisition and analysis, revealing patterns and processes in aquatic systems, enhancing scientific communication, and fostering new pathways for participatory science. We will open the session with a brief overview tracing the development of AI in aquatic science and assessing its current capabilities and future potential. We will then set the stage for speakers to showcase concrete examples of how AI is being applied across the aquatic sciences to tackle fundamental questions and pressing issues, and to outline emerging opportunities poised to reshape the field. The session aims to spark dialogue within the aquatic science community, emphasizing AI's striking capacity to accelerate research and address key environmental sustainability and biodiversity conservation challenges that intersect with aquatic systems.

presentations.title: AI in small streams: applications and lessons learned
presentations.abstract: AI may be particularly beneficial in aquatic sciences because many hydrologic processes are challenging to generalize and expensive to measure and because the biota is often cryptic and difficult to observe. New AI-based solutions that are faster, cheaper and better at uncovering complex patterns and that provide new opportunities are coming online rapidly and will likely revolutionize aquatic sciences. We describe recent examples of AI approaches including measuring and modelling stream flow, joint modeling of stream flow and temperature, tracking individual fish, and the opportunity that AI provides for integrating among and across hydrological and ecological areas of study. As it is also very important to make AI models openly available to users, we also discuss strategies for operationalizing AI models in aquatic sciences.

presentations.title: AI-ENHANCED IN SITU IMAGING FOR MONITORING PLANKTON AND SUSPENDED PARTICLES DURING ROBOTIC HULL CLEANING
presentations.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping aquatic observing systems by enabling automated, high-resolution analysis of dynamic processes. We present a compact in situ imaging system that applies AI-based computer vision to quantify suspended particle fields during ship-hull cleaning operations, where environmental verification is essential. The instrument integrates telecentric illumination, a high-resolution camera, and embedded computing capable of autonomous image acquisition, segmentation, feature extraction, and convolutional neural-network (CNN) classification. Originally developed for plankton imaging, it was adapted to resolve suspended particulate matter (≥15 µm) and to quantify its horizontal and vertical distributions at high spatial and temporal resolution. Field deployments in the Baía da Ilha Grande (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) combined CTD profiling with AI-driven image processing to characterize physical conditions and background particle loads before, during, and after robotic hull-cleaning events. The cleaning ROV incorporates an onboard containment system that retains removed fouling material; thus, particle release is not expected. The imaging system provides independent, AI-supported verification by detecting fine-scale fluctuations in particle concentration and distinguishing natural variability from unintended releases, demonstrating its application in real-time environmental monitoring to support safer, data-driven hull-cleaning technologies.

name: Aquatic Primary Production Across Scales: Drivers, Dynamics, and Consequences
lead_organizer: Stuart Jones, Grand Valley State University
co_organizers: Paul Hanson, University of Wisconsin - Madison
Isabella Oleksy, University of Colorado Boulder
Chris Solomon, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
Kathleen Weathers, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
description: Primary production is the engine of aquatic ecosystems, fueling food webs, regulating biogeochemical cycles, and shaping ecosystem responses to environmental change.
