Yet, understanding how primary production varies across spatial and temporal scales—from microbial interactions in localized patches to global patterns in lakes, rivers, and oceans—remains a critical scientific challenge.

presentations.title: DIATOM TRAITS AND GEOCHEMICAL DATA PROVIDE EVIDENCE FOR A SHIFT IN PRIMARY PRODUCTION DRIVEN BY EUTROPHICATION
presentations.abstract: Long-term lake records are necessary to determine how external nutrient inputs alter the functional diversity of freshwater diatoms, a critical group of primary producers. Here, we examined a ~140-year record of diatom community dynamics, their traits, and lake geochemistry from a single sediment core from West Okoboji Lake, Iowa. Using CONISS analysis on the diatom and geochemical data, we identified three statistically significant zones with boundaries at ~1940 and 2000 CE. The transition at ~1940 CE was characterized by a shift in species composition toward large planktic Aulacoseira spp. During this period, stable nitrogen isotope values and total organic carbon increased, likely driven by intensified agricultural activity within the watershed. The shift at ~2000 CE was characterized by a sharp decline in biogenic silica from peak values observed just prior to the transition. From ~2000 to 2017 CE, small planktic diatoms persistently dominated, coincident with reported increases in cyanobacteria, suggesting the lake now sustains small copiotrophic phytoplankton. Using non-metric multidimensional scaling, we assessed the temporal trajectory of the diatom community and found a transition from a less productive to a more productive state. Together, these results demonstrate that eutrophication altered not only the magnitude of primary production but also diatom species composition and their functional diversity, highlighting the value of trait-based approaches for detecting ecological reorganization relevant to future lake resilience.

presentations.title: PHYTOPLANKTON AND BACTERIAL PRIMARY PRODUCTIVITY ACROSS TROPHIC, SEASONAL AND ANNUAL SCALES IN LAKE ONTARIO USING RADIOISOTOPE TRACERS AND ACTIVE FLUORESCENCE
presentations.abstract: Lake Ontario is a large temperate lake shared by Canada and the United States. It is generally oligotrophic, although eutrophication of nearshore areas is common. Fisheries and Oceans Canada has maintained long term monitoring programs in the oligotrophic western region of the Lake as well as in the hyper-eutrophic embayment of Hamilton Harbour that include radioisotope based measures of phytoplankton (14C) and bacterial (3H) primary productivity over the May – October period. In the offshore waters of Lake Ontario, phytoplankton productivity peaks at 6 – 7 mg C m-3 h-1 mid summer whereas in Hamilton Harbour, values can exceed 80 mg C m-3 h-1. Similarly, bacterial productivity offshore peaks at about 0.2 mg C m-3 h-1 compared to 1 – 2 mg C m-3 h-1 in the harbour. Beginning in 2025, we added active fluorometry to our ongoing assessments of phytoplankton primary productivity and we will provide some technical comparisons with the 14C method to further the discussion. The goal of the current study is to compare and contrast phytoplankton and bacterial primary productivity these different habitats and consider some of the underlying nutrient and chemical drivers over multiple years.

presentations.title: Phytoplankton Production between the Detroit River and Maumee River Plumes in Western Lake Erie
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton production is the basis of aquatic food webs. The Western Basin of Lake Erie has strong gradients of primary producer biomass and abiotic conditions affecting productivity, yet there have been few measurements of phytoplankton production contrasting the low nutrient inputs from the Detroit River and high nutrient inputs from the Maumee River. We conducted a series of 13C uptake experiments at 3 sites between the Detroit and Maumee River once a month between May-October in 2023 and 2024. Across all dates, mean areal primary productivity was highest at the site closest to the Maumee River (155.81 mg C hr-1m-2) and lowest at the site closest to the Detroit River (16.37 mg C hr-1m-2), likely due to differences in phytoplankton biomass. Areal production peaked in August, averaging 153 mg C hr-1m-2 across all sites. Mean water column integrated biomass specific production peaked in May (383.63 mg C hr-1mg chl-1), was highest at the intermediate site (356.90 mg C hr-1mg chl-1), and lowest at the site closest to the Maumee River (118.37 mg C hr-1mg chl-1). Pmax (the maximum chlorophyll-corrected photosynthesis rate at light saturation) was highest closest to the Maumee River. The response of productivity to low light intensities (alpha) was highest in May, potentially indicating that phytoplankton were more efficient at using low levels of light early in the season.

presentations.title: THE INFLUENCE OF ESTUARINE OPTICAL PROPERTIES AND CONSERVATIVE MIXING ON PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES IN A SOUTHEASTERN ESTUARY
presentations.abstract: In aquatic systems, optical properties influence phytoplankton communities because their photosynthetic efficiency depends greatly on light availability. Light availability varies with optical elements in the water column, such as colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) and turbidity. These elements are common and variable in estuarine systems. Consequently, estuarine regions display a wide range optical properties and, therefore, a dynamic light field for phytoplankton. This study examined the optical properties of the Winyah Bay estuary in South Carolina using mixing diagrams and related these factors to phytoplankton biomass and community composition across the salinity gradient. Results showed that the behavior of optical properties and their relationship to chlorophyll-a changed under various environmental conditions. Notably, the estuary acted as both a source and a sink for CDOM depending on river flow. Additionally, CDOM and chlorophyll-a showed different correlations—positive or negative—based on river discharge and wind direction. These results have implications for remote sensing of phytoplankton biomass as algorithms should not rely on fixed CDOM correction factors to estimate biomass across varying environmental conditions in estuarine waters.

presentations.title: RESPONSES OF LAKE PRIMARY PRODUCTION TO NUTRIENT AMENDMENTS AND REDUCED LIGHT SUPPLY BY BROWNING
presentations.abstract: Increases in magnitude and frequency of extreme precipitation events are a predicted consequence of global climate change. Environmental consequences include pulsed supplies of nutrients and colored dissolved organic matter (cDOM) to surface waters, which may particularly threaten clear-water lakes. As the effects of nutrients and cDOM on lake productivity are likely opposed, it remains challenging to predict their combined effect. Here we present results from a large-scale, full-factorial enclosure experiment conducted in a clear-water lake during the summer of 2021, where we assessed the responses of primary production (PP) to recalcitrant cDOM (2 mg L-1 HuminFeed©), N and P supply over four weeks. PP was largely driven by fluctuations in solar radiation related to weather conditions, with light saturation observed in the upper water layer. Browning decreased Secchi depth by a factor of two but had no significant effect on light use efficiency. Nutrient supply, in contrast, stimulated PP, independent of browning. Moreover, after two weeks, PP in the enclosures initially receiving cDOM with no nutrients added was consistently higher than in the clear-water controls. Our data on phytoplankton growth rates and light-use efficiency indicate that this unexpected stimulation was not due to nutrients delivered with the nutrient-poor cDOM. Instead, the response likely resulted from the recycling of nutrients formerly released from plankton impaired by shading and exploited when browning declined following photooxidation and other loss processes of cDOM.

presentations.title: Global declines in marine primary production in the ocean color era
presentations.affiliation: University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science
presentations.abstract: The key role of net phytoplankton production (NPP) in providing ecosystem services and influencing global biogeochemical cycles has given rise to an ongoing pursuit of accurate, synoptic estimates at high resolution in both time and space. Satellite remote sensing is the only platform that offers this capability, and past and present earth observing missions collectively provide an unbroken global time series. We present a 25-year global assessment across two satellite missions (SeaWiFS and MODIS-Aqua) to investigate how a warming ocean has influenced NPP in conjunction with underlying metrics of nutrient limitation. We show that statistically significant decreases in NPP have occurred in almost half of the ocean and these changes are dominated by declines in the tropical and subtropical stratified ocean. A deeper analysis confirms that strengthening nutrient limitation is largely driving declining NPP. Climate- mediated shifts in NPP represent a fundamental perturbation to biogeochemical cycles that can further weaken global fisheries. This presentation will review the current state of the art in remotely-sensed primary production, and discuss interoperability in freshwater ecosystems.

name: Aquatic Primary Production Across Scales (Posters)
lead_organizer: Stuart Jones, Grand Valley State University
co_organizers: Paul Hanson, University of Wisconsin - Madison
Isabella Oleksy, University of Colorado Boulder
Chris Solomon, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
Kathleen Weathers, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
description: Primary production is the engine of aquatic ecosystems, fueling food webs, regulating biogeochemical cycles, and shaping ecosystem responses to environmental change.

presentations.title: CONTRASTING SENSITIVITIES OF PHYTOPLANKTON AND PERIPHYTON TO VARYING NUTRIENT REGIMES IN RESTORED WETLANDS
presentations.abstract: Agricultural eutrophication impacts aquatic ecosystems and the services they provide globally. Water quality treatment wetlands can mitigate nutrient pollution by intercepting runoff and fostering microbial denitrification, uptake by vegetation, and sediment burial. Beyond improving water quality downstream, restored wetlands may offer additional co-benefits through the provisioning of critical wildlife habitat. However, despite their important roles in nutrient cycling and supporting aquatic food webs, little is known about the relative sensitivities of (pelagic) phytoplankton and (benthic) periphyton to agricultural runoff under realistic field conditions. To reveal how these communities respond to varying concentrations and ratios of key macronutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus), we surveyed nine restored wetlands (and three reference sites) on Iowa's Des Moines Lobe. Phytoplankton and water quality measurements were collected three times across the open water season in 2024, whereas passive periphyton samplers were deployed twice. Samples were processed to estimate the taxonomic and functional composition of communities and assess their ecological health and sensitivity to nutrient dynamics over time.

presentations.title: PALEOECOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT OF CHIRONOMID-INFERRED HYPOLIMNETIC OXYGEN DYNAMICS UNDER ANTHROPOGENIC STRESS IN SIMON LAKE (SUDBURY, ONTARIO)
presentations.affiliation: Cooperative Freshwater Ecology Unit, Vale Living with Lakes Centre, Laurentian University
presentations.abstract: Algal blooms pose an increasing threat to freshwater ecosystems, with their occurrence influenced by anthropogenic stressors including eutrophication, urbanization, and climate change. Simon Lake, located within the Junction Creek Watershed (Sudbury, Ontario), is a eutrophic urban lake where yearly filamentous green algal blooms have occurred for decades. Nutrient enrichment and the magnitude of internal loading stimulated by hypolimnetic oxygen loss are key drivers of blooms. However, long-term nutrient and oxygen records for Simon Lake are lacking, leaving baseline conditions uncertain. Using paleolimnological methods on a 58-cm 210Pb-dated sediment core, we examined temporal changes in chironomid assemblages, reconstructed historical oxygen conditions preceding major anthropogenic and climatic disturbances, and tracked trends in whole-lake primary production using spectrally inferred sedimentary chlorophyll-a. Pronounced shifts from chironomid taxa with higher oxygen optima (e.g., Sergentia coraina-type and Polypedilum spp.) to those characteristic of lower oxygen conditions (e.g., Chironomus spp., Parachironomus varus-type, and Endochironomus spp.) occurred. Coupled with a ~41% decline in species richness over the past 150 years, community changes indicate declining hypolimnetic oxygen concentrations in recent decades, while increases in sedimentary chlorophyll-a suggest heightened primary production.

presentations.title: MACROPHYTES AS PHYSICAL FILTERS: IMPACTS ON METABOLIC EXPRESSION IN EUTROPHIC RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Aquatic metabolism integrates light-driven production and respiratory oxygen consumption, and is strongly shaped by physical controls on gas exchange and light availability. In hypereutrophic systems, dense floating macrophyte stands act as structural modifiers of the water column, constraining irradiance penetration and altering dissolved oxygen (DO) dynamics independently of biological demand. We examined how macrophyte cover regulated physical drivers of metabolism in a tropical reservoir by comparing two 14-day periods: one under extensive surface cover and another after mechanical removal. High-frequency DO, temperature, light profiles, and wind speed were recorded every 15 minutes. Light availability in the mixed layer, represented by mean irradiance (Emean), dropped sharply under macrophyte cover, coinciding with persistently low DO concentrations and dampened diel amplitudes that restricted metabolism estimates for several days. Following removal, DO levels increased and diel variability was restored, although gross primary production, respiration, and net ecosystem productivity (NEP) showed no statistical differences between periods.

presentations.title: SECCHI DEPTH IN THE LAKES OF THE KAWARTHA HIGHLANDS: UNRAVELING SHORT- AND LONG-TERM VARIABILITY IN WATER CLARITY
presentations.abstract: Secchi depth (SD) is one of the commonly measured limnological parameters due to its simplicity and low cost. As a result, SD data is widely available for many lakes and frequently used as a primary indicator of water quality and lake trophic state. Here, we characterize SD in lakes from the Kawartha Highlands region of southcentral Ontario, using a combination of contemporary and historical data. Our central goal was to evaluate the key determinants of SD in this region and assess how SD has changed over the past several decades. Our analysis used SD measurements collected from historical sources dating back to the early 1970's, values obtained from the Ontario Lakes Partner Program, and ten years of our own measurements. In all, we amassed over 5000 Secchi depths from 30 lakes in the Kawartha Highlands. Over the past 10 years, average SD was 4.5 m with most values between 2 m and 7 m. While there were some differences among lakes, much of the short-term variability was not explained by lake chlorophyll or dissolved organic carbon. Over the past thirty years, SD increased, decreased, or remained static depending on the lake examined.

presentations.title: STABLE STATES AFFECT METABOLISM AND CARBON DIOXIDE CONCENTRATION IN PONDS
presentations.abstract: Ponds can exist in multiple stable states, including clearwater with macrophytes and turbid dominated by phytoplankton. While stable states are directly linked to the dominant primary producer, the relationship to metabolism and CO2 concentration is less clear. In this study, we used experimental ponds that differed in stable states to quantify (1) ecosystem metabolism using dissolved oxygen and (2) pond carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations. We studied 6 experimental ponds with two exhibiting phytoplankton dominance, two exhibiting macrophyte dominance, and two existing in an intermediate state (limited macrophytes but clearwater). In each pond, we measured CO2 concentrations, temperature, and dissolved oxygen during the summer. Despite pronounced differences in water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, gross primary production and net ecosystem productivity did not differ substantially among stable states, indicating that a pond's dominant primary producer does not reliably predict whole-system metabolic rates. Surface CO₂ concentrations did, however, differ significantly across stable states, though these patterns were not explained solely by ecosystem metabolism.

presentations.title: EVALUATING PRIMARY PRODUCTIVITY RATES AND PHOTOSYNTHETIC EFFICIENCY OF REPRESENTATIVE PHYTOPLANKTON TAXA UNDER FUTURE OCEAN CONDITIONS
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton play a critical role in the global carbon cycle by converting atmospheric CO₂ into organic carbon through photosynthesis and are estimated to produce up to half the atmospheric oxygen. Phytoplankton are highly sensitive to environmental carbonate and temperature conditions; consequently, their rates of carbon fixation and primary productivity are expected to change under future ocean conditions. However, the trend and magnitude of these changes remain poorly constrained, limiting a predictive understanding of future primary production. This study captures the physiological responses of five representative phytoplankton species across three paired carbonate and temperature conditions. These include a present-day scenario for the subtropical north Atlantic (420 ppm pCO₂, 22°C), a high-emission end-of-century condition for the same region (1135 ppm pCO₂, 25.3°C) and a far-future high warming condition (1850 ppm pCO₂, 28.6°C). The chosen species represent major phytoplankton functional groups–coccolithophores, green algae, diatoms, and cyanobacteria–each with unique carbon-concentrating mechanisms and are therefore expected to implement different strategies to acclimate to future conditions.

presentations.title: EXPLORING THE BUILDING BLOCKS OF LAKE METABOLIC REGIMES
presentations.abstract: Ecosystems, including lakes, are often classified by geographic location, size and shape, and biological productivity. An additional classification, traditionally applied to terrestrial ecosystems and more recently to streams, is the annual pattern of energy flow or metabolic regime. Although limnologists have long examined seasonal phytoplankton succession and the effect of storms on lake metabolism, we still lack a formal theory describing lake metabolic regimes. To explore plausible emergent lake metabolic regimes and identify the dominant drivers of annual patterns in lake primary production and ecosystem respiration, we developed a quantitative framework for predicting and interpreting these regimes. Our approach integrates simple established physical and biological models to translate ultimate drivers - solar radiation, air temperature, land use - into proximate controls on lake primary production and ecosystem respiration - light climate, water temperature, and nutrient availability.

name: Microbial-DOM Coupling in Inland Waters in the Light of Biogeochemical Cycles (Posters)
lead_organizer: Paola Ayala-Borda, University of Lethbridge
description: Microbes and dissolved organic matter (DOM) both play key roles in the biogeochemistry of inland waters. Microbes are the most abundant and important biological component responsible for recycling DOM, either from autochthonous or allochthonous sources. They participate in the fixation and oxidation of carbon molecules, shaping the organic matter pool throughout the microbial life cycle. DOM is the most mobile form of organic matter, distributing carbon and nutrients across ecosystems and affecting the complexation, solubility and transport of metals and contaminants.

presentations.title: ROLE OF COLLOIDAL ORGANIC MATTER IN TRACE ELEMENTS MOBILITY IN A SUBARCTIC CATCHMENT
presentations.abstract: Subarctic ecosystems are under pressure from global environmental changes. Particularly, permafrost thaw mobilizes a vast pool of organic matter (OM) and associated trace elements (TE). The aim of this project is to study the extent to which colloidal OM influences the mobility of TE in subarctic catchments. We study both TE that form cations, such as rare earth elements (REE), and oxyanions, such as arsenic (As) and selenium (Se). We seek to understand the complexes form between those elements and organic colloids mobilized by permafrost thawing. To do so, we sampled surface water from two rivers near the community of Whapmagoostui-Kuujjuaraapik, in Nunavik, Québec, in 2025. The Great Whales River (GWR) and the Sasapimakwananisikw (SAS) river drain a sporadic permafrost valley and flow into the Hudson Bay in a land-ocean continuum, presenting a salinity gradient at their mouth. The SAS river is highly charged in colloidal OM compared to the GWR. This range of physicochemical conditions allows the study of the complexation of TE by colloids under different parameters. We characterized the size and shape of colloids using asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation (A4F), then their molecular and elemental composition by Pyrolysis-GC-MS and ICP-MS. Preliminary results suggest a strong affinity between As and Se oxyanion and colloids in the presence of iron and calcium, while REE might be more linked to the OM in colloids.

presentations.title: Saltwater intrusion and freshwater restoration drive long-term transformation of dissolved organic matter composition in the Florida Everglades
presentations.abstract: Changes in the dissolved organic matter (DOM) source and composition of coastal wetlands can result from climate- and human-driven changes in fresh and marine hydrology. We analyzed a decade (2012-2022) of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations and DOM compositions from monthly surface water samples collected at n = 14 sampling stations along two transects (Shark River Slough; Taylor Slough/Panhandle) spanning freshwater peat and marl marsh, mangrove, and seagrass ecosystems in Everglades National Park (Florida, USA). DOM composition was assessed using indices derived from fluorescence excitation emission matrices coupled with parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC). We quantified six distinct PARAFAC components, which varied with both subtropical seasonal (wet-dry season) hydrology and pulsed inputs from freshwater restoration.

presentations.title: Biomarker–Optical Evidence for DOM Transformation in the San Francisco Bay Estuary
presentations.abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) in estuaries reflects variable contributions from riverine inputs, wetlands, agricultural drainage, and in situ production, all shaped by seasonal hydrology. To resolve how these drivers regulate DOM cycling in the San Francisco Bay Estuary (SFBE), we integrate molecular biomarkers (lignin phenols, amino acids, neutral sugars) with optical properties (SUVA, spectral slopes, fluorescence indices) across winter, spring, and summer flow regimes. Winter high flows export lignin-rich terrestrial DOM with limited alteration. Spring snowmelt introduces degraded upland material together with amino-acid-rich algal production. Summer low flows increase residence time, enhancing photobleaching, microbial reworking, and wetland and agricultural drainage influence.

presentations.title: Linking best management practices, dissolved organic matter and microbial communities in agricultural streams
presentations.abstract: Numerous practices have been suggested to mitigate the negative impacts of intensive agriculture on water quality, but quantification of their real-life efficiency is limited because the biological processes and patterns involved in the receiving streams remain poorly understood. The objective of this study is to determine the links between agricultural best management practices (BMPs), dissolved organic matter (DOM) and microbial communities in agricultural streams. We will sample draining fields with contrasting crop cover, drainage density, and BMPs (including buffer strips and cover crops) at key moments of the growing season in the St. Lawrence Lowlands (Québec, Canada) to determine the links between DOM and the taxonomic composition (16S rRNA) and metabolic functions (predictive models) of aquatic bacterial communities.

presentations.title: Metabolic scope of dominant marine bacteria: with great abundance comes great divergence
presentations.abstract: Microbial communities drive marine biogeochemical cycles, yet their metabolic capacities and substrate preferences remain poorly understood. Here, we compare metabolites from model strains of the most abundant marine bacteria, SAR11 and SAR202, using direct reversed-phase liquid chromatography ultrahigh resolution mass spectrometry. Intracellular metabolic profiles revealed an abundance of retinaldehyde and diverse glycerolipids within SAR11 cells, whereas SAR202 was enriched in amino acids, nucleobases, organic acids, sugars, and aminoacyl lipids. SAR11 preferentially consumed amino acids and osmolytes while storing mainly sugars and lipids and releasing nucleobases and organic acids. In contrast, SAR202 utilized amino acids and organic acids while preserving nucleobases, amino acids, and lipids and releasing primarily nucleobases and organic acids. Both cells shared similar amino acid and derivative transformations but also exhibited potential compound tradeoffs.

presentations.title: Inherent resistance of aromatic compounds to microbial degradation
presentations.abstract: The quantitative difference between bioavailable DOM and unavailable DOM is generally vast, with only ~10% readily available to microbes. Given the abundant presence of oxygen in most aqueous environments, and reduced carbon structures that clearly have stored energy available, why haven't microbes fully evolved the capacity to be able to take advantage? The two most widely accepted hypotheses invoke 1) inherent structural recalcitrance in which the energy required to break down an organic molecule through enzyme formation is greater than the energy returned, and 2) the dynamics of concentration thresholds, in which dilution increases energy costs to the point that microbes can't make a living. Aromatic compounds are frequently invoked as a class that is too energy-poor for microbes to degrade, but this has only been inferred. To directly test this, we conducted a series of pilot incubations utilizing freshwater inocula with aromatic compounds as the sole source of carbon. Initial experiments with vanillic acid (VAD), a lignin-derived compound, demonstrated that microbes will readily utilize VAD, with near complete loss of VAD after 14 days while maintaining residual DOC that could be either microbially-sourced, or incomplete breakdown products from VAD.

name: Sediment Derived Nutrients, Cyanobacteria and Climate Change
lead_organizer: Gertrud Nürnberg, Freshwater Research
description: As a sediment researcher, nutrient (P and N) specialist, or someone studying eutrophication and cyanobacteria proliferation in lakes world-wide, we invite you to participate in this special session.

presentations.title: VARIABLE CLIMATE FACTORS CONTRIBUTE TO INTERNAL PHOSPHORUS LOADING AND CYANOBACTERIA BLOOMS IN DIFFERENT BASINS OF LAKE CHAMPLAIN
presentations.abstract: Lake Champlain is a large natural lake characterized by several distinct basins with varying morphometry and catchment properties. Cyanobacteria blooms are common in several areas of the lake, typically characterized by ephemeral shoreline blooms in the deep central basin, and by more widespread bay-wide booms in the shallow eutrophic bays. Different basins are susceptible to different climate influences, but in both shallow, polymictic bays and in deep stratified areas, the evidence suggests that climate change is increasing cyanobacteria bloom frequency. In the deep 'Main Lake' basin, internal loading does not appear to be a dominant factor in the development of blooms, but changes in dissolved nutrient loading from catchments, increasing water temperature, and lower wind speed may increase the likelihood of conditions promoting the emergence of surface blooms and the transport of blooms to lake shorelines.

presentations.title: Climate-sensitive iron biogeochemistry drives cyanobacterial bloom succession in Lake Okeechobee
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms in Lake Okeechobee, Florida, USA, are highly seasonal despite the lake's subtropical climate, suggesting biogeochemical controls beyond temperature and light alone. We present an integrated, multi-disciplinary investigation demonstrating that sediment iron (Fe) cycling plays a central and previously under-recognized role in structuring nutrient availability, optical environment, and bloom community composition. High-resolution datasets of sediment geochemical characterization, voltammetric redox profiling, optical and acoustic HAB sensing, and advanced particle/light characterization reveal tightly coupled sediment–water exchanges of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) that nonlinearly vary across seasons. During winter and spring, replete nitrate and limited soluble reactive phosphorus favor Microcystis spp., whereas summer ferric Fe reduction liberates P, stimulates N fixation, and transitions blooms toward diazotrophic cyanobacteria.

presentations.title: NON-STEADY-STATE SEDIMENTARY PHOSPHORUS CYCLING AND INTERNAL LOADING TRAJECTORIES IN HAMILTON HARBOUR, LAKE ONTARIO, CANADA
presentations.abstract: Hamilton Harbour, a eutrophic embayment of western Lake Ontario, has experienced sustained reductions in external phosphorus (P) and iron (Fe) loading, yet internal P release and nuisance algal blooms remain a concern. We applied a reactive-transport sediment diagenesis model to simulate the evolution of sedimentary P cycling and internal loading from 1987 to 2060. We linked these fluxes to hypolimnetic and epilimnetic water quality using a box model. The sediment model resolves organic matter mineralization, Al- and Fe-bound P, and sulfur processes, and we used decision-tree analysis and year-specific local sensitivity analyses to identify the dominant controls on internal P release. Simulations project an increase in internal P loading relative to 1980-2010, with a transient peak between 2010 and 2030, followed by a new quasi-steady state after about 2035.

presentations.title: PHOSPHORUS LOADING AT FALL TURNOVER IN CHAUTAUQUA LAKE, NY
presentations.abstract: Internal loading can contribute a great deal of phosphorus to inland lakes that experience anoxia during seasonally stratified periods. This process may stimulate increases in algal biomass and harmful algal blooms (HABs) if the phosphorus reaches the epilimnion when physical conditions are right for a bloom. However, much of the phosphorus released from sediments during stratified conditions is sequestered in the hypolimnion until a mixing event such as fall turnover or mechanical disturbance takes place. Here we assess the spatio-temporal phosphorus distribution in Chautauqua Lake, NY, USA before and after fall turnover using sensor data, physical samples, and hydrodynamic modelling. Our results show increasing phosphorus in the hypolimnion leading up to fall turnover.

presentations.title: Forms and Fate of Phosphorus from Resuspension and Diffusive Flux in Lake Erie's Western Basin
presentations.abstract: The large fetch and shallow depth of Lake Erie's western basin leads to frequent resuspension of surface benthic sediments. Resuspended sediments can interact with phosphorus (P) pools in the water column and have been implicated as a source of P to support phytoplankton. We performed controlled laboratory experiments with sediment cores from Lake Erie to measure the amount, forms, and fate of P resuspended from locations in the western basin. Overall, resuspension caused by weak bottom stress (0.06 pascal) increased particulate P forms, but there was little evidence for increased dissolved P concentration through desorption. Higher levels of stress (0.15 pascal) substantially increased particulate P, but exchangeable P was a minor component and dissolved P changed little due to resuspension.

presentations.title: Water residence time as an important predictor of internal phosphorus loading effects on water quality in lakes
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms have been increasingly associated with internal phosphorus (P) load (IL). We explored IL variations in six Finnish lakes with different water residence time (t). t varied in the lakes between 18 d and 435 d, and it is changed in one lake through hydrological alteration from 430 d to 230 d. We characterized sediment P release by measuring redox potential, sediment P release rate (RR) by diffusion and sediment density by sonar scanning. The IL for the six lakes was estimated as the product of RR and anoxic area factor (AA, measure of anoxia). Variations in IL were explained by the concentration and proportion of sediment iron-bound P. The content of organic P in sediment total P (TP) was highest in the hydrologically manipulated lake (37%). IL estimates (24-235 mg/m2/summer) were lowest at short and highest at long t. The contribution of IL to TP summer load correlated with the cyanobacterial share in the phytoplankton biomass.

name: Sediment Derived Nutrients, Cyanobacteria and Climate Change
lead_organizer: Gertrud Nürnberg, Freshwater Research
description: As a sediment researcher, nutrient (P and N) specialist, or someone studying eutrophication and cyanobacteria proliferation in lakes world-wide, we invite you to participate in this special session.

presentations.title: Benthic cyanobacterial Mats Enhance Recycling on Nitrogen in Eutrophic Lacustrine Sediments
presentations.abstract: Benthic cyanobacterial mats have a significant influence on nutrient cycling in eutrophic lacustrine sediments, yet their role in nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) dynamics remains understudied. This study investigates Microseira (Lyngbya) wollei, a globally prevalent, non-heterocystous cyanobacterium that forms perennial benthic and seasonal pelagic mats that are capable of releasing toxins and fixing atmospheric nitrogen (N₂ fixation). The goal of this study is to investigate the contribution of benthic M. wollei mats to nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and iron (Fe) dynamics at the sediment-water interface. From March to October 2023, excluding April and May, we sampled one of two locations at Lake Wateree, South Carolina. To distinguish the contributions of M. wollei, two sites were sampled within each location, one with benthic M. wollei mats and one without. Results show denitrification was the primary pathway for bioavailable N removal, with no detectable anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) activity. Denitrification rates correlated with mat thickness when mats were present (r = 0.77, N=13, P=0.002), although the presence of M. wollei did not significantly impact N removal rates.

presentations.title: EXPLORING INTERNAL IRON LOADING IN SHALLOW BAYS AS A POTENTIAL DRIVER OF CYANOBACTERIA BLOOMS IN A LARGE, SUBARCTIC OLIGOTROPHIC LAKE
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacteria bloom formation has been increasing in lakes across trophic scales and latitudes because of climate change. The prevailing view is that climate change is altering lake biogeochemical dynamics, resulting in changes in the spatial coverage, severity, and longevity of anoxia development and associated internal loading of nutrients. The internal loading of phosphorus (P) and ferrous iron (Fe2+) is fairly well understood in deep waters, where stronger and longer thermal stratification (and associated oxygen depletions) occurs. Sediment anaerobia in shallow waters has received less attention, and its link to increasing cyanobacteria abundance and dominance of the phytoplankton community has been theorized but is not well established. The goal of this research is to investigate if internal iron and phosphorus loading in shallow waters promotes cyanobacteria growth in a large, subarctic lake (Sambaa K'e) located in the southern Northwest Territories.

presentations.title: NUTRIENT AND TRACE METAL RELEASE FROM SEDIMENTS: UNDERSTANDING THE INFLUENCE OF BIOLOGICAL, CHEMICAL AND PHYSICAL PROCESSES ON NUTRIENT DYNAMICS
presentations.abstract: The impact of internal nutrient inputs deriving from lake sediments has become a major concern in recent decades due to its role in promoting eutrophication and delaying lake recovery. Under different physiochemical conditions such as low oxygen, sediments can shift from a sink to a source, remobilising stored nutrients into the overlying waters. Several studies have utilised the terms hypoxia (0.5 < O2 < 2 mg L-1) and anoxia (< 0.5 mg L-1) to define low oxygen conditions in the water column. However, inconsistencies in defining these terms and documenting dissolved oxygen concentrations in studies has made it difficult to determine the effects of oxygen on nutrient release patterns. This research focuses on comparing hypoxia and anoxia to better understand how they influence the release of various nutrients from the sediments. A controlled laboratory experiment was conducted over 28 days to compare the release of nutrients from sediments under oxic, hypoxic and anoxic conditions in the overlying waters. The experiment revealed that hypoxia and anoxia differentially influence the release of nutrients and trace metals.

presentations.title: Assessing the impact of hypolimnetic anoxia on water quality in a eutrophic reservoir: experimental and modelling insights
presentations.abstract: Dam reservoirs are often affected by eutrophication-related problems due to the accumulation of nutrients - primarily nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) - originating from the watershed and from internal sediment loading. Although significant efforts have been made to reduce external inputs, these measures are often insufficient because a substantial share of nutrients is released from the sediments. Dissolved oxygen (DO) concentrations at the sediment-water interface (SWI) play a key role in controlling internal sediment loading. This study combines fieldwork, laboratory experiments, and modelling to evaluate how DO levels at the SWI influence the water quality of central France largest reservoir, Eguzon Lake. Sediments were collected from the reservoir and used in a microcosm experiment to quantify nutrient and metal fluxes at the SWI under oxic and anoxic conditions. Anoxic treatments resulted in the release of ammonium, phosphate, iron, and manganese, whereas oxic conditions promoted nitrate release from the sediments.

presentations.title: Y2KANSAS: RAPID INCREASES IN CYANOBACTERIA AT THE START OF THE 21ST CENTURY IN KANSAS RESERVOIRS
presentations.abstract: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) are primarily driven by phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N), in addition to temperature and light, and are a widespread water quality concern. Despite management efforts, with climatic changes, mechanisms underlying observed shifts in HABs are not always apparent. To address this issue, we collected complete sediment cores from each of 12 reservoirs within Kansas River Basin, Kansas, and aggregated historical water quality data to evaluate trends of nutrients and phytoplankton relative to those recorded in the fossil record. In addition to establishing sediment chronology using fossil Plutonium, we analyzed phytoplankton pigments and DNA in reservoir sediments to reconstruct changes in the magnitude, timing, and composition of phytoplankton communities. Beta-carotene, a red-orange pigment used as a proxy for total phytoplankton, increased two- to 10-fold since impoundment among the reservoirs, primarily due to increased cyanobacteria.

name: Sediment Derived Nutrients, Cyanobacteria and Climate Change (Posters)
lead_organizer: Gertrud Nürnberg, Freshwater Research
description: As a sediment researcher, nutrient (P and N) specialist, or someone studying eutrophication and cyanobacteria proliferation in lakes world-wide, we invite you to participate in this special session.

presentations.title: Controls on the Release of Redox-Sensitive Metals Under Artificially Eutrophied Conditions in a Shallow Lake
presentations.abstract: Water quality in lakes and reservoirs is globally at risk, affected by a myriad of stressors. A key concern globally is the occurrence of cyanobacteria. One proposed theory for mitigating cyanobacterial blooms in freshwater is to suppress sediment-water fluxes of key micronutrients, including redox-sensitive metals, by maintaining an oxic sediment-water interface. A whole-lake experiment was conducted on a small, polymictic headwater lake in northwestern Ontario to test the effects of oxidized nitrogen (NO3) on the release of redox-sensitive metals and the implications for phytoplankton bloom dynamics. Specifically, we looked at the fluxes of bioavailable iron (Fe(II)), as cyanobacteria require significantly more iron than their eukaryotic competitors. We predicted that maintaining a water column concentration of 2 mg N-NO3 L-1 would sufficiently oxidize the sediment-water interface in a shallow lake throughout the open-water season; however, we discovered that the lake did experience periods of hypoxia and low redox despite high doses of nitrate.

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL DIVERGANCE, PHYSIOLOGICAL CONVERGANCE: INVESTIGATING PHYTOPLANKTON IRON-MEDIATED PSII EFFICIENCY ACROSS TROPHIC GRADIENTS IN BOREAL LAKES
presentations.abstract: Climate driven eutrophication shifts freshwater algal communities toward cyanobacteria-dominated harmful algal blooms (cHABs). While phosphorus (P) management has been prioritized, cHABs are often limited by iron (Fe). Sediment-water interface oxidation with nitrate (NO3-) prevents the reduction of Fe(III) to bioavailable Fe(II) (REDOX). Fe(II) is the primary component of phytoplankton photosynthetic performance (PSI/PSII), yet how intracellular Fe (FeInt) limitations affect NO3- availability, biomass, and phytoplankton community speciation on PSII efficiency remains not well understood. Dissolved Fe (DFe), FeInt, chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), and PSII efficiency (Fv/Fm) were measured across five boreal lakes of varying trophic statuses (TP: 2.4-23.9 ug/L) in 2024.

presentations.title: IMPACT OF WHOLE-LAKE NITRATE ADDITIONS ON SEDIMENT REDOX AND CYANOBACTERIA BLOOM FORMATION IN TWO LAKES IN THE EXPERIMENTAL LAKES AREA, CANADA 2019-2025
presentations.abstract: A whole-lake experiment was designed to test the hypotheses that low sediment redox results in cyanobacteria bloom formation and bloom onset is mediated via internal ferrous iron (Fe(II)) loading from anaerobic sediments when other conditions for formation are suitable. Conversely, high sediment redox prevents bloom formation. Two oligotrophic lakes, one polymictic (L303) and one deep enough to thermally stratify (L304) were dosed weekly with phosphate (P) in 2019-2025 excluding 2020 and 2021. High nitrate applications began in L303 in 2024 and in L304 in 2025. Equivalent amounts of N as urea will be added in future years. Dialysis incubations with ferrozine at the sediment-water interface captured Fe(II) in non-nitrate years but not when nitrate was applied, inferring effective nitrate oxidation of the SWI.

name: From Immediate Shocks to Long-Term Shifts: Terrestrial Disturbances and Aquatic Ecosystem Responses
lead_organizer: Guillaume Grosbois, UQAT
co_organizers: Hélène Masclaux, Université de Bourgogne Franche-Comté
description: Freshwater ecosystems are essential components of global landscapes and are closely connected to their terrestrial surroundings through complex physicochemical, biological and ecological interactions.

presentations.title: TWO PATHS TO RECOVERY: WHAT 40 YEARS OF MONITORING REVEAL ABOUT ACIDIFIED LAKE RESPONSE UNDER DIVERGING STRESS REGIMES
presentations.abstract: Acid rain damaged thousands of Boreal Shield lakes and was a widespread international problem in the 1970-80s. Impacts around Sudbury, Ontario, were severe, with many lakes also affected by metals deposition from smelters. Major reductions in SO2 emissions initiated the world's largest experiment in regional lake recovery. Although acidification and pollution recovery have been studied extensively, our work is the first to integrate decades-long concurrent monitoring of chemical, physical, and biological conditions, revealing recovery alongside emerging stressors from urbanization and climate change. Using some of the best long-term monitoring records in the world, we examined the extent, timing and dynamics of recovery of two severely acidified lakes: one in a remote wilderness setting (White Pine) and one affected by historic metal contamination and ongoing urban development (Clearwater). Both lakes had declines in water clarity, shallower epilimnia, and increases in cold-water habitat associated with recovering DOC, which was more pronounced in the urban lake.

presentations.title: TRACKING INDUSTRIAL AND URBAN LEGACIES IN A FLUVIAL LAKE (SUDBURY, ONTARIO): A COLLABORATIVE INDIGENOUS PALEO-ECOTOXICOLOGICAL STUDY
presentations.abstract: European settlement in Sudbury, Ontario (Canada) in the 1850s spurred industrialization and introduced unprecedented stressors to nearby aquatic systems. Most notably, large-scale mining and smelting operations caused regional metal contamination and environmental degradation. Simon Lake, a small, shallow system on the boundary between the City of Sudbury and Atikameksheng Anishnawbek First Nation Reserve, lies downstream of historically impacted lakes within the Vermillion River watershed. Due to legacy pollution and recurrent algal blooms, Simon Lake has been culturally eutrophied, with a ten-year mean total phosphorus concentration of ~40 µg/L. To investigate long-term changes, we analyzed a dated sediment core (~200 years) using paleo-ecotoxicological methods, including subfossil diatoms, Cladocera, sedimentary metals, and inferred chlorophyll-a.

presentations.title: Sedimentary environmental DNA (sedDNA) reveals long-term reductions in lake animal diversity associated with historical mining and smelting contamination
presentations.abstract: Understanding long-term ecological changes in freshwater ecosystems is crucial for evaluating the impacts of human activities and guiding conservation and management efforts. In this study, we aimed to reconstruct 160 years of changes in fish populations, microbial eukaryotes, and plant communities in two boreal lakes of the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of Quebec, Canada and correlate these results with trace element concentrations. We used sedimentary DNA (sedDNA) extracted from sediment cores collected in both littoral and deep zones of two lakes differing in anthropogenic impact: Osisko Lake, subjected to mining and urban discharges as well as atmospheric emissions from the Horne smelter, and Dufay Lake, minimally influenced by these anthropogenic activities.

presentations.title: Tributaries of the Doce River basin, southeastern Brazil, support high regional fish diversity
presentations.abstract: The Doce River is historically one of the most impacted basins in Southeastern Brazil, with its environmental condition further worsened by the collapse of a huge mining tailings dam that virtually wiped out the biodiversity of the river's main channel in 2015. Despite these pressures, knowledge about fish diversity and distribution remains limited. We sampled fish and characterized local physical habitat, slope and altitude in 45 river sites. We then estimated the importance of each site to the regional biodiversity using the Local Contribution to Beta Diversity metric (LCBD).

presentations.title: Timber's Toll: Short and long-term impacts of submerged log extraction in boreal lakes
presentations.abstract: Historic log driving left large volumes of submerged wood in boreal lakes and rivers, altering geomorphology, water physico-chemistry and food webs structure and dynamics during centuries. Currently, submerged log extraction is promoted both as a source of valuable timber and as a potential restoration practice. Of particular concern is the potential mobilization of methylmercury. This study assessed short and long-term impacts of log extraction in lakes from the Témiscamingue and Mauricie regions of Québec.

presentations.title: Long-term trends of Hg isotopes in lake sediments reveal shift in Hg sources in a remote boreal lake
presentations.abstract: Mercury (Hg) atmospheric pollution presents a significant threat to both environmental and human health. We studied Hg stocks and cycling in a small boreal watershed (Lake Laflamme) on the Canadian Shield integrating isotopic measurements of Hg in soils and dated lake sediments. The long-term Hg sediment record shows a continuous increase in Hg concentration since about 1800. The Hg isotope composition of the sediments exhibits a strong shift, particularly after the 1970s, with the more recent sediments converging toward the isotopic composition of the catchment organic soils. Overall, the data suggests that the nature of Hg now entering the lake has changed from an atmospheric to a terrestrial source in the last decades.

name: From Immediate Shocks to Long-Term Shifts: Terrestrial Disturbances (Posters)
lead_organizer: Guillaume Grosbois, UQAT
co_organizers: Hélène Masclaux, Université de Bourgogne Franche-Comté
description: Freshwater ecosystems are essential components of global landscapes and are closely connected to their terrestrial surroundings.

presentations.title: CLEANER AIR, BROWNING WATERS: USING A BREAKPOINT ANALYSIS TO BETTER UNDERSTAND DISSOLVED ORGANIC CARBON TRENDS IN RECOVERING LAKES
presentations.abstract: Many lakes throughout northeastern North America and northern Europe have exhibited increases in dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations in recent decades, a phenomenon known as 'browning,' because it often imparts a brownish hue to water color. This phenomenon has primarily been attributed to recovery from historical acidification and concomitant water chemistry changes. To understand the potential drivers and characterize relative rates in browning, we analyzed long-term trends in DOC concentrations among lakes throughout northeastern North America and northern Europe. We focused on distinguishing between linear, accelerating, and decelerating trends over time by identifying statistically significant breakpoints that separate time periods differing in browning magnitude and direction.

presentations.title: COMPARING SPACE-FOR-TIME AND PALEOLIMNOLOGICAL METHODS TO STUDY THE EFFECTS OF FORESTRY MANAGEMENT ON LAKE BROWNING
presentations.abstract: Browning of freshwater systems is a global concern due to the complex changes it may cause to the functioning of aquatic ecosystems. Forest management practices are an important driver of browning, increasing the leaching of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and nutrients from the soil. This PhD project studies how forestry practices have influenced the browning of small boreal lakes by combining space-for-time methods and lake sediment time series. In 2025, we sampled 22 lakes with 0-33% of the catchment ditched and 0-45% clearcut in the past 20 years. Preliminary results indicate that DOC correlated strongly with the area of ditching (r=0.63, p=0.002) and clearcuts (r=0.38, p=0.08) in the catchment.

presentations.title: PHOSPHORUS IN SEDIMENTS OF AN URBAN EUTROPHIC RESERVOIR AND TRIBUTARIES
presentations.abstract: This study assessed total phosphorus (P) concentrations in sediments from a highly impacted, eutrophic urban reservoir (Ibirité Lagoon, MG-Brazil), its tributaries, and a downstream site, evaluating the influence of physicochemical conditions, seasonality, and catchment land use and cover. Surface sediments were sampled in May (dry season) and November (rainy) 2024. In the reservoir, P concentrations were higher in the rainy season. Organic matter and fine grains percentage were positively associated with P concentrations in both seasons.

presentations.title: INFLUENCE OF LAND USE AND LAND COVER ON THE SPATIAL DISTRIBUTION OF TRACE ELEMENTS IN SEDIMENTS OF AN URBAN RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Urban water bodies are subject to trace element contamination resulting by different land use and land cover (LULC). The Ibirité Reservoir, located in Minas Gerais (Brazil), is a highly polluted lentic system under intense urban and industrial stress. This present study evaluated how LULC, as well as sediment properties, influence trace element concentrations in the reservoir and its main tributaries. In tributaries, trace element composition was explained by upstream LULC, especially agricultural land and low vegetation cover, together with sediment organic matter.

presentations.title: THERMAL REFUGIA AT THE WATER-FOREST INTERFACE: IMPLICATIONS FOR FRESHWATER TURTLE CONSERVATION IN EASTERN CANADA
presentations.abstract: Le biome boréal couvre près de 30 % des forêts mondiales et est largement exploité pour ses ressources. De nombreux écosystèmes aquatiques situés dans ces forêts dépendent des zones de rejet des eaux souterraines, dont les températures stables créent des refuges thermiques essentiels aux ectothermes boréaux. L'objectif de ce projet est d'évaluer la dépendance des tortues d'eau douce aux écosystèmes aquatiques associés aux rejets d'eaux souterraines par les eskers, et d'évaluer comment ces habitats peuvent orienter les stratégies de conservation.

presentations.title: Diatom Assemblages and Water Quality Dynamics in High Alpine Drainage Lake (Grizzly Reservoir) in Colorado, USA
presentations.abstract: High alpine lakes in the Rocky Mountains are sentinels of climate change. Grizzly Reservoir in the Roaring Fork Watershed (Colorado, USA) receives acid mine drainage from a historical mine called Ruby Mine. This study uses diatom assemblages preserved in a lake sediment core to construct historical water quality conditions and evaluate whether recent climate change is driving unprecedented shifts in this system. Diatoms are sensitive indicators of water chemistry and their morphological deformities (teratology) can signal heavy metal stress and other pollutants.

presentations.title: IMPLICATIONS OF RAPID LAKE BROWNING FOR MICROBIAL NUTRIENT REGIMES ACROSS AN ARCTIC LANDSCAPE
presentations.abstract: Arctic lakes in West Greenland were rapidly transformed from blue to brown lake states after the autumn of 2022, when a series of compound climate extremes occurred in this area. This coherent browning event significantly altered microbial diversity and function, shifting lakes from carbon sinks to carbon sources. Prior to browning, these lakes were characterized by low-color, autochthonous dissolved organic matter (DOM). After browning, these lakes are characterized by high-color, allochthonous DOM that is low in nitrogen.

presentations.title: Impacts of permafrost degradation on water supply and dissolved organic matter dynamics in thermokarst lakes
presentations.abstract: In the Arctic, ice-rich permafrost degradation alters the hydrological connectivity between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. In thermokarst lakes, permafrost thaw contributes to inputs of dissolved organic matter (DOM), which can be further degraded in lakes. Our study focuses on three lakes in southwestern Yukon, which remain underexplored. To characterize the impacts on water and carbon cycles, we analyzed water stable isotopes, dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations, and optical parameters of DOM in the active layer, permafrost and lake water column.

presentations.title: Ecological thresholds of ichthyofauna in response to environmental changes in a highly impacted basin, southeastern Brazil
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic disturbances are leading to habitat loss and to severe changes in biological communities. Such impacts can be pronounced in river systems and their ichthyofauna, but ecological threshold to these alterations can vary across different taxa. Here, we studied the ecological thresholds in freshwater fish sampled along 44 six- to nine-order river stretches in Doce River basin, Brazil. We selected 8 metrics related to land use in the catchment, local physical habitat, and water quality.

presentations.title: Eutrophication risk under contrasting land use and sustainability scenarios in Brazilian biomes
presentations.abstract: Human activities continue to alter nutrient cycles worldwide and intensify pressures on freshwater systems, raising concerns about water quality and ecosystem health across Brazilian biomes. Here we integrate a Eutrophication Risk Index with a spatially explicit land-use modeling framework to evaluate how contrasting national sustainability scenarios reshape phosphorus contributions to aquatic environments. Agricultural practices remain the dominant source of phosphorus losses, with scenario-specific hotspots of eutrophication risk.

name: Complexity in Space and Time: From Optical Properties to Ecosystem Processes
lead_organizer: Carina Seitz, University of Nevada Reno
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada Reno
Catherine O'Reilly, University of Minnesota Duluth
description: Inland water ecosystems and their watersheds are constantly reshaped by the complex interplay of their physical, chemical, and biological connections.

presentations.title: Hindcasting a century of winter thermal conditions in the upper Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Only recently have multi-year, whole year time series of thermal structure been available for the Laurentian Great Lakes. These data show that the formation of winter stratification and thermal structure in general across the Great Lakes varies in character not just between lakes, but interannually within lakes. An analysis of heat content and Schmidt stability shows that there is an empirical heat content threshold that must be exceeded for winter stratification to form, and a strong relationship between winter air temperature and minimum heat content. This analysis suggests that Superior has been and remains reliably dimictic, Huron is in the process of transitioning from forming winter stratification to cooling below the temperature of maximum density but not forming stratification, and Michigan experiencing more frequent years in which it does not cool to the temperature of maximum density.

presentations.title: SPATIOTEMPORAL VARIABLITY OF FISHING EFFORT AND HARVEST ACROSS A DYNAMIC TROPICAL INLAND FISHERY: A REMOTE SENSING APPROACH IN CAMBODIA'S TONLE SAP LAKE
presentations.abstract: The Tonle Sap Lake supports one of the world's most productive inland fisheries, yet tools and essential information for management of this complex, dynamic flood pulse ecosystem are lacking. Using high-resolution (<80 cm) satellite imagery (2021–2023), paired with 2023 drone surveys and catch sampling in Siem Reap Province, we present a quantitative assessment of spatiotemporal heterogeneity in effort and catch for one of the lake's dominant gears, arrow-shaped traps. From 2021-2023, we mapped 1,025 ± 276 traps in the study area. Although effort remained consistent throughout the study, trap counts indicate a substantial increase in effort over the past two decades.

presentations.title: 20 years of Drought in the Colorado River Drainage: Limited impacts on Lake Mead (Reservoir)
presentations.abstract: The Colorado River Basin has been in a sustained drought for over 20 years. Lake Mead, an impoundment of the Colorado River, provides water for urban, industrial, and agricultural purposes for much of the Western United States including over 25 million people. During this drought, water storage in Lake Mead has been reduced to 35% of full capacity, a loss of more than 50 m of depth. Despite these large changes in the hydrology of the system, the limnological characteristics of the reservoir have persisted largely unchanged. The reservoir continues to demonstrate a warm monomictic stratification pattern, mixing completely 1 out of every 2 years.

presentations.title: Float around and find out: Patterns and processes of thermal spatiotemporal heterogeneity in the Upper Snake River, WY
presentations.abstract: Understanding spatial and temporal variation in river temperature is critical for managing and conserving cold-water species under changing environmental conditions. This study examines patterns and drivers of thermal heterogeneity in the Upper Snake River, Wyoming, USA with a focus on thermal conditions supporting Snake River Cutthroat Trout. To evaluate thermal spatiotemporal heterogeneity, we conducted longitudinal temperature surveys (<5m) and monitored fixed-site temperature loggers (15min) across a 42 km reach of the Upper Snake River.

presentations.title: Analyzing the spatial and seasonal variability of zooplankton community composition, biomass, and diel migration patterns at Lake Tahoe
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton spatial and temporal heterogeneity profoundly influences essential ecosystem processes. The spatial distribution of zooplankton results from a complex interplay of biotic and abiotic factors. We investigate the spatial and seasonal variability in the composition, biomass, and migration patterns of the zooplankton community in oligotrophic Lake Tahoe (USA). Zooplankton were sampled at ten sites across multiple depths during the day and night in four seasons of 2023. Results reveal pronounced diel vertical migration and seasonal and spatial variability.

presentations.title: SPATIAL PATTERNS OF DISSOLVED OXYGEN STATES AFFECT LAKE FOOD WEB STRUCTURE THROUGH THE RESPONSE OF COLD-WATER FISH
presentations.affiliation: Tokyo university of agriculture and technology
presentations.abstract: Surface water warming and bottom water oxygen depletion, accelerated by global warming, restrict the vertical distribution of cold-water fish in the pelagic areas of temperate lakes. Although hypoxic conditions in temperate lakes are often spatially heterogeneous, little is known about how this heterogeneity affects the distribution of cold-water fish and the resulting food web dynamics. We investigated the distribution of cold-water fish (kokanee and rainbow trout) in a temperate lake in Japan using a hydroacoustic system and environmental DNA.

name: Complexity in Space and Time: From Optical Properties to Ecosystem Processes (Posters)
lead_organizer: Carina Seitz, University of Nevada Reno
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada Reno
Catherine O'Reilly, University of Minnesota Duluth
description: Inland water ecosystems and their watersheds are constantly reshaped by the complex interplay of their physical, chemical, and biological connections.

presentations.title: Forty years of zooplankton: long-term community stability with increasing biomass following invasive species disruption in a large oligotrophic mountain lake
presentations.abstract: One of the best-known examples of food-web disruption after establishment of an invasive species is the massive re-arrangement of the fish assemblage in Flathead Lake following the proliferation of non-native Mysis in the early 1980's. However, the effects of this invasion on the zooplankton are less well-appreciated and little is known about the durability of these disruptions. Since 1985, year-round sampling has characterized the abundance and biomass of crustaceans and rotifers in the lake. Flathead Lake zooplankton community structure was remarkably stable during the 40-year observation period. Zooplankton biomass increased by ~60% during the study period (seasonal Mann-Kendall analysis, p<0.002), driven by increases in the dominant copepod L. ashlandi.

presentations.title: COMPARATIVE SPATIOTEMPORAL DYNAMICS OF WATER QUALITY IN TWO CONTRASTING WYOMING, USA RESERVOIRS
presentations.abstract: Reservoirs are inextricably linked to human uses such as water supply, flood control, recreation and are biogeochemically complex, functioning along a continuum from lotic to lentic systems. Jackson Lake and Boysen Reservoir are two reservoirs in Wyoming, USA that starkly contrast in their trophic status (oligotrophic vs. eutrophic), elevation, and hydrologic regime. We aimed to identify how spatiotemporal variability of water quality parameters are structured within and between these two contrasting reservoirs. Higher spatial variability suggests internal processes (e.g., primary productivity) are important mechanisms driving observed patterns.

presentations.title: Understanding Changes in Carbon Quality During Anoxia in Temperate Lakes
presentations.abstract: The development of anoxia in the hypolimnion of lakes can contribute to the release of sediment-bound constituents, such as phosphorus and dissolved organic matter (DOM). However, the release of DOM under anoxic conditions is poorly understood. We collected high-frequency measurements of dissolved oxygen and fluorescent dissolved organic matter, along with manual samples of dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved absorbance and excitation-emission matrices (EEMs) from three lakes with varying trophic states (eutrophic, oligotrophic and dystrophic), in the Pocono Mountains of Pennsylvania, USA. Our data shows that hypolimnetic DOM changes rapidly and consistently with the onset of anoxia.

presentations.title: SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL VARIABILITY OF PH LEVELS IN A HYPEREUTROPHIC SALINE LAKE
presentations.abstract: California's Salton Sea, a rapidly deteriorating inland hypereutrophic lake, generates public health challenges due to its emission of highly elevated hydrogen sulfide (H2S) concentrations. Given that pH influences the solubility and reactivity of H2S, this study characterizes pH variability across various spatial and temporal scales. Random forest results suggest that bottom temperature is consistently an important predictor of both surface and bottom pH at shallow and deep sites.

presentations.title: CONNECTING SCALES OF MICROBIAL MONITORING USING IN SITU IMAGING FLOW CYTOMETRY
presentations.abstract: Aquatic ecosystems exhibit strong spatial and temporal heterogeneity, demanding observational strategies that bridge instantaneous, fine-scale measurements with long-term, large-area monitoring. In situ imaging flow cytometry is increasingly replacing traditional bottle sampling and laboratory microscopy, offering high-resolution characterization of microbial communities and particles directly in the environment. The CytoSense design was conceived around these principles 25 years ago and has since evolved toward higher sensitivity, enhanced imaging performance, autonomous operation, and deployment flexibility.

presentations.title: LIMNOLOGY OF THE KAWARTHA HIGHLANDS: WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED?
presentations.abstract: While the eastern Canadian landscape is largely dominated by boreal ecosystems on the Canadian Shield, the St. Lawrence Lowlands are also an important feature of southern Ontario and Quebec. Here we describe the limnology of Kawartha Highland lakes, which are found in an ecotone between the Canadian Shield and the St. Lawrence Lowlands. Lakes in the region exhibit vary in surface area, volume, and maximum depth. The widest variation among lakes is in dissolved calcium (~2-30 mg Ca/L).

name: Breaking the Flow (Posters)
lead_organizer: João Miguel Merces Bega, University of São Paulo
description: Rivers and streams act as reactive conduits for carbon and nutrients transport from terrestrial landscapes to coastal systems.

presentations.title: LEAF TRAITS, CONDITIONING, AND SHREDDERS DRIVE FPOM PRODUCTION, COMPOSITION, AND MICROBIAL COMMUNITIES IN LEAF LITTER DECOMPOSITION
presentations.abstract: The breakdown of riparian leaf litter is a key pathway by which terrestrial carbon enters stream food webs, driving shredder growth but also influencing the quantity and composition of fine particulate organic matter (FPOM). The mechanisms regulating FPOM production, particularly the roles of leaf traits, microbial conditioning, and shredder identity, are insufficiently resolved. We conducted two batch experiments where we (1) fed variously conditioned (oxic vs. anoxic) leaf resources (alder, beech, and maple) to one shredder (Sericostoma sp.) and (2) one leaf species (alder) to shredders differing in identity and ontogenetic stage. Our results identify shredders as drivers of FPOM quality rather than just quantity.

presentations.title: THE IMPACT OF A SEQUENCE OF EXTREME RAINFALL EVENTS ON THE BIOGEOCHEMICAL CYCLING IN A LARGE GULF-REGION OF FRESHWATER INFLUENCE
presentations.abstract: The increasing frequency of extreme rainfall events presents a major threat to coastal water quality and ecosystems. This study examines the impact of a sequence of high rainfall events and the resultant biogeochemical dynamics across the land-ocean continuum of a large estuarine system, the Tikapa Moana -o- Hauraki/Firth of Thames. Background saturation amplified pollutant delivery to the coastal environment, prolonged thermohaline stratification, and enhanced loading of nutrients.

presentations.title: Impacts of seasonal extremes on carbon and mercury mobilisation in two temperate watersheds
presentations.abstract: Climate change is leading to more intense and frequent extreme events, such as heavier precipitation or drought periods, while also altering the length of seasons. However, the extent to which these events impact the budget of carbon (C) and associated contaminants (e.g. mercury, (Hg)) remains poorly constrained at the watershed level. We sampled incoming stream water, lake outlet and throughfall every two weeks of two temperate watersheds for over a year, which allowed us to capture extreme rain (>130mm within 24h) and drought events.

presentations.title: RIPARIAN RESTORATION EFFECTS ON STREAM CARBON DYNAMICS
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are globally important bioreactors for carbon transformation and emission. Globally, streams are net sources of carbon emissions to the atmosphere. Small streams contribute disproportionately to riverine CO2 emissions. In this project, we aim to quantify carbon fluxes and burial in small streams and ditches in the agricultural areas of British Columbia's Lower Fraser Valley and to determine if restoring the riparian vegetation of these systems may help to shift the carbon balance towards net uptake.

name: Connecting Habitats (Posters)
lead_organizer: Jérôme Comte, INRS
description: Water bodies are interconnected within hydrological networks linking aquatic habitats to each other and to the terrestrial environment.

presentations.title: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF NUTRIENT POINT SOURCE POLLUTION ON RECEIVING SEDIMENT MICROBIOMES
presentations.abstract: Essex County, Ontario Canada is a unique location in the Canadian Lake Erie watershed as it hosts the second largest greenhouse operations in the world. The size and density of this industry have doubled between 2011 to 2025. The increased density of greenhouse stormwater retention ponds (GSWP) in the area have been cited as possible vectors for both phosphorous and nitrogen inputs to the adjacent watershed. This research evaluates the impacts of localized high nutrient point sources (N and P) on GSWP contributions using sediment microbial functional activity.

presentations.title: ASSESSMENT OF BIOFILM COMMUNITY COMPOSITION ACROSS THE CAP ROUGE RIVER WATERSHED (QUEBEC, CANADA) USING METAGENOMICS
presentations.abstract: Algal biofilms were collected in the summer of 2023 to track changes in microorganism assemblages at 23 stations located across the Cap Rouge River watershed, Quebec (Canada). Biological integrity as determined by the Eastern Canada Diatom Index (IDEC) was used as a proxy for water quality. Long-read metagenomic (GridION, Oxford Nanopore Technologies) sample analysis was performed to assess biofilm composition along the up/downstream gradient.

presentations.title: Exploring the functional adaptation of microbial communities from thermokarst pond waters and permafrost soil: development of metaproteomic protocols
presentations.abstract: Permafrost is composed of a deep permanently frozen layer and an active layer that undergoes seasonal thawing. Accelerated by global warming, the thawing of permafrost leads to the collapse of the active layer and promotes the formation of thermokarst ponds. This presentation focuses on the development of reliable and reproducible protocols for recovering and characterising the metaproteome of microbial communities inhabiting thermokarst pond waters, sediments, and the active layer.

presentations.title: Connectivity-driven microbial assembly mediate organic matter degradation and methane cycle in high-arctic transitioning permafrost
presentations.abstract: As continuous permafrost thaws, thermokarst ponds form and act as hotspots for greenhouse gas emissions. We investigated microbial community assembly and functional potential from three permafrost cores, three thermokarst, and three non-thermokarst soil–water continua (Bylot Island, Canada) using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing and gene and genome-resolved metagenomics. Thermokarst ponds showed soil microbial mass effects, with characteristic genomes encoding pathways for degrading terrestrial aromatic compounds.

name: Species Diversity and Community Shifts of Freshwater Phytoplankton Along Environmental Gradients
lead_organizer: Man Xiao, NIGLAS, CAS
description: Lakes and reservoirs function as sentinel ecosystems, integrating and amplifying signals of environmental change through shifts in their biological communities.

presentations.title: Phytoplankton trends across a nearshore-offshore gradient in the Laurentian Great Lakes
presentations.affiliation: Natural Resources Research Institute, University of Minnesota
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton in the Laurentian Great Lakes are a critical base component of a diverse and complex food web. The US EPA's Great Lakes Biology Monitoring Program examines the offshore pelagic phytoplankton community. Recently, in collaboration with USEPA's Cooperative Science and Monitoring Initiative, we added a suite of nearshore sampling stations to understand phytoplankton diversity and abundance on a nearshore-offshore gradient. An initial study on Lake Superior revealed that phytoplankton communities were similar in biovolume between stations in the pelagic versus nearshore, though there was somewhat higher diversity at nearshore stations.

presentations.title: Biological and Physiological Drivers of Competition between Bloom-Forming Cyanobacteria: Evidence from Several Lakes
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial blooms (CyanoHABs) have increased markedly in recent decades and are projected to intensify further due to the combined impacts of eutrophication, elevated CO2 levels, and global warming. Although colonial Microcystis remains dominant in many freshwater systems, the proliferation and persistence of bloom-forming filamentous cyanobacteria (FC) are increasing across diverse geographical regions. Emerging evidence suggests certain filamentous species can utilize phosphonates to support growth in phosphorus-limited conditions. A case study from Honghu lake illustrates a shift in ecosystem state.

presentations.title: UNDERSTANDING PLANKTONIC CYANOBACTERIA DYNAMICS UNDER DIVERSE ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS IN A NATIONAL PARK IN NOVA SCOTIA, CANADA
presentations.abstract: Kejimkujik National Park (KNP) and National Historic Site contains some of the most pristine aquatic systems in Atlantic Canada, attracting many visitors each summer. This project aims to characterize and determine biotic and abiotic variables associated with planktonic cyanobacteria communities in KNP and track how these communities change throughout the summer months. Surface samples were collected from 18 lakes in the park over three sampling periods. Cyanobacteria proliferation strongly abides by specific environmental thresholds in the park, consisting of higher relative abundances in systems with low total phosphorus, low total organic carbon, and pH levels greater than 5.5.

presentations.title: Long-term physico-chemical and phytoplankton trends from two Brandenburg (Germany) lakes in response to catchment restoration
presentations.abstract: Lake ecosystems are under pressure from multiple anthropogenic stressors, including excessive nutrient inputs and climate change. We analysed long-term data from two well-studied lakes in Brandenburg (Germany) after the catchment restoration that began around 1990: Scharmützelsee (a dimictic lake) and Langer See (a very shallow polymictic lake). Cluster analysis confirms a clear shift in phytoplankton community composition in both lakes with the clusters relating to trophic status.

presentations.title: Reconstructing climate and environmental change in central Chile during the Common Era using diatom assemblages
presentations.abstract: Central Chile has been experiencing a mega-drought for over a decade, which has drastically impacted over ten million people, water availability, vegetation, and forest fires. We analyzed sediment cores from two lakes, Lago Verde Tolhuaca (VTL) and Lago NN Tantauco (NNT) using diatoms as an effective proxy for climate change. The dominant taxa found in Lake VTL were Pinnularia, Aulacoseira, Navicula, whereas Lake NNT was dominated by Eunotia, Frustulia and Staurosirella.

presentations.title: Reconstructing 150 Years of Genus-Specific CyanoHAB Responses to Seasonal Temperatures Using Integrated Paleolimnological Proxies
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cyanoHABs) are intensifying in temperate lakes, yet the seasonal mechanisms that shape genus-specific bloom development remain poorly understood. We reconstructed ~150 years of cyanobacterial abundance for three cyanoHAB genera—Gloeotrichia, Dolichospermum, and Microcystis—across nine lakes in Maine, USA spanning gradients of trophic status and climate warming. Preliminary results show that winter and spring temperature trends are often stronger predictors of Gloeotrichia and Dolichospermum abundances than summer or annual averages, consistent with their dependence on overwintering akinetes and spring recruitment.

name: Freshwater Phytoplankton (Posters)
lead_organizer: Man Xiao, NIGLAS, CAS
description: Lakes and reservoirs function as sentinel ecosystems, integrating and amplifying signals of environmental change.

presentations.title: Short-term nutrient enrichment triggers rapid phytoplankton reorganization: insights from a large drinking water source reservoir
presentations.abstract: Nutrient-driven shifts in phytoplankton communities are a key driver of harmful algal blooms. We conducted an in situ microcosm experiment in eutrophic Danjiangkou Reservoir – China's primary water source for the South-to-North Water Division Project. Phosphorus emerged as the primary limiting nutrient, with total algal and cyanobacterial cell concentrations increasing sharply when DIP increased from 0P to 0.05P.

presentations.title: Spatio-temporal distribution of bacterial communities in Quebec lakes
presentations.abstract: Microorganisms play a fundamental role in lakes. They support the entire aquatic ecosystem by forming the base of the food web and drive the ecosystem metabolism.
