This project aims to characterize the spatial and temporal distribution of microbial communities in surface water of 60 lakes, in the southern region of Quebec, using environmental DNA and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Preliminary results show that the 16S community composition does not reflect the variation in the measured environmental parameters.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF HYDROLOGICAL HETEROGENEITY AND MAINTENANCE DRAWDOWNS ON ALGAL DYNAMICS IN A FRESHWATER RESERVOIR SYSTEM (LAKE SINCLAIR, GEORGIA, USA)
presentations.abstract: As human-made systems, reservoirs experience regulated flow rates and periodic drawdowns. Lake Sinclair (Georgia, USA) is a reservoir providing critical recreation, drinking water, and hydropower benefits. The lake's dendritic morphology creates deep basins and shallow coves. In 2020, median time-averaged algal biomass was 5.8-fold higher in shallow vs. deep sites (p = 0.03). PCA revealed lower community variability among deep sites, suggesting a 'core' algal community.

presentations.title: EFFECTS OF THE MONSOON SEASON ON PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITY COMPOSITION IN TWO TROPICAL PONDS IN BANGLADESH
presentations.abstract: Monsoonal forcing is expected to influence both abiotic drivers and plankton community structure in tropical freshwater ecosystems. We analyze biweekly time series gathered over the course of two years (2002-2004) from two tropical ponds in Matlab, Bangladesh: Matlab Centre, a square artificial pond, and Shilmondi, a natural pond. Surface water temperatures in both ponds ranged between 25–31°C pre-monsoon and 17–20°C during the colder winter months.

presentations.title: Phytoplankton dynamics in a eutrophic tropical reservoir: does macrophyte coverage matter?
presentations.affiliation: Universidade do Estado de Minas Gerais
presentations.abstract: The Ibirité Reservoir is a eutrophic tropical urban reservoir with episodes of cyanobacterial blooms. Part of its water surface is currently covered by Pontederia crassipes. The spatial and temporal dynamics of phytoplankton were evaluated based on bimonthly samplings performed at five points in the reservoir between July 2024 and July 2025. No spatial variation of phytoplankton was observed within the reservoir, however temporal differences were observed between all samplings.

presentations.title: IMPACTS OF CLIMATE CHANGE ON TEMPERATURE AND PLANKTON PHENOLOGY OVER TIME IN LAKE WHATCOM, WASHINGTON (USA)
presentations.abstract: Lakes are important sentinels of climate change due to their sensitivity and response to environmental shifts. Lake Whatcom (Washington, USA) serves as a drinking water source for over 120,000 people and has been routinely monitored for water quality since 1988. Monthly samples for plankton and water quality parameters, including temperature and chlorophyll a, have been collected for 30 years. Preliminary results indicate that surface water and air temperatures have increased over time.

name: Plastic Pollution from Freshwaters to Oceans
lead_organizer: Veronica Nava, University of Milano-Bicocca
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada, Reno
description: The role of aquatic ecosystems in the global plastic cycle is increasingly acknowledged.

presentations.title: PLASTIC0PYR SWITCH: A CITIZEN SCIENCE INITIATIVE TO TACKLE PLASTIC POLLUTION
presentations.abstract: Plastic pollution is a widespread environmental problem resulting from poor control of consumable plastic products and poor management of the waste they generate. The Plastic0pyr Switch project, created in 2021, aims to raise social awareness of plastic pollution and global change by applying a detailed but fairly simple procedure for the quantitative and qualitative assessment of such pollution in river systems. In total, participants collected, classified and measured 2,340 pieces of waste from 20 stream-riparian reaches.

presentations.title: Ostracods as bioindicators of recent environmental contamination in the mangroves of Guadeloupe
presentations.abstract: Nanoplastics < 1 μm, are emerging environmental contaminants and a growing concern in coastal ecosystems, yet their fate in mangroves and calcifying organisms remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the occurrence of nanoplastics in sediments and carbonate-forming microcrustaceans (ostracods) across sites in the Guadeloupe (Caribbean) mangrove. Results show a widespread occurrence of polystyrene (PS), polypropylène (PP) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC), in both sediments and ostracod valves.

presentations.title: Are Ice Rinks Sources for Microplastics and other Emerging Contaminants?
presentations.abstract: Ice hockey, curling, and skating are among Canada's most beloved sports, with ice quality being critical to player performance. While much focus is placed on ice quality for optimal play, less attention is paid to the potential release of emerging contaminants from ice rinks into the environment. This study investigated the presence of emerging contaminants including microplastics and persistent, mobile, and toxic (PMT) plastic additives, in ice shaving from the Mattamy Athletic Centre located in the City of Toronto. Microplastics were detected at high concentrations ranging from 59 to 2,063 particles per 100 mL of melted ice shaving.

presentations.title: Synergistic Effects of Photooxidation and Mechanical force on the Degradation of Commercial Polyethylene Mesh in Coastal Waters
presentations.abstract: Polyethylene (PE) mesh are widely used in coastal habitats, such as oyster-reef restoration, yet their long-term environmental fate remains poorly understood. Previous works focus on photo-degradation alone, often ignoring the combined effects of wave-driven mechanical forces. Here, we conducted laboratory incubations that coupled sunlight exposure through a solar simulator and mechanical wave simulation. Our results show that solar irradiation significantly oxidized the PE mesh materials. However, mechanical forces appeared to peel off the oxidized surface layer, making the plastics 'fresher'.

presentations.title: Ultraviolet Radiation Accelerates the Release of Nanoplastics from Polyethylene Microspheres Under Shear-Mixing in Water
presentations.abstract: This study examined the shear-driven fragmentation of the UV-aged and unaged polyethylene microspheres (180-212 µm) in water. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that UV aging and shear mixing altered the particle surface morphology. After shear-mixing, nanoparticle tracking analysis revealed a one-magnitude higher nanoparticle concentration in UV-aged suspensions than in the pristine ones by 120 min.

presentations.title: Life history of three cladoceran species exposed to the pesticide imiprothrin, microplastics and combinations
presentations.abstract: The excessive use of pyrethroid pesticides including imiprothrin has led to them being classified as emerging pollutants. In this study we evaluated the acute and chronic effects of imiprothrin and 30 µm sized microplastics, alone and combined, on the life history of each cladoceran. LC50 values for imiprothrin were 0.248, 0.307 and 0.336 mg L-1 for C. dubia, S. vetulus and A. cf. glabra, respectively.

name: Plastic Pollution from Freshwaters to Oceans
lead_organizer: Veronica Nava, University of Milano-Bicocca
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada, Reno
description: The role of aquatic ecosystems in the global plastic cycle is increasingly acknowledged.

presentations.title: First insights into the mechanisms and biological dynamics of nanoplastic interactions with two Arctic microalgae
presentations.abstract: Nanoplastics (< 1 µm) have been detected in the Arctic Ocean. There is a notable lack of research addressing Arctic phytoplankton and their exposure to nanoplastics. In this context, our study aims to elucidate the physical and biological mechanisms governing nanoplastics interaction with Arctic phytoplankton. Two Arctic strains, Gephyrocapsa Huxleyi and Chaetoceros neogracilis, were grown in batch culture and exposed to polystyrene, polypropylene and polyethylene. Our results indicate that higher concentrations and smaller particle sizes decreased photosynthetic efficiency, chlorophyll-a content, the cell abundance and sizes.

presentations.title: Response of the Plankton Food Web in a Whole-Lake Microplastic Addition Experiment
presentations.abstract: Following the collection of 4 years of baseline data, microplastic (MP) fragments were added biweekly to a small lake at the IISD Experimental Lakes Area in northwestern Ontario. Loading rates simulated inputs from urban storm flows. MPs rapidly cleared from the water column following each addition and water concentrations were generally below 4 MPs/L. We observed small decreases in the biomass of total phytoplankton, zooplankton, and Chaoborus but no strong effects on community composition.

presentations.title: THE DUAL ROLE OF BIOFILMS AS SINKS AND SOURCES OF MICRO- AND NANOPLASTICS
presentations.abstract: Plastic pollution is a global concern, yet freshwater systems—key transport pathways to marine ecosystems—remain understudied. This study explored the role of biofilms as sinks and sources of micro- and nanoplastics (MP/NP). MP/NP concentrations ranged from 1.23 to 1239 ng/mg of biofilm dry weight. Polystyrene was the most frequently detected polymer, while polyvinyl chloride showed the highest concentrations.

presentations.title: Plastic physical properties and season influence macroplastic litter colonization by freshwater biota
presentations.affiliation: Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research – UFZ
presentations.abstract: Plastic debris in freshwater systems is still less studied compared to marine systems, particularly regarding interactions with biota. We here investigated the colonization of macroplastic particles by aquatic biota in a reservoir. We identified 15 phyla on the collected substrates among which Rotifera, Nematoda, and Ciliophora were the most abundant. Both the physical properties of plastics and seasonality affect how plastic debris is used as substrate or shelter by lentic biota.

presentations.title: A comparative metagenomics approach reveals a common functional potential of plastisphere microbiomes across oceans
presentations.abstract: Over the last decades trillions of plastic particles have accumulated in the oceans, which are heavily overgrown with biofilms (termed plastisphere). We examined the functional potential of open ocean plastisphere microbiomes based on genome-resolved metagenomics in comparison to the surrounding seawater plankton. The plastisphere displayed a distinct microbiome that is taxonomically comparable across oceans but different to the surrounding seawater.

presentations.title: PLASTISPHERE EFFECTS ON FRESHWATER ECOSYSTEMS ACROSS ENVIRONMENTAL GRADIENTS
presentations.abstract: Plastics are now pervasive across environments, yet their ecological roles remain poorly understood compared to their chemical and toxicological impacts. In this presentation, we synthesize results from geographically widespread experiments examining plastisphere development, biodiversity, and metabolic effects across freshwater systems with contrasting hydromorphological and trophic characteristics. Our findings show that the plastisphere expands substrate availability for biofilm-forming organisms, effectively creating a novel 'floating–benthic' habitat.

name: Plastic Pollution from Freshwaters to Oceans (Posters)
lead_organizer: Veronica Nava, University of Milano-Bicocca
co_organizers: Sudeep Chandra, University of Nevada, Reno
description: The role of aquatic ecosystems in the global plastic cycle is increasingly acknowledged.

presentations.title: Plastic flows (micro and nano): Analytical development and environmental behaviour
presentations.abstract: For many years, global plastic production has increased significantly. The objective of this presentation is to present a study showing the distribution of nanoplastics and microplastics in the St. Lawrence River and estuary with unique spatial resolution. Based on our results, it is clear that the St. Lawrence River, one of the most anthropized rivers in the world, is a significant source and accumulation zone for this plastic waste in the northern hemisphere.

presentations.title: Tracing nanoplastics from glacier to the ocean: transport pathways and environmental fate
presentations.abstract: Anthropogenic particles and emerging contaminants, particularly plastics, are now widespread in the environment at the nanoscale (<1µm). This study investigates the behavior of NP in fjords influenced by major marine-terminating or land-terminating glaciers in the western Greenland. Along the salinity gradient, samples collected near the glaciers and influenced by freshwater inputs show higher concentrations of NP in the colloidal phase.

presentations.title: Spatial and Temporal Variation in Stormwater-Derived Debris Input
presentations.abstract: The spatial and temporal dynamics of stormwater-derived debris remain understudied. We quantified debris inputs across Rochester, New York, using community-based debris audits and storm-drain debris input assessments conducted through the use of catch basin debris interception devices known as LittaTraps. Tobacco products and food/beverage packaging were most common.

presentations.title: Interception of Stormwater-Driven Anthropogenic Debris in Monroe County, NY
presentations.abstract: Stormwater has been identified as a key driver of anthropogenic debris transport in urban and suburban environments. We quantified input of debris to the stormwater system using LittaTraps installed in nine storm drains in Rochester and Brighton, NY, USA. Using two years of input data, we built a predictive model to identify potential hotspots of debris input.

presentations.title: Detection of Microplastics in the Deep Layers of Lake Biwa
presentations.abstract: Microplastics in freshwater environments are increasingly recognized as an emerging pollutant, yet their vertical distribution in deep lake waters remains poorly understood. We conducted a survey of microplastics in the deep water of Lake Biwa, Japan, collecting samples from a depth of 80 m. No microplastics were detected in the 1.0 mm fraction; however, three particles were identified in the 100 μm fraction (two PE, one PS).

presentations.title: THE PHYSICAL FATE OF MICROPLASTICS IN THE LITTORAL ZONE OF A WHOLE-LAKE MICROPLASTIC ADDITION EXPERIMENT
presentations.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are ubiquitous across all ecosystems. To bridge this gap, we measured abundance of MPs in the littoral zone of an experimental lake (L378) across five different compartments: water, macrophytes, periphyton, rocks, and sediment. We found that periphyton was the greatest reservoir of MP, followed by surface water, and periphyton was the only compartment which appeared to accumulate MP over the season.

presentations.title: CHARACTERIZATION AND QUANTIFICATION OF NANOPLASTICS IN MANGROVES
presentations.abstract: Mangroves are ecotones between land and sea, whose submerged roots create habitats for many marine species. This project aims to characterize and quantify nanoplastics in selected biotic and abiotic matrices, and to assess their spatial distribution within mangroves. Preliminary results reveal the presence of PVC, PS, PP, and PE in both sediments and organisms.

presentations.title: Earthworm-Driven Mobilization of Microplastics Toward Soil–Water Interfaces
presentations.abstract: Microplastics from agricultural films accumulate in soil, yet their movement toward groundwater or surface waters is poorly understood. Earthworm bioturbation may enhance this transfer by creating macropores. To examine this mechanism under realistic outdoor conditions, we conducted a small-scale lysimeter experiment.

presentations.title: CHARACTERIZING THE ABUNDANCE, COMPOSITION, AND FATE OF MICROPLASTIC IN THE ANAEROBIC DIGESTION OF FOOD WASTE
presentations.abstract: With the food industry accounting for more than a third of global plastic packaging, plastics discarded with food waste may hitchhike alongside. Here, we quantify and characterize MP abundance in liquid digestate from four digesters treating food waste at different manure:food waste ratios. MP abundance and composition varied substantially across sites, ranging from 400-25,033 particles per liter.

presentations.title: LINKING SPATIAL, TEMPORAL, AND COMPOSITIONAL VARIABILITY OF MICROPLASTICS TO HUMAN EXPOSURE RISK AND POTENTIAL INPUT SOURCES
presentations.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are a pervasive contaminant in the Great Lakes. This study examines the spatial, temporal, and compositional variability of MPs in the nearshore region of Lake Ontario by analyzing samples from the water column, sediment, and fish tissue. Across all matrices, fibers were the dominant morphology, suggesting strong influence from textile-derived or wastewater-associated sources.

presentations.title: TROPHIC GUILDS INFLUENCE MICROPLASTIC PREVALENCE, TISSUE DISTRIBUTION, AND COMPOSITION IN FRESHWATER FISH FROM A HIGHLY IMPACTED RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Microplastic (MPs) contamination in aquatic ecosystems is an increasing global concern. This study assessed the prevalence, abundance, and composition of MPs in four tissues of carnivorous and omnivorous fish from a Neotropical freshwater system in Brazil. MPs prevalence reached 100% of individuals. Omnivores accumulated more MPs in all tissues.

presentations.title: PHYSICOCHEMICAL TRANSFORMATION AND DEGRADATION OF POST-CONSUMER PLASTICS UNDER REAL-WORLD ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS
presentations.abstract: Plastic pollution is prevalent globally, yet the transport, transformation, and ultimate fate of plastics in freshwater systems remain poorly understood. We incubated three plastic types in a full-factorial batch experiment using in-lake mesocosms at ambient, increased temperature, decreased pH, and increased temperature + decreased pH conditions for 135 d.

presentations.title: Investigating the interactions of anthropogenic pollutants (nanoplastics and UV filters) occurring in the Lake Balaton ecosystem using the great pond snail (Lymnaea stagnalis) as a model organism
presentations.abstract: Lakes are increasingly exposed to multiple stressors such as climate change, eutrophication, and anthropogenic pollutants, including nanoplastics (NPs) and UV-filter compounds. We aimed to investigate the single and combined ecotoxicological effects of two sizes of polystyrene nanoplastics (40 nm and 500 nm) and three commonly used UV-filter compounds on the embryonic development of the great pond snail.

presentations.title: IMPACT OF MICRO- AND NANOPLASTICS ON HOST-PARASITE INTERACTIONS IN FRESHWATER ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are under increasing threat from human activities. Plastic debris entering freshwater ecosystems undergo continuous aging and fragmentation. This study investigates clone-specific responses of Daphnia and its parasite to nanoplastic (NP) exposure, and how these differential effects potentially impact ecological functions.

presentations.title: IDENTIFICATION OF PCL-DEGRADING BACTERIA FROM THE ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
presentations.abstract: Microplastic pollution in the St. Lawrence River (SLR) is pervasive. We sampled water and sediment from Verdun Beach in October 2024. Two colonies were identified through 16S rRNA sequencing as being members of Pseudomonas spp., one of which was identified as Pseudomonas chlororaphis. Our findings suggest local bacteria may contribute to biodegradable plastic degradation.

presentations.title: PLASTIC POLLUTION AFFECTS MICROBIAL COMMUNITY COMPOSITION AND NUTRIENT AVAILABILITY IN A LABORATORY SETUP
presentations.abstract: The presence of plastic in water has raised concerns about its implications for ecosystem functioning. Here, we investigated the role of plastic as an anthropogenic substrate for microorganisms, affecting the microbial community composition and dynamics in a lab-based experiment. We observed several changes, including an adaptation in algal community composition, marked chemical alterations, and a significant change in the extracellular polymeric substances.

name: Multiple Stressor Effects on Freshwater and Marine Ecosystems in a Changing Climate
lead_organizer: Mechthild Schmitt-Jansen, Helmholtz-Centre for Environmental Research UFZ
co_organizers: Sabine Hilt, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries

presentations.title: ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS AND FOOD WEB STRUCTURE DRIVE INTERMEDIATE NATIVE PREDATOR DYNAMICS IN WYOMING, USA RESERVOIRS
presentations.abstract: Intermediate fish species, or species that occupy the core of food webs linking lower trophic levels to apex predators and vice versa, are often understudied despite often dominating consumer biomass and playing a crucial role in aquatic food web dynamics. Recruitment, growth, and mortality rates are key demographics that define population dynamics of fish species and can be assessed through age and growth analyses to determine frequency and magnitude of reproduction, growth rates, age of maturity, and population age and size structure. To quantify these metrics for white sucker (Catostomus commersonii), we aged 100 individuals using otoliths from three distinct populations in Wyoming, USA reservoirs. These reservoirs span a gradient of environmental conditions, food web structure, and management strategies, allowing us to investigate the role of both biotic and abiotic factors on the growth of white suckers. We used stable isotope analysis to quantify food web interactions between white sucker and walleye (Sander vitreus) and compared population structure between the two species to identify biotic drivers of white sucker age, growth, and size structure. We also modeled annual growth of white sucker against temperature, water level, and water clarity to identify abiotic drivers of growth. By understanding population dynamics of these species across multiple ecosystems, fisheries managers can identify how populations, communities, and food webs may be altered by changing environmental conditions, shifts in apex predator populations, and management actions.

presentations.title: HYDROLOGICAL MEDIATION of CUMULATIVE THERMAL STRESS DRIVES NONLINEAR POPULATION DECLINES in Salvelinus fontinalis: AN 14-YEAR EMPERICAL THRESHOLD ANALYSIS
presentations.abstract: Climate change is increasingly threatening freshwater biodiversity, with cold-water species like brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) particularly vulnerable due to their narrow thermal tolerances. While acute thermal thresholds (e.g., >19°C reduced growth, >22°C recruitment failure) are well-documented, the effects of chronic, sublethal warming in natural systems remain poorly understood. Using an 11-year dataset (2012–2022) from nine hydrologically diverse streams in eastern Canada, we quantified how cumulative warming and precipitation variability drive population declines. Our results reveal a critical cumulative thermal threshold of 11.6°C-years (95% CI: 10.2–13.1), beyond which brook trout abundance declines nonlinearly, demonstrating that prolonged sublethal stress can collapse populations before acute thresholds are reached. Hydrological regime mediated responses: groundwater-fed streams buffered warming initially but showed delayed declines (e.g., LC: -13.6% abundance/°C), while rainfall-dependent systems exhibited boom-bust dynamics tied to extreme events (e.g., UO summer spikes >19°C). Wet-season precipitation exacerbated declines (β = -16.4 fish/mm), likely due to hydrological stress during biologically sensitive periods. Small populations were disproportionately vulnerable to extremes (93% declines in hot years), suggesting demographic and genetic constraints. These findings redefine climate vulnerability for cold-water fishes by emphasizing cumulative stress over acute extremes, with direct implications for conservation: protecting groundwater recharge, prioritizing rainfall-stream restoration, and using the 11.6°C-year threshold as a management benchmark.

presentations.title: CEMPRA : a tool to assess cumulative effects of land use and climate change on Atlantic Salmon
presentations.affiliation: Institut National de la Recherche Scientifique
presentations.abstract: For several decades, aquatic ecosystems have been facing an increase in pressures affecting the quality of their habitats. Pressures resulting from land use and climate change have increased, leading to changes in the structure of fish communities. The Atlantic Salmon (Salmo salar), an endemic species of the North Atlantic Ocean, has suffered significant population declines over the past 50 years, and even local extinctions. As in many salmon rivers worldwide, those in southern Canada undergo similar declining trends. These decreases in abundance result notably from land-use changes and climate change (e.g. increase in water temperature, river discharge) which influence the vital rates (i.e. survival, reproduction, growth) of Atlantic Salmon. To implement robust and sustainable conservation and restoration actions, it is necessary to study the responses of Atlantic Salmon to the cumulative effects resulting from land-use modification and climate change. To address this issue and to help river managers, the CEMPRA (Cumulative Effect Model for Prioritizing Recovery Actions) tool allows the identification of hydrographic entities where habitat quality is degraded. Composed of a model of cumulative effects and population dynamics, this tool is based on monitoring data from river systems, the vital rates of the species, and the suitability indices of the species according to the stressors and life stages. Thanks to these data, CEMPRA allows predicting the population dynamics of Atlantic Salmon under different scenarios of land-use change or climate change.

presentations.title: Interactions between global change stressors on submerged plants depend on null models, plant traits and experiment conditions
presentations.abstract: Submerged plants play key roles in shallow aquatic ecosystems, and are affected by multiple, simultaneously occurring global change stressors. However, understanding the interactive effects of these stressors remains challenging due to the influence of null model selection, experimental conditions (external factors), and plant traits (intrinsic factors). To test the impact of these moderators, we compiled 176 published full-factorial experiments with pairwise global change stressors affecting the growth of submerged plants, and applied three commonly used alternative null models (additive, multiplicative, and dominance) to capture the interactive effects of stressors. We compared the direction of stressor interactions across null models and tested how experimental conditions and plant traits moderated interaction outcomes. Across all null models, the average interactive effect was additive. All three models consistently identified 26% of interactions as antagonistic, whereas the proportion of synergistic effects ranged from 13% to 15% depending on null model choice. Agreement among null models was limited: only 30% of antagonistic interactions were consistently identified by all three models, compared with 51% and 58% for synergistic and additive interactions, respectively. Both experimental conditions and plant traits significantly influenced stressor interactions. Antagonistic interactions were more likely in experiments conducted under high nutrient conditions, in the absence of fish, or involving snails. Similarly, experiments targeting not warm-tolerant species, eutrophic-sensitive species, and species with a C3 photosynthetic strategy more frequently exhibited antagonistic effects. These patterns likely reflect non-linear stressor responses and co-tolerance. Overall, our results demonstrate that the interactive effects of global change stressors are highly context dependent, and no general interaction pattern can be derived from existing studies. presentations.title: HOW RESTORATION CAN LEAD TO RESILIENT COASTAL SCAPES
presentations.abstract: Coastal zones feature a concentration of social-ecological assets, whose interactions lead to increasing conflicts. By restoring river-coast connectivity and shore dynamics, natural resilience can be enhanced, effectively reducing risks within adaptation-through-restoration plans. This approach will be here illustrated by the Ebro river-delta-coast system in the Spanish Mediterranean, where combined models and observations have been applied to assess the ecosystem services of river pulses (to enhance solid discharges) and coastal roughness (to reduce erosion and flooding). The observations include data from open top chambers, reproducing future temperatures in vertical erosion/accretion at the deltaic plain. The same models are part of the developed early warning (EWS) and climate warning (CWS) systems, which steer short- to long-term decisions for deltaic resilience. The obtained results are enriched within Coastal Restoration Platforms, which support the implementation of adaptation plans, including co-selected interventions and co-defined thresholds for the EWS and CWS. The newly generated knowledge on restoration and resilience has enabled the preparation of Coastal Restoration Agreements, which promote nature-based solutions coexisting with rigid infrastructure to achieve short-term risk reduction with long-term climate adaptation needs. Such a joint approach supports rethinking a new land-water planning which cares for coastal systems and is being now disseminated from two on-going EU research projects (REST-COAST and COAST-SCAPES). This research was funded by the REST-COAST project (European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation grant agreement No 101037097).

presentations.title: Ecosystem based management targets in a changing climate – challenges for the EU Water Framework Directive assessment framework
presentations.abstract: Climate change is increasingly impacting aquatic ecosystems through temperature rise, altered hydrology, geochemical shifts, and sea-level rise. The current water legislation in the European Union (Water Framework Directive) relies on ecosystem based environmental objectives that are anchored in type-specific reference conditions. Ongoing climate change may complicate the assessment of ecological quality and the implementation of measures because of the difficulty to isolate climate impacts from other pressures including nutrient pollution and hydromorphological changes. EU countries increasingly recognize that this is a problem and are working towards common solutions. The challenge is to ensure that environmental objectives remain achievable and at the same time to avoid blaming climate change where other pressures are the cause. The focus should be on implementing measures to counteract negative effects of climate change in combination with other pressures wherever possible. But in some cases, it may be necessary to adapt the assessment framework – e.g. if a previously perennial river becomes intermittent as a result of the changing climate. This requires transparency and adaptive management, based on high-quality monitoring information for all pressures and their impacts linked to climate change. Key to progress is to develop a context specific list of parameters to help authorities understand the influence of climate change on their aquatic systems. Only by incorporating all driving parameters can a systems status be understood and management solutions forwarded

presentations.title: MITIGATING FLOW REDUCTION WITH WASTEWATER REUSE: PROMISE OR PERIL FOR STREAM HEALTH?
presentations.abstract: In many parts of the world, climate change reduces summer baseflow and promotes flow-intermittency. The resulting reduction in dilution capacity of point sources is often considered a threat to aquatic ecosystems. Therefore, water managers often store treated wastewater in summer and release it in winter when flow is high. Today, this strategy is being questioned, as the stored wastewater could be used to sustain flow during summer. Few studies compare the hydrological, chemical and ecological effects of different wastewater discharge strategies, especially on temperate headwater streams. We chose 3 effluent-fed headwater streams in Brittany (France) and monitored discharge hourly, chemistry bi-weekly, biofilm communities monthly and aquatic invertebrate communities annually. In 2025, we implemented reduced wastewater discharges while increased or pulsed discharges are planned for 2026. In 2025, treated wastewater strongly contributed to the stream discharge (maximum between 39% and 87% from June to September). Effluents significantly altered the water quality, with an increase in mean temperature and nutrient concentrations (+2.2 °C, +21.5 mg/L for nitrate, +0.9 mg/L for phosphate). Diatoms dominated the communities and we observed a considerable increase of 517% in mean concentration from downstream to upstream. Aquatic invertebrate samples are still under analysis. We conclude that, even reduced, treated wastewater already substantially contributes to the natural discharge and highly influences the stream’s chemical and ecological conditions.

presentations.title: WARMING, PRODUCTIVITY SHIFTS AND HABITAT RISK FOR OIL SARDINE IN THE SOUTHEASTERN ARABIAN SEA: AHP–PCA BASED VULNERABILITY ASSESSMENT
presentations.abstract: Oil sardine (Sardinella longiceps) is a climate-sensitive pelagic species supporting major coastal fisheries in the southeastern Arabian Sea. This study assesses its climate vulnerability using a 20-year (2005–2024) dataset and an integrated AHP–PCA framework. Environmental variables including SST, chlorophyll-a, salinity, dissolved oxygen, mixed layer depth, pH, nutrients, and major climate indices (ENSO, IOD, PDO) were extracted and analysed using Python. PCA identified dominant environmental drivers, while AHP generated weighted exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity indices. The present study shows a clear warming trend across the region, with higher SST coinciding with reduced habitat stability and shifts in sardine suitability zones. Declining chlorophyll and changes in nutrient availability indicate weakening productivity, directly influencing potential feeding conditions and spawning environments. Increased salinity variability was found to coincide with periods of lower predicted suitability, suggesting sensitivity during early life stages. Variability in mixed layer depth and upwelling intensity further highlights fluctuating nutrient supply and consequent changes in favourable habitats. Collectively, SST anomalies, productivity decline, and altered upwelling emerged as the strongest drivers influencing sardine vulnerability. The composite vulnerability index indicates moderate to high vulnerability in core fishing grounds, underscoring the need for climate-ready fisheries management aligned with SDG-14.

presentations.title: Warming, food web simplification and surface runoff pollution additively reduce the functioning of shallow freshwater ecosystems
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Hydrobiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Global declines in biodiversity are driving food web simplification, which threatens the functioning of freshwater ecosystems. These impacts are strongly affected by climatic and anthropogenic stressors, which further reduces biodiversity. However, how these stressors operate in concert to alter ecosystem functioning is still poorly understood. Here, we used 48 large-scale field mesocosms to test how the individual and combined effects of warming, surface runoff pollution (SRP), and food web simplification (FWS) affect the functioning of standing waters. We found that warming and pollution significantly altered primary producer community composition in simplified food webs by reducing the production of submerged macrophytes, with the associated reduction in shading increasing the growth of periphyton. Warming also suppressed the growth of submerged macrophytes, particularly M. spicatum. SRP (inorganic particles, organic matter and nutrients) stimulated filamentous algal (FLA) growth, as macrophytes provided suitable growth surfaces and the algae had stronger competition ability than macrophytes with pulse nutrient released into water. We further calculated the temporal stability of each primary producer group and found it decreased for macrophytes in the simplified food web treatments, while stability of FLA increased under SRP. Our findings demonstrate that when faced with an increasing range of global environmental stressors, which is often the case in natural ecosystems, shallow freshwaters lose functioning as the system shifts away from submerged macrophytes and towards benthic algal dominance. Our study provide a mechanistic basis for conservation strategies aimed at preserving shallow freshwater ecosystem functions.

presentations.title: Salinization and warming effects on zooplankton community in Mediterranean shallow lakes: a mesocosm experiment
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems in the Mediterranean climate zone are increasingly threatened by declining precipitation and rising evaporation, which reduce lake volumes, flushing out and in turn increase salinity. The effects of warming and salinity are often studied separately, while their combined influence is poorly understood. We elucidated how zooplankton communities respond to the combined effects of salinity and warming under future climate scenarios. A three-month mesocosm experiment was conducted in fall 2023 in Mediterranean Türkiye, applying two salinity levels (4 g/L and 40 g/L) crossed with two temperature treatments (ambient temperature and +4.5°C warming). Results showed a difference in community composition between salinity treatments. At 4 g/L, large-bodied cladocerans dominated the zooplankton community, whereas 40 g/L mesocosms were dominated by halotolerant small-bodied rotifers. Diversity and richness were consistently higher under low salinity treatment. PERMANOVA results indicated that warming had no significant effect on biomass. GAM analyses revealed salinity in combination with warming predominantly led to reduced zooplankton diversity with an additional small but significant non-linear effect of water clarity. The model explained 66% of the variation in Shannon diversity. Overall, our findings emphasize that increasing salinization, particularly with warming, may impoverish zooplankton community structure and induce major shifts in zooplankton community composition in Mediterranean lakes.

presentations.title: Hydrological and ecosystem impacts of in-stream artisanal aggregate and tin mining in central Rwanda
presentations.abstract: The integrity of freshwaters is vital to maintaining healthy aquatic (and terrestrial) ecosystems. Though humans rely on freshwaters as a key natural resource and these systems support uniquely high levels of biodiversity, they are exceptionally threatened and highly exploited. The extraction of geologic commodities, including critical minerals and aggregate materials (sand, gravel, etc.), often occurs in river channels and/or the waste materials of these activities interact with water courses. Artisanal and small-scale mining is often overlooked in the evaluation of mining’s environmental impact and contribution to sustainable development. Understanding the hydrological and ecological responses to landscape disturbances caused by artisanal in-stream mining is important for the management of aggregate and mineral resources, freshwaters, and freshwater biodiversity. This work presents the case study of the Rusine River in Rwanda, in which both artisanal aggregate and tin mining occur. Primarily relying field data but supported by remote sensing, we present comprehensive data describing the abiotic and biotic components of the freshwater system along the course of the watershed. We explore the localized and system-scale impacts of these mining activities, evaluating the integrity of the watershed and its ecosystem functioning. We compare this system to similar rivers lacking some of the exploitative land uses in the Rusine. This work provides insight into responsible natural resource management in rural Rwanda with global lessons in preserving freshwater ecosystem services.

presentations.title: PHYTOPLANKTON BIOMASS RESPONSES ARE AMPLIFIED WITH ELEVATED TEMPERATURE UNDER NITROGEN-LIMITING CONDITIONS
presentations.abstract: The availability and relative abundance of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) in lake ecosystems can have a high degree of seasonal variability, which can influence the nutrient limitation dynamics of phytoplankton communities. Along with nutrient inputs, temperature plays a key role in promoting phytoplankton growth, further intensifying eutrophication in water bodies. In this study, we combined classic N and P nutrient limitation bioassays with an elevated temperature treatment to investigate seasonal limitation patterns and the extent to which warming alters nutrient effects on the phytoplankton community in a hypereutrophic reservoir. From May to October, we quantified biomass responses of the total phytoplankton assemblage and the three dominant divisions present: chlorophytes, cyanobacteria, and diatoms. The total phytoplankton community was P-limited from spring through August, then shifted to co-limitation for the remainder of the study. Chlorophytes and diatoms showed similar late-summer co-limitation patterns, whereas cyanobacteria instead shifted to strict N limitation. Temperature did not directly influence nutrient limitation status, but during periods of N limitation, elevated temperatures significantly increased the phytoplankton biomass response of the +N and +NP treatments. Therefore, our results suggest that elevated temperatures may magnify cyanobacteria blooms under N-limiting conditions. These findings indicate that reductions in both N and P are necessary for effective eutrophication management, especially as global temperatures continue to rise.

presentations.title: GLOBAL ADVANCES IN SPRINGS CONSERVATION: THE IUCN INTER-COMMISSION GLOBAL SPRINGS TASK FORCE
presentations.abstract: Springs are among the most biologically diverse and ecologically significant freshwater ecosystems on Earth, yet they remain critically understudied, underreported, and underprotected. As biodiversity hotspots, refugia, and vital ground-to-surface linkages, they support unique plant, invertebrate, fish, and amphibian assemblages found in few other habitats. Despite their importance, springs are lost at unprecedented rates due to groundwater extraction, land-use change, infrastructure development, and climate pressures. In response, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) identified the need for an Inter-Commission Global Springs Task Force (GSTF) to bring experts together from the Species Survival Commission, the World Commission on Protected Areas, and the Commission on Ecosystem Management. The GSTF will define, classify, and map springs globally, identify priority sites for biodiversity conservation, integrate springs into global conservation frameworks, and develop policy guidance and best management practices. By synthesizing existing datasets, conducting field inventories, and using emerging tools, the GSTF will build the first comprehensive global inventory of springs ecosystems. This presentation showcases the GSTF objectives, early findings, and strategies for elevating springs to global conservation priority. By revealing their ecological, hydrological, and cultural value, the GSTF seeks to ensure that these critical ecosystems—and the species they sustain—are recognized, studied, and safeguarded as keystone components of planetary biodiversity.

presentations.title: ECOLOGICAL SURVEY OF SPRINGS IN THE SAN ANDRES MOUNTAINS: MACROINVERTEBRATES AND WATER QUALITY ASSESSMENT
presentations.affiliation: University of Texas at El Paso
presentations.abstract: Springs in the Chihuahuan Desert region are unique ecosystems that are often hydrologically distinct from larger freshwater bodies. These springs are small, pristine, and environmentally constrained, making them ideal for biodiversity studies. Here we aim to characterize rotifer and macroinvertebrate communities in springs throughout the San Andres Mountains, a region that has not been extensively explored in terms of freshwater biodiversity, due to its position on a military installation. Water quality and environmental parameters (e.g., temperature, pH, salinity) were also measured to identify their influence on species distribution. We hypothesized that conductivity is the most important driver of species richness and that hydroperiod is the most important determinant of community structure. Findings from pilot surveys of >20 springs have identified several taxa of bdelloid and monogonont rotifers and many macroinvertebrates in San Andres springs. This aligns with a 2018 report which documented a general site level richness of 1-27 taxa, with one outlier site that contained 53. Preliminary results of our study recovered 1-15 taxa across sites. Recent findings revealed that ~40% of the springs were dry during the sampling period. Additional sampling is needed to determine trends in species diversity and water quality of sites over the last ~20 years. The results achieved from this project can inform conservation efforts for spring ecosystems and improve our understanding of how climate change may impact freshwater invertebrate communities in mountainous desert regions.

presentations.title: INTEGRATING SATELLITE DATA INTO WATER QUALITY FORECASTING WORKFLOWS IMPROVES FORECAST ACCURACY AND UNCERTAINTY ESTIMATES
presentations.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems are experiencing many changes due to human activities, resulting in increased variability of environmental conditions. Near-term iterative forecasting has been shown to be a valuable tool to predict how these ecosystems will change in the future, thus improving both water management and ecosystem understanding. Many water quality forecasting systems require high-frequency sensor data as input, which limits scalability to only sites with existing sensor monitoring systems. To scale near-term iterative forecasting methods to waterbodies with little or no in situ sensor data, new tools are needed. Here, we evaluated how the assimilation of satellite data into a process-based hydrodynamic model using the open-source Forecasting Lake And Reservoir Ecosystems (FLARE) system affected forecast performance and uncertainty estimates for ten lakes across the United States. We estimated surface water temperature using the Landsat-8/9 Surface Temperature product. Comparisons of forecasts with satellite data assimilation vs. forecasts with no data assimilation reveal that satellite data can improve forecast estimates across 1- to 14-day horizons into the future at the water surface. This study shows great promise for satellite remote sensing as a key freshwater forecasting data constraint, especially in waterbodies without in situ sensor data, and demonstrates an automated workflow for accessing satellite data and incorporating them into forecasts.

presentations.title: Are all projected impacts of climate change on marine ecosystems more of the same? Not if uncertainty has anything to do with it!
presentations.abstract: With rising sea temperatures, due to climate change, new methods and tools are necessary to provide policy makers clear guidance in the management of complex marine ecosystems. This study looks beyond the direct increased temperature effects upon species and examines the indirect effects of cascading causalities within the ecosystem. Ecosystem models are an example of a toolset that provides the user the ability to project changes and the policy maker with much required information. The large degree of uncertainties associated with model scenario testing, and the complexity of the marine ecosystem, complicates the ability to provide policy makers with high quality, and reliable, projections of the impacts of climate change on the marine ecosystem. We use deep uncertainty tools to determine the plausible impacts of climate change on several marine ecosystems, from the North Sea to the Eastern Mediterranean. Uncertainty is incorporated into the climate projections and the model parameters, while ensuring biological validity, in order to determine the range of impacts on the ecosystem. The results identify the differences between the responses of the very different ecosystems and highlight the difficulty in assuming a general ecosystem response to climate warming. The objective of the paper is to build upon existing ecosystem models and comprehensively incorporate all the sources of uncertainty, to characterize the breadth of system outcomes. The identification ot these outcomes will then allow for the creation of realistic policies which take system uncertainty into account.

presentations.title: ACCOUNTING FOR GROUNDWATER IN DAILY SPATIAL STREAM TEMPERATURE MODELS: IMPLICATIONS FOR FUTURE COLD-WATER REFUGIA
presentations.abstract: Water temperature is a fundamental attribute of riverine ecosystems, determining water quality, ecosystem processes, and habitat suitability for organisms. While widespread stream warming is anticipated under climate change, groundwater availability and other landscape factors are expected to mediate warming rates across river networks. Areas most resistant to warming offer important thermal refuge for cold-water species. Despite recent improvements in data collection and modelling, our ability to accurately predict daily stream temperatures at spatial scales relevant for the detection of cold-water refugia (<1 km stream reaches) is limited by a lack of accurate, high-resolution data describing groundwater availability. We combined stream temperature data collected over 11 years (2013-2023) at 78 locations across the upper Snake River watershed, Wyoming, USA with climate and landscape covariates, including a novel metric of groundwater availability, to parameterize a daily spatial stream temperature model (RMSE=1.4°C, MAE=1.08°C). Using locally downscaled future climate projections, we predicted stream temperatures every 300 meters through 2100. Model results show that groundwater plays an important role in buffering increases in temperature in upper Snake River watershed stream habitats, creating cold-water refugia that will persist into the future. Our results can be used to identify current and future suitable thermal habitat for vulnerable species across a large river network, providing needed guidance for habitat protection efforts under climate change.

presentations.title: Tracing the flow: Tracer-based insights for improved longitudinal dispersion forecasting
presentations.abstract: (liannika@alumni.ethz.ch) Advancing adaptive management of aquatic ecosystems requires integrating empirical data, process-based models, and reliable forecasts. As part of early warning systems in the event of accident-related water pollution, the German Federal Institute of Hydrology investigates dispersion processes in rivers to improve predictions of solute transport. Longitudinal dispersion is shaped by channel morphology and hydrological variability, but commonly used empirical coefficients often fail to represent this complexity, especially under changing climate conditions. To refine model calibration, we combine numerical modelling with targeted tracer studies in major German rivers. Our recent synthesis of over 700 tracer experiments shows that no ideal tracer currently exists for large-scale (>100 km) applications. Tritiated water is theoretically optimal due to its conservative behavior but is restricted by regulation and logistics. Sulphorhodamine G (SRG) emerges as the most viable alternative, offering real-time detection with acceptable environmental performance. To evaluate practical suitability, we conducted a real-time field experiment over 240 river km, directly comparing tritiated water and SRG under identical hydrological conditions, providing new insights into their ability to capture travel times, dispersion dynamics, and recovery. Both tracers performed well but also showed limitations, reinforcing the need for multi-tracer strategies and continued tracer development to improve model parametrization and, ultimately, support more adaptive and resilient management of connected aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: From Scale to Database: A Digital End-to-End Workflow for Standardized Fish Data Collection and Analysis
presentations.abstract: The analysis of fish scales is central to fisheries biology, providing insight into age, growth, population dynamics, and ecosystem conditions. Yet scale analysis is still largely manual and fragmented, limiting reproducibility, comparability, and long-term data integration. We present a digital workflow that standardizes and automates the entire process—from field sampling to data analysis and storage. During sampling, biometric data and contextual metadata (e.g., date, location) are digitally recorded and stored in a local database with a unique identifier. This information is also printed on the sample envelope, ensuring consistent and unambiguous identification. In the lab, a dedicated imaging unit captures high-resolution scale images. Using the unique identifier, images are automatically matched with their corresponding metadata and stored on a centralized web platform supporting data management, collaborative annotation, quality control, and long-term accessibility. New software enables automated and semi-automated extraction of biological information, including annuli counts, circuli patterns, and scale metrics. Compared to manual stereomicroscopic analysis, this approach provides faster, reproducible, and operator-independent results. By linking all steps in one workflow, the system minimizes errors, prevents data loss, and provides a scalable foundation for standardized monitoring and sustainable stock assessment.

presentations.title: POSEIDON: A Watershed-to-Waterway Nutrient Intelligence Platform
presentations.abstract: Managing aquatic ecosystems requires tools that can translate complex environmental data into actionable understanding. This is especially true for nutrient pollution, where limited monitoring makes it difficult to understand how terrestrial activities translate into downstream impacts. Addressing this gap requires transforming sparse water-quality samples into meaningful estimates of nutrient loads and connecting them back to the land. In this talk, we introduce POSEIDON, a decision-support platform built around three complementary components that move users from data to knowledge to action. First, WQPredict uses AI-based models to transform sparse stream nutrient concentration data into continuous daily estimates of concentrations and loads—metrics widely used and directly linked to coastal and inland lake eutrophication and algal blooms. Next, TREND characterizes nutrient inputs from the landscape—agricultural, urban, and point-source contributions—to map the terrestrial pressures influencing nutrient pollution. Finally, LAND2WATER then links these dimensions by quantifying how watershed nutrient inputs relate to observed stream loads, revealing the drivers of nutrient export and identifying where management actions will have the greatest impact. Together, these components allow POSEIDON to diagnose nutrient hotspots, evaluate management options, and support the development of targeted nutrient-reduction strategies. By integrating stream conditions with landscape nutrient inputs, POSEIDON provides a powerful foundation for adaptive, data-informed watershed management.

presentations.title: CONSERVATION PLANNING TOOL FOR SUMMIT LAKE LAHONTAN CUTTHROAT TROUT
presentations.abstract: The Lahontan cutthroat trout (LCT) is a threatened species of large-bodied inland trout native to the Great Basin ecoregion. Summit Lake, located in northern Nevada, is the only desert terminal lake to host a native, self-sustaining LCT population. We used over 10 years of capture-mark-recapture data collected by the Summit Lake Paiute Tribe to estimate many critical demographic parameters, such as adult and juvenile survival and spawning frequency. We used these parameters, along with additional information gathered from the literature, to develop a demographic simulation model for the Summit Lake LCT population, which forecasts population dynamics as a function of lake level and stream flow. The model also incorporates additional parameters which allow it to simulate scenarios such as harvest, drought, and stream restoration. A web-interface application was built using RShiny to allow for natural resources managers and decision makers to quickly run different scenario tests. This is crucial for monitoring the long-term sustainability of threatened species such as the LCT.

presentations.title: THE NATIONAL ECOLOGICAL OBSERVATORY NETWORK: PROVIDING CLEANED AND GAP-FILLED DISCHARGE DATA TO EXAMINE LONG-TERM TRENDS IN AQUATIC SYSTEMS ACROSS SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL SCALES
presentations.abstract: Calculating accurate discharge timeseries data is a critical component of assessing biological and climatic functionality within aquatic ecosystems. NEON produces continuous discharge data at 27 stream and river monitoring sites across the United States. Beginning in the 2025 data release, NEON discharge data are cleaned and gap-filled to produce a timeseries that is, to the greatest extent possible, free of both gaps and erratic periods. During data cleaning, data are reviewed, and quality flags are applied to gaps and periods that require correction. Constant offsets are applied where data shifts have occurred. Flagged periods are then corrected using gap-filling methods such as linear interpolation (for short gaps) and regression coefficients (for longer gaps) based on relationships between co-located sensors, or co-located monitoring stations (e.g., USGS gauges). The quality and continuity of the NEON Water Year 2022 – 2024 discharge dataset was evaluated by assessing the strength of the relationship between field discharge measurements (treated as truth) and modelled estimates and by calculating the number of gaps present in the record. The analysis found that NEON discharge data are well-correlated with field measurements during this period and that the record is essentially continuous across sites. These findings support the use of data cleaning and gap-filling methods to improve data quality and continuity and indicate that NEON discharge data are suitable for use in answering critical research questions in freshwater ecology at the continental scale.

presentations.title: Bridging Ecological Narratives and Quantitative Prediction Through Meta-Analysis and Probabilistic Networks
presentations.abstract: Ecology seeks to understand relationships between organisms and their environment. Traditionally, these associations have been described qualitatively through narratives, conceptual frameworks, or graphical representations such as flow charts and decision trees. While such narratives synthesize decades of research, they often remain semantic, providing insight without predictive capacity. Meta-analyses quantitatively synthesize ecological patterns across broad scales, allowing estimation of general trends and consistent relationships among ecological variables. Here, we present the first global synthesis of parameter estimates across five key riverine organism groups - bacteria/archaea, algae, macrophytes, invertebrates, and fish - in response to seven stressors. From 22,120 screened papers, we extracted 276 studies with 1,332 stressor-response relationships. Consistent responses were found for salinity, oxygen depletion, and fine sediment accumulation, while effects of nutrient enrichment and warming varied among groups. However, these estimates are not yet embedded in a unified network. It is proposed combining meta-analysis with probabilistic networks, enabling aggregated estimates to generate predictions and explore relations. This approach merges quantitative synthesis with qualitative ecological knowledge, allowing literature-derived information to inform predictive models. It extends meta-analytic results into a probabilistic, predictive framework, bridging the gap between ecological narratives and quantitative predictions.

presentations.title: Chloride Effects on Zooplankton Biomass are Strongly Modified by Co-occurring Ions and Regional Context
presentations.affiliation: Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Freshwater lakes are increasingly impacted by salinization. While local-scale studies and experiments have provided valuable insights into chloride (Cl-) effects on zooplankton, how those results translate to different ecological contexts of lakes in a broad range of eco-climatic settings remains largely unknown. To fill this gap, we studied how Cl- and major ions relate to zooplankton communities while accounting for ecological context across thousands of lakes. We analyzed data for 2,304 lakes using chemical, biological, and natural context variables from three years of the U.S. National Lakes Assessments and the LAGOS-US Research Platform. We found that zooplankton responses to Cl- varied substantially by taxonomic group, ecoregion, and lake ion composition. Large and small cladoceran biomass generally showed initial increases at low Cl- levels, followed by declines at higher concentrations. Calanoid and cyclopoid copepods displayed more linear or region-specific trends, while rotifers showed limited or inconsistent relationships with Cl-. We also found interactive effects between Cl- and calcium, potassium, and sulfate ions, with interactions varying considerably across ecoregions. In most cases, interactions between Cl⁻ and potassium or sulfate explained more variation in zooplankton biomass than with calcium ions. Our macroscale analysis reveals how Cl- and ion interactions shape zooplankton communities across broad eco-climatic gradients in ways that have not been captured by local or experimental studies.

presentations.title: CLIMATE-DRIVEN BIODIVERSITY TURNOVER IS AMPLIFIED AT ECOREGION BOUNDARIES
presentations.abstract: Climate change is reshaping ecological communities worldwide, yet we still know little about where biodiversity change is most pronounced across landscapes. Ecotones, or the boundaries between ecoregions, are often predicted to be hotspots of climate sensitivity due to steep environmental gradients and high species turnover, but empirical evidence has been limited. Using the BioTIME database, we analyzed 36,745 freshwater, marine, and terrestrial community time series to test whether temporal turnover is elevated near ecoregion boundaries and whether this sensitivity interacts with regional climate change. We quantified species turnover using the Jaccard index between all pairwise years of each time series and modeled turnover using ordinal beta regression with rate of temperature change, equatorward or poleward distance to ecoregion boundary, and temporal distance as predictors, including all interactions. Contrary to earlier work showing weak or inconsistent boundary effects, we found strong evidence that communities closer to ecoregion boundaries experience significantly higher temporal turnover. Boundary-proximal assemblages show approximately 4-42% higher replacement rates over a decade than communities in biome interiors. Moreover, the boundary effect was magnified in regions experiencing the fastest warming, where turnover near boundaries was 45-240% higher than in slowly warming regions after a decade. This interaction between climate and ecoregion boundary suggests that ecotones act as amplifiers of biodiversity change under rapid climate forcing, likely reflecting both shifting species ranges and heightened ecological reorganization where biotic and abiotic gradients are steepest. These results provide new empirical support for long-standing predictions about ecotone vulnerability and identify ecoregion boundaries as emerging hotspots of biodiversity change.

presentations.title: BIODIVERSITY RESPONSES TO CLIMATE-DRIVEN HYDROLOGIC CHANGE IN FRESHWATER MUSSELS, CRAYFISH, AND AQUATIC INSECTS
presentations.affiliation: Illinois Natural History Survey, Prairie Research Institute, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, IL
presentations.abstract: Macroinvertebrates typically comprise most biodiversity in streams and rivers, and groups such as mussels and crayfish often dominate benthic biomass. Yet these taxa are rarely assessed for climate related vulnerability and almost never evaluated together, limiting cross-taxa comparisons and prioritization. Climate-driven shifts in the timing and magnitude of extreme high and low flows, snowmelt, and evapotranspiration may shift biodiversity hotspots or reveal climate-resilient watersheds. We compiled an occurrence dataset of ~500 lotic species of stoneflies, caddisflies, crayfish, dragonflies, and mussels. Using ecological niche models, we predict each group’s change in species richness between a baseline (1981–2006) and future (2030–2059) period within HUC12 watersheds across the U.S. Midwest—an area highly vulnerable to increasing precipitation extremes. Hydrologic inputs from five global climate models allow us to assess which taxa are most sensitive to climate-driven change. We expect richness to vary across watersheds, with those containing higher-order catchments supporting more species due to increased habitat heterogeneity and sustained flows. Lower-order streams may be particularly vulnerable to hydrologic change. Their limited groundwater buffering and strong dependence on local precipitation suggest that alterations in flow magnitude, timing, or variability could strongly limit species persistence thereby reducing richness. Across taxa, we anticipate richness variation driven by species- and group-specific sensitivities related to differences in life history, dispersal, and hydrologic dependence. Overall, this work identifies where macroinvertebrates are most at risk, providing a foundation for targeted biodiversity conservation.

presentations.title: Consistency in Zooplankton-Environment Relationships over Time in Lakes across the World and Implications for Space-for-Time Substitution
presentations.abstract: Understanding and predicting how environmental change affects zooplankton community structure and function are critical given the pivotal role zooplankton play in maintaining aquatic ecosystem functioning and serving as bioindicators. Space-for-time substitution (SFTS) surveys are often used to infer temporal changes because zooplankton time series data are relatively scarce. However, the central SFTS assumption of space-time equivalence remains largely untested and, thus, inferences about temporal responses within the SFTS framework are uncertain. Using time series from 50 lakes with more than 8 years of data over 4 continents in the Zooplankton International Geospatial (ZIG) dataset, we tested the hypotheses that the relationships between zooplankton density and three potential explanatory variables (water temperature, chlorophyll-a, and pH) are (1) consistent across years within lakes, and (2) more consistent as zooplankton density is aggregated at higher levels of organization (e.g., community > order > genus). Analyses were conducted using generalized linear mixed-effect models. Preliminary results suggest that the relationships between zooplankton density and the potential drivers were consistent between years, and these relationships were stronger for density aggregated at the community level compared to genus level. These results provide empirical support for SFTS analyses widely used in the aquatic sciences, though we suggest caution when considering finely resolved taxonomic responses relative to community-level SFTS dynamics.

presentations.title: TRACKING INVASION PATHWAYS THROUGH LAKE NETWORKS: VALIDATING LANDSCAPE-SCALE PREDICTIONS WITH BROAD-SCALE MONITORING DATA
presentations.abstract: Predicting freshwater invasions across lake-rich landscapes requires understanding how hydrologic networks, accessibility, and landscape structure shape opportunities for species movement. In 2015, we developed a landscape-scale model of invasion potential for Ontario’s inland lakes, using connectivity, network configuration, and environmental suitability to identify pathways most likely to facilitate the spread of warm- and cool-water fishes. A decade later, we evaluate whether such network-based predictions anticipate real establishment patterns. Here we pair our published invasion-potential surfaces with nearly fifteen years of observations from Ontario’s Broad-Scale Monitoring (BsM) Program, which samples more than 1,500 lakes across four 5-year cycles using both repeat lake samples and probabilistic draws. By comparing predicted risk with occurrences of established and emerging invaders, we test how network position, landscape accessibility, and thermal context relate to subsequent invasion status. Preliminary comparisons suggest alignment for several taxa, alongside cases where sparse temporal coverage may obscure early establishment. This synthesis shows how long-term monitoring can ground-check network-based invasion frameworks, offering a scalable and pragmatic approach for refining landscape predictions without reanalyzing underlying environmental layers.

presentations.title: A PALEOLIMNOLOGICAL SYNTHESIS OF CLADOCERAN DYNAMICS ACROSS CANADIAN LAKES OVER THE PAST ~200 YEARS
presentations.abstract: With accelerating anthropogenic stress across the Canadian landscape comes a responsibility to understand, protect, and restore the health of freshwater lakes. Developing a national portrait of ecological changes requires synthesis of long-term archives that cover periods prior to intensive human stressors. Paleolimnology is a powerful tool for uncovering large-scale trends in lake dynamics over the past ~200 years. For instance, hyperspectral chlorophyll records of 80 Canadian lakes showcased a widespread increase in primary production in the last century, consistent with prior syntheses documenting a rise in cyanobacteria pigments from the Northern Hemisphere. Here, we are developing a Canada-wide spatio-temporal dataset of zooplankton community trends, using cladoceran subfossil remains of ~75 lake sediment records. These remains can help elucidate the effects of anthropogenic stressors on lake food webs. We will quantify diversity and community changes over time, space, and key environmental gradients. Preliminary analyses show that the alpha-diversity trends are relatively dynamic through time, and many lakes show a rise in eutrophication-tolerant Chydorus brevilabris. By focusing on a keystone trophic level of lake food webs, we are able to infer ecological consequences for other trophic levels (i.e. phytoplankton, fish). Our approach compliments a recent primary producer synthesis, extends our understanding of the temporal dynamics of freshwater invertebrate communities in Canadian lakes, and ultimately guide restoration priorities.

presentations.title: THE CONTRIBUTION OF AUTOCHTHONOUS AND ALLOCHTHONOUS ORGANIC MATTER IN LENTIC ECOSYSTEMS' FOOD WEBS: A GLOBAL META-ANALYSIS
presentations.affiliation: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
presentations.abstract: Freshwater food webs are fueled by autochthonous organic matter (auto-OM) and allochthonous organic matter (allo-OM). Allo-OM is more abundant but has lower nutritional quality and assimilation efficiency by freshwater consumers than auto-OM. These discrepancies in nutritional quality are likely to generate differences in food webs' structure. Auto-OM-based food webs might show higher taxonomic and functional diversity than their allo-OM-based counterparts. However, land use and climate changes threaten freshwater biodiversity and might alter the contribution of auto-OM to food webs. Riparian deforestation can increase light incidence in freshwater ecosystems, boosting algae stocks but reducing their nutritional quality. Climate change increases freshwater animals' consumption of auto-OM and affects the stocks of both OM sources. We aim to evaluate how the contribution of auto and allo-OM in lentic ecosystems' food webs will taxonomically and functionally shape these communities. Our main hypothesis is that auto-OM will support greater taxonomic and functional diversity due to its higher nutritional quality when compared with allo-OM. We propose a global meta-analysis to test whether the most taxonomically and functionally diverse aquatic communities correlate with higher auto-OM contribution to lentic food webs. We expect that freshwater communities will exhibit greater taxonomic and functional diversity when auto-OM contributes more than allo-OM to energy flow because of the greater assimilation efficiency associated with high-quality auto-OM.

presentations.title: SPATIO-TEMPORAL DYNAMICS OF LAKE WATER QUALITY USING MULTI- AND HYPERSPECTRAL SATELLITE INTEGRATION
presentations.abstract: Integrating hyperspectral and multispectral satellite images is crucial for improving lake water quality monitoring in the context of actual global warming and related climate extreme events. Multispectral sensors provide long time series, extensive coverage and consistent observations, which facilitate the identification of broad-scale trends in turbidity, chlorophyll-a and surface dynamics in the context of present climate change. Hyperspectral sensors complement these capabilities by capturing fine spectral details that improve the identification of optically complex water constituents and enable the development of more accurate bio-optical models. We have combined different hyperspectral (PRISMA, DESIS, ENMAP, EMIT, PACE) and multispectral (Landsat-8, Sentinel-2A/B, Sentinel-3A/B, MODIS-Aqua/Terra and VIIRS-SNPP/JPSS) sensors in order to improve our understanding intra- and inter-daily phytoplankton dynamics and characterise the status of water quality of three Italian lakes (Garda, Trasimeno and Varese) characterised by different optical properties. In situ instruments are available in all three lakes that allow continuous measurements of either reflectance or water quality throughout the day. In addition, we used the ECOSTRESS sensor to derive surface water temperature. The results on water quality parameter concentrations, derived from bio-optical model application, confirmed that multi-sensor analysis was crucial for detecting rapid changes in the lakes, mainly due to variations in temperature.

presentations.title: Satellite-Detected Seasonal Water Storage Variability: Contrasting Roles of Lakes and Reservoirs in Climate Adaptation
presentations.affiliation: Nanjing Institute of Geography & Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The seasonal redistribution of water storage by lakes and reservoirs is critical for water security, yet their distinct roles in regulating the global water cycle remain poorly quantified. Here we fuse multi-source satellite observations to reveal how natural lakes and human-made reservoirs buffer seasonal changes in terrestrial water storage (TWS). We find that lakes and reservoirs collectively buffer 10.9% of seasonal TWS variability, with this effect being most prominent in the Northern Hemisphere (16-27%). Reservoirs alone contribute to 48.5% of such buffering capacity globally and significantly reshape the spatial and temporal pattern of surface water storage. These systems operate in starkly different ways. Lakes, which prevalent in humid high-latitudes, typically align with the natural seasonal water cycle. In contrast, reservoirs which concentrate in arid and populated mid-to-low latitudes, are actively managed, with operations altering the natural seasonal timing of the water cycle across 62 of 118 major basins. These management strategies are tailored to distinct regional priorities, from seasonal water supply in the US and Europe, to capturing autumn/winter resources in India and West Africa, and mitigating flood risk in monsoon-dominated basins like the Yangtze. These findings highlight the profound impact of human water management on planetary-scale hydrology and underscore its critical role in building resilience in an era of increasing hydrologic extremes.
