presentations.title: HEATWAVE AND MICROPLASTIC EXPOSURE REDUCE THE NUTRITIONAL QUALITY OF A COMMON FRESHWATER PHYTOPLANKTON, TETRADESMUS OBLIQUUS
presentations.abstract: The increased occurrence of heatwaves (HW) and microplastic (MP) pollution may be decreasing the productivity of aquatic ecosystems. Elevated temperatures reduce the nutritional quality of phytoplankton, largely by decreasing polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) content, but it is unclear whether HW elicit a similar or stronger response. The effect of MP, and the combination of HW and MP, on the nutritional quality of phytoplankton is similarly unknown. To address these knowledge gaps, we examined the effects of constant warming (CW), HW, and MP on the lipidome of a common freshwater green alga, Tetradesmus obliquus. Although we applied the same total amount of heat in the CW and HW treatments, we saw clear differences in the lipid profile. The lipidomic response under HW involved a transient induction of more numerous and acute changes, whereas changes accumulated over time with CW. Extraplastidial membrane lipids and PUFA significantly decreased under both heat treatments, but neutral lipids decreased only under HW. Interestingly, plastidial lipids increased in all treatments, suggesting a protective response within photosynthetic organelles. The co-occurrence of MP induced a unique response under CW only. Upon return to ambient conditions, T. obliquus showed signs of recovery from both treatments, particularly with MP present, but maintained differences in the lipid profile one-week post-heating. Our findings suggest that future global change may have significant consequences for freshwater algal nutritional quality and thus the productivity of aquatic food webs.

presentations.title: Dynamics and drivers of mercury deposition in Canadian lake sediments over the past ~200 years
presentations.abstract: Mercury is a persistent, adverse environmental pollutant due to its ability to bioaccumulate and its resistance to biodegradation. Lake sediments provide a record of mercury deposition, of which the greatest source in North America is industrial activity, which comprises both local and distant sources of industrial pollution. Understanding the effects of mercury pollution on lake ecosystems, however, is complicated by the effects of climate and land-use changes, which are shifting the dynamics of lacustrine mercury deposition and cycling. For example, increases in dissolved organic carbon (DOC) inputs to lakes, associated with climate change-induced increases in temperature and precipitation, can enhance the delivery of mercury to these ecosystems. In contrast, land-use intensification in lake watersheds often increases nutrient inputs and sediment deposition, which may dilute the accumulated mercury in lake sediments. We used measurements of sedimentary total mercury concentrations as well as time series of chlorophylls and dissolved organic carbon (based on spectroscopic approaches) to infer past changes in sediment cores collected from 90 lakes across Canada. By applying generalized additive models and ordination techniques, we evaluated the relative strength of different drivers of mercury deposition including both within-lake factors (chlorophyll and DOC) and between-lake factors (climatic and land-use records). These analyses will disentangle the relative contributions of individual and synergistic drivers of mercury dynamics as recorded in lake sediment archives across Canada.

presentations.title: NON-TARGET SCREENING OF MICROPOLLUTANTS IN SURFACE WATER AND SEDIMENTS FROM AN URBAN EUTROPHIC RESERVOIR IN BRAZIL
presentations.abstract: An increasing number of anthropogenic compounds, including pharmaceuticals, pesticides, PFAS, and other micropollutants occur in urban reservoirs worldwide. Despite reduced concentrations, they have the potential to affect aquatic fauna. In this study, non-target screening (NTS) of surface water (n = 50; July 2024–July 2025) and sediment (n = 20; November 2024 and May 2025) from an urban eutrophic reservoir located in Minas Gerais State, Brazil, was performed to characterize chemical pollution and identify potential sources in the study area. Water samples (100 mL) were spiked with 50 μL of an isotopically labeled standard solution prior to solid-phase extraction (SPE), and a procedural blank was prepared for each sample batch. Sediment samples (2–5 g) were freeze-dried prior NTS of >10,000 chemicals. Analytical determination was performed using nanoflow liquid chromatography (Dionex Ultimate 3000 NCS‐3500RS Proflow, Thermo Scientific) coupled with high-resolution accurate-mass spectrometry (Q Exactive HF Orbitrap, Thermo Scientific). Analyses were conducted in collaboration with the Department of Environmental Resource Engineering, Technical University of Denmark. NTS analysis is crucial for uncovering unknown or unexpected contaminants beyond conventional target lists and provides a comprehensive framework for detecting xenobiotics and transformation products, generating detailed chemical fingerprints of the Ibirité Reservoir, and supporting evidence-based management of urban aquatic systems through more holistic environmental risk assessments.

presentations.title: Carbon stable isotope reveal transgression to bicarbonate uptake during cyanobacteria blooms
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacteria blooms can seriously affect ecosystem health. Moreover, these events can also affect turnover of aqueous carbon, including dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and particulate organic carbon (POC). Interactions of these three phases also influence their carbon stable isotope ratios. These relationships were shown in a freshwater pond that was investigated over a period of 23 months with several cyanobacterial blooms. During this investigation period we were able to map turnover and sources of aqueous carbon before, during, and after bloom events. During bloom events POC isotope values (d13CPOC) increased up to −17.4 ‰. This increase coincided with a decrease of aqueous CO2 (CO2(aq)) below the atmospheric equilibration value of 412 μatm. Associated carbon isotope enrichment between CO2(aq) and POC (εCO2-phyto) ranged from 2.0 to 21.5 ‰ with lowest enrichments at pH values above 8.9. The increase of d13CPOC and decrease of εCO2-phyto values at low CO2 and high pH was most likely caused by the activation of the carbon concentrating mechanism (CCM) by cyanobacteria. This mechanism correlated with preferential assimilation of the naturally 13C-enriched HCO3−. Surprisingly, this mechanism became dominant much later than expected and CO2(aq) remained a dominant input even at low pCO2 values. Our data show that CO2(aq) still contributed with more than 50 % to the POC pool even at pCO2 values as low as 150 μatm. Only after this threshold, the reduced εCO2-phyto value suggested increased incorporation of 13C-enri9ched HCO3−.

presentations.title: Using stable isotopes to quantify nutrient uptake in cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms
presentations.abstract: Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CHABs) are a persistent problem in western Lake Erie. These seasonal blooms are largely dominated by Microcystis aeruginosa, which produces the cyanotoxin microcystin, a nitrogen-rich molecule. Microcystis is capable of using several forms of nitrogen, including urea. It is important to understand how Microcystis is utilizing available urea, because it is a common component of the agricultural runoff that may contribute to the annual blooms. Previous studies observed incorporation of both the nitrogen and carbon from urea by Microcystis. However, we hypothesize that Microcystis primarily utilizes the nitrogen from urea, and that carbon from urea is secondary to dissolved inorganic carbon as a source of carbon for photosynthesis. We performed an experiment to test whether Microcystis incorporates carbon from 13C/15N dual-labelled urea over 4-hour incubations. Samples were collected and assessed with nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (nanoSIMS) isotopic imaging to determine biomass assimilation by comparing measurements of 13C/15N to 12C/14N. We observed that Microcystis in urea-amended samples did take up urea-derived nitrogen, but not carbon, providing insight into the nutrient usage by Microcystis under natural bloom conditions.

presentations.title: Snowmelt and groundwater interactions in water-limited mountains: Insights from water isotopes
presentations.abstract: he interactions between snowmelt and groundwater in Morocco's High Atlas Mountains, Tifnoute Valley in Lake Ifni’s catchment, is investigated in this research. Within over 20 years of monitoring (2004–2025), 208 water samples of snow, precipitation, springs, rivers, and lake water were gathered over various elevations and seasons. To better describe regional isotopic behavior, we established a new Local Meteoric Water Line (LMWL) and altitudinal gradient using observed and simulated precipitation isotope data. Extensive spatial and seasonal variability are observed in isotope values, mainly due to elevation differences, snowpack distribution, and geological settings. Unexpectedly, evaporation appears to have little effect on the isotopic signature, perhaps due to the high elevation, cold temperature, and high infiltration rates, which reduce extensive surface water exposure. A local recharge was identified for the lake and springs mainly from snow-covered areas in the upstream. The isotope mass balance results further show that snowmelt is a major contributor to local recharge processes, accounting for around 50–60% of the groundwater and around 68% of inflow to Lake Ifni. Additional comparison of the previous findings of snowmelt contribution to groundwater using isotope mass balance suggests a significant decline between the years 2016 and 2024, which strongly aligns with an extensive decrease of snow cover area. By elucidating the role of snow and rain in surface and groundwater recharge, this research better understands hydrological processes in arid mountain environments and offers new insights into water resource management under conditions of climatic uncertainty and increasing water demand. Keywords: Snowmelt; Groundwater dynamics; Stable isotopes; Lake Ifni; Atlas Mountains; Semi-arid regions

presentations.title: ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITY COMPOSITION ALONG AN URBANIZATION GRADIENT – BERLIN PONDS AS A MODEL SYSTEM
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: (jiayi.fan@igb-berlin.de) Urbanization is accelerating worldwide, intensifying anthropogenic stressors that reshape aquatic biodiversity. In pond ecosystems, urban-related changes, such as pollution, eutrophication, and altered land use, might strongly modify zooplankton communities, which are sensitive indicators of environmental change. We examined zooplankton communities from 65 ponds along an urbanization gradient at both local (100 m radius) reflecting urbanization in the immediate neighborhood of the pond and at the regional (3200 m radius) scale, reflecting embedment in an urbanized area. This distinction is highly relevant for a city like Berlin, which has extensive green areas. We found strong shifts in cladoceran composition, community-wide mean body size, and diversity patterns along the urbanization gradient. Highly urbanized ponds were dominated by smaller-bodied taxa, whereas less urbanized ponds supported higher species richness and more large-bodied species. Urbanized ponds also showed elevated chlorophyll-a concentrations. Ponds located in larger green areas (low urbanization at 100 m scale) outside the city center did show higher biodiversity despite the high regional-scale urbanization. This suggests that surrounding green areas can buffer urban impacts and sustain local diversity. To assess longer term dynamics, we reconstructed historical zooplankton communities by analyzing dormant egg banks from five urbanized ponds along the urbanization gradient. Analysis revealed that increasing anthropogenic activities over the past five decades have driven Total Phosphorus enrichment and biodiversity decline, with stronger effects in more urbanized ponds. Our combined contemporary and historical approach highlights how urbanization shapes biodiversity and might influence the functioning and resilience of urban pond ecosystems, for instance, through a change in community-wide body size.

presentations.title: DAPHNIA POPULATIONS SHOW SUBSTANTIAL GENETIC VARIATION IN THE ACUTE TOLERANCE TO FIVE URBANISATION-ASSOCIATED POLLUTANTS
presentations.abstract: (felix.mende@igb-berlin.de) Urban ponds are increasingly exposed to novel chemical stressors originating from wastewater spills and road runoff. By asserting a top-down control on primary producers, Daphnia water fleas play a vital role in these ecosystems but are threatened by the influx of chemical pollution. Standing genetic variation can facilitate rapid local adaptation in such fast-changing urban environments. Yet, studies on the potential for local adaptation of D. magna to urbanisation-associated pollutants are scarce. Given the complex pollution burden in urban environments, a multi-stressor perspective becomes vital in the context of adaptation. Here, we investigated whether D. magna from urban and rural ponds differ in their tolerance to five common pollutants: the tire wear chemical 1,3-Diphenylguanidine, the pharmaceutical Metformin, the insecticide DEET, the antimicrobial Triclosan, and Caffeine. Using a hierarchical design that allowed us to analyse acute tolerance across multiple biological levels—from clones to populations to land-use categories—we evaluated a) the extent of genetic variation in tolerance within populations, b) whether populations differ in tolerance, and c) whether these differences are linked to urbanisation (i.e. land-use). The key result of our analysis is that both urban and rural populations showed pronounced genetic variation in their pollution tolerance, and this was strongly pollutant- and clone-dependent. The presence of such clonal variation suggests that populations from both land-use categories show potential for local adaptation to chemical pollutants.

presentations.title: Light pollution in urban waters shapes the ecology and evolution of Daphnia water fleas
presentations.abstract: (ndmtzn@gmail.com) Artificial light at night (ALAN) is an increasingly pervasive urban stressor, yet its ecological and evolutionary impacts on freshwater organisms, and consequently on whole ecosystems, remain poorly understood. I will present novel results from common garden experiments and population growth trials using Daphnia as a focal species where we aimed to examine how ALAN shapes ecological functions and drives evolution in urban populations. In large-scale common garden experiments, we have tested >80 genotypes of Daphnia magna originating from ponds that are exposed to a gradient of light pollution in Berlin. Genotypes were tested for their life-history traits and grazing rates, under control (dark nights) and ALAN conditions. We have discovered substantial variation both within and between populations, indicating a large potential for evolution in this system. Next to common garden experiments, we have also tested for ecological effects of ALAN, specifically on a newly discovered species interaction between Daphnia and predatory flatworms. ALAN dramatically shaped the outcome of this interaction, with preliminary results suggesting a strong genotype-dependent pattern. Importantly, we are currently testing how ALAN may be driving the evo-to-eco feedback between trait differentiation (evolution) and species interactions (ecology). Our work illustrates how ALAN, which itself is strongly linked to socio-economic dynamics, can have effects at various biological levels, from organismal traits to population dynamics and species interactions, and ultimately ecosystem functioning.

presentations.title: SOCIO-ECOLOGICAL DYNAMICS OF URBAN BLUE SPACE: THE INFLUENCE OF AFFLUENCE ON BIODIVERSITY AND PERCEPTIONS OF PONDS IN BELGIAN CITIES
presentations.abstract: Urban ponds are vital yet understudied components of cityscapes, supporting biodiversity and contributing to human well-being. However, the extent to which socio-economic factors shape their ecological characteristics and biodiversity perception remains unclear. This study investigates how affluence influences biodiversity patterns, and the human perceptions of urban freshwater ponds across Brussels and Antwerp. Using a multidisciplinary approach that combines traditional biodiversity assessments, environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding, and social surveys, we examine socio-ecological feedbacks between urban pond ecosystems and people. Sampling of zooplankton, macroinvertebrates, and eDNA has been completed, the social surveys have been finalised, and data analyses are ongoing. Results will reveal patterns associated with the “luxury effect”—the correlation between wealth and biodiversity—in freshwater systems. They will also explore how urban ponds contribute to well-being, how accurately people estimate biodiversity, and how shifting baselines shape these perceptions. By integrating ecological and social data, this research aims to clarify the role of urban blue spaces in supporting ecosystem services, informing sustainable urban planning, and promoting equitable access to nature. A pilot study on ponds in Brussels is being finalized for publication, both these findings, and preliminary findings from the larger study will be presented.

presentations.title: MULTIPLE RESPONSES OF THE ICHTHYOFAUNA TO ANTROPOGENIC STRESSORS IN A HIGHLY URBANIZED NEOTROPICAL BASIN
presentations.abstract: Urbanization is one of the most important contemporary anthropogenic stressors, leading to profound alterations in ecosystems. However, studies addressing the multiple responses of aquatic biodiversity to urbanization are still incipient in Neotropical freshwaters. Here, we investigated changes in fish populations and communities along gradients of environmental degradation in streams (N = 11) from a highly urbanized watershed in southeastern Brazil. We detected morphological deformities in species such as the guppy Poecilia reticulata, with 20% of individuals sampled in streams draining industrial areas exhibiting lordosis. At the community level, despite a higher richness of native species (75% of the ichthyofauna), 80% of total numerical abundance was accounted for non-native species in the basin, a pattern consistent with predictions of the Urban Stream Syndrome. The number of inhabitants without access to sewage treatment, used as a proxy for sewage load in the streams, had a positive effect on non-native species richness (R² = 0.29; p = 0.04). For native fish species, both richness (R² = 0.66; p = 0.002) and abundance (R² = 0.55; p = 0.006) showed a strong decline along the urbanization gradient (expressed as % urban area upstream from each sampling site), highlighting how intense changes driven by urban landscapes pose a threat to the maintenance of aquatic biodiversity. We expect this study represents an important step toward understanding the effects of urban degradation on freshwater fish populations and communities from the Global South.

presentations.title: Impact of Microscale Landscape Heterogeneity on Urban Reservoir Water Quality: A Regression Study in the Ibirité Lagoon Watershed, Brazil
presentations.abstract: The Ibirité Lagoon, an urban reservoir in the Belo Horizonte Metropolitan Region, experiences accelerated eutrophication and high sediment input driven by rapid anthropogenic expansion and Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) changes. Understanding peri-urban dynamics requires quantifying how LULC influences local hydro-limnological degradation. This study examines, at a micro-watershed scale, the quantitative relationship among LULC patterns, sanitation coverage, and key water quality parameters in the Lagoon’s tributaries. The approach integrates LULC data and periodic in situ measurements in a GIS environment. Dependent variables include Turbidity, Total Suspended Solids (TSS), and nutrient concentrations (Total Phosphorus – TP and Total Nitrogen – TN). Independent variables include upstream LULC percentages (residential/industrial areas, bare soils, agriculture) and sewage coverage in each sub-basin. Multiple Regression Models (MRM) are being used to assess relationship strength. Preliminary findings show that specific LULC classes are statistically significant, and that high landscape heterogeneity helps reveal distinct microscale cause-and-effect patterns. Intensified urban occupation and low sanitation coverage correlate strongly with increased diffuse inputs of sediments and nutrients, reflecting the reservoir’s advanced trophic state. This initial assessment of peri-urban landscape influence supports the development of targeted territorial management strategies to mitigate LULC impacts and preserve the ecological functionality of the Ibirité Lagoon.

presentations.title: Investigating how Urbanization-Linked Salinity Variation Shapes Tissue-Specific Microbiomes in the Gulf killifish, Fundulus grandis
presentations.abstract: Coastal urbanization has increased rapidly in recent decades, altering key abiotic factors in coastal ecosystems. These changes, including intensified salinity fluctuations during precipitation events, can vary across sites and shape local biota. The Gulf killifish (Fundulus grandis) is a euryhaline species uniquely found in both urbanized and natural coastal habitats in the Gulf, making it an ideal model for studying the consequences of salinity variability from different avenues. While recent and ongoing research by the Bernal lab at Auburn University has explored the molecular responses to osmotic stress, the role of salinity variability in shaping the killifish-associated microbiome remains obscure. Here, we investigate how tissue (e.g., skin, gill, and gut) microbial community structure of F. grandis is shaped by salinity across seasons using amplicon sequencing. This ongoing study compares microbial communities across four populations with exposure to different levels of coastal urbanization and offers a multi-tissue perspective that could establish a framework for understanding host–microbe interactions for euryhaline species. Results will advance our understanding of whether and how salinity influences microbial community structure and will provide insight into bacterial communities that may constitute osmotic plasticity in the euryhaline Gulf killifish.

presentations.title: CONSEQUENCES OF CONTROL: AQUATIC CARBON DYNAMICS IN A NEWLY ESTABLISHED URBAN FLOOD CONTROL PROJECT IN TORONTO, CANADA
presentations.affiliation: University of Toronto | Royal Ontario Museum
presentations.abstract: Globally, cities are being forced to respond to the increasing threat of flooding and storm damage, as the repercussions of extreme weather events are amplified by climate change and the continued development of impermeable urban surfaces. In response, many metropolitan areas are adopting natural climate solutions that modify and redirect urban hydrology to reduce flood risk. One such example—considered by some to be perhaps the largest urban climate adaptation project on the planet—is the Port Lands Flood Protection Project, including the newly opened Biidaasige Park, located at the mouth of the Don River in Toronto, Canada. This initiative has highlighted the resilience of ecosystems and urban benefits from naturalized flood protection efforts. However, the consequences of such projects to aquatic carbon cycling dynamics are rarely considered. We present aquatic metabolism data from newly constructed flowing and still-water environments at Biidaasige Park. Pairing diel oxygen curve analyses with water chemistry data and experiments in planktonic and biofilm productivity, we reveal aquatic ecosystem dynamics within such developments, contributing data that can guide government agencies and stakeholders when evaluating the broader implications of new directions in urban design.

presentations.title: URBANIZATION AND SEWAGE POLLUTION DRIVE FUNCIONAL HOMOGENIZATION OF FISH ASSEMBLAGES IN NEOTROPICAL HEADWATER STREAMS
presentations.abstract: Urbanization represents a severe threat to the ecological integrity of neotropical stream ecosystems. We evaluated the effects of land use (% urbanization) and organic pollution (sewage access) on the functional structure of fish assemblages in the Ibirité Reservoir basin, Brazil. Fish were sampled in 10 streams during dry (September 2024) and rainy (April 2025) seasons. Species were classified into trophic guilds (Omnivores, Invertivores, Carnivores, Algivores, and Iliophages) and we applied a Community Weighted Mean (CWM) approach to assess shifts in functional composition along the degradation gradient. Linear models were used to test the relationship between environmental predictors and trophic structure. Sewage load positively predicted the dominance of Omnivores (R2=0.23, p=0.04), primarily driven by the proliferation of tolerant species like Poecilia reticulata in impacted sites. In contrast, specialized guilds such as Algivores displayed a negative trend in response to sewage (R2=0.20, p=0.06) and urbanization, indicating a loss of grazing functions. Invertivores and Iliophages showed no significant associations with urban stressors. The replacement of specialized traits by generalist strategies suggests a functional simplification of the community and a potential impairment of ecosystem services, such as benthic cleaning and nutrient cycling. These findings indicate that urban stressors act as environmental filters, favoring tolerant generalists and leading to biotic homogenization.

presentations.title: Urbanization and Infrastructure Development as Drivers of Reservoir Shrinkage: A Multi-Temporal Geospatial Analysis of Soil Movement and Water Surface Dynamics
presentations.abstract: The preservation of reservoir ecosystems is a critical challenge, often undermined by anthropogenic disturbances in catchments. This study investigates the direct link between urban sprawl, major infrastructure developments, including earthworks from road construction, and the retraction of reservoir surface area. The objective is to develop a predictive geospatial model to estimate rates of water body shrinkage based on multi-temporal observations of influencing factors. The method involves a sequential four-stage process: First, soil movement dynamics are quantified through the analysis of historic aerial/orbital images spanning the last five decades. This long-term temporal series is crucial for understanding baseline and rates of erosion. Second, the "peak moment" of sediment transport is identified for each sub-catchment, correlating these periods with specific phases of intense urban development and infrastructure deployment. Third, a predictive geographic model based on weights of evidence is constructed using the derived soil movement and historic water area data. Finally, this calibrated model is applied to the new proposed Belo Horizonte Metropolitan Ring Road to estimate the projected volume of soil to predict its impact on water surface retraction. This research presents a robust quantitative framework for evaluating the direct impact of sediment loading driven by human activity on the limnological characteristics and volumetric capacity of freshwater reservoirs. Findings are essential for urban planning, environmental impact assessment, and the effective management of water resources in rapidly developing regions.

presentations.title: HIGH RATES OF SULFIDE PRODUCTION IN A SHALLOW, SEASONALLY-STRATIFIED URBAN LAKE
presentations.abstract: Anoxic and sulfide-rich (euxinic) environments have played a significant role in the history of Earth. Today, they are restricted to specific habitats, such as anoxic fjords, mangrove sediments, meromictic lakes, and marine basins (e.g. the Black Sea). Here, we report high rates of S2- production in an urban gravel pit, in Lake Salbker South, Germany. In 2023 and 2024, the hypolimnion became anoxic and H2S production started within one day of the onset of stratification. After 27 and 16 days, 570 and 240 mmol S²⁻ m⁻² had accumulated, corresponding to production rates of 21 and 15 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹. We interpret the high S2- production by a convergence of three essential factors: (i) the supply of sulfate-rich groundwater (~20 mmol L-1) originating from Zechstein formations, (ii) the high availability of phosphorus in the lake (~0.28 mg L-1), which causes the accumulation of cyanobacterial biomass to levels at the upper end of the trophic scale (Chla 100-400 µg L-1) and results in strong diurnal epilimnetic O2 fluctuations (0 to >20 mg L⁻¹), and (iii) the warm temperatures in the shallow hypolimnion, which are maintained by the complex morphometry that impedes wind-driven mixing. Hypolimnetic S2- production rates are among the highest documented in marine and limnetic environments, though they are surpassed in hypersaline alkaline systems. Nitrate absence during summer does not appear to limit the production of organic matter and S2- in this euxinic environment, as hypothesized earlier.

presentations.title: WALKING THE LINE OF STATISTICS AND SCIENCE COMMUNICATION WITH THE ADIRONDACK LAKE ASSESSMENT PROGRAM
presentations.abstract: The Adirondack Lake Assessment Program (ALAP) has been a pillar of science and stewardship for decades, serving the Adirondack Park’s six million acres of protected wilderness, abundance of freshwater resources, and local communities since 1997. As a collaborative effort between Protect the Adirondacks and the Paul Smith's College Adirondack Watershed Institute, ALAP is the largest community-led water quality monitoring program in the region, engaging hundreds of volunteers and dozens of lake associations each year. From a scientific perspective, the program’s goal is to use long term data to inform how lakes respond to environmental stressors like eutrophication, acid deposition, road salt, and climate change. However, ALAP also strives to promote community engagement through scientific monitoring and aspires to serve as an accessible data repository that residents, lake associations, and local governments can use to support water quality protection efforts. Although reports are regularly compiled and shared in support of these objectives, the accessibility of the reported information to the volunteers and communities the program serves has remained unclear. Could the traditional reporting style be improved upon to address this disconnect, making the data more applicable to both scientists and community members alike? As a pilot effort, using a combination of explanatory language and graphic design, the most recent comprehensive report detailing ALAP’s 26th sampling season was reformatted in an attempt to walk the line of scientific reporting and science communication.

presentations.title: CITIZEN SCIENCE & PARTICIPATORY ART: FINDING CONNECTIONS WHERE METHODS INTERSECT
presentations.abstract: Community/student workshops that combine careful observation of freshwater with collective participatory art create images that capture elements at precise moments in time. Gesturing toward BACI (before-after-control-impact) experiments in ecology, we ask participants to consider what before/after information their images might archive, and what might be possible to “know” or infer from them. Can artistically-generated products constitute scientifically-useful data? In a series of established and evolving workshops, we guide participants through the process of creating images exposed and developed by ambient light from the sun over a prolonged moment along, around, and within waterways. Camera-less prints are created by placing objects and materials in direct contact with analog, gelatin silver photographic paper. This method of slow, repeated observation and collation results in visuals that record characteristics of vegetation, sediment, rocks, and wood debris that comprise important habitat elements for aquatic species. Ideally, prints directly interact with the water itself by being fully or partially submerged during exposure. This direct, durational process emphasizes the deep time embedded within land and water continually re-shaped by disturbances, both observable and invisible. While comparisons to the scientifically-accepted practice of repeat photography are within easy reach, we are interested to explore questions around whether engaging in this process might capture something even more meaningful, deeper, or at least a bit different.

presentations.title: HOW TO RECOVER A (ONCE) MIGHTY RIVER? SUBMERGED AQUATIC VEGETATION COLLAPSE AND CITIZEN SCIENCE ACTIVATION IN THE MIDDLE ST. JOHNS RIVER, FLORIDA
presentations.abstract: The St. Johns River (SJR) in eastern Florida, USA, is a shallow, slow-flowing system often described as “a river of lakes.” Lentic and lotic portions of the middle SJR historically supported extensive submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) beds dominated by Vallisneria americana and, by the late 20th century, non-native Hydrilla verticillata. Over the past two decades, however, total SAV coverage in the middle SJR – including Lake George, the second largest lake in Florida – has collapsed by up to 99%, dramatically affecting wildlife and fisheries. Although government agencies have invested substantial resources into SAV research and restoration, there is broad agreement that these efforts have not produced sustained ecosystem recovery. In early 2024, a group of local anglers, recreationists, and business owners dissatisfied with agency methods, outcomes, and explanatory narratives formed a new citizen-science organization, Mighty River Recovery (MRR). Drawing on extensive historical knowledge and volunteer-led monitoring, MRR has advanced alternative hypotheses for ecosystem decline and potential recovery. Perhaps most contentiously, MRR has questioned longstanding aquatic plant management paradigms in the middle SJR and initiated citizen science-based monitoring of aquatic plant control impacts. The MRR case study, though still in its infancy, highlights both the promise of citizen science in generating new lines of inquiry outside traditional agency frameworks, as well as the daunting challenges of achieving the research rigor expected in scientific and regulatory contexts.

presentations.title: Buoys become bridges: Engaging communities with real-time Instruments in the Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Based out of the University of Windsor and part of the Global Water Futures Observatories (GWFO), the Real-Time Aquatic Ecosystem Observation Network (RAEON) provides infrastructure, staff, and data management support for integrated Great Lakes research. RAEON deploys real-time sensing instruments, including buoys and autonomous underwater vehicles, to support the development of an early warning system for harmful algae blooms in the western Lake Erie basin. Data are open and publicly available on the Great Lakes Observing System (GLOS)’s Seagull platform. However, openness alone does not guarantee use or impact. Data collected by buoys, gliders, and other real-time sensing systems are critical for understanding lake dynamics, yet typically operate far from shore and out of public view. To address this, we developed a community science and public engagement initiative with a goal of reframing freshwater monitoring instruments as public engagement and science communication tools, bringing them into public spaces, parks, schools, community events, and art exhibits. Hands-on encounters create opportunities to tell different stories about Great Lakes health, solicit qualitative insights from communities, and broaden pathways for participation in community-based water monitoring and data collection. Using these instruments as engagement tools facilitates multisided knowledge exchanges that increase public awareness of Great Lakes research, while also providing opportunities for researchers to gain insight into community priorities, questions, and concerns.

presentations.title: NOT JUST LAKES: INTEGRATING LIMNOLOGY INTO COMMUNITY CONNECTIONS AND NEW DIRECTIONS IN URBAN DESIGN
presentations.abstract: Communities around the world are rapidly transforming themselves in ways that reflect both climate change mitigation (e.g., upgrading infrastructure to improve feasibility of net zero goals) and adaptation (e.g., reengineering aquatic landscapes for improved resilience from flooding events). However, the role that limnologists can play in helping communities navigate such changes is often overlooked, both within and beyond our scientific community. In this talk, I will present potential opportunities and strategies for limnologists interested in this liminal space, drawn from my own experiences carrying forward a research focus on aquatic metabolism into a community and climate-oriented curatorial position at Canada’s largest museum in the heart of Toronto. This will include insights associated with work on Crawford Lake, Ontario, which was announced in 2023 as the candidate “golden spike” of the proposed Anthropocene epoch, as well as more recent work in the newly opened Biidaasige Park in Toronto, which is located in what some have described as the largest urban climate adaptation project on the planet.

presentations.title: ASSESSING ARTIFICIAL AERATION AS A RESTORATION TOOL IN A SUBTROPICAL URBAN LAKE: LESSONS FROM URUGUAY’S FIRST WHOLE-LAKE EXPERIMENT
presentations.abstract: Artificial aeration is commonly applied to mitigate eutrophication by improving deep-water oxygen conditions and reducing internal phosphorus loading, yet its effectiveness in relatively deep urban lakes of subtropical regions remains understudied. Here, we evaluate Uruguay’s first aeration-based restoration, implemented in Lake Javier, a 10 m-deep eutrophic lake in southern South America, using a four-year Before-After Control-Impact design including an unmanipulated reference lake. Monitoring encompassed thermal structure, dissolved oxygen, nutrients, transparency, and chlorophyll-a, combining periodic sampling with high-frequency automated monitoring. Aeration partially reduced thermal stability but failed to maintain persistent hypolimnetic oxygen. Total phosphorus decreased substantially between 2020 and 2024, while total nitrogen increased slightly, reinforcing phosphorus limitation. Phytoplankton, dominated by cyanobacteria, exhibited pronounced temporal fluctuations, reflecting the resilience of the eutrophic state despite improved nutrient conditions. This initiative involved local community, municipal government, and academia, integrating scientific and management perspectives. As the first whole-lake aeration experiment in Uruguay, it provides regionally novel empirical evidence and emphasizes the importance of adaptive, multi-scale strategies to enhance the sustainability and social relevance of urban lake restoration under changing climatic and anthropogenic pressures.

presentations.title: ASSESSING MICROALGAL POTENTIAL FOR DOMESTIC WASTEWATER REMEDIATION: GROWTH DYNAMICS AND NUTRIENT REMOVAL EFFICIENCY
presentations.abstract: Freshwater is an essential resource for the survival of humanity and biodiversity. However, improper waste disposal activities have generated environmental and public health impacts. In the face of this crisis, the development of technological methods and nature-based solutions for the treatment of wastewater has become essential. This study aimed to evaluate the capacity of microalgae to remove contaminants from domestic wastewater. The microalga genera Chlorella was cultivated for a period of 14 days using domestic wastewater, along with separate negative and positive controls using deionized water and BG-11 medium, respectively. Optical density and pH were monitored daily in the three cultures to evaluate algal growth. Turbidity was measured daily in the wastewater culture. The concentrations of phosphorus, total nitrogen, ammonium, nitrate and chemical oxygen demand in the wastewater culture were evaluated before and after treatment. The microalgae presented steady cell and pH growth in the BG-11 and H2O mediums. In the wastewater culture, there were fluctuations in growth and pH for the first 8 days, before falling abruptly and subsequently maintaining a flat growth rate and returning to fluctuating in pH. The wastewater culture presented a removal efficiency of 99.27% for phosphorus, 33.84% for total nitrogen, 52% for ammonium, and 99.99% for chemical oxygen demand. However, nitrate increased by 164.8%. These findings contribute to limnological applications of biotechnology and support the advancement of nature-based solutions for wastewater management.

presentations.title: Linking Watershed Socioeconomics to Lake Molecular Chemistry: A Novel Framework Using Census Data and FT-ICR MS
presentations.abstract: Effective lake management requires a mechanistic understanding of how human activities drive changes in water quality, moving beyond simple correlations to actionable, process-based insights. This study proposes and applies a novel diagnostic framework designed to achieve this by integrating spatial watershed data, census-derived socioeconomic variables (e.g., income, population density), and advanced molecular-level analysis via Fourier Transform Ion Cyclotron Resonance Mass Spectrometry (FT-ICR MS). This framework was applied to a robust dataset comprising 40 temperate-to-boreal North American lakes, with water sampling conducted across five distinct seasons to capture temporal variability. By directly coupling the molecular-level "fingerprint" of lake organic matter with socioeconomic data, we test the hypothesis that human land use and population density are not just correlated with, but directly shape, the biogeochemical environment of a lake. We aim to explore whether socioeconomic factors can serve as predictors for shifts in DOM chemodiversity. This integrative approach is anticipated to provide managers with a powerful and nuanced diagnostic tool. By identifying the specific molecular signatures associated with different watershed pressures, it can guide targeted monitoring efforts towards the most significant pollution sources and inform the development of precise, cost-effective management strategies for lake restoration and long-term health.

presentations.title: BLOWING IN THE WIND: INSIGHTS FROM LONG-TERM SENSOR DATA ON IMPACTS OF WIND IN A SHALLOW DRINKING WATER RESERVOIR
presentations.abstract: Wind is a critical driver of physical and biogeochemical dynamics in lakes and reservoirs, shaping mixing patterns, stratification, and nutrient distribution. In drinking water reservoirs, wind-driven processes are particularly consequential because they influence raw water quality and the risk of harmful algal blooms, creating significant treatment challenges. High-intensity wind events can resuspend bottom sediments of shallow lakes increasing turbidity and modifying light conditions, while also releasing sediment-bound nutrients that may stimulate algal growth. Conversely, periods of low wind promote strong water column stability, creating favorable conditions for bloom-forming phytoplankton to establish and persist. In this study, we use insights from ten years of buoy-based monitoring in Buffalo Pound Lake, Canada – a shallow drinking water reservoir – to characterize the changes associated with wind-driven sediment resuspension, particularly related to bloom formation and progression, and assess how quickly the lake returns to antecedent conditions after these events. We further pair these in-lake observations with long-term meteorological records to estimate the historical frequency of critical winds and evaluate whether sediment resuspension events have become more common over recent decades. Preliminary data analysis has shown that 245-315° winds above a speed threshold of ~30 km/h are linked to high turbidity events. Other lake variables, including water temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen saturation, exhibit same-day responses, but while some recover within a few days, others require longer to re-establish their baseline state.

presentations.title: COMPARING SEDIMENTS AND POREWATERS OF TWO SCOTTISH UPLAND DRINKING WATER RESERVOIRS WITH PERIODICALLY ELEVATED MANGANESE CONCENTRATIONS
presentations.abstract: Elevated concentrations of manganese (Mn), a trace element linked with human neurological conditions, pose a growing threat to drinking water quality globally. In Scotland, several drinking water reservoirs experience seasonally high concentrations, as sediments release Mn into the overlying waters. The exact controls of these releases remain unknown. We compare sediments from two reservoirs with differing Mn patterns. Loch Bradan experiences periodic summer-autumn peaks in both dissolved and total Mn concentrations, whereas Daer Reservoir shows episodic elevated total Mn but rarely elevated dissolved Mn. Sediments were collected by gravity corer, then dried and milled. Total Mn was determined by a HBF4 digest and analysed by ICP-MS. Mn’s spatial distribution within the sediment matrix was explored by SEM-EDX and solid phase speciation by XPS. Porewater Mn fractionation and water–sediment-interface associations were investigated by Size Exclusion Chromatography and FT-ICR-MS. We found elevated Mn concentrations in upper porewaters and sediments of both reservoirs. Truly dissolved Mn was marginally more abundant in Daer’s than Loch Bradan’s porewaters. Sediments were highly organic, and large organic-Mn complexes in the colloidal fraction are dominant in Loch Bradan’s surface sediment porewaters. The detailed characterisation of sediments and porewaters improves our understanding of Mn release mechanisms and the forms entering overlying waters. This information is crucial for understanding conditions triggering mobilisation events and the fate of Mn in the water column.

presentations.title: Setting priority straight : the use of geochemical landscapes to identify integrative conservation targets
presentations.abstract: SETTING PRIORITY STRAIGHT : THE USE OF GEOCHEMICAL LANDSCAPES TO IDENTIFY INTEGRATIVE CONSERVATION TARGETS Émilie Pastore1, Eric Harvey1 and Raphaël Proulx11. Département des sciences de l'environnement, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières Current indices to identify conservation priority are generally based on the presence of specific species (fine filter) or aim at regional representativity in geostructure (coarse filter). Both approaches generally lead to the protection of a restricted number of species while ignoring the local variations in ecological processes that sustain biodiversity in the first place. As such, a call was made by experts for the development of more integrative indices that could integrate biodiversity, but also its supporting functions (biotic interactions, energy flows, etc.). The goal of my project is to evaluate the potential of using geochemical element composition as a new index for conservation priority by testing whether geochemical hotspots, that is sites with the most unique elemental signature, are also biodiversity hotspots. To do so, we will use an extensive public dataset, produced from mining prospection, on the geochemistry of streams to build an “elemental community matrix” from which we will identify streams with unique composition of geochemical elements. The unique signature will be determined with a local contribution to beta diversity (LCBD) analysis, which calculates, based on a data matrix of geochemical elements, the contribution of different zones to the variation of geochemical element composition of a predetermined area. In the summer of 2026, 20 to 30 streams along a unicity gradient will be sampled to identify potential links with the biodiversity present (macro-invertebrates and diatoms).

presentations.title: Warming promotes picophytoplankton and increases the carbon use efficiency of the Elbe Estuary during summer
presentations.abstract: Warming in temperate estuaries affects primary production, oxygen dynamics, and plankton structure, yet impacts on microbial communities in the dynamic, human-influenced Elbe estuary remain unclear. We conducted a four-week indoor mesocosm experiment with natural plankton from the tidal freshwater reach under +0 °C, +2 °C, and +4 °C scenarios. We measured phytoplankton community composition, as well as viral, bacterial, and heterotrophic nanoflagellate biomass, alongside whole-community gross primary production and carbon use efficiency. All treatments showed a succession from centric diatoms to chain-forming cyanobacteria, but the cyanobacterial increase and resulting microphytoplankton biomass were lower at +4°C. Picoeukaryote and picocyanobacterial biomass increased at +2 °C compared to the control, and picoeukaryote abundance also rose significantly at +4 °C, whereas cryptophyte biomass declined at both warming levels. Viral-like particles increased over time but showed significantly less increase at +4 °C, while bacteria and heterotrophic nanoflagellates showed no significant temperature response. Mass-specific gross primary production was highest in picophytoplankton and exhibited limited warming sensitivity; carbon-use efficiency remained stable. Together, these results show that a month of warming reshapes microbial size structure and viral dynamics in Elbe estuary plankton communities without diminishing overall carbon-processing capacity. Such shifts in microbial composition under warming may influence food-web pathways and biogeochemical cycling in temperate estuaries

presentations.title: Individual and joint effects of heatwave and resuspension on the aquatic food web depend on nutrient loadings: implications for shallow lake restoration
presentations.abstract: Shallow lakes provide many vital ecosystem services, particularly when dominated by submerged macrophytes. However, these lakes face increasing ecological degradation due to multiple stressors, including eutrophication and climate change. These stressors can occur individually or in combination, and in the latter case, they may interact, complicating ecosystem management and restoration efficacy. Despite their ecological importance, the combined effects of these stressors—and potential recovery trajectories after their removal—remain poorly understood. Using outdoor mesocosms, we investigated the individual and interactive effects of heatwaves and resuspension on aquatic food webs under low (oligotrophic) and high (eutrophic) nutrient conditions, along with their legacy effects post-disturbance. Our results showed that heatwave significantly increased the macrophyte cover percentage in the disturbance stage under oligotrophic conditions (i.e., low nutrient loading), suggesting a positive effect of heatwaves on macrophyte growth. In contrast, the combined effects of heatwaves and resuspension significantly enhanced the phytoplankton biomass (measured as chlorophyll a) while reducing the macrophyte cover, indicating strong stressor interactions that are positive for phytoplankton but negative for macrophytes. Notably, heatwaves exerted legacy effects: under eutrophic conditions, chlorophyll a remained elevated during recovery (positive legacy). Our results revealed that resuspension alone increased gastropod density during the disturbance phase under eutrophic conditions, while heatwaves left a positive legacy on copepod biomass in oligotrophic systems. Additionally, resuspension enhanced trophic transfer efficiency in the oligotrophic state. Our findings demonstrate that stressor effects and legacy responses are highly context-dependent, varying with nutrient status and food-web components. Our results highlight the need for multi-stressor management approaches to ad

presentations.title: LIGHT SPECTRUM MATTERS: INTERACTIVE EFFECTS OF LIGHT AND NUTRIENTS ON PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES AND TROPHIC TRANSFER
presentations.abstract: Light is a major driver of trophic energy transfer from phytoplankton to zooplankton, and while the impact of light intensity is well investigated, the role of the light spectrum for trophic transfer is unclear. Underwater, both the available light intensity and wavelength spectrum change with depth, affecting phytoplankton’s efficiency in light use. We conducted in-situ incubations to determine the combined effects of nutrients (ambient, enriched), water depth (0.5 m and 2.5 m), and light quality (full, blue, green, red spectrum) on a natural lake phytoplankton community by analyzing the community structure and biochemical composition (nutrient stoichiometry and fatty acids). The field experiment was combined with a subsequent laboratory study to determine food quality impacts on Daphnia pulex growth through alterations in phytoplankton food quantity and quality parameters. We found that light spectrum influences both the species composition and biochemistry of phytoplankton communities, highly dependent on water depth and available nutrients. The light spectrum was important when light, but not nutrients, limited phytoplankton growth. In addition, abiotic factors altered the prevalent growth constraints of Daphnia from phosphorus limitation to limitation by essential fatty acids. Hence, the effects of different light spectra were propagating from the primary producer level to the consumers. We demonstrate that the light spectrum is a significant component of the abiotic environment that influences both plankton dynamics and trophic transfer in aquatic ecosystems.

presentations.title: Advancing In Situ Methods for Studying Microplastic Fate in Freshwater Sediments
presentations.affiliation: Faculty of Science and Mathematics, University of Nis, Serbia
presentations.abstract: Understanding vertical microplastic (MP) transport in freshwater sediments is essential for evaluating their mobility toward groundwater under hydrodynamic and bioturbation-driven influences. This study examined MP movement in karst lake sediments using the In Situ Microplastics Assessment System (ISMAS), a cylindrical in situ mesocosm with mesh-covered openings that allow natural water exchange while retaining particles. Each unit contained natural sediment and mock population created with 100 Chironomus riparius larvae. Two treatments received secondary polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) MPs (>500–50 μm), while a third served as a biological control. Systems were deployed for three months in Lake Šasko (Montenegro) and retrieved by divers to minimize disturbance. Four sediment cores per unit were extracted and frozen in the field, sectioned into 2 cm layers, and processed using ZnCl₂ density separation. Results indicate consistent vertical MP movement in both polymer treatments, with particles largely retained in upper layers but detectable across deeper sections. No major differences between PE and PP were observed at this stage. Ongoing analyses will refine depth-dependent patterns and clarify contributions of hydrodynamics and bioturbators. These findings advance empirical understanding of MP mobility and retention in freshwater sediments, providing needed evidence for assessing their environmental fate.

presentations.title: SUCCESSION, GRAZING IMPACT AND SELECTIVITY OF MICROZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES IN RESPONSE TO A SUMMER HEAT WAVE IN THE ELBE RIVER ESTUARY
presentations.abstract: Microzooplankton exert strong grazing pressure on their prey and their activity highly depends on temperature, making it crucial to study the effects of heatwaves, especially in nutrient-rich estuaries. In a 4-week indoor mesocosm experiment, we investigated how three warming scenarios affected the microzooplankton dynamics of a summer community from the Elbe estuary. Sampling occurred every other day, with weekly dilution experiments to analyze growth rates of phyto- and microzooplankton and grazing rates of micro- and mesozooplankton. Our findings showed a significant decline in overall biomass across all treatments over time, independent of temperature. Notably, dinoflagellate biomass decreased significantly at highest temperatures. Warming also reduced richness, evenness, and diversity of the microZP community, with stronger reduction effects at higher temperatures. As a result, microZP communities diverged over time. Among the environmental factors analyzed, pico- and microphytoplankton abundance, dissolved oxygen, and temperature were the most influential in shaping community structure. Growth rates were strongly altered by temperature, with varying responses between plankton groups. Overall, growth rates of pico- and nanoplankton declined over time, with few exceptions. Grazing rates also declined over time in all treatments, though enhanced grazing rates for picocyanobacteria and picophytoplankton were found at highest temperatures. Heatwaves have the potential to strongly alter the plankton community of the Elbe during summer months.

presentations.title: ASSESSING THE IMPACT OF NUTRIENT IMBALANCE ON MULTI-TROPHIC LEVELS IN AN AQUATIC MESOCOSM EXPERIMENT
presentations.abstract: Human activities have altered the nitrogen (N): Phosphorus (P) ratio, with a faster increase of anthropogenic N inputs compared to P inputs (see Peñuelas and Sardans, The global nitrogen-phosphorus imbalance, Science, 2022). Peñuelas and Sardans report a global N:P increase from about 19:1 in the 1980s to 30:1 in 2020. To investigate the impact of this N:P imbalance for aquatic ecosystems we performed an outdoor mesocosm experiment in the North West of the UK. The aim of the experiment was to establish four replicates of N:P ratios of 10, 50 and 100, in addition to a control, and maintain them for 6 months (April to November) while monitoring chemical, physical and biological parameters. Using a multi-method approach we characterised changes in abundance and diversity in response to N:P across all taxonomic groups from bacteria to macroinvertebrates, in addition to cladoceran and copepod size measurements and stoichiometry. The N:P ratio impacted across all taxonomic levels, causing shifts in both abundance and diversity, with zooplankton size analysis currently ongoing. Cladocerans and copepods managed to maintain homeostasis at some of the higher N:P ratios.

presentations.title: QUANTIFYING THE CONTRIBUTION OF ZOOPLANKTON DIEL VERTICAL MIGRATION TO DOWNWARD CARBON FLUXES IN STRATIFIED LAKES USING A MESOCOSM-BASED APPROACH
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton exhibit diel vertical migration (DVM) in stratified lakes, residing in deeper waters during the day to avoid fish predation and migrating to surface waters at night to feed on phytoplankton. Zooplankton are expected to exhibit more pronounced DVM behavior in lakes with higher predation risk from planktivorous fish. However, zooplankton functional groups differ in their evasion capabilities, which may drive diverse behavioral responses to planktivory. Zooplankton DVM contributes to the downward transport of organic carbon to deep water layers and sediments in the ocean, but DVM-mediated carbon flux has not been quantified in lakes. We manipulated planktivorous fish densities in 14 experimental enclosures (9 m diameter, 20 m deep) in Lake Stechlin, Germany for six weeks in spring 2023 to investigate differences in DVM behavior of zooplankton functional groups and quantify impacts of DVM on carbon cycling. DVM was quantified using AI-supported high-resolution in situ video (modular Deep-focus Plankton Imager). Our experiment revealed that larger individuals and taxa with weaker evasion capabilities increased DVM extent in the presence of planktivores. We applied models of zooplankton respiration, fecal pellet production, and depth-integrated community metabolism, and measured particulate and dissolved carbon concentrations in the water column and sediment traps to explore how DVM drives carbon flux dynamics through changes in respiration and excretion across time and depth. Our results provide a first quantification of DVM-mediated downward carbon fluxes in lakes.

presentations.title: BIG TROUBLES IN LITTLE LAKES: BOTTOM-UP AND TOP-DOWN CONTROLS DRIVE CYANOBACTERIAL BLOOM DYNAMICS IN MESOCOSMS
presentations.abstract: (A.Grenier-Journe@nioo.knaw.nl) Harmful cyanobacterial blooms represent a major ecological and socioeconomical threat to inland waters around the world. Temperature and nutrients play a key role in driving cyanobacterial bloom dynamics, but it remains a challenge to separate individual from combined effects on natural communities. To elucidate the individual and combined effects of warming and nutrients on cyanobacterial bloom dynamics, we conducted a mesocosm experiment with natural cyanobacterial communities from spring to autumn 2025, and exposed these to ambient versus warmed (+5°C) as well as nitrogen-limited (TN:TP = 2) versus balanced conditions (TN:TP = 16). We hypothesized that warming would lead to faster cyanobacterial growth, but also stronger top-down control, and that nitrogen limitation will benefit N2-fixing cyanobacteria, particularly when combined with warming. We observed cyanobacterial blooms in all tanks during the late spring, although the timing and intensity of these blooms were different between treatments. For example, nitrogen-limited mesocosms experienced blooms one to two weeks later than the nutrient-replete mesocosms, with lower cyanobacterial biomass. Moreover, during summer, cyanobacterial biomass dropped substantially and was likely driven by top-down control including zooplankton grazing. Overall, we observed that warming and nutrients influenced cyanobacterial dynamics directly during the early stages of the experiment, and later indirectly by altering multiple top-down control factors.

presentations.title: Bottom-up and top-down control of arctic phytoplankton community dynamics in mesocosm experiments
presentations.abstract: Major transformations in the Arctic Ocean (AO) hydrosphere and cryosphere are reshaping phytoplankton dynamics. Increasing Atlantic inflows are introducing warmer waters depleted in silicate, while the ongoing reduction in sea-ice extent and duration is lengthening the potential growing season. These changes alter phytoplankton phenology, leading to earlier nutrient exhaustion and modifying the timing and strength of phytoplankton-zooplankton interactions. As a result, both bottom-up and top-down controls are likely to shift, affecting phytoplankton assemblages, growth, and physiological performance. To explore these combined stressors, we conducted two complementary experiments targeting different phases of the productive season. In spring, a controlled mesocosm experiment at Qikiqtarjuaq manipulated two key environmental drivers, silicate availability and grazing intensity, to examine their interactive effects on emerging phytoplankton communities in 180-L mesocosms. Later, at the end of the productive season, surface phytoplankton assemblages were collected in the Canadian Arctic Archipelago during the CCGS Amundsen expedition and incubated for 12 days in 18-L on-deck mesocosms. Across both experiments, we tracked changes in community structure, biomass accumulation, and photophysiological responses. Together, these experiments offer new insights into how phytoplankton respond to concurrent environmental changes in the AO and contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms driving shifts in Arctic phytoplankton communities amidst a rapidly changing climate.

presentations.title: Investigating the impact of environmental character on dissolved organic nutrient uptake by freshwater biota using mesocosm experiments
presentations.abstract: Multiple anthropogenic stressors are causing rapid freshwater ecosystem decline, driving increased nutrient fluxes to freshwaters (particularly carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus), promoting harmful algal blooms, excessive macrophyte growth and decline in biodiversity. Organic nutrient fractions can be the dominant fraction in oligotrophic freshwaters (>80% of the total nutrient load), comprise at least 20% of the total nutrient load in eutrophic freshwaters, and are highly bioavailable to microbial and primary producer groups. Whilst the impacts of inorganic nutrient enrichment on freshwater biota have been widely researched, there is a less focus on how organic nutrient fraction composition and environment interact to influence the rates and pathways of dissolved organic matter (DOM) uptake in freshwater ecosystems. Here, we conducted three stable isotope dosing experiments in replicate mesocosms in streams with differing underlying chemistries (chalk, clay and peat) under ambient conditions, and under experimentally altered streamflow and warming conditions (+2.3oC, based on RCP 6.0). Results suggest different patterns of 13C and 15N uptake according to DOM chemistry, similarities in bulk 13C15N nutrient uptake rates regardless of environmental character, changes in uptake rates under climate change, and organic nutrient uptake at rates equal to or in excess of inorganic nutrient uptake rates. Further work currently underway will determine gene x environment interactions controlling relative nutrient use efficiency and metabolic responses to these differing DOM chemistries.

presentations.title: TROPHIC INTERACTIONS AND NUTRIENT STOICHIOMETRY, RATHER THAN WARMING, SHAPE MESOZOOPLANKTON DYNAMICS IN THE ELBE ESTUARY
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Marine Ecosystem and Fisheries Sciences (IMF), University of Hamburg
presentations.abstract: Two mesocosm experiments were carried out to explore how warming, nutrient stoichiometry, and the presence of zooplankton influence plankton communities and trophic interactions in the Elbe estuary water column. In the first experiment, conducted over four weeks in summer 2024 with ambient, +2 °C, and +4 °C treatments, the mesozooplankton community consistently shifted from copepods toward cladocerans. This transition occurred in all temperature treatments, suggesting that warming by itself was not responsible for the change. Instead, alterations in the lower trophic levels point to prey availability (phytoplankton and microzooplankton) as a likely driver. A second mesocosm study in spring 2025 manipulated N:P ratios (Ambient, 16:1, 32:1, and 64:1) and included initial mesozooplankton additions in half of the tanks. Stable-isotope measurements (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) revealed enriched seston signatures and clear separation between producers and consumers under Redfield and moderately P-limited conditions, whereas the most P-limited treatments produced more depleted baselines and changed the spacing among trophic levels. When mesozooplankton were added, seston and consumer isotope values became more tightly clustered, indicating stronger trophic coupling under higher grazing pressure. Taken together, the two experiments demonstrate that nutrient stoichiometry and prey availability can, under certain circumstances, have a greater impact on short-term estuarine food-web structure than warming alone.
