presentations.title: THE WORLD’S OLDEST MAN-MADE BIOLOGICAL EXPERIMENT - ANCIENT STONE JARS AS NATURAL MESOCOSMS FOR STUDYING ECOLOGICAL STRUCTURE IN TEMPORARY AQUATIC ECOSYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Biological experiments are often short-lived, yet effects on communities and processes require time to emerge. Consequently, conclusions become more robust with longer durations. A striking real-world example can be found in central Laos, where thousands of large stone jars are scattered throughout the landscape. For ~2000 years, rainwater interacting with jar geology and varying tree cover has created unique and replicated aquatic ecosystems. Their clustered layout enables testing of ecological and evolutionary questions. Here, we report how these ancient mesocosms can be used to test ecosystem responses to local abiotic variation and disturbance. The jars contained between 5 to 254 liters, but the capacity of the jars was substantially larger (from about 45 to over 1,000 liters). We show that tree cover dominates every jar ecosystem’s state, with variations in tree cover density creating gradients in oxygen (O2) and nutrient concentrations among jar ecosystems. Litter contribution to aquatic ecosystems leads to higher nutrient levels and lower O2 concentration, even in systems under different long-term selection, in the oldest man-made ecosystems ever analyzed. The jar communities, obtained from environmental DNA, reveal very distinct composition in each jar shaped by abiotic conditions and a seemingly high degree of idiosyncrasy. This system provides a rare long-term perspective on how alternate wetting and drying together with terrestrial inputs influence aquatic ecosystems, providing insights into resilience, biodiversity, and ecosystem function in a changing world.

presentations.title: REDUCED METHANE EMISSIONS FROM POND MESOCOSMS USING A NOVEL AERATION TECHNOLOGY
presentations.abstract: Methane is the 3rd most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, contributing 28 times the impact of CO2 emissions on a per mass basis, therefore an ideal target gas to remove from the atmosphere. This study explores a tool to reduce methane emissions from aquatic systems. EM Fluids (EMF) has developed a solar-powered device that enhances gas mass transfer rates (e.g., like oxygen) across the air-water interface by ~2x with minimal energy input. The EMF device is hypothesized to increase methanotrophic activity, while decreasing methanogenic activity through increased oxygenation in the water column. Further, by increasing gas mass transfer, the treatment may aid in gas transport from ebullition into the water column, making it more readily available to methanotrophs. In lab water columns, methane mass transfer rates from bubbles into the water column significantly increased using the EMF device. In field-based pond mescosms, net methane emissions, net methane oxidation, and gas-mass transfer during ebullition were observed over the summer months; preliminary analyses found net methane emissions were reduced and net methane oxidation was increased under EMF treatment. The study provides insight into future applications of EMF technology in large freshwater bodies to reduce methane and overall greenhouse gas emissions.

presentations.title: Are laboratory-based stable isotope dosing experiments representative of field-based experiment outcomes when exploring the role of dissolved organic matter in freshwater ecosystems?
presentations.abstract: Within the EU, an estimated 1 billion tonnes of livestock-derived organic matter are produced annually. These products frequently enter streams via urination or defecation of livestock directly into streams or by leaching of manures and fertilisers through soil. Our recent research has shown that DOM can be highly bioavailable as a nutrient resource for freshwater biota. Investigating this uptake relative to inorganic nutrient uptake using stable isotope dosing in mesocosms is a novel approach developed by our group and applied in the field. Such experiments are often considered optimal as they run under natural ambient stream conditions, but they can be costly, requiring large amounts of staff time to set up and run. An alternative approach is to perform experiments in a controlled, laboratory setting which can minimize staff time needed to set up field-based equipment, while also allowing for tight control over key limiting factors such as temperature and light during the experiments. A common criticism is that such laboratory experiments do not represent natural conditions. Here, we report the results obtained from 2 stable isotope dosing experiments in replicate mesocosms conducted in both the field and laboratory in an attempt to investigate if laboratory-based experiments can produce findings comparable to those generated under field ambient conditions. Preliminary results suggest that similar patterns are observed in bulk 15N and 13C uptake in both biofilms and bryophytes in laboratory and field-based experiments, though absolute rates of uptake vary between the two approaches. Further work is currently underway to examine these patterns and determine how accurate laboratory mesocosm experiments are at simulating field-based experiments.

presentations.title: PHYTOPLANKTON CONTROLS ON NUTRIENT INFLUXES: EVIDENCE FROM FRESHWATER MESOCOSM SYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Interactions between nutrient availability and phytoplankton growth play a foundational role in shaping lake ecosystem function. However, climate change has disrupted the rate and timing of nutrient delivery to lakes via extreme storm events, drought, changing ice cover, and altered mixing regimes. Increased and variable nutrient loading can stimulate changes in phytoplankton biomass, community composition, and functional diversity. To investigate the impact of changing nutrient delivery timing on phytoplankton functional diversity and biomass, we deployed 16 pelagic (closed-bottom) mesocosms on Lake Champlain, Vermont, USA. We tested three nutrient addition treatment groups and a control over a 14 day period: all nutrients at once (pulse), daily additions (press) and sporadic (random pulse). Besides the control group, all treatments were increased by the same nutrient concentration by the end of the 14 days (84 µg NH4-N/L and NO3-N/L and 31 µg PO4/L), manipulating only the rate of delivery. The treatments were meant to simulate natural occurrences of nutrient pulses into lakes such as agricultural run-off, mild or extreme rain events, intermittent mixing, and snow melt. Preliminary results indicate variability in phytoplankton response between treatments, with ongoing analyses examining differences in metabolic carbon flux. These results provide insight into phytoplankton traits that are conserved across disturbance events and will facilitate prediction of community composition and functional diversity of phytoplankton communities with intensifying climate change.

presentations.title: USING A MESOCOSM EXPERIMENT TO TEST HOW AMBIENT PH INFLUENCES PHOSPHORUS SENSITIVITY OF CALCAREOUS PERIPHYTON MATS
presentations.abstract: Limestone-based freshwater ecosystems, such as the Everglades in South Florida, are dominated by CaCO3-rich periphyton mats that are sensitive to phosphorus (P) enrichment. Previous research shows pH also strongly influences diatom assemblages and is indistinguishable from P as a primary driver, highlighting the need for experiments to disentangle pH effects from P. Using a 10-day ex situ mesocosm experiment, we tested how ambient pH influences the P sensitivity of calcareous periphyton mats from Everglades National Park (EVER) and Big Cypress National Preserve (BICY). We applied low (6.0) and high (8.0) pH across a P gradient (0–1000 µg P/L) and assessed periphyton attributes and algal assemblage composition using a randomized block design. Low pH and higher P were associated with increased algal content (pH: β = 0.43, p = 0.03; P: β = 0.08, p = 0.04), mat total P (pH: β = 0.80; p < 0.001; P: β = 0.24; p < 0.001), and gross primary production on some days (Day 2 pH: β = 2.16, p = 0.002; Day 8 P: β = 0.42, p = 0.01) compared to the high pH and lower P treatments. The pH x P interaction was not significant, and neither pH, P, nor their interaction affected mat organic content or algal assemblage composition. EVER mats and assemblages responded more strongly to low pH and P than BICY mats, likely due to lower mineral content. These findings suggest low-pH environments may stimulate algal production and demonstrate the value of a mesocosm approach for testing stressor interactions that may be difficult to assess in observational studies or large-scale field experiments.

presentations.title: USING MESOCOSMS FOR MITIGATION STUDIES - FROM WASTE TO RESOURCE: RECYCLING OLIVE OIL WASTEWATER FOR SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE
presentations.affiliation: IGB - Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries
presentations.abstract: The environmental impact of olive mill wastewater (OMWW) is a major concern in the Mediterranean and other regions where olive oil production is a key economic activity. OMWW has a high organic load, high phenolic content, and low biodegradability, which can cause toxicity to aquatic life and disrupt freshwater ecosystems when discharged untreated, especially in areas experiencing water shortages. To address these concerns, the EU PRIMA CYCLOLIVE project (https://www.cyclolive.eu) explores sustainable strategies for recycling olive oil byproducts through both technological innovation and ecological assessment. One critical aim is to develop affordable, nature-based local solutions, such as constructed wetlands, to effectively treat both OMWW and solid waste in a cyclic, sustainable way. Here, we present the first results from mesocosm experiments designed to simulate OMWW discharge scenarios under standardized conditions and quantify the effects of both untreated and treated OMWW on aquatic ecosystems. The experiments serves to: 1) observe short-term responses of planktonic communities and water quality to OMWW inputs, allowing for a better understanding of its ecological effects under controlled, but near-real conditions, and 2) most importantly to investigate what mitigation potential establishing constructed wetlands could have to both decrease the detrimental effects of olive oil byproducts the aquatic environment, while also using the treated wastewater in intelligent low-cost irrigation systems, to mitigate the water shortages and support the farming communities.

presentations.title: THE IMPACT OF SALINIZATION AND WARMING ON SHALLOW LAKES THROUGH COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH BY EARLY-CAREER SCIENTISTS USING MESOCOSM STUDIES
presentations.affiliation: Federal Rural University of Pernambuco, WasserCluster Lunz and Middle East Technical University
presentations.abstract: Climate change and salinization are important threats to freshwater ecosystems, especially shallow lakes. To investigate the interactive effects of climate and salinity, we conducted three parallel mesocosm experiments in cold semiarid and warm Mediterranean Türkiye. Salinity was manipulated as a gradient (0-50 g/L) or as factorial treatments (4 and 40 g/L), combined with temperature treatments (ambient, heatwave, constant warming). In the first, an eight-month-long experiment with 16 different salinities (0-50 g/L), we found a unimodal response of key variables. Total nitrogen, phosphorus, chlorophyll a, alkalinity, and suspended solids increased with salinity. Water clarity peaked at 17 g/L, whereas it was lower at both low and high salinities in both climates. In the second experiment, lasting 8 weeks, we tested the impact of salinity (4 and 40 g/L) and a 2-week heatwave (+6 °C) across two climates. Higher salinity and a warmer climate enhanced phytoplankton biomass. The heatwave had negligible effects on key variables. The third experiment highlighted the stronger influence of higher temperature (+4.5 °C) on oxygen concentration, pH, and alkalinity, particularly in warmer climates and at salinity 40 g/L. All of these were made possible through the collaboration of more than 40 volunteers, interns, MSc and PhD students, supported by METU and TÜBİTAK, as well as 19 researchers supported by the EU-H2020 AQUACOSM-plus project. In conclusion, salinization is a critical stressor in shallow lakes, with its effects modulated by climate and temperature.

presentations.title: SALINIZATION SUPPRESSES EBULLITION AND LOWERS GLOBAL METHANE EMISSIONS FROM AQUATIC SYSTEMS
presentations.abstract: Aquatic ecosystems are the largest natural source of methane (CH4) to the atmosphere, yet their future contribution to the global CH4 budget remains uncertain. A key but overlooked driver of this uncertainty is the rapid salinization of inland waters, accelerated by climate change, sea-level rise, pollution, and poor water management. While local effects on aquatic CH4 emissions have been reported, the global climate relevance remains poorly understood. Here, we provide a global assessment of salinization impacts on aquatic CH4 production, oxidation and emissions by combining a systematic literature review, a large-scale salinization field experiment, microbial activity assays, and analyses of microbial community composition. We provide evidence that salinization globally leads to a substantially greater reduction in aquatic CH4 emissions than previously recognized. This historic underestimation stems from methodological biases that predominantly focus on diffusive CH4 emissions and neglect or underestimate ebullition. Our literature synthesis suggests that CH4 ebullition is more sensitive to salinization than diffusive emissions, notably, this important pathway remains under-quantified in the literature. Our long-term (>4 years) salinization experiment indicates that salinity changes the microbial community resulting not only in lower methanogenesis rates but also lowering its temperature sensitivity, resulting in a markedly weaker temperature response of ebullition under brackish conditions. This antagonistic interaction between salinity and warming highlights that salinization dampens the temperature-driven increase in CH4 emissions. Extrapolating the global salinity–CH4 relationship to plausible salinization scenarios suggests that inland-water CH4 emissions may decline by about 5% (95% CI: 2-12%). Together, these findings identify salinization as a key, previously underestimated regulator of the global CH4 budget with major implications for predicting greenhous

presentations.title: Effects of Salinization on Nutrient Cycling and Sediment Carbon Dynamics: evidence from short-term laboratory experiments and long-term field experiments
presentations.abstract: Aquatic ecosystems are heavily impacted by eutrophication and play a major role in C emission to the atmosphere. Nutrient and C cycling in the sediment play a key role in these processes. Salinization of inland waters, driven by climate change, sea-level rise, pollution, and water management, poses a serious threat to the functioning of inland waters, strongly impacting nutrient and C cycling. Although its effects on these biogeochemical processes are widely recognized, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. By integrating the results of short-term laboratory and long-term field experiments on effects of salinization, we gained important insights into how salinization affects nutrient and C cycling. We found that salinization influences nutrient availability in the short term by mobilizing NH4 and P. Additionally, long term salinization decreases the capacity of the sediment to bind nutrients which may lead to N limitation in the water column due to increased P mobility. The impact of salinization on eutrophication, however, depends on sediment composition (organic matter, S, P, Fe and N concentrations) and salinization history. Salinization decreases CH4 production and emission due to inhibition of methanogenic microorganisms. It however remains difficult to predict the effect of salinization on CO2 emissions and hence the overall net effect on C fluxes to the atmosphere in terms of global warming potential. We summarize the effects of salinization on sediments and identified key drivers for the consequences of salinization on nutrient and C cycling.

presentations.title: Combined effects of rising temperature and seawater intrusions on organic matter decomposition in coastal wetlands: a mesocosm approach
presentations.affiliation: Institute of Marine Sciences, Middle East Technical University, 33731 Mersin, Türkiye
presentations.abstract: Coastal wetlands play a vital role in carbon cycling by regulating the decomposition and accumulation of organic matter. Yet these ecosystems are increasingly threatened by climate-driven stressors such as seawater intrusion and global warming, which may alter key biogeochemical processes. This study investigated how these stressors influence the decay constant (k) of contrasting litter types—labile green tea and more refractory rooibos tea and macrophyte litter. Mesocosms (each with 5000 L) were inoculated with plankton, macrophytes and fish to mimic natural coastal wetlands. All tanks were initially maintained at 4 ppt salinity for four weeks. To simulate seawater intrusion, salinity was subsequently increased to 7 ppt and 10 ppt (n = 8 per level) for six weeks by seawater additions, resulting in three salinity treatments crossed with two temperature levels (ambient and +2.5 °C warming). Ecosystem variables including temperature, chlorophyll-a, nutrients, sedimentation, and C dynamics (DOC and POC) were monitored to assess responses. Decomposition rates were mainly driven by warming, litter type, and incubation time. Green tea decomposed fastest (k = 0.027 ± 0.0002 day⁻¹), followed by rooibos (k = 0.011 ± 0.0001) and macrophyte litter (k = 0.010 ± 0.0004). Warming moderately accelerated decay, especially for green and rooibos tea, while seawater intrusion had little effect, likely because labile material was lost before salinization began. These findings highlight how warming and salinity interact to shape organic matter turnover in coastal wetlands under future climate scenarios.

presentations.title: FUNCTIONAL RESILIENCE OF A BENTHIC ALGAL METACOMMUNITY EXPOSED TO GROUNDWATER SEAWATER INTRUSION
presentations.abstract: Seawater intrusions from groundwater into coastal freshwater wetlands may be especially impactful on wetland function due to increased phosphorus liberation and reduced opportunity for functional continuity via exchanges of compensatory species. To examine the functional resilience of an oligotrophic coastal wetland in response to groundwater-derived seawater, we conducted in-situ open-water experimental manipulations exposing benthic algae (periphyton) across a coastal seawater ecotone to additions of salinity and phosphorus. We measured dispersal and periphyton functional rates of production in response to treatments and regional conditions. We hypothesized that cross-regional dispersal would enable periphyton in fresh and brackish regions to exhibit high functional redundancy, adaptive species transitions, and functional resilience when exposed to groundwater-derived seawater. Contrary to expectations, dispersal and functional redundancy between regions was low. There were large regional differences in periphyton taxa, and significantly reduced productivity in the brackish region. Brackish periphyton was largely unaffected by treatments, but freshwater periphyton exhibited compounding decreased functions in response to salt and phosphorus. However, “mass effects” from highly productive freshwater periphyton mats may have supported resilience of periphyton taxa and functions at both local and cross-regional scales. Overall, we found that periphyton resilience was dependent on the spatial scale of disturbance, the degree of metacommunity dispersal, and prior history of seawater exposure.

presentations.title: HYDROLOGICAL AND BIOGEOCHEMICAL DRIVERS OF SALINIZATION IN PRAIRIE PONDS
presentations.abstract: Salinization threatens freshwater sustainability, and as climate change intensifies drought and extreme precipitation, prairie ponds are increasingly vulnerable to sulphate accumulation that degrades water quality and affects aquatic life and livestock health. We used a holistic framework to assess how hydrological and biogeochemical processes shape salinization in prairie ponds, identify systems most at risk, and evaluate management options. Monthly surveys were conducted in 35 reservoirs, three of which were dredged in the fall of 2021 and 11 wetland ponds across Saskatchewan, Canada, between May and August of 2021 and 2023. Ponds were classified as discharge or recharge systems based on permanence and seasonal conductivity patterns. We predicted that salinization would reflect sediment and soil characteristics, hydrology, and surrounding biophysical features. To test this, we assessed sulphate dynamics in upland soils, water columns, and sediments, evaluated sulphate retention in upland soils, and identified environmental drivers of salinization. Sediment acted as the primary sulphate reservoir, with upland soils as a secondary source and water reflecting short-to-long term fluxes. Structural equation modelling identified hydrology as the dominant driver, supported by effects of sediment and soil sulphate, organic matter, total dissolved nitrogen, water depth, and vegetation cover. Overall, groundwater connectivity strongly influences pond salinization, and sediment removal and vegetation conservation can help mitigate salinity in prairie pondscapes.

presentations.title: A paleolimnological investigation of the effects of long-term chloride enrichment on the ecological structure of 15 urban lakes
presentations.abstract: Chloride contamination in freshwaters is often viewed as an acute stressor, yet in lentic systems chloride accumulates gradually over extended periods of time. We used paleolimnological techniques to evaluate whether long-term chloride enrichment has altered the ecological structure of 15 urban lakes in Minnesota, USA, spanning a wide gradient of contemporary chloride conditions from low impact to severely impaired. Radiometrically dated sediment cores were used to reconstruct historical community and environmental conditions from diatom assemblages, core geochemistry, and fossil pigments. Our results reveal nuanced and potentially compounding effects of salinization on lake structure and aquatic food webs. We found strong evidence of recent increases in water-column stratification, likely reflecting interactions between rising salinity, climate-driven warming, and nutrient loading. We did not find evidence of chronic salinity impacts on the community structure of biological indicators; however, the period of most rapid salinization coincided with other pervasive anthropogenic disturbances like catchment urbanization, nutrient enrichment, and climate change. Overall, the records of lake response to long-term chloride enrichment were more muted than we hypothesized. In highly urbanized landscapes, long-term disturbance regimes may overshadow or mask potential chloride effects, complicating efforts to isolate salt-driven ecological changes in paleolimnological archives.

presentations.title: IMPACT OF WATER ABSTRACTION AND GLOBAL WARMING ON WATER BALANCE, SIZE AND ECOSYSTEM STRUCTURE OF INLAND AND COASTAL LAKE ECOSYSTEMS IN ARID AND SEMI-ARID REGIONS OF TÜRKIYE
presentations.abstract: Globally, temperature and precipitation patterns are predicted to change markedly due to climate change. Particularly, the regions with a cold or hot semi-arid climate and the Mediterranean climate zones are expected to be strongly affected, leading to shrinking of lakes and increased salinity. In this talk, we will give a brief overview of ongoing changes in freshwater and saline lakes in arid and semi-arid central Anatolia and the Mediterranean regions of Türkiye based on results from a 4-year TÜBITAK project (CLIM-SALTLAKES) studying the climate change effects on trophic structure and dynamics in saline and brackish lakes. Focus will be on results from a comprehensive snap-shot sampling of 49 inland and coastal saline lakes and on changes in the water balance, size and ecosystem structure of lakes in two of its large, closed basins (Konya and Burdur), as well as the future perspective for lakes in these areas.

presentations.title: Salinity thresholds shape global patterns of freshwater biodiversity
presentations.abstract: Accelerating human-driven environmental changes are reshaping ecosystems worldwide, raising critical questions about whether biodiversity responses to stressors are gradual or characterized by abrupt thresholds. Freshwater ecosystems are particularly vulnerable to these pressures due to their limited extent and high biodiversity. Among the most pervasive threats is salinization, which is increasing globally due to land use change and climate impacts. Using macroinvertebrate community data from 684 globally distributed lakes, we identified distinct threshold responses to salinization. Species richness and rarefied richness sharply declined once salinity exceeded approximately 160 mg/L, whereas community evenness showed sensitivity at even lower salinity (~42 mg/L). In contrast, total macroinvertebrate abundance remained stable until salinity surpassed ~10,000 mg/L, indicating a phased degradation pattern—initial diversity loss followed by ecosystem collapse at higher levels of salinity. These biodiversity shifts were driven by differential tolerances among taxonomic, functional and trophic groups. Our findings highlight the prevalence of nonlinear ecological responses to anthropogenic stressors, emphasizing the necessity of identifying ecological thresholds to guide effective conservation and management efforts.

presentations.title: Assessing trajectories of ecosystem recovery in storm surge-impacted lakes of the outer Mackenzie Delta (NT, Canada)
presentations.abstract: Low-lying, coastal ecosystems within Canada’s Arctic regions are experiencing an increased frequency and intensity of storm surge events, which can potentially lead to saltwater inundation following stormwater intrusion. Following a severe storm surge that took place in September 1999, lakes in the northwest Mackenzie Delta (Northwest Territories) were fundamentally altered. This research employs a paleolimnological approach, using lake sediments from impacted lakes of the outer Mackenzie Delta, to evaluate recent storm surges dynamics and trajectories of ecosystem recovery. The last sediment cores from lakes impacted by the 1999 storm surge (called the “Dead Zone”) were collected in 2010 and showed no recovery from the 1999 storm surge event and its impacts. In 2025 we re-sampled a series of lakes in the Dead Zone to assess trajectories of ecosystem recovery over the last several decades. Further, mercury in sediment cores has not been measured in impacted lakes of this region before and may also represent an important source of contamination in the lakes, given the changes that have occurred following salinization, and coastal mercury dynamics. This research will explore the possibility that more recent saltwater intrusion events may have interrupted ongoing ecosystem recovery, leading to a “new normal” where the return interval between storm surge impacts may be shorter than the time required for ecosystem recover in these Arctic lake environments.

presentations.title: COMPARING THE IMPACT OF INORGANIC (NACL) AND AN ORGANIC (BEET JUICE) DE-ICERS ON AQUATIC COMMUNITIES EXPERIENCING EUTROPHICATION
presentations.abstract: De-icing agents, largely sodium chloride, are driving freshwater salinization via chloride (Cl-) pollution. Cl- can impact freshwater ecosystems by re-structuring food webs and provoking the decline of salt-sensitive taxa. To mitigate these effects, there has been an interest in “eco-friendly” alternatives whereby organic additives (i.e. beet juice) are combined with NaCl. Research on the effects of beet juice on aquatic communities is understudied, particularly in the context of multiple stressors. Using an outdoor mesocosm system at the Gault Nature Reserve, QC, I compare the effects of NaCl, beet juice de-icer and nutrient enrichment on the composition of plankton communities. I hypothesize that the combination of these stressors will have interactive effects on the plankton communities. I expect that de-icing agents will negatively impact zooplankton abundance, with beet juice having larger toxicity effects, but that phytoplankton growth provoked by nutrient enrichment will buffer toxicity via a larger stock of food. Thirty-two 1000L mesocosms were filled with water from Lac Hertel. Aquatic communities were exposed to a factorial design of either NaCl, a beet salt brine mixture at low or high nutrient levels, for 30 days. Results showed strong effects of organic de-icers on zooplankton, regardless of trophic status. Most strikingly, we observed dominance of mosquito larvae in treatments with organic de-icers, likely mediated through competitive and olfactory/visual recruitment effects. Furthermore, this study revealed a previously unreported change in the thermal regime– a water-cooling effect through beet juice addition. Put together, this work furthers our understanding of the impact of de-icers, allowing us to incorporate site-specific contexts (i.e. trophic status) when implementing policies for de-icer application.

presentations.title: ADAPTIVE RESPONSES OF DAPHNIA MAGNA TO INCREASED SALINITY
presentations.abstract: Freshwater salinization is a global trend driven by human activities such as road de-icing, mining, and agriculture. Increased salinity imposes stress on the overall functionality of the ecosystems, as well as the inhabiting organisms. The keystone herbivore Daphnia has shown adaptive tolerance to increased salinity, both in experimental evolution studies and in natural systems. Although such adaptations to anthropogenic stressors may facilitate resilience in a changing world, the mechanisms underlying them are poorly understood. We address this knowledge gap by experimentally studying various phenotypic traits of D. magna populations from the Pannonian Plain area. This area hosts inland saline waters with a strong salinity gradient, soda pans in Austria and bomb craters in Hungary, inhabited by salinity-tolerant species. These ecosystems display patterns of both regional and local genetic differentiations in salinity tolerance of D. magna. While in both cases there are improved survival rates in high salinity, we have a very limited picture of the animals’ fitness and the mechanism behind the tolerance. Hence, we assessed survival in presence of abroad experimental salinity gradient, as well as juvenile growth rate of the different Daphnia populations. Additionally, we measured trehalose levels of the populations to examine its role in alleviating osmotic pressure. Our results provide new insights into the physiological aspects of the observed adaptations and a more complete overview of the tolerant animals’ fitness.

presentations.title: From fresh to brackish: Salinity dynamics and ecosystem responses in prairie wetlands
presentations.abstract: Human activities are increasing salinity across inland aquatic networks worldwide, with far-reaching consequences for ecosystem functioning and biogeochemical processes. Here, we synthesize our team’s recent work on the patterns and impacts of salinization in wetlands of the western Canadian prairies. Drawing from regional surveys, controlled experiments, ecosystem mass balances, isotopic tools, and food-web analyses, we identify several key insights. (1) Where multi-decade records exist, most ecosystems show rising salt concentrations, mirroring trends in regional rivers. (2) Across agricultural landscapes, wetland salinity is consistently lower in cropped than rangeland settings, with strong dependence on local hydrology and landscape position. (3) In wastewater-fed wetlands, salts accumulate and are minimally processed, creating downstream risks. (4) Wetland salt storage and export fluctuate widely with drought–flood cycles. (5) Salinity strongly alters food webs and the processing of carbon and nutrients, with the largest and most non-linear effects occurring at the transition from freshwater to sub-saline conditions. Together, these results reveal how salinization can reshape prairie wetland ecosystems and highlight the need for management strategies that account for hydrology, land use, and long-term salt budgets.

presentations.title: Variable Drivers of Summer Chloride Concentrations in Urban Surface Waters
presentations.abstract: Excessive chloride concentrations threaten the structure and function of urban aquatic systems. While road salt is a well known driver of chloride levels, other factors moderate the persistence and impact of chloride in surface waters but are much less well understood. This study aimed to discern and predict how urban surface waters are variably affected by chloride during the summer, considering impacts of hydrology, land use, surface water type, and winter inputs across diverse surface waters in the Twin Cities Metropolitan Area (TCMA), Minnesota. Upwards of fifty springs, streams, ponds, and lakes in the TCMA were sampled over two years for chloride and biogeochemical tracers to infer water sources. Tracer and hydrologic connectivity metrics were used to examine how variation in water sources (e.g. surface runoff, groundwater) affects chloride levels in common surface water types. We found a positive relationship between groundwater contributions to stream flow and chloride concentrations, demonstrating persistent chloride from winter road salt applications through the entire year in some settings. Further, we found a strong influence of seasonal precipitation on summer chloride as indicated by consistent decreases in chloride concentrations from 2023 (a very dry summer) to 2024 (a very wet summer). Our work shows that chloride in urban freshwaters is determined by the interplay of climate, seasonality, land use, and hydrologic connectivity, suggesting that the development of strategies tailored to local contextualizing factors can help in managing road salt impacts.

presentations.title: SALT STRESS RESPONSES IN FRESHWATER PHYTOPLANKTON: INSIGHTS FROM YEAR-ROUND MONITORING AND SALINITY BIOASSAYS
presentations.abstract: Freshwater salinization is an increasingly pervasive stressor in inland lakes; however, its ecological and biogeochemical impacts remain underexplored compared to nutrient enrichment. Yet, even relatively minor increases in chloride concentration can affect osmotic conditions and alter freshwater microbial communities. Lake Acton (located in southwest Ohio) is a hypereutrophic reservoir that receives agricultural runoff and chloride loading from road salts and fertilizers. While Lake Acton has been the site of long-term ecological monitoring, the diversity and function of the microbial phytoplankton, particularly over seasonal timescales, have been understudied. In this study, we first describe year-round phytoplankton dynamics in Lake Acton using algal biomass measurements from the Fluoroprobe/Algae Lab Analyzer (ALA) and 18S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial phytoplankton communities exhibited seasonally specific trends in alpha-diversity and community structure. We then tested the impact of salinity stress in bioassays from lake water collected at distinct seasonal timepoints (winter, fall, summer). By integrating observational data with experimental manipulations, this work provides insight into how salinization shapes microbial food-web structure. We will discuss how our results contribute to broader efforts to understand anthropogenic drivers of salinization and inform monitoring and management strategies for urban-agricultural freshwater ecosystems.

presentations.title: INTERACTIVE EFFECTS OF SALINITY AND WARMING ON PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES IN A FRESHWATER LAKE MESOCOSM EXPERIMENT
presentations.abstract: Freshwater salinization from road salt, combined with rising water temperature due to climate warming, is expected to alter lake ecosystems by reshaping plankton communities. Although both stressors have independent effects on plankton, their interactive influence during summer conditions remains poorly understood. Previous studies have relied on land-based mesocosms or single-stressor designs, limiting our ability to evaluate how temperature and salinity jointly structure natural plankton communities. To address this gap, a four-week in-situ mesocosm experiment was conducted at Lac Hertel, manipulating three salinity concentrations (0, 700, 2000 mg Cl⁻/L) crossed with ambient or moderate warming (+2–3°C). Eighteen mesocosms filled with lake water were monitored using data loggers and weekly plankton sampling. Preliminary results show patterns indicating that elevated temperature and higher chloride levels can influence phytoplankton dynamics, with several groups exhibiting reduced biomass or altered trajectories under combined stress. While treatment differences appear to be modest at this early analysis stage, warming tended to suppress algal growth relative to ambient conditions, and elevated chloride sometimes coincided with lower or more variable biomass. These early results suggest that the combined effect of warming and salinity may exert additive pressures on summer phytoplankton communities. Findings will provide insights into the ecological impacts of road salt use, informing strategies to improve management practices.

presentations.title: Multi-year methane emissions from multi-biome lakes measured with comparable methodology within the SITES GHG flux program
presentations.abstract: Lakes represent one of the main sources of methane (CH4) to the atmosphere, contributing in the order of 5-15% of the total global yearly emissions. While the scientific interest in understanding and modelling these emissions are rapidly increasing, methodologically consistent long-term measurement programs of lake CH4 fluxes are largely missing globally. Here we present results from the Swedish Infrastructure for Ecosystem Science (SITES) program on lake CH4 emissions. Five lakes distributed across Sweden, including the subarctic alpine, boreal and north temperate conditions, were consistently monitored during 2016-2022 in ways that considered variability in space and time within lakes and that allowed between-lake comparisons. The data includes total CH4 fluxes, diffusive fluxes and surface water concentrations along with some other common physical and chemical lake variables. Briefly, the data show the need of appropriate consideration of ebullition and space-time integration to properly represent whole lake CH4 emissions. We further show that CH4 fluxes have an apparent temperature dependency that are modulated by depth-zones and that can differ among lakes. Also, yearly open water CH4 flux estimates were consistently shaped by temperature in all lakes, with modest increases in whole season mean water temperature resulting in substantially increased CH4 emissions. Finally, we propose that temperature-normalized fluxes should be used in lake emission inter-comparisons to achieve more robust results.

presentations.title: High-Resolution Measurement of CH4 Fluxes in Reclaimed Wastewater-Fed Mediterranean Reservoirs
presentations.abstract: Inland aquatic systems contribute nearly half of global methane (CH4) emissions, with reservoirs accounting for more than 5% – a contribution projected to rise with warming and reservoir expansion. Yet, reservoir CH4 emissions remain highly uncertain, as flux estimates are sparse and episodic, making scaling across heterogeneous space and time challenging. Reservoirs differ from marine systems due to substantial terrestrial and anthropogenic nutrient inputs that stimulate algal production, particularly in warm conditions. Enhanced algal biomass supplies labile organic matter that fuels methanogenesis and drives CH4 fluxes. Despite these important interactions, high-resolution observations linking nutrient inflows, thermal structure, and CH4 dynamics in reservoirs are still limited. To address this, we are conducting continuous biweekly measurements of CH4 (and CO2) fluxes in two agricultural reservoirs supplied with reclaimed wastewater in a Mediterranean climate. These measurements are integrated with remote sensing, water-column profiling, water and sediment chemistry analyses, and algal biomass assessments to characterize stratification patterns, redox gradients, nutrient availability, and temporal shifts in algal dynamics. By capturing nutrient and thermal structure at high resolution, these measurements offer mechanistic insights into CH4 dynamics and support improved representation of reservoir CH4 emissions at regional and global scales.

presentations.title: TEMPORAL AND SPATIAL VARIABILITY OF EBULLITION IN THE SHALLOW WATER ZONE OF A LARGE LAKE
presentations.abstract: Ebullition is a major pathway for CH₄ emissions from lakes, but it remains difficult to quantify, and data are rather limited, especially in large systems. This study investigates the temporal and spatial variability of ebullition in the littoral zone of a large lake. Using automated ebullition flux funnels, we measured time series of ebullition fluxes over weeks to months and at several stations in the shallow water zone of Lake Konstanz, resolving changes in these ebullition fluxes at time scales of a few minutes. In addition, we measured surface waves, water temperature, and hydrostatic pressure. These data illustrate that surface waves trigger ebullition, thus causing variability in the ebullition flux at short time scales. Ship waves, even after traveling long distances, induce pressure drops that are regularly sufficient to induce gas-bubble release from shallow sediments. Although these events occur only during brief ship-wave passages, they can contribute substantially to overall CH₄ emissions. On seasonal time scales, ebullition typically increases from spring to summer and decreases again from August to September when ebullition essentially ceases. During summer, average ebullition fluxes differ among sites, but at almost all sites, the time series of the ebullition fluxes are characterized by a regular diurnal pattern. We will present these observations and discuss physical and environmental mechanisms that explain the observed patterns in the ebullition fluxes.

presentations.title: From Well-Constrained to Uncertain CH4 Reservoirs Budget: Insights from the GHG-CARE Project
presentations.abstract: Carbon emissions in reservoirs, just like in any other waterbody, is fundamentally the end-product of an ensemble of key, interacting processes that occur at varying rates in time and space. Canada's reservoirs exhibit a wide variety of attributes (sediment composition, light extinction coefficient, biological rates, and so on) and may serve different purposes, thereby expressing unique features, for e.g., flow management, physical configuration, that regulate their emissions uniquely. Carbon emissions in reservoirs have therefore proven notoriously difficult to quantify. As part of the GHG-CARE field project (2023 to 2025), we collected continuous and synoptic field data, at different times of the open-water season. Our intent was to capture the temporal and spatial variability of hydrodynamics and gas dynamics in 18 contrasting, managed reservoirs in Canada. We will present reservoir examples where physical and biological rates are reasonably well-constrained in space and time using simple models while poorly constrained in others, thereby driving uncertainty in carbon budgets and emissions. In this presentation, we wish to highlight the difficulties encountered and provide guidance for improved large-scale application of mechanistic models.

presentations.title: The importance of plant traits for improving methane flux estimation in littoral zones of inland waters
presentations.abstract: Around half of the global methane (CH4) emission stems from aquatic ecosystems, with inland waters being the largest contributor. This estimate, however, comes with great uncertainties. In particular, CH4 emissions in vegetated aquatic habitats can be extensive and highly variable, but are still poorly understood. Characterizing how different macrophytes mediate CH4 production and emission pathways is key to reduce the uncertainty when quantifying and predicting ecosystem-scale emissions. Investigating not only the magnitude of CH4 emissions of a range of species, but connecting those to specific plant traits, will allow for more robust extrapolations. We conducted a greenhouse mesocosm experiment investigating 16 different macrophyte species representing all life forms (emergent, floating and submerged). Over the course of 4-6 weeks, transparent chambers were used to measure carbon dioxide and CH4 fluxes from the mesocosms. In addition, CH4 ebullition and concentrations of dissolved gases in surface water and in sediment pore water were monitored. Subsequently, all plants were analysed regarding a series of plant traits hypothesised to influence CH4 production and emission. These included several leaf traits, root traits and whole plant traits (e.g. leaf area, nutrient content and biomass). Greenhouse gas fluxes and concentration of dissolved surface water and pore water gases differed clearly between species and between life forms. Preliminary analysis indicate that the observed trends correlate with several plant traits, particularly root-related traits and biomass.

presentations.title: VARIABILITY OF METHANE EBULLITION WITHIN AND BETWEEN STREAMS, AND ITS RELATIONSHIP WITH SEDIMENT CHARACTERISTICS
presentations.affiliation: Global Change Research Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Methane ebullition is one of the primary processes by which methane is transported from streams into the atmosphere. However, it is challenging to extrapolate ebullition due to its high spatiotemporal variability and the multiple driving factors involved. Although ebullition is typically higher in very fine, organic-rich sediments than in coarse sediments, the process rates across the grain size and organic matter content gradient are poorly understood in the heterogeneous conditions found in streams. Understanding these patterns could help to upscale methane emissions from streams. We measured methane ebullition in six streams in Czechia and Austria with 20 bubble traps per stream over a period of 15 days in four seasons. Sediment samples were collected under each trap to investigate the relationship between methane ebullition and sediment characteristics. A total of 480 sediment samples were collected and analysed in relation to methane ebullition. While the methane ebullition rates varied substantially between streams due to differences in environmental characteristics (seasonal mean per stream: 0.01–89.41 mg CH4 m-2 d-1), the seasonal pattern followed the temperature changes as expected. The proportion of total methane emissions accounted for by ebullition ranged from 0.1% in winter to 79% in summer. Ebullition rates and methane content in bubbles exhibited high small-scale variability within streams (0–527 mg m-2 d-1 and 0.01–72%, respectively), and their relationship with sediment characteristics will be discussed in detail in the presentation.

name: Reducing the Uncertainties in Methane Emissions from Aquatic Environments
lead_organizer: Mina Bizic, TU Berlin
co_organizers: Paul del Giorgio, Université du Québec à Montréal
Yves Prairie, Université du Québec à Montréal

presentations.title: SPATIOTEMPORAL VARIABILITY AND DRIVERS OF BENTHIC METHANE PRODUCTION POTENTIAL IN STREAMS
presentations.abstract: In streams and rivers, methane (CH4) emissions and related fluxes and production in the sediment are not well understood despite their high contribution to the global CH4 budget. To unravel the magnitudes and drivers of benthic CH4 production, we measured the CH4 production potential and related sediment properties from six streams in Czechia and Austria once in all four seasons over one year. We took samples at three locations in each stream (total of 71 sediment samples) and measured the methane production potential in five replicates. First results showed that the CH4 production potential rates differed by five orders of magnitude. The mean CH4 production potential ranged from 1.34 x 10-4 ± 1.43 x 10-4 to 20.67 ± 11.17 µg CH4 gDW-1 d-1 (mean ± SD, n = 5), varying largely within and between streams and seasons. The largest variance in CH4 production potential was explained by within stream differences, demonstrating the high heterogeneity of occurrences and production of methanogenic archaea in small streams. Further, preliminary results indicate sediment organic matter content as the more influential driver of spatial variability of benthic CH4 production potential compared to the proportion of fine sediments. This highlights the important role of organic matter as a source for methanogens for benthic methane production.

presentations.title: EXPLORING A NOVEL AERATION TECHNOLOGY TO MITIGATE METHANE EMISSIONS FROM A WETLAND
presentations.abstract: Wetlands have a large amount of stored carbon with high oxygen demand, and relatively stagnant water. Consequently, dissolved oxygen tends to be low, favouring anaerobic processes such as methanogenosis. E M Fluids Inc. has developed a novel aeration technology (EMF), that increases gas exchange across the air-water interface, allowing more oxygen into the system, potentially suppressing anaerobic processes. The objective of this study was to determine whether EMF treatment can effectively suppress net emissions of methane from a wetland by increasing oxygen exchange. Six wetland mesocosms (3 reference and 3 treatment) were established at a field research station. Over the 2025 summer season, methane flux measurements were made weekly over a 10-week period, using removable tents as gas chambers, and measuring methane using gas-chromatography. Data were analyzed using a repeated measures ANCOVA model, with pressure, temperature, radiation, and wind as covariates. Wetlands under EMF treatment supported faster plant growth (p = 0.045) and higher net methane emissions (p = 0.032) compared to reference mesocosms. The higher emissions were accounted for by higher direct release by plants rather than emissions from soil. Coupled with higher growth this may suggest effects of treatment on plant physiology, studies on which are ongoing.

presentations.title: TOWARDS A COMPREHENSIVE UNDERSTANDING OF METHANE FLUX: THE ROLE OF AQUATIC VEGETATION IN A NORTHERN BOREAL LAKE
presentations.abstract: In northern (>50°N) freshwater ecosystems, aquatic vegetation is expanding, potentially enhancing methane (CH4) emissions through plant-mediated transport. Despite this, most studies do not directly measure CH4 fluxes from shoreline emergent vegetation. To better understand the contribution of vegetation to overall CH4 flux, we measured diffusive, ebullitive, and plant-mediated CH4 flux in open (non-vegetated) and vegetated shoreline areas of an oligo-mesotrophic glacial lake in Kaska ancestral territory (British Columbia). Methane fluxes from vegetated zones (24.6 ± 6.1 mg C m-2 d-1; diffusion + plant mediated) were approximately two times greater than diffusive fluxes from open areas (14.3 ± 4.2 mg C m-2 d-1). Ebullition was a small contributor to overall flux, representing 0.96 ± 1.24 mg C m-2 d-1 and 0.93 ± 1.31 mg C m-2 d-1 from vegetated and open zones, respectively. Linear regressions revealed that the combined diffusive and plant-mediated flux was negatively correlated with water depth (R2 = 0.25; p-value = 0.009). Plant-mediated fluxes increased with plant greenness, represented by the Green Chromatic Coordinate calculated via field photos before each flux measurement (R2 = 0.36; p-value = 0.004). Pending stable carbon isotope data and benthic vegetation CH4 production incubations will provide more insights into production pathways. Our preliminary results suggest that CH4 emissions from large glacial lakes are likely to increase and play a more important role in the northern CH4 budget with the expansion of emergent vegetation.

presentations.title: Investigation of Bubble Trap Uncertainties in the Laboratory Using CH4, CO2, N2 and Air
presentations.abstract: Bubble traps with pressure sensors have been used to provide a continuous record of the head space within the trap. A natural expectation is that these records provide a direct measure of ebullitive flux. However, there are uncertainties associated with this technique. For example, we have conducted laboratory experiments that show the headspace can shrink or grow without ebullition. Temporal changes in the height of the headspace were continuously recorded with time lapse imaging while logging water pressure and temperature. A control experiment with atmospheric gas (i.e. air) showed that the head space varied in height with temperature and pressure according to the ideal gas law. Experiments with N2 in the headspace showed an initial increase in the height of the headspace of approximately 0.010 cm/hr, while CO2 showed an initial decrease of 1.5 to 2.2 cm/hr and CH4 with an initial decline of 0.21 cm/hr. These differences are attributable to the differences in solubility and diffusivity of the gases. Our laboratory observations provide a possible explanation for previously unexplained field measurements with bubble traps.

presentations.title: Changes in methanogenesis potential in response to whole-lake nutrient enrichment
presentations.abstract: Many lakes are progressively undergoing eutrophication as climate pressures increase. Eutrophication has been shown to increase methane production, but uncertainties remain about the degree of within-season change in methanogenesis with eutrophication. We leveraged a series of whole-lake manipulations over two years in which one lake was fertilized, and the other was fertilized and had a light-blocking dye added, to evaluate changes in the methanogenesis potential in surface sediments. Weekly, we collected water and sediment from the lakes’ profundal and littoral zones, placing them in bottles which were flushed with nitrogen and incubated at 4C to measure the change in methane concentrations in the headspace. We hypothesized that methanogenesis rates would increase in the fertilized lake and the lake with the dye addition compared to an unmanipulated reference lake, due to an increase in algal substrate and anoxic volume. While methanogenesis potential rates were higher in the profundal zone in both the reference and dyed and enriched lake, there was no difference in rates in the enrichment only lake. Methanogenesis rates did not vary among years in the enriched lakes but were significantly different between years in the unmanipulated reference lake. These results suggest that eutrophication may stabilize methanogenesis rates among years compared to more variable rates in oligotrophic ecosystems.

presentations.title: BUBBLE TRAP ESTIMATES OF EBULLITION AT A PIT LAKE
presentations.abstract: Base Mine Lake Demonstration (7.9 km2, 57° 1'N, 112° 31'W) is a pit lake in the oil sands region of northern Alberta, Canada. The lake consists of a 10 m water cap, on top of approximately 40 m of fluid fine tailings. Within the underlying fluid fine tailings, methane bubbles are generated that rise through the water cap throughout the year. These bubbles can transport particles (turbidity) and residual hydrocarbons from the tailings into the water column. We examine pressure variations with bubble traps for multiple deployments in Base Mine Lake. These pressure records allow near continuous estimates of the ebullitive gas flux. The fluxes are highly variable horizontally (between coincident deployments) and episodic. Here we discuss the variations in the distributions of the continuous fluxes with the goal of attaining more meaningful statistics of ebullitive flux including the mean and higher order statistics. We also apply methods used to develop intensity duration frequency curves for our records similar to those typically used for precipitation rto the flux records. Finally, the observed ebullition was compared to fluxes computed using methane eddy-covariance at BML as well ebullition at other sites using various measurement techniques.

presentations.title: Acetone, acetaldehyde, and methanethiol as precursors of aerobic methane photoproduction in seawater
presentations.abstract: Methane (CH₄) production in natural waters has traditionally been considered to occur only under strictly anoxic conditions. However, surface ocean waters that are fully oxygenated are mostly supersaturated with CH₄, a phenomenon known as the oceanic methane paradox. Photochemical CH4 production from dissolved organic matter has been proposed as a potential explanation, yet the specific precursors responsible for this photochemical CH4 source remain poorly constrained. We evaluate three methyl-containing compounds commonly found in surface seawater, acetone, acetaldehyde, and methanethiol as potential CH₄ precursors. Each compound was dissolved in air-saturated artificial seawater and irradiated in time and concentration series. CH₄ concentrations increased linearly with irradiation time and with precursor concentration. At the concentration of 5 μmol L⁻¹, acetone yieled the highest CH₄ formation rate (7.75 × 10⁻³ ± 1.46 × 10⁻³ nmol CH₄ L⁻¹ h⁻¹), followed by acetaldehyde (5.65×10⁻³ ± 1.23 × 10⁻³ nmol CH₄ L⁻¹ h⁻¹) wile methanethiol yielded negligible CH₄ photoproduced. CH4 photoproduction rates from acetone and acetaldehyde decreased exponentially between 280 and 345 nm and was mainly a primary photochemical process. Ongoing experiments using ¹³C-labeled acetone aim to further elucidate this mechanism. Ongoing experiments using ¹³C-labeled acetone aim to further elucidate this mechanism. This study identified acetone and acetaldehyde as potential precursors of aerobic CH₄ photoproduction in sunlit surface waters and improved our understanding of its photochemical mechanism.

presentations.title: INVESTIGATING LITTORAL RESTRUCTURING AND GREENHOUSE GAS DYNAMICS UNDER EXTREME WATER LEVEL RISE IN A TEMPERATE SEEPAGE LAKE
presentations.abstract: Rising water levels have been observed in many lakes worldwide since the 2000s, including parts of the U.S. Midwest where agricultural practices and shoreline development are common. These hydrologic changes transform the littoral zone by flooding terrestrial soils, vegetation, and infrastructure, with unknown consequences for greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics in this productive habitat. Fish Lake in southern Wisconsin, USA, has risen >5m in the past decade, nearly doubling its surface area and creating extensive newly inundated littoral habitat composed of former forest, farmland, and roadway substrates. To evaluate how novel substrates may influence GHG dynamics, we quantified weekly summertime surface water concentrations of CO2 and CH4 at three littoral sites containing distinct flooded terrestrial substrates plus one central pelagic reference site. Average CO2 and CH4 concentrations in littoral sites (12.1 and 0.18 µmol/L-1) were greater than those in the pelagic (10.4 and 0.13 µmol/L-1) but were variable among sites, suggesting spatial heterogeneity in GHG production. However, the flooded roadway site with minimal organic substrate, exhibited the highest CH4 concentration (0.56 µmol/L-1). Elevated CH4 concentrations may be driven by organic matter being transported through wind generated wave action from the adjacent eutrophic wetland that is now merged with Fish Lake. These findings suggest that rising water levels that increase connectivity between habitats can create new pathways for carbon inputs and alter GHG production in expanding littoral zones.

presentations.title: TRACKING NUTRIENT FLOW IN THE CHANGING ARCTIC: COMBINED USE OF COMPOUND-SPECIFIC AMINO ACID ISOTOPES AND FATTY ACIDS
presentations.affiliation: UCSC University of California, Santa Cruz
presentations.abstract: Rapid glacier retreat is transforming high-latitude landscapes and creating thousands of new lakes, offering natural experiments for understanding how environmental change shapes nutrient flow in aquatic ecosystems. We combined compound-specific stable isotope analysis of amino acids (CSI-AA) with fatty acid analysis to trace nutrient transfer from primary producers to the top of food webs (fish) across a suite of Greenland lakes spanning the glacial–lacustrine transition. Essential amino acid fingerprints revealed striking shifts in basal protein sources, from algal production in glacial lakes to increasing detrital contributions in clear-water ones, contrary to expectations. In parallel, fish long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs), vital organic nutrients, increased by more than 60% along the successional gradient, driven largely by the rise of omega-6 fatty acids as turbidity drops, and the decreasing importance of detritus in later stages. We also found increasing egg cannibalism under stronger glacial influence, associated with high accumulation of marine-derived LC-PUFAs. Where such subsidies were absent, fish appeared to compensate for low LC-PUFA availability through endogenous biosynthesis of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), as evidenced by precursor accumulation. We demonstrate the power of integrating methods to reveal both food-web foundations and structure (CSI-AA) and the transfer of LC-PUFAs to consumers. Our results highlight that environmental change reshapes food webs, with consequences for the availability of organic nutrients to top consumers.

presentations.title: Expanding the Isotopic Toolbox: Graph-Theoretical Insights into Trophic Structure
presentations.abstract: Stable-isotope data provide an integrative view of trophic organization, yet most analytical tools capture only limited aspects of ecosystem structure. We show that representing isotopic data as an isotopic network substantially expands the ecological information extractable from isotopic space. Using whole-network metrics such as connectivity, modularity, and nestedness, we reveal emergent properties of trophic organization, including interrelationships, segmentation, and assembly gradients. At the organism level, node metrics such as degree, closeness, eigenvector, and betweenness centrality identify differentiated species roles and highlight taxa that act as structural connectors within communities. These network-based descriptors uncover community-wide properties, contrasts among isotopic guilds, and the functional importance of key species—patterns that remain undetected using traditional approaches such as Layman metrics. Their lack of association with conventional isotopic metrics shows that network analysis captures novel and complementary dimensions of trophic structure. Because graph theory offers a large suite of methods linked to biological processes, it provides a framework to interpret isotopic data in a richer and more mechanistic way. Our results position isotopic-network analysis as a promising tool for extracting deeper ecological insight from stable-isotope datasets. Integrating graph-theoretical metrics with existing isotope approaches enhances our ability to detect functionally relevant patterns in community assembly and ecosystem functioning.

presentations.title: AMINO ACID COMPOUND-SPECIFIC ISOTOPE ANALYSIS REVEALS TROPHIC COUPLING BETWEEN COASTAL AND OLIGOTROPHIC OFFSHORE FOOD WEBS IN THE NORTH PACIFIC SUBTROPICAL GYRE
presentations.abstract: Nearshore waters of tropical Pacific islands often exhibit higher productivity relative to surrounding oligotrophic environments, potentially subsidizing offshore food webs. Around the Hawaiian Islands, micronekton in the Mesopelagic Boundary Layer (MBL) community migrate nightly from 350-700 m toward coastal waters, presumably to exploit enhanced zooplankton biomass. However, direct evidence of energy and nutrient transfer between nearshore and offshore systems remains limited. We used compound specific isotope analyses of amino acids (CSIA-AA) to measure δ13C and δ15N values in two micronektonic assemblages with contrasting migration behaviors: (i) island-associated MBL species that migrate horizontally and vertically toward shore, and (ii) offshore diel vertical migrators (DVM) that remain distant from the islands. This comparison enables evaluation of the island mass effect (IME) on pelagic food-web structure and quantification of nearshore-offshore nutrient exchange. Preliminary results reveal distinct isotopic baselines and trophic positions, with DVM species occupying higher trophic levels than MBL species. Comparisons with zooplankton isotopic values suggest that inshore-derived nutrients are important resources for MBL micronekton, whereas offshore species rely more on deep-sea zooplankton. These findings underscore the value of CSIA-AA in resolving trophic pathways that link coastal productivity to pelagic food webs, offering essential insights for reef conservation and sustainable pelagic and fisheries management.

presentations.title: MEASURING d13C OF FATTY ACIDS IN GREY SEAL (HALICHOERUS GRYPUS) BLUBBER: DIET EVALUATION AND ASSESSMENT OF FRACTIONATION
presentations.abstract: Debate concerning diets of grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) in the NW Atlantic persists, with conflicting information arising from analysis of DNA of stomach contents, bulk stable isotopes and fatty acid (FA) signature analysis. Here, we offer another perspective on diet analysis and have determined d13C values of FA in blubber of grey seals sampled on Sable Island, NS. We collected blubber biopsies from male and female seals in winter and spring 2000 and females in winter 2023/24 to identify differences in foraging preferences with sex, season and year. We measured d13C values in a suite of 11 FA that were consistently present at levels >1 % of total FA mass. Females from 2023/24 were also sampled longitudinally at the beginning and near the end of lactation, allowing us to assess fractionation of stable carbon isotopes with FA mobilization from blubber. We did not find any difference in d13C values of FA due to sex or season in 2000, suggesting that males and females consumed similar diets with little variation in early winter and late spring. In contrast, we found substantial variation between females sampled in winter of 2023/2024 and 2000, suggesting a diet shift over the 20-year period, and supported by FA proportional data. Finally, we found obvious fractionation due to hydrolysis as FA were mobilized from blubber during fasting, with blubber FA d13C values increasing during the fast. Such information about fractionation is critical in establishing routine methods to evaluate diet using this technique.

presentations.title: Biogeochemical interactions in deep-sea sediments exposed by novel in-situ experimental systems
presentations.affiliation: Marine Biological Laboratory, University of Chicago
presentations.abstract: Deep-sea sediments serve as the Earth’s largest organic carbon sink, yet nutrient cycling and energy flow in the massive ecosystem is poorly understood. This knowledge gap stems from both the inaccessibility of sediments kilometers below the surface ocean, and the lack of techniques for examining microbial metabolisms responsible for biogeochemical cycling in these habitats. Here, we performed in-situ incubations with organic carbon substrates of varying complexity and lability in sediments at 3600 meters below sea level. This was accomplished by developing novel deep-sea experimental systems involving injector push cores, which were deployed for 0 days, 4 days, and 18 months in the eastern North Pacific Ocean. By combining 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, metagenomics, and geochemical data, we identify microbes stimulated by the injected substrates. Analyses of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from individual species revealed the different roles and mechanisms behind responder and degrader microbes. Moreover, microbial community succession and trophic interactions were elucidated. These results are essential for effective modelling of complex sediment food webs and carbon cycling. Collectively, we expose the characteristics of rare, uncultivated microbes in sediments thousands of fathoms below the surface ocean and overall community dynamics, providing new insights into the ecology and metabolic activities of deep seafloor microbiomes.

presentations.title: PROTECTING THE FUTURE BY LEARNING FROM THE PAST: SALMON NURSERY LAKE ECOSYSTEM RECONSTRUCTION THROUGH SHOTGUN SEQUENCING OF SEDIMENTARY DNA
presentations.abstract: Pacific salmon are keystone species to North Pacific ecosystems, but many populations have declined or become more variable due to anthropogenic impacts and climate change. Long-term records are needed to understand past changes, identify ecosystem stressors, and guide restoration. Here, we use sedimentary DNA (sedDNA) to reconstruct ecological trajectories across five Pacific salmon nursery lakes in British Columbia, spanning centuries to millennia. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we examined ecosystem-level changes encompassing organisms from bacteria to fish. Multiple fish species were successfully detected, allowing reconstruction of fish community dynamics over time. We also recovered diverse algal and zooplankton DNA, enabling exploration of food-web interactions across multiple trophic levels. Notably, our plant assemblage data reveal a long-term shift from tree-dominated DNA signatures toward increasing dominance of grasses and flowering plants, accompanied by a rise in aquatic macrophyte detection - patterns consistent with landscape-level vegetation change and potential nutrient enrichment. Across multiple lakes, we detected increased representation of the toxin-producing cyanobacterium Microcystis, suggesting shifts in water quality over recent centuries. Overall, our findings demonstrate that sedDNA provides taxonomically rich, long-term insights into aquatic and terrestrial ecological dynamics, which are foundational for understanding and protecting salmon nursery habitats.
