presentations.title: Regulation of Microzooplankton Grazing on Unicellular Cyanobacterium in the Western North Pacific
presentations.affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Marine Environmental Science, Xiamen University
presentations.abstract: Major advances have been made in understanding the diversity, activity and environmental controls of marine N2-fixing microorganisms. However, top-down controls on these pivotal diazotrophs remain poorly understood. Here, we employed modified dilution assays coupled with flow-cytometry and quantitative PCR to quantify the growth and grazing mortality rates of unicellular diazotrophs. Across the Western North Pacific (WNP), the community structure of unicellular diazotrophs exhibited clear regional heterogeneity. Environmental clustering delineated two biogeographic provinces, the South China Sea (SCS), the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG). The NPSG was characterized by weaker nitrate supply, along with lower Chl a and net primary production (NPP) than the SCS, presenting a marked contrast in nutrient levels and productivity. In the NPSG, UCYN-B experienced significantly reduced grazing mortality and pressure—an apparent pattern that was mirrored, albeit to a lesser extent, in the picocyanobacterial community when compared to the SCS. In contrast, UCYN-A in the SCS displayed moderately higher growth and grazing rates compared to the bulk phytoplankton community, suggesting a higher biomass turnover rate. Notably, nano-eukaryotes (Euk) and UCYN-A showed coherent trends in their vital rates across basins, likely attributable to the symbiotic association between UCYN-A with its eukaryotic host. Collectively, our findings highlight the importance of top-down processes in facilitating the ecological success of UCYN-B in oligotrophic waters, while also indicating the efficient transfer of UCYN-A-derived nitrogen to higher trophic levels in the SCS.

presentations.title: PEELING BACK THE LAYERS: THE INFLUENCE OF WATER COLUMN STRUCTURE ON PELAGIC FOOD WEBS IN THE NORTHERN GULF OF MEXICO AND SOUTH ATLANTIC BIGHT
presentations.abstract: The South Atlantic Bight (SAB) and the northern Gulf of Mexico (nGoM) are both subtropical shelf seas that transition seasonally between vertically mixed and strongly stratified conditions; however, they differ in the mechanisms that drive productivity, resulting in distinct biological and biogeochemical dynamics. In the SAB, stratification is primarily driven by temperature and enhanced by offshore intrusions, whereas in the nGoM, it is dominated by riverine freshwater input. To better understand how these differences influence pelagic food webs, this study characterizes the food-web structure in these regions using stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes, to assess how water-column heterogeneity shapes trophic organization in ecosystems with differing physical and biological dynamics. Zooplankton samples representing a wide range of traits (body composition, trophic level, feeding mode), as well as size-fractionated particulate organic matter (POM) were collected for bulk 13-C and 15-N stable isotope analysis. Samples were collected from the SAB and nGoM during August and November of 2024 and 2025 to capture periods with and without significant water-column stratification. Preliminary results suggest that predatory gelatinous zooplankton exhibit greater trophic variability in the nGoM than in the SAB under stratified conditions.

presentations.title: The effects of seaweed and shellfish mariculture on the fecal carbon flux and feeding habits of zooplankton in a mariculture base of southern China: Implications for the biological pump
presentations.abstract: Zooplankton play a pivotal role in the marine ecosystem, with their fecal pellets constituting the primary component of passively sinking particles in the ocean. Mariculture activities are extensively practiced along the coastline of China. Surveys were carried out in different mariculture areas around Nan'ao Island in the South China Sea from March to June 2023 during seaweed Gracilaris lemaneiformis cultivation. A total of 36 zooplankton species were identified, including 27 copepod species. Zooplankton abundance ranged from 500 to 2760 ind. m−3, with the highest abundance observed in the G.lemaneiformis cultivation area (P<0.05). Furthermore, the Shannon-Wiener diversity index of the zooplankton community in the G.lemaneiformis area surpassed that of the shellfish and control areas (P<0.05). The abundance of zooplankton fecal pellets fluctuated between 12 and 283 pellets m−3, and the fecal pellet carbon flux ranged from 0.004 to 0.976 mg C m−2 d−1. The fecal pellet abundance and carbon flux of zooplankton peaked in the G.lemaneiformis cultivation area (P<0.05). Sequences of red algae and brown algae were detected in the zooplankton. Results showed mariculture activities affect zooplankton community structure and their fecal pellet carbon flux; the large-scale cultivation of G.lemaneiformis enhances zooplankton diversity and effectively increases the carbon flux of fecal pellets in the coastal waters. These findings could provide new management strategies for mariculture environments with increasing anthropogenic stressors in the Anthropocene Epoch.

presentations.title: Project Breathless: Highlights of hypoxia impacts in three great “Dead Zones”
presentations.affiliation: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
presentations.abstract: We studied the effects of declining oxygen on fishes in three well-studied hypoxic regions. We used a combination of biomarkers in otoliths, eye lenses, and muscle tissue for direct assessments of impacts of hypoxia on growth, niche breadth, and mercury exposure. Otoliths provided information on hypoxia exposure from manganese uptake; movement information from variations in strontium and barium; and metabolic status from magnesium. Eye lenses and muscle tissue provided lifetime and static information, respectively, on mercury exposure. Muscle stable isotope ratios revealed differences in dietary niche breadth, which for all but one species, became narrower in hypoxia. Models of Baltic Sea fish communities showed that cod shifted its diet as benthic foods became less available with hypoxia, and that cod also became smaller. Finally, we used data sonification to create “fish songs” to communicate about hypoxia to the public, featured in a science museum in Stockholm and elsewhere.

presentations.title: Seasonal variability of the Oxygen Minimum Zones off the Mexican tropical Pacific and consequences on zooplankton vertical distribution
presentations.abstract: Oxygen concentrations were obtained and analyzed for the area in the entrance of the Sea of Cortés during different seasons, a total of 6 cruises were analyzed. A comparison of the depth of the Oxygen Minimum Zone (OMZ), shows and important seasonal variability being shallower and more pronounced during summer. The Vertical distribution of zooplankton was studied during Autumn and Winter. The Habitat Compression Hypothesis (HCH) was verified, with most zooplankton groups showing an abscence, or limited vertical migration. The distribution of euphausiids was studied. The dominant species were the low-oxygen-adapted Euphausia distinguenda, for spring, and Euphausia lamelligera for autumn. However, the autumn second dominant non-migrant species Stylocheiron affine was drastically reduced during the spring cruise, in favor of low-oxygen tolerant species like Euphausia tenera and Euphausia eximia, in coincidence with a shallower OMZ. A comparison of a 48 hours of continuous vertical distribution sampling, confirm the HCH, but with more accentuated differences between shallow and deeper waters in spring than in autumn, and on the day/night differences.

presentations.title: TOWARDS INCLUSION OF ZOOPLANKTON PREY QUALITY AS A FUNCTIONAL TRAIT: APPLICATION OF LIPIDOMICS IN ECOSYSTEM MONITORING
presentations.abstract: Food quality, particularly the availability of essential fatty acids and diverse lipid classes (e.g., triacylglycerols, phospholipids), is a key biochemical trait of zooplankton that shapes fish fitness and marine food web dynamics. Essential fatty acids such as DHA and EPA are critical for fish growth and reproduction, while lipid classes indicate energy storage, membrane integrity, and stress responses. These compounds influence prey quality and reflect organismal condition, affecting population dynamics and trophic interactions, key indicators of ecosystem health. However, these biochemical traits are rarely measured in ocean monitoring programs, leaving a critical gap in our ability to link zooplankton quality to fish condition and ecosystem productivity. To address this gap, our project comprehensively measures the lipid composition of major zooplankton taxa that serve as key prey for juvenile fish and other higher trophic levels. This approach provides species-specific insights into essential fatty acids and lipid classes, which are critical for understanding prey quality and energy transfer. To achieve this, we are developing lipidomics-based methods within Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s continental shelf monitoring program along the West Coast of Vancouver Island during spring and summer cruises. Lipidomics enables detailed profiling of these biochemical traits, offering new opportunities to characterize zooplankton functional diversity and link organismal condition to ecosystem productivity in a changing ocean. Understanding zooplankton species-specific lipid composition changes across time and space is critical for predicting how climate-driven changes in zooplankton quality cascade through marine food webs and influence fish survival. By integrating lipidomics into long-term monitoring, this work provides a framework to track functional traits alongside abundance, enabling more accurate assessments of ecosystem health and resilience under climate change.

presentations.title: Invasive species reshape plankton interaction networks under warming and nutrient change: an emperical modelling test
presentations.affiliation: Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Climate change, nutrient fluctuations and species invasions are fundamentally altering freshwater ecosystems; yet their interactive effects on plankton community structure and pelagic food-web stability remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to forecast essential ecosystem services. Here, we investigate how warming temperatures, changing nutrient levels and fish reshape plankton interactions in several temperate lakes that support recreation, fisheries and drinking-water supply and have undergone eutrophication, climate change and repeated biological invasions. Using long-term time series of plankton and whitefish, we apply empirical dynamic modelling to reconstruct time-varying plankton interactions and quantify emergent ecosystem properties such as connectance, modularity and stability. We hypothesise that plankton interactions exhibit nonlinear responses to environmental drivers, with shifts in ecosystem stability and modularity emerging at critical temperature–nutrient thresholds. We expect that if whitefish abundance increase, then we will detect marked reorganisations of pelagic interaction networks and to alter the timing and magnitude of ecosystem responses to climate and nutrient change. Identifying the timing and mechanisms of shifts in plankton interactions and emergent properties will enable scientists and managers to better anticipate future lake states and develop resilient, evidence-based management strategies for ecosystems increasingly shaped by invasive species.

presentations.title: Spatial, Temporal, and Ontogenetic Variation in the Trophic Ecology of Blackfin Flounder (Glyptocephalus stelleri) on the Eastern Coast of Korea Using Stable Isotopes
presentations.affiliation: 1. East Sea Research Institute, Korea Institute of Ocean Science & Technology. 2. University of Science & Technology, South Korea
presentations.abstract: This study investigated the spatial, seasonal, and ontogenetic variation in the trophic ecology of blackfin flounder (Glyptocephalus stelleri) on the eastern coast of Korea using stable isotope analysis. Dorsal muscle tissues were collected from Ayajin and Hupo (n = 261) between 2023 and 2024, oven-dried, homogenized, and analyzed for δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N using an Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer (IRMS). Trophic positions were calculated from δ¹⁵N values, using copepods as the primary baseline, and isotopic niche width (SEAc) and overlap were quantified using SIBER and nicheROVER in R. PERMANOVA revealed significant effects of season, station, and maturity on isotopic composition (p < 0.01), with significant interactions between season and maturity (p < 0.01) and between maturity and station (p < 0.05). Seasonal δ¹³C ranged from −20.82‰ to −16.30‰ and δ¹⁵N from 10.87‰ to 13.64‰, with Hupo individuals more enriched than those from Ayajin. Immature fish had lower δ¹³C (−18.92‰) and δ¹⁵N (11.58‰) than mature individuals (δ¹³C: −18.4‰; δ¹⁵N: 12.35‰). Isotopic niche size varied seasonally (summer 0.65‰², winter 0.66‰², autumn 0.68‰², spring 0.78‰²), spatially (Ayajin 0.44‰², Hupo 0.47‰²), and ontogenetically (immature 0.46‰², mature 0.80‰²). Niche overlap ranged from 52.2% (autumn–winter) to 90.8% (spring–summer), and trophic positions varied with season (3.29–3.53), ontogeny (3.29–3.51), and location (Ayajin 3.26, Hupo 3.53). These findings indicate that blackfin flounder exhibit flexible feeding strategies, with trophic ecology strongly influenced by season, location, and developmental stage. Mature individuals exploit broader trophic niches, and high intraspecific niche overlap highlights substantial resource sharing, emphasizing the value of multidimensional approaches in trophic studies and fisheries management.

presentations.title: Impact of Aerobic Anoxygenic Phototrophic bacteria on the aquatic carbon cycle
presentations.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries, Stechlin, Germany
presentations.abstract: Microbial respiration is commonly measured as oxygen consumption after dark incubations. Aerobic anoxygenic photoheterotrophic (AAP) bacteria are a functional group characterized by their relatively large size, high metabolic activity, and rapid growth, which can be partially attributed to their ability to harvest extra energy from light via bacteriochlorophyll-a-containing type II reaction centers. Despite their widespread occurrence and contribution (1–23% of aquatic bacterial communities), their ecological roles remain insufficiently understood. To better understand their role in the carbon cycle and microbial food webs, we conducted four complementary field studies and measured the microbial respiration in the presence of infrared light, able to be absorbed by AAP bacteria but not by oxygenic phototrophs. We found that light-derived energy enables AAP bacteria to reduce microbial respiration while enhancing carbon uptake, suggesting that dark incubaton measurements overestimate microbial respiration by 15% in a meso-oligotrophic freshwater lake. AAPs are also present substantially in coastal marine waters, where they were notably more abundant in the particle-attached fraction during the most productive seasons. AAP bacteria peak during spring phytoplankton blooms and correlating with the primary producers. Our results suggest their ability to thrive on carbon-rich particles while minimizing respiratory carbon loss highlights their potential to channel organic matter efficiently through microbial food webs toward higher trophic levels.

presentations.title: INVESTIGATING MICROBIAL INFLUENCES ON SEDIMENT NUTRIENT INTERNAL LOADING MECHANISMS IN THE GREAT LAKES CANADA
presentations.abstract: Eutrophication poses significant threats to freshwater ecosystems globally. Internal nutrient loading has become a dominant long-term driver of eutrophication, especially in North American large lakes. Sediment microbes can mediate nutrient cycling thus impacting the internal loading potential. However, previous studies have primarily focused on abiotic nutrient release mechanisms, while ignoring the role of microorganisms. In this study, we correlate sediment nutrient dynamics from elemental and molecular interpretation of the sediment microbiomes using high-throughput DNA and cDNA sequencing of 16S rRNA genes in Lake Erie western and central basin. We observed significant chemical and microbial gradients across western to central basin. Differences in the sediment Al/Fe stoichiometry (molar ratios were <3) were observed, phosphorous associated with apatite/mineral-bound forms. Collectively, DNA sequencing showed uniform distribution of Acidobacteriota taxa across all sites, while cDNA indicated Pseudomonadota was the most active. Functional metabolisms show gradients of nitrogen cycling, and phosphorous mobilization potential, which corresponds to identified active communities involved in nitrogen cycling. In this study our results were able to show significant dependence between nitrogen and phosphorous internal loading potential at the sediment water interface in these systems across the western basin of Lake Erie. This talk will highlight some of these observations and discuss impacts on large lake systems responses to eutrophication.

presentations.title: Microbial and Redox Archives in Great Lakes Sediments: Linking Biogeochemistry to Environmental Change
presentations.abstract: Sediment cores are vital recorders of natural biogeochemical processes and the cumulative effects of human impacts and pollution. As part of the Great Lakes Sediment Surveillance Program, we investigated vertical profiles of the sediment microbiome and redox capacity across cores from all five Laurentian Great Lakes. We compared the phylogenetic composition of the metabolically active microbial community to the total community, and quantified the sediment's electron-donating and accepting capacities using mediated electrochemical analysis, alongside key redox species. The overall electron exchange capacity, an indicator of the total redox-active sites, was shaped by sediment depth and microbial community structure. Most cores exhibited stratified redox layers corresponding to oxygen availability (0-3cm), progressing from oxygen respiration to iron reduction, and methanogenesis. In contrast, Lake Superior core retained deep oxygen penetration down 10 cm, dated to ~1850, supported by dominance of aerobic and oxidase-positive genera including ammonia oxidizers, sulfur oxidizers, and methanotrophs. Distinct microbial and redox profiles among lakes reflected anthropogenic influences and environmental stressors such as organic loading and invasive species. This integrated approach linking sediment microbiomes with redox capacity provides valuable archives for understanding ecosystem dynamics and offers insights for environmental management and forecasting ecological change.

presentations.title: Relation between river-talik system, organic matter remobilization, and the microbial community
presentations.affiliation: Institut National de la Recherche Scientifique
presentations.abstract: Access to safe drinking water all year round remains a major challenge for most communities in the North. In Nunavik (northern Québec), surface water is usually the main source for drinking water. The quantity and quality (chemical and microbiological) of surface water in arctic regions, however, can fluctuate considerably, requiring appropriate treatment procedures and alternative sources to prevent shortages. Taliks, which are zones of permanently unfrozen ground in permafrost regions, can contain pumpable good quality groundwater all year round. Yet few northern communities use groundwater for their drinking water needs. This study aims to provide better insight into the viability and potential of river-talik systems as a source of drinking water. Specifically, this study aims to characterize (i) the taxonomic and functional diversity of the microbial communities; and (ii) the fate and mobility of polycyclic aromatic compounds (PACs) in a talik underneath the Kuuguluk River in Salluit, Nunavik. Fieldwork was carried out in August 2025 and included surface water, groundwater, and soil sampling. Bacterial DNA from filtered (0.22 um) water and soil samples were extracted and sequenced using an Oxford Nanopore Technologies PromethIon sequencer. Microbial communities were described using long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing and Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs) were assembled at some sites to study potential functional diversity. PACs present in soil and water were analysed using gas chromatography – mass spectrometry (GC-MS).

presentations.title: UNVEILING DIEL MICROBIAL DYNAMICS: EDNA TRACES FUNCTIONAL CHANGES ON MICROBIAL STREAM COMMUNITIES
presentations.affiliation: IHCantabria - Instituto de Hidráulica Ambiental de la Universidad de Cantabria
presentations.abstract: Microbial communities exhibit diel patterns in metabolic and physiological activities, shaped by environmental cues and often regulated by intrinsic clocks. Understanding their short-term responses is key to elucidating the role of microbial behavior and on ecosystem functioning. We investigated diel patterns in riverine bacterial activity using 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding and functional predictions based on PICRUSt2 and KEGG Orthology. For the first time, we applied environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding to detect fine-scale temporal dynamics in microbial composition and potential functions over a 24-hour cycle. Significant shifts in the relative abundance of specific taxa suggest changes in metabolic activity, while overall diversity remained stable, indicating functional adjustments rather than taxonomic turnover. Functional predictions revealed circadian-like behavior, with taxa showing temporally structured activity aligned with environmental cycles. Daytime peaks occurred in carbohydrate and energy metabolism, aerobic respiration, and nutrient transport, whereas detoxification, stress response, and regulatory pathways increased towards the afternoon and night. These findings highlight the dynamic nature of microbial communities in lotic ecosystems and underscore the value of eDNA-based approaches for capturing diel microbial dynamics, offering insights for environmental monitoring and biogeochemical cycling.

presentations.title: ASSESSMENT OF HEAVY METAL CONCENTRATION IN FRESH WATER PRAWNS (MACROBRACHIUM SPP) IN THE CALABAR RIVER, NIGERIA
presentations.abstract: This study assessed concentrations of heavy metals (chromium (Cr), cadmium (Cd), and nickel (Ni)) in two freshwater prawn species, Macrobrachium macrobrachion and Macrobrachium vollenhovenii, from the Calabar River, Nigeria, to evaluate potential ecological and human health risks. Prawns were collected between May and July 2024 from artisanal fishermen at Esuk Nsidung and Eserebom, preserved on ice, and analyzed using Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry following acid digestion. Mean concentrations in M. macrobrachion were 0.031 ± 0.01 mg/kg (Cr), 0.0081 ± 0.008 mg/kg (Cd), and 0.339 ± 0.21 mg/kg (Ni); in M. vollenhovenii they were 0.031 ± 0.016 mg/kg (Cr), 0.0071 ± 0.0071 mg/kg (Cd), and 0.077 ± 0.04 mg/kg (Ni). Statistical analysis (Student’s t-test) revealed no significant differences (p > 0.05) between the two species for all metals. All detected concentrations were below World Health Organization (WHO) permissible limits, indicating that prawn consumption from this river poses no immediate toxicological risk. Comparative analysis with previous studies showed lower or comparable metal levels, suggesting reduced anthropogenic pollution inputs in the sampling area. These findings provide baseline data for environmental monitoring and highlight the need for continuous surveillance to ensure long-term food safety and ecosystem health.

presentations.title: TRACKING RESOURCE-RESPONSIVE PHENOTYPES IN OLIGOTROPHIC DIATOMS
presentations.abstract: The oligotrophic surface ocean is typically dominated by picocyanobacteria, however irregular increases in microeukaryotes such as diatoms can increase primary production and carbon (C) export. Here, we used Lagrangian in situ sampling and shipboard incubations to identify patterns in diatom biodiversity and phenotype with metatranscriptome sequencing. Surface ocean diatom populations increased in a North Pacific Subtropical Gyre (NPSG) water mass by the mid-point of the Lagrangian timeseries. In concurrent shipboard nutrient-addition experiments, diatom populations increased in all treatments with added nitrogen (N). In both the timeseries and N-amended incubations, the diatom increases were dominated by Cylindrotheca, a pennate diatom which has repeatedly increased with N addition in studies from prior years. All of the N-responsive genes in Cylindrotheca identified in the incubations were similarly expressed in situ where Cylindrotheca increased in abundance. This shared transcriptional response suggests that an increase in bioavailable N was an essential shared driver of these Cylindrotheca populations. Even subtle changes in N availability may play a key role in community composition dynamics in the oligotrophic ocean. Ongoing work is investigating whether Cylindrotheca is a ‘resource specialist’ relative to other oligotrophic diatom phenotypes, better attuned to respond to resource availability than other diatoms.

presentations.title: MICROBIAL ECOLOGY AND CARBON BIOGEOCHEMISTRY IN A HIGHLY VARIABLE SHALLOW EUTROPHIC LAKE
presentations.abstract: Inland aquatic ecosystems are globally-relevant sites of carbon dioxide and methane cycling. In ponds and shallow lakes, short-term mixing events can result in dramatic temporal changes in temperature, oxygen availability, and the distribution of nutrients and organic matter. Recent work emphasizes the potentially outsized contribution of these systems to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, yet the response of the microbial communities responsible for GHG production and consumption remains poorly resolved. To quantify the response of microbial communities to stratification variability and the relative contributions of ecological, chemical, and physical processes to dissolved gas concentrations, we conducted repeated sampling of a shallow, eutrophic water body at six sites. We measured in-situ temperature, dissolved oxygen, and pH water column profiles and observed temporal changes indicative of frequent mixing. We also sampled three depths to quantify concentrations of nutrients, chlorophyll a, and dissolved gases. To determine the composition and metabolic potential of microbial communities, we performed shotgun metagenomics and analyzed the phylogenetic and biogeographic distribution of relevant pathways. We find that microbial community composition mirrors stratification changes and highlights the role of differential methane production and consumption. Examining diversity at different levels of organization in response to environmental change is critical to understanding the influence of microbial ecology on carbon cycling dynamics.

presentations.title: HOW OPTICS AND THERMODYNAMICS SHAPE METHANE EMISSIONS FROM LAKES
presentations.abstract: The interactions of light regime and physical stratification can be argued to dictate greenhouse gas flux through determining the thermodynamics in lake systems. Using geochemical profiling and metagenomics, we reconstructed metabolic networks in a wide range of lakes including ferruginous (iron-rich) and euxinic (sulfide-rich) systems. We observed significant methane accumulation in the anoxic monimolimnion—up to 420 µM in ferruginous lakes—yet surface levels remained low, indicating a highly efficient biofilter at the chemoclines. We identified a tight thermodynamic coupling between phototrophs and methanotrophs driven by oxidant regeneration. In ferruginous lakes, anoxygenic phototrophs likely use reduced iron (Fe2+) as an electron donor. This process regenerates oxidized iron (Fe3+), while in euxinic lakes light energy is utilized to recycle essential electron acceptors such as SO42- (e.g., Chlorobium), required for anaerobic methane oxidation. Oxygenic phototrophs (e.g., Cyanobium) detected at and above the chemocline likely provide oxygen. This supply sustains aerobic methanotrophs like Crenothrix and Methylobacter even in suboxic waters. Hence methanotrophic capacity is ultimately constrained by optical properties selecting for low-intensity light anoxygenic or high-intensity oxygenic phototrophs. Consequently, levels of chromophoric dissolved organic matter determine methane oxidation rates. We conclude that chemoclines function as dynamic, light-powered engines for methane removal, sensitive to brownification and climate-induced shifts in stratification.

presentations.title: Vertical patterns in microbial community structure and metabolic potential in warm Central Texas ponds
presentations.abstract: Small warm ponds are important sites of biogeochemical cycling, yet little is known about how microbial communities in these systems respond to extreme summer heat and seasonal changes in the water column. Understanding how these communities function under such conditions is essential for predicting biogeochemical responses to climate driven warming. We examined two Central Texas ponds that routinely exceed 32C to determine how microbial taxa and metabolic functions vary with depth and season. We sampled every other month for one year, with metagenomic and water chemistry analyses planned for both surface and bottom waters. Metagenomes were used to evaluate community composition and metabolic potential across major biogeochemical pathways. Results from June show that organic carbon oxidation and fermentation dominate carbon cycling at the surface. Methanotrophy appears in only a few genomes, suggesting limited surface methane consumption during high temperature periods. Nitrogen cycling potential is present but modest, including nitrogen fixation and nitrite ammonification. Sulfur cycling is more prominent, with widespread sulfur oxidation and limited evidence of reductive sulfur processes. These findings indicate that during peak summer heat, surface microbial communities are driven primarily by aerobic carbon processing with selective contributions to nitrogen and sulfur transformations. Ongoing analyses across seasons and depths will clarify how thermal structure influences microbial function in warm pond ecosystems.

presentations.title: Bioaccumulation of Heavy Metals and microbial loads and its heavy risk in mudskipper from Buguma creek of Niger Delta, Nigeria.
presentations.affiliation: Nigerian Institute for Oceanography and Marine Research,Lagos,
presentations.abstract: Mudskipper (Perrophtal Moclon)are benthic burrowers, sediment feeders and widely consumed in most areas of Niger Delta, Nigeria. They are usually affected with different types of pollutants from agricultural produce, pipeline destruction, chemical activities, transportation effluent. They are used in aquatic ecotoxicology studies. However microbial load and heavy metals pollution in most creeks, coastal swamps and estuaries has been a major concern that threatens aquatic ecosystem water quality and biodiversity. These poses threat to livelihood, food security. Heavy metals such as pb, cd, fe, Hg, faecalcoliform and Vibro were analysed in mudskipper.The mudskipper were digested and examined for heavy metals concentration using flame atomic absorption spectrophotometer. The sample organisms for microbal load were homogenised using 200ml sterile ,0.2% saline water for 2 minutes .A tenfold dilution of 107 of the homogenates were used .1 ml of fresh sterile dilutors to plates of the 5- tube MPN (most portable numbers) method described by Geihariat et al (1996) was used. Enumeration of bacteria was done using Thiosulphate citrate sugar Agar (TCBS), 0.1ml of samples pipettes was added aseptically into TCBS plate in triplicate and spread with a sterile like glass rod. The vibro species were enumerated using standard microbiological technique(BAM,1998).The levels of pb, cd, fe, hg, ranged between 20±0.006 to 3.20 ±0.008mg/kg, 0.02 to 1.23 ±0.001mg/kg, 2.80±0.004 to 5.20 ±0.009mg/kg and 0.01 ±0.009 to 0.03±0.008mg/kg respectively while the faecal coliform and vibro recorded.0.3 x105 to1.5 x105 and 1.8x105 to 2.0x105 CFU. The pb, cd and Hg recorded higher values than the safe levels according to the FAO|WHO and USEPA. Hence, there is a healththreatening risk to consumers in neurological, carcinogenic, Kidney and cardio vascular diseases, diabetes, and gastrointestinal issues.

presentations.title: Auxotrophy in freshwater Nanopelagicaceae strains revealed by genomic and culture-based analyses
presentations.abstract: Free-living bacteria in oligotrophic ecosystems often exhibit genome streamlining, resulting in auxotrophic dependencies on essential cofactors under nutrient-limited conditions. In this study, strains belonging to the Candidatus Nanopelagicaceae, an abundant group of free-living freshwater bacteria, were investigated to assess their physiological reliance on heme, riboflavin, and NAD, essential cofactors required for fundamental metabolic processes. We isolated Nanopelagicaceae strains from Lake Soyang in Korea using a dilution-to-extinction approach and sequenced to obtain complete genomes. Phylogenetic analysis assigned the strains to the Ca. Planktophila (acI-A1, A4, A6, and A7 tribes). Genomic analysis revealed the absence of key genes required for the de novo biosynthesis of essential metabolites, suggesting metabolic dependence on external sources. This inference was supported by culture-based experiments, which demonstrated that growth occurred only when the required cofactors were supplied. These findings shed light on the diverse unexpected external dependencies of this lineage and suggest that such traits may influence their niche patterns and ecological roles within freshwater microbial communities.

presentations.title: Tiny Organisms Making Big Waves: Microbial Communities and Dynamics in Regions Across the South Indian Ocean
presentations.abstract: The Indian Ocean is reported to be warming at higher rates than other oceans, with anticipated consequences for biodiversity and primary productivity. Indian ocean microbial ecology is understudied, especially in the South Indian Ocean (SIO) where little is known about microbial community connectivity and structure. Here, we address this knowledge gap using samples collected on a GEOTRACES cruise across the SIO from Durban, South Africa to Fremantle, Australia in December 2024 to January 2025. Phytoplankton and non-photosynthetic prokaryotes were enumerated via flow cytometry, 16S rRNA gene amplicons were sequenced, and biogeochemical measurements were made. Analyses exposed diversity across the phytoplankton, bacteria and archaea–across latitudinal and vertical gradients. Growth rates of the phytoplankton Prochlorococcus, the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth, were also assessed using cell cycle analysis of flow cytometry samples collected over day–night cycles in the open ocean. We compared photic-zone microbial community structures from coastal Madagascar, the open ocean, and coastal Australia. Because Madagascar is subject to strong currents and eddy shedding, the central open ocean region is highly oligotrophic, and western Australia's coast has moderate upwelling, we were able to investigate how the differing communities were shaped by ocean conditions. Better understanding the microbial communities of the SIO and their dynamics is vital as a baseline for future work to see potential changes in food webs and primary production under climate change.

presentations.title: It’s not easy being green: seasonal and decadal shifts in phytoplankton community composition in the subtropical North Atlantic
presentations.abstract: The North Atlantic subtropical gyre (NASG) is characterized by annual spring phytoplankton blooms followed by less productive stratified periods. On a multiyear scale, surface waters of the NASG are increasing in temperature, salinity, and acidity. These trends are expected to continue, with anticipated corresponding changes in phytoplankton community diversity and function. Phytoplankton in this region have been characterized across the decades so that general seasonal changes are well documented. Here, we draw on 30 years of monthly sampling at the Bermuda Atlantic Time-Series (BATS) site in the northwestern Sargasso Sea to investigate seasonal and decadal changes in phytoplankton community structure and dynamics. We examine phytoplankton groups at the species and amplicon sequence variant (ASV) levels using 16S rRNA gene amplicons (that capture both cyanobacteria and eukaryotic phytoplankton) and connect trends to environmental data and satellite-derived chlorophyll a-based phenology. Although there was not an overall decrease in the chlorophyll a signature during spring blooms, the relative abundances of green algae, major spring bloom contributors, have declined in recent years. The relative stability of bloom-time chlorophyll signals coupled with seasonal shifts in other phytoplankton groups, with predatory mixotrophs expanding their seasonal ranges. These observations demonstrate the ongoing effects of changing ocean conditions on key phytoplankton groups, with anticipated effects on primary production, food webs, and biogeochemical processes.

presentations.title: Patterns of local adaptation in a deep-water specialist Chloroflexota population across the Laurentian Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Deep water is marked by cold temperatures, complete darkness, high hydrostatic pressure, and low nutrient concentrations, all of which culminate in lower and slower biological activity compared to surface regions that may impose unique constraints on molecular evolution. The Laurentian Great Lakes (LGL) constitute the deepest large lake ecosystem on Earth and host a diversity of deepwater specialist microorganisms that must contend with steep environmental gradients throughout the system, particularly during seasonal mixing. Here, we utilize metagenomic read-mapping and pangenomics to analyze the microdiversity structure of the phylum Chloroflexota CL500-11 clade across the LGL, a freshwater deep-water specialist that comprises 10-30% of the bacterial community in the LGL hypolimnia. This work reveals remarkably low population diversity within the CL500-11 clade despite its numerical dominance, with population substructure primarily emerging from Lake Erie, which is unique in nutrient load, depth, residence time, and surrounding land use among the otherwise oligotrophic LGL. CL500-11 metagenome-assembled genomes from Lake Erie are enriched in enzymes that metabolize the plant-associated sugars xylose, arabinose, and rhamnose, highlighting a potential adaptative response to increased concentrations of algal-derived metabolites in Lake Erie. Together, this work examines the influence of the environmental conditions in deep water on the microdiversification of a dominant deep-water bacterial lineage.

presentations.title: Investigating Genomic Markers of Microbial Oil Biodegradation in Arctic Marine Ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Rapid arctic warming and declining sea ice are opening northern waters to increased shipping and resource extraction. This raises the likelihood of accidental oil spills that pose serious risks to Inuit communities and Arctic marine ecosystems. Because the presence of sea ice limits access to oil contaminants for mechanical or chemical cleanup, biodegradation by natural microbial populations is the most viable response strategy. Despite its importance, our limited understanding of how microbial communities degrade petroleum oil in ice-laden waters continues to hinder the development of effective spill-response strategies. To address this gap, we conducted 8-week mesocosm experiments at the Ocean-Sea Ice Mesocosm (OSIM) Facility in Churchill, Manitoba. This state-of-the-art facility allows us to add large volumes (118 L) of diesel to expansive pools of ice-laden seawater (255 m³ each) in a controlled setting. To track the response of microbial communities under realistic arctic conditions, we leveraged metagenomics with longitudinal modeling to catalogue taxa and genes indicative of oil biodegradation. Preliminary results indicate that diesel-impacted communities exhibit slow (>20 days), but pronounced shifts in community composition, including substantial increases in known oil degraders (e.g., Cycloclasticus). Integration of genomic and geochemical datasets is nearly complete and will further resolve the capacity and constraints of microbial oil biodegradation within sea ice and underlying ecosystems in the Arctic Ocean.

presentations.title: DIGGING INTO THE UNKNOWN BIODIVERSITY OF MANITOBA’S SALINE SPRING SEDIMENTS
presentations.abstract: Extreme environments provide a prime opportunity to study biodiversity, biogeography, evolution, and population dynamics. The discontinuous nature of these habitats results in independent evolutionary pressures and trajectories for the organisms that inhabit them. Examples of these environments are the saline springs located on the west bank of Lake Winnipegosis, Manitoba, which host diverse microbial communities, but have lacked targeted study using modern molecular techniques until recently. Here, we sampled four of the >60 saline springs and used these samples for metagenomic DNA extraction and sequencing. Sequence reads were assembled and binned to recover metagenome-assembled genomes of organisms - some representing novel taxa as high as the phylum level. The reconstructed genomes were leveraged to guide cultivation efforts through inferring metabolisms, community roles and ecosystem functions. Overall, this data will support taxonomic descriptions of numerous novel taxa. As the first molecular data generated from these springs, this will also serve as benchmark for prokaryotic community composition in these spring systems. The high level of novelty in the uncovered microbial diversity is expected to provide insights into biogeography, as studies of these environments will now be targeted at uncovering microbial endemicity. Although the saline springs are all derived from the same subterranean saline aquifer, the springs are geographically isolated and physicochemically diverse, contributing to the different evolutionary drivers experienced by these communities.

presentations.title: METABOLICALLY ACTIVE SEDIMENT MICROBIAL COMMUNITIES INDICATE TROPHIC STATUS AND ANTHROPOGENIC INFLUENCES IN DISTURBED LAURENTIAN GREAT LAKES
presentations.abstract: Biogeochemical cycles in freshwater systems can vary across ecological gradients, such as the interconnected Laurentian Great Lakes, which offer a unique opportunity to investigate how microbes, the primary drivers of biogeochemical cycles, respond under natural fluctuations and anthropogenic stressors. As part of the Great Lakes Sediment Surveillance Program, we assessed both the total (DNA) and active (RNA) communities in the surface sediments of all five Laurentian Great Lakes to identify spatially explicit diversity in phylogenetic composition and the breadth of metabolic capabilities contributing to major biogeochemical cycles. Our results show that oligotrophic lakes (Superior, Huron, Michigan) exhibit greater spatial homogeneity in functional gene profiles compared to eutrophic lakes (Erie, Ontario). Lakes with stronger anthropogenic stressors demonstrated border metabolic capabilities, including aromatic hydrocarbon degradation and chlorate reduction, as indicated by predicted functional profiles. Microbial community composition clustered along nutrient availability gradients, specifically Huron and Superior are tightly clustered, whereas Erie, Ontario, and Michigan show more dispersed patterns. A higher functional capability gradient across the trophic statuses of the Laurentian Great Lakes underscores the influence of external factors, including nutrient loading and human activity, in shaping the functional capacities of freshwater sediment microbial communities.

presentations.title: Transient Dynamics in the Vertical Competition Between Sinking and Buoyancy-Regulating Phytoplankton Species
presentations.abstract: In the temperate zone of the Northern Hemisphere, lakes typically exhibit seasonal patterns of thermally stratified and fully mixed periods. Global warming is altering these cycles, particularly by prolonging summer stratification. Phytoplankton dynamics are closely linked to these patterns: spring bloom formation is typically associated with higher average light availability with the onset of summer stratification, yet stratification also increases the risk of cells sinking out of the euphotic layer. To avoid sinking, many phytoplankton species have evolved motility traits such as flagella or buoyancy regulation. Observations from deep, clear-water lakes in the Northern Hemisphere suggest that especially low-light-adapted cyanobacteria, such as Planktothrix rubescens, might benefit from extended stratification periods through their capacity to vertically migrate via active buoyancy regulation. This trait may confer a competitive advantage over sinking species. Using a 1D model, this study investigates competition between sinking and buoyancy-regulating phytoplankton species along the vertical water column. Species compete for light and nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus) along heterogeneous depth gradients, making use of a modified Droop model. Specifically, we examine how seasonal stratification patterns influence phytoplankton dynamics and how physiological traits related to resource utilization and vertical movement strategies influence transient dynamics. Overall, this work provides new insights into the early development of phytoplankton blooms under changing lake stratification regimes.

presentations.title: Phytoplankton intraspecific traits variation and trade-offs along environmental gradients
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton traits vary substantially both across and within species. Interspecific trait variation plays a key role in shaping community interactions and underlies species sorting in response to environmental change. Beyond variation across species, research increasingly recognizes the importance of differences within species. This intraspecific variation can drive population structure and dynamics and underpins adaptive responses to shifting environments. Such variation arises not only among genotypes but also within genotypes through single-cell differences. Yet both levels of intraspecific trait variation remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the extent of trait plasticity, potential trade-offs, and their consequences for population dynamics in natural environments. Here, we synthesize recent advances on intraspecific variation, plasticity, and trade-offs in phytoplankton traits, and propose an approach for untangling genotypic and single-cell contributions to trait diversity to more accurately represent population responses to environmental change. We also highlight existing and developing techniques that jointly address both sources intraspecific trait variation.

presentations.title: Long-term shifts in phenology of nearshore zooplankton in Lake Ontario
presentations.abstract: Seasonal succession of nearshore zooplankton reflects the physical environment and biological competition and predation. Nearshore habitats are important spawning areas for fish, and thus recruitment success is largely determined by the alignment in the timing of zooplankton peaks with the larval fish emergence and growth at early life stages. We use a thirty-year (1995-2025) biweekly time series from May-October of seven nearshore (10 m depth) sites in Lake Ontario to track shifts in zooplankton community phenology. The seven sites are distributed along the US southern shore tracking a well-known west to east gradient in thermal structure. Copepod populations are first to peak in May with cyclopoid followed by calanoid species peaks. As the nearshore habitat warms we see bosminid and then daphniid grazers dominate. In late summer and fall, predatory cladocerans are a small component of overall biomass but have a major impact on zooplankton community structure. Sites were grouped by similarity in phenology that reflected geographic patterns. We evaluate whether zooplankton phenology has changed over this critical time period marked by climate change and the expansion of invasive species. This timing is then put in context of the life history of fish species known to utilize nearshore habitat.

presentations.title: The effects of freshwater phytoplankton germination at population and community scales
presentations.abstract: Dormancy, a process by which an organism enters a reversible state of low metabolic activity, is an important shared trait across phytoplankton taxonomic groups as both a bet hedging strategy and a method to survive unfavorable conditions. Phytoplankton use dormancy in response to many biotic and abiotic cues, including temperature and light. The ecological effects of germination from dormant individuals in benthic sediments are largely unknown. We conducted experiments to investigate: (1) how environmental conditions and sediment age affect the abundance and identity of germinating phytoplankton, and (2) how strongly contributions from sediment affect community assembly and dynamics. We created a series of microcosms by incubating alpine lake sediment samples from 0 to 86 years old under different temperature and light conditions. Age of sediment, incubation temperature, and photoperiod affected overall community growth and composition, with functional groups like diatoms and green algae responding favorably to different temperatures and photoperiods. To investigate how such germination affects the whole microalgal community, we also need to understand how germinants interact with the contemporary phytoplankton community. In a second microcosm experiment, we added sediment to unfiltered lake water, using sediment or lake water alone as controls. Over three weeks, we observed differences in the growth rate and composition of these communities, likely influenced by different assembly patterns.

presentations.title: Thermal Limits and Decline of Synechococcus under Accelerated Warming and Marine Heatwaves
presentations.affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Marine picophytoplankton contribute roughly 20% of global oceanic primary production, including thermally resilient taxa such as Synechococcus, which dominate warm oceans and are projected to benefit from future warming. Tropical populations exist near their upper thermal limits, making them highly vulnerable to further warming, a largely unexplored risk for Synechococcus. Here, we combine high-frequency in situ observations and laboratory experiments to examine the thermal tolerance of Synechococcus in one of the warmest marine ecosystems. Over a seven-year period (2018–2024), we monitored population dynamics alongside continuous sea surface temperatures, capturing the increasing frequency and duration of marine heatwaves (MHWs) in 2023–2024, the warmest years on record. Abundance of Synechococcus increased with temperature and peaked at ~30.2°C, but extreme temperatures recorded in 2023–2024 surpassed the thermal capacity of Synechococcus populations. Laboratory experiments of Synechococcus clades isolated from the warmest Red Sea, confirmed strain-specific optima ranging from ~25°C (clade IIIa) to ~33°C (clade IIa), with maximum thermal limit up to 35.2°C. During the unprecedented warming of 2023–2024, when sea surface temperatures exceeded 35°C and MHWs persisted for up to 55 days, Synechococcus blooms weakened by ~4.5-fold. While bloom timing and growth rates remained stable, lower initial abundances at bloom onset drove the decline, signaling a shift in population dynamics under intensified thermal stress. Comparison with published temperature–abundance models demonstrates prior datasets fail to capture responses to extreme warming. Our results provide direct evidence of ecological niche loss in tropical Synechococcus, challenging predictions of their future dominance and highlighting the vulnerability of even the most heat-tolerant primary producers to accelerated warming. These findings underscore the capacity of extreme warming events to rapidly destabilize

presentations.title: HOW BIODIVERSITY MODULATES BLOOM FORMATION: EVIDENCE FROM NATURAL PHYTOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton communities in freshwater systems are characterized by their capacity to form rapid, transient biomass increases, known as blooms, in response to shifting abiotic and biotic conditions. The ability of potential bloom species to monopolize resources depends on their life-history traits, their ecophysiological alignment with environmental conditions, and interactions shaped by community diversity. Diversity can influence bloom dynamics through two opposing mechanisms: selection effects, where high diversity increases the likelihood that a highly competitive species dominates, and complementarity effects, where diverse assemblages partition resources more efficiently, reducing the chance that any single species achieves bloom-level dominance. Grazing pressure further modulates these processes by altering resource monopolization and biomass accumulation. We examined potential bloom formations in natural phytoplankton communities spanning a broad diversity gradient and shaped by long-term environmental history. Communities of naturally different diversity were collected from multiple freshwater lakes and subjected to a mesocosm experiment manipulating grazing and nutrient supply. We quantified community- and species-level bloom metrics across the diversity gradient and compared these results to previous laboratory experiments using artificial communities.

presentations.title: Strong and weak trait–environment associations in subarctic stream diatoms
presentations.abstract: Ecological traits are functional characteristics measurable at the species level and provide valuable insights into how organisms respond to environmental constraints. Here, we investigated how diatom trait groups and individual species respond to environmental variables. Diatoms were sampled at 129 sites in the subarctic streams of Norwegian islands and mainland, and were categorized into three trait groups: high-profile, low-profile and motile diatoms. Data were analyzed using a recently developed method known as Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities, which is a flexible framework for joint species distribution modelling. We found that diatom trait-groups responded relatively weakly to measured environmental variables but showed positive or negative relationships with major ion levels of the water (e.g., conductivity, calcium [Ca2+]). Variance partitioning showed a similar, important contribution of the chemical variables for all the trait groups, while the contributions of physical variables and especially random (spatial) factors were notably lower for all trait groups. Our findings also highlighted considerable variation among species in their relation to environmental variables within the trait groups. Notably, we identified a high number of indicator species within each trait group that were explained by specific environmental factors, mostly chemical variables. Our study suggests that certain diatom species can be considered as useful environmental indicators but the variability in species preferences within the trait group may in some circumstances hamper the use of ecological traits in environmental assessments. Thus, we suggest using species-level ecology combined with trait information to better track environmental change when using diatoms as indicators.

presentations.title: BOREALIZATION OF ZOOPLANKTON COMMUNITIES AND TROPHIC IMPLICATION FOR BOWHEAD WHALES (BALAENA MYSTICETUS) IN WEST GREENLAND
presentations.abstract: The bowhead whale is the only baleen whale that resides in the Arctic year-round. Each spring, hundreds of bowhead whales from the Eastern Canada–West Greenland population migrate to Disko Bay where they consume large amounts of zooplankton. They rely heavily on large, lipid-rich Arctic Calanus species (C. hyperboreus and C. glacialis), while the smaller boreal species C. finmarchicus offers lower energetic value. Rapid climate-driven shifts in zooplankton communities indicate increasing replacement of Arctic taxa by boreal species, potentially altering the energetic landscape available to bowheads during a critical feeding period especially for adult females. This study examines evidence of zooplankton borealization in Disko Bay over the past decade and evaluates its consequences for the size and lipid reserves of Calanus species. Taxonomic composition of existing time series (2017-2025) will be compared with the most recent sampling campaign to quantify recent community changes. Zooplankton samples were collected in April and July 2025 using 150-µm nets. Lipid content is estimated using standardized image-based methods and used as an indicator of prey energy value. These values will be compared with recent estimates of bowhead whale energetic requirements during their spring residency in Disko Bay. Preliminary analyses show an increasing dominance of C. finmarchicus, which is smaller and less lipid-rich than the Arctic species. This trend suggests a decline in the average energetic quantity of available zooplankton, with potential implications for bowhead whale foraging success.

presentations.title: Environmental drivers of zooplankton functional diversity in European pond ecosystems
presentations.abstract: Functional diversity is increasingly recognised as a key driver of ecosystem processes and resilience. Yet, most research has focused on terrestrial ecosystems (mainly terrestrial plants) while freshwater systems, especially small waterbodies such as ponds, remain relatively understudied. Ponds are crucial habitats for biodiversity, supporting a large proportion of the freshwater species pool in the landscape, while also providing essential ecosystem functions and services, such as climate change mitigation, nutrient cycling and pollination. In this study, we quantified the functional richness (i.e., number of functional traits) of zooplankton species in 130 ponds across Europe to identify the environmental factors shaping these communities and their potential vulnerability to climate change. We found that nutrient concentrations and pond morphometric characteristics, including depth and area, were the strongest predictors of zooplankton functional assemblages. Importantly, our results suggest that temperature increases can alter zooplankton functional diversity by shifting the relative abundance of species with different feeding traits, for instance, favouring herbivorous cladocerans over more carnivorous copepods. These shifts can cascade through the ecosystem, influencing phytoplankton densities and broader community dynamics. Our findings highlight the urgent need to preserve and carefully manage pond ecosystems to maintain functional diversity and safeguard ecosystem processes amid multiple anthropogenic pressures.

presentations.title: Environmental filtering of phytoplankton functional strategies across arid reservoirs
presentations.abstract: Phytoplankton communities in arid reservoirs experience strong physical and chemical constraints, making them ideal systems to assess how environmental filtering shapes functional strategies. We analysed phytoplankton communities from four arid reservoirs in north-western Algeria using in-situ measurements, laboratory analyses, Reynolds' Functional Groups, functional indices, and a species trait database. RLQ and fourth-corner analyses were used to link traits with environmental gradients, and zooplankton data were examined to provide complementary community patterns. Assemblages were mainly structured by salinity, depth, and organic enrichment, with oxygenation and temperature acting as secondary drivers. These gradients filtered functional strategies: small, motile or mixotrophic species dominated mineralized waters, whereas larger taxa with siliceous structures characterized deeper and more stable conditions. Functional traits explained community structure more clearly than taxonomy, highlighting their relevance for predicting community responses in arid systems. Trait-based approaches thus were more sensitive of ecological responses than species composition alone and are promising for understanding and monitoring arid reservoirs under environmental change.

name: Weathering the Storm: Motivational Tools for Professional and Personal Resilience
title_full: EC02 Weathering the Storm: Motivational Tools for Professional and Personal Resilience - A 'Voices for Well-being in Aquatic Sciences' live presentation
description: Staying motivated while balancing work and life can be a difficult task for many. Moreover, the many challenges early career researchers (ECRs) face such as uncertain career paths, intense competition for funding and publications, long and often remote field seasons, and even visa requirements can exacerbate motivation. In this 'Voices for Well-being in Aquatic Sciences' installment, ASLO's early career committee will host Dr. Richard Koestner, a professor of Psychology at McGill University, where he has conducted research on human motivation for over 30 years. SDT highlights three basic psychological needs - autonomy, relatedness, and competence that are essential for staying motivated, functioning well, and maintaining mental well-being.

name: Closing Lake Superior's Carbon Budget After 20+ Years
title_full: TH01 Closing Lake Superior's Carbon Budget After 20+ Years
description: Lake Superior (USA/Canada) plays an important role in global biogeochemical cycles because of its size despite having the lowest productivity and nutrient concentrations of the five Laurentian Great Lakes. While inland lakes have a disproportionate impact on global carbon (C) cycling relative to their global surface coverage, Lake Superior's C budget remains poorly constrained. In this town hall, we will discuss recent updates to Lake Superior's C budget with participants, including identifying any missing pools or processes, prioritizing pools and processes in need of constraint, and identifying recent studies or unpublished data to be integrated into estimates.

name: Workshop: Harmonization of distributed data
title_full: WS02 Workshop: Harmonization of distributed data in aquatic sciences
description: With the emergence of machine learning models, re-use of publicly available data in aquatic science has become increasingly common, and in some cases required by funding agencies. Pooling of data across distributed sources has numerous advantages including expanded geographic coverage and increased modeling power. FAIR (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability and Reusability) have become guiding principles in scientific data management. This workshop seeks to bring together a diverse group of aquatic scientists from academia, management agencies, and the private sector.
lead_organizer: Bobby Hensley, National Ecological Observatory Network

name: Synthesize it: Big Data to Test Watershed Hypotheses
title_full: WS03 Synthesize it: Using Big Data to Test Watershed Hypotheses
description: Synthesis lies at the heart of discovery in aquatic science, connecting individual studies into collective insight. This 90-minute, hands-on workshop will introduce participants to the power and practice of synthesis through an interactive, community-driven session centered on a Shiny app developed from a multi-site water-quality dataset.
lead_organizer: Lienne Sethna, St. Croix Watershed Research Station

name: Vibecoding Interactive Tools for Ocean Science
title_full: WS13 Vibecoding Interactive Tools for Ocean Science Communication and Analysis: A Hands-On Tutorial
description: Programming is essential to the work of many ocean scientists, including their data analysis and mechanisms for sharing their results with the public. During this workshop, we will introduce ocean science professionals to what is known as vibecoding. When someone vibecodes, they create computer programs with AI but without touching much of the code themselves. Vibecoding is performed using agentic AIs, such as Claude, Copilot, or Cursor, which interact directly with programming tools and code.
lead_organizer: Caroline Berger, Aarhus University

name: R-Coding and Skill-Building Workshop
title_full: WS09 R-Coding and Skill-Building Workshop
description: Join Dr. Kateri Salk and the ASLO Student Committee for a hands-on R-coding and skill-building workshop. This workshop will guide participants through a workflow using a real-world example of publicly available limnology data. During the session, participants will work through a partially pre-coded R script.
lead_organizer: Alia Benedict, University of Minnesota Duluth

name: From Values to Practice: Inclusive Science Spaces
title_full: WS08 From Values to Practice: Everyday Actions for Inclusive Science Spaces
description: Many researchers in aquatic sciences recognize the importance of equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) but remain unsure how to translate these values into consistent, everyday practice. Organized by the SIL EDI Task Force, this interactive workshop aims to bridge that gap by focusing on small, realistic actions that individuals can take in laboratories, fieldwork, classrooms, and scientific meetings to foster more welcoming and equitable environments.
lead_organizer: Anas Mohamed Usoof, The University of Winnipeg

name: Weaving Indigenous Knowledge and Western Science
title_full: WS05 Opportunities and Challenges in Weaving Indigenous Knowledge and Western Science
description: There are a growing number of research programs in many parts of the world that are working in partnership with indigenous knowledge holders to improve understanding and design more salient solutions for the protection and sustainable future of water and water resources. In this workshop, we will facilitate a discussion around a co-construction and value proposition between Indigenous knowledge holders and western scientists to work together on waters.
lead_organizer: Fanny Noisette, Université du Québec à Rimouski
co_organizers: Kianna bear-Hetherington, Water Guardian, Wolastoqey Nation
Katrine Turgeon, Université du Québec en Outaouais

name: Reciprocity, Data Sovereignty, and Equitable Attributions
title_full: WS10 Reciprocity, Data Sovereignty, and Equitable Attributions in Ocean Research
description: Relationships, data, and connections lie at the confluence of science, people, and knowledge. Research projects focused on an understanding of natural systems are needed to make better, holistic resource management decisions. In Heʻeia, Hawaiʻi, researchers from the university, state agencies, non-profit organizations, and the local, Indigenous communities led the effort in 2017 to conceptualize a guiding document, Kūlana Noiʻi, for equitable and reciprocal community-research partnerships. In this workshop, we will embark on small-group discussions using exercises and case studies on real-life scenarios of research-community partnerships, Indigenous data sovereignty, and appropriate attributions and authorships.
lead_organizer: Yoshimi Rii, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa

name: Tutorials in Physical Limnology for Biologists and Chemists
title_full: WS11 Tutorials in Physical Limnology for Biologists and Chemists
description: The hydrodynamics within lakes leads to transport of solutes and particulates such as phytoplankton. Processes causing such transport include convection from heat loss at the water surface, the turbulence induced by 'breaking' of internal waves, incoming stream or river water. The goal of these tutorials is to present fundamental knowledge of the hydrodynamics of lakes, new developments in instruments and understanding of processes, and models that describe the processes and linkages.
lead_organizer: Sally MacIntyre, University of California - Santa Barbara

name: Walking with Water: Art-Science Collaborations
title_full: RE03 Walking with Water: Art-Science Collaborations and Experiences
description: Professor Elizabeth (Liz) Miller, Communication Studies at Concordia, with expertise in Art-Science collaborations and co-creation, will host a workshop with Dr. Konstantinos Vaziourakis, a limnologist who explores scientific concepts through art, and Soren Brothers, a limnologist and the first ever Science-Climate Change Curator at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto. The workshop will be followed by a guided walk on L'île Sainte-Hélène 'Scales of Waste: An Island, an Archipelago and a River,' using the 'WasteScapes' App.
lead_organizer: Elizabeth Miller, Concordia University
co_organizers: Soren Brothers, Climate Change Science Curator, Royal Ontario Museum

name: Plenary & Opening Ceremony
title_full: PL01 Plenary & Opening Ceremony
description: Andrea Reid, University of British Columbia. Indigenous fisheries, community-based research, and the science of what works. Andrea Reid is a Nisga'a citizen and scientist engaged in community-partnered work on fish and fisheries, critically examining their pasts and envisioning just futures. Her research and teaching, based out of the Nass River Valley on the British Columbia North Coast, centre approaches that are intergenerational, land-based, and relational. Dr. Reid is a Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Fisheries Science, leading the Centre for Indigenous Fisheries at The University of British Columbia.
lead_organizer: ASLO Meetings, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography

name: Plenary & SIL Baldi Award
title_full: PL02 Plenary & SIL Baldi Award
description: Thomas Bianchi, University of New Hampshire - Carbon Processing in Aquatic Critical Zones: Biogeochemical Challenges in the 21st Century. Bianchi holds an M.S. in Ecology and Evolution from Stony Brook University (New York) and a Ph.D. in Marine Sciences from the University of Maryland. Bianchi currently serves as a Research Professor at the University of New Hampshire's Institute for the Study of Earth, Oceans, and Space. Claudia Bonecker, State University of Maringá, SIL Baldi Award Winner - Long-Term Ecological Research in a Neotropical floodplain, Brazil.

Louis Legendre, Sorbonne University and Laval University, ASLO Redfield Award Winner. description: SIL Naumann Thienemann Award Winners: Judit Padisák (University of Pannonia) - leading limnologist known for her foundational contributions to phytoplankton ecology and functional group theory; Dr. Warwick Vincent (Université Laval) - internationally recognized for his pioneering research on high-latitude and polar freshwater ecosystems; Dr. David Hamilton (Griffith University) - internationally respected freshwater scientist whose work in water-quality modelling and ecosystem dynamics has shaped lake and river management worldwide. Alanna Lecher, Lynn University, ASLO Yentsch-Schindler Early Career Award Winner.

title_full: PL05 Plenary & SIL Kilham Award
description: Mak Saito, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution - Exploring the Functional Biogeochemical Capabilities of Microbes in Aquatic Systems as Indicators of Changing Environmental Metabolism. His laboratory studies the nutritional role of metals in marine microorganisms and their influence on global biogeochemical cycles. Sylvia Bonilla, Universidad de la República, Montevideo, Uruguay, SIL Kilham Award Winner - Bloom-forming cyanobacteria: Insights from South America. Cyanobacteria are a distinctive photolithotroph group characterized by high physiological flexibility, unique pigment structure, high morphological diversity and tolerance to extreme environmental conditions.

name: Plenary & ASLO Martin Award
title_full: PL06 Plenary & ASLO Martin Award
description: Sapna Sharma, York University - On thin ice: Are lakes feeling the heat? Sapna Sharma is a Professor in the Department of Biology at York University and York Research Chair in Global Change Biology. Her research highlights how lakes worldwide respond to climate change, including rapid ice loss, warming water temperatures, degrading water quality, and changing fish distributions. Andréa G Grottoli, The Ohio State University, ASLO Martin Award Winner - Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. The 2026 Martin Award is being presented to 'Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals' for fundamentally altering our understanding of coral nutrition and resilience in an era of climate change.

title_full: PL07 Plenary, ASLO Bertics Memorial Presentations and Closing Remarks
description: Robert Arlinghaus, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries - How to integrate across disciplines and among science and society to achieve outcomes that make a difference in the real world: lessons from fisheries science. Robert Arlinghaus is professor of integrative fisheries management at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and group leader at Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries. ASLO Bertics Memorial Presentations: Jan Peter Amend, Sarah M. Collins, Elizabeth (Beth) Hundey. Closing Remarks.
lead_organizer: ASLO Meetings, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography.

name: How to review a manuscript with the ASLO editors
title_full: WS14 How to review a manuscript: a workshop with the ASLO editors
description: Peer review of manuscripts is a key part of scientific publishing. Reviewing is an opportunity to participate in the publishing process. As a reviewer, you are tasked with assessing the work of your colleagues and sharing your thoughts with an editor. In this workshop, the editors of the ASLO journals will answer questions and present guidance on providing an effective review.
lead_organizer: Krista Longnecker, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

name: ASLO-SIL Dance Party
title_full: SE05 ASLO-SIL Dance Party
description: Get ready to dance the night away at the 2026 ASLO–SIL Joint Meeting Dance Party! Join fellow aquatic scientists for an evening of music, movement, and community at the Palais des Congrès de Montréal on Friday, 15 May from 19:30–22:30. title_full: SE01 Opening Reception
description: Celebrate the beginning of the ASLO-SIL Joint Meeting! Complimentary finger food is included in the registration fee and a cash bar is available for beverages. Be sure to pick up your registration badge and attend the Opening Ceremony before joining us
