name: Late Breaking Posters
title_full: LBP01 Late Breaking Posters
description: Late Breaking Posters
lead_organizer: ASLO Meetings, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography

presentations.title: DIVERGENT NEUROENDOCRINE FEEDING RESPONSES IN FISH EXPOSED TO TWO MICROCYSTIS EXUDATES
presentations.abstract: Feeding disruption and energetic metabolism inhibition are key mechanisms underlying fish health decline during cyanobacterial bloom events. Driven by global climate change and habitat alteration, dominant bloom-forming species in plateau lakes, such as Lake Dianchi, are shifting from Microcystis aeruginosa to M. wesenbergii. Using Acrossocheilus yunnanensis as a model organism, this study systematically investigated feeding responses and potential neuroendocrine mechanisms under exposure to these ecologically significant cyanobacteria. We conducted a 96-hour exposure assay utilizing logarithmic-phase cell-free exudates or whole bloom co-cultures. We found that M. aeruginosa induced feeding suppression via a two-phase anorexic effect. This study reveals that the succession from M. aeruginosa to M. wesenbergii in eutrophic lakes may profoundly alter food web structures and functions by disrupting feeding-related neuroendocrine systems in fish.

presentations.title: Chytrid biodiversity across watersheds in Maine: insights from a three-year multi-method survey
presentations.abstract: Chytrids are important in aquatic ecosystems, playing essential ecological roles as parasites and decomposers. Their distribution, taxonomy, and ecological functions are poorly understood, however. To better understand the biodiversity of these fungi in Maine, we integrated eDNA metabarcoding with traditional baited culturing surveys across four freshwater to marine watersheds. To date, we have cultured 124 pure chytrid isolates, mostly from freshwater samples, and 61 thraustochytrid isolates, which dominated the marine samples. From 18S metabarcoding, we found 535 chytrid ASVs spanning many major chytrid lineages. Overall, we found that merging traditional and eDNA methods is crucial for understanding the biodiversity and ecosystem functions of these important fungi.

presentations.title: TEMPERATURE EFFECTS ON CHYTRID ZOOSPORE VIABILITY AND INFECTION PREVALENCE IN PLANKTOTHRIX AGARDHII
presentations.abstract: Lake ecosystems are particularly vulnerable to global warming, as climate stress is expected to intensify aquatic infections, affecting trophic interactions, host populations, and nutrient cycling. Parasitic fungi (Chytridiomycota) infect phytoplankton and play a key role in controlling cyanobacterial blooms while providing alternative food sources within food webs. Here, we used a host-parasite system consisting of the toxigenic cyanobacterium Planktothrix agardhii and its obligate chytrid parasite Rhizophydium megarrhizum to investigate how temperature affects zoospores viability. Zoospore suspensions were incubated at four temperatures for up to 48 hours.

presentations.title: FROM DATA TO DISCOVERY: UNDERSTANDING CANADA'S OCEANS WITH CIOOS
presentations.abstract: Ocean data are critical for effective ocean management. The Canadian Integrated Ocean Observing System (CIOOS) is a national collaboration to make high-quality data from our coast and oceans discoverable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. By bringing together data from multiple sectors — scientific, governmental, community and industrial — into one user-friendly platform, CIOOS builds a coherent information ecosystem, essential to understanding the oceans' changes and making informed decisions. Looking ahead, CIOOS plays a key role in advancing open science by promoting transparent, rigorous research that adheres to international best practices.

presentations.title: Hierarchical control of marine bacterial surface roughness by environmental factors and community diversity in coastal waters
presentations.affiliation: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC)
presentations.abstract: Organic nanoparticles are an important nutrient source for marine bacteria, yet the mechanisms underlying their utilization remain poorly understood. In this study, we conducted a year-long time-series survey at four coastal sites on Okinawa Island, Japan. Surface roughness was measured for 2,245 individual bacterial cells using atomic force microscopy, and bacterial community structure was analyzed based on 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Mean surface roughness varied by up to threefold among samples, indicating pronounced spatiotemporal variability. Statistical analyses revealed that surface roughness was primarily controlled directly by environmental factors such as temperature, salinity, and nutrient concentrations, which together explained 42% of the observed variation.

presentations.title: Wildfires mobilize arsenic from legacy mining-contaminated subarctic catchments
presentations.abstract: Wildfire is a natural ecosystem process, but climate change has led to unparalleled increases in the frequency and severity of wildfires, with impacts observed across aquatic ecosystems. The Yellowknife area was impacted by more than 50 years of atmospheric arsenic-bearing mining emissions and the legacy of these impacts persists on the landscape. In 2023, the ZF015-23 wildfire encroached on the city of Yellowknife. During 2024 and 2025, soil porewater, surface runoff, and stream water samples were collected, and volumetric streamflow data was measured, from burned and unburned catchments. Dissolved arsenic concentrations were significantly higher in burned vs unburned areas (p<0.001).

presentations.title: Differential temporal dietary patterns of highly migratory Northwest Atlantic sharks
presentations.abstract: Dietary patterns of highly migratory marine species are inherently difficult to study. Previous research typically relies on relatively low sample sizes and has lacked a long-term time horizon. In this study, we used a long-term food habits dataset to investigate temporal changes in dietary patterns of pelagic sharks. A multivariate statistical analysis was used to investigate differential dietary patterns across species demographics of a generalist and specialist feeder. Both species displayed statistically significant differences in diet temporally, as well as significant differences in diet between maturity levels.

presentations.title: STORM AFTER STORM: CARBON AND IRON EXPORTS FROM BOREAL ENVIRONEMNTS FOLLOWING INTENSE STORMS
presentations.affiliation: Memorial University of Newfoundland and Labrador
presentations.abstract: The island of Newfoundland is located in the North Atlantic Ocean, and is a sparsely populated island dominated by peatland and boreal forest. The rivers of Newfoundland are high in dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and iron inputting large amounts into the coastal region. Eastern Newfoundland experienced two extreme weather events over a 5-day period, the arrival of post-tropical cyclone Melissa and a weather bomb. Three rivers were sampled prior to the arrival of these events, directly after the events and five days after to investigate the change in DOC concentrations, quality, and iron concentrations.

presentations.title: AI-Assisted Food Web Model Construction: Narragansett Bay as a Proof of Concept for Scalable Ecosystem Modeling
presentations.abstract: Food web models are powerful tools for understanding ecosystem structure and informing management, yet their construction remains prohibitively slow. Building a single model demands years of literature synthesis, diet matrix parameterization across dozens of functional groups, and iterative mass-balance adjustments. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI offer a transformative opportunity to accelerate this process. Here, we present Narragansett Bay (Rhode Island, USA) as a proof-of-concept for an AI-assisted food web construction workflow. Using LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), we automate functional group identification, diet matrix construction, and mass-balance parameterization.

presentations.title: CASTING OFF, SETTING SAIL, AND REACHING NEW SHORES: THE ASLO EMERGING FELLOWS
presentations.abstract: The demand for aquatic scientists across academia, government, industry, not-for-profits, and the private sector is growing —yet pathways into this field remain opaque for many students. To address this need, ASLO has launched a new initiative that builds on our society's decades of experience fostering the next generation of aquatic sciences leaders, the ASLO Emerging Fellows. Our vision for ASLO Emerging Fellows is to bring perspective and talent of underrepresented groups to bear on urgent environmental challenges, while supporting emerging scientists in finding fulfilling careers, and well-compensated positions.

name: The Scientific Publishing Lunch Group
title_full: EC04 The Scientific Publishing Lunch Group – tips on writing, reviewing, and publishing for ECRs by ECRs
description: 'Science is not finished until it's communicated' (Mark Walport). We receive training on how to conduct scientific research as students and early career professionals (jointly referred to as ECRs), but opportunities to develop skills in scientific communication and, more specifically, scientific publishing, are not as abundant. As the Fellowship reaches its 10th year, past and current Fellows will come together during this lunch session to share some of their tips and lessons learnt on writing, reviewing, and publishing.
lead_organizer: Rita Franco-Santos, Oceans Institute, University of Western Australia

name: Gulf of Maine Zooplankton Meet-up
title_full: MT07 Gulf of Maine Zooplankton Meet-up
description: Within the Gulf of Maine, zooplankton represent the primary food source for many ecologically and economically important species, but their abundances are changing in part due to rapid warming in the region. We invite all those studying zooplankton in the Gulf of Maine and nearby regions to join in a collaborative discussion regarding current monitoring efforts, methods, and experiments.
lead_organizer: Patricia Thibodeau, University of New England

name: Aquatic Nitrogen Fixation RCN Social
title_full: SE06 Aquatic Nitrogen Fixation Research Coordination Network Social
description: Do you have a nitrogen fixation? We do too! We invite anyone interested in nitrogen fixation across all aquatic habitats, from headwater stream to the open ocean, to join us to celebrate the advances made over the last five years by the Aquatic Nitrogen Fixation Research Coordination Network. The goal of this event will be to promote networking among RCN participants, discuss outcomes of RCN working groups, and brainstorm future diazo-focused research initiatives.
lead_organizer: Amy Marcarelli, Michigan Technological University

name: How to publish in RIO for Aquatic Mesocosm facilities
title_full: WS15 How to publish in RIO to make your Aquatic Mesocosm facility more visible
description: Aquatic environments worldwide are facing critical challenges (pollution, salinisation, drought, temp increase, invasions etc.) that cause severe problems for biodiversity and human well-being. The AQUACOSM-RI consortium and the virtual network of aquatic mesocosm installations comprise aquatic mesocosm facilities around the world. To support increased national and international project collaboration in mesocosm-based research we offer a workshop on how to easily make your Aquatic Mesocosm facility more visible as RIO publication in a topical collection.
lead_organizer: Stella A. Berger, Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries

name: CyaNut Working Group Meeting
title_full: WG04 CyaNut Working Group Meeting
description: The aim of this SIL working group is to provide a longer-term platform for collaboration to evaluate, consolidate and systematise the vast amount of dispersed information on nutrient control of eutrophication, specifically of cyanobacterial blooms. At our current stage we finished the first two review manuscripts concerning the remaining controversy about the nutrient to address, N or P or both, for mitigating cyanobacterial blooms.
lead_organizer: Sylvia Bonilla, Universidad de la República

name: SIL PEG meeting (Plankton Ecology Group)
title_full: WG05 SIL PEG meeting (Plankton Ecology Group)
description: This will be a hybrid/in-person meeting to bring together and rekindle the SIL working group called PEG (Plankton Ecology Group). This working group was active in the past decades producing highly cited papers and the textbook PEG succession model. The PEG meeting will be about developing strategies for building a collaborative network of plankton ecologists and related fields that can operate during and in between physical meetings.
lead_organizer: Ali Ger, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte

name: Late Breaking Posters
title_full: LBP02 Late Breaking Posters
description: Late Breaking Posters
lead_organizer: ASLO Meetings, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography

presentations.title: Seasonal dynamics in a macrophyte community: Comparison of traditional and environmental DNA techniques
presentations.abstract: Macrophytes are vital members of aquatic ecosystems, contributing to the food web, biogeochemical cycles, and habitat structure. Macrophyte communities within Quebec lakes are typically monitored using traditional methods (e.g., underwater surveys or raking). However, these methods are costly and time-consuming, resulting in lakes being surveyed at most once annually. Our goals are to investigate seasonal variation in a temperate lentic macrophyte community in Quebec, Canada, using traditional and eDNA approaches, and to compare the congruence of the methods over a macrophyte growth season as well as their ability to detect invasive species.

presentations.title: 'IRONING' OF INLAND WATERS: INVESTIGATING WATER COLOR-IRON COUPLING AND POTENTIAL DRIVERS IN EASTERN CANADIAN LAKES
presentations.abstract: Inland waters across the Northern Hemisphere have exhibited a browning trend for several decades. Increases in iron (Fe) concentrations have also been reported, although to a lesser extent, suggesting a coupling between water color (Col) and Fe. We studied 40-year trends in dissolved organic carbon (DOC), Col, and Fe in 106 lakes across eastern Canada. Significant increases in Col and Fe were observed in 70% and 46% of lakes respectively, whereas decreases occurred in 4% and 8%. Cluster analysis revealed that Fe trends closely tracked Col trends, with strong Fe increases observed in lakes with higher mean concentrations and trend slopes in Col and DOC.

presentations.title: Using eDNA tools to identify and quantify the bloom-forming taxa of an unusual algae bloom in a mesotrophic north temperate lake
presentations.abstract: The identity of phytoplankton causing nuisance algal blooms can have large ecosystem and management implications, but traditional monitoring techniques are less useful for small-sized phytoplankton. A two-tiered eDNA approach was used to identify and quantify the bloom forming taxa in a mesotrophic north-temperate lake. We used amplicon sequencing of the 18S and 16S rRNA genes to identify a nano-sized green alga, Rhexinema spp, as the dominant eukaryotic phytoplankton and members of the pico-sized cyanobacteria order, Synechococcales, as the dominant cyanobacterioplankton.

presentations.title: COMPARING AND RECONCILING REFERENCE AND DISTURBANCE CLASSIFICATION METHODS FOR STREAM BIOMONITORING
presentations.abstract: Biomonitoring relies on a reference condition approximating the least-disturbed ecological state, with deviation from this reference measuring human-caused disturbance. Multiple methods exist to define reference and disturbed states, each with advantages and limitations. We compared three methods (professional judgment, principal component analysis, and cluster analysis) to classify low-gradient and hard-bottom stream sites as reference or disturbed by dominant stressor type. Results were reconciled into a unified classification recognizing all disturbance types.

presentations.title: Using a 60+ year dataset of late winter water temperatures to investigate climate change in the lower Great Lakes
presentations.abstract: Understanding the drivers of interannual variability in Great Lakes thermal conditions is essential for predicting ecosystem responses to climate change. In this study, we examine the relationship between large-scale atmospheric forcing and late winter (April) surface and water column water temperature in Lakes Ontario, Huron, and Michigan using data since the late 1960s. Our analysis of long-term records shows a consistent warming trend in April surface water temperature across all lakes. We find a strong linkage between winter (DJF) air temperature and the subsequent the April lake temperature suggesting that winter atmospheric conditions exert strong control on spring thermal structure.

presentations.title: A Novel Autonomous USV System for High-Resolution Freshwater Carbon Accounting
presentations.abstract: Freshwater greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are a critical component of the global carbon cycle; however, accurate quantification remains hindered by sparse sampling and limited site accessibility. To address these challenges, we developed an intelligent unmanned surface vehicle (USV) platform for the autonomous monitoring of surface water GHG emissions. By integrating a USV with a floating flux chamber, a real-time CO₂/CH₄ analyzer, and cloud analytics, this system delivers highly efficient, high-resolution measurements across multiple sites.

presentations.title: MICROPLASTICS IN SURFACE WATER AND SEDIMENT OF HALIFAX, NOVA SCOTIA
presentations.abstract: Microplastics have attracted significant attention over the past twenty years as emerging marine pollutants. We investigated the occurrence of microplastics at three locations within Halifax Harbor (Nova Scotia, Canada): commercial ports, shipyards, and a marina. Surface water and sediment were analyzed for large microplastics (>300 µm) and classified according to size, morphology, color, and polymer composition using optical photothermal infrared (O-PTIR) spectroscopy. Across all locations, fibers were the most prevalent (49%), followed by fragments (38%) and films (13%).

presentations.title: FISHING VESSELS REDISTRIBUTE THEIR ACTIVITY ACROSS STAGES OF OFFSHORE WIND ENERGY DEVELOPMENT IN SOUTHERN NEW ENGLAND
presentations.abstract: In Southern New England, where fishing continues to be a way of life and pillar of commerce, a decade of offshore wind energy development (OWED) has altered fishery dynamics. This study explores spatial patterns of vessel presence and apparent fishing effort across three stages of OWED that encompass ten years of pre-construction, construction, and operation at South Fork Wind and Revolution Wind. Vessel GPS tracking data from the Automatic Identification System were used to calculate mean vessel presence hours and mean apparent fishing hours within and surrounding these offshore wind farms for each development stage.

presentations.title: A MOLECULAR TOOLBOX FOR RAPID AND SENSITIVE DETECTION OF THE HARMFUL DIATOM PSEUDO-NITZSCHIA
presentations.abstract: The pennate diatom Pseudo-nitzschia produces the neurotoxin domoic acid (DA) which can impact both humans and marine wildlife when consumed. Over 50 species have been identified globally, and DA production varies both across and within species. To address the need for rapid, species-specific tools, we developed a molecular toolbox targeting species-specific markers, including the internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) region, the small subunit of Rubisco (rbcS), and the domoic acid biosynthesis gene dabA. Assays were developed for both quantitative PCR (qPCR) and CRISPR-Cas12b LAMP diagnostics.

presentations.title: UNEXPECTED, STRONG HETEROGENEITY IN POPULATION DENSITIES OF MAJOR CLADOCERAN TAXA, IN THE RESPONSE TO PREDATION OF TRIOPS CANCRIFORMIS
presentations.abstract: Cladocera and Notostraca at first seem like a classic predator – prey relationship. Both orders represent the class Branchiopoda and are known to coexist in temporary aquatic ecosystems, long enough to mutually induce and develop evolutionary changes in each group. In this work, we present a subset of data resulting from a large-scale mesocosm experiment, aimed to assess the role of large branchiopods - in this case Triops cancriformis - as keystone species in temporary pond ecosystems. The results show that some taxons thrive much better in the presence of Triops than others.

name: Multilingual Science Blogging
title_full: WS16 Multilingual Science Blogging: Translating Science into Connection
description: Blogging is an effective tool used for communicating scientific information to a broader audience. Science blogging has become a popular tool among scientists, early-career researchers, graduates, and undergraduate scholars to share their findings and highlight the broader relevance of their work beyond academic spaces. This workshop will introduce participants to the value of science blogging as a science communication tool. Participants will learn the basic structure of a blog, writing strategies for science blogging, and approaches for translating or adapting content for multilingual audiences.
lead_organizer: Angelique Rosa Marín, Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography

name: Amplifying Voices in Aquatic Sciences: Aquatic Confluence
title_full: AV001B Amplifying Voices in Aquatic Sciences: Aquatic Confluence
description: In an era of accelerating global change, it is crucial to pause and reflect on how our actions today affect and alter our planet. Addressing the pressing current and future environmental challenges faced by aquatic systems, especially at the interfaces with other ecosystems, requires international and multidisciplinary research efforts to ensure inclusive, holistic, and innovative solutions. The ASLO Early Career Committee (ECC) seeks to enhance global collaboration and networking opportunities for early career researchers (ECRs).
lead_organizer: Pascal Bodmer, Cornell University
co_organizers: Bianca M. Rodríguez-Cardona, International Institute of Tropical Forestry
Mina Bizic, Technical University of Berlin
Members of the Early Career Committee (ECC), Association for the Sciences of Limnology and Oceanography, ASLO

presentations.title: Assessment of harmful algae in selected mangrove oyster communities along the coast of Ghana
presentations.abstract: Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs) have been identified as a major threat to biodiversity in coastal ecosystems. A study was undertaken to identify and characterise harmful algae in two coastal water bodies in Ghana - Narkwa lagoon and Densu estuary. Field sampling was conducted over a three-month period (March–May 2025), during which nine physico-chemical parameter including temperature, DO, salinity, nutrient concentration, pH, transparency and turbidity was measured. Algae species were characterised using microscopic and environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding of 18S rDNA gene. eDNA results indicated several harmful algal species, including Prorocentrum minimum, Heterocapsa rotundata, Karenia mikimotoi, Karlodinium veneficum, Fibrocapsa japonica, and Dinophysis acuminata.

presentations.title: Beyond visible blooms: persistent microcystin-LR in a warm monomictic lake of south-central Chile
presentations.abstract: Cyanotoxin risk in freshwater ecosystems is commonly inferred from the visual presence of cyanobacterial blooms; however, toxin occurrence may remain undetected when blooms are not apparent. In this study, the persistence of microcystin-LR (MC-LR) was assessed in Lake Laguna Avendaño, a lake in south-central Chile under marked anthropogenic pressure. Limnological variables, nutrient concentrations, chlorophyll-a, trophic status, and microcystin-LR were monitored between August 2023 and November 2024. MC-LR was detected throughout the study period despite the absence of visible blooms, with concentrations ranging from 0.2 to 1.8 µg·L⁻¹.

presentations.title: Dissolved methane dynamics in a tropical urban wetland: spatial gradients and seasonal variation driven by anthropogenic impact
presentations.abstract: Urban wetlands in tropical regions are highly dynamic ecosystems with a significant role in the global carbon cycle, acting as both sinks and sources of greenhouse gases, including methane (CH4). This study estimated dissolved CH4 concentrations (CCH4) and their spatial and seasonal variation across the urban lacustrine wetland of Xochimilco (Mexico City) in relation to anthropogenic impact. Seven sites with contrasting characteristics were monitored during the dry and rainy seasons. All seven sites were supersaturated with CH4 in both seasons, confirming their role as potential atmospheric sources.

name: Transforming your abstract into a performing act
title_full: WS17 Transforming your abstract into a performing act
description: In recent years, aquatic scientists have increasingly collaborated with artists to explore new ways of engaging with and communicating research. A growing movement involves intentional partnerships in which scientists and artists co-create performances that translate scientific findings, concepts, and environmental challenges into emotionally resonant experiences. This interactive workshop explores how a scientific abstract can be transformed into a short performing act. The goal is to provide participants with practical tools to reimagine their research through embodied storytelling, theatrical techniques, and collaborative creativity.
lead_organizer: Konstantinos-Marios Vaziourakis, Uppsala University
